Anthropic, Musk outline duelling approaches to AI-era philanthropy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
20:35:28 UTC
05:35:28 KST

Anthropic, Musk outline duelling approaches to AI-era philanthropy
Anthropic and Elon Musk laid out starkly contrasting approaches to redistributing part of the proceeds of the AI boom, with the Claude developer committing 5% of its shares to an unprecedented new fund for the “public good,” while Musk pledged to give one SpaceX share to “every kid in America,” arguing for such direct distributions as the burgeoning sector faces growing public scrutiny.
AI safety concerns have multiplied following security breaches by AI systems and dire warnings from industry heads about the possibility of severe, even existential, risks of runaway AI development in addition to public concerns about potential job losses.
While Anthropic is betting on distributing wealth through ways including nonprofit donations and direct contributions to specific populations, Musk has said he recommends “giving the shares directly to the public”.
“Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many,” Musk, who runs Anthropic rival SpaceXSI, said in a post early on Oct 19. He held about 6.42 billion shares in the company as of June.
SpaceX shares were up about 1% in afternoon trading.
Anthropic said that its initiative will give it more flexibility and scale to make donations for the benefit of humanity.
The company is planning one of the biggest IPOs in history as a public benefit corporation, a legal structure that requires management to balance broader public interests with profitability goals.
The flotation could value it at roughly US$2 trillion (S$2.6 trillion), although Reuters exclusively reported last week that some investors are weighing a lower valuation of around US$1.5 trillion. That would value a 5% stake toward the fund in a range of US$75 billion to US$100 billion.
That would dwarf the still substantial potential value of Musk’s share giveaway, which would be worth roughly US$11 billion at current share prices based on US census figures showing there are 72 million children in America.
“Giving shares, which are stakes in the future economy, directly to the people is the way,” Musk argued.
Musk’s move comes months after the White House launched “Trump Accounts,” a cradle-to-adulthood investment programme that will provide US citizens born between 2025 and 2028 a government-funded investment account of US$1,000 that families can build on.
With the option for individuals and corporations to donate equity shares to the accounts, many top US companies have already pledged support for the programme with employer matches or additional funding, including Dell, Visa, Micron and Delta Air Lines.
Earlier in 2026, SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell and her husband pledged a share of their SpaceX stock to each of more than two million children under the Trump initiative.
It was not immediately clear whether Musk’s share donations would be linked to Trump Accounts or come with any kind of lockup period. SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for more details.
“That’s a lot of shares ... I’m sure somebody will be happy to take them,” said Robert Pavlik, senior portfolio manager at Dakota Wealth Management, who does not hold SpaceX shares in the portfolios he manages.
“It feels like a publicity stunt ... Will it create positive public sentiment? Perhaps.”
Michael Dell and his wife, Susan, have pledged US$6.25 billion in cash for Trump Accounts, aimed specifically at underprivileged children. In contrast, the value of Musk’s contribution will depend on SpaceX’s often volatile share performance.
Most of Musk’s philanthropic efforts have been through the Musk Foundation, which reportedly holds more than US$14 billion in assets.
Berkshire Hathaway Chairman Emeritus Warren Buffett, one of the most prominent figures in philanthropy, is reported to have given away US$60 billion so far, with most of the rest of his roughly US$150 billion fortune slated for philanthropy too.
The Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation has distributed more than US$100 billion since its founding in 2000, with some of that fuelled by donations from Buffett.
Labour market impact cited
Anthropic, which has positioned itself as a safety-first AI lab, has said AI could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”
The company said in its blog post its Public Benefit Fund could support initiatives including direct distributions to specific populations and efforts to address AI’s impact on the labour market, building on a previously announced US$200 million commitment to study and address labour-market disruption.
Its proposed fund would be established as a wholly owned limited liability company and would receive an additional 2% of Anthropic’s shares, at the board’s discretion, for every 50% increase in the company’s value above a baseline that has yet to be disclosed.
Global companies have cut thousands of jobs after investing heavily in AI, with many, primarily tech firms, pointing to higher efficiencies from the technology’s rapid adoption.
Not for political giving
The AI giant said none of the equity held by its fund would be used for lobbying or political giving in the US or abroad.
US policymakers are weighing greater oversight of AI and companies are stepping up efforts to shape how the technology is regulated.
Combined with its co-founders’ pledge to donate 80% of their equity and an employee donation matching programme, roughly 20% of Anthropic’s shares will be dedicated to public purposes, excluding any additional shares added later.
Anthropic said it would say more soon on the fund’s governance, structure and the valuation thresholds that could expand its ownership stake. REUTERS

Trump signs order launching women’s health division at NIH, White House
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Trump signs order launching women’s health division at NIH, White House
First Lady Melania Trump has championed the executive action as a ‘transformative moment’ for US women’s health.
United States President Donald Trump has signed an executive order that will establish a dedicated women’s health division within the National Institutes of Health (NIH), as well as a White House task force focused on the subject.
During a signing ceremony in Washington on Monday, First Lady Melania Trump praised the initiative as setting “a new standard for women’s health in America”.
“This is a transformative moment for women in America. Beginning today, we will change the reality of women’s health,” she said.
“Previous generations fought for women’s rights. Our generation will fight to discover the cures that will ensure a woman can live her life in health and to the fullest.”
The newly minted project, spearheaded by the first lady, requires the new health division to be established within 90 days.
It aims to accelerate scientific discoveries, expand clinical access for women’s health and modernise care throughout every stage of a woman’s life.
The new division at the NIH will not replace the agency’s Office of Research on Women’s Health but will have a broader mandate beyond research, according to the White House.
Melania Trump gestured to “super intelligence, advanced biotechnology and groundbreaking therapies” as tools that offer a “unique chance to reinvent women’s healthcare”.
The first lady’s office has identified “five pillars” for innovation in the field. One involves funding targeted research to develop cures for diseases that affect women, such as endometriosis.
Another calls for a quicker timeline for “promising therapeutics” to reach female patients.
“In 2026, medical advances can do more than just prolong life,” said Melania Trump. “It should give women the freedom to live life to its fullest, to pursue our dreams, experience love, discover, create, travel and lead.”
The White House task force will be co-chaired by the newly cancer-free White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, as well as Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr.
While Monday’s executive order mandates that the HHS must fund the administrative costs of the task force, the order itself does not include any specific funding targets or dollar amounts.
Experts have noted that Melania Trump has kept a relatively low profile during Trump’s second term.
Her public appearances have been fewer than during Trump’s first term, though she has stepped into the public spotlight to promote improvements to foster care and the role of technology, such as artificial intelligence in education.
During Trump’s first term, the first lady launched the “Be Best” campaign focused on child well-being, safe social media and countering opioid abuse.
But critics have questioned how effective Monday’s executive order might be, given the cuts Trump has made to the federal workforce since his second inauguration.
Thousands of employees have been laid off at the NIH alone, with Kaiser Health News reporting that its workforce is at its lowest level in decades.
The NIH was also given a deadline to slash spending by 35 percent across all of its divisions, amounting to a massive $2.6bn budget reduction.
In April 2025, the HHS drew widespread condemnation and a multi-state lawsuit after abruptly moving to terminate regional contracts for the Women’s Health Initiative, the nation’s largest longitudinal study on older women’s health at the time.
Critics warned that the move would jeopardise life-saving research on cardiovascular disease, cancer and osteoporotic fractures for senior women.

Supreme Court may strike down school policies that limit Asian students
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
20:27:48 UTC
05:27:48 KST

Supreme Court may strike down school policies that limit Asian students
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Magnet programs exist across the country, including in California and Los Angeles, and were conceived as a form of voluntary integration.
- Los Angeles Unified has an extensive magnet system, 66 whole-school magnets and 268 magnet centers within a larger campus.
WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court agreed Monday to consider outlawing school diversity policies that limit Asian American students at magnet programs and selective high schools.
Three years ago, the court ruled that Harvard and other universities may not discriminate on whom they admit based on the race of their applicants. Evidence in that case showed that Asian applicants with very high test scores were often turned down.
But the justices have been divided over admissions rules for highly selective high schools in Boston, New York and Fairfax County, Va., as well as magnet programs for gifted middle school students.
In most instances, judges have said school officials may use “race-neutral” policies to achieve racial diversity. For example, giving an automatic admission to the top 5% of the students in all of a big city’s high schools or its middle schools could achieve greater racial and ethnic diversity.
The Justice Department has petitioned to join a lawsuit challenging LAUSD’s decades-old desegregation policy that provides extra resources and smaller classes to predominantly minority schools.
But the court’s conservatives, led by Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel A. Alito, have condemned such policies as thinly disguised racial discrimination.
Magnet programs exist across the country, including in California and Los Angeles, and were conceived as a form of voluntary integration — a way to get white students to attend the same schools as nonwhite students, without having to resort to forced busing.
The idea was that a special school program would be attractive enough to serve as a “magnet” for white students to enroll at a school they might not otherwise attend. A mix of white and nonwhite students was seen as a benefit to the nonwhite students, because white students would be sharing the fate of the nonwhite students.
Asian students were frequently part of that original equation on the nonwhite side of the ledger and counted with other students classified as nonwhite, such as Black or Latino students. But in terms of student achievement, Asian students have performed more like white students, frequently surpassing white students academically.
One subset of magnet schools requires a selective admissions process, and these are at the center of the current dispute.
The court agreed to hear an appeal from parents in Montgomery County, Md., who were upset by a sharp drop in Asian students at its four magnet schools for gifted students.
For a decade, the school board had been troubled that fewer than 15% of the students at its magnet schools were Black or Latino, even though they made up about half of the student population.
In contrast, Asian students were less than 15% of the county’s student population but made up about half of the enrolees at the magnet programs.
After several years of debate, school officials dropped the use of a countywide competitive test and chose top performing students at all of its middle schools using a lottery.
That prompted a lawsuit that reached the U.S. 4th Circuit Court of Appeals.
Fairfax County in northern Virginia had adopted a somewhat similar policy for the Thomas Jefferson High School for Science & Technology. A federal judge ruled for Asian parents and said their students had been deprived of a “level playing field” in competing for admission.
But the 4th Circuit, by a 2-1 vote, disagreed and said Asian American students were still winning more seats than their percentage of the school population.
The Assn. for Education Fairness, the parents group in Montgomery County, lost for the same reason in the 4th Circuit. The number of admitted Asian students had declined, but their percentage remained well above their share of school population.
They appealed and urged the Supreme Court to rule on their case and to clarify the law.
“School districts across the country have overhauled admissions criteria for competitive public schools after concluding that existing systems produced undesirable racial enrollment patterns,” they said.
They said the court should end this type of racial discrimination against Asian students.
However, a longtime champion of admissions policies that rely on social and economic fairness said he hoped the court would side with Montgomery County.
“The Supreme Court has long disfavored racial preferences and pointed to race-neutral programs that look at factors like socioeconomic disadvantage as the right way to do affirmative action,” said Richard D. Kahlenberg, director of the American Identity Project at the Progressive Policy Institute.
Federal authorities charge 28 people in California with alleged illegal voter registration or voting, escalating the Trump administration’s fight with state election officials.
He said the Maryland school board followed that rule.
“It essentially provided an admissions break to students based not on race, but on the economic disadvantage of the elementary school they attended. The question now opened is whether the court will stand by precedent or move the goal posts. Is the court opposed to racial preferences, or to racial diversity itself?”
Los Angeles Unified, the nation’s second-largest school system, has an extensive magnet system, with 66 whole-school magnets and 268 magnet centers within a larger campus.
At this point, many of the magnets provide no discernible integration benefit and are viewed instead as inducements for any student to enroll. Many magnets are nearly all students of color because few white students apply.
A few schools, however, have more applicants than spaces, and the district relies on “the Magnet Priority Point System and the need to maintain a racially balanced enrollment, and by available space.”
Parents must mark one federally recognized race or ethnicity on the application, or it won’t be processed. A family gets points, for example, if a student applied unsuccessfully for a magnet in the past.
In L.A. Unified, 53 schools are designated for students rated as “gifted,” and there are four campuses with programs for highly gifted students, typically identified by a professional evaluator.
Available recent data for the highly gifted program at North Hollywood High indicated that the largest percentage of students, about 38%, were Asian. Overall, the district’s enrollment is about 3.5% Asian.
The justices will hear arguments in the case early next year.
Savage reported from Washington and Blume from Los Angeles.

The president's remarks came the same day that a Russian daytime drone strike in a public park killed six people, including two children. The night before, Russia attacked Kyiv with over a dozen ballistic missiles and targeted nearly 30 critical energy facilities across the country.
But Trump had nothing to say about any of that, choosing instead to praise Russian President Vladimir Putin for his restraint in both Ukraine and Iran.
When asked if he was open to a trilateral meeting with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping, Trump said he was, but that such a meeting wouldn't be for Ukraine's sake — since Russia, apparently, "has been fine on Ukraine." He said the main purpose of the meeting would be to discuss nuclear disarmament.

Trump then said he would be willing to talk to Xi about Ukraine, saying "he's been very fair with Ukraine. He hasn't been much involved, and same with Russia."
"They haven't been nearly what they could have been, and I appreciate that."
It's not clear whether Trump was referring to China's support for Russia, or Russia's aggression in Ukraine.
read also
Trump defended his recent deals with Putin and sanctions waivers for Russia, saying the U.S. was negotiating with the Kremlin regarding the release of a high-profile hostage. He also said Russia was "very well-behaved on Iran."
"We also have a very good situation with respect to Iran. (Putin's) laying off Iran," Trump said.
"It's nice because we're hitting Iran very hard, as you know, economically as well as militarily, and Russia's done nothing there that we can see, and I think that's a very positive."
Russia is Iran's close ally and has pledged to assist Tehran in its war with the U.S. Multiple media outlets have reported on Russia shipping weapons to Iran, aiding in missile development, and providing intelligence to help Iran attack U.S. bases in the Middle East.

While Ukraine sent its experts to help shoot down Iranian drones attacking Gulf states, Putin pledged to supply Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian with all "the necessary goods" and support the country during the war.
But in his remarks to the media on Oct. 19, Trump seemed convinced that Putin, not Zelensky, was his true ally.

The U.S. president again lashed out at Zelensky, saying Ukraine should consider getting someone new to negotiate on their behalf.
"We've given a lot to Ukraine. They've given nothing to us."
Ahead of the U.S. midterm elections, Trump has taken a hard turn toward Moscow in an apparent bid to lower domestic fuel prices: On Oct. 9, he announced a plan to purchase Russian diesel, despite years of U.S. sanctions on Russian energy products. He also ordered Ukraine to stop attacking Russian oil refineries.
Lawmakers and critics from both political parties pointed out that the war in Iran was the main driver of the surge in global oil prices, and condemned the deal for rewarding Moscow even as it continued pummeling Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure.

Schools in UK, Hungary, Serbia sent hoax bomb warnings
BELFAST - Hundreds of schools in Northern Ireland, Scotland, Hungary and Serbia were sent bomb threats on Oct 19 with some evacuated as the authorities said the warnings appeared to be a hoax.
It is not yet known whether the incidents were connected to each other.
“Police investigating the circumstances of threatening emails sent to schools across Northern Ireland this morning ... are treating the matter as a hoax,” police said.
Northern Ireland police said up to 300 schools had received “the same emailed message which contained a generalised threat” which was also received by “some schools across the UK”.
Earlier on Oct 19, Northern Ireland Education Minister Paul Givan said the emails appeared to be “from Islamists threatening that Sharia law will be brought into our country and that there are viable devices within those school settings”.
Givan said the email was “signed off ‘Allahu Akbar’” and some schools had closed as a result.
“I want to absolutely condemn the actions of those who sought to disrupt our education system today by issuing threatening emails to our schools,” Givan added.
Meanwhile, Scottish police said “threatening messages” had also been sent to “a number of schools across Scotland”.
“These are being treated as a hoax and officers are investigating,” Police Scotland said in a statement.
In central Europe, Hungary saw emails sent to local media, claiming that bombs had been placed in over 70 schools across the country, according to police.
Many of the establishments were evacuated, but officials said no bombs were found.
“Based on the investigations carried out so far, this morning’s threats have proved to be unfounded,” Hungary’s interior minister Gabor Posfai said on Facebook.
In neighbouring Serbia, state broadcaster RTS reported that more than 100 schools had also received bomb threats.
The nature of the messages outside of Northern Ireland remained unclear, and the Northern Irish education authority said in a statement that “the majority of schools remained open”. AFP

Lockheed Delivers C-130J to Become Navy’s TACAMO Plane
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
20:23:29 UTC
05:23:29 KST

The U.S. Navy on Oct. 15 accepted a C-130J-30 Super Hercules plane that it will modify to become the first of its new nuclear command, control, and communications aircraft—a route the Air Force is considering for a similar NC3 mission under congressional direction.
Manufacturer Lockheed Martin delivered the aircraft to the Navy at its Marietta, Ga., facility, the company said in an Oct. 16 statement. When the modifications are complete, the C-130J-30 airframe will be designated an E-130J Phoenix II.
The E-130J is envisioned as the next-generation aircraft to take on the Navy’s TACAMO, mission. TACAMO, short for “Take Charge and Move Out,” is the mission of receiving, verifying, and relaying orders from the President, Secretary of Defense, and other military leaders, mainly to nuclear-armed submarines.
Since the late 1990s, the Navy has executed the TACAMO mission with the E-6B Mercury, derived from the Boeing 707. The Strategic Communications Wing 1 flies the mission from an Air Force installation—Tinker Air Force Base in Oklahoma.
Officials say the E-6B fleet, which includes 16 aircraft, is aging and must be replaced. The Navy announced in late 2020 its plan to buy new C-130Js for the purpose. From 1963 to 1993, the Navy flew the EC-130Q as its TACAMO platform.
“The C-130J platform has a storied history supporting our strategic communications mission, and accepting this first C-130J-30 marks an exciting new chapter,” Navy Capt. Roger Davis, airborne strategic command, control and communications program manager, said in Lockheed’s statement. “Lockheed Martin’s delivery of this battle-proven airframe provides the structure and performance backbone our mission requires as we transition into mission systems integration to field the E-130J Phoenix II.”
Now that the Navy has its first C-130J, the plane will transition into the mission systems integration process, led by Northrop Grumman as the prime contractor, U.S. Strategic Command said in a release. RTX’s Collins Aerospace will provide Very Low Frequency systems.
“This delivery marks a historic milestone for the U.S. Navy, Lockheed Martin, and the nation’s strategic communications network,” Trish Pagan, vice president of air mobility and maritime missions for Lockheed, said in the company’s statement. “The C-130J-30 Super Hercules continues to evolve and adapt to the needs of our customers, carrying the proven reliability of its lineage while transforming into a new, strategic mission set. It is built to deliver the capabilities our joint force demands and built to last through any operational challenge.”
The Navy wants a total fleet of 31 E-130Js; three are currently under contract.
The C-130J-30 is an extended version of the standard C-130J, which adds 15 feet to the plane’s fuselage. Yet the aircraft is still smaller than the E-6B, and the Navy’s use will be slightly different too.
For decades, the E-6B has been responsible for both the TACAMO and “Looking Glass” missions—Looking Glass is the nickname given to the Airborne Command Post mission—aircraft that fly with the systems and crews needed to receive and relay orders from the President and launch intercontinental ballistic missiles via the Airborne Launch Control System. But the E-130J will only perform the TACAMO mission, and the Air Force is taking back over the Looking Glass mission it performed from 1961 to 1998.
The Air Force is in the early stages of defining what it calls its “Looking Glass-Next” program. One option is to fold it into the still-in-development E-4C Survivable Airborne Operations Center, which is meant to replace the E-4B “Doomsday” plane as the flying command post for national leaders to direct nuclear and conventional forces, execute emergency war orders, and coordinate civil response actions in case of a major emergency.
Congress also included a section its 2026 National Defense Authorization Act directing the Air Force to submit a report on its acquisition strategy for Looking Glass-Next, including “options to expand production of the C-130J-30 Super Hercules aircraft to provide additional airframes to preserve the Airborne Command Post capability.”

The leader of a Kenyan cult that drove people to starvation has been found guilty of the murder of 190 children
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
23:16:14 EEST
05:16:14 KST

The leader of a Kenyan cult that drove people to starvation has been found guilty of the murder of 190 children
Kyiv • UNN
A Kenyan court found Paul Mackenzie and around 30 accomplices guilty of the deaths of 190 children and an adult. More than 400 bodies were found in the Shakahola forest.
A Kenyan court found the leader of a cult that practiced starvation, Paul Mackenzie, as well as about 30 other people, guilty of murdering 190 children and one adult. The event became one of the most horrific cult-related tragedies in recent world history, UNN reports, citing The Guardian.
Mackenzie was arrested in 2023 after police received information to that effect. Within weeks, law enforcement officers began finding bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola Forest, near the coast in southeastern Kenya.
According to prosecutors, Mackenzie and his organization, the "Good News International Church," created an apocalyptic Christian cult. Its followers were ordered to starve themselves and their children — in order to go to heaven before the end of the world.
Mackenzie denied the murder charges, saying that he had not forced the victims to starve, but the court rejected this argument.
More than 400 bodies were discovered in the Shakahola Forest in total. Many of them had undergone severe decomposition, and only 26 could be identified.
The court verdict delivered on Monday concerns 191 deaths, while investigations into the other fatalities are ongoing.
During the court hearing, which lasted more than eight hours, Judge Diana Kavedza Mochache noted that in some cases children were isolated and deprived of food in front of their parents.
Mackenzie himself was present in the courtroom; he was wearing a striped polo shirt and red trousers and was sitting beside his wife, who is also an accused person in the case.
Before the decision was announced, he remained silent, staring blankly.
Relatives of some of those who died in the forest gathered at the Mombasa High Court to hear the verdict.
Sixty-two-year-old Francis Wanje lost eight family members to the cult, including two grandchildren.
Before the verdict was announced, he said: "For our family, this has been a huge burden that has led to serious psychological problems… I had been waiting for this day for a long time."
In addition
The tragedy in Shakahola shook Kenya after mass graves were discovered in the coastal forest more than three years ago. This raised questions about how Mackenzie had managed to continue his activities despite having been on law enforcement's radar since 2017, when police searched his premises. According to police, authorities shut down Mackenzie's church in 2019, after which he moved to the Shakahola Forest.
The case also prompted calls for tighter oversight of churches and other religious organizations in a country where religious faith plays an important role in public life.
Kenyan President William Ruto said in 2023 that government agencies should have prevented these deaths. He added that, as president, he accepted responsibility for what had happened.
People with direct knowledge of the cult's activities said that Mackenzie had planned the mass starvation in three stages: first children, then women and young men, and finally the remaining men.
Some of Mackenzie's followers told Reuters (in a 2023 report) that he — a former taxi driver — prohibited cult members from sending their children to school or seeking medical care when they were ill, calling such institutions "satanic."
The cult members lived in makeshift dwellings built from plastic sheeting and straw. Mackenzie divided the area into zones, giving them biblical names — for example, "Jerusalem" and "Judea."
The dire situation of his followers became known in mid-March 2023, when a local resident reported to police that his brother and sister-in-law, following Mackenzie's orders, had starved their children to death in the forest.
Mackenzie was arrested but later released on bail. According to relatives, after that he moved forward the date of the end of the world that he had previously announced to his followers. In April 2023, police arrested him again, began more systematic searches of the forest, and exhumed bodies from mass graves.
In connection with the deaths in the forest, Mackenzie has also faced other charges, including terrorism-related charges; he himself denies the allegations.
According to prosecutors, while in custody, he also issued instructions that led to the deaths of 52 people in the village of Kwa-Binzaro, located approximately 30 kilometers (18 miles) from Shakahola. Mackenzie has pleaded not guilty in that case.

Art crime detective Arthur Brand warns: 'All museums have been, and will be, victims of theft'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

20:16:10 UTC

Art crime detective Arthur Brand warns: 'All museums have been, and will be, victims of theft'
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on: Modified:
François Picard is pleased to welcome art crime detective Arthur Brand. "In the old days they stole a painting, but a painting is unique; you cannot cut it in two," explains Brand, "In the last 10 years they have been targeting more and more objects made of gold, silver". He examines the transformation of international art theft, warning that increasingly sophisticated criminal opportunism is shifting attention from irreplaceable paintings towards precious metals and gemstones that can be dismantled, melted down or dispersed.
He identifies a disturbing proliferation of copycat museum robberies across Europe, fuelled by the apparent ease with which criminals penetrated the Louvre and escaped within minutes. Challenging the popular 'Hollywood' mythology of elaborate criminal masterminds, he instead describes a landscape shaped by opportunism, institutional security failures and the lucrative disposability of stolen cultural treasures.
The spectacular theft of €90 million worth of jewels from the Louvre have exposed vulnerabilities extending far beyond the security of France's most celebrated museum.
While estimating the chances of recovering the missing jewels at "50-50," Brand suggests that French investigators may know considerably more than they have publicly disclosed. His assessment raises broader questions about the protection of cultural heritage in an era when the commercial value of stolen objects may increasingly outweigh their historical and artistic significance.

Catalan separatist leader Carles Puigdemont can return to Spain without being arrested after a Supreme Court judge on Monday confirmed the withdrawal of an arrest warrant for him, nearly nine years after he fled the country following a failed independence bid.
Judge Pablo Llarena upheld his Oct. 6 decision to lift the arrest warrants for Puigdemont and former Catalan Cabinet Ministers Antoni Comin and Lluis Puig, rejecting an appeal by the far-right Vox party.
The judge said a recent Constitutional Court ruling meant Spain's amnesty law could apply to their cases.
However, he stressed that the decision only concerned the arrest warrants and did not mean Puigdemont had been formally granted amnesty.
A final decision on whether to dismiss the criminal proceedings against him must be made by the Supreme Court's criminal chamber.
The ruling follows a Constitutional Court decision in favor of former Catalan Labor Minister Dolors Bassa, which rejected the Supreme Court's interpretation of whether embezzlement linked to the 2017 independence referendum was excluded from Spain's amnesty law.
Llarena acknowledged that the Constitutional Court's interpretation was binding, although he criticized its reasoning and defended the Supreme Court's previous position.
Puigdemont, who led Catalonia's regional government during its 2017 independence referendum and subsequent unilateral declaration of independence, fled to Belgium that October to avoid prosecution.
He has remained abroad since then, although he briefly returned to Barcelona in August 2024 to address supporters before leaving again without being arrested.
Spain's parliament approved the amnesty law in 2024 following an agreement between Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez's Socialist Party and Puigdemont's Junts party, whose parliamentary support helped Sanchez secure another term after the 2023 general election.
The Supreme Court had previously refused to apply the amnesty to Puigdemont's embezzlement charge, arguing that the alleged misuse of public funds involved a personal financial benefit.
The Constitutional Court subsequently rejected that interpretation, opening the way for the amnesty to be applied to Puigdemont's case.
Last week, Puigdemont asked the Supreme Court to apply the amnesty law without further delay and definitively close the proceedings against him.
He did not publicly comment on Monday’s ruling and Spanish media cites sources saying he intends to return only if he has been formally granted amnesty.
Monday's ruling also comes amid political uncertainty in Spain after Sanchez called an early general election for Nov. 29.

AI-generated photos falsely claiming to show an elderly couple being “stripped and robbed” during unrest in France have racked up millions of views. Amplified by far-right accounts, the images fuelled inflammatory claims about Muslims, Jews and the riots. The FRANCE 24 Observers traced one image to an AI photo montage published by a pro-Israel account. The images were created using OpenAI tools, and the alleged assault remains unverified, with no official reports confirming the attack.
Two AI-generated photos falsely claiming to show an elderly couple in their 80s being “stripped and robbed” during unrest in France have racked up millions of views online. The images spread widely on X, particularly among far-right accounts. Some users described them as “the most horrific image of October 17th”, while others claimed they showed that “France has fallen” and warned that the rest of Europe and the UK would be next.
Several accounts also claimed the couple were Jewish, accusing French President Emmanuel Macron of failing “the Israeli people” and comparing the alleged attack to a 1941 pogrom in Ukraine.
American far-right conspiracy theorist Alex Jones also shared one of the fake images, blaming the alleged violence on “criminal consortium of Muslims and communists, who are unified by their hatred of the west and white people”.
The images did not only circulate on social media. French digital media outlet Sirenes shared one on Instagram, while Israeli right-wing news channel C14 published it under the headline “Islam Conquers Europe”.
However, both images are AI-generated.
The FRANCE 24 Observers confirmed their artificial origin using SynthID, an invisible digital watermark designed to help identify AI-generated content. Both images were detected as having been created using OpenAI tools.
There are also several visual clues that point to manipulation in one of the photos. The woman’s hand appears to have only four fingers, with an enlarged, deformed thumb. Two masked heads are visible despite there being only one body, while a bollard lying on the ground does not resemble the type typically found in Paris.
With the help of the European Broadcasting Union’s Spotlight network and Belgium’s RTBF fact-checking team, the FRANCE 24 Observers traced the source of the image: a montage published late on October 17 by the pro-Israel account Infos-Israel.news. The montage contained several AI-generated images and was flagged as AI content.
The same white border visible around the image in the original montage also appears in posts circulating on X, indicating that the photo was lifted and re-shared directly from that collection.
But while the images are fake, what about the underlying claim that an elderly couple was assaulted?
The allegation gained traction after French journalist Dominique Rizet said on air on BFM that an elderly couple had been attacked in Paris, citing a police source. His report was subsequently picked up by other media outlets, though no official photos or sources confirmed the alleged assault.
FRANCE 24 contacted Rizet, who said he had received the information from a police source at 8:47 pm on Saturday and that it had been “confirmed”.
However, the fact-checking service CheckNews of French newspaper Libération contacted the Paris prosecutor’s office, which said that, as of Monday - around 48 hours after the alleged incident - there had been no reports to that effect to date.
As of now, other credible sources or official reports have confirmed the alleged attack.

In addition to the ban, Ronaldo will have to pay a fine of €255.
According to a ruling by the association's disciplinary committee, part of the player’s suspension has already been served, as he had already been suspended.
Ronaldo, who now plays his club football for Saudi side Al-Nassr, began his punishment on 1 October, leaving 11 days left to serve. That means he could be available for the national team’s upcoming matches against Denmark on 14 November and Wales on 17 November.
'Mitigating circumstances'
The ruling said Ronaldo had asked that "mitigating circumstances be taken into account," in particular his "lack of any disciplinary record in the current season and the previous three seasons, provision of services of relevance to football, commendations for sporting merit and contribution to establishing the material truth."
"With regard to the mitigating circumstances of providing services of relevance to football and commendations for sporting merit, the defendant Cristiano Ronaldo submitted his sporting CV, including the awards and recognitions he has received over the course of his career," the document reads.
It adds that, in terms of "contribution to establishing the material truth," the player referred to the statement published on his Instagram page on 6 October.
The ruling sets out in detail the sequence of events after Ronaldo left the training camp.
On 30 September, the former Real Madrid and Manchester United star walked out of a camp before a training session at Parken Stadium in Copenhagen.
The player is said to have left without notifying anyone from the FPF or the squad in advance.
The document states that the player informed FPF President Pedro Proença of his decision by phone, saying that he did not feel in the right frame of mind to play.
"During the aforementioned telephone conversation, the defendant player informed the president of the FPF that he was not in an emotional condition to remain with the National Team at the training camp," the disciplinary committee noted.
Media coverage
In assessing the case, the committee acknowledged Ronaldo's services to football and his multiple awards. The body also took into account "his conduct after the events, in particular the remorse shown in the statement of 06.10.2026."
Even though certain mitigating factors were recognised, there were also aggravating elements in the FPF's view, notably the media coverage of the case and his role as team captain.

People who are more considerate of others show less “me first” bias in quick decisions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
20:00:27 UTC
05:00:27 KST

A study conducted in the U.K. found that people who were more socially mindful, meaning more attentive to other people’s needs and choices, showed a weaker egocentric bias when making quick decisions. Specifically, they showed a smaller tendency to identify their own belongings faster and more accurately than objects belonging to a friend. The paper was published in Consciousness and Cognition.
People tend to process information related to themselves differently from information related to other people. This tendency is known as self-bias. One common example of this is self-prioritization, in which objects associated with oneself are recognized more quickly and accurately than objects associated with someone else. Even trivial possessions can acquire this advantage, suggesting that merely linking an object to the self can influence decision-making.
Researchers increasingly view this effect not as an automatic feature of cognition, but as a flexible bias that depends on the situation and on characteristics of the individual. One proposed mechanism is an egocentric “default-to-self” tendency, in which people initially assume that an object is more likely to belong to themselves than to another person. This assumption can speed decisions about self-related objects by reducing the amount of evidence needed before responding.
One characteristic that may weaken this tendency is social mindfulness. Social mindfulness is the tendency to consider other people’s needs, wishes, and freedom of choice when making decisions. People who are more socially mindful also tend to be more cooperative, generous, empathic, and trusting in their interactions with others. Greater consideration of other people may therefore reduce the cognitive advantage normally given to self-related information and make self-prioritization less pronounced.
Study author Marius Golubickis of United Arab Emirates University and his colleagues hypothesized that greater social mindfulness would be associated with less self-bias. More specifically, they expected that more socially mindful individuals would show smaller differences in the speed and accuracy of their responses to their own objects compared with a friend’s objects, and that this would be explained by a weaker default-to-self assumption.
Study participants were 100 adults tested in a laboratory at the University of Aberdeen in Scotland, each paid £10 (about $13). Sixty-four were women, and their average age was 28. Nine participants were later excluded for not following instructions, leaving 91 for the analysis.
Participants completed two tasks: an object classification task, which measured self-bias, and an object-selection task, which measured social mindfulness. In the object classification task, the computer assigned one category of objects to the participant and the other to a named best friend. The two categories were pens and pencils, and which item went to whom was varied across participants.
After learning which objects belonged to whom, participants saw a brief picture of either a pen or a pencil and had to report, as quickly and accurately as possible, who owned it. Each participant completed 10 practice trials followed by two blocks of 100 trials.
In the object-selection task, participants were shown sets of three or four objects in which one item was unique and the others were identical. The task was presented as if it was being played with a partner, a stranger they would never meet, and the participant always chose first. Choosing one of the identical items was considered socially mindful because it preserved the partner’s ability to choose between different options, whereas taking the unique item removed that choice.
As expected, participants responded faster to objects they owned (542 milliseconds, on average) than to objects owned by their friend (557 milliseconds), and they were slightly more accurate with their own objects (94% vs. 92%). This confirmed that participants showed self-prioritization. However, the effect was smaller among participants who were more socially mindful, for both speed and accuracy, and some participants even responded faster to their friend’s objects. Social mindfulness accounted for a modest share of the differences between people, about 5% for speed and 11% for accuracy.
To explore the mechanism behind these findings, the researchers used a computational model of decision-making that separates how efficiently people process what they see from any bias they bring to a decision before the object appears. The model showed that participants tended to begin each decision already leaning toward the answer that the object belonged to them. This lean was weaker among people higher in social mindfulness, which the authors interpret as reduced egocentrism. Participants also processed their own objects slightly more efficiently than their friend’s, but this advantage was not related to social mindfulness.
“Collectively, these findings further underscore the malleability of self-prioritization and provide a computational account of how social mindfulness impacts decision-making,” study authors concluded.
The study sheds light on individual differences in decision-making. However, the study examined ownership decisions about only two kinds of trivial objects, pens and pencils, and results might differ for more important possessions. In addition, all participants were from the U.K., and the authors note that culture may shape both social mindfulness and self-bias.
The study was also correlational, so it cannot show that social mindfulness causes reduced self-bias, and the researchers did not check whether participants believed they were really choosing alongside another person. Social mindfulness was measured with a single behavioral task, which may not capture all aspects of consideration for others.
The paper, “Social mindfulness is associated with reduced self-bias: A computational approach,” was authored by Marius Golubickis, Siobhan Caughey, Esther S. Selvaraj, Parnian Jalalian, Yadvi Sharma, Jessica Highfield, Rinki Kanakraj, and C. Neil Macrae.

Finland seeking one million land mines as it eyes Russian threat
Unknown

Finland seeking one million land mines as it eyes Russian threat
Helsinki recently joined regional peers in withdrawing from the UN Charter banning munitions as it eyes its eastern border.
Finland is seeking to acquire one million anti-personnel mines.
The plan to spend 100 million euros ($112 million) on the munitions comes after Helsinki and regional peers withdrew from a United Nations compact rejecting their use.
With Moscow increasingly accused of mounting hybrid warfare against supporters of Ukraine, and possibly planning military provocations, Finland exited the Ottawa Convention last year.
Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania and Poland, all also among the staunchest allies of Ukraine, also quit the agreement, citing the potential threat from Moscow.
Colonel Riku Mikkonen of the Army Command told Finland’s national news agency STT that officials are now gathering information from suppliers regarding the deal, the AFP news agency reports.
Helsinki would like domestic manufacturers to supply the mines, with contracts signed by the end of 2027 and production up and running by 2028.
“It would be useful in many ways if Finnish companies produced the anti-personnel mines in Finland,” Mikkonen said. About half a dozen Finnish firms qualify, he told STT.
“However, at this stage, buying the mines from abroad is not totally ruled out,” he added.
Finland joined the Ottawa Convention, a humanitarian treaty aimed at eliminating anti-personnel landmines and destroying more than a million of them, in 2012.
However, it announced that it was withdrawing in April 2025, citing a worsening security climate, and stopped being bound by the treaty in January.
Prime Minister Petteri Orpo has called Russia, which sits on Finland’s eastern edge, a long-term threat.
Finland shares a border of roughly 1,340 kilometres (830 miles) with Russia. It has beefed up its defences since Moscow’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, and reported that migrants have been pushed across from the east.
Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen on Monday urged the EU to stop issuing tourist visas to Russians until the war ends.
“As long as Russia continues its invasion, Russian citizens should not be issued tourist visas,” she said, adding that it is “not right” for Russians to enjoy Europe’s freedoms “while their country bombs the homes of Ukrainians”.
Valtonen noted that Schengen countries granted nearly half a million tourist visas to Russians in 2025. Finland banned such visas in 2022, and she argued the rest of the bloc should follow suit.

France faces reckoning with public order policing after violent protest weekend
France reeled Monday after a weekend of nationwide unrest sparked by mass protests against the rising cost of living and in support of high school students’ demands over education funding. In the violent clashes that erupted, law enforcement officers and protesters were wounded, public buildings were set ablaze and businesses were looted, raising significant questions about the French police's approach to public order.
French and international front pages kicked off the week Monday with images of the country in flames and headlines focused on “chaos” or “disaster” after polarising mass demonstrations rocked the country over the weekend.
Demonstrators marched across France on Saturday in massive protests drawing about 550,000 people, according to authorities while organisers put the turnout at 800,000. Following scenes of violence involving the police and certain demonstrators as well as looting, arson and at least 2,400 arrests, France is facing a debate over its maintien de l'ordre (public order) police doctrine.

Sparked in high schools in France’s overseas territories and taken up by schools in under-served Parisian suburbs, student blockades quickly spread across the country in recent weeks, with students demanding more resources for education and complaining about dilapidated infrastructure and a lack of teachers. The movement morphed this weekend into national demonstrations with unions, student organisations and activists hoping to revitalize the Yellow Vests movement, which emerged in November 2018 in protest of fuel prices and the high cost of living.

Protests turned into scenes of turmoil and clashes with the police with many demonstrators reporting being sprayed with tear gas and police using “intermediary force” weapons which are used in crowd control by French law enforcement and have become a focal point of debate in recent weeks following several high school students being wounded in protests.
On Saturday, in Saint-Étienne in southeastern France, a 17-year-old lost his hand to a grenade while in Mulhouse, in the northeast, a young woman of the same age lost use of her eye. One protester died on the fringes of a demonstration in Paris following a “probable cardiac arrest” but local authorities said they did not yet know the circumstances surrounding his death.

‘Non-lethal weapons’
Prisca Ancion, a lawyer who works in the Paris suburb of Seine-Saint-Denis and a member of Collectif d'Action Judiciaire – a collective of lawyers founded and run by members of hard-left party Révolution Permanente – has closely followed the high school student protest movement. She said the weekend’s protests showed how heavily armed the French police have become.
“In 2026 we are at a point where the police have never been as armed and trained,” she said. “This is a consequence of a series of budgets which, while imposing austerity measures across a range of sectors – notably education – have allocated substantial funding to the police and armed forces.”

Ancion said special police units such as the CRS (the branch in charge of crowd and riot control) and the BAC (the anti-crime brigade) carry equipment classified as A2 – military-grade weapons – under France’s internal security code, including stun grenades, crowd dispersal grenades, rubber bullet launchers (also known as “flashballs” or “LBDs”) and tear gas labelled as “non-lethal”.
“In reality we should call them ‘less lethal’ weapons but they can be, at a minimum, mutilating,” she said.
Oliver Davis, a professor and head of the Department of French at University College Cork, said terms like “non-lethal” are “euphemisms”, and that these weapons, which entered French public order policing in the 1990s, can be extremely dangerous.
“They can create awful injuries if they're fired at the face, at the genitals or at soft parts of the body, they can ruin people's lives,” he said. “They are not 'sort of' toys, which is how they sometimes seem when they're described by the spokespeople of the policing forces.”
In an article for The Conversation, Davis traces the history of public order policing in France and the creation of the CRS at the end of World War II. According to him, these units tend to be far more militarised and confrontational than riot police in most other European countries. He added that Greece is one of few EU countries with a comparable approach in which de-escalation is not the guiding principle.

According to Olivier Cahn, a specialist of criminal law at the University Paris-Nanterre, there was a shift in national policy for crowd control in 2016 during the Nuit Debout (Up All Night) protest movement against proposed labour reforms, which came a year after the Charlie Hebdo terror attacks.
That shift was further formalised in 2025 with a "National Urban Violence Scheme” which led to an overall harsher policing doctrine.
“We have adopted a much more brutal policing doctrine, effectively consisting of a combination of kettling (corralling) tactics, extensive use of weapons – whether grenades or LBDs – and interventions within protests by law enforcement officers to bring protesters to justice,” he said. “We can see that the result is perhaps not an improvement in the quality of policing, but rather a considerable increase in the number of injured police officers and a sort of rallying of protesters against the police.”
For Davis, the early policing of the high schoolers’ movement reflected a failure by the Ministry of the Interior to restrain officers. In his view, the government paired heavy-handed policing tactics with “the pretence of listening” in an attempt to contain the movement. Instead, he said, images of injured teenagers have drawn more people into the protests.
‘Lack of anticipation’
On Saturday, some protesters also looted multiple stores and set fire to buildings – such as Limoges' city hall, the roof of which collapsed, or Lyon's tourism office.
President Emmanuel Macron said in a televised address Sunday that the country felt “anger” and “shame”, and that those responsible would be “held accountable”. He said he had told local prefects to work with mayors to protect public buildings and businesses, including by banning protests if necessary.
Read moreLive: France issues curfew for parts of central Paris
Macron also rejected Minister of the Interior Laurent Nunez’s offer of resignation, who said he “felt responsible for everything that happened”.
According to Cahn, French territorial intelligence services, those meant to “prevent and suppress urban violence”, had estimated about 200,000 demonstrators, far fewer than the at least half a million who turned out.
Nunez admitted there had been a “lack of anticipation” on Saturday and that the approximately 60,000 law enforcement staff deployed that day had been insufficient to deal with the large crowds, and that they had “lost control” in some cities.

French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu asked local authorities to impose “partial curfews” in certain cities Monday evening and said that the state of emergency could potentially be declared “if needed”. Some northern cities introduced curfews for Monday and Tuesday nights and authorities in the capital issued an overnight curfew in two neighbourhoods.
While it seems unlikely that the current doctrine of public order will be reexamined by the government given their recent statements, people in the French political sphere, particularly on the left, are increasingly calling it into question.
Green Party leader Marine Tondelier called for police doctrine to be "reviewed quickly", citing risks for both protesters and police officers and the infringement of civil liberties, while Marseille's socialist Mayor Benoît Payan called for "explanations" regarding the government’s approach to policing.

Anti-Netanyahu bloc plots swift Knesset takeover after election, but internal divisions threaten plan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
19:56:05 UTC
04:56:05 KST

The anti-Netanyahu bloc is preparing to move quickly to seize control of key Knesset positions immediately after the October 27 election, with plans to replace the parliamentary speaker and block controversial judicial overhaul laws from taking effect. But even before voters head to the polls, disagreements within the opposition are raising doubts about whether the parties can secure the votes needed to carry out their plans.
Representatives of the parties have been holding a series of meetings to coordinate their strategy for the first days after the election, drafting legislation and identifying parliamentary moves that could be carried out even before a new government is formed. Their most pressing concern is a set of laws passed by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition that are scheduled to take effect after the election, leaving little time for opponents to intervene.
The plan begins with gaining control of the Knesset's Arrangements Committee, which oversees parliamentary business during the transition to a new government. Opposition officials believe that controlling the committee could allow them to replace the Knesset speaker within days and begin advancing legislation to repeal or delay the coalition's laws.
But the strategy depends on cooperation from lawmakers across several parties, and that is where concerns are emerging. At a recent meeting, some representatives warned that candidates on certain opposition lists had previously supported elements of the judicial overhaul and might refuse to vote for their repeal.
The legislation at the center of the dispute includes measures concerning the attorney general, changes to the Police Internal Investigations Department that would place it under the Justice Ministry, and a law altering the composition of the Judicial Selection Committee. The latter is scheduled to take effect immediately after the election.
The latest meeting brought together Oded Forer of Yisrael Beytenu; Shaul Meridor and Orit Farkash representing Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar! party; Liran Avishar Ben-Horin and Gili Haushner from Naftali Bennett's Beyahad party; and Ram Shefa of the Democrats.
Some participants raised concerns about the decision-making process within Eisenkot's Yashar! party, particularly after its representatives asked for time to consult before providing answers on certain legislative proposals. Others pointed to previous statements by candidates on opposition lists who had publicly supported some of the coalition's judicial changes.
"Some people on these lists promoted and publicly supported the judicial overhaul laws," one source in the anti-Netanyahu bloc said. "And that's where the problem lies."
A senior figure involved in the discussions said the absence of clear positions from some parties was making it difficult to reach binding agreements before election day. "Some parties are not stating their positions clearly," the official said. "There are parties with a range of opinions, and we don't know what their guiding position is. Certain issues came up in the meetings, and there was hesitation. Not everything can be taken for granted, and there is a lack of clarity on some matters."
Despite the disagreements, working groups have begun preparing legislative proposals aimed at reversing existing laws and advancing measures they believe must be approved quickly. The goal is to complete as much of the groundwork as possible before the election, rather than spend the first days afterward negotiating over legal language and parliamentary procedure.
The preparations also account for a possible election outcome in which neither political bloc emerges with a clear majority, but the anti-Netanyahu parties hold a narrow parliamentary advantage. Under that scenario, they hope the president would give their bloc the mandate to attempt to form a government, a development they believe could also help them secure control of the Arrangements Committee.
"Our goal is for the president to give the mandate to our bloc," opposition officials said. "The importance of receiving the mandate is not only the ability to try to form a government, but also gaining control of the Arrangements Committee. If we control the committee, we can replace the Knesset speaker within a day or two, or at the beginning of the following week."
The officials stressed that the timetable would be tight, making advance agreements essential. Closer to election day, the parties intend to assess how individual candidates are likely to vote, with particular attention to those whose positions on judicial legislation remain unclear.
That effort is also intended to prepare the bloc for political pressure from Likud. Opposition officials believe Netanyahu's party will try to persuade individual lawmakers to withhold support from efforts to repeal the coalition's legislation, potentially depriving the anti-Netanyahu camp of a majority on critical votes.
"There is legislation that must be advanced as soon as possible after the election," a senior opposition official said. "If the people we're concerned about don't vote with us, we may not be able to repeal the coalition's laws. We're certain Netanyahu will apply enormous pressure, and we need people who can withstand it."
Those concerns follow an earlier report by ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth that Likud had established a dedicated team to examine new candidates on opposition party lists, including their family connections, social circles and influential associates. The reported aim is to identify potential avenues of influence that could prevent lawmakers from voting against Likud after the election.
For the anti-Netanyahu bloc, the parliamentary battle is therefore taking shape before the election itself. Its parties are preparing to move rapidly against the outgoing coalition's legislative agenda, but their ability to do so will depend not only on the number of seats they win, but also on whether they can maintain unity when the first crucial votes are called.

One man down and on a flattening pitch, Boland and Starc continue to shine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
19:55:32 UTC
04:55:32 KST

As the afternoon meandered on and the stubbornly soggy outfield of St George's Park threatened to waste another day of the second Test at Gqeberha, South Africa had good and bad fortune to ponder.
The good news was that upon the game's long-awaited resumption at 3:45pm local time, Australia would be without one member of its intimidating quartet of fast bowlers due to illness. The bad news, with no disrespect to the others, was that it wasn't Scott Boland.
Sure enough, within 10 minutes of the restart, the Victorian had struck again to remove debutant opener Marques Ackerman — Boland's third wicket in five typically compelling overs.
Worse still for the Proteas, Mitchell Starc, who'd been a little out of sorts in his brief spell on day one, was hitting his straps too. Bowling with fluency and at speeds nudging towards 150km/h, the left-armer soon struck as well thanks to a lazy waft outside off stump from Matthew Breetzke and a smart catch from Alex Carey.
At that stage, South Africa was 4-40 and staring into the abyss.
What transpired in the hour that followed was heartening for South Africa, though perhaps not enough to shift the course of this truncated contest.
The pitch — whose lack of hessian coverings during the worst of the downpours was said to be predictive of imminent mayhem — seemed to flatten out and not behave so treacherously at all.
The batting, circumspect but not unadventurous, started to look less fragile as Proteas skipper Temba Bavuma got going with South Africa's recast number six, Ryan Rickelton. And the missing bowler, Josh Hazlewood — who Cricket Australia says will return on day three — was suddenly looking like a real hole in the bowling rotation.
Loading Twitter content
Indeed, a bubbly 50-run partnership later, and with stumps not far away, Bavuma could have permitted himself some satisfaction that he and Rickelton had pulled things out of the fire so calmly. He might also have felt his side's bad luck was starting to turn when a sun-blind Marnus Labuschagne put down Rickelton at leg slip.
As ever, though, Boland had other ideas. Well, one idea, to be honest: hammer away on a patch of the pitch roughly the size of a Wisden cricketers' almanac and wait for the ball to seam either way.
The burly right-armer duly took Rickelton's outside edge and Matt Renshaw, at first slip, took a catch that could be charitably described as fortunate; it looked like Carey's, but the keeper didn't move a muscle; Renshaw did, on a significant delay, grasping it in one hand when the ball was past him and then slowly mouthing some easily-made-out words of relief: "Oh. My. God."
Thus, from a relatively promising position, the Proteas finished the day 5-97 from the 43 overs that have been possible so far. Boland, with 4-31 from 14 overs, was not simply the pick of the bowlers but a one-man show who single-handedly lifted the contest out of its torpor, his every delivery imbued with potential.
Now that he is ranked in the world's top 10 Test bowlers without commanding regular selection, it is often said that Boland is unlucky. Another way of looking at it is that, at 37 — an overripe age for a fast bowler of any kind, let alone one so vigorous and impactful — he simply knows his own virtues and limitations better than he did as a younger man, and can conserve and channel his energies in ways the regulars cannot.
It is also, surely, a minor triumph of man management. That Boland and, perhaps more so, Starc continue to glide to the crease in such prolonged spells and with such devastating impact is not a matter of luck. Today, again, Starc, who is also pushing 37, was a genuine menace: a 148km/h bouncer to Bavuma was as scary as anything he bowled in his 20s.
We talk often of Starc's eye-popping strike rate of 45 — six better than Dennis Lillee and Mitchell Johnson, seven better than Glenn McGrath and Jeff Thomson, 12 better than Starc's old sparring partner Shane Warne — but it is now his longevity that is so unusual to the point of freakishness.
Playing in his 109th Test, Starc is bowling at a level that history suggests should be impossible. Jason Gillespie and Brett Lee, the express quicks of preceding decades, were done with Test cricket at 31 and 32 respectively; like Johnson, they'd strung together 70-something Tests between the inevitable injuries.
Touch wood, Starc will feasibly play 50 or 60 more Tests than that — a coda of similar length to Merv Hughes's entire Test career. The way Cricket Australia has balanced Starc's financial and physical preparation requirements for the last decade is an organisational triumph that should be studied. If only it, and Starc himself, were replicable.
As for South Africa, what they can replicate remains to be seen, but it's very unlikely, as in Durban, that promising 50-partnerships will get this one done.

"I think it's time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine because what's happened? A tremendous number of people are dead. They're losing their male population," he said.

"Zelenskyy is not helping matters much. I think he doesn't want to stop it, but I want to see people not die."
"We've given a lot to Ukraine. They've given us nothing," he added.
 
Possible talks with Putin, Xi on Ukraine
Asked whether he had agreed to a trilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping on Ukraine, Trump said he had not but was open to such talks.
"No, but I would do it. Not so much for Ukraine because Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine," he said.
Trump indicated that nuclear disarmament would be a priority in any such meeting.

Asked whether he would meet Putin and Xi to discuss ending the war without Zelenskyy present, Trump said he would do "anything I can do to end the war, whether somebody's there or not."

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told the Journal that discussions were underway but there was no clear understanding yet on the meeting or its agenda, though all three sides acknowledged the “hypothetical possibility” of such a meeting.
The report came on the heels of Trump announcing a deal to buy Russian diesel fuel and later signing an executive order waiving key sanctions on Moscow, a move Zelenskyy criticized.
"Any easing of sanctions against Russia without a clear and lasting de-escalation agreement with Russia is an obvious weakness," Zelenskyy said.
 
Russia, China, and Iran

"Russia could have done a lot more to help Iran. Russia's done very little for Iran. China could have done a lot more for Iran," he said.
"I view that as being a very positive thing," Trump added.

Rubio puts Trans-Caspian trade and critical minerals at centre of Central Asia talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
19:53:16 UTC
04:53:16 KST

The US and five Central Asian governments backed closer transport and industrial cooperation at a C5+1 meeting in Samarkand. Rubio also held bilateral talks, while Uzbekistan signed the Artemis Accords.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the foreign ministers of five Central Asian countries agreed to deepen cooperation on transport, critical minerals and security at a C5+1 meeting in Samarkand on Monday.
The talks brought together the United States, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan. In a joint statement, they backed investment in the Trans-Caspian trade route, closer industrial cooperation and simpler customs procedures.
A trade route to Europe
The Trans-Caspian route, also known as the Middle Corridor, connects Central Asia with European markets through the Caspian Sea, the South Caucasus and Turkey, bypassing Russia.
"We're going to enhance the infrastructure of the Trans Caspian trade route and give our partners more ways to reach American and Central Asian markets," Rubio said.
Washington also wants to diversify supplies of critical minerals used in energy technologies and advanced manufacturing. The six governments identified mineral processing, energy cooperation and cybersecurity among their priorities, but the joint statement gave no figures for new infrastructure funding.
Uzbek Foreign Minister Bakhtiyor Saidov proposed cooperation extending from mineral exploration to processing and local industrial clusters. He also called for closer links between the C5+1 diplomatic forum and the B5+1 business platform to involve companies in identifying projects.
The US push comes as the five Central Asian states maintain extensive economic ties with Russia and China. Speaking separately to Euronews in Samarkand, Rubio said Washington was seeking competition, not exclusivity.
"This is not about coming here to say, stop talking to somebody else or stop working with some other country," he told Euronews.
Bilateral talks with the five ministers
Rubio also held separate meetings with each of his Central Asian counterparts.
Kazakhstan's Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tileuberdi discussed trade, energy, critical minerals and technology with Rubio. Kazakhstan's Foreign Ministry said the US Secretary of State expressed interest in visiting the country after the G20 summit in Miami in December, although no date was announced.
The US State Department said they also discussed Kazakhstan's commitment to join the Abraham Accords, a US-backed framework for normalising relations with Israel.
Rubio also met Kyrgyzstan's Foreign Minister Jeenbek Kulubaev to discuss bilateral cooperation. Tajik Foreign Minister Sirojiddin Muhriddin raised trade, investment and regional security, according to his ministry.
Rubio held talks with Turkmenistan's Rashid Meredov, with the two countries preparing another round of political consultations in Ashgabat in November.
Uzbekistan and the US held the first session of their Enhanced Strategic Partnership Dialogue, covering trade, energy, technology and security. Following the talks, Foreign Minister Saidov signed the Artemis Accords in Rubio's presence, making Uzbekistan the 77th country to join the international framework for peaceful space exploration.

US arrests over 2 dozen in California sweep targeting alleged non-citizen voters
The Justice Department said all those arrested are lawful permanent residents but not US citizens who are permitted to legally vote
US federal authorities arrested over two dozen foreign nationals on Monday in California as part of a statewide sweep targeting people who officials say have illegally registered and voted in the country’s midterm elections.
They also reflect a further escalation in a simmering voter roll fight between the federal government and California that came into focus last week when the Justice Department sued the state and later warned that local election workers who knowingly process or tabulate ballots submitted by non-citizen voters are at risk of investigation and potential prosecution.
The Justice Department said all those arrested as part of a sweep dubbed Operation Protect the Vote are lawful permanent residents – but not US citizens who are permitted to legally vote.

Salah strikes again as Trabzonspor beat Besiktas 2-0 in Super Lig
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
19:51:59 UTC
04:51:59 KST

Halis Sunnetci
19 October 2026•Update: 19 October 2026
Mohamed Salah scored his eighth league goal of the season as Trabzonspor defeated Besiktas 2-0 at Papara Park on Monday in the final match of Week 8 of the Turkish Super Lig.
The visitors started brightly, with goalkeeper Andre Onana denying Olaitan’s close-range header in the 10th minute before Nwaiwu blocked Dusan Vlahovic’s first-time effort four minutes later.
Onana was called into action again in the 17th minute, saving Vaclav Cerny’s deflected strike from outside the penalty area.
Despite Besiktas’ early pressure, Trabzonspor broke the deadlock in the 21st minute through Ozan Tufan.
Ernest Muci drove into the box from the left and fired a shot from a tight angle that goalkeeper Alexander Nubel parried into the path of Tufan, who converted the rebound with a half-volley.
The hosts nearly doubled their advantage in the 38th minute when Salah launched a counterattack and found Muci, whose pass released Franculino, but Nubel denied the striker in a one-on-one situation.
Besiktas came close to equalizing three minutes later as Onana parried Leandro Trossard’s powerful effort into the path of Murillo, whose rebound struck the woodwork.
Despite enjoying nearly 65% possession, the visitors struggled to break down Trabzonspor’s organized defense after the interval.
Trossard fired narrowly wide from the edge of the box in the 70th minute before Salah doubled the hosts’ advantage a minute later.
Franculino raced onto a lofted pass from Aral Simsir down the left flank and delivered a low cross for the Egyptian forward to finish first time from close range.
The goal took Salah’s tally to eight goals and three assists in eight league matches, moving him clear at the top of the Super Lig scoring chart.
Trabzonspor continued to threaten on the counterattack, with Nubel making two successive saves in the 82nd minute to deny Noah Saviolo and Salah.
Salah missed another chance three minutes later, curling a left-footed effort wide after being picked out by Muci inside the penalty area.
Substitute Ilhan Fakili forced Onana into a save in the 87th minute, but Besiktas failed to threaten again as Trabzonspor secured their fourth consecutive victory in all competitions under new head coach Thomas Reis.
The victory lifted Trabzonspor to fourth place in the Super Lig standings with 16 points, while Besiktas dropped to fifth with 15 points.
