More than three dozen members of US Congress have had their offices targeted with envelopes containing white powder, less than three weeks before the 3 November midterms, as federal agents try to identify who is behind the campaign.
The latest is the Virginia Democrat Suhas Subramanyam, whose Leesburg district office was evacuated on Monday after an envelope containing a suspicious substance arrived. He said the office was cleared quickly, adding that “acts of political intimidation have no place in our country”.
Subramanyam’s office said preliminary tests showed the powder was not hazardous.
Law enforcement sources told ABC News that more than 100 letters thought to contain white powder are circulating in the US mail system. The FBI, Capitol police and US Postal Inspection Service are investigating, according to a notice sent to Senate staff on Thursday.
Election offices in at least 15 states had reported receiving or being targeted by suspicious mail by Thursday evening, according to the Tampa Free Press, which cited federal authorities. No suspect has been named, and federal authorities have not released a confirmed figure.
The FBI declined to confirm “specific instances or letters”, but said in a statement: “The FBI and US Postal Inspection Service are investigating a series of suspicious mailings sent to various addresses nationwide, including secretary of state offices and their related election offices, and congressional offices.
“Some of the letters contained an unknown substance and we are working closely with our law enforcement partners to respond to each incident. We are also working with our partners to identify the individual or individuals responsible for the letters. This FBI and the US Postal Inspection Service will continue to safeguard the public and secure elections for American citizens.”
Senators have been targeted across the political spectrum, and country. Letters addressed to the Democratic Senate minority leader, Chuck Schumer, and California senator Alex Padilla were intercepted by authorities, while Chris Murphy of Connecticut said the FBI, the Senate sergeant at arms and Capitol police alerted his team of a letter as well. Republicans in South Dakota, Texas and Nebraska were also targeted, with Mike Rounds saying his Sioux Falls office was evacuated, along with Pete Ricketts and Ted Cruz also reporting a suspicious letter.
In the House, at least 10 people were exposed after white powder was sent to the offices of the New York Democrats Hakeem Jeffries, Ritchie Torres and Tom Suozzi. In California, Jimmy Panetta said a staffer opened an envelope at his Santa Cruz office, then cleared the room and called 911. He said such attempts to intimidate “will not deter us from doing our job”. In Massachusetts, five staffers left Seth Moulton’s Salem office while police investigated, and testing found no substances of concern.
Investigators have described several common features connecting the suspicious letters sent to public officials and election centers.
The FBI has stated that the recovered envelopes were processed through a north Texas mail processing center and carry a postmark or stamp reading “Thinking of You”. Senate staff and House offices were warned to watch for plain white envelopes featuring these distinct markings.
The vast majority of these envelopes were intercepted by the US Postal Inspection Service and screening facilities before being delivered.
In 2024, election officials were targeted in 17 states before the 2024 presidential election, and no suspect has been named in this case.

Inside the disappearing investment scheme with possible terrorism links
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
19:05:28 UTC
04:05:28 KST

From Sydney to the Caribbean via Dubai: How a CEO with possible terror links allegedly took millions
A licensed investment company allegedly scammed its customers out of their life savings — and now its CEO may have links to terrorism. 
It has sparked concerns about deep flaws in Australia's financial regulatory regime.
Shirtless, adorned in reflective sunglasses and holding a pineapple, Karim Farag looks like an ordinary holiday goer.
But the 32-year-old Egyptian has landed in a web of lies involving a suspected sham investment, ghost addresses leading to the Caribbean, a famous Australian cricketer and alleged links to terrorism.
Karim Farag is the former chief executive of Main Group FX, a licensed investment firm in Australia that disappeared three years ago, leaving at least 13 investors collectively $2 million in the red.
Now the ABC can reveal Mr Farag has alleged connections to an organisation accused of funding terrorism.
Mr Farag maintains he has nothing to hide and is willing to cooperate with authorities.
The 'euphoric' Sydney event that lured investors
It all began at a four-star hotel in the heart of Sydney in 2023.
As they enjoyed free food and cocktails, Main Group investors could never imagine that, by the end of the year, the company hosting the event would vanish, and their life savings along with it.
Investor Jean Giles, a former public servant from Western Australia, thought she bonded with her account manager over a glass of red wine as he confided that his daughter had died in a hit-and-run in New York.
"The Sydney event was the clincher for me. I came away from there feeling quite euphoric," she said.
"I'd found something that was going to give my husband and I enough money to enjoy our retirement."
Main Group claimed to trade in futures and commodities, including oil and gold.
Its headquarters were in Sydney, and it spruiked algorithmic trading software that allowed investors to "set and forget" their money.
With monthly dividends and the ability to cash out at any time, users could start with as little as US$250.
Ms Giles invested a small amount and, over several months, with moderate returns, was coaxed into giving away more to the tune of $176,000.
Also at the Sydney event was Melbourne truck driver Dean Butterworth, who eventually invested $217,000 from a workers' compensation payout he received after injuring his back.
He was among an estimated 40 guests who met several Main Group FX staff flown in from the Cyprus head office to "put a face to the voice", as the event was advertised.
It was to be the first and only time meeting Robin Mahfouz, the Australian director of Main Group FX, and account managers Oscar Allison and Alex Morrison.
Mr Allison and Mr Morrison did not respond to requests for comment. The ABC is not suggesting they were aware of any wrongdoing.
"Going to this event sort of made me feel comfortable knowing that we're meeting real people, it's not over the phone, it's not emails or anything like that," Mr Butterworth said.
Adding to the appeal, cricket legend Shane Watson was spruiked as a potential special guest as Main Group's "Australian ambassador" but ended up being a no-show.
The firm's enigmatic chief executive Mr Farag was quoted in a paid advertorial saying: "We are thrilled to partner with a world-class talent like Shane Watson!"
Mr Watson had previously posed for the company in a photo shoot that included a Main Group FX-branded cricket bat and clothing.
Loading...
"Being able to partner with Main Group FX, that's one of their incredible strengths, is educating people, educating traders and people who don't really know a lot about trading to be able to give them the best chance of success," Mr Watson said in the video.
He told the ABC he cut ties with the group in November 2023, had no involvement in its management, and had tried to get the photos removed.
The unravelling
A few months after the lavish conference, investors said monthly dividends stopped, they could not withdraw their money, and all trace of Main Group FX disappeared.
Main Group FX never entered administration or bankruptcy and the company is now deregistered, with customers no longer receiving returns and unable to recover their initial investment.
It has essentially vanished, and there is no established way for investors to salvage their missing money. They now have to take matters into their own hands, with some pursuing action from police and regulators.
"At the moment, financially, I'm barely holding it together. Bankruptcy is on the books," Mr Butterworth said.
He was forced to return to work despite his back injury while Ms Giles sold her home.
"The axe fell and I realised that everything that we'd put in there, all the money I'd taken out of our mortgage, had gone,"
she said.
So what is Main Group FX?
Loading...
Main Group FX boasted of its "Sydney headquarters", but the ABC found it was initially listed at a luxury residential address in the CBD.
A month later, its address switched to an office-space-for-hire in Chatswood.
Staff told the ABC they never saw anyone come in from Main Group.
But the most interesting address for this investment was hidden deep in company documents: Suite 5 at the Griffith Corporate Centre, Kingstown in St Vincent and the Grenadines.
The Caribbean location has previously been the subject of an ABC investigation, and the Australian and UK corporate regulators have issued multiple warnings about dozens of entities allegedly using this exact address as a base to perpetrate dubious online trading schemes.
Loading...
Even the identity of some of the directors of this company raises questions about its legitimacy.
ASIC records show a 21-year-old international student was registered as Main Group's first director in February 2023.
She told the ABC she had no idea her name had been used.
Just a month later, the directorship changed to Australian-Lebanese citizen Robin Mahfouz, who was based in Cyprus at the time and attended the Sydney event.
A man born in Moldova took over in January 2024 as the scheme was imploding.
Company director claims she was a victim
The ABC was able to track down Main Group's registered director, Robin Mahfouz, who declined to comment.
In an unsworn affidavit the ABC has obtained, as it was circulated among investors, Ms Mahfouz said she had no idea the company was potentially a scam and blamed her boss, Main Group's chief executive Karim Farag.
She alleged Mr Farag said she would be paid a higher salary if she allowed her name to be used on business registration documents.
She also told customers her grandparents' address in western Sydney was used on official company records.
Karim Farag's full name appears as "Karim Farag Mohamed Abdelhamid" on ASIC records where he is listed as a shareholder of Main Group.
In March 2024, his name appeared somewhere else — somewhere that left customers horrified.
Karim Farag's alleged links to terrorism
Karim Farag Mohamed Abdelhamid is one of 599 names that appear on a list from the Israeli defence minister accused of having cryptocurrency accounts that may have funded a terrorist group.
Loading...
In 2024, Israel's National Bureau for Counter Terror Financing announced the seizure of cryptocurrency wallets it alleged were linked to an organisation called Dubai Company for Exchange, a group it said had provided "substantial assistance" to Hamas.
Mr Farag's full name, birth date, and details of his Binance cryptocurrency account were included in the order.
The Australian government has designated Hamas a terrorist organisation.
The Israeli government did not provide details on the value of the crypto seized, nor the value of each account or direct financial assistance by Mr Farag.
Snir Levi, an Israeli expert in blockchain intelligence, told the ABC the names on the warrant were alleged to have provided support to terror financing by using the infrastructure of Dubai Company For Exchange.
The US government has similar concerns. In July, the US Treasury Department also designated a group called El-Kahira for General Trading, another name for Dubai Company For Exchange, as a terrorist group.
US authorities said El-Kahira provided "underground banking services" through money and cryptocurrency to known Sweden-based organised crime groups.
It is not known whether Mr Farag knew of the company's links to Hamas, or what the extent of his involvement in the platform was.
Possible terrorism links 'very concerning'
Ken Gamble, the director of Australian intelligence firm IFW Global, has been investigating Karim Farag on behalf of some of Main Group's investors and was "pretty shocked" to discover the possible terrorism links.
"So the [Israel] government had published this list, and I immediately became very concerned," Mr Gamble said.
Speaking generally, he said: "It's not uncommon for terrorist groups to look at raising money through online investment fraud."
"It's actually very clever because online investment fraud is a very low risk offence. It goes undetected mostly. And yet there's massive amounts of money that can be obtained."
Dubai Company For Exchange
More light has been shed on Dubai Company For Exchange's alleged potential links to terrorism following court action in the United States.
In July this year, a group of Israelis who survived the October 7 attack filed a civil lawsuit against major cryptocurrency exchange Binance in the US District Court, accusing it of allowing terror financing on its platform.
The untested court claim stated $US50.89 million ($72.8m) flowed between Binance and Dubai Company For Exchange-attributed wallets from 2022 onwards.
Loading...
Dubai Company For Exchange provided Hamas with cryptocurrency services, including the ability to convert crypto tokens into normal currency, the claim also stated.
It added that the designated terror group allegedly held a large number of Binance accounts "to transfer funds intended for terrorism".
In a statement, Binance said the claims were untrue and said it planned to file a motion to dismiss the case.
The ABC contacted a defunct Facebook page linked to Dubai Company for Exchange but was unable to find any current contact details.
Mr Farag declined an interview with the ABC and did not respond to detailed questions, but said he had nothing to hide.
"If there is a legitimate legal matter concerning me, I am more than willing to cooperate directly with the appropriate police authority, court, regulator or other competent government authority through proper legal channels," he said.
He said in a statement that he did not give permission for his details to be published and reserved his legal rights.
"To date, I have received no court order, summons, formal police notification, regulatory notice or other official legal communication requiring me to participate in an investigation or provide information concerning this matter," he wrote.

Man convicted of bribing former senior Rivlin adviser to advance requests to government ministries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
19:02:50 UTC
04:02:50 KST

The Haifa District Court on Monday convicted Mazid Hamdan of giving bribes to a former senior adviser to former president Reuven Rivlin in exchange for help advancing his own interests and those of his clients with public authorities, the State Attorney’s Office announced on Monday.
Hamdan admitted the offenses under a plea agreement based on an amended indictment. Prosecutors and defense lawyers agreed to seek a six-and-a-half-month custodial sentence to be served through community service, alongside a suspended sentence and a fine whose amount would be determined by the court.
Judge Dr. Muhammad Ali convicted Hamdan of bribery offenses involving Ze’ev Dolinsky, who served as Rivlin’s personal and senior adviser. Proceedings against the remaining defendants continue, prosecutors said; Hamdan’s admission does not determine their guilt.
According to the amended indictment, Hamdan, a resident of Yanuh-Jatt near Acre with political connections, helped people advance requests with government bodies, sometimes for payment. He and Dolinsky had known each other for years through their activities in Likud.
Hamdan bribed Dolinsky for planning approvals, advancing passport applications
The first count covers their dealings between 2018 and 2020. Hamdan admitted paying Dolinsky at least NIS 6,000 in 2018 through two sums of NIS 3,000 made available for cash withdrawal, in return for assistance with matters in which Hamdan had a financial interest.
The requests ranged from planning approvals and entry permits to medical training and government grants. The indictment describes Dolinsky using his official title and contacts to approach public officials on Hamdan’s behalf.
One request concerned Hamdan’s plan to build a gas station on land he owned. According to the account Hamdan admitted, Dolinsky approached a Transportation Ministry official and a planning committee secretary to advance the application. He presented the request to the secretary as though it had also been submitted to the President’s Residence, although it was unrelated to that office.
Hamdan also sought help renewing a hunting-rifle license that had previously been revoked, securing permission for an Abu Dhabi resident and two Jordanian citizens to enter Israel, and advancing an application for an Israeli passport.
Other approaches concerned a medical residency at Galilee Medical Center in Nahariya and a doctor’s request for a NIS 250,000 grant for working in the periphery. The residency application was rejected, the indictment says.
Hamdan paid to appeal failed Health Ministry licensing examinations
The second count concerns payments intended to advance appeals against failed Health Ministry licensing examinations in occupational therapy.
According to the amended indictment, another defendant, Marwan Rayan, approached Hamdan concerning his son and niece after they took the examinations. When they learned that they had failed, the two submitted appeals.
Hamdan admitted arranging for Rayan to pay Dolinsky in return for assistance with those appeals and instructing him to meet the adviser. The indictment describes a payment of an unspecified amount at a January 14, 2019, meeting in Jerusalem, followed by repeated approaches to a Health Ministry employee.
The conviction is part of a broader case in which Nissim Cohen, a former parliamentary aide to then-MK Yitzhak Vaknin, previously admitted multiple offenses of accepting bribes and money laundering.
Cohen was sentenced earlier this year to two and a half years in prison, subsequently reduced on appeal to 22 months, according to the prosecution.
Hamdan’s case now moves to sentencing, when the parties will present their agreed request to the court.

Israel’s next government must confront the future of the West Bank - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
19:02:45 UTC
04:02:45 KST

The first task of Israel’s next government should be to confront a question that can no longer be postponed: What does Israel intend to do with the West Bank?
This is not merely a question of territory. It is a question of Israel’s security, its relations with its neighbors and allies, its democratic character, and its future as a Jewish state.
In February 2026, the government took a series of decisions concerning the West Bank, including authorizing the resumption of land-registration procedures in Area C. It allocated an initial NIS 244 million to the process for 2026-30 and created new positions to carry it out.
Critics, including hundreds of former senior members of Israel’s security and governmental establishments who filed a petition to the High Court of Justice, have argued that these measures, together with other changes in the administration of the West Bank, amount to a process of de facto annexation.
The government has presented the measures in different terms, short of annexation, including as steps related to security, land administration, and strengthening Israeli control.
That distinction matters. Except for the annexation of east Jerusalem neighborhoods immediately after the war, Israel did not annex any part of the West Bank during the close to six decades elapsed since then.
But sovereignty does not necessarily arrive in a single dramatic act. It can also emerge incrementally – through changes in land administration, planning, settlement, jurisdiction, regulation, and the exercise of governmental authority.
The question before Israel, therefore, is not only whether it has formally declared annexation. It is whether fundamental changes to the status and governance of the territory are taking place without an explicit national decision on their ultimate destiny.
The February measures and other recent policies have generated legal challenges and international criticism.
Whether one accepts every legal argument advanced by the petitioners or every characterization of the government’s policies, the underlying democratic question remains: A transformation of this magnitude should not occur through administrative accumulation. It should result from an explicit decision by Israel’s elected government and Knesset, following a transparent public debate about its consequences.
Those consequences extend far beyond the legal status of particular parcels of land or the application of military and administrative orders.
First, there are the security consequences.
The Palestinian Authority has serious shortcomings, but Israeli security officials have for years regarded security coordination with it as an important instrument for preventing terrorism and disrupting attacks.
Policies that weaken the PA – whether through territorial fragmentation, economic pressure, or other measures – could increase the risk of its eventual collapse.
The result could be a vacuum that fundamentalist radical armed organizations would seek to exploit, leaving Israel with greater responsibility for security and civilian administration across the West Bank.
That would come at a considerable cost. The Israel Defense Forces would face the task of maintaining security among a large Palestinian population while protecting Israeli communities and confronting threats on multiple fronts. Direct Israeli responsibility for civilian administration would also impose substantial financial and administrative burdens.
In addition, the decisions in question are liable to be interpreted as providing a tailwind to disastrous acts of Jewish terrorism which are on the rise while state authorities either turn a blind eye or convey silent encouragement through decisions such as the granting of governmental legitimacy to Israeli-Jewish takeovers of lands in the Judea and Samaria area. This is liable to spur further violence.
Second, there are legal and diplomatic consequences. Unilateral changes to the status of the West Bank could intensify disputes with international institutions and governments over international law and the framework established by the Oslo agreements. The Oslo II agreement envisioned the gradual transfer of territorial powers in the West Bank to the Palestinians, with permanent-status issues – including borders and settlements – to be resolved through negotiations.
Israel must account for the possibility that further unilateral changes could expose the country, its officials, and military personnel to additional international legal and diplomatic pressure. The international response to settlement and annexation-related policies is already affecting relations with governments and international institutions.
Third, there are regional consequences. Jordan’s security relationship with Israel is particularly important. Jordan has a direct interest in developments in the West Bank and in preventing instability or displacement from spreading across the Jordan River. Egypt likewise has a central role in Gaza, Sinai security, and the Israeli-Egyptian peace treaty.
The same applies to Israel’s broader relationship with Arab states that have established or developed ties with it. Policies that make Palestinian statehood or a negotiated regional framework more remote violate an explicit Israeli commitment included in the Abraham Accords and could complicate further normalization, as well as make it much harder to construct a broader regional security and economic architecture, such as has been envisioned with Saudi Arabia.
Fourth, there is a fundamental question about Israel’s political character and national identity. If Israel ultimately extends sovereignty over the West Bank, it will have to confront the political status and rights of the Palestinians living there.
Granting Israeli citizenship and full political rights to Palestinians in the territory would have profound implications for Israel’s demographic and political structure. Maintaining Israeli sovereignty while denying those rights would leave different political and legal arrangements for different populations living under Israeli authority and would amount to apartheid.
This is therefore not simply a debate about borders. It is a debate about what kind of state Israel intends to be.
'Freedom, justice, and peace'
Israel’s 1948 Declaration of Independence pledged that the state would be based on “freedom, justice, and peace” and would ensure equality of social and political rights to its citizens. Any long-term arrangement involving the West Bank must therefore be measured not only against security considerations but also against the principles Israel has proclaimed as part of its national foundation.
There is also a profound question for world Jewry. Israel’s relationship with Jewish communities abroad has never rested only on security or national identity. It has also been connected to a shared commitment to democratic values. Permanent Israeli sovereignty over millions of Palestinians without full political rights could deepen disagreements within parts of the Jewish world over Israel’s direction and its relationship to democratic principles.
Such a fissure with the Jewish world, in which Israel operates against its own Declaration of Independence, violates the fundamental reason for Israel’s existence – to be a secure and democratic home for the Jewish people.
None of this means that Israel can ignore security threats emanating from the West Bank, nor does it mean that the PA or Palestinian political system should be idealized. It means that the consequences of changing the territory’s status are too consequential to be determined incrementally.
The next government, following the October 27 election, should therefore make the question of the West Bank a priority.
It should define it in explicit terms and initiate a thorough, transparent, and sustained national process for deciding the future of the West Bank and, in coordination with relevant actors, Gaza.
It should begin by reviewing measures that could alter Israel’s long-term strategic position, starting with the recent measures enacted last February, and determining which, if any, should be suspended pending an explicit national decision.
It should also present the Knesset and the public with a clear assessment of the security, legal, diplomatic, economic, and democratic consequences of the available alternatives.
Israel can choose its future. But it should do so consciously, transparently, and through its democratic institutions – not by allowing a historic transformation to occur one administrative decision at a time, without a clear decision by the Israeli public about where that process leads.
The central question is therefore unavoidable: Does Israel intend to move toward permanent sovereignty over the West Bank, toward a negotiated territorial arrangement, or toward some other defined political framework?
Whatever answer Israel ultimately chooses, it should be explicit – and its consequences should be understood before the choice becomes irreversible. Continuing with measures that lead to annexation will be catastrophic.
V.-Adm. (ret.) Ami Ayalon is a former director of the Israel Security Agency (Shin Bet) and commander of the Israel Navy.
Gilead Sher, a fellow at Rice University’s Baker Institute and a reserve colonel in the IDF, is a former senior peace negotiator and chief of staff to prime minister Ehud Barak.
Orni Petruschka is a social activist, philanthropist, and former technology entrepreneur.

Ex-Soroka doctor jailed for ISIS membership after collecting explosives, poison manuals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
19:02:44 UTC
04:02:44 KST

The Beersheba Magistrate’s Court sentenced a former Soroka Medical Center doctor to 27 months in prison on Sunday for membership in ISIS, finding that his pledge of allegiance and years of collecting the terrorist organization’s material went beyond ideological interest to developing practical capabilities.
Dr. Muhammad Azzam was also fined NIS 15,000 and given a 12-month suspended sentence. Prosecutors said his details had been referred to the Health Ministry for consideration of revoking his medical license.
Judge Shoshana Shitrit ordered that time already spent in custody be deducted from the prison term. Azzam, who spent more than 17 months in detention before being placed under electronic monitoring, must report to Dekel Prison on November 8.
The sentence follows his conviction on April 27 after a contested trial. The conviction was for membership in a terrorist organization; the judgment does not establish that he attacked or harmed patients.
According to the court’s findings, Azzam regularly consumed ISIS propaganda from 2014 until his arrest on July 16, 2024, watching footage of battles, executions, and beheadings and sometimes sharing material with others.
Former Soroka doctor pledged allegiance to ISIS, downloaded explosives and poison manuals
After the October 7 Hamas-led massacre attack and the outbreak of the Israel-Gaza War, he pledged allegiance to the organization’s leader. The court found that his conduct became more extreme afterward, including downloading practical manuals on explosives and poisons while working at Soroka in 2024.
Investigators found material systematically arranged in folders on his electronic devices, some protected by passwords. Shitrit concluded that the collection and organization of operational guides reflected deliberate learning and preparation for possible future use, rather than curiosity.
The judgment also cited exchanges in which Azzam expressed delight at the October 7 atrocities and shared footage of them. In another conversation, concerning wounded soldiers brought to Soroka, he expressed a wish that one of the soldiers would die.
Shitrit treated his work as a doctor as an aggravating factor, citing his direct access to vulnerable civilians and wounded soldiers. Her assessment concerned the potential danger arising from that position, rather than a finding that he had used it to injure anyone.
Defense argues former Soroka doctor had no intention of carrying out attack
The defense argued that Azzam’s membership was entirely passive and that he had taken no practical step toward an attack. His lawyers said he had neither purchased materials for terrorism nor planned to travel abroad to join the organization, and had no intention of harming anyone.
A central issue at trial was whether an oath recited privately, without direct personal or digital contact with an ISIS representative, could establish membership. According to the sentencing judgment, by closing arguments the defense had abandoned its factual denials and focused on that legal question.
The court convicted him, finding that the oath, considered alongside his sustained identification with ISIS and the evidence on his devices, established membership.
Prosecutors sought a deterrent prison sentence, emphasizing the prolonged radicalization, his decision to join during wartime and his failure to accept responsibility.
In mitigation, the defense described difficult detention conditions and the impact on his wife and two young daughters. Azzam told the court he wanted to move forward and rebuild his family life.
Shitrit gave weight to his lack of previous convictions, his family circumstances and the difficult conditions of his detention, placing the sentence toward the lower end of the range she considered appropriate.
The suspended sentence will apply if he commits specified terrorism or state-security offenses within three years of his release. He was informed of his right to appeal.

Israel is overestimating its leverage in Washington - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
19:02:22 UTC
04:02:22 KST

Israel can secure a good new military aid agreement with the United States, but doing so will require a clear understanding of what each country gains from the relationship and the limits of Israel’s influence.
More than a month ago, I outlined in this newspaper the recommendations of the Nagel Committee on the Defense Budget regarding a new memorandum of understanding (MOU) with the Trump administration. The task facing the current negotiating team is much harder and entirely different from the one we faced a decade ago, when I had the honor of leading the negotiations for the unprecedented $38 billion agreement signed toward the end of the Obama administration, with excellent cooperation from an outstanding interagency team.
Still, I believe a reasonably good agreement is possible, provided we take the necessary measures with determination, even though some will describe the task as “mission impossible.”
Since then, I have often been asked why the United States should sign a new agreement with Israel at all. What does it offer the superpower? What does it offer Israel beyond the assistance itself? What does the special relationship with Israel offer the United States, and where does it end?
I have also repeatedly been asked why, contrary to irresponsible statements by commentators and even some Israeli policymakers, past and present, continued assistance is not directly tied to Israel’s political independence from the United States. The claim that it is directly tied is simply incorrect. Anyone who argues otherwise does not understand the balance of power or the geopolitical relationship between the two countries.
To answer the first question, I will refer to a slide the MOU negotiating teams drafted jointly about a decade ago. It explained why the agreement was so important to the United States. A corresponding slide explained why the agreement benefited Israel, but that is less relevant to this article. I believe the reasons presented in the slide remain largely accurate.
Agreement demonstrates long-term US commitment to Israel
The agreement demonstrates the United States’ long-term commitment to Israel and implements part of the legislation concerning Israel’s qualitative military edge (QME). It prevents the need for active US military intervention on Israel’s behalf and presents Israel as a bulwark against radical Islam and an effective security guarantor for Jordan. It also enables the United States to strengthen its security cooperation with Gulf states by providing significant military capabilities and supporting military cooperation and joint development.
It is also important to understand the main direct and indirect contributions that Israel’s government, defense establishment, and civilian and commercial sectors bring to the relationship. While there is legitimate debate over their precise economic value, those contributions are worth far more than the US assistance itself.
In many cases, Israel provides the United States with immediate solutions to urgent operational problems or gaps in the field, largely because Israel is more flexible and quicker to identify threats and develop working solutions. In some cases, after receiving that immediate assistance, the United States invests enormous resources and its best people in its defense industry and security establishment, eventually surpassing Israel in those capabilities.
Areas in which Israel has helped and continues to help the United States include intelligence and cyber capabilities; defense against short-, medium- and long-range ballistic missiles; unmanned aerial vehicles and drones; space technologies, particularly lightweight satellites; technologies for detecting and neutralizing tunnels; operational concepts, doctrine and experience; and counterterrorism technologies and prototypes. They also include selected partnerships with the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA), the research laboratories of the US Army, Navy and Air Force, and US national laboratories.
Israeli startups, research centers established in Israel by multinational corporations, and Israeli academia also contribute direct and indirect contributions from technologies and breakthroughs. These are, of course, specific and sometimes niche technologies. It would be wrong to claim that Israel is solely responsible for all, or even a large share, of the revenue generated by any of the companies mentioned here.
Examples include Mellanox/Nvidia, Amazon, Meta, Google, Palo Alto Networks and Check Point, as well as developments in life sciences, medicine, quantum technologies and cybersecurity startups working in both defensive and offensive fields. They also include defense technologies transferred through broad partnerships between Rafael Advanced Defense Systems, Israel Aerospace Industries, Elbit Systems and smaller Israeli companies, and major US corporations or second-tier suppliers.
Still, despite all of the above, my unequivocal position is that those who argue that the United States could not “survive” without Israel’s technological contribution, and that Israel is therefore indispensable, are overstating the case. I wish I could agree.
There are two considerations here. Israel’s value and contribution to the United States are beyond doubt, including its direct and indirect, though partial and limited, contribution to US capabilities against adversaries such as Russia and China.
Dangerous to claim US cannot 'survive' without Israel
But claiming that the United States cannot do without Israel, and acting on that assumption, is very dangerous. This is particularly true of proposals to base the next MOU primarily on technological cooperation rather than security assistance, which has been its basis until now.
The political changes taking place on both sides of the US political spectrum do not alter this assessment. Such an approach could backfire on Israel and leave the Israel Air Force with no viable path to procuring its main platforms in the future.
Signing a new MOU adapted to changing realities will require a focused, uncompromising effort by all relevant parties. It will preserve the strategic alliance and cooperation with the United States and reaffirm America’s long-standing commitment to Israel, despite the changes taking place in the relationship.
The writer, a brigadier-general in the reserves and a professor, is a senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies (FDD) in Washington. He served as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s national security adviser and as acting head of Israel’s National Security Council.

Palestinian activist Mahmoud Khalil asks US Supreme Court to hear case seeking to avoid re-arrest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
19:02:12 UTC
04:02:12 KST

Columbia University graduate Mahmoud Khalil on Monday asked the US Supreme Court to overturn a ruling that opened the door for President Donald Trump's administration to re-arrest and deport the Palestinian activist.
Khalil's lawyers asked the justices to take up his case after the Philadelphia-based 3rd US Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that federal immigration law barred a lower-court judge from ordering his release from US Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody.
Khalil was among the most prominent foreign students to be arrested last year as the Trump administration pursued a campaign to detain and deport noncitizens who engaged in pro-Palestinian activism on college campuses.
His lawyers say the Supreme Court should make clear that immigration law does not prevent noncitizens from pursuing cases arguing they have been detained to punish them for speech that is protected by the US Constitution's First Amendment.
"If the Trump administration can punish someone for their pro-Palestine speech, this or any future administration can punish anyone for any speech," Khalil told reporters on Monday.
Khalil faces possible re-arrest and deportation pending Supreme Court ruling
If the 3rd Circuit's decision is allowed to stand, Khalil faces the prospect of arrest and deportation, after the Board of Immigration Appeals in April rejected his challenge to an immigration judge's order that he be removed to Algeria or Syria.
A lower court order barring him from being re-detained remains in place for now until the Supreme Court rules. A separate appeal of the immigration judge's order remains pending.
A spokesperson for the US Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, in a statement said the Trump administration acted within its authority in Khalil's case, and it encouraged him to self-deport.
Khalil, a prominent figure in pro-Palestinian protests against Israel's war in Gaza, is an Algerian citizen who was born in a Palestinian refugee camp in Syria.
Immigration agents arrested him in March 2025 in the lobby of his university residence in Manhattan despite his being a lawful permanent resident, or green-card holder. His wife and their 1-year-old son are both US citizens.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio had invoked an obscure provision of the Immigration and Nationality Act to deem Khalil removable, citing his involvement in "antisemitic protests and disruptive activities" at Columbia in 2024 that the government said fostered a hostile environment for Jewish students.
He was released from a Louisiana detention center in June 2025 after the New Jersey-based US District Judge Michael Farbiarz, an appointee of former President Joe Biden, ordered the Department of Homeland Security to release him.
Federal appeals court overturns ruling that secured Khalil's release
In January, a 2-1 panel of the 3rd Circuit overturned Farbiarz's decision, saying that under the Immigration and Nationality Act, Khalil's claims could not be addressed through a district court and instead could be raised in an appeal of a removal order from an immigration judge.
After the full appeals court declined to reconsider the case, Khalil turned to the Supreme Court.
Federal appeals courts are split on whether district judges may hear challenges like Khalil's or whether such claims must proceed first through immigration courts, which are not part of the federal judiciary but are instead run by the US Department of Justice.
The Trump administration last month asked the Supreme Court to overturn a ruling in a similar case favoring Georgetown University scholar Badar Khan Suri, another pro-Palestinian advocate detained by ICE who was ordered released.

France: Curfews issued in Paris, Nice after unrest
Published October 19, 2026last updated October 19, 2026
What you need to know
- France announces curfews for parts of Paris, northern cities and Nice after unrest
- French cities experienced rioting and looting over the weekend amid anti-government protests.
- Italy's Meloni considering curfew after riot in Milan
- Albania's PM says 'red line' must be drawn' after anti-government demos and clashes
Follow below for the latest on the protests and unrest in France and other parts of Europe on Monday, October 19:
Foreign governments issue France travel warnings
Several countries around the world, including China, Malaysia, Germany and the United States, have advised citizens traveling to France to avoid large crowds and exercise caution in the wake of large-scale protests and looting in major cities.
China's Foreign Ministry urged Chinese nationals in France to remain alert to potential risks, increase safety precautions, and avoid areas where demonstrations are taking place.
Malaysia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said that, while travel to France remains unrestricted, Malaysians are advised to consider postponing non-essential trips until the situation improves.
The Malaysian embassy in Paris has issued an advisory urging citizens already in France to exercise caution and remain vigilant.
The US State Department issued an alert on Monday warning Americans to avoid demonstrations in major French cities, while an alert issued by the American embassy in Paris noted new curfews ordered in cities including Paris and Lille.
"Avoid the areas of the demonstrations," the warning said.
And in Europe, some of France's direct neighbors have also issued travel advice to citizens.
The German Foreign Ministry said further riots couldn't be ruled out and urged German nationals to follow instructions from local police. It warned citizens that they could face fines if they fail to adhere to requests to leave unauthorized demonstrations.
Governments in the Czech Republic, the Netherlands, Poland, Denmark, Sweden, Finland and Norway also issued warnings to avoid protests.
Albania: Prime Minister Rama says protesters crossed 'red line'
Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama said on Monday that protesters had crossed a "red line" after a police station was set ablaze during anti-government demonstrations.
"Protests are a right, whereas violence is a crime," Rama wrote on social media. "This red line must be drawn clearly at this critical stage of our democratic development."
Demonstrators in Albania have been clashing with police since last Tuesday after months of protests over university conditions and political corruption came to a head.
Fresh unrest broke out again in the capital Tirana on Monday evening, with protesters throwing Molotov cocktails at the interior ministry and riot police responding with water cannons, tear gas and rubber bullets.
Prime Minister Rama said he was prepared to engage in dialogue, but not with those who commit violence or political parties which fail to distance themselves from it.
"Violence is not a solution, but the government also needs to reflect deeply to understand this revolt," one 22-year-old student protester told the AFP news agency.
"We are not criminals; we want social peace and better living conditions in our country. We will continue our movement until Rama resigns."
Around 300 people have reportedly been injured in the clashes, according to local authorities, more than half of them police officers,.

Famous Siberian cave yields remains of yak-like Ice Age mammal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
19:01:01 UTC
04:01:01 KST

Famous Siberian cave yields remains of yak-like Ice Age mammal
Oct 19 - A Siberian cave already famous for yielding the first remains of an extinct human lineage called the Denisovans, who once roamed widely in Eurasia, has now produced evidence of a previously unknown large Ice Age mammal closely related to today's yak.
Researchers said they discovered small bone fragments of the animal in Denisova Cave in the Altai Mountains of southern Siberia in Russia, and obtained DNA that showed these remains belonged to a bovine species distinct from others already known, living and extinct.
In all, the researchers studied 20 bone fragments from this species — 14 from Denisova Cave and 6 from other sites in the broader region. The oldest specimen dated to about 250,000 to 200,000 years ago, and the youngest to about 27,000 years ago.
The bones themselves were so fragmentary that their shape alone did not reveal that they belonged to a previously unknown large mammal. But the researchers were able to generate 20 ancient genomes from the bones, and these showed that this was a unique species whose evolutionary lineage diverged from the ancestors of the modern-day yak approximately 400,000 years ago.
"It is unusual, especially to recognize a large mammal species from small, unidentifiable fragments," said evolutionary geneticist Love Dalén of the Centre for Palaeogenetics, a collaboration between Stockholm University and the Swedish Museum of Natural History, senior author of the research published in the journal Current Biology.
"I'd say that this is related to the advances in the field of ancient DNA, as genetics is a powerful new layer of information applied to ancient materials," said Alexandre Gilardet, a doctoral student at the Centre for Palaeogenetics and co-lead author of the study, along with Centre for Palaeogenetics postdoctoral researcher Jonas Oppenheimer.
Genetic evidence alone is not sufficient to allow for giving a scientific name to a new species, so the researchers are calling this one "Yak X."
THE ICE AGE LANDSCAPE
Dalén said Yak X lived alongside other bovines including steppe bison and the aurochs, the extinct wild ancestor of today's domesticated cattle. It also shared the Ice Age landscape with woolly mammoths, woolly rhinoceroses, horses and large predators such as cave hyenas and brown bears, Dalén said.
"I'd expect it to have looked more like a yak than a bison, given its close relationship to modern yaks," Dalén said.
Yaks are sturdily built animals with horns, long fur and a hump at the shoulders, looking a bit like a hairy ox. The largest males can weigh as much as a ton. Wild yaks are restricted to higher elevations of the Tibetan Plateau.
The Yak X discovery deepens the understanding of the diversity of large Ice Age mammals and adds another species to the long list that disappeared at around the end of that epoch.
"Using the long, 200,000-year time span of our sampling, we can see that the species may have undergone a population decline during a period of warming around 120,000 years ago, and went extinct some time after our youngest sample, about 27,000 years ago," Oppenheimer said.
The vast Siberian expanse was a grassland ecosystem called the mammoth steppe, known as such for its largest denizens. Most of the region was left uncovered by the immense ice sheets that had blanketed large swathes of North America and Europe.
The Yak X lineage diverged from the ancestors of modern yaks around the same time as the evolutionary split that occurred between the ursine lineages that led to today's brown bears and polar bears.
THE DENISOVANS
It was in Denisova Cave in 2008 that scientists unearthed a finger bone that offered the first evidence of the existence of Denisovans, extinct cousins of Neanderthals and our own species, Homo sapiens. Since then, more remains of Denisovans have been discovered in the cave and in several far-flung parts of Asia.
Some modern populations of people, especially those in Melanesia and Papua New Guinea, carry a small percentage of DNA from Denisovans, indicating interbreeding with Homo sapiens before the Denisovans became extinct under circumstances that are not well understood.
Denisovans were hunter-gatherers who survived in many different types of environments. The Yak X species might have been among the prey that they hunted.
"It seems reasonable that Yak X was on the Denisovan menu," Dalén said. REUTERS

Columbia University graduate Mahmoud Khalil has asked the US Supreme Court to overturn a ruling that opened the door for President Donald Trump's administration to re-arrest and deport the Palestinian activist.
Khalil's lawyers asked the justices on Monday to take up his case after the Philadelphia-based 3rd US Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that federal immigration law barred a lower-court judge from ordering his release from US Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody.
Khalil was among the most prominent foreign students to be arrested last year as the US administration pursued a campaign to detain and deport noncitizens who engaged in pro-Palestinian activism on college campuses.
His lawyers say the Supreme Court should make clear immigration law does not prevent noncitizens from pursuing cases arguing they have been detained to punish them for speech that is protected by the US Constitution's First Amendment.
If the 3rd Circuit's decision is allowed to stand, Khalil faces the prospect of arrest and deportation, after the Board of Immigration Appeals in April rejected his challenge to an immigration judge's order that he be removed to Algeria or Syria.
A lower court order barring him from being re-detained remains in place for now until the Supreme Court rules. A separate appeal of the immigration judge's order remains pending.
Khalil, a prominent figure in pro-Palestine protests against Israel's genocide in Gaza, is an Algerian citizen who was born in a Palestinian refugee camp in Syria.
Immigration agents arrested him in March 2025 in the lobby of his university residence in Manhattan despite being a lawful permanent resident, or green-card holder. His wife and their 1-year-old son are both US citizens.
Supreme Court intervention
Secretary of State Marco Rubio had invoked an obscure provision of the Immigration and Nationality Act to deem Khalil removable, citing his involvement in "antisemitic protests and disruptive activities" at Columbia in 2024 the government said fostered a hostile environment for Jewish students.
He was released from a Louisiana detention centre in June 2025 after the New Jersey-based US District Judge Michael Farbiarz ordered the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, to release him.
In January, a 2-1 panel of the 3rd Circuit overturned Farbiarz's decision, saying that under the Immigration and Nationality Act, Khalil's claims could not be addressed through a district court and instead could be raised in an appeal of a removal order from an immigration judge.
After the full appeals court declined to reconsider the case, Khalil turned to the Supreme Court.
Federal appeals courts are split on whether district judges may hear challenges like Khalil's or whether such claims must proceed first through immigration courts, which are not part of the federal judiciary but are instead run by the US Department of Justice.
The US administration last month asked the Supreme Court to overturn a ruling in a similar case favouring Georgetown University scholar Badar Khan Suri, another pro-Palestinian advocate detained by ICE who was ordered released.

====================================================================================================

‘Crucial opportunity to act’ as study finds most of Europe’s wild bee species in decline
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
19:00:04 UTC
04:00:04 KST

Most of Europe’s wild bee species and about half of its hover fly species have declined over the last century, a study has found, as a UN biodiversity summit begins in Armenia.
Records since 1921 show more bee species are declining than increasing in all parts of Europe except the Alpine region. The richness of bee and hover fly species suffered a persistent drop in the Atlantic and Continental regions, the study found, though trends in other regions were mixed or even positive.
The data, which covers 88% of bee and hover fly species across the continent, suggests pollinator communities have been reshaped by the “gradual loss of sensitive species and the rise of a resilient few”, according to the scientists. They warned of “deeper functional disruptions” if existing trends were not addressed.
Nearly 90% of wild flowering plants, as well as more than three-quarters of major food crop types, depend in part on animal pollination. The UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization has warned the decline of pollinators sets off a chain reaction that threatens wildlife and weakens the ability of ecosystems to withstand climate change and environmental stress.
Carlos Martínez-Núñez, an ecologist at the Spanish National Research Council and lead author of the study, said the findings showed that biodiversity loss could remain hidden behind apparently stable species numbers, “giving us a crucial opportunity to act before further declines occur”.
“The fact that some species are increasing today does not mean they will remain winners as climate change and habitat loss intensify,” he added.
The findings come as diplomats gather in Yerevan for the 17th UN conference on biodiversity. The summit, known as Cop17, will focus on the conservation and sustainable use of the natural world, and the shared benefits of its genetic resources.
The study found 91% of the species logged over the last century had also been recorded at least once in the modern period, between 2001 and 2020. Although this suggests as many as 9% of species could have been wiped out in Europe, many of the species not spotted recently occur only rarely in the historical record, and the researchers said they “do not expect widespread extinctions to have occurred yet”.
However, the species’ occupancy – the probability of being found at a given site – had mostly fallen.
Ainhoa Magrach, an environmental researcher at the Basque Centre for Climate Change (BC3), who was not involved in the study, said it “confirms what has long been suspected: many pollinator species are losing populations, and the decline is not affecting all of them equally”.
“Until now, most of the evidence came from a few north-western European countries, such as the UK, Belgium and the Netherlands,” she said. “This work shows that the pattern extends across the continent, although some regional differences exist.”
Wildlife is dying out at an unprecedented rate as humans destroy habitats, spray pesticides, and warp the weather with planet-heating pollution. Despite far-reaching consequences for humanity, including threats to food systems and further breakdown of the climate, governments have not met a single UN target on nature since the biodiversity convention was created in Rio in 1992.
The Cop17 summit is expected to focus on assessing progress toward this decade’s targets, which include protecting 30% of land and sea, reforming $500bn (£375bn) of environmentally damaging subsidies and restoring 30% of the planet’s degraded ecosystems.

A Russian satellite is stalking a U.S. spacecraft in orbit. Experts are worried
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
18:55:52 UTC
03:55:52 KST

A Russian satellite came dangerously close to a Finnish-American satellite this weekend in a provocative maneuver that could foreshadow the new norm for space warfare.
According to public orbital tracking data, KOSMOS-2612, a Russian satellite launched in April with very few details disclosed, approached too close for comfort to ICEYE-X36, an imaging satellite from the Finnish company ICEYE that is owned by its U.S. subsidiary and has been used by the Ukrainian military. Nobody knows quite what KOSMOS-2612 did or what its intentions were, but the two satellites were, at most, a few hundred meters apart, with some estimates putting the distance at within 30 meters. Though the exact distance is unclear, the encounter still appears to be the closest known deliberate and uninvited interaction between two active spacecraft in low-Earth orbit.
No explanatory or corroborating statements have emerged from Russian or U.S. defense officials or from ICEYE, leaving outside experts to speculate about the apparent orbital game of cat and mouse that unfolded overhead.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Such a maneuver is not inherently aggressive or ill-intentioned, says Victoria Samson, head of space policy at the Secure World Foundation. But when taken in the context, the close approach is concerning.
“You’re looking at what Russia is doing here, not in terms, specifically, of what’s happening in space but as part of a larger examination of what’s happening on Earth,” Samson says. “Russia and Ukraine are literally at war with each other. And so it’s kind of tinting how you view Russia’s activities here.”
This maneuver is known as a rendezvous and proximity operation (RPO), and it’s not quite as straightforward as the simple formation flying that is routinely performed with airplanes. To get close to another object in orbit, a spacecraft needs to get itself into the same orbital plane and then change its velocity until it essentially matches the speed as its target so that the two don’t just zoom by each other.
Besides raising the odds of a catastrophic collision, such maneuvers usually require burning a lot of propellant, which is a nonrenewable resource. So satellite operators tend to only attempt them for very compelling reasons. In this case, the reason seems obvious: Russian officials have been unhappy about Ukraine’s purported use of ICEYE-X36’s synthetic aperture radar imaging, which can see through clouds and smoke to track and guide activity on the ground below. A Ukrainian official confirmed to Axios that the nation’s military works with the Finnish satellite company, and ICEYE announced earlier this year that it had signed a collaborative agreement with Ukraine’s defense ministry. ICEYE-X36 launched in 2024, two years after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
KOSMOS-2612’s stalking could be chiefly a warning meant to signal capability, or it could instead be intended for more direct and nefarious action: During an RPO, an aggressor satellite can do any number of things to its target, including taking pictures, jamming communications, blocking sensors or even physically disabling and pushing the other spacecraft out of orbit. Under pressure, the operators of ICEYE-X36 could well decide the spacecraft must burn precious propellant of its own to escape or elude KOSMOS-2612 or other threatening satellites, shortening the mission’s operational lifetime.
Russia’s maneuver has also come as Ukraine has faced broader interference with space-based support for its defense against Russia’s ongoing invasion: Ukrainian war fighters and Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky have reported widespread throttling of SpaceX’s satellite-based Starlink and Starshield services on the battlefield.
The technology to accomplish RPOs is rapidly improving: China, the U.S., Russia and several private companies have all been independently testing their RPO capabilities for the past several years. Radar tracking data show that, since May, other KOSMOS satellites have been maneuvering around ICEYE-X36 in provocative maneuvers that have been explicitly called out by the U.S. Space Force.
There are few official international regulations related to these types of maneuvers, and conducting one nonconsensually breaks norms and crosses ill-defined lines for mutual safe operations on-orbit, Samson says. Unsolicited RPOs might be interpreted as aggressive—or even as an act of war. And already high tensions on the high frontier now seem set to soar: last month the U.S. Space Force announced that it had placed weapons in space. (The U.S. did not disclose many other details about the weapons, but some experts believe they’re communication jammers with RPO capabilities.)
Although ground-based surveillance now allows close tracking of most satellites, without public statements from operators of secretive spacecraft, it’s harder to know what, exactly, they’re up to when conducting maneuvers such as this one. Samson says there’s little to do, for now, besides watching the mysterious drama play out overhead.
“We’re going to wait and see what happens,” she says. “This kind of thing can change quickly, but I would hold off hysterical speculation until we know more about it.”

Election Offices in at Least 32 States Have Received Suspicious Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
18:55:05 UTC
03:55:05 KST

At 12:20 pm last Tuesday, an official in the Louisiana secretary of state’s office opened a mailed letter and white powder fell out. The office was immediately evacuated and the employee was rushed to the emergency room. The employee was not injured and subsequent tests showed that the substance was not harmful. By Wednesday, the office was back open.
“Tuesday’s event did not impact any election operations in preparation for the upcoming election,” Trey Williams, a spokesperson for Louisiana’s secretary of state, tells WIRED.
But the incident was not isolated. A WIRED investigation has found that over the course of the following days, election offices in at least 31 other states were targeted with similar letters as they prepared for the midterms that are now just two weeks away. Many of the states have made public statements acknowledging the receipt of these letters, but WIRED’s accounting of all the incidents shows the full scale of this campaign for the first time.
The vast majority of letters were intercepted by the United States Postal Service before they reached their intended targets, state officials tell WIRED, but in Arizona, Delaware, Oklahoma, South Carolina, and Louisiana the letters were not intercepted, leading to election offices being evacuated when white powder was discovered.
The states that confirmed receipt of a letter are: Alaska, Arizona, California, Connecticut, Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Idaho, Illinois, Kansas, Louisiana, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Mississippi, Nebraska, New Hampshire, New Mexico, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Utah, Virginia, Washington, Wisconsin, and Wyoming.
Election officials in 10 states—Vermont, Michigan, New York, Rhode Island, Texas, West Virginia, Colorado, Kentucky, Indiana, North Carolina—and DC tell WIRED they have not received any suspicious packages. The eight remaining state election offices did not respond.
The white powder contained in the letters that have been opened so far has been reported as not harmful, but election offices remain on high alert.
“We are deeply concerned by these incidents,” the National Association of Secretaries of State and the National Association of State Election Directors wrote in a joint statement. “As we have each stated in the past, threats against election officials and workers have no place in our democracy. Those who administer our elections should never fear for their safety while carrying out their essential duties.”
As news of the letters being sent emerged last week, federal agencies alerted other election offices in some states that a potentially dangerous package was on the way. The FBI notified authorities in Alaska on Friday that an envelope was expected to arrive the following day. At about 9 am Saturday morning, the USPS identified the suspicious package, the Juneau Independent reported.
In Utah, officials told WIRED on Friday that they were preparing for a threatening letter to be sent. “We have been in contact with postal service employees who are actively monitoring our mail for a similar letter so they can intercept it before it reaches our office,” a spokesperson for Utah lieutenant governor Deidre Henderson told WIRED. On Sunday, Henderson posted an image of the suspicious letter that had been intercepted to Threads. The letter was sent in a white envelope with a handwritten address on the front.
The top left hand corner of the letter lists the sender as DSA, seemingly standing for the Democratic Socialists of America organization, with the New York ZIP code associated with the group. The DSA has denied any involvement in the campaign.
Like many election officials responding to this apparent intimidation, Henderson was defiant. “Nothing is going to disrupt the midterm election,” she said. “We won’t let it happen.”
The US Postal Service directed WIRED to the FBI when reached for comment, and the FBI refused to say how many letters it had identified as part of this campaign or whether it had any leads on who was behind the campaign.
“The FBI and US Postal Inspection Service are investigating a series of suspicious mailings sent to various addresses nationwide, including Secretary of State offices and their related election offices,” the FBI tells WIRED in a statement. “Some of the letters contained an unknown substance and we are working closely with our law enforcement partners to respond to each incident.”
“Based on the events in other states, we were notified to expect a suspicious letter, but it was intercepted by the USPS and [Homeland Security Investigations] before it got to our office,” Elizabeth Jonson, a spokesperson for the Mississippi secretary of state, tells WIRED. “It has now been turned over to the FBI, and we were informed the contents were non-hazardous.”
A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson says that its “Federal Protective Service has responded to a series of suspicious-letter incidents affecting congressional offices in federal facilities over the past week,” though they did not comment on the letters sent to election offices.
The letters targeting election offices coincided with similar letters being sent to congressional offices across the country, targeting both Democratic and some Republican lawmakers including senators Ted Cruz, Chris Murphy, and Alex Padilla. One letter was sent to Michigan representative Hillary Scholten, a Democrat, who said in a statement that it warned of an impending “civil war” beginning after the midterms.

Could Labor's trust tax be as much as 60 per cent? Yes, but there's a reason
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
18:50:43 UTC
03:50:43 KST

Could Labor's trust tax be as much as 60 per cent? Yes, but there's a reason
Try to understand Labor's proposal to levy a 30 per cent new tax on trust funds and you can fall quickly down a rabbit hole. This bewildering area of tax law can confuse even seasoned observers.
But you don't need expertise to raise an eyebrow at the claim, made by some of the government's critics, that some small business owners could be stung with a tax rate of 60 per cent or more. That sounds a lot higher than 30 per cent.
So is the claim true? Is this a hidden sting in the tail of the government's tax package? Asked on the ABC's Insiders on Sunday, Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino declined to answer, saying only that "each situation is different".
The short answer is easy: yes, there are circumstances where Labor's new tax could result in a tax rate of 60 per cent. But there's a reason why, and it sheds some light on what the government is trying to achieve with its trust tax.
How trusts can be used to pay less tax
A trust is a financial vehicle used to manage properties, businesses or other assets. It is a popular management tool for those with a lot of wealth, or with complex financial affairs, including many business owners.
For those who use them, trusts can offer greater privacy, control and flexibility than other financial vehicles. But there have long been concerns that they can be used to pay less tax — sometimes much less.
The simplest trust strategy is to split up one person's income among many people. For example, someone who earns $500,000 in a year could use a trust to split that income into five chunks of $100,000 for themselves, a spouse and three children.
To unlock more advanced tax opportunities, a trust owner can create what is known as a "bucket company" — effectively, a dumping place for their money. The company pays the 30 per cent company tax rate, and the family members are made shareholders.
The money can then be given out as dividends at any point in the future. The 30 per cent is refunded as a franking credit, and the family members pay their personal tax rates, opening up additional flexibility to time earnings for tax purposes.
It's complicated, but the use of a bucket company can dramatically expand the tax benefits of trusts. ANU academics Bob Breunig and Tristram Sainsbury have estimated someone can avoid $150,000 of tax on just $500,000 of income in this way.
How the government's trust crackdown works
The government says this is unfair and has proposed a 30 per cent minimum tax on trust income for "discretionary" trusts — those with the flexibility to allow this kind of planning.
The idea is to minimise any benefits from income splitting. Money can still be split up, but will be taxed at least 30 per cent from the very first dollar, whoever it goes to.
But for bucket companies, there is a harsher rule. This, at last, is where the 60 per cent tax rate comes in.
How 30 becomes 60
Under the government's proposal, money going into a bucket company from a discretionary trust will be taxed twice — first the 30 per cent trust tax, and then the 30 per cent company tax.
This double-up does not happen when the beneficiaries are family members. In this case, a refund rule ensures there is no double tax. The 30 per cent is paid only once (though it may be a higher rate if the person is in a higher tax bracket).
But the government has chosen not to extend this refund to bucket companies, to discourage their use.
The tax is not airtight. Trustees will be able to escape the minimum tax if they simply agree to give each beneficiary (people and bucket companies) the same share of income each year.
But Sonali Walpola, an associate professor of tax law at the ANU who supports the new tax, says she believes it will still make discretionary trusts and bucket companies less popular as an option for tax minimisation.
"On equity grounds, this is definitely a step in the right direction," she says.
"I think it will curb some of the more aggressive uses of trusts for tax minimisation.
"Advisers actively market bucket companies as a tax minimisation tool. They are companies that have no operations and serve no other purpose than to cap residual trust income at the corporate tax rate."
Small business concerns
But the tax has encountered fierce opposition from business groups which say they are a legitimate vehicle used by small business owners who are already taxed enough.
Andrew McKellar, chief executive of business group ACCI, says discretionary trusts give small business owners the flexibility to keep family-owned businesses within the family.
"If you think family pharmacies, small and medium-sized home builders, small retailers, restaurants, cafes … they're using these trusts as a flexible mechanism to protect the assets that they have and to provide succession planning," he said.
"We're not saying that there isn't a way to ensure that tax avoidance or tax minimisation is not occurring where it's illegitimate. But what we're not open to is an assault on legitimate small businesses who are trying to have a go."
Jenny Wong of CPA Australia says bucket companies are useful "to hold profits for reinvestment, to buy equipment, hire staff and get through a bad year … Taking [tax] twice on the way in goes well beyond closing a deferral advantage".
Some critics say the worst examples of tax minimisation can be stamped out with guidance from the tax office, or with "integrity provisions" in the law, rather than a new tax.
Sonali Walpola says the integrity provision in the tax law for trusts has been largely ineffective in practice.
"There have been less than 10 litigated cases over more than 45 years," she says.
"Administratively, it's very difficult for the ATO to apply."

Trump signs order creating NIH division, task force for women’s health
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
18:50:29 UTC
03:50:29 KST

Trump signs order creating NIH division, task force for women’s health
WASHINGTON - US President Donald Trump signed an executive order alongside first lady Melania Trump on Oct 19 creating a White House task force and a National Institutes of Health division focused on women’s health.
The task force will be led by White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, who recently announced that she is cancer-free, and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr, Trump said at a White House event.
It directs the federal government to pursue a comprehensive approach to women’s health across all life stages, strengthening research to speed up prevention, diagnosis, and treatment and translating those findings into clinical practice and policy, according to a White House fact sheet.
The task force will hold its first meeting on Oct 19, Trump said, during what he noted was Breast Cancer Awareness Month. Wiles recently finished treatment for breast cancer.
“The executive order I’ll sign in just a moment will direct the Department of Health and Human Services to establish a new women’s health division within the National Institute of Health,” Trump said at the event.
“That’s a big deal. They’ve been after it for a long time,” he said. “Who the hell wouldn’t have a woman’s health division? Melania said they don’t have it.”
The NIH has an Office of Research on Women’s Health, established in 1990.
The new division will operate in coordination with that office rather than replace it, and must be established within an appropriate NIH institute or centre within 90 days, according to the order.
The White House said the move is meant to broaden the government’s focus beyond research and prioritise translating discoveries into clinical care for women and girls.
It will focus on speeding up diagnosis and improving treatment of women’s health conditions that remain understudied, boosting the inclusion of women and girls in clinical trials, and holding grant recipients accountable for considering sex as a biological variable.
Conditions affecting women disproportionately
The division will study conditions that uniquely or disproportionately affect women, including cardiovascular disease, cancer, autoimmune and inflammatory conditions, chronic pain, endometriosis, fibroids, polyendocrine metabolic ovary syndrome, infertility, menopause, Alzheimer’s disease and osteoporosis, the Department of Health and Human Services said in a statement.
The order was first reported by USA Today.
Melania Trump, whom Trump credited with conceiving the initiative, said the effort should “ensure that medical breakthroughs are accessible and affordable to women, regardless of their financial circumstances” and “replace generations of silence with open conversation, education and compassion.”
Trump and his administration have pushed for healthcare cuts, including at NIH, and in 2025 moved to downsize the federal healthcare workforce.
During Trump’s second term, his administration sought to cut NIH grants for research on diversity-related topics and reportedly is moving to allow political appointees to control health-research funding.
The order revokes former President Joe Biden’s March 2024 executive order on advancing women’s health research, which was championed by then-first lady Jill Biden, as well as a November 2023 memorandum that created a White House initiative on the issue.
The Trump administration has also launched a safety review of the abortion pill, mifepristone, that could pave the way for restrictions.
Major medical groups have criticised the move as politically motivated while anti-abortion groups argue the review is moving too slowly. Earlier in October, US officials told a court the review would be completed by March.
US health officials also removed a longstanding safety warning from many hormone replacement therapy products, tightening supplies and leading to shortages, and have urged more manufacturers to study testosterone therapies for women that could support future approvals of female-specific products.
HHS has also targeted family planning funds, announcing earlier in 2026 that for the first time it would require applicants for Title X funding to align their programmes with Trump’s political priorities, prompting legal action. REUTERS
