Japan’s MMX Mission Wants to Bring Martian Moon Samples Back to Earth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
18:45:06 UTC
03:45:06 KST

It’s difficult to imagine a more daunting journey than one to an alien moon named after the Greek god of fear—especially when three other attempts to make that journey have failed.
And yet, as Japan’s space agency, JAXA, and its collaborators gear up to send a spacecraft to Mars’ formidably named moon, “all the members are filled with a quiet sense of excitement,” says Kiyoshi Kuramoto, who leads the mission’s slew of international scientists.
This mission, called the Martian Moons eXploration (MMX), is set to launch from Japan’s Tanegashima Space Center in the wee hours of Tuesday in Japan (Monday afternoon in the US). After almost a year of travel, the spacecraft will reach Mars and its two moons: Phobos, meaning fear in Greek, and Deimos, meaning dread. MMX will observe the pair from afar and collect samples from Phobos in a bid to answer a looming scientific question: How, exactly, did the moons come to be?
Researchers have been attempting similar gambits for decades. Since the 1980s, Russia has sent three probes to Phobos, all of which failed. Still, researchers are anxious to achieve this mission impossible because the origin of Phobos and its sibling remains a mystery. Some of their attributes, such as the pattern of visible light they reflect, suggest they are asteroids captured into Mars’ orbit by its gravity. But the moons’ circular orbits in line with the Martian equator indicate that they could have formed from debris left over from a collision between a nascent Mars and a gigantic asteroid, Tom Statler, MMX program executive at NASA, said at a press briefing.
The new mission is designed to help settle the debate by surveying Mars and the moons in detail using a suite of scientific instruments. With MMX’s MEGANE instrument, for instance, researchers will determine the elemental makeup of Phobos by measuring the neutrino particles and gamma rays it emits. If Phobos ends up having more volatile elements such as hydrogen or potassium, it could lean closer to the captured-asteroid hypothesis, while fewer volatiles could support the impact idea.
“We know nothing about Phobos' elemental composition,” says David Lawrence, who leads the MEGANE team from Johns Hopkins University. “For me, that’s what’s exciting—making a measurement nobody’s done before.”
These observations are “going to give us a hint at some of the answers to the really big questions we have about Phobos,” says Abigail Fraeman, an MMX team member at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory. “But really, the return samples are going to nail those questions.” After scoping out Phobos with its onboard instruments and a rover—which will land ahead of the spacecraft to explore the new terrain—the spacecraft will land on the moon to collect at least 10 grams of material using two different sampling methods. The goal is to bring them to Earth by 2031, which would make them the first ever samples returned from a moon other than our own.
Researchers suspect Phobos’ surface soil contains Martian material, and analyzing it could paint a better picture of how the planet evolved over billions of years. But MMX will also provide insight into our solar system at large. Laboratory analysis of the samples will help determine the origin of leftover material from the early solar system and how it was transported, Statler said during the briefing.
Undertaking this research will require overcoming daunting obstacles. Because scientists currently know little of Phobos’ surface, they can’t pick a landing spot until taking up-close observations of the moon, Kuramoto says. The mission also uses two sampling methods as a safeguard in case one fails, he adds. “Returning samples from a Martian moon is a world-first challenge that is not easy.”
Still, the number of researchers involved and their depth of expertise give the team confidence that it can succeed where others have failed. MMX is a feat of international collaboration with scientists from NASA, the European Space Agency, and Germany’s and France’s space agencies. “That kind of compounded set of expertise and contributions really helps make the mission objectives very achievable,” says Elliot Sefton-Nash, MMX project scientist at ESA.
JAXA also has a proven track record of successful sample-return missions. Despite some setbacks, its Hayabusa mission became the first mission to return a sample from the surface of a near-Earth object when it brought back material from asteroid Itokawa in 2010. Its successor, Hayabusa2, delivered samples from the primitive asteroid Ryugu in 2020. Many Hayabusa2 members have helped design the MMX mission, but sampling Phobos will be different—its orbit and gravity are different from Ryugu’s, for instance, Kuramoto says.
Still, “JAXA's learned and achieved so much with their sample-return missions that they are really well positioned to be able to do this,” Fraeman says.

Ukraine's military uses Starlink's military-grade satellite internet service Starshield for battlefield communications amid Russia's invasion.

Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since 2022 and is now facing an acute humanitarian crisis caused by Russian restrictions on civilian movement and humanitarian access. Russian forces have blocked regular food and aid deliveries, while mined roads and persistent drone attacks have made evacuation routes extremely dangerous, leaving around 2,000 residents trapped in the city with severe shortages of food, medicine, water, electricity, and other essentials.
“We are now moving towards agreeing the final details on ensuring a ceasefire and evacuating everyone who wishes to leave, not just from Oleshky elsewhere, but directly to territory controlled by the Ukrainian government,” Lubinets stated.
“There are still some difficult issues, so to speak, but I hope that in the near future we will all see results from these negotiations,” he continued.
The evacuation would cover Oleshky and six nearby settlements, Ukrainska Pravda wrote.
Ukraine estimates that around 6,000 civilians may remain in the area, including up to 200 children. Up to 2,000 people are believed to remain in Oleshky itself.
Lubinets emphasized that negotiations with the Russian side are taking place every day.
“I can’t disclose many details, but I can say that, in my view, we have made as much progress as possible,” he added, according to Ukrainska Pravda.
Days earlier, Pope Leo XIV called on Russian leader Vladimir Putin to agree to a ceasefire around Oleshky so food and medical aid could reach civilians and residents could evacuate safely. He raised the issue directly during an October 16 phone call with Putin focused on the humanitarian situation in the occupied city.

400-plus Indian-origin scholars, alumni from 27 countries warn against ‘anarchy’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

It calls for resolving differences through “debate, discussion, dialogue and dissent” within the constitutional framework
NEW DELHI: Days after competing groups of Harvard-linked Indians took opposing positions on protests against the Election Commission, more than 400 Indian-origin students, researchers and alumni associated with universities across 27 countries have issued a statement warning against efforts to erode public trust in constitutional institutions and attempts to replace democratic debate with street confrontation.Titled “Spare India from Anarchy”, the statement carries 402 names, including individuals linked to Harvard, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), Oxford, Cambridge, Stanford, Princeton, Yale and Columbia universities, as well as the London School of Economics, National University of Singapore and University of Toronto.The signatories allege that “a frenzy of election denial” and a preference for ‘street over Sansad’ have taken hold in some quarters. They argue that unfavourable election results are being used to question electoral procedures, adverse court rulings to cast doubts on judicial independence and even the armed forces are being drawn into partisan debate.“An unconscionable and devious plan of sowing seeds of doubt in Indian democracy has been hatched,” the statement claims, accusing unspecified groups of turning matters before courts into campaigns on the streets.
The intervention follows a public disagreement among Harvard affiliates over the October 10 protests in Delhi against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls. A group of around 100 Harvard-linked signatories criticised alleged police excesses and detentions, while 44 others subsequently warned against attacks on the credibility of constitutional institutions.The latest appeal widens that dispute beyond Harvard, though it does not name the Election Commission, the SIR exercise or the Delhi protests explicitly.Invoking BR Ambedkar’s warning about the “grammar of anarchy”, the statement says dissent remains essential to democracy but should not become a cover for undermining its institutions. It calls for resolving differences through “debate, discussion, dialogue and dissent” within the constitutional framework.
The accompanying document says the signatories are based in, or have studied in, countries across four continents. It also makes clear that the listed university affiliations do not amount to endorsements by the institutions themselves.

Burnham urges officials to come up with more radical options for Thames Water
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
18:37:14 UTC
03:37:14 KST

Andy Burnham has told officials to rip up their plans for how to fix Thames Water and present him with more radical options for what to do with the stricken company.
In an early test of his promise to bring “the essentials of life” under public control, the prime minister is urging his advisers to go back to the drawing board and create a new list of policies for the utility.
One option being looked at is to convert about £100m of outstanding fines into a government stake in the company, saving its creditors money but giving ministers some say in how it is run.
Burnham previously said he would nationalise Thames, which is running out of cash and recently asked its creditors for an additional £2.4bn, but is struggling to find a way to do so without spending billions of pounds, getting tied up in a lengthy court battle, or both.
Sources familiar with the prime minister’s thinking say he has now told policy officials across Whitehall to contemplate options that were not previously considered feasible, even if that means spending taxpayer money and going to court.
One government source described the fate of the company as a “litmus test” on whether the government could deal with challenges in the medium term, rather than just immediate cost of living support and longer-term structural changes.
“There are more options than people have assumed to date including ones that have never been properly considered,” the source said.
Another said the prime minister had told his officials to “look at all the options and not feel constrained”, in a departure from the advice under Burnham’s predecessor, Keir Starmer.
Burnham has promised to end what he calls “40 years of neoliberalism” and has instructed his ministers to draw up a 10-year plan for government later this year, including detailed proposals for bringing utilities under public control.
Meanwhile, Angela Eagle, the environment secretary, is working on a water bill that will lift a Thatcher-era cap on government ownership of water companies and could rewrite how the bankruptcy regime works for the industry.
Government advisers believe changes to the “special administration regime” (SAR) would make it easier to take companies such as Thames into state control in the future.
But Burnham is also looking for a more immediate solution to Thames’s problems.
When the prime minister came to office, government insiders say he was presented with two main options for Thames: strike a bailout deal with the American hedge funds that own its debt, or pursue an SAR.
Thames’s creditors had proposed a £10bn rescue plan for the company, but Emma Reynolds, the previous environment secretary, made clear her opposition to such a plan before Burnham became prime minister.
Government lawyers also believe it will be difficult to have the company placed into SAR given that it is being kept afloat financially by its creditors and has managed to keep services running.
Among the other options being discussed is the waiving of the approximately £100m in environmental fines the company still owes and taking a stake in it instead. Then, if and when the company is fined again, the government would automatically increase its share rather than collecting the cash.
While some believe this would be a relatively straightforward way to give the government a say in how the company is run, many also believe it would fall short of Burnham’s promise to nationalise the company outright.
The prime minister is under pressure to go further, for example by stripping Thames of its licence, pushing for it to go into SAR immediately and then taking it out of administration without offering anything to the existing creditors.
Such a plan will inevitably be challenged in court, but Burnham is understood to be more willing to take on legal action than Starmer was. One adviser said: “Litigation was always a 100% certainty.”
The prime minister’s advisers also believe they can go further with Thames than with other companies because international investors see the company as a unique case, and not an indication of how the government intends to treat every water company.
Officials say other water companies are likely to be dealt with in different ways, through a mixture of stricter regulation and increased oversight by elected officials such as mayors.
Ewan McGaughey, a professor in law at King’s College, London, said: “The government’s best option is to start a special administration process for Thames Water before it runs up more debts, and sends billions more overseas.
“An orderly transition to public ownership does not require that banks in control are bailed out – on the contrary, the law says polluters should pay.”
Lena Swedlow, deputy director of the Compass campaign group, said: “The obvious solution is to put Thames Water into SAR, and then brought into public ownership so it truly works for everyone.
“While reform of the failing regulatory mechanisms is welcome, any recapitalisation and debt-to-equity schemes that do not seek to permanently wrestle the company from private hands will fail to be in the interests of the workers, stakeholders, and the 16 million people Thames serves. Everything else is noise in the wind.”

We've watched policial violence grow overseas. Now it's arrived on our shores
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
18:35:09 UTC
03:35:09 KST

analysis
Alleged attack on Helen Haines brings spectre of political violence to our shores
The fragility of Australia's democracy was in plain sight yesterday when one of parliament's most well-respected politicians was critically injured in what the prime minister described as an attack outside her electorate office.
Helen Haines had returned from Mansfield to her electorate office in Wangaratta to speak to my program Afternoon Briefing about the appointment of a new National Anti-Corruption Commission (NACC) head after a turbulent first four years for the federal integrity body.
She has fought for integrity in politics and was instrumental in establishing the NACC.
She deserved to be treated with respect and integrity too.
Instead, she is apparently Australia's first victim of a targeted attack on a politician at this scale this century, and the consequences for Australian democracy are profound.
This is something we've come to expect in countries like the United Kingdom and the United States, but in Australia we have been living on the edge.
We've been bracing for the worst but hoping that the horrific violence which is increasingly being normalised across the world is something that escapes our island home.
Democracy only functions when we are free to speak without fear. That includes the right to stand for parliament, argue an unpopular position and to meet the people you represent without fearing for your life.
If the attack on Haines makes anyone fearful about participating in democracy, we must find every way we can to resist it.
'Australians used to disagree better'
Political analyst and Redbridge polling group director Tony Barry has warned the fragmentation of current politics is creating a tinderbox.
"Deepening political polarisation, economic insecurity, and the rise of identity-driven tribalism have created a very volatile and fragmented electorate," he said.
"Australians used to disagree better, but with the rise of tribalism and a breakdown of consensus we are unlikely to see less volatility."
Much has been said about how well liked and respected Helen Haines is, and it's true. She is one of the most well-regarded authentic people in parliament.
But even if this were not the case, even if she peddled contentious and controversial ideas, she would still deserve the right to be safe to do her job as an elected member of parliament.
To live in a democracy free from violence is not selective; it should never be determined by who people like. It is a central and incontestable part of what it is to be in a free and democratically robust liberal democracy.
Australian Federal Police data shows it received 1,067 reports of threatening, harassing, nuisance and offensive behaviour directed towards parliamentarians, high office holders and associated offices and facilities in 2025–26, an increase of 12 per cent on the previous year.
We have a problem in this country, and we must now truly reckon with what it means.
Campaigners warned about safety
In the coming days we will have a fierce debate about how to keep politicians safe in their electorates and accessible to their constituents. There will be discussions about the political temperature and the level of security politicians need.
But underlying it all is the brutal reality that something has changed in this country and the innocence we once enjoyed has been shattered.
Victoria goes to the polls next month. Last night, Labor's state director, Steve Staikos, warned campaigners about their safety.
In an email he wrote: "I would also like to remind all campaign workers and volunteers to remain alert to potential safety risks throughout the campaign."
He warned them not to campaign alone. "Whether you are doorknocking, at a train station or a polling booth, I ask that you please attend in pairs at a minimum. Ideally, please campaign in teams of three or greater."
The Centre for Public Integrity, an independent research institute with a longstanding relationship with Helen Haines, said if the alleged incident was intentional, it would be an "act of democratic violence".
In a statement, it said it was "devastated" by the reports, describing Haines as an "extraordinary parliamentarian and an extraordinary person", adding it was "shocked by the increasingly hostile environment in which Australian parliamentarians are working".
Loading
Threats increasing for years
On 7.30, the prime minister called for respectful political debate.
"We can have differences. They should be debated out in a democracy, but they shouldn't be the subject of personal rancour and the calling into people's motivation where it's not appropriate to do so."
Threats against Australian politicians have been increasing for several years. Yesterday afternoon that fear became reality, and one of the most widely respected politicians in the federal parliament was the victim of unspeakable violence.
The whole system relies on a functional society.
British Labour MP Jo Cox was murdered in 2016 while on her way to meet constituents. The judge sentencing Cox's murderer stressed the importance of MPs being able to "meet their constituents safely and fearlessly".
Haines should have been able to walk in her office and speak to the nation about the integrity reset she had campaigned for.
The fact that the nation wasn't able to hear her articulate her vision is a travesty.
This is our moment to stand up and ensure that Haines remarkable democratic commitment is honoured.
Democracy must be fiercely protected.
Patricia Karvelas is host of ABC News Afternoon Briefing at 4pm on weekdays on ABC News Channel, co-host of the weekly Party Room podcast with Fran Kelly and host of politics and news podcast Politics Now.

A pandemic-era record has returned. The next chapter looks different
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
18:30:51 UTC
03:30:51 KST

In brief
- Australians are moving from the nation's cities to its regions at an increasing rate.
- Data shows some are looking further afield than traditional satellite cities.
Australians are moving from the cities to the regions at rates not seen since the COVID-19 pandemic, with a regional Western Australian city the fastest-growing hotspot.
The Commonwealth Bank and the Regional Australia Institute's (RAI) latest Regional Movers Index shows capital-to-regional migration in the June quarter had matched the record levels of the same quarter in 2021.
The report reveals capital city residents moving to the regions outnumber those moving in the opposite direction by 30 per cent.
While established satellite cities such as the Sunshine Coast and Geelong continue to attract the largest share of movers, the data shows some are looking further afield.
The Western Australian regional centre of Greater Geraldton had the highest year-on-year growth, with net inflows from capitals rising by 225 per cent to June 2026.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
NSW's Clarence Valley and South Australia's Murray Bridge ranked second and third, with growth of 167.3 per cent and 150 per cent, respectively.
Queensland's Toowoomba recorded growth of 147.1 per cent after topping the rankings in the March 2026 quarter. Bathurst in NSW rounded out the top five with growth of 122.4 per cent.
Sydney and Melbourne continue to be the largest sources of regional movers, respectively accounting for 52 per cent and 36 per cent of net outflows across all capital cities.
In overall numbers, the Sunshine Coast, about 100km north of Brisbane, remained the most popular regional destination, receiving 8.7 per cent of the share of total net migration.
It was followed by Greater Geelong, south of Melbourne, with 5 per cent, Lake Macquarie on the NSW Central Coast with 4.1 per cent, Fraser Coast in Queensland with 3.9 per cent and Moorabool in Victoria with 3.6 per cent.
The inter-regional migration index, tracking movement between regional areas, was above its long-term average but below its June quarter peak in 2023.
When including inter-regional migration, Central Goldfields in Victoria, about 140km northwest of Melbourne, experienced the strongest growth, with net internal migration inflows increasing 312 per cent over the year.
It was followed by Burdekin in north Queensland at 285 per cent, Snowy Monaro in southern NSW at 233 per cent, and the Tablelands and Douglas, both in far north Queensland, at 223 per cent and 221 per cent, respectively.
While Burdekin's growth was mostly driven by arrivals from capital cities, Tablelands benefited from a mix of capital city and regional migration.
Growth in the other regions was primarily driven by migration from other regional areas.
Country appeal remains 'incredibly strong'
RAI chief Liz Ritchie said 2026's high June quarter numbers were particularly noteworthy as internal migration typically slowed during this period, with fewer Australians tending to move during the cooler months.
"This tells us the appeal of country living remains incredibly strong all year round, even outside the traditional peak moving periods," she said.
"Australians are increasingly considering a broader range of regional communities when deciding where to live, with the benefits of regional living extending beyond popular coastal towns and inland communities."
Ritchie said the RAI's regional population planning report had found regional growth outpaced government projections by 114,000 people over the past decade.
"With more Australians choosing regional communities, we need population planning that anticipates growth and ensures housing, infrastructure and essential services keep pace," she said.
Commonwealth Bank's regional and agribusiness banking executive general manager, Kylie Allen, attributed North Queensland's growth to investment in diversifying local economies.
Burdekin, south of Townsville and home to Ayr and Home Hill, was supported by agriculture, manufacturing and renewable energy, she said.
The Tablelands, inland from Cairns and including Atherton, benefited from strong agribusiness and tourism sectors.
Douglas, which includes Port Douglas north of Cairns, was supported by a thriving tourism industry and ongoing investment in local infrastructure.
"Across northern Queensland, local investment is helping regions capitalise on their distinct strengths and drive broader economic growth," she said.
"When local businesses invest and expand, the benefits flow through the wider economy, creating jobs, attracting skilled workers and strengthening the services and supply chains that help regional communities thrive."

====================================================================================================

'Terrifying': The parents who dread having adult kids who won't leave home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
18:30:40 UTC
03:30:40 KST

How are parents raising resilient kids in an age of constant judgement and conflicting advice? From gentle parenting to tough love, we hear from parents navigating generational differences, social pressures and childhood baggage. Watch Insight episode Modern Parenting on SBS On Demand.
Carmen (not her real name) lives in a two-bedroom apartment in Sydney with her 18-year-old daughter, who’s currently doing end-of-school exams. Carmen is happy in life and adores her daughter, but she’s quietly counting the days until she moves out.
But it wasn’t always this way.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"When she was a young child, I absolutely loved being a mother," she told SBS Insight. "Now I’m feeling like her maid and I’m no longer feeling that warm maternal rush of, 'oh, I just want to look after her'."
Underneath it all is a sense that she’s given enough.
"It’s all about looking at the sacrifices that we’ve made as mothers for so many years and reaching middle age and saying ... Actually, I don’t want to spend my entire life sacrificing."
Having left home when she was 17, Carmen also believes fostering her daughter's independence is part of the job.
"If she's still at home with me in her late 20s, I don’t think I would be doing my daughter any favours."
Brisbane mum Amanda (not her real name) says she is "absolutely" looking forward to the day her three children leave home.
She had her first child nine months after finishing university, and she now has a 22-year-old, two teenagers plus a 16-year-old stepchild.
"My whole adult life has been about balancing kids and career. I just want some time for me," she says. "I've never seen my children as the central part of my life."
Amanda (not her real name) says she loves her kids, but she sees her job as turning them into independent adults.
"The longer they stay with me, the less I’ve done my job properly," she says.
She also looks forward to travelling outside school holidays, not driving kids around every day, and spending time with her partner without children, which she's never had.
"The idea of living alone and not having anybody else to disturb us is just the greatest joy to us."
That doesn’t mean pushing her children out. Her son is living at home rent-free while he saves roughly three months’ worth of rent, and she wants to help him do it.
But she says the thought of her children still at home in their mid to late 20s is "terrifying".
"I'd just want them out of my house."
Kids at home for longer
Around three quarters (77 per cent) of 19 to 20-year-olds and almost half (48 per cent) of 23 to 24-year-olds live with their parents, according to an August 2026 Australian Institute of Family Studies report.
About 85 per cent of them say they’re concerned about housing affordability.
Social researcher Mark McCrindle says cost is a key driver of children staying at home for longer, though social shifts play a part too. Young people are studying longer, carrying more debt and starting their earning years, and their own families, later.
"We’ve institutionalised adolescence," he says.
"Plus parents these days are also a lot more relaxed. The children have a lot more freedom, and there’s not the same social stigma of living with parents well into their adult years."
Not every parent wants them gone
For plenty of families and cultures, having adult children at home isn’t a problem to solve.
Professor Roger Wilkins, co-director of the annual Household, Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia survey, says there are upsides. More young people can study, and their parents are "probably the wealthiest generation of parents yet and better placed to keep supporting their children into adulthood".
Parents interviewed by McCrindle’s team said that despite occasional tension, they value the connection of having adult children at home.
"It keeps that most important bond of family together right at the time that those young adults are about to move into that next stage of having their own kids."
The impact on relationships, finances and wellbeing
However, children staying longer at home is a common reason for parents seeking support and "absolutely" puts more strain on parents and family dynamics, says the CEO of Relationships Australia NSW, psychologist Elisabeth Shaw.
"We see people who have real fears that it’s just too comfortable at home and are not really sure how this phase is going to end," she says.
There’s a "reluctant camaraderie" among parents in the same boat, which normalises the situation.
"It’s now, 'well, if I was a really good parent, I should be open to supporting and housing them for as long as they need me'."
Ongoing costs
Then there's the money — though Wilkins stresses the experience varies widely.
"Plenty of parents feel they need to support their adult children and are finding that quite a burden," he says.
Many families are keen to downsize from servicing a large family home, he adds, especially as rent and mortgage costs continue to rise.
Carmen would like to cut her hours, rent out her apartment and travel.
"I’m burnt out as a person," she says. "I do kind of feel stuck working."
Amanda and her partner rent a six-bedroom house in inner Brisbane and have a deposit saved to buy something smaller, but they want to wait until at least some of the kids have left.
"We don’t want to own a six-bedroom home, but you know, rents keep going up," she says.
McCrindle says the strain sets in when there’s no certainty about when young adults will leave, and it often continues even once they have jobs.
With life milestones arriving later, many parents don’t become empty nesters until their 60s, and they can find themselves caring for adult children and ageing parents at the same time.
"You have parents who are sandwiched in the middle from a financial, time pressure, relational and emotional burden perspective."
Learning to have ‘difficult conversations'
Shaw says many families dodge the 'when are you leaving?' talk because they’re afraid of upsetting someone.
"I can't tell you the number of people I’ve seen who are going silent because they feel bad for saying anything, but they’re stockpiling resentment," she says.
Often the strain comes from treating adult kids as kids, while the kids expect adult freedoms, she adds.
So how do you start the conversation?
"Begin with open questions about the future, like what your kids hope for after school, then share your own plans and ask how they fit," she suggests.
"It’s trying to talk to them as adults, but own your own goal."
McCrindle suggests going a step further and putting the arrangement in writing, covering duties, financial contributions and broader family commitments, with a review after 12 months.
Amanda says she's never explicitly discussed with her children when she expects them to move out "because that feels rude", but says she's been clear about her and her partner's future plans.
"We've talked about living overseas for a year when the kids move out and that they're welcome to visit us if they want to."
Shaw clarifies having children at home isn’t a problem in itself. It’s how the family feels about it.
"The questions to ask are, is the family in conflict? Are there silences full of seething resentment? Is someone in the family being held back? And is the young person failing to thrive in other aspects of their lives?"
Shedding the guilt
For those experiencing guilt for looking forward to their kids leaving home, Shaw offers a different way to see the situation.
"Sometimes a push is actually a thing that we do as parents, and it’s a very healthy thing to do."
But knowing that doesn’t make it easy. Carmen understands the logic, and she still feels guilty.
"It's almost like life exists in these little chapters and I'm moving forward to a different chapter but I have to keep rereading the last pages over and over," she says.
"This is a beautiful young woman and I'm enjoying seeing her grow and thrive and I want to become her really good friend. But it's not quite there yet.
"I'm in that weird in-between."

Pezeshkian calls for stronger Iran-Russia cooperation to advance peace and multilateralism
TEHRAN – Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has called for faster implementation of agreements between Tehran and Moscow, citing energy, transport, trade and power generation as priority areas for expanding bilateral cooperation.
Pezeshkian made the remarks on Monday during a meeting with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov in Tehran, where the two sides discussed the strategic partnership between the countries, the implementation of existing agreements and developments in the region and beyond.
The president said the two countries could play an effective role in strengthening peace, sustainable security and a multilateral international order by drawing on their shared capabilities and regional and international mechanisms.
The Iranian president welcomed the continued expansion of relations between Tehran and Moscow, stressing the need to deepen bilateral cooperation, strengthen political and diplomatic coordination, and ensure that previously reached agreements translate into practical results.
Referring to his recent meetings and telephone conversations with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Pezeshkian said the two leaders had been following up on bilateral understandings, implementation plans and joint projects through ongoing consultations. He expressed hope that his upcoming visit to Moscow would help advance the agreements and produce tangible outcomes in areas of mutual interest.
He also thanked the Russian president, government and people for their support and solidarity during the recent war against Iran, emphasizing the importance of continued mutual support and closer political and diplomatic cooperation in pursuit of the two countries’ shared interests.
Turning agreements into practical projects
Pezeshkian also highlighted understandings reached on the Caspian Sea and trade as a foundation for expanding economic and regional engagement. He said agreements in energy, transport and power generation should move towards implementation through clearly defined operational arrangements, practical mechanisms and specific timelines.
The president’s remarks underscored Tehran’s emphasis on translating the strategic partnership into concrete projects rather than allowing bilateral understandings to remain at the level of political commitments. He said the upcoming visit to Russia would provide an opportunity to pursue this objective.
Energy cooperation, transport links, trade and power generation were identified as key priorities, alongside broader coordination through regional and international organizations. Pezeshkian argued that stronger economic ties between Iran and Russia could serve the interests of both countries while creating wider opportunities for regional cooperation.
Iran calls for a regional approach to peace and security

He stressed that the attacks took place while Iran was pursuing dialogue and diplomatic engagement.
The president said Iran would not accept a situation in which a country used its military power and instruments of pressure to impose its will on other nations. Tehran, he said, sought an international order founded on mutual respect, the rights of nations, constructive cooperation and multilateralism. He added that Iran and Russia shared common ground on these principles.
Pezeshkian also stressed that Iran had no fundamental disagreements with countries in the region, pointing to the historical, cultural and religious ties linking Iran with its neighbors and other Muslim nations. He said Tehran remained committed to developing relations through dialogue, fraternity and mutual cooperation, and was ready to address existing challenges through understanding and regional mechanisms.
He said US intervention and divisive policies have contributed to tensions in the region. The president also criticized the presence of US military bases in regional countries, arguing that they had brought greater tension, division and insecurity rather than lasting stability.
Pezeshkian said sustainable regional security should be based on mutual trust, the participation of regional countries and respect for the legitimate interests of all parties. Iran, he added, welcomed joint initiatives with neighboring states in peace and security, economic development, cultural and scientific cooperation, and people-to-people exchanges.
His remarks placed regional diplomacy and cooperation among neighboring countries at the center of Tehran’s approach to security, rather than reliance on external military deployments.
Multilateral institutions as platforms for cooperation
Elsewhere in his remarks, Pezeshkian said developments in the international system had made it increasingly necessary to move beyond unilateral approaches and strengthen inclusive mechanisms for cooperation. Iran, he stressed, was determined to play an active role in building a fairer multilateral order based on mutual respect.
He pointed to Russia, China and other members of the BRICS group, the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) and the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) as having considerable potential to expand economic, political and security cooperation and strengthen the role of multilateral institutions in international affairs.
The president called for making fuller use of these platforms to expand economic engagement, facilitate trade, develop transport and transit infrastructure, and deepen regional cooperation. He said closer Iran-Russia relations, combined with the effective implementation of bilateral agreements and the use of regional and international mechanisms, could advance shared interests and strengthen cooperation at both regional and global levels.
Lavrov reaffirms Moscow’s commitment to the partnership

He reaffirmed Moscow’s intention to expand cooperation in oil and gas, energy, transport, communications, media, culture, science and higher education.
The Russian foreign minister also emphasized the alignment of Iranian and Russian views on international issues and the importance of continued diplomatic consultations to promote peace and security. Referring to agreements concerning the Caspian Sea, he called for closer coordination to protect the two countries’ interests and strengthen regional cooperation.

The two diplomats reviewed bilateral relations under the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty, as well as developments in the Persian Gulf, the Caucasus, Ukraine and West Asia.
Araghchi said Tehran and Moscow agreed that regional disputes required political solutions rather than military action. They also discussed Palestine, Lebanon, Yemen, security in the Strait of Hormuz and recent incidents involving commercial vessels and port infrastructure in the Caspian Sea.
Both sides reaffirmed their opposition to unilateralism and their commitment to multilateral cooperation through international institutions, including BRICS and the SCO. Lavrov reiterated Russia’s commitment to its agreements with Iran, citing humanitarian assistance and the gradual return of Russian specialists to the Bushehr nuclear power plant. He also said Moscow intended to continue implementing its economic and investment commitments to Tehran.
Lavrov expressed hope that Pezeshkian would visit Russia in the coming days to attend a summit of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum in Moscow, providing another opportunity to advance bilateral cooperation.

Suggesting that Scotland’s coast is undefended is both inaccurate and irresponsible, the Defence Secretary told the Commons, offering in the same answer to work with the Scottish Government on the defence of the United Kingdom regardless of constitutional differences.
Lara Bird, the Scottish National Party member for Arbroath and Broughty Ferry, asked the Secretary of State to station a warship permanently on Scotland’s north coast, and set the request against what she described as a sevenfold difference in defence spending between south east England and Scotland.
Bird said: “Scotland is currently on the front line of defending the High North. And yet, despite the very real threats that we face, the UK government currently spends seven times more on defence in the south east of England than in the whole of Scotland combined. And so, given those very real threats that we face, and given that our coastline is currently undefended by the Royal Navy, will the Secretary of State commit to placing a surface level vessel permanently on the north coast of Scotland?”
Wes Streeting, the Secretary of State for Defence, said: “Can I just sort of say gently to the hon. Member that I think it is both inaccurate and irresponsible to suggest that Scotland’s coast is undefended, and in the same spirit, just to underscore to her, I am very willing to work with the Scottish Government in defence of the United Kingdom, regardless of our constitutional differences. It is important that we work together and I hope we can do so in the question.”
His Majesty’s Naval Base Clyde at Faslane is the Royal Navy’s largest site in Scotland and the home of the submarine service, holding the Vanguard class boats that carry the deterrent and the Astute class attack submarines alongside them, with the whole submarine flotilla consolidating there.
RAF Lossiemouth flies the P-8A Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft that track Russian submarines through the Greenland Iceland United Kingdom gap, and holds Typhoons at quick reaction alert for the northern half of British airspace. River class offshore patrol vessels work Scottish waters on fishery protection and maritime security tasking, and the Fleet Ready Escort is held at short notice to shadow Russian warships as they transit.
HMS Prince of Wales and her strike group deployed to the High North this month on Operation Firecrest, with F-35B Lightning jets flying from the carrier in the North Atlantic, and the Royal Navy has spent the year building the pattern of surface deployments north of Scotland that the deployment sits within.
Versions of the claim have reached the Commons before, and this publication has examined an earlier assertion that there are no Royal Navy vessels in Scottish waters, and has tested the related argument that Scotland is short changed on defence spending.
Figures published last month put Ministry of Defence spending with Scottish industry at £2.53 billion, a thirteen per cent real terms increase on the previous year, worth £460 a head and supporting 12,200 jobs. The House of Commons Library, working from the previous year’s regional statistics, puts spending with industry in South East England at £7.9 billion, or £820 a person, against a United Kingdom average of about £460.
The Arctic Policy Framework published last week named Russian activity around undersea cables and pipelines as a threat to critical national infrastructure and described the shadow fleet as a systemic risk, which puts official policy close to Bird’s description of where Scotland sits. The Lunna House Agreement signed with Norway commits the two navies to protecting those links across the North Atlantic, and the Defence Committee is running an inquiry into the High North, with written evidence submitted this month setting out how uncrewed platforms and Type 26 frigates would provide persistent anti-submarine surveillance in the gap.

Jalen Hurts Has Deep Vein Thrombosis and Blood Clots in His Lungs. Here’s What to Know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
18:26:48 UTC
03:26:48 KST

Jalen Hurts is expected to miss the rest of the NFL season after doctors diagnosed blood clots in both lungs, ESPN and NFL Network reported.
The Philadelphia Eagles quarterback has deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and bilateral pulmonary emboli, according to an Oct. 19 statement from the team. He is clinically stable and has no significant functional limitations, they said, but needs blood thinners—and can’t participate in contact activities, including football, while taking them.
“Jalen’s prognosis is very good, and we expect a full recovery,” the statement said.
The news raises questions beyond football: How do you recognize a blood clot? What does treatment involve? And why can some people stop blood thinners after a few months while others take them for life? We asked doctors who aren’t involved in Hurts’ care what everyone should know.
How to recognize a possible blood clot
Deep vein thrombosis, or DVT, occurs when a clot forms in a vein deep inside the body, often in the leg. Those veins carry blood back toward the heart. They’re different from superficial blood clots——Hurts’ original diagnosis—which form closer to the skin, explains Dr. Geoffrey Barnes, a cardiologist and vascular medicine specialist at University of Michigan Health.
The distinction matters because deep-vein clots are more likely to break loose and travel through the heart into the lungs. Once a clot lodges in an artery there, it causes a pulmonary embolism.
DVT often causes pain, swelling, and redness or a darker skin color. Patients commonly tell Barnes, “My entire calf and ankle are swollen.” One leg might look noticeably different from the other.
An injury can make those symptoms easier to dismiss. “If you’re worried that you have a DVT, it’s important that you get medical care quickly,” Barnes says. Seek a same-day evaluation through your doctor, urgent care, or an emergency department rather than waiting to see whether it goes away.
Unexplained shortness of breath, chest pain, coughing up blood, or fainting require emergency care because they can signal a pulmonary embolism. A dry cough without a cold, pain when taking a deep breath, or a racing heart can also be clues, says Dr. Stephan Moll, a hematologist and professor of medicine at the University of North Carolina who runs an Athletes and Blood Clots Clinic.
Some pulmonary embolisms cause only mild symptoms—or none at all. People can mistake the discomfort for bronchitis, pneumonia, or a strained muscle, Moll says.
Clots become more common with age. Other risk factors include surgery, injury, prolonged inactivity, cancer, certain inherited conditions, and estrogen-containing medications. But young, active people can develop them, too.
How doctors diagnose and treat blood clots
To check for a leg clot, doctors usually use ultrasound. They move a handheld device over the skin to get pictures of the veins underneath, gently pressing as they go. A normal vein should flatten under that pressure.
With a clot, “you can’t squeeze it closed because that solid clot is in the way,” Barnes says.
Doctors typically use a specialized CT scan to look for clots in the lungs. Finding them in both lungs doesn’t, by itself, establish how sick someone is, Barnes says. Doctors also check oxygen levels, blood pressure, and whether the heart is struggling to pump blood through the lungs.
Pulmonary embolisms range from mild cases to medical emergencies, Moll emphasizes. Some people need treatment in the hospital, including medication that dissolves clots or a procedure to remove them. Many others can be treated with anticoagulants, commonly called blood thinners.
Blood thinners help keep clots from growing and prevent new ones from forming. “They do not dissolve blood clots,” Moll says. Your body gradually breaks down the existing clot, though some people are left with scar tissue.
Many people with DVT can take medication at home, Barnes says. Some people with lower-risk pulmonary embolisms can, too.
Treatment for DVT or pulmonary embolisms generally lasts at least three months. “For the first three months it’s uninterrupted blood thinners,” Moll says.
After that, doctors weigh the chance of another clot against the risk of bleeding from continued medication. What caused the clot helps guide that decision. Someone who developed one after surgery may be able to stop once treatment is complete and that temporary risk has passed. “But if this kind of came out of the blue,” Barnes says, longer-term treatment may make sense. Cancer, continued immobility, and certain clotting disorders can also affect the decision.
Having a scan that looks better doesn’t automatically mean it’s time to stop medication, Moll says. Doctors generally follow symptoms rather than ordering repeated scans to watch a clot disappear.
Even someone who stops daily medication may need a prevention plan for future surgery or another period of increased risk. “Risk factors vary, and the length of treatment varies, and the recovery varies,” Moll says.
What recovery looks like
A blood-clot diagnosis doesn’t necessarily mean you need to stay on the couch.
“I’m not asking them to go for a jog or run a marathon,” Barnes says. “But I want them to be up and walking around as much as they can tolerate,” gradually doing more every day.
Getting tackled is another matter. Blood thinners make bleeding harder to stop, so a collision or fall—especially one involving a head injury—can become much more dangerous. When it comes to contact sports like football, “I would not let an athlete play on blood thinners,” Moll says.
For some athletes who need long-term treatment, specialists may consider a carefully managed, intermittent medication schedule after the initial three months, Moll says. It isn’t suitable for everyone and requires expert oversight; patients shouldn’t skip doses to play sports. Ask your doctor which activities you can safely return to and when.
Keeping your legs moving can also help reduce the risk of future clots. On long flights, Barnes recommends getting up to walk every one to two hours. While you’re seated, pretend your big toe is a pen and trace the alphabet with it to get your ankle moving and help pump blood through your legs. “You can do that just sitting in your seat. Nobody knows,” he says. If you’ve recently had a clot, check with your doctor before flying.
Some people feel much better relatively quickly. Others experience lasting damage to the veins after DVT, which can leave blood struggling to flow back up the leg. That can result in what doctors call post-thrombotic syndrome: “chronic swelling, chronic pain, chronic leg heaviness,” Moll says. After a pulmonary embolisms, some people continue to have shortness of breath, chest discomfort, or fatigue, particularly if the clots haven’t fully cleared.
Depending on what’s causing the symptoms, treatment might include compression stockings for leg swelling, specialized rehabilitation, or a procedure to address damaged veins or lingering clots. Tell your doctor if those symptoms linger. “We have treatments that we can offer to try and make that better,” Barnes says.

Palestinian activist Mahmoud Khalil asks US Supreme Court to hear case seeking to avoid re-arrest
Oct 19 - Columbia University graduate Mahmoud Khalil on Monday asked the US Supreme Court to overturn a ruling that opened the door for President Donald Trump's administration to re-arrest and deport the Palestinian activist.
Khalil's lawyers asked the justices to take up his case after the Philadelphia-based 3rd US Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that federal immigration law barred a lower-court judge from ordering his release from US Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody.
Khalil was among the most prominent foreign students to be arrested last year as the Trump administration pursued a campaign to detain and deport noncitizens who engaged in pro-Palestinian activism on college campuses.
His lawyers say the Supreme Court should make clear immigration law does not prevent noncitizens from pursuing cases arguing they have been detained to punish them for speech that is protected by the US Constitution's First Amendment.
"If the Trump administration can punish someone for their pro-Palestine speech, this or any future administration can punish anyone for any speech," Khalil told reporters on Monday.
If the 3rd Circuit's decision is allowed to stand, Khalil faces the prospect of arrest and deportation, after the Board of Immigration Appeals in April rejected his challenge to an immigration judge's order that he be removed to Algeria or Syria.
A lower court order barring him from being re-detained remains in place for now until the Supreme Court rules. A separate appeal of the immigration judge's order remains pending.
A spokesperson for the US Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, in a statement said the Trump administration acted within its authority in Khalil's case, and it encouraged him to self-deport.
KHALIL'S BACKGROUND AND ARREST
Khalil, a prominent figure in pro-Palestinian protests against Israel's war in Gaza, is an Algerian citizen who was born in a Palestinian refugee camp in Syria.
Immigration agents arrested him in March 2025 in the lobby of his university residence in Manhattan despite his being a lawful permanent resident, or green-card holder. His wife and their 1-year-old son are both US citizens.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio had invoked an obscure provision of the Immigration and Nationality Act to deem Khalil removable, citing his involvement in "antisemitic protests and disruptive activities" at Columbia in 2024 that the government said fostered a hostile environment for Jewish students.
He was released from a Louisiana detention center in June 2025 after the New Jersey-based US District Judge Michael Farbiarz, an appointee of former President Joe Biden, ordered the Department of Homeland Security to release him.
In January, a 2-1 panel of the 3rd Circuit overturned Farbiarz's decision, saying that under the Immigration and Nationality Act, Khalil's claims could not be addressed through a district court and instead could be raised in an appeal of a removal order from an immigration judge.
After the full appeals court declined to reconsider the case, Khalil turned to the Supreme Court.
Federal appeals courts are split on whether district judges may hear challenges like Khalil's or whether such claims must proceed first through immigration courts, which are not part of the federal judiciary but are instead run by the US Department of Justice.
The Trump administration last month asked the Supreme Court to overturn a ruling in a similar case favoring Georgetown University scholar Badar Khan Suri, another pro-Palestinian advocate detained by ICE who was ordered released. REUTERS

Federal prosecutors allege that the defendant, Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, was in frequent communication with an unnamed member of the Saudi royal family and that a Saudi military official paid for a one-way plane ticket for Alfozan’s wife and young son to return to Saudi Arabia after his arrest, according to the court document, made public late on Sunday.

The case has highlighted security challenges around sensitive AI research as companies and governments compete fiercely for an edge in the transformational technology.
“The defendant went to significant lengths to create customized, encrypted recording devices to secretly record highly sensitive meetings involving senior OpenAI personnel and executives, high-level business counterparts, and government officials, all while communicating with individuals of significance in Saudi Arabia and pursuing opportunities in — and making plans to travel to — Saudi Arabia,” prosecutors wrote in a detention memo.
The Saudi government media office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. A lawyer for Alfozan did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The lawyer, William Pernik, previously asked for Alfozan to be released from custody, subject to conditions including location monitoring and surrendering his passport, and said Alfozan had spent the last 15 years in the US and had applied to become a citizen.

Before his arrest, Alfozan was scheduled to fly to Riyadh during a planned two-month parental leave. His wife told investigators that she and their son planned to move permanently to Saudi Arabia and that Alfozan eventually intended to join them, according to prosecutors.
In an Arabic-language interview on the Identity Capital podcast last month, Alfozan said that he visits Saudi Arabia three or four times a year, follows developments there and advises or mentors Saudi startups.
He said meeting Prince Mohammed bin Salman, then deputy crown prince, during a 2016 gathering with young Saudi tech workers in Silicon Valley persuaded him to learn at a top tech company before bringing those skills back home.
While Alfozan was working at Facebook, he and other Saudis in Silicon Valley formed a consulting initiative that linked Saudi public- and private-sector organisations with expertise in big data, the internet of things and machine learning.

Despite the denials from Washington, many in Kyiv suspect the issues are not a coincidence.
On Monday morning, Zelensky wrote on social media: "Overnight two ballistic missile attacks were reported on the capital, one without warning, the second with only minimal time to take shelter."
Hours earlier, an interview the president did with NBC was published, in which he said intelligence sharing had been restored after a three-day pause.
"We are very thankful for this," he said. "Only [the] United States has this unique intelligence to tell our side when Russia uses ballistic missiles."
But Beskrestnov told the BBC that American intelligence continued to be incomplete and inconsistent, and that the US had failed to provide a clear explanation for the issue.
"This looks very strange," he said. "Sometimes we receive this information before the attack, another time we [do] not."
He continued: "And for example, last night we received it, but... one minute before the attack."
However, he said other collaboration with US continues, adding: "Intelligence data keeps flowing, and the issue is solely with the air raid alert component."
Beskrestnov also said the US had given no clarity about who was responsible for the ongoing restrictions to the Starlink internet network and its military service Starshield, which Kyiv uses to provide connectivity for drones, helicopters and military communications.
Last week, Starshield restricted the speed at which mobile units could move while staying connected to the network to 100mph (160km/h).
This has limited Ukraine's ability to shoot down incoming drones or to launch mid-range drone attacks into Russian-occupied areas.
Starlink owner Elon Musk said last week that the US government ultimately controls access to Starshield, which was designed for the Pentagon, suggesting it may therefore be behind the restrictions. Trump has denied involvement.
Beskrestnov said he thought both issues occurring at the same time was "probably" a deliberate move to put pressure on Ukraine.
He told BBC News: "It's probably the United States trying to say [to] us, 'let's have the conversation, negotiation with Russia, you should find the compromise'."
Beskrestnov also said Ukraine had its own radar data to provide some limited warning of incoming attacks, but was urgently looking into using alternative communication systems.
He added: "Now we understand that something begins to happen with Starlink, and we're not sure what will be the next step.
"We understand that we should be prepared for some problems in future. And now we're thinking about an alternative for Starlink, not only for air defence, for communication between our forces, between our staff, for civilians also, because we don't know what we should expect in future regarding Starlink."
On Monday, when asked about intelligence sharing, Trump said: "We've given a lot to Ukraine. They've given us nothing."
Earlier, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio had said there had not been a "pause" to intelligence sharing.
"I don't know where [Zelensky is] getting these things or why he's saying these things to the press," he told reporters on Monday.
Rubio said he could not comment on the incident, adding: "I know a few nights ago there was a software problem involving their early warning system."
The BBC has contacted Starlink for a response.
A White House official said there were no changes to intelligence sharing operations between the US and Ukraine.
The official spoke on background to discuss intelligence matters. Trump is focused on ending the war, the official said, and added that the US has provided more aid to Ukraine than any other country.
Russian attacks continued late on Monday, with Ukrainian officials saying at least six people were killed - including a toddler in her pram and an 11-year-old girl - in a drone strike near a park café in the north-eastern Kharkiv region.
Zelensky described the attack in which another 14 people were injured as "absolute atrocity".

Netanyahu’s new security doctrine: Regional strategy or election ploy?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
18:21:06 UTC
03:21:06 KST

Netanyahu’s new security doctrine: Regional strategy or election ploy?
Experts say Netanyahu’s security doctrine and map of regional alliances serve his political ambitions ahead of elections.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has unveiled an updated national security doctrine and displayed a map of rival regional alignments, signalling a security approach that prioritises preemptive military action, the expansion of buffer zones, and the pursuit of new regional partnerships.
The document was developed with the assistance of Israel’s National Security Council and published by the Prime Minister’s Office on Sunday, just nine days before Israel’s parliamentary elections that could spell the end of Netanyahu’s time in office. It outlines a formal policy of preventing perceived threats through military action rather than containment – a policy that has already been seen in action over the past few years, as Israel pursues multiple wars and attacks on its neighbours.
Electoral survival strategy
The timing of the map’s release carries particular political significance, with Netanyahu fighting to retain power amid criticism of his conduct in power, the ongoing corruption trial he faces and his handling of the October 7, 2023, attacks, as well as the wars that followed.
As the October 27 election day draws closer, Netanyahu is attempting to bolster his credentials as Israel’s ‘Mr Security’, hoping to get the votes of Israelis who may not like some of his other policies or behaviour, but still view him as the most likely leader to defend the country.
Netanyahu, who did get the endorsement of US President Donald Trump on Sunday, said during the briefing that Israel could face the possibility of a far less supportive administration in Washington in two years, after the end of the Trump presidency.
“In two years, a president… who is extremely hostile to Israel could come to power [in the United States],” Netanyahu warned.
He therefore argued that Israel must “expand our network of alliances and develop capabilities that make us a valuable asset” to other countries as a way of protecting itself if US policy towards it changed.
The comments, according to analysts, suggest that Netanyahu is seeking to portray his leadership as essential to navigating both Israel’s regional military challenges and its diplomatic isolation, all while keeping a fearful electorate reassured.
Mohanad Hage Ali, deputy director for research at the Malcolm H Kerr Carnegie Middle East Center, explained that the strategic presentation centred on competing regional blocs and buffer zones.
That framework “incubates and nurtures existential fears, which would lead Israeli voters to feel the need for a decisive leader”, Hage Ali noted.
In his assessment, Netanyahu stands to benefit from the Israeli public’s fear of regional threats by presenting himself as a familiar leader capable of managing them, making him “the devil you know”, as the analyst put it, to voters reluctant to embrace political change at a sensitive time.
Netanyahu’s political opponents have been quick to push back against that narrative.
Gadi Eisenkot, one of the prime minister’s main challengers in the upcoming election, said that the published doctrine was “two hollow pages, full of slogans that have nothing to do with a security concept”.
Another, former Prime Minister Yair Lapid, described the document as “superficial”.
Expanding security zones
The map displayed during Netanyahu’s briefing was originally published in May by Friedrich-Ebert-Stiftung, a German political foundation. It divides the Middle East and parts of Africa into competing blocs, highlighting the region’s complex network of alliances and rivalries.
Those networks include states, unrecognised entities and non-state actors.
The map identifies an Israel-United Arab Emirates alignment, described as the “Hexagon Alliance”, alongside a separate grouping of Egypt, Turkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia – the latter three of which signed the Mecca mutual defence pact in August – labelled the “Sunni Diamond Alliance”. It also depicts Iran and its regional allies as a separate axis.
The map serves to illustrate the issues outlined in the published security doctrine, presenting a region where Israel faces multiple threats, the alliance that Israel is seeking to cultivate across the wider region, and the perceived need for “buffer zones” – the occupation of territory in other countries.
Israel’s existing illegal occupation of territory in Gaza and southern Lebanon illustrates the potential consequences of expanding the buffer zone approach.
Hage Ali warned that continuing to pursue an approach built around expanding military control could lead to “more conflict and more ethnic cleansing” under the guise of security buffers.
Embracing regional factions
A striking element of the map displayed by Netanyahu is its explicit designation of non-state actors as friendly entities.
The map highlights territories controlled by the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces in Sudan and Khalifa Haftar’s self-styled Libyan National Army within an alignment deemed cooperative to Israel and the United Arab Emirates.
Israel views these actors as pragmatic partners or at least cooperative entities in a broader strategic grid, Hage Ali explained. However, the public association of these groups with Israel threatens to damage their domestic standing across the Arab world.
That reflects Netanyahu’s immediate priorities, where “what Israelis think matters more than the reputation of your allies and the viability of these alliances”, Hage Ali added.
The portrayal of the Middle East as a region divided into competing alliances also carries risks for Netanyahu’s broader diplomatic ambitions.
Earlier this year, Netanyahu proposed a “hexagon of alliances”, envisaging cooperation between Israel, India, Greece, Cyprus and unnamed Arab, African and Asian partners, against what he described as “radical” regional alliances.
The proposed grouping has not been established as a formal alliance, and commentators in Israel and the international press have described the project as a branding exercise rather than a binding military pact, noting that countries like India prioritise non-alignment and pragmatic trade over ideologically rigid blocs.
For Tehran and its regional partners, the map also offers potent political leverage.
Hage Ali emphasised that the visual layout “will certainly help their propaganda machine”, providing Hezbollah and other Iranian allies with evidence to reinforce the narrative that Israel seeks to expand and dominate the region.

Russia’s strategic plans for 2026 thwarted – Biletsky on importance of Operation Vivaldi
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
21:20:23 EEST
03:20:23 KST

The successful execution of Operation Vivaldi has thwarted the Russian Federation’s strategic plans, which included plans to encircle the Sloviansk-Kramatorsk agglomeration by closing a ring near the settlement of Barvinkove, announced Brigadier General Andriy Biletsky, commander of the Center grouping of forces.
As reported by an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent, the brigadier general explained at a press conference in Kharkiv that the primary objective of Operation Vivaldi was specifically to disrupt the enemy's offensive operations.
"The enemy’s key plan for 2026 has been destroyed. Therefore, the strategic significance of this operation is not measured in kilometers, but in the fact that the enemy’s core objective has been thwarted, namely, the encirclement of the entire Donetsk region, including Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, with an advance toward Barvinkove, intended to seize Donetsk region through two converging strikes. This plan has been thwarted," Biletsky stated.
He identified the forces opposing the Ukrainian units: the 1st Guards Tank Army, along with the 20th and 25th Combined Arms Armies (drawn from the West grouping). These forces had been tasked with advancing from a bridgehead established on the Chornyi Zherebets River toward the city of Sviatohirsk and the settlement of Rubtsi. "The Russian Federation’s strategic objective was to split our forces on the eastern bank of the Oskil River into two, destroy them, and then advance toward the town of Barvinkove, located in the south of Kharkiv region. The plan involved a two-pronged maneuver: one thrust through the Sviatohirsk salient, which we have since eliminated, bypassing Lyman to envelop Sloviansk-Kramatorsk urban agglomeration from the north; and a second thrust, passing through the town of Dobropillia toward Barvinkove, to complete the total encirclement of Donetsk region," Biletsky explained.
Thus, as the general emphasized, the Russian Federation sought to "achieve a key political objective" set by the Kremlin: the complete seizure of Donetsk region. Biletsky added that this was originally a Russian plan for 2026, which the occupiers began attempting to implement in 2025.
"They were supposed to reach Barvinkove by 2026. Now, as we approach the end of 2026, this is the situation: the destruction of that bridgehead and the offensive force has effectively resulted in the defeat of the 20th Army’s 144th Division... With their offensive force routed, the enemy has, for the time being, abandoned attempts to bypass and encircle Donetsk region," the brigadier general noted.
According to Biletsky, the occupiers have a few remaining options in Donetsk sector. Specifically, Russia might attempt a "frontal assault" on Sloviansk and Kramatorsk—a move that, the general noted, would require significant resources, entail heavy casualties, and offer no guarantee of success. "The enemy has temporarily abandoned this plan, though they intend to resume it," he added.
As the general noted, the Russian Federation effectively has only one remaining area of focus—Dobropillia—since the occupiers achieved some success there and have not yet abandoned this "pincer" maneuver.
"Therefore, the primary significance of this operation does not lie in the distance covered nor in the fact that the Third Corps reached the Chornyi Zherebets River, thereby shortening its front line and gaining the ability to significantly densify its infantry positions, as well as the concentration of UAVs and artillery per square kilometer (essentially making their defense denser, more stable, and impenetrable). Rather, the operation’s importance lies in the fact that the Russian Federation’s strategic designs were thwarted. This is what is meant by forcing an adversary to abandon their plans—that is the key point. Now, they face the need for serious planning and replanning; it is a complex and costly undertaking," Biletsky emphasized.
He described Operation Vivaldi as unique, not least because it was carried out under exceptionally difficult conditions. Biletsky underscored that Ukraine conducted an offensive while being outnumbered by the enemy, yet still achieved a truly significant success.
The operation was carried out by personnel from the 3rd Assault Brigade, the 60th Separate Mechanized Brigade, the 125th Separate Territorial Defense Brigade, the 3rd Separate Reconnaissance Battalion, the 25th Separate Anti-Tank Battalion, and the 21st Separate Special Purpose Battalion KRAKEN, as well as attached units: the 66th Separate Mechanized Brigade, the 3rd Border Detachment, the 10th Mobile Border Detachment Dozor, tactical groups from the 8th Special Operations Forces Regiment, the National Guard of Ukraine’s Lasar's Group, the K-2 unit of the Special Operations Forces (SOF), and unmanned systems units from the Special Operations Center A (Alpha).
