Living with non-stop air raids: how Kharkiv, Dnipro, Zaporizhzhia, Odesa and Kyiv have adapted to the jet-powered war of 2026
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
21:20:00 EEST
03:20:00 KST

Living with non-stop air raids: how Kharkiv, Dnipro, Zaporizhzhia, Odesa and Kyiv have adapted to the jet-powered war of 2026
In 2026 the war has been reaching ever deeper into Ukraine, no longer confined to the combat zone. Russia has been striking civilian targets with drones and missiles for nearly five years now.
Since September 2026, following the large-scale emergence of jet-powered Shahed attack drones, attacks on the rear have entered a new phase of escalation. Russian forces regularly strike Ukrainian metals companies, industrial facilities, retailers' warehouses, railway stations, trains, shopping centres, petrol stations and even kindergartens. There are now almost non-stop air-raid warnings in both major cities and the surrounding regions.
As the Ukrainian Air Force looks for ways to counter Russia's jet-powered attacks, people in the country's major cities are learning to live their lives differently, adapting to yet another set of challenges that the Russia-Ukraine war has brought them.
Ukrainska Pravda reached out to fellow journalists at four local media outlets – Odesa-based Intent, Vidbudova Zaporizhzhia (Zaporizhzhia Recovery), Kharkiv-based Gwara Media and Dnipro.media – to compare notes and learn about how Ukraine's major cities are coping amid constant air raids.
No cities in Ukraine's west are included in this overview because they are further away from the front line and experience fewer air-raid warnings – and long may that remain the case. Cities located too close to Russian forces, including Kherson and Sumy, have also been left out.
In this article, we look at what life is like for people in Odesa, Zaporizhzhia, Dnipro, Kharkiv and Kyiv these days, how everyday life has changed, what new inconveniences have emerged, and how residents, local authorities and businesses are adapting to the new challenges of the war.
Odesa
We propose to tell this story from south to north, with Odesa our first stop. On 18 September 2026, Odesa had 20 air-raid warnings in just one day – an all-time record for the city since the full-scale war began.
The constant attacks and strikes have not brought life in Odesa to a halt. The city has much to endure, but there has been no mass closure of businesses. Entrepreneurs have adapted to the ever-present danger, although they continue to suffer financial losses caused by damage to their premises and consequent repairs, forced downtime, and expenditure on generators, batteries and backup internet connections. There have even been cases where businesses near the site of a strike have reopened immediately after the clean-up, provided the premises were still fit for use.
Large shopping centres and retail chains in Odesa generally have formal emergency protocols in place. Increasingly, however, their response will depend on the type of threat. Missile threats prompt a more serious response, with businesses suspending operations, but not all shops close completely when the threat is of a drone attack. Large centres use car parks or other premises as shelters, while small businesses rely on the nearest municipal shelters and often ignore air-raid warnings.
The regular attacks have not stopped people from going shopping in stores and shopping centres, although they are making more use of delivery services. Some supermarkets and other businesses, such as Metro and McDonald's, close when an alert is issued, but the ATB food retail chain remains open.
With air-raid warnings now a constant in our lives, another question that arises is how to keep children safe at school. Schools in Odesa are trying to keep in-person learning going as much as possible, but the constant interruptions disrupt timetables: the children have to move to shelters and then go back to their classrooms, and when there are several alerts in a single day, the teachers' plans are effectively derailed. In a small number of schools, lessons continue inside the shelters; others switch to remote learning.
The city suffers from a shortage of public transport, but services continue to run when the sirens sound. They can, however, be disrupted by strikes, road closures, damage to overhead power lines or power cuts. Privately-owned buses are the most flexible means of transport in such situations and often continue operating, while municipal trams and trolleybuses are more dependent on centralised decisions and the state of the power grid. Air-raid alerts also cause frequent delays to intercity buses and trains arriving in or departing from Odesa.
As for petrol stations, there is no single citywide rule requiring them either to close completely or switch to self-service when an alert is issued. Over the past month, however, more and more petrol stations in Odesa have started closing when air-raid warnings are in place.
Air-raid sirens have become part of everyday life in the city, sounding dozens of times a day, particularly when there are waves of drone attacks. Overall, Odesa is at constant risk of strikes by drones, missiles, ballistic missiles, and more recently guided aerial bombs as well. As a result, residents are increasingly assessing the level of risk for themselves and tend to take the threat of ballistic missiles more seriously than, for example, a prolonged alert prompted by UAVs.
The number of shelters in Odesa has increased, including mobile shelters, but access remains uneven across different parts of the city. Some people regularly go down to shelters, while others have grown accustomed to the danger and are ignoring air-raid warnings more and more often.
There is currently no mass exodus from Odesa comparable to the one seen in spring 2022, although some families temporarily leave for western regions of Ukraine or go abroad after particularly severe attacks.
Employers, meanwhile, have become much more tolerant of employees arriving late because of prolonged alerts, overnight attacks, transport issues or power cuts. Where possible, they use hybrid working arrangements, adjust schedules, or simply take into account that part of the working day may have to be spent in a shelter.
Odesa's cultural life is alive and well, with concerts, theatre performances, festivals, talks and other events still taking place. Event organisers are now required to have a plan of action in case of an air-raid warning: pausing the event, evacuating people to a shelter, postponing it, or resuming once the all-clear has been given.
Even Odesa's nightlife has survived, especially in the Arcadia resort and the city centre, where hundreds of tourists and locals can still be seen out in the evenings. These activities are now, however, constrained by the curfew and the continuing risk of attacks.
Zaporizhzhia
Unlike Odesa, Zaporizhzhia is a frontline city. As such, it faces an onslaught from the full range of Russian weaponry.
Residents say they have been particularly affected by the recent wave of attacks on shopping centres. The Russians have destroyed all the Epicentr home improvement stores, most of the Amstor supermarkets, and the largest shopping centre, City Mall. This leaves only a handful of large shopping centres in the city.
The destruction of the shopping centres also means that local businesses lose the premises where they used to operate – shops selling branded clothing, handmade items, mobile phone accessories, electronics, furniture, jewellery and many other products.
Overall, the situation regarding shopping centres in the city is challenging: the Russians have destroyed almost all the major ones. Those that remain appear to be open, but some of the shops have either closed or moved to other locations. Smaller neighbourhood shopping centres are faring better and are still open.
People in Zaporizhzhia are making more use of delivery services – and not only because the places where they used to shop nearby may have been destroyed, but also out of a reluctance to make unnecessary trips to shopping centres that could be targeted by Russian attacks.
But the most significant long-term impact – which also has a knock-on effect on small businesses – has been caused by Russia's attacks on large industrial companies. For example, in September the Zaporizhstal steelworks suspended operations following a series of missile strikes. Since the plant is one of the city's main employers, this has had a huge impact on both residents' incomes and the local budget's revenue from personal income tax.
Almost all of the city's 92 schools use a hybrid learning model, meaning students attend school in person periodically.
The city also has 10 "underground schools" – shelters equipped for people to spend several hours in relative comfort, where lessons can be held and students can take breaks. Two such schools were completed in early autumn, with another two due to be completed by the end of the year. The most important thing is that lessons in these underground schools can continue uninterrupted despite the air-raid alerts.
Public transport in Zaporizhzhia is increasingly coming under attack from FPV drones, which target both municipal buses and privately operated minibuses. Municipal transport was attacked by drones at least twice in September.
The situation in the Kushuhum hromada A hromada is an administrative unit designating a village, several villages, or a town, and their adjacent territories. , located between Zaporizhzhia and the line of contact, is indicative of this. In early summer, as Russian FPV drones began penetrating further into the region, minibuses started being fitted with anti-drone protection in the form of metal cages. By the end of the summer, even the protected minibuses had stopped serving the southern parts of the hromada closest to the front line.
The situation with rail travel is even more difficult: passengers almost always have to take a bus to Dnipro and catch a train from there.
Petrol stations in Zaporizhzhia continue to stay open, with no queues or fuel shortages. Following a series of attacks on petrol stations over the summer, many are now protected with netting and gabions.
Mobile and internet connections in the city have so far remained available. During prolonged power cuts, mobile internet can become unreliable, and fixed internet connections that do not use fibre-optic cables may stop working. Nevertheless, some form of connection remains available at all times.
Adapting the healthcare system to the new reality of life under constant attack appears to be one of Zaporizhzhia's priorities. The city authorities regularly report on renovated shelters, backup power supplies and stockpiles, although more in the context of preparing for a hard winter than the security situation. Overall, healthcare can be said to be operating as normal. In addition to the public hospitals, there are several large private medical facilities, meaning that medical care remains accessible.
Air-raid warnings are in effect almost all the time. The city authorities recently created a distinction between oblast-wide and city-specific alerts, adding a separate warning for guided aerial bombs.
There are several threat levels. FPV drones usually strike seemingly random targets – cars, apartment blocks, public transport. Several such drones have already effectively reached the city centre and hit buses waiting at junctions. The Zaporizhzhia Oblast State Administration building has also been attacked several times.
Shahed drones are primarily used to target factories or energy infrastructure. Residential areas are also affected by them.
During the summer, the city was regularly hit by four or five guided aerial bombs as many as three times a day. Such strikes are now rare.
The use of missiles against Zaporizhzhia is relatively infrequent, with most attacks involving ballistic missiles targeting factories or Kalibr cruise missiles.
Despite its frontline status, the city hosts many small cultural events organised by individual venues and arts centres. Zaporizhzhia celebrated City Day on 3 October, and more than 10 fairs and other events were held at various venues to mark the occasion, some of which attracted large crowds.
Well-known performers come to Zaporizhzhia to give concerts, and there are comedy shows by both local stand-up comedians and household names.
Several cinemas, theatres, the philharmonic and many other venues are still open and can get quite busy, particularly at weekends.
Kharkiv
Like Zaporizhzhia, Kharkiv is a frontline city. In the first half of 2026, 589 new companies were registered in Kharkiv Oblast, indicating that the market is gradually adapting. Factories continue to operate to some extent. The IT industry largely operates remotely and companies do not open offices in the city.
Shopping centres stay open when the sirens sound, although some individual shops close, mostly those belonging to large chains. In one shopping centre, some shops even rent space in the car park, which is designated as a shelter.
Schools without certified shelters are closed. Children in Kharkiv study either online or at metro schools and underground schools. According to Kharkiv Mayor Ihor Terekhov, 52% of the city's schoolchildren will be able to study in a blended format during the 2026-2027 academic year, combining in-person and remote learning.
Public transport is free and does not stop during air-raid alerts. The downside is that passengers sometimes have to wait more than 7-10 minutes for a train on the metro, compared with, for example, 2-5 minutes in Kyiv.
At the Kharkiv Oblast Clinical Hospital, an underground hospital connected to the main building is being built. Medical facilities are equipped with shelters, generators and backup power supplies. When there were power cuts across the city, hospitals, as critical infrastructure, continued to be supplied with electricity.
The healthcare system becomes overwhelmed in the aftermath of attacks, as the number of casualties is often high. Doctors therefore have to prioritise operations, postponing scheduled procedures in order to save critically injured patients. Seriously injured people from all over the oblast are often taken to the regional hospital in Kharkiv, which has greater capacity to treat them.
Hospitals also admit wounded military personnel from the front line, and this places medical staff under further strain.
On average, around 10 air-raid warnings are issued in the city every day, with an average duration of almost an hour and a half. On 30 September, for example, an air-raid alert in Kharkiv remained in effect for 10 hours.
The Russians' most frequent target is civilian infrastructure, with petrol stations among the sites increasingly hit in recent attacks. People rarely go to shelters. Even during an attack, life largely goes on as normal in the streets, unless the strike occurs very close by.
Concerts, performances and other events are permitted in designated safe spaces. Some independent theatres, NGOs and activists may hold events at ordinary venues, provided they ensure the audience or visitors have access to a shelter. In practice, however, shelters are rarely used, and events generally continue uninterrupted when the sirens sound.
Restaurants, cafés and other venues in Kharkiv stay open in the evenings until around 20:00-22:00, while most shops close at around 21:00-22:00, with some staying open until 23:00.
Dnipro
On the way back to the capital on our virtual journey, we arrive in Dnipro, a major city that has learned to keep going amid ballistic missile threats and daily warnings of attacks. And although alerts have become far more frequent – in September 2026, for instance, they were issued five times as often as in September 2025 – the city has not ground to a halt.
Large businesses and shopping centres have been forced to adapt in the wake of strikes. Some shopping centres close completely whenever there is any threat, while others base their response on the level of danger. People often ignore the alerts, however, and simply wait outside the doors.
Strikes on metals plants and the Interpipe industrial site have posed particular challenges for the city.
Mobile service providers and postal services suspend operations whenever an alert is issued, disrupting business logistics. Despite the attacks, privately operated buses and municipal public transport continue to operate, while the metro serves as a free shelter. Railways remain the most vulnerable, with many trains cancelled or delayed. The situation is further complicated by the fact that mobile and GPS signals are jammed when the threat is high (so that electronic warfare can function properly), turning journeys across the city into something of a blind navigation exercise.
Education and healthcare in Dnipro have also shifted into emergency mode. Officially children attend school in person, but in practice they spend several hours a day in noisy basements, prompting parents to complain of a dramatic decline in educational standards.
Hospitals try to keep going without interruption. Public hospitals cancel appointments only when the threat level is classified as red [indicating missiles or large-scale drone attacks – ed.], while private clinics often stay open during air-raid alerts, sometimes requiring patients to sign waivers releasing them from liability.
Safety remains the biggest problem, as there is a critical shortage of shelters close to people's homes and workplaces, and mobile concrete shelters often end up turning into rubbish dumps because of poor sanitary conditions. As a result, most residents rely on the two-wall rule A safety rule whereby a person keeps two walls without windows between them and the street during attacks. and only rush to seek shelter when there is a ballistic missile threat or explosions can be heard.
Despite people's exhaustion and constant stress, there has been no mass exodus from Dnipro: leaving is expensive, and people fear losing their jobs. Instead, the city has become a hub for displaced people from frontline areas.
Even cultural life has endured. Theatres are still open, pausing performances when audiences need to move down to shelters. The famous House of Organ and Chamber Music has been closed since it was damaged by a Russian attack, but concerts are held at other venues or simply in the metro.
Kyiv
Our final stop is Ukraine's capital. Kyiv has long been subjected to regular Shahed drone and missile attacks, but from September onwards, the situation has become considerably more difficult.
In September 2026, not a single day in the capital went by without air-raid warnings. Alerts were in place for a total of 242 hours and 40 minutes – that's 33.7% of the month. In effect, Kyiv residents spent a third of September under the threat of attack.
The authorities did not immediately respond to the relentless air attacks. On 10 September, the Kyiv Defence Council shortened the curfew, which now runs from 01:00 to 05:00.
Nevertheless, the city did introduce a more flexible system for operating under a yellow threat level, allowing public institutions and administrative service centres to continue providing services when there is no direct missile or drone threat. However, given that a jet-powered UAV can cross the entire city in eight minutes, it's hard to describe any situation as genuinely risk-free.
Most business losses are now caused by strikes on warehouses and disruptions to logistics, including bridge closures and the return of power cuts.
Recent decisions by the city authorities allow businesses to operate more flexibly when the threat level is relatively low. During large-scale drone or ballistic missile attacks, however, all major shopping centres close and ask shoppers to go to shelters.
Shopping centres have not extended their opening hours despite the shorter curfew.
The capital's schools teach mainly in person or in a blended format. School shelters have been prepared, but frequent alerts throughout the school day force children to spend hours in basements, disrupting lessons. The Kyiv City State Administration's Department of Education has already recommended that schools have an autumn half-term break from 26 October to 1 November, although each school may adjust these dates depending on the security situation in its area.
The quality of education depends on how well individual schools are prepared to organise the learning process. For example, one school in the Solomianskyi district has three semi-basement spaces. All lessons are held, but they are only 35 minutes long [rather than 40-45 – ed.]. Students in grades 1-5 (primary school) and 10-11 (high school) attend in person, while the others (middle school) study online.
Schools without shelters, however, have had to switch to remote learning. Kyiv residents are often forced to move to other cities for the sake of their children's education, as the constant air raids make regular school attendance in the capital extremely difficult.
Shahed drone attacks have significantly affected transport links between the right and left banks of the capital. In early September, the government made an attempt to keep the overground section of the metro's green line running even when an alert was in effect; previously, trains had only run on the underground section.
But the initiative ended in failure after the first drone attacks on the Pivdennyi (South) Bridge, when a Shahed narrowly missed a metro train.
Since the beginning of October, Kyiv has made major changes to how traffic on its bridges is managed when an alert is in effect:
- Pivdennyi (South) Bridge: traffic from the right bank to the left bank is restricted for 15 minutes after an air-raid alert is issued, but there are no restrictions on left bank-right bank traffic.
- Podilsko-Voskresenskyi Bridge: after an air-raid warning is issued, traffic from the left bank to the right bank is temporarily suspended for 15 minutes.
- Pivnichnyi (North) Bridge, Darnytskyi Bridge, Paton Bridge and Metro Bridge: no restrictions on traffic during air-raid warnings.
The result is that Kyiv is paralysed during alerts, as the transport links between the two banks are disrupted. Overground public transport still stops during alerts, although the shorter curfew means public transport now runs for an hour longer in the evening.
Kyiv managed to avoid strict rolling power outages throughout September and early October, but on 6-7 October the capital and the surrounding region once again returned to scheduled stabilisation and emergency power cuts.
For safety reasons, petrol stations stop serving customers as soon as an alert is issued.
With the return of scheduled power cuts in October, mobile internet connections in some areas have once again begun to deteriorate, as Russian forces have been actively targeting Kyiv's data centres.
Postal operators also close branches when the sirens sound.
Under a Kyiv Defence Council decision of 10 September, medical facilities and hospitals now operate under updated protocols. They continue to provide services during a yellow threat level, but when there is a direct threat, staff and patients must move to shelters. Hospitals are equipped with generators – vital now that power cuts have returned – and try to avoid cancelling scheduled operations except during large-scale missile attacks.
Kyiv residents take shelter in underground car parks, basements and the metro, which is open to shelter in around the clock. People in Kyiv have begun responding to air-raid alerts more frequently since the October strikes on infrastructure, although the two-wall rule remains the most common form of protection. The city authorities have promised to install mobile shelters.
The main change is that Ukraine's major cities are no longer experiencing "war lite". Life hasn't stopped, but it has been transformed into a harsh, pragmatic mode of survival in which flexibility, self-sufficiency and willingness to work underground have become the defining rules of the new reality.
Analysis and reporting by Volodymyr Fomichov, Ukrainska Pravda.

He said Congress would reaffirm that Ukraine is an indispensable ally and Russia a self-declared enemy of the US.

Starlink limits still cripple Ukraine’s drones
Separately on Monday, President Volodymyr Zelensky reiterated that Ukrainian units were still losing satellite connections.
After a report from the Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU), Maj. Gen. Mykhailo Drapatyi, Zelensky said that Starlink and Starshield equipment still stops working at 130-160 km/h (81-100 mph) along various parts of the front.
Russia Strikes Ecosoft, Planeta Plastic With Ballistic Missiles
The restrictions are significantly slowing frontline logistics and limiting the use of several types of drones, including mid-strike drones and the interceptors Ukraine relies on against jet-powered Shahed drones.
“This must be raised with partners once again at all levels,” Zelensky said. “Speed matters for protecting lives.”
The limits first disrupted Ukrainian drone operations overnight on Oct. 13-14; around the same time, Ukrainian authorities also reported that they hadn’t received a partner warning about Russian ballistic missiles.
The next day, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk claimed that the US military, and ultimately Trump, sets speed limits on Ukraine’s Starshield terminals – not his company.
The Telegraph later reported, citing four sources, that Musk himself had proposed throttling the service and that Trump approved it. Trump, however, rejected that account.
“I don’t know if it was somebody, because it wasn’t me, and I don’t think it was Elon,” Trump told reporters. “And, as far as I understand, everything is the same as it’s always been.”
Sanctions waiver deepens rift
The Starlink dispute is unfolding alongside a growing public feud between Kyiv and Washington.
The tensions date back to Oct. 9, when a Ukrainian delegation met senior US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Miami, hoping to reach a breakthrough on ending Russia’s aggression.
During the talks, the envoys reportedly warned that Washington would cut off intelligence sharing if Kyiv kept striking Russian oil refineries.
Several US outlets also reported that the administration threatened to suspend the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL), the mechanism through which European allies buy American weapons for Ukraine, including Patriot interceptors.
US Ambassador to NATO Matthew Whitaker denied any changes to the PURL on Oct. 13.
Currently, Ukraine is facing a critical shortage of Patriots, which are the only weapons systems capable of deterring Russia’s ballistic missiles.
While the talks were still underway, Trump announced a diesel deal with Putin in Washington, under which Russia would supply hundreds of thousands of tons of fuel to US and global markets.
The US Treasury then lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports through April 2027.
Around the same time, Trump slammed Kyiv for refinery strikes and called for a new president in Ukraine. “Zelensky could have settled this war many, many times, but he chooses not to,” Trump told reporters. “I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president.”
On Oct. 14, a total of 12 senators – six Republicans and six Democrats – signed a joint letter urging Trump to rescind his deal with Putin, calling it a gift to Moscow and a betrayal of Ukraine.
“This deal is a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our Allies; it should be rescinded,” the senators wrote, demanding the president to enforce the new Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, signed by Trump just three weeks before striking the deal.
Despite condemnation from Ukraine, the EU and his own party members, Trump signed an executive order Friday, Oct. 16, waiving sweeping Russia sanctions and tariffs set to take effect Sunday, Oct. 18.
The White House defended this decision, saying it will allow for a peaceful resolution to Russia’s war.

US adds ‘wrongful detention’ warning for Americans travelling to China
US State Department is updating its travel advisory to alert Americans of the risk of being detained arbitrarily under Chinese law
The US State Department has added a “wrongful detention” warning to its travel advisory for China, alerting Americans to the risk of being detained arbitrarily under Chinese law.
On Monday, the official China travel advisory added the “D” risk indicator for wrongful detention, while maintaining the country’s overall advisory level at Level 2, or “Exercise Increased Caution”.
The advisory urges Americans travelling to mainland China to exercise caution due to the “arbitrary enforcement of local laws, the use of exit bans without a fair and transparent process under the law, and the risk of wrongful detention”.
The move comes as Washington and Beijing seek to maintain an improving bilateral relationship following a warm welcome for Chinese President Xi Jinping by US President Donald Trump during the September visit to Washington. The two leaders are expected to meet twice more this year.

Iran welcomes regional security initiatives that do not include the "presence or intervention of foreign forces,” said the nation’s foreign minister on Monday.
"We welcome any initiative that leads to the establishment of security based on regional capabilities and collective security arrangements among regional countries, without the presence or intervention of foreign forces, and consider it a step in the right direction," Abbas Araghchi told a joint news conference alongside Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov in Tehran, according to Iran's state-run news agency IRNA.

Tehran and Moscow have strengthened political, economic, and military cooperation in recent years amid Western sanctions imposed on both countries.
In early 2025, Pezeshkian and Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a 20-year Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty in Moscow, covering cooperation in defense, security, energy, trade, and transportation.
The agreement also provides for closer coordination on regional and international issues, although it does not establish an obligation for mutual defense.

Benny Gantz drops out of Israel’s election race
Decision comes after polls showed his Blue and White party below the 3.25 percent threshold needed to enter the Knesset.
Benny Gantz, a former Israeli army chief and defence minister, has withdrawn from Israel’s election race after polls showed his party falling short of the threshold for entering parliament.
The leader of the Blue and White (Kahol Lavan) party announced on Monday he will not run in the October 27 polls, saying he will “continue to work for unity”.
The 67-year-old is expected to hold a news conference later on Monday.
Opinion polls in the lead-up to next week’s vote had consistently shown Gantz’s party hovering below the 3.25 percent threshold needed to enter the 120-seat Knesset, or Israel’s parliament.
A former main opposition leader, Gantz sat in a national unity government with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu from 2020 to 2021.
He also joined Netanyahu’s war cabinet that was formed to oversee Israel’s genocidal war against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip after the Hamas-led attacks in southern Israel on October 7, 2023. Gantz quit the emergency cabinet in early June 2024, saying Netanyahu “is preventing us from advancing toward true victory”.
Reporting from Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, Al Jazeera’s Nour Odeh said Gantz’s election withdrawal announcement “was not really expected”, but added that many would see it as being “in line with how he’s conducted himself” after entering politics in 2018.
“This is a man who entered into unity governments with leaders – especially Netanyahu – that he expressly opposed,” said Odeh.
Gantz’s message for unity is narrow, Odeh added, as it referred to “a unity government of Zionist parties, so no Palestinian Israeli parties, no non-Zionist parties in the government, even if that means bringing in Netanyahu again”.
‘Irrelevant and inconsequential’
Netanyahu’s Likud party and the far-right coalition it leads is locked in a tight race with a self-styled Zionist opposition alliance heading into the election, according to recent polling, although neither side appears on track to win a parliamentary majority.
Two Arab-led electoral lists representing the Palestinian citizens of Israel, who make up about 20 percent of the population, are projected to win 13 seats and could be critical to any post-election coalition – but both main blocs have ruled out forming a government with them.
Opposition leaders, including Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot, who is seen as a potential prime minister candidate, welcomed Gantz’s decision as “correct” and “responsible”.
Alon Pinkas, a former Israeli ambassador and consul general in New York, told Al Jazeera Gantz’s exit from the race does not change the playing field as he was not going to have a major impact on the election.
“Electorally, his departure from the political system is completely irrelevant and inconsequential,” he said. “In terms of the politics, it is also inconsequential,” adding that Gantz had lost “a lot of his aura” when he “overstayed his welcome in the Netanyahu government”.

continuous vertical gardens and layered planters wrap 111 house in são paulo

continuous vertical gardens and layered planters wrap 111 house in são paulo
designed by isay weinfeld with landscape design by rodrigo oliveira, 111 house features a continuous ring of perimeter planters that filter light and preserve privacy across a four-level são paulo residence.
prefer designboom on google
VERTICAL PLANTERS ENCLOSE FOUR-LEVEL RESIDENCE IN SÃO PAULO
Designed by Isay Weinfeld with landscape architecture by Rodrigo Oliveira, 111 House is a four-level residence in São Paulo, Brazil, created for a family of contemporary art collectors. Positioned on a compact urban plot, the house organizes its footprint along the left site boundary, leaving a lush, full-depth garden strip along the right side. This arrangement allows the primary living spaces, breakfast room, and upper-level bedrooms to open directly onto outdoor greenery, optimizing natural light and cross-ventilation across every level. A rear setback further opens up the lower level, creating a sunken lightwell court that brings illumination into subterranean spaces.
SMALL-FOLIAGE FLORA FILTERS 111 House’s FACADE OPENINGS
The architecture by design studio Isay Weinfeld uses a neutral material palette and clean geometric lines to double as a gallery space for the family’s art collection. Along the northwest elevation, perpendicular concrete wall projections extend outward at varying depths, serving as structural brise-soleil to shade interior spaces from harsh afternoon sun while organizing ground-floor social areas and compartmentalizing upper-floor bedrooms.
Defining the home’s exterior identity is a continuous ring of perimeter planters that wrap every floor slab, extending from the ground-level entryway up to the rooftop terrace and swimming pool. Rather than relying on the broad-leafed tropical flora typical of Brazilian landscapes, landscape designer Rodrigo Oliveira specified wind-resistant, cold-climate species, fine-textured foliage, and varied flowering plants. As the vegetation grows, stems and leaves overflow the planter edges to dissolve the structural concrete boundaries. The layered greenery filters natural light entering the home, softens interior views, and establishes a privacy screen along all four levels without isolating the home from its surroundings.

Israeli police detain 10 people in rare raid against West Bank settlers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
18:05:14 UTC
03:05:14 KST

Israeli police have detained 10 people in a rare raid against settlers, after a weekend of extreme violence in the occupied West Bank including an attack on US photojournalist Heidi Levine, which she described as an “attempted lynching”.
She was knocked down, kicked and beaten by a group of masked Israeli men as she covered the olive harvest in a Palestinian village on Friday. The militants broke four vertebrae and a rip, ripped open her finger so it required surgery and left her with lacerations across her body.
“I was practically, basically lynched by a gang of Jewish settlers in the area of Ramallah,” Levine said, in an interview with the BBC from her hospital bed on Monday.
The day after that assault, Israeli militants armed with sticks and iron bars attacked a group of European diplomats and Palestinians harvesting olives outside the town of Taybeh, assaulting a visiting French mayor, smashing the window of an official car, and causing severe injuries to a young Palestinian man.
The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, questioned the accounts of Israeli militant violence, ignoring extensive video and witness evidence.
He referenced an “alleged attack” on Levine, whose severe injuries were visible in interviews from her hospital bed, and “unproven allegations” the diplomats had been targeted by militants.
The attacks and his response drew a furious international reaction, including from the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee – generally considered a staunch ally of the current Israeli government – European nations and the editor of the Washington Post, Matt Murray.
On Monday morning Israeli police released footage of a rare raid on settlers, and said they had detained 10 people connected with the attacks on foreigners and construction of an illegal outpost.
Hours later a court extended the detention of six men connected with the attacks on foreigners, to between three and four days.
There has been little response to extreme violence against Palestinians across the West Bank, and Levine said the global focus on her attack highlighted extreme double standards.
“People are dealing with this, undergoing attacks, losing property, losing family members, being injured all across the West Bank and nothing is being done,” she said.
Israelis target Palestinians with near total impunity in the occupied West Bank, where arrests are unusual, indictments rare and convictions even more unusual.
Israeli human rights group Yesh Din has documented 561 incidents of settler and soldier violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank over three weeks since 27 September. That is an average of more than 26 each day.
“It is telling that it took attacks on foreign nationals to prompt a significant response from Israeli authorities,” said the group’s executive director, Ziv Stahl. “Palestinians have endured years of systematic settler violence, with 94% of investigations into cases of settler violence against Palestinians closed without indictments.
Levine said her body armour and helmet had prevented even more serious injuries, and she considered herself “lucky” given the ferocity of the attack. Netanyahu’s attempt to cast doubt on the attack felt like a “a big slap on my face”, she added.
Netanyahu’s statements, apparently undermined by security forces arrests days later, were widely seen as an attempt to court far-right voters inside Israel, as the country heads into the final days of an election campaign.
His coalition partners include extremist settlers, who support the campaign of violence that has driven thousands of Palestinians from their homes and land in the occupied West Bank over the last three years.
Haaretz reported on Monday that political pressure was preventing the army from confronting “Jewish terrorism” in the West Bank, even when the targets were foreigners including diplomats and journalists.
Commanders are reluctant to challenge settler leaders, or take action against Israeli civilians and soldiers who attack Palestinians, Israeli defence officials told the paper.
Formal investigations and disciplinary procedures are limited and undermined by unofficial but clear messages of support from top commanders, the report said.
It cited the response to an attack on a CNN crew in March. Central Command chief Maj Gen Avi Bluth suspended the battalion responsible from operational duty and announced disciplinary action against soldiers involved.
Later that night, the brigade commander came to a base where the soldiers were staying to express his support and join them in prayer, Haaretz said.

The protests on the Indian Ocean archipelago began last week over water shortages and the rising cost of living, but violence exploded after a police officer shot and seriously wounded a woman on Saturday.
“The curfew currently in effect will not be extended, effective today,” the office of Prime Minister Navin Ramgoolam said in a statement.
“The last curfew ended at 4:30am on Monday 19 October, and it has not been extended. Roads are open, all schools have reopened with classes running as usual, and daily life is back on track,” the Mauritius Tours tourism operator confirmed on its website.
The unrest saw at least 188 people arrested on charges including looting, arson, damage to police stations, and possession of explosives in the following days.
The police officer who shot the woman in the neck has been arrested and brought to court, authorities said.
The island nation of Mauritius is usually viewed as a model of stability and prosperity in Africa. The last major unrest was in 1999, when a renowned singer died in police custody.
However, the unrest provoked a British government update of its travel advice, which urged people travelling to the popular holiday destination to take care.
“The Government of Mauritius introduced temporary curfews during the evenings and overnight, covering most areas of the main island, which lasted from 12 October to 18 October, ending at 4.30am on Monday 19 October,” the British government said in a statement.
“Stay away from demonstrations and large public gatherings and follow the advice of local authorities,” it warned tourists.

People with darker personalities tend to prefer partners like themselves, study suggests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
18:00:32 UTC
03:00:32 KST

People generally want a romantic partner who is kind and cooperative, yet some individuals are drawn to manipulative personalities and even violent criminals. A new study published in Evolution and Human Behavior suggests that preferences for these dark traits largely track people’s own personalities, with those higher in such traits rating them as more desirable in a partner. The study also found that a hypothetical partner described as manipulative and as having committed physical assault was rated as highly undesirable, and adding fame, wealth, or good looks did not make that person any more appealing.
When people look for a romantic partner, evolutionary biology suggests they should favor prosocial traits like kindness, trustworthiness, and cooperation. These qualities help build stable relationships and help ensure that both partners invest in raising children. Despite this general rule, some people are attracted to antisocial personalities, and at the extreme, to people who have committed serious crimes, a sexual attraction known as hybristophilia.
Public fascination with notorious offenders such as the American serial killer Ted Bundy helped inspire the new investigation. “The idea for this study came from observing the attraction to famous criminals, such as Ted Bundy, who famously received many love letters during his imprisonment,” study lead author Katharina P. da Silva told PsyPost. “This observation led me to question whether there might be an evolutionary basis for being attracted to individuals with socially undesirable traits, given that these traits could bring disadvantages to those who form relationships with them.”
To understand why someone would choose a partner likely to exploit or harm them, psychologists often examine the Dark Triad of personality. The Dark Triad is a cluster of three distinct but overlapping socially offensive traits: narcissism, Machiavellianism, and psychopathy. Narcissism involves grandiosity, entitlement, and a constant need for admiration. Machiavellianism is defined by strategic manipulation, deceit, and a belief that the ends justify the means, while psychopathy is characterized by callousness, impulsivity, and a lack of empathy or remorse.
These traits exist on a spectrum in the general population, meaning people can display everyday, non-clinical levels of selfishness and manipulation without being diagnosed with a personality disorder or committing crimes. Early evolutionary research into these traits suggested they might actually offer an advantage in the dating pool. For instance, a 2008 survey of college students found that men with higher Dark Triad scores tended to have more casual sexual partners and a stronger preference for short-term relationships.
Building on this idea, a 2013 experiment asked women to rate written descriptions of fictional men and found that the Dark Triad personality was rated as more attractive than a regular control personality. However, subsequent research questioned whether dark traits are inherently appealing or if they simply piggyback on other attractive qualities. The new study’s authors refer to this idea as the desirability by-product hypothesis, which proposes that people are not actually drawn to manipulation or cruelty itself, but rather to desirable traits like physical beauty, social status, or wealth that happen to appear alongside a dark personality.
Another competing explanation for the appeal of dark personalities is homogamy, also known as assortative mating, which is the tendency for people to choose partners who are similar to themselves. Under this view, manipulative or callous individuals actively prefer partners who share their worldview and lifestyle. For example, a 2016 study found that women who scored high in narcissism preferred male faces digitally altered to look narcissistic, though this self-similarity effect did not appear for Machiavellianism or psychopathy.
Da Silva, who holds a master’s degree in experimental psychology, developed the research in the Behavior, Evolution and Sexuality Lab at the Institute of Psychology at the University of São Paulo under the supervision of Jaroslava V. Valentova, with whom she and co-author Marco Antonio C. Varella also recently published a book chapter on Dark Triad traits and casual sex across cultures. Now a doctoral student at the Laboratory of Translational and Behavioral Neuroscience at the Federal University of São Paulo, she and her colleagues set out to directly test both homogamy and the desirability by-product hypothesis in a single study.
The researchers wanted to see whether attraction to Dark Triad traits is linked to a person’s own dark traits and risk-taking tendencies, and whether adding fame, wealth, or good looks to a violent criminal profile could make an antisocial partner seem desirable.
The researchers recruited 400 Brazilian adults between the ages of 18 and 60, with an average age of about 28. The sample included 193 women, 176 men, and 31 participants who identified as non-binary, identified as a Latin American trans-feminine identity known as travesti, or chose not to state their gender. Because the non-binary and travesti groups were small, the researchers excluded those 31 individuals from statistical models that specifically tested for gender differences, leaving 369 participants for those specific comparisons.
Participants completed a series of online questionnaires measuring their own personalities and behavioral tendencies. To measure Dark Triad traits, the authors used a 12-item survey called the Dirty Dozen, which asks respondents how much they agree with statements reflecting narcissism, Machiavellianism, and psychopathy on a 1-to-5 scale. Participants also completed an adapted version of this same scale to rate how desirable they found each of those 12 dark traits in a potential romantic partner.
To measure risk-taking and thrill-seeking, the researchers administered two additional questionnaires. One was a 10-item scale assessing sexual sensation-seeking, which measures a person’s desire for novel and varied sexual experiences. The other was the 12-item sensation-seeking portion of an impulsivity questionnaire, which measures the tendency to seek out exciting, risky activities.
For the experimental portion of the study, each participant was randomly assigned to read one of six short written vignettes describing a hypothetical person. The descriptions were kept completely neutral regarding gender, age, and race, and no photographs were used so that physical facial features would not accidentally bias the ratings. After reading their assigned profile, participants rated how willing they would be to enter a casual, short-term relationship and a stable, long-term relationship with that person on a scale from 1 (extremely unwilling) to 7 (extremely willing).
The first vignette served as a prosocial control condition, describing an intelligent, kind, and helpful person who enjoys teamwork and cares about how their actions affect others. The second vignette described a person with Dark Triad traits but no criminal record, portraying them as calculating, persuasive, and willing to do whatever it takes to get ahead because they believe the ends justify the means. The third vignette used this exact same Dark Triad description but added that the person had committed the crime of physical assault.
The remaining three vignettes tested the by-product hypothesis by pairing the Dark Triad and physical assault profile with a major desirable attribute. In the fourth scenario, the assault gained media attention, and the person became famous with a large social media following. In the fifth scenario, the person was described as wealthy and of high social status, able to post bail after the assault arrest. In the sixth scenario, the person was described as extremely physically attractive, drawing media focus for their good looks after being sent to jail for the assault.
When analyzing the personality questionnaires, the researchers found evidence consistent with the homogamy hypothesis. Across the board, participants who scored higher on Dark Triad traits rated those same traits as more desirable in a romantic partner. People’s own scores correlated with their preference for the same trait at about 0.59 for Machiavellianism, 0.66 for psychopathy, and 0.69 for narcissism, on a scale where 1 is a perfect relationship. Even when controlling for gender, sexual sensation-seeking, and thrill-seeking in a combined statistical model, a person’s own levels of Machiavellianism, psychopathy, and narcissism remained the primary predictors of their preference for those respective traits in a mate.
While sexual sensation-seeking and thrill-seeking were weakly linked to dark trait preferences in simple one-to-one comparisons, their influence disappeared once the participants’ own Dark Triad scores were accounted for. This suggests that thrill-seeking does not explain preferences for dark traits beyond its overlap with people’s own dark traits. As a further check, the researchers compared each participant’s preferences with the self-ratings of randomly paired participants and found that people’s preferences sat closer to their own scores than chance pairings would predict.
These findings align with research covered by PsyPost in October 2024, which examined real-world romantic couples rather than ratings of hypothetical profiles and similarly found that partners tend to share similar levels of Machiavellianism, narcissism, and psychopathy. The results are also consistent with a study covered by PsyPost in August 2024, which evaluated real-world couples and found that people with dark personalities feel more satisfied in relationships when their partners share similar levels of psychopathy and narcissism.
“It is worth noting that, to the best of our knowledge, this is the first evidence of assortative mating for antisocial traits in a Brazilian sample,” da Silva noted. “We hope these findings encourage further investigation into the underlying factors driving such attraction in Latin American populations.”
In the experimental vignette portion of the study, the desirability by-product hypothesis was not supported. On the 1-to-7 willingness scale, the kind, prosocial control profile received an average rating of 5.92, making it by far the most desirable option. When the profile switched to a calculating Dark Triad personality without a criminal record, average willingness to date the person dropped sharply to 2.40.
“The main takeaway is that, despite evidence showing some attraction to antisocial traits and criminal individuals, prosociality still remains a far more desirable trait in the context of mate choice,” da Silva explained.
Adding a history of physical assault caused desirability to fall even further, down to an average rating of 1.52. Pairing that profile with fame, wealth, or extreme physical attractiveness did not improve its appeal. The famous criminal received an average score of 1.46, the wealthy criminal scored 1.49, and the physically attractive criminal scored 1.60, none of which were statistically different from the plain criminal profile.
“Given the extensive literature supporting attraction to traits such as fame, high socioeconomic status, and physical attractiveness, it was an interesting surprise when the byproduct hypothesis was not confirmed,” da Silva said. “However, this finding suggests that the effect of antisocial traits combined specifically with the crime of physical assault may have acted as a dealbreaker, that is, a negative trait in a potential partner that carries more weight in attraction than any positive characteristics presented by them.”
The researchers also looked at whether these preferences changed depending on whether the relationship was casual or long-term. Overall, participants expressed slightly higher willingness to engage in short-term relationships than long-term ones across all profiles, and men gave slightly higher willingness ratings than women for short-term dating. Contrary to the authors’ expectations, however, the dark and criminal profiles gained no special advantage in the casual context; the gap between them and the prosocial profile was similar for flings and for stable relationships.
This general rejection of dark personalities is in line with a study covered by PsyPost in February 2025, which also used written vignettes of hypothetical partners and found that people generally prefer low levels of Dark Triad traits for both short-term and long-term dating. The results also differ from the 2013 experiment described earlier, in which women rated a fictional man with Dark Triad traits as more attractive than a control character. Similarly, the new findings stand in tension with a 2016 speed-dating study covered by PsyPost, which found that narcissism and psychopathy were linked to greater short-term dating success. That study involved real face-to-face meetings rather than written profiles, and in person, charm and body language might mask a person’s underlying manipulation.
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider when interpreting these findings. In the personality survey, most participants rated themselves and their ideal partners very low on the Dark Triad scale, clustering near the bottom of the 1-to-5 range. For example, average self-ratings were 1.62 for Machiavellianism, 1.58 for psychopathy, and 2.45 for narcissism, which creates a “floor effect” where the lack of high scores can artificially inflate the statistical similarity between self-ratings and partner preferences. The homogamy results also reflect stated preferences rather than the partners people actually choose.
There are also a few methodological details to keep in mind regarding the online survey tools and vignettes. The researchers noted that the brief 12-item Dirty Dozen scale had slightly weaker internal consistency for Machiavellianism and psychopathy than is ideal, and the survey did not include attention-check questions to weed out distracted readers.
The researchers also did not check whether participants saw the added fame, wealth, and looks as desirable, or whether they viewed the assault as equally serious across profiles. In addition, using written descriptions of beauty, wealth, and fame may not trigger the same automatic emotional reactions as seeing an actual photograph of a gorgeous person or interacting with someone of high status in real life.
The specific crime chosen for the vignettes, physical assault, may also help explain why the desirable traits failed to make the criminal profiles appealing, since violence may signal a direct threat to a partner’s safety. In addition, every profile with fame, wealth, or good looks also described an assault, so the study could not test whether those attributes would make a manipulative but law-abiding partner more appealing. Those profiles were also rated near the bottom of the scale, leaving little room to detect any improvement. Future studies could test whether non-violent offenses, such as financial fraud or white-collar crime, are more easily forgiven when a potential partner is wealthy, famous, or good-looking.
Finally, the study relied on a convenience sample of Brazilian internet users. Even though Brazil has high rates of violent crime overall, the participants were more educated than the general population and were recruited mainly through university channels and social media, so they may not reflect people in settings where crime is more common.
“It’s important to say that the use of a convenience sample may have limited the representation of individuals who are attracted to partners with criminal records, as this preference is likely rare in the general population,” da Silva added. “This could have diluted the observed effects of criminal behavior on mate preferences. Additionally, it is essential to remember that our research was performed in a Brazilian sample, and that no single sample can represent humanity. Also, this reinforces why it is so important to do research on diverse, ‘in-between’ populations such as ours, which are unfortunately still underrepresented in the literature, building a more robust evolutionary psychological science.”
Looking ahead, the researchers hope to explore whether these mating preferences shift in different social environments where aggressive, dominant behavior might be viewed by some as a practical form of protection or resource acquisition. “Future research could benefit from employing targeted sampling strategies (e.g., in high-crime areas or specific subcultures) to test whether the observed mechanisms are amplified in ecologies where the cost-benefit ratio of criminality is altered,” da Silva said.
The study, “Dark side of mate choice: homogamy drives attraction to dark triad, but desirability of antisocial traits and criminal behavior is not enhanced by fame, wealth, or looks,” was authored by Katharina P. da Silva, Bruno H. Amaral, Marco Antonio C. Varella, and Jaroslava V. Valentova.

The dark forces driving discontent across the developed world
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

analysis
The dark forces driving discontent across the developed world
Disillusion is rapidly turning to discontent and open conflict.
Over the weekend, demonstrators took to the streets across France, Spain, Portugal, Italy and Belgium, battling police, torching public buildings and looting shops.
The scenes have mirrored events on the other side of the Atlantic, as the political chasm dividing America has grown, with outbursts of public anger against authorities gaining momentum.
Across the developed world, including here in Australia, political momentum has shifted from the centre to the fringes in an increasingly bipolar world that, if it continues, ultimately will render any attempt at consensus futile.
Populist leaders, experts at whipping up fury for personal gain, are in the ascendancy despite offering little in the way of solutions.
While the catalysts in each country may differ, the root cause largely is the same: the economy.
The compact — the unwritten agreement — between workers and the democratic state is fraying.
Lower- and middle-income workers feel they're going backwards. And they're not imagining it.
Wages have not kept pace with inflation as asset prices have soared. Property ownership in many Western nations is almost out of reach of ordinary workers while rents have skyrocketed.
That has concentrated wealth in an increasingly smaller cohort of wealthy households.
The "cost-of-living crisis" has become a transnational phenomenon.
And as prices continue to surge, central banks have responded in unison by raising interest rates, piling further pressure on those already most affected.
The cost of inequality is beginning to manifest itself.
Why you feel poor
Here's a snapshot of why workers are angry.
If you take inflation into account, Australian incomes are back to where they were in 2011.
There was the post-pandemic inflation hangover piled on top of Russia's invasion of Ukraine, which sent energy prices into orbit, that's now been followed by America's war in Iran.
The combination has not just obliterated income growth. It has sent it into reverse.
It's a story writ large across the Western world.
Just how intractable the problem has become is on full display right here at home.
The opposition and a large posse of economic commentators point to federal government spending. It's firing up inflation, they argue, and driving interest rates higher.
That's not entirely true. For a start, there are huge global forces at work. But let's look at the domestic situation.
Spending alone isn't the problem. It is the imbalance between tax revenue and spending. There's not enough tax to pay for all that spending, and the shortfall, the deficit, must be funded by debt.
There are two levers you can pull here. One is raising taxes, which no-one will ever support. And the other is cutting spending, which no-one will ever support.
From 2013 to the pandemic, Australia, a resource-exporting nation, ran up deficits during the greatest resources boom in history.
The government of the day decided to throw away a resources tax, a decision that has cost the country dearly.
And to this day, we continue to sell our resources, charging a fraction of the taxes other nations apply.
In the meantime, lobbyists continually agitate for cuts to income and company taxes, even as we stare into the abyss of ongoing deficits.
Their universal fix is to raise the Goods and Services Tax, which, if you hadn't already guessed, hits low- and middle-income earners the hardest.
Remember the three-stage income tax cuts, the ones that really benefited higher-income earners?
Apparently, they were going to be self-funding. They were going to generate so much economic activity that the cuts would increase government revenue.
Instead, they've created a structural imbalance in our federal finances.
And whenever the idea of spending cuts is raised, there is an almighty burst of outrage.
Just ask Joe Hockey. His 2014 federal budget was howled down.
This year's budget, meanwhile, targeted welfare payments to the wealthy, which, given our circumstances, should have been a no-brainer.
The hugely generous discounts to capital gains tax and the loophole created by negative gearing were wound back, along with a tightening of the generous tax arrangements surrounding family trusts.
Five months later, and the outcry against the changes continues.
Tax concessions may not seem like spending, but, in essence, they are. That's because they cost the budget as revenue is foregone while the benefits accrue to a targeted cohort.
Other taxpayers, paying the full rate, end up subsidising the beneficiaries.
And it is wealthier households that overwhelmingly benefit from those concessions.
Loading
The Trump legacy: higher interest rates
Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) governor Michele Bullock has confirmed what many of us feared.
Higher interest rates are here to stay.
"I don't know if this particular level is the new normal, but what I do know is that we're not going back down to interest rates of zero or very close to zero, policy rates of that," she said after the RBA rate hike this month.
Inflation is no longer an Australian-only concern. It's rising across the developed world.
The US Federal Reserve has already raised rates once this year and, after hotter-than-expected inflation stats this month, could go again before Christmas.
In the past few weeks, bond markets have pushed interest rates on longer-term US government debt dramatically higher as concerns about US government debt continue to rattle investors.
Tax cuts for the wealthy, under Donald Trump's Big Beautiful Bill, coupled with huge outlays for the war in Iran, have sent US debt into orbit.
As you can see below, America's debt-to-GDP is now at 126 per cent, far higher than during World War II.
The interest bill on that debt is now the second-biggest expense in the US Budget and outstrips defence spending. With soaring US bond rates, that bill is now becoming ever more expensive.
As a much smaller nation that imports capital for investment, longer-term Australian government debt rates have soared alongside the greenback.
Add in the trillions of dollars earmarked for artificial intelligence investment over the next few years, and the global demand for debt funding is likely to keep interest rates elevated for years.
Higher inflation and higher interest bills eat into worker salaries.
When did the rot set in?
Some point to the global financial crisis (GFC).
Governments and central banks bailed out the culprits while workers were left to fend for themselves.
What followed was mass unemployment and an acceleration of the globalisation trends that sent much of the world's manufacturing industries to China.
Inflation all but disappeared and interest rates, in what now appears to be an aberration, plummeted.
Stock markets boomed and real estate soared, giving a false impression of rapidly rising national wealth across the Western world. The gap between the have-mores and the have-nots grew ever wider but was largely ignored.
But the GFC was merely a flashpoint when the tectonic forces that had been building for years finally snapped.
For decades, the great economic experiment of the 80s appeared a resounding success.
Reagan and Thatcher pushed through financial deregulation and allowed market forces to dominate, liberated debt markets, allowed trade to flow freely, increased wealth and raised living standards across the globe.
There was a dogmatic application of the theory of free markets and globalisation as detractors were denigrated and discarded.
For more than 30 years, it seemed to work, until it all blew up.
But even then, it appears we only paid attention to one side of the Yin and Yang of an economic revolution.
And now the costs are mounting.

Stamp duty is hundreds of years old and removing it could boost home ownership
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

Stamp duty is one the oldest taxes and removing it could boost home ownership
Whether it is bidding at an auction or buying at a private sale, most people purchasing property in Australia will pay one of the world's oldest taxes, stamp duty.
But research suggests shifting away from the more than 300-year-old tax on property transactions could ease housing affordability and help boost economic activity.
Across the country, all jurisdictions have stamp duty, with only the ACT planning to phase the tax out over a 20-year period.
e61 Institute economist Nick Garvin said stamp duty was not a neutral tax because it dis-incentivised people from moving.
"An ideal tax is one that is neutral in the incentives that it generates. So basically it doesn't change people's behaviour," Dr Garvin said.
Removing stamp duty could increase home ownership
According to research from the e61 Institute, stamp duty has a direct impact on housing transactions.
The research found that after Queensland increased stamp duty in 2011 by about one percentage point, housing purchases declined.
It estimated removing stamp duty in New South Wales could result in about 100,000 more home purchases per year, while in Victoria it could be about 90,000.
Dr Garvin said a solution would be to move to an ongoing land value tax because it was difficult to dodge and it did not affect people's behaviour, unlike stamp duty.
A 2022 NSW Treasury report found replacing stamp duty with a land value tax could increase home ownership in the state by about 6.6 per cent in the long term.
"If people want to own a home or own the land that a business is built on, there's no way to avoid paying the tax,"
he said.
"Another benefit is it generates less volatility in government revenue. It's kind of more a steady ongoing payment by each owner, so government revenue is more predictable."
How does Australia compare to other places?
Across the ditch, New Zealand does not charge stamp duty; however, its GST is higher at 15 per cent, compared with Australia's 10 per cent.
Grattan Institute housing expert Matthew Bowes said it could be one factor that explained why planning reform in New Zealand had facilitated more townhouse and apartment building.
"They don't have a tax on people moving into new homes that we have here," Mr Bowes said.
"I think it is part of what clogs up our housing market and stops people taking up these opportunities created by the planning reforms we've seen in Melbourne and Sydney."
The United States has a similar tax to stamp duty called mortgage tax in eight states, and a "mansion tax" in seven states which only affects properties sold above a certain price. Neighbouring Canada has a land transfer tax, which is similar to stamp duty.
The United Kingdom's Conservative Party has committed to abolishing stamp duty on the primary home.
"So this is my guarantee: no stamp duty when you buy your home," Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has said.
But the UK does not regularly update its housing valuations, so introducing an ongoing land tax would be difficult, according to London School of Economics housing expert Kath Scanlon.
Under the Conservative policy, the revenue lost by abolishing stamp duty would be mitigated by making cuts to spending, something Ms Scanlon cautioned against.
"Abolition of stamp duty would definitely stimulate the housing market, but there are good reasons for having some taxation of property, if well designed," she said.
The only place in Australia planning to abolish stamp duty
In 2012, the ACT government announced a series of tax reforms including plans to replace stamp duty with a land value tax over a 20-year period, and in July it abolished it for first home buyers.
Researchers from Victoria University found changes the government had made since 2012 to being phasing out the tax had raised economic activity by about 80 per cent, and also increased property transactions in the ACT.
They also found that in the 2022-23 financial year, people in Victoria paid $12 billion to move homes, with $9 billion going to stamp duty.
It meant Victorians moving house paid an effective tax rate of 300 per cent, which added $40,000 to the cost of purchasing an average home.
Mr Bowes said a universal land value tax was better for the economy because it incentivised the development of under-utilised land.
"If there's valuable land people are sitting on, making them pay a tax for sitting on it increases the probability places [with] good land that should be used are developed," he said.
But Mr Bowes said despite the advantages, a land tax could be seen as less politically popular.
"In the context of that purchase, spending $50,000 or whatever large amount on stamp duty doesn't feel as costly as, say, getting a rates notice for a similar amount over a couple of years," he said.
"So the challenge is that it's incredibly convenient for governments to tax us at a point in time when we are prepared to spend the money, even if that has downsides in terms of its economic implications."

While Australia scrambled for fuel, millions of litres were being exported offshore
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

While fuel pumps ran dry, Australia sold megalitres of homegrown fuel overseas
In short:
Australia has about three days' worth of readily available fuel supply made from ethanol, sugarcane and other biofuels, but the vast majority is sold overseas.
The newly formed Biofuel Producers Alliance says a mandate on fuel importers and refiners could shore up Australia's fuel stocks, buffer against price shocks and support Australian farmers.
What's next?
The federal government is consulting on whether to create a "volumetric mandate" that would require fuel companies to buy Australian-made fuels.
Australia is exporting tens of millions of litres of biofuels that could instead add at least three days of supply to the nation's petrol and diesel stocks.
Petrol prices have risen again to an average $2.42 per litre as the war in Iran drags on longer than anticipated.
There are fresh concerns about Australia's vulnerable fuel stocks heading into the summer holidays, as the United States mulls a ban on diesel exports.
Australia currently holds 41 days of petrol supply and 33 days of diesel, more than when the Iran war began because of emergency measures imposed earlier in the year, but still well below the international requirement to hold 90 days of supply.
With the country's fuel security vulnerabilities exposed, the government is looking at whether to force petroleum companies to buy Australian-made fuels that are being sold overseas to help buffer the country from price and supply shocks.
Australian fuel being sold overseas instead
A new alliance of Australian biofuel producers has formed to encourage the federal government to require the major petroleum importers and refiners to buy Australian biofuels, made from the waste by-products of wheat, sugarcane, cooking oils and other farming feedstock.
The Biofuel Producers Alliance, made up of Manildra Group, Wilmar Sugar and three biodiesel companies, already has about 470 megalitres of ethanol and biodiesel capacity, which amounts to about three days' extra supply.
But in the first six months of the year, when Australia was scrounging for additional fuel, more than 60 megalitres produced in Australia was sent overseas because there is little demand from petroleum importers and refiners to buy Australian biofuels.
"When we were sitting in March and April, and all of this was unfolding, E10 was one of the first fuels to drop out in service stations, and at the same time we shipped out 24 million litres of ethanol to South-East Asia, Korea and other places for them to use with their cars," Biofuel Producers Alliance chief executive Matt Hobbs said.
"At a time of a fuel crisis, we ignored fuel that we made here and instead sent it to other countries."
Mr Hobbs said if the federal government introduced a national biofuel blending requirement from 2027, it could shore up stocks and ease the pain at the bowser by several cents a litre during price shocks.
"It's good for consumers because you have got good supply, it doesn't go on a boat. Fuel made in Australia should be used in Australia, and not shipped overseas."
The federal government is consulting on whether to make fuel companies purchase low carbon liquid fuels, including biofuels, which it acknowledges may be the only pathway to reducing CO2 emissions for some current fuel uses, including in aviation.
The government's consultation paper proposes introducing a "volumetric mandate" that would begin in 2029, requiring certain amounts of alternative fuels to be supplied or acquired in order to create demand and support domestic fuel production.
Once the sector has been established, after 2035 the requirement would shift to require more efficient fuels based on carbon intensity, rather than prescribing specific fuel types and amounts.
The Biofuel Producers Alliance said there was capacity for a mandate to begin now and quickly soften fuel pressures, rather than waiting until 2029.
The Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (ACCI) said Australia's current project pipeline could potentially support 2 billion litres of domestic low-carbon fuel production, and as much as a fifth of the country's fuel imports could be replaced with domestic production by 2040 with further investment in fuel refining.
However, the ACCI said the government should not impose demand-side measures to develop the sector, but rather give temporary assistance.
"Broader demand-side market obligations should only proceed where it is proven that sufficient fuel is available at a competitive price and … that the market, infrastructure and compliance systems are ready," the business group said in its submission to the government.
The ACCI said that as the vehicle fleet electrified, any policy should be increasingly focused on hard-to-abate sectors including aviation, heavy freight, mining and defence.
The Australian Institute of Petroleum, whose members include Ampol, BP, Mobil Oil and Viva Energy, said in August it supported policies to stimulate demand for low-emission fuels.
"AIP members have long been advocating that low-carbon liquid fuels, such as renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel, can substantially cut emissions from hard-to-abate sectors such as heavy transport, agriculture and mining," chief executive Malcolm Roberts said.
"Fuel suppliers have robust international supply chains which have ensured continued supply to Australia despite the Middle East crisis. Local refining and in-country fuel reserves also strengthen our fuel security."
Iran war fuel crisis 'proved' demand failure
More than 60 countries have mandates requiring petroleum companies to purchase biofuels, including the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, European Union nations and Singapore.
The alliance said Australia was exporting nearly 80 per cent of its cooking oil and canola, mainly to Europe and Asia, where it was refined into renewable diesel and aviation fuel and then sold back into markets, including to Australia.
Just 0.1 per cent of Australia's diesel last year came from biodiesel, 1/50th of the rate consumed in the US and EU where there are established local biodiesel industries using by-products of soybean oil, animal fats and other goods.
But Mr Hobbs said when the fuel crisis began in February and fuel prices skyrocketed, ethanol-blended petrol recorded its weakest month since 2010 outside of the pandemic.
He said the four major fuel companies in Australia did not have commercial reasons to buy Australian biofuels, since they were vertically integrated and it was financially advantageous for them to buy their own supplies.
"There's great opportunity with current facilities to expand supply, and for farmers and others to get good prices for their commodities … at a good price for consumers," Mr Hobbs said.
In August, the Manufacturing Workers' Union, Australian Workers' Union, National Farmers' Federation, and grain and sugar farmers jointly wrote to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese advocating for a national ethanol and biodiesel mandate.
