I am an Israeli rabbi. I cannot stay silent about settler violence - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

This week in the West Bank was brutal. It was also, in many ways, a regular week.
On October 16, Palestinian farmers in Abu Falah were attacked by Israeli settlers while harvesting olives. Trees were burned, residents were assaulted, and Heidi Levine, an American Jewish photojournalist for The Washington Post, was beaten so severely that she required hospitalization and surgery. She was wearing a vest clearly marked PRESS. She was there to document the violence. She became one of its victims.
The following day, European diplomats visiting the Palestinian village of Taybeh to express solidarity with its residents and olive harvest were reportedly attacked as well.
These incidents are horrifying. But what should frighten us even more is how ordinary such violence has become.
Settler violence against Palestinians does not begin with the olive harvest, and it does not end when the harvest is over. It is a recurring reality across the West Bank: farmers threatened on their land, families living under intimidation, property damaged or destroyed, and people struggling to carry on with ordinary life without fear.
The olive harvest brings volunteers, journalists, and international attention to some of these incidents. It does not create the underlying violence. It exposes a reality that too often remains invisible to Israeli society.
Those responsible must be held accountable. Their actions, however, must not be used to assign collective blame to the wider Jewish population living in the West Bank. Accountability requires identifying and confronting perpetrators, not condemning an entire community.
Confronting violence against Palestinians
As an Israeli rabbi and co-chair of Rabbis for Human Rights, I encounter this reality not as an abstract political debate but as a moral challenge. I cannot accept that violence against Palestinians has become routine.
On October 16, Rabbi Dov Lior, the former chief rabbi of Kiryat Arba, issued a halachic ruling permitting Jews to harvest olives from Palestinian-owned groves. He argued that Palestinian farmers who had been unable to access their crops had already received sufficient benefit from previous years when they could harvest them. He further argued that taking the olives would demonstrate Jewish ownership of the land and fulfill a religious commandment.
This reasoning turns a farmer’s inability to reach his own trees into a justification for taking his livelihood. The more vulnerable the farmer becomes, the easier it supposedly becomes to dispossess him.
A religious ruling cannot turn theft into a mitzvah.
The Torah is explicit: “You shall not steal” (Leviticus 19:11), and “You shall not rob your neighbor” (Leviticus 19:13). These commandments do not come with an exception for national or religious aspirations. Nor can we separate property rights from the dignity of the person whose property is being taken.
Lior’s ruling rests on the assertion that the Land of Israel belongs to the Jewish people and that Palestinians therefore have no legitimate claim to it. But Jewish tradition does not speak with one voice in support of this position. The Tzohar rabbinic organization rejected the ruling, emphasizing that theft is forbidden whether the victim is Jewish or non-Jewish.
Genesis 1:27 teaches that every human being is created b’tzelem Elohim, in the image of God. In Bereshit Rabbah 24:7, Rabbi Tanhuma further emphasizes the dignity inherent in that image. No one loses that dignity because they are Palestinian, Muslim, or belong to a people with whom we are in conflict.
The sanctity of those who live on the land
As a rabbi, I cannot accept an interpretation of Judaism that invokes the sanctity of the land while disregarding the sanctity of the people who live on it.
For Palestinian families, olive trees represent far more than an agricultural resource. They connect generations to the land, sustain livelihoods, and preserve family traditions. Yet farmers across the West Bank face intimidation, assaults, burned trees, stolen crops, and obstacles to accessing their groves.
Levine’s beating makes this reality impossible to ignore. Her press identification did not protect her. We should be asking why Palestinian farmers need protection simply to harvest their own olives – and why journalists documenting attacks on them are themselves at risk.
At Rabbis for Human Rights, we organize volunteers to accompany Palestinian farmers during the harvest. We arrive early in the morning and stand alongside families who should never have to depend on our presence to exercise their basic rights. We call ourselves a human wall. We cannot guarantee every farmer’s safety, but we can refuse to abandon people facing intimidation.
Our presence is essential, but it also exposes the limits of what volunteers can accomplish. We cannot substitute for a state that has a duty to protect the people living under its control.
The Israeli government must ensure safe access to agricultural land, prevent attacks, investigate allegations, and hold perpetrators accountable. Condemnations alone are not enough.
I understand the fear and grief that have shaped Israeli society since October 7. I understand the insecurity many Israelis experience and the desire to protect our communities. But trauma cannot become a license to inflict suffering on others. Our pain does not erase Palestinian suffering. Our attachment to this land does not cancel someone else’s attachment to it.
I do this work because I love Israel. The Jewish people’s historical connection to this land carries responsibilities as well as rights. If we speak of being a light unto the nations, we must hold ourselves accountable to the moral standards we proclaim.
Neither Israelis nor Palestinians are going anywhere. We share this land, and we must find a way to live here together in peace. That peace must be built on dignity, justice, and equality for all – not on fear, dispossession, or the denial of another people’s rights.
I want to live in a country where Palestinian farmers can walk to their olive trees without fear, where violence is met with accountability, and where every person enjoys equal rights and protection under the law.
This is not a dream separate from our Jewish tradition. It is a demand that emerges from its deepest teachings. Our task is not simply to claim this land but to help build a society in which everyone who lives here can flourish.
That is the Israel I love – and the future I will continue to work for.
The writer is co-chair of Rabbis for Human Rights.

What will Russia and the world look like in 2038? For Meduza’s 12th anniversary, we asked 12 people to share their hopes and predictions.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
17:58:32 UTC
02:58:32 KST

What will Russia and the world look like in 2038? For Meduza’s 12th anniversary, we asked 12 people to share their hopes and predictions.
Meduza is 12! When we were just starting out in 2014, the world was a very different place — no COVID, no President Trump, no mass exodus of Russians. Russia’s war against Ukraine had already begun, though, and of course there was Putin (who had been in power long before that). What will the world and Russia be like in 12 years? And what would you like them to be like? We put these questions to 12 people we trust.
Galina Timchenko, Meduza co-founder and publisher
The honest answer to this question sounds pretty harsh, but what can you do: “I don’t know.” No, it’s worse than that: “Nobody knows.”
There are too many variables, too many forks in the road. We’re still managing a precarious balancing act, but the risk of tumbling into catastrophe is greater than ever. Some things are obvious, like the AI “big bang”; others are less so, like the “rightward turn” in many countries.
Making predictions is a thankless business. My only hope is that in 12 years, no one will remember them.
As for what I’d like the world to be like in 12 years, John Lennon put it best in his famous song “Imagine.”
Boris Grebenshchikov, musician
Fortunately, I cannot see the future at all, and I wouldn’t want to, because it depends on how we act now. We can only act authentically by listening to our hearts. Knowing the future would keep us from acting sincerely, as our hearts tell us to.
Lyubov Sobol, politician
I see Russia as a wonderful country. Without wars. Without restrictions. With leaders elected by its own citizens, working to make people’s lives better: so they can live happily, grow, work and earn a living, raise children, and think about the future, rather than struggle to survive in a toxic present. With advanced technology, high-quality healthcare and education, and a commitment to protecting the environment and ensuring everyone’s well-being.
A country that builds partnerships with its neighbors and with countries willing to work with us. Without coercion, blackmail, or threats, and to everyone’s benefit. Russia is neither an appendage of the West nor a colony of China. We can learn from other countries’ mistakes and successes while finding our own way. Right now, we’re falling behind in everything, from the AI race to human rights, but why can’t we succeed at both? Russia can be a wonderful country. That’s worth fighting for.
Maria Kolomychenko, journalist at The Bell who researches technology and internet restrictions
It’s hard for me to predict the future more than a decade ahead, but I’ll try. I’ll focus on a subject I’ve covered for years: how governments regulate the internet. I’ll be only too happy if this prediction doesn’t come true =)
Given current trends, I expect the line between how democracies and autocracies regulate the internet to blur by 2038. Experiments with “digital sovereignty,” partial restrictions on minors’ internet access, and surveillance through lawful interception (in other words, the same thing as Russia’s SORM surveillance system) — all of this is already happening in European and other democratic countries. The technologies used to exert control and the arguments for using them increasingly resemble those employed by authoritarian states such as Russia.
As a result, children growing up now and those born in the next few years will probably never know an anonymous, truly free internet — in Russia, and possibly in Europe and the U.S. as well. They’ll learn from books that people once used the internet without having to show ID every time they logged in, and without fearing that every action and every like could be traced back to them.
Artificial intelligence will bring many benefits, but also new problems — and we’re already seeing the first signs. Government agencies responsible for censorship and repression are already trying to incorporate AI into their work. Over the next decade, Russia will probably use it increasingly for mass surveillance of internet users, primarily to automate the analysis of the vast amounts of data collected by SORM and other government systems.
The question is whether Europe will use these technologies the same way Russia does, or whether it will manage to draw a line between security and total surveillance. I don’t have an answer.
Georgy Trishkin, rocket launch analyst and author of the Telegram channel Tekhassky Vestnik (The Texas Herald)
Predicting the future is a thankless task, but let’s assume that in 12 years, high-speed satellite internet will be commonplace and having no internet on a plane will be a thing of the past. Streams of tens of thousands of satellites will be visible in the night sky, and reusable rocket launches will happen daily, if not hourly. Several private and national space stations will replace the International Space Station, but the militarization of space will recall the frenzy of the 1980s.
By then, astronauts from the United States, China and Europe will have landed on the Moon, perhaps joined by Russians or Japanese astronauts taking part in other countries’ missions. And Mars? It will still be inhabited by robots, but scientists on Earth will already be studying samples of its soil. The world will see both the metallic core of a protoplanet and the methane glaciers of Titan, and witness Apophis’s close approach. Both Voyager probes will, sadly, fall silent after a half-century mission. Sightings of passing interstellar objects will become more common, and they’ll continue to fuel conspiracy theories. We’re unlikely to find traces of other life or discover the nature of our own, but as before, we’ll be one step closer. What matters, though, is that the next 12 years, like the last 12, pass without any loss of human life in orbit.
Anton Dolin, film critic
Probably David Lynch’s famous quote: “I’m wearing dark glasses today because I’m seeing the future, and it’s looking very bright.”
Asya Zolnikova, architecture journalist and art historian
According to the U.N., two-thirds of the world’s population will live in cities by the middle of the 21st century. Cities will be even bigger and more crowded, and competition for housing, education, and healthcare will intensify. Everyone has to decide for themselves what to do about that, but it’s certainly something to prepare for.
Now for the second part of the question — what I’d like Russia to be like.
I’ve lived in Moscow all my life and saw the city change for the better in the 2010s. But at the same time, restrictions and repression kept growing. I vividly remember the day in 2012 when members of Pussy Riot were sentenced — I was already working as a news reporter then. The two-year sentence completely threw the newsroom. It was a shock. After work, I went to the Oktyabrskaya subway station, near where I was living at the time, and saw that part of Muzeon Park had reopened after renovations, with landscaping and pavilions unlike anything we’d seen before. I don’t remember whether the ship Bryusov was there yet, but it certainly was a couple of years later, when things in Russia had gotten even worse. I walked along, thinking about that two-year sentence, unable to understand how all of this could exist side by side: the sentence was handed down at Moscow’s Khamovniki District Court, just a couple of kilometers from the park.
I’ve lost some of my idealism since then, but I’d really like beautiful parks and architecture to stop being a consolation or a smokescreen.
Maria Moskaleva, a student who left Russia after being persecuted over an antiwar drawing
Many readers may be hoping to find pure, childlike optimism here — touching visions of a happy future for Russia and a world that still has a chance at a decent, rational future.
But I had to take off my rose-colored glasses long ago. I had to face reality — its cruelty and uncomfortable truths, and the candor that people so rarely show.
It seems to me that Russia has no hope left. There are too few people who care about life itself — and I want to remind you how much that word means. And even that small percentage of people can’t truly change, or even shake, what has taken hold in the country. What hope there is lies with young people capable of clear thinking.
A fascist regime has seized control of Russia. Thousands, hundreds of thousands of shattered lives. Poverty. Wars. Illegally seized territories. But behind all of this, there is one cause that seems to me the most important. How people think.
Not everyone becomes truly human simply by being born. What makes us human is the path we take through life. A path toward the kind of thoughtful reasoning society badly needs. But while this problem has deep historical roots in Russia, things don’t look much better in the rest of the world. Just look around, read the international press, and see what’s happening.
It’s hard for me to imagine how many years, decades, or even centuries will have to pass before Russia can be called a free and democratic country, before tens of thousands of people finally wake up and rise up against the bloodstained regime. That takes a leader.
People no longer understand words whose meanings should be impossible to forget.
Love. Happiness. Goodness.
Without understanding what these words mean, people continue to support bloodshed, their own humiliation, and the destruction of their loved ones’ lives.
The world is changing in complicated ways, but certainly not for the better. Money dictates everything. Too many people in power don’t care about human lives, and that trend can only grow stronger.
I won’t make predictions or guess at the future. But there will never be heaven on earth. There will never be a time of perfect harmony, complete tranquility, happiness and well-being. No. That world doesn’t exist and never will.
And yet the most frightening thing is something else: we’re driving ourselves deeper and deeper into the abyss. Every day. With our actions, words, and thoughts.
We have only ourselves to blame for what happens around us and for the suffering we endure.
And so there’s no point anymore in shouting, “Come to your senses!”
It’s too late.
Though I’d like to believe it isn’t.
Angelina Davydova, environmental journalist
I want to see a more peaceful, calmer world with greater solidarity, where people and governments in different countries work to solve global problems, including climate change, biodiversity loss, plastic pollution, inequality, and treatment for rare diseases.
A world where humanity works across borders on comprehensive solutions to environmental and social problems, while trying to build a new system of economic and social governance that doesn’t deplete resources, pollute the environment, or deepen inequality. A world where people have the resources, energy, opportunities and time to pursue these goals without facing threats to their lives, freedom, or health.
But we probably won’t see such dramatic changes for the better in 12 years. For now, many parts of the world seem to be heading toward destruction instead: International relations and agreements, international organizations, and joint efforts to solve problems are breaking down. Ongoing wars and conflicts, new races for resources, the rise of authoritarianism and other undemocratic forms of government amid political crises in traditional democracies, growing social inequality and divisions within societies, and the lack of real action on global environmental problems are all pushing many parts of the world further toward the destruction of existing political, social, civic, and international structures.
I very much hope that this period of upheaval and destruction, as the world we know disappears, will eventually hit rock bottom, after which countries and regions will try to begin a new era of renewal, joint action, and cooperation. I’d like to see that new world. For now, we can only guess what it might look like.
Dmitry Kuznets, Meduza’s military analyst
The future, as physicists and philosophers tell us, is fundamentally unpredictable. Yet many people try anyway, passing off outcomes they consider likely as certainties. I’m not comfortable making forecasts, but if you insist, I’ll give it a try too.
In a short-term forecast — and 12 years isn’t far off — the likeliest outcomes are those in which the world doesn’t change very much. After all, it’s barely changed in the past 12 years: The Russian army was fighting in Ukraine in 2014, too; Meduza was working out of Latvia, and most of its readers were in Russia.
There are differences, of course. The war between Russia and Ukraine will be over by 2038. But, alas, Russia has already mortgaged its future — in every sense — to fight it, and no “victory,” whatever that word is supposed to mean, will get it out of that debt trap.
We can, of course, hope (or fear) that artificial general intelligence will sweep everything away like a mighty hurricane and let every country and society start with a clean slate. (What’s a 12-year forecast without AI?) But here, too, it’s better to make a cautious prediction: Don’t expect AI to solve all the mysteries of the universe, dramatically increase labor productivity, or wipe out all of humanity and put us all out of work.
AI advances will be adopted fastest in warfare: We’ll almost certainly soon see vast numbers of fully autonomous drones deciding for themselves whether to kill. That will certainly happen before people trust AI to fly commercial airliners or perform other safety-critical tasks.
What the AI industry will take from us is money. In the U.S., capital investment in this sector already exceeds investment in all other industries combined. News organizations are especially vulnerable: Their reporting is already being taken without compensation and delivered to paying users by AI agents. We’ll be sure to discuss all of this on Meduza in 12 years.
Whatever the world is like in 12 years, I hope we’ll still be able to explore it in all its beautiful and terrible diversity. I’d like to believe that efforts to correct globalization’s mistakes won’t lead to closed borders, and that technological progress won’t exclude people from pursuing knowledge.
Apart from that, progress has so far made the world better and more interesting (even if many people disagree), and there’s no reason to think that trend will change by 2038.
Alexey Uvarov, historian
How inevitable a good or bad future seems depends in large part on how we feel at the time. In the fall of 1940, for instance, hundreds of thousands of Londoners endured constant bombing by the Nazi Luftwaffe and later lived to see the Beatles and the Moon landing. How much of that future could they possibly have imagined back in 1940?
The thing is, we’ve grown used to living in a world that’s moving in the “right” direction, a world destined for progress. But for millennia, humanity lived in a different kind of world, including one that saw two world wars, genocides, the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, and the nuclear disasters at Chornobyl and Fukushima. None of these terrible tragedies condemned future generations to eternal suffering, though the suffering of those who lived through these horrors is immeasurable.
Perhaps that’s where our hope lies: Neither the “course of history” nor the “logic of human development” makes progress or self-destruction inevitable. It all depends on us — on people — and recognizing our power to shape events can help restore our faith in the future.
In hindsight, we tend to see many tragic events as inevitable, but in fact nothing is predetermined. So we shouldn’t expect either flying cars or the ashes of a nuclear apocalypse in 2038. It will be a new, changing world, in some ways less balanced and less predictable than ours.
But the question is what we ourselves can do for our future, rather than which direction the world is heading. I believe and hope that the world in 2038 will be a place where everyone takes more responsibility for their own life and future.
Galina Yuzefovich, literary critic
From where we stand today, it’s hard to imagine a bright future, but I’ll try.
By 2038, even if the world hasn’t entirely abandoned the idea of war as a way to resolve differences (that’s too much to hope for), it will at least have entered another long period of relative peace.
Clearly, artificial intelligence isn’t going anywhere (though as a natural-born Luddite and technological pessimist, I wouldn’t mind if it did). But I’m almost certain that agreements setting standards for AI use will be reached before long, so I’m not worried about a machine uprising or a total catastrophe in the job market (including creative work) by 2038.
As for my own field, I think we’ll very soon see intellectualism and serious reading come back into fashion. In fact, that’s already happening, but I see it as a “long-term trend” that won’t run out of steam in 12 years — it will gather strength instead. Society will inevitably celebrate print books, long novels, and the slower pleasures of sustained attention, while Instagram Reels and other “fast” content will become a little embarrassing, like fast food.
I’ll take the liberty of referring readers to John Lennon’s song “Imagine,” which expresses my ideals best, and focus on books. I very much want to believe that by 2038, reading will really be back in fashion — that it will return not just as an activity society approves of (in that sense, it will definitely come back — it’s already coming back), but as something more. That books will once again be at the center of public attention, that people won’t just put them on shelves and take pretty photos of them, but actually read them, discuss them, and share them with one another.
With all the enormous upheavals we’re witnessing, and those we can only foresee for now, this may seem like a trivial detail and wishful thinking on the part of someone who simply loves to read. But I really am convinced that reading is what allows both individuals and humanity as a species to maintain a certain depth and complexity.
Books also foster empathy and provide a foundation for constructive, civil debate — something a genuinely democratic society cannot exist without. In the future I hope to see, reading will matter again — both as an individual pursuit and a shared social activity.

Ukraine war latest: Ukraine evacuates wounded soldier from front line by drone for first time, military says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
17:57:43 UTC
02:57:43 KST

Ukraine war latest: Ukraine evacuates wounded soldier from front line by drone for first time, military says
Key developments on Oct. 19:
- Ukraine evacuates wounded soldier from front line by drone for first time, military says
- Ukraine brings home 23 children from Russian occupation
- Ukraine, Russia nearing agreement on evacuation of civilians from occupied Oleshky, ombudsman says
- 3 waves of Russian missiles slam Kyiv overnight, killing at least 1, injuring 8
- 'Absolute atrocity' — Russian drone strike on park in Kharkiv Oblast kills children
- Russia strikes 28 critical energy facilities across Ukraine in latest wave of attacks, Zelensky says
Ukrainian forces have carried out what they describe as a "first-of-its-kind" aerial evacuation of a wounded soldier directly from a front-line position by drone, the Ukrainian military and defense company Gurzuf Defense announced on Oct. 19.
The operation involved Ukraine's 92nd Separate Assault Brigade, 30th Separate Mechanized Brigade, and 10th Army Corps, along with Ukrainian drone manufacturer Gurzuf Defense.
The Ukrainian military did not disclose the date of the operation or the section of the front line where it took place.
The wounded soldier, serving with the 30th Brigade, had spent nearly 500 days at a front-line position "under constant threat of death." His fellow soldiers maintained contact with him and delivered food, water, ammunition, and medicine by drone, Gurzuf Defense said.
After the soldier suffered a severe injury, evacuating him by ground became impossible because of Russian drone activity in the area and mined terrain. Attempting to reach him on foot or with a ground robotic vehicle, the usual way of evacuating the wounded, would have put the rescue team at risk.
Ukrainian troops used a heavy-lift hexacopter drone, the Heavy Shot Ayudag-6.
The team first delivered special equipment with carabiners to the wounded soldier, then sent the drone equipped with a winch. Guided remotely by fellow soldiers who remained in contact with him, the soldier secured himself to the evacuation system, Gurzuf Defense said, calling the operation an "unprecedented mission."
The drone then transported him to a safer position, where other soldiers met him and arranged further evacuation to a hospital. The mission lasted 1 hour, 14 minutes, and 36 seconds, covering a distance of 62 kilometers (39 miles).
The company said the operation required close monitoring of the airspace and electronic warfare protection throughout the flight. The soldier is now receiving treatment and rehabilitation, and his life is no longer in danger, according to the 30th Separate Mechanized Brigade.
"An extremely complex operation, but a successful one. This is a historic event," "Napalm," a 92nd Brigade programmer who was involved in preparing the operation, said.
"It marks the next stage in the evacuation of the wounded, which we will all eventually reach. Now the serious, systematic work begins to ensure that such missions take place on a regular basis," Napalm added.
Gurzuf Defense co-founder Pavlo Feldblium warned that aerial evacuation should not be treated as a routine practice, citing the risks to wounded soldiers during flight. Each mission would need to be planned individually for the specific circumstances and location, he said.
"Air rescue is a last resort when there is no other way to save a person," Feldblium said.
According to the Ukrainian outlet Ukrainka Pravda, the hexacopter Heavy Shot Ayudag-6's platform has a flight range of up to 25 kilometers (15.5 miles) and an operational altitude of 150–300 meters (500 to 1,000 feet), while the aircraft itself weighs about 98 kilograms (215 pounds) and can carry 70–90 kilograms (150 to 200 pounds).

Ukraine brings home 23 children from Russian occupation
Ukraine has brought home 23 more children from Russian-occupied territory over the past week, the presidential initiative Bring Kids Back UA announced on Oct. 19.
The rescued children are now receiving psychological support and assistance in restoring their Ukrainian documents, Bring Kids Back UA said.
Among the children returned to Ukrainian-controlled territory is 9-year-old Stefan, who was forced to undergo military training at a school under Russian occupation, including instruction in handling grenades and firearms, the statement said.
Another child returned to Ukraine was 13-year-old Polina, who survived a Russian combat drone strike near her home and was later afraid to go outside, the statement said.
Russian troops also raided her home and destroyed communication devices to limit access to information, according to Bring Kids Back UA.
As of September 2026, Ukraine's Justice Ministry has officially confirmed 20,610 cases of deportation and forced transfer of Ukrainian children to Russia.
Ukrainian human rights groups estimate that hundreds of thousands of Ukrainian children are under Russian control, including those who have been deported or forcibly transferred and those who remain in occupied territories and are at risk of deportation.
Ukrainian officials estimate the real figure of abducted children could be far higher. Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets puts the number at up to 150,000, while Presidential Commissioner for Children's Rights Daria Herasymchuk has given a range of 200,000–300,000.
In 2023, the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Russian President Vladimir Putin and Russia's Commissioner for Children's Rights Maria Lvova-Belova for their role in state-sanctioned child abductions.

Ukraine, Russia nearing agreement on evacuation of civilians from occupied Oleshky, ombudsman says
Ukraine and Russia are nearing an agreement on the final details of civilian evacuation from the front-line town of Oleshky and nearby settlements in the Russian-occupied part of Kherson Oblast, Ukrainian Human Rights Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said on Oct. 18.
Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since the early days of the full-scale invasion. Residents face severe shortages of food, water, and electricity, while mined roads, constant drone attacks, and interrogations by Russian troops at checkpoints make safe evacuation virtually impossible.
The two sides are discussing a local ceasefire to allow residents to be evacuated directly to Ukrainian-controlled territory, rather than having to travel first through Russian-occupied areas and then through Russia and Belarus, Lubinets said in an interview with Ukrainian broadcaster Espreso.
"We are making as much progress as possible. We are now moving toward agreeing on the final details to ensure a ceasefire and evacuate everyone ... directly to territory controlled by the Ukrainian government," Lubinets said.
Lubinets did not specify what direct evacuation to Ukrainian territory entails, but one possible option is to transfer civilians across the Dnipro River to the Ukrainian-controlled western bank.
He added that Kyiv has been holding daily negotiations to unblock the humanitarian evacuation and that Moscow has begun considering a proposal Kyiv put forward long ago.
"We still have some difficult issues to resolve, but I hope that in the near future we will all see concrete results from these negotiations," Lubinets said.
No final agreement has been publicly announced, and it remains unclear when an evacuation could begin.
Lubinets said on Sept. 16 that more than 6,000 people possibly remain in Oleshky and the surrounding area, including about 200 children. His office said it had verified 358 people who urgently need assistance to leave safely.

3 waves of Russian missiles slam Kyiv overnight, killing at least 1, injuring 8
At least one person was killed and eight others injured after multiple waves of Russian missiles struck Kyiv overnight on Oct. 19.
Several explosions rocked the capital just before 11 p.m., with further attacks around 3 a.m. and 7 a.m., Kyiv Independent journalists on the ground reported. Ukraine's State Emergency Service (DSNS) said damage was reported in at least three districts.
One person was killed in the Desnianskyi District where a non-residential building caught fire and a metro station was damaged, DSNS said. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko earlier reported a fatality was that of 21-year-old woman.
The above-ground Chernihivska and Lisova metro stations were temporarily closed for repairs, city officials said.
Later on Oct. 19, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said more than 70 workers were repairing the damaged metro infrastructure, with the most difficult work involving power supply and train control systems. Repairs had continued since overnight but were being slowed by air raid alerts, which forced crews to take shelter.
Train service between Lisova and Akademmistechko stations was expected to resume that evening, with trains skipping Chernihivska until repairs were completed, Klitschko added.
Five people were injured in the Solomianskyi District when a 25-story residential building was damaged, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported. It is not yet clear where the other injuries occurred.
The Cosmo Multimall shopping and entertainment center sustained significant damage in the Solomianskyi District. Its administration said no employees were injured and that the mall was working to resume operations as soon as possible. The center did not disclose the extent of the damage or provide a timeline for repairs.

Russia strikes 28 critical energy facilities across Ukraine in latest wave of attacks, Zelensky says
Russian attacks struck 28 substations and other critical energy facilities across Ukraine, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 19, following another wave of missile and drone attacks on the country's energy infrastructure.
At least 550,000 households lost power overnight, Zelensky said, following a coordination meeting on the situation in Ukraine's regions.
Russian forces targeted energy infrastructure in 11 oblasts overnight and on the morning of Oct. 19, First Deputy Energy Minister Artem Nekrasov reported. Additional power outages caused by Russian strikes and ongoing hostilities were reported in four other oblasts.
One energy worker was injured in an attack on an energy facility in Vinnytsia Oblast, Nekrasov said.
Repair crews are working to restore electricity wherever security conditions allow, although prolonged air raid alerts and the threat of renewed Russian strikes are slowing restoration efforts, according to the Energy Ministry.
During the overnight attacks, Russia launched 16 ballistic missiles and more than 200 drones in several waves in what Zelensky described as a "targeted attack on Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast."
Zelensky said Ukraine had "once again" received no advance warning from its partners about the strikes.
Nekrasov said that over the past week, Russia carried out 87 targeted attacks on Ukraine's energy, oil, and gas sectors. Authorities recorded 224 incidents that caused damage to energy, oil, and gas infrastructure during that period.
Russia has carried out 2,147 attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure since July 16, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said in an interview with BBC News Ukrainian published on Oct. 19, citing figures as of Oct. 17.
"Not a single day has passed without attacks on energy infrastructure," Koretskyi said.

Kazakhstan tops FIE men’s team épée world rankings for the first time
The Kazakhstan men’s épée team has reached the No. 1 spot in the International Fencing Federation (FIE) World Rankings for the first time in the country’s history, Qazinform News Agency reports.
The historic milestone follows a run of international titles over the past twelve months, culminating in a gold-medal performance at the 2026/27 FIE World Cup season opener in Casablanca, Morocco.
Kazakhstan's rise to the top of the FIE rankings caps an impressive winning streak. The team secured consecutive gold medals: at the Islamic Solidarity Games in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, in November 2025; the Asian Fencing Championships in New Delhi, India, in June 2026; the World Fencing Championships in Hong Kong in July; and the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, in September.
Long dominated by traditional fencing powerhouses such as France, Italy, Hungary, and Switzerland, as well as Asian heavyweights Japan and South Korea, the men’s team épée rankings are now led by Kazakhstan. Kazakhstan arrived in Casablanca ranked third behind Switzerland and France, but its victory at the Moroccan event pushed the squad past both rivals to take the No. 1 spot.
Kazakhstan achieved the top ranking with a revised lineup featuring Kirill Prokhodov, Vadim Sharlaimov, Alexandr Fedotov, and Kirill Pavlov. En route to the title, the squad defeated France — a 23-time world champion in men's team épée.
Qazinform reported earlier that President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev congratulated Kazakhstan’s men’s épée fencing team on their triumph in Morocco.

Brazil's government says $4 billion budget reshuffle needed for Lula measures in 2027
BRASILIA, Oct 19 - Brazil's Planning Ministry said on Monday that the budget reallocations needed to accommodate measures recently announced by President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva as he seeks re-election in next Sunday's vote amount to about 20 billion reais ($3.95 billion) in the 2027 budget.
In a statement, the ministry said the amount represents just over 1% of total primary expenditure subject to spending limits under Brazil's fiscal framework, adding such adjustments will be made while preserving both the overall spending cap and the government's primary budget target.
• Leftist Lula has unveiled a string of measures ahead of Sunday's runoff after trailing right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro in the first round
• Announcements range from free nationwide weekend public transport, which has yet to be formally submitted to Congress, to a 15% increase in the Bolsa Familia welfare program that is already being implemented
• The government said the Bolsa Familia increase alone would cost 22 billion reais in 2027
• The Planning Ministry did not explain how the budget reallocations required to fund the broader package of measures would amount to less than that
• The ministry said estimates circulating publicly about the total fiscal impact wrongly combine measures with different funding sources and implementation timelines, arguing some policies, such as fuel tax relief, have been offset by higher oil-related revenue
• It added that public policy implementation should not automatically be viewed as election-driven spending REUTERS

MOSCOW, October 19. /TASS/. Researchers from Giredmet company, a member of Rosatom's research division, have developed a technology and organized the production of thallium nitrate, eliminating the domestic electronics industry's reliance on foreign supplies for this critical component, the company’s press service said.

The work was carried out under a government contract with the Russian Ministry of Industry and Trade.

Thallium nitrate is used in various industries, primarily in microelectronics and microwave electronics. It is added to electrolytes for the gold-plating of contacts and microchip components. It is also used in semiconductor manufacturing and the doping of thin films.

The strike came as Saudi Arabia canceled a major international investment conference following repeated Houthi attacks on its territory.

According to a Yemeni military official, the attack occurred as newly recruited soldiers were lining up for a training session. The provincial government warned that the death toll could rise as authorities assessed the casualties.
The Shabwa authorities condemned the strike as a major escalation, saying it had targeted recruits undergoing training and preparation. They called on Yemen's presidential leadership and the Saudi-led coalition to accelerate the deployment of air defense and early warning systems to protect the province against further attacks.
Rashad al-Alimi, chairman of Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council, promised a "firm response," accusing the Houthis of resorting to terrorist attacks when facing military pressure. The rebels acknowledged carrying out the strike, claiming that the camp was operated by Saudi officers and that some had been killed. They provided no evidence to support that assertion, and Saudi authorities did not immediately comment.
The attack marks another escalation in Yemen's civil war, which has intensified since the broader conflict involving Iran began in February. The renewed fighting shattered a ceasefire established in 2022 that had largely halted major hostilities between the Houthis and government forces.
The Houthis, who control Yemen's capital, Sanaa, and much of the country's north, have expanded their military operations in recent weeks, targeting Saudi airports, oil infrastructure and military facilities while also capturing territory along the Red Sea coast near the strategically important Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
On Monday, the rebels claimed to have conducted six additional attacks against Saudi Arabia, including strikes targeting oil facilities, military installations and Riyadh's international airport. They did not specify when the operations occurred. Saudi Civil Defense authorities issued danger alerts, although there were no immediate reports of casualties or damage from those latest claims.
The continuing attacks have begun disrupting major economic events in the kingdom. Saudi Arabia announced Monday that it was canceling an international investment conference scheduled for the following week, which had been expected to attract senior executives from Wall Street and other international financial institutions. The decision underscored the growing consequences of the Houthi campaign for Saudi Arabia's economy and international business activities.
The latest escalation follows a series of deadly incidents inside Yemen. On Sunday, the Houthi-run Health Ministry accused Saudi-led forces of carrying out an airstrike in the rebel-held northern province of Saada that killed at least nine people, including five children and two women. The rebels said additional strikes over the weekend had left more than 30 people dead or wounded. Saudi Arabia did not immediately respond to those allegations.
Saudi Arabia entered Yemen's civil war in 2015 after the Houthis seized Sanaa and large areas of northern Yemen. Riyadh has long viewed the movement's military capabilities and its ties to Iran as a threat to its security. According to U.N. experts, Iran and allied groups in Lebanon and Iraq have provided the Houthis with military expertise, training and advanced weapons, although Tehran denies supplying arms to the rebels.
The conflict has taken on renewed strategic importance as Houthi forces advance near Bab el-Mandeb, a vital maritime chokepoint connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. Earlier this month, the Saudi-led coalition launched a major offensive aimed at removing the rebels from recently captured territory along the coast.
Meanwhile, the U.S. State Department renewed its demand Monday for the release of more than 20 Yemeni employees of the American Embassy in Sanaa, marking five years since their detention by the Houthis. The embassy suspended operations in 2015, but local employees continued providing security and maintenance services. Washington called for their immediate and unconditional release.

====================================================================================================

Will Trump's endorsement enhance Netanyahu's standing in the eyes of Israeli voters? - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
17:51:50 UTC
02:51:50 KST

In June, US President Donald Trump reportedly told Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu he would be in prison if not for him. On Sunday, he told Israelis to give the prime minister another term.
What happened?
How did Trump go from acknowledging that he had called Netanyahu “f**king crazy” during their June conversation to praising him on Truth Social as “strong, brave, and brilliant” and giving him his unequivocal endorsement?
That is one question.
Another is whether this endorsement, the first explicit, written endorsement of this type in the country’s history, will matter.
US presidents have made their preferences in Israeli elections crystal clear before. Usually, however, they have left Israeli voters to connect the dots.
Previous US presidents set precedent for expressing views on Israeli elections
In March 1992, three months before an Israeli election, then-president George H. W. Bush announced that he would not approve $10 billion in long-sought housing loan guarantees to help absorb immigrants from the former Soviet Union unless prime minister Yitzhak Shamir froze settlement construction.
Shamir lost to Yitzhak Rabin, who signed an agreement with Bush for the guarantees two months after his victory. Aaron David Miller, an administration official at the time, later wrote that the perception that Shamir had mismanaged relations with Washington hurt him badly, and that the Bush administration helped orchestrate that perception.
In 1996, president Bill Clinton went to extraordinary lengths to boost Shimon Peres over Netanyahu, later acknowledging as much in a television interview. He also tried to help Ehud Barak stave off defeat at the hands of Ariel Sharon in 2001. Neither effort produced the desired electoral result.
Barack Obama pointedly refused to meet Netanyahu when he came to address Congress in 2015, just weeks before that year’s election. And Joe Biden’s 2022 visit, after another election had been called, gave then-prime minister Yair Lapid an opportunity to look prime ministerial alongside an American president.
Trump's explicit support for Netanyahu deviates from past presidents
So American involvement in Israeli elections is nothing new. What distinguishes Trump’s intervention is how little he has left to interpretation.
In April 2019, Trump helped Netanyahu through policy decisions, foremost among them the recognition of Israeli sovereignty over the Golan Heights. This time, he dispensed with the need for voters to infer his preference from his policies. He endorsed Netanyahu much as he might endorse a favored candidate for Congress.
“Please let this Letter serve to represent my Complete and Total Endorsement of Bibi Netanyahu in his upcoming Race for Re-Election as Prime Minister of Israel,” he wrote. “BIBI NETANYAHU WILL NEVER LET YOU DOWN!”
Blunt? Certainly. Surprising? Given Trump’s previous interventions in Israel’s domestic affairs, less so.
In June 2025, Trump took to Truth Social to demand an end to Netanyahu’s corruption trial, calling it a witch hunt and a travesty, and invoking American military support for Israel in what sounded like a veiled threat.
“It is terrible what they are doing in Israel to Bibi Netanyahu,” he wrote. “The United States of America spends Billions of Dollars a year, far more than on any other nation, protecting and supporting Israel. We are not going to stand for this.”
Sunday’s endorsement also came with a warning. Trump suggested that an Israeli government headed by anyone else could leave the US to confront Iran alone – something he said he was reluctant to do.
“If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work [attack Iran] ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so,” he wrote.
The message went beyond saying that Netanyahu was his preferred candidate. It suggested that the choice Israelis make could affect Washington’s willingness to act against Iran.
That is a considerable weight to place on the Israeli voter.
Trump recently hesitated to endorse Netanyahu
But why intervene now? In a Newsmax interview as recently as Thursday, Trump stopped short of an endorsement and, when asked whether he trusted Netanyahu, said he trusted no one in politics. By Sunday, those reservations were gone.
One explanation is straightforward: Trump always intended to endorse Netanyahu and was waiting for the moment when he thought it would have the greatest impact.
The final stretch before an election is when parties roll out the big guns they were saving for maximum impact. Trump, in campaign terms, is a very big gun.
Netanyahu’s opponents offered less flattering explanations.
Lapid, number two on the B’Yachad list, said in a radio interview that Netanyahu had begged Trump for an endorsement instead of pressing him to act against Iran.
Yashar head Gadi Eisenkot offered his own explanation: Netanyahu had “lied” to Trump about Eisenkot’s willingness to attack Iran. Throughout the campaign, Netanyahu has portrayed Eisenkot as reluctant to take aggressive military action against Hamas, Hezbollah, and Iran.
Another theory being floated is that Trump had seen private polling suggesting Netanyahu was faring considerably better than the public polls indicated. According to this theory – and without access to the polling supposedly driving this decision, it is only a theory – Trump, having backed Viktor Orban’s losing bid in Hungary earlier this year, was reluctant to risk another unsuccessful endorsement. Once persuaded that Netanyahu had a chance to win, he felt comfortable backing him.
Trump-Netanyahu disagreements may remain after endorsement
The endorsement also makes a broader point about the Trump-Netanyahu relationship, which has been marked by growing disagreements and tensions in recent months, as seen in Trump’s expletive-laden June phone call to the prime minister.
The president’s endorsement does not mean that those disagreements have disappeared. It means that, despite them, Trump still prefers Netanyahu to the alternatives. Frustration with a prime minister and support for his reelection are not mutually exclusive.
But Trump’s preference is one thing. The weight Israeli voters give it is another. This brings us to the second question: will his endorsement make a difference at the ballot box?
Is there really a substantial pool of voters in the anti-Netanyahu camp – Yashar or B’Yachad voters, for instance – who will read Trump’s endorsement, suddenly see the light, and switch to Likud?
Unlikely.
Trump’s endorsement might have carried greater weight in March, following the first week of the war with Iran, when Israeli confidence in him was running high. Since then, that confidence has diminished.
The Israel Democracy Institute found that the share of Jewish Israelis who believed Israel’s security was a central consideration for Trump fell from 64% in March to 26% in a survey published in early July.
That measures something different from personal popularity, but it is directly relevant to the argument Trump is now making: that Israelis should take his preference into account when deciding who can best protect them.
Still, converting Netanyahu’s opponents is only one way an endorsement could matter.
Its more plausible effect is within the right-wing camp: reassuring wavering Netanyahu supporters, encouraging them to turn out, or persuading voters considering smaller right-wing parties that Likud is the safest bet for their vote.
It also gives Netanyahu a fresh answer to those questioning his management of Israel’s most important relationship. After months in which the disagreements with Trump were on public display and his opponents charging that he has badly mismanaged Israel’s relations with the US, he can now point to an unequivocal endorsement from the president himself.
The campaign message practically writes itself. Whatever the arguments, whatever the tensions, Netanyahu is still the man Trump wants across the table.
Whether that moves enough votes to change the coalition arithmetic is another matter. American presidents have tried to influence Israeli elections before, only to find the Israeli voters an independent lot determined to reach their own conclusions.
Trump, in his inimitable style, has made his choice clear. The question now is whether Israeli voters will agree that his choice should also be theirs.

Two newly established Syrian state universities specializing in defense and security have barred women from enrolling in most courses, in admission policies condemned as discriminatory by Human Rights Watch (HRW), according to reports and statements from Damascus.
Syria’s Higher Education Ministry announced on September 30 that admission to law, economics and management, and social sciences programs at the National University of Defense Sciences would be restricted to men. At the Syrian University for Security Sciences, women may apply only to cybersecurity programs. Meanwhile, several public universities specializing in kindergarten education, midwifery, and nursing are now admitting only female students.
Applications closed on Monday, and the admission rules are unchanged despite the controversy.
HRW warns of 'concerning pattern' of discrimination
HRW warned that the restrictions violated Syria’s Constitutional Declaration and its international legal obligations, forming part of a “concerning pattern” of state actions restricting women’s roles in Syrian society and reinforcing gender stereotypes.
“Syria’s authorities are rebuilding the army and the security forces without women,” said Hiba Zayadin, senior Syria adviser at HRW. “Women can’t train as officers, and they can’t even study to be the army’s lawyers or administrators. This is discrimination, plain and simple.”
Although the September announcement has sparked international criticism, a former Higher Education Ministry official told Agence France-Presse last month that some gender-based admission policies had long been in place. However, excluding women from defense and security universities is a new development.
Many of the newly established defense universities, including the National University of Defense Sciences, require male students to commit to military service. This requirement does not apply to female students in the limited number of courses open to them.
Women effectively denied pathway to joining army
Human Rights Watch noted that, despite the opening of the Women’s Police Institute, whose first class graduated in September, restrictions on women’s admission to most defense university courses have effectively denied them a pathway into the army.
The exclusion follows an August decision by Syrian authorities to bar members of the Women’s Protection Units (YPJ), the all-female component of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces, from joining the army.
Restrictions extend beyond the defense and security sectors. State technical institutes specializing in oil and gas and railway studies also admit only male applicants.
The new Syrian authorities have also repeatedly raised questions about women’s roles in public life. In December 2024, a government spokesperson suggested that women might be biologically unsuited to certain political roles and said their ability to serve as judges “could be an area of study and research for specialists.” The following month, the governor of Latakia banned female state employees from wearing “excessive” makeup, threatening legal action against those who failed to comply.
“Women are underrepresented in parliament, the police, and some public offices, and are now shut out of the army,” Zayadin said. “The authorities have promised to respect women’s rights, but their actions directly contradict those promises. Women’s full participation, in all roles and sectors, is essential to building a brighter future for Syria.”
Sally Obeid, a founding member of the Syrian Christian Congress, condemned the admission rules on X, insisting that Damascus’s “goal” was “to kill women’s minds, clone Taliban policies, and confiscate Syrian women’s right to seats in engineering and law.”

Global Jewish life profoundly reshaped by impact of Israeli-Palestinian conflict, INSS report shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
17:51:40 UTC
02:51:40 KST

A new report published by the Institute for National Security Studies (INSS) on October 10 contends that the ongoing Israeli-Palestinian conflict has evolved past a localized Middle Eastern affair to profoundly reshape everyday Jewish life across diaspora communities.
The report, titled “No Longer on the Sidelines: How the Israeli-Palestinian Conflict Impacts Diaspora Jews,” was authored by INSS senior researchers Theodore Sasson, a professor at Middlebury College, and Avishay Ben Sasson-Gordis, head of the US-Israel field.
Drawing on six months of discussions between an INSS Joint Working Group and leaders of major Jewish organizations across the US, Canada, France, the UK, and South America, the authors note that local fallout from Israel’s conflict choices makes global Jewry genuine stakeholders in Israeli policy. They have identified four major impacts: normalizing hostility, dividing communities, diminishing political influence, and fueling antisemitism.
The authors explain that hostility toward Israel has normalized across Western societies due to interpretations of the IDF’s conduct in Gaza and the West Bank.
The report highlights that a March 2026 Pew poll showed 60% of Americans view Israel unfavorably, up from 53% in 2025 and 42% in 2022, with 75% of young adults (18-29) holding negative views. Israel’s US standing now mirrors hostile nations like Iran, China, and Russia rather than allies like the UK and Germany.
Controversy over Israel penetrates global politics
Beyond polls, Israel has entered domestic politics via midterm primaries, where left-wing candidates challenge arms sales and AIPAC funding. In Europe, pariah designations have advanced further. UK participants noted that “Israel is South Africa” across cultural institutions, while French participants warned that anti-Zionism risks becoming a cultural norm.
Consequently, Jewish institutions – such as synagogues hosting aliyah sessions, camps hiring IDF veterans, Hillel groups, and BDS-targeted businesses – face intense protests, turning ordinary Jewish life into counter-cultural activity.
The authors examine how the decline in support for the two-state solution in Israel has fractured diaspora communities internally.
For decades, the two-state paradigm allowed diaspora supporters to reconcile backing Israel with democratic values by viewing the “occupation” as temporary. The abandonment of this horizon leaves defenders unequipped to counter outside critics, compounding feelings of alienation.
This alienation, particularly among young adults, intensified alongside relentless media imagery of civilian death and suffering in Gaza and the West Bank, coupled with widespread narratives accusing Israel of intentionally inflicting harm. As one working group participant warned, communities under-informed about Palestinian terror threats and saturated with reports of Israeli transgressions are becoming dangerously alienated from the moral case for Israel.
Public opinion data underscore this trend: a June 2026 AP-NORC survey reported that 24% of American Jews feel “not at all” emotionally attached to Israel, a steady rise from 20% in 2025, 14% in 2020, and 12% in 2013, with 39% of young adults aged 18 to 29 reporting no attachment. The authors’ secondary analysis of the data indicates that low emotional attachment is closely associated with secularism, skepticism regarding the justification of military actions in Gaza, and beliefs that Israel committed genocide.
Growing disagreements over Israel-Hamas war fracture communities
While Jewish organizations continue advocating for Israel, growing dissent has fractured communities, particularly in liberal regions like US blue states and coastal metros, straining central bodies and reducing their capacity to represent the community as a whole.
As the pro-Israel lobby fragments into competing right-wing, centrist, and liberal camps, and some individual synagogues divide, the rise of newly launched non-Zionist and anti-Zionist groups has caused further division and altered the public image of organized Jewish life.
The authors analyze the erosion of diaspora political influence. The absence of a viable political horizon for resolving the conflict, coupled with controversial rhetoric and policies from Israeli figures, has made pro-Israel advocacy exceedingly difficult, forcing diaspora defenders to navigate accusations that supporting Israel contradicts core democratic values.
This weakened leverage is evident internationally. In the US, anti-Israel candidates have won primary races despite heavy AIPAC spending. In Canada, the government has advanced arms embargoes and recognized Palestinian statehood while dismissing communal leaders. In the UK, authorities have pushed forward with West Bank settlement product bans over community objections.
The authors emphasize that this diminished political capacity not only harms Israel’s national security; it also inflicts a heavy toll on diaspora communities themselves. Having invested massive resources into building robust political lobbies, global Jewry now faces an erosion of its broader political power, undermining its ability to advocate effectively for its own local community interests and needs.
Diaspora Jews concerned that Israel backlash contibutes to antisemitism
The report details how the war’s management and rhetoric from senior Israeli officials have provided fuel for antisemitism and heightened anxiety, with a late 2026 Mellman Group survey showing 56% of American Jewish voters deeply concerned that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s actions have worsened antisemitism.
This perception is matched by data; AJC polling shows 93% viewing antisemitism as serious, and ADL audits document steep surges in Israel-related incidents across the US. Left-and-right political polarization has left many American Jews experiencing political homelessness, while skyrocketing security costs force communal organizations to divert critical funds away from Jewish life.
In Canada and the UK, physical violence, including arson, stabbings, and a 2026 Yom Kippur synagogue shooting in Ontario, has accelerated, with protests targeting Jewish neighborhoods and leading some Canadian Jews to consider an “exit strategy.” Meanwhile, in parts of Europe, mounting threats have driven an ongoing process of “marranization,” where Jews feel compelled to conceal their identities to stay safe.
In their analysis, the authors address a core grievance voiced by diaspora leaders: while avoiding harm to Israel has historically been paramount, the Israeli government appears largely unconcerned with how its conflict choices impact diaspora well-being, often undermining international law through damaging ministerial rhetoric, restrictive aid policies, or unchecked settler violence.
The report stresses that the deepest long-term risk stems from the political deadlock over a permanent one-state reality without democratic rights for millions of Palestinians, which alienates Western allies and exhausts community advocacy.
Although domestic Israeli politics and public hardening post-October 7 have sidelined peace frameworks, post-election leadership must weigh broader national security needs, including democratic preservation and global Jewish ties.
While diaspora leaders have traditionally avoided criticizing Israeli policy due to a perceived lack of “skin in the game,” that premise is shattered. And yet, public critique remains intensely sensitive due to fears of aiding adversaries and internal communal divides. Ultimately, the compounding toll of these interlocking dynamics makes the diaspora’s stake in Israel’s strategic decisions undeniable, while hurting Israel’s own soft power and international standing.
INSS researchers urge Israeli officials to avoid divisive rhetoric
The report concludes with a series of concrete recommendations for Israeli policymakers to mitigate the conflict’s local fallout and help restore global advocacy capacity.
The authors urge Israeli leadership to ensure cabinet ministers avoid rhetoric that inflames human rights allegations and to publicly disavow any such statements when made. Furthermore, authorities must crack down on West Bank extremist violence and hold perpetrators accountable.
Politically, Israel must maintain a diplomatic horizon to prevent a slide into a non-democratic single-state reality while proactively communicating its commitment to a viable resolution.
The report also calls for institutional reforms. Israel must establish sustained dialogues with diaspora organizations, build collaborative strategies to improve international standing, and formally integrate systematic reviews within cabinet ministries to evaluate how domestic policy choices impact world Jewry.
The authors noted that the report’s conclusions and recommendations belong solely to the researchers and do not necessarily represent the views of every participating organization.

Syrian textbooks show pan-Arab content replaced by Islamist ideology, IMPACT-se finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
17:51:37 UTC
02:51:37 KST

An in-depth review of 130 Syrian school textbooks implemented under the administration of Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa shows that Baathist, pan-Arabist, and secular governance frameworks have been substantially replaced by Sunni-Muslim identity and political Islamism.
The findings were detailed in a report titled "The New Syria: Education Under al-Sharaa: Review of Syria’s National School Curriculum, 2025–2026," published on Monday by the Institute for Monitoring Peace and Cultural Tolerance in School Education (IMPACT-se), covering the 2025–2026 academic year.
Authored by researchers Matan Perchikov, Itam Shalev, and Yonatan Negev, PhD, the report systematically analyzed thousands of textbook pages across Grades 1-12. The researchers applied content and discourse analysis using UNESCO-derived standards for peace and tolerance, comparing current textbooks side by side with earlier editions from 2017-2018 or 2011-2012 to trace specific alterations, omissions, and updates.
The report maps out a structural transformation in how national identity is framed, substituting secular Syrian patriotism and pan-Arab nationalism with broad pan-Islamist and religious constructs. Local loyalty to the national homeland is consistently subordinated to the broader transnational Muslim community, while traditional celebrations of Arab nationalism are replaced by an emphasis on Islamic civilization.
Historical narratives have been revised to reflect this theological reorientation, with seminal events such as the Great Arab Revolt of 1916- 1918 no longer taught as a popular liberation movement against Ottoman Turkish occupation, but instead framed strictly as a rebellion aimed at breaking away from the Ottoman State.
Scientific theories heavily edited, removed as Islamization extends across subjects
This Islamization of knowledge extends deeply across subjects, targeting foundational scientific theories like evolution, the Big Bang, and biological development, which have been heavily edited or removed. It attributes natural phenomena directly to divine creation, with primary science texts replacing phrases like "nature’s giving" with "Allah’s giving."
At the same time, the curriculum normalizes armed struggle and self-sacrifice, elevating historical and regional militant figures while systematically romanticizing Palestinian armed resistance, rocket fire, and suicide bombings as acts of supreme martyrdom and justified defense.
The instructional materials also marginalize Syria’s diverse ethnic and religious minority populations. While Christianity maintains a restricted and legally subordinate presence, ethnic groups such as the Kurds, Turkmen, and Druze are nearly invisible across the curriculum, and prominent historical figures from these backgrounds are stripped of their ethnic identities. Sectarian divisions are further reinforced through the contestation of Shi’ite and Alawite symbols, including the explicit delegitimization of the Fatimid Caliphate and the sidelining of Alawite leadership figures.
The curriculum addresses Jewish communities through traditional theological grievances, repeating allegations of treachery, deceit, and broken covenants while entirely erasing centuries of local Syrian Jewish history. Jewish national identity is dismissed outright, with textbooks portraying Jews as a disjointed mix of populations rather than a legitimate nation. Israel is subjected to intense hostility, consistently referred to by derogatory designations such as the "Zionist entity" or simply the "enemy," and omitted entirely from regional maps. In historical units covering the 1948 war, military operations undertaken by the Israeli side are explicitly likened to Nazi crimes against Jews, and all past peace agreements involving Israel are condemned.
Gender roles within the new curriculum have likewise shifted sharply toward traditionalist constraints, diminishing the public visibility and rights of women. References guaranteeing gender equality under civic law have been excised, leaving women defined primarily through domestic family roles as obedient wives and mothers. Visually, textbook illustrations of women and girls have been altered to reflect stricter Islamic dress codes, frequently through the retrofitted addition of hijabs, alongside explicit curriculum content advocating for the full-body-covering burqa.
The curriculum also completely scrubbed the Baathist political legacy. Content associated with former ruler Hafez al-Assad, Bashar al-Assad, and their family has been systematically erased, dismantling the longstanding Assad personality cult and recasting the former rulers in the texts as corrupt, sectarian autocrats. Consequently, the 2011 civil war and the subsequent 2024 uprising are taught as a morally righteous restoration of authentic Islamic-Arab rule.
IMPACT-se CEO: Syria has 'rare opportunity' to revamp education system post-Assad
"The post-Assad era presents Syria with a rare opportunity to create an education system and a society based on inclusion, tolerance, and a shared civic identity, said IMPACT-se CEO Marcus Sheff. "Instead, these textbooks show a very concerning shift from one damaging ideological framework to another."
Sheff warned that the marginalization of minorities and women alongside the glorification of religiously framed violence risks shaping a generation far away from peaceful coexistence.
"This report should raise serious concerns among international leaders who hope to see Syria emerge as a partner in building a peaceful and prosperous Middle East," Sheff added.
He noted that IMPACT-se is working with policymakers in Washington and internationally to drive meaningful reforms to Syria’s school curriculum, seizing a critical opportunity for change as the new Syrian government seeks international assistance and support.

As diaspora minister, Naftali Bennett helped establish the southern prayer space in 2013. Benjamin Netanyahu’s government approved the broader agreement intended to secure its status, then froze it.
Neither leader’s record amounts to delivering the full compromise.
“In recent years, and especially since October 7, we have all come to recognize how important - even critical - our ties with Diaspora Jewry are to the existence of the Jewish people and the State of Israel,” Women of the Wall said.
“Yet Israel has repeatedly slammed the door on Diaspora Jews, sending an unmistakable message that they have no place here with us.”
For the organization, the Western Wall exemplifies that contradiction: a site meant to connect Jews to their shared heritage has become a recurring source of exclusion and political confrontation.
Bennett’s B’Yachad party approaches the issue through the language of belonging and reconciliation. Its doctrine addresses the Wall under the heading “Only Together Can We Create a Home for Every Jew.”
“The Western Wall is a sacred and unifying place, and it should be a place of Shalom Bayit [domestic harmony], not civil strife,” the document states.
Women of the Wall: Preservation is not enough
Its practical commitment is to preserve the southern prayer space while maintaining Orthodox arrangements at the main plaza.
“In this spirit, the Ezrat Yisrael solution on the southern end of the Western Wall – intended to facilitate prayer and gatherings in diverse ways – should be preserved, without disrupting Orthodox prayer arrangements at the Western Wall Plaza.”
That wording supports the continued existence of a space accommodating diverse forms of Jewish worship. It does not explicitly promise to implement the full 2016 compromise, establish its proposed management framework, or complete specified improvements within a stated timetable.
The distinction matters because Ezrat Yisrael predates the broader agreement.
In August 2013, Bennett’s Jerusalem and Diaspora Affairs Ministry announced the completion of a roughly 450-square-meter prayer platform near Robinson’s Arch. Developed in coordination with the Prime Minister’s Office and Jewish Agency chairman Natan Sharansky, it was presented as an interim solution for egalitarian and pluralistic prayer ahead of the High Holy Days.
Netanyahu’s government approved the agreement in January 2016, and it went further. It called for a recognized egalitarian prayer area, a management framework with representatives from the Reform and Conservative movements and Women of the Wall, and state funding for maintenance and services. Orthodox authorities would retain control of the main plaza. The government froze the plan in 2017 under pressure from haredi parties.
Women of the Wall described the agreement as an effort to provide a dignified, equal place for women and to represent liberal Jewish movements representing millions of Diaspora Jews. Its statement blamed haredi and hardline religious Zionist pressure for the freeze and called for the agreement’s implementation.
More recently, the dispute has extended beyond infrastructure to the authority to determine permissible prayer practices.
Last February, the Knesset advanced a private bill sponsored by far Right Noam MK Avi Maoz that would give the Chief Rabbinate authority to determine what constitutes desecration at Jewish holy sites and make it the religious representative consulted over regulations. The proposal passed its preliminary reading 56–47 and still required further readings to become law.
Netanyahu had prevented the proposal from receiving the Ministerial Committee for Legislation backing by canceling its meeting, reportedly to avoid a crisis with Diaspora Jewry. Nevertheless, it advanced by a free vote, with support from Likud Justice Minister Yariv Levin, who called for completing the legislation to end High Court intervention in the Wall’s management, a move Shas and United Torah Judaism also supported.
Women of the Wall cited Maoz’s proposal, alongside legislation submitted by Shas leader Arye Deri in 2023, as measures that it said sought to exclude liberal Jews and women and undermine the prayer rights of Diaspora Jews.
Its criticism places the issue within a broader argument about Jewish peoplehood: decisions negotiated among Israeli coalition partners also affect communities abroad whose religious practices differ from those enforced at the main plaza.
Bennett’s record raises a separate question about the distance between support for egalitarian prayer and the ability to overcome coalition opposition.
During negotiations to establish the Bennett-Lapid government in 2021, implementation of the compromise had been included in the coalition agreement at Yisrael Beytenu’s request.
This arrangement envisaged access from the main Western Wall complex and a governing board including progressive Jewish and Women of the Wall representatives.
By January 2022, however, Bennett acknowledged that his government could not implement the full plan. Speaking to The Jerusalem Post that year, he cited opposition within Yamina and New Hope, and said his government instead intended to pursue physical improvements without implementing the agreement’s other provisions.
Women of the Wall is asking parties to make that additional commitment. It urged the next government to take a broad, farsighted approach that weighs the relationship with Diaspora Jewry and the future of the Jewish people alongside political alliances with haredi parties.
