The cycle of trauma and violence is failing us - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
17:51:28 UTC
02:51:28 KST

When we first arrived in the Palestinian village of Turmus Ayya, a man shouted at us with a kind of passion that stopped me in my tracks.
“You steal our olives, burn our homes.”
My heart shattered.
I found myself wondering what this man had experienced in his life. What pain, what loss, what fear had brought him to a place where a group of Jews arriving in his village could represent, to him, everything that had gone wrong?
I don't know his story. I won't pretend to. But I couldn't stop thinking about it.
The cycle of trauma and violence between Israelis and Palestinians has become so entrenched that we've started treating it as inevitable. It isn't. And it is heartbreaking, infuriating, and profoundly unhelpful to those of us who are genuinely trying to build a better future for both peoples.
Today, I witnessed just how dangerous that cycle has become.
I agreed to join a public relations trip to several Palestinian villages organized by Regavim, an organization whose values and political outlook I do not share. I made that clear when I accepted the invitation.
I'm a liberal Zionist, an educator, and an activist. My work is to help people understand Israel, its complexities, and the realities facing Israelis and Palestinians. I take that responsibility seriously. And I believe that if I'm going to speak about a place, a conflict, or a community, I have an obligation to see it for myself.
How can I educate people about something I haven't made an effort to understand firsthand? What credibility does my voice have if I'm only willing to visit places that confirm what I already believe?
Throughout my career, I've accepted invitations to visit places around the region that are complicated, uncomfortable, and sometimes dangerous. I've visited Rawabi and Kalkilya and pre-October 7 would go to speak to Gazans on the border as they cross in and out for work. I've spent time in Jewish settlements. I've spoken with people on different sides of the conflict, listened to their stories, and tried to understand the realities they live with.
That is the job. Not to agree with everyone you meet. Not to endorse every organization that invites you. And certainly not to abandon your principles at the door. It's to look, listen, ask questions, and learn enough to speak honestly about a reality that is rarely as simple as any one political camp would like it to be. But nothing about my commitment to understanding this conflict prepared me for what happened next.
Our second stop was in Area B of the West Bank. It is important to make that distinction: we were not in Area A. We were in Area B. Initially, nothing seemed particularly alarming. A couple of teenagers were riding bikes nearby. Then they pulled out their phones. They appeared to be making calls.
A few minutes later, we reached a point where a car carrying Palestinians blocked our way. The people inside began yelling at us, asking if we were Jews. Several people were on their phones, apparently telling others that Jews had arrived.
We were traveling in three cars. Fleur Hassan-Nahoum was in the first car with Cindy Seni and Jessica Cohen. I was in the middle car, and Bellamy Bellucci and Golda Daphna were behind us in the third.
The people blocking us told us we couldn't be there. We didn't argue. We didn't try to push our way through. We agreed to turn around. But more people began arriving. Cars, people on foot, teenagers on bikes. It felt as though word had spread and people were converging on us. The car blocking the road had cut off our way forward, so we turned around and started to leave.
People were shouting at us as we drove away.
Then, perhaps 30 seconds later, they began throwing what I can only describe as boulders at our cars. These weren't little rocks. They were enormous chunks of concrete.
Our guides and security personnel, who were driving us and were armed, told us to duck and cover our heads. We did exactly what they said. There was no point in stopping to get out or drawing a weapon; that would only have escalated an already dangerous situation. We needed to get out safely.
I could feel the car shaking as the concrete slammed into it. In the first car, a chunk came through the window. Cindy was injured.
It was terrifying.
We soon made it back into Israel proper and pulled over to the side of the road. We called Magen David Adom and the police. Baruch Hashem, we were all okay. But we had just experienced something I struggle to find the right words for.
It was an attempted lynching. We were targeted as Jews.
Our presence had been identified, our way forward had been blocked, and when we turned around and tried to leave without confrontation, people began hurling enormous chunks of concrete at our cars. One came through the first car's window, injuring my friend Cindy.
I don't use those words lightly. We were trying to leave peacefully. We were told to duck and cover our heads as concrete slammed into our vehicles. We were terrified, and we were fortunate to get out safely.
Whatever one believes about the politics of the organization that brought us there, none of that justifies what happened to us. No disagreement over land, no political grievance, and no history of suffering makes it acceptable to target people for being Jewish.
And yet, I keep returning to the man who shouted at us when we first arrived in Turmus Ayya.
I keep thinking about his anger, and about the possibility of the pain and fear behind it. I can acknowledge that Palestinians have experienced profound suffering without excusing an attack on Jews. I can condemn violence against Palestinians without minimizing violence against Israelis. These principles are not mutually exclusive. They have to coexist if we are ever going to move beyond this.
That is precisely why what happened today makes me so sad. The cycle of trauma and violence is not making either people safer. It is deepening the fear, anger, and mistrust that make a better future harder to imagine.
I went on this trip because I believe that seeing things firsthand matters. I still believe that. I will not allow a frightening experience to convince me that looking, listening, and learning are mistakes. Nor will I allow my disagreement with an organization to prevent me from examining the realities it wants to show me.
But bearing witness also means telling the truth about what happened, even when that truth is uncomfortable. It means refusing to look away from Palestinian suffering, and refusing to look away when Jews are attacked. It means being honest about the people and organizations we disagree with, without surrendering our own judgment.
I am a liberal Zionist because I believe Israel can and must be a country committed to democracy, human rights, and equality. I believe in Israel's future, and I believe that future requires taking the lives and dignity of Palestinians seriously, too.
That doesn't mean ignoring the threats Israelis face, excusing violence, or pretending that good intentions are enough. It means being willing to confront uncomfortable realities, including the ones that challenge our own worldview.
I went to these villages because I believe you cannot understand this conflict from a distance. What happened to us today will not make me stop asking questions or listening to people whose experiences differ from my own. But listening cannot mean looking away when people are hurt, and understanding someone's pain cannot mean excusing what they do with it.
I left Turmus Ayya thinking about the man who shouted at us. I left the West Bank thinking about the concrete that came through the window. Both experiences matter. Neither cancels out the other. And if we cannot hold both truths at once, we will keep repeating the same cycle and wondering why nothing changes.
The writer is an activist and content creator. A third-generation IDF veteran with over a decade in Israel advocacy, she has created and executed content for dozens of major organizations. She is an associate at the Tel Aviv Institute.

The European Commission released a statement condemning the violence in Albania on Sunday, saying it had "no place in a democratic society" and that the response "must remain within the law and proportionate."
Edi Rama has accused some of those taking part in anti-government protests in Albania as having crossed a "red line" as demonstrations continued across the country on Monday.
Anti-government "Flamingo" protests have been ongoing in Albania for months amid calls for Rama to resign as prime minister, but clashes ramped up early last week as a student movement calling for action over high tuition fees launched fresh demonstrations.
"Protests are a right, whereas violence is a crime, and this red line will be drawn firmly at this critical stage of our democratic development," Rama wrote in a post on social media on Monday.
"The rioters must and will bear the legal and financial consequences of their blindness," he continued, whilst also urging protesters to "distance themselves" from rioters.
"I and the governing majority are ready for dialogue with anyone except the rioters and political parties that do not distance themselves from violence," Rama added.
Violent clashes with police in recent days have seen protesters set buildings alight, hurl molotov cocktails, and shoot fireworks at officers, who have responded with rubber bullets, water cannons, and tear gas.
Hundreds of people, including police officers, have reportedly been injured in the violence.
"We will continue our movement until Rama resigns. We are not criminals, we want social peace and better living conditions in our country," Leka Sina, a 22-year-old student, told the AFP news agency.
"Violence is not a solution, but the government also needs to reflect deeply to understand this revolt," Sina added.
Rama has sought to pin the blame for the unrest on foreign influence.
The European Commission released a statement condemning the violence in Albania on Sunday, saying it had "no place in a democratic society" and that the response "must remain within the law and proportionate."
"Freedom of assembly and expression are fundamental rights and core European values, to be respected and exercised peacefully," the Commission said in its statement. "In a candidate country firmly committed to the EU accession process and making important progress on its EU path, grievances should be handled through constructive dialogue and in a peaceful manner."

Netanyahu or Eisenkot? Where their visions for Israel’s security align - and collide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
17:51:24 UTC
02:51:24 KST

While there are many national security strategies, the next government will ultimately come down to a choice between two visions.
One is the vision of current Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces pressure from the Right.
The other is the vision of Yashar party leader and former IDF chief Gadi Eisenkot, who faces pressure from both his right and his left.
Netanyahu, Eisenkot differ on how to confront Iran - but not on the threat
There are few major differences between Netanyahu and Eisenkot on the Iranian threat, though there are some nuances. Both will oppose a "bad deal" if US President Donald Trump's administration opts for such a deal.
Despite Trump's endorsement of Netanyahu and statement that he probably will not help attack Iran again, the US president has few positions set in stone and is likely to act on whatever whim is convincing to him at any particular moment: Whether to cut a deal, to return to war, or to continue a marathon economic standoff of competing blockades.
In that sense, the main differences are that Netanyahu would likely be more open about opposition to a bad deal to try to influence American public opinion, even at the cost of trying to improve the deal behind the scenes.
Eisenkot, by contrast, would likely keep his opposition private in order to try to improve the deal quietly, while viewing American public opinion as something he has less control over.
Both Netanyahu and Eisenkot would be ready to attack Iran in some circumstances where the nuclear or ballistic missile threat became too close for comfort. Both of them have shown they will not jump at attacking Iran at every moment.
Most would agree that at this stage Netanyahu would be willing to take on more risk to attack Iran and might interpret the point of no return as an earlier point than Eisenkot.
Israel's political leaders have no clear plan for Gaza
Neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot has a real plan for Gaza. Both have promised to eliminate Hamas's control of the Strip, but neither has a clear path to doing so.
Netanyahu's path is thoroughly unconvincing because he has had three years to achieve this goal. While Hamas is substantially weakened, it is still quite clearly in power.
In a recent briefing to which he invited only a small portion of the Israeli military reporters' group, leaving out The Jerusalem Post, other English-language Israeli outlets, and the vast majority of Hebrew-speaking reporters, he refused to back away from his commitment to "absolute victory" over Hamas, despite there being no evidence that he has come any closer to that goal since October 2024, when Yahya Sinwar was killed and all 24 of Hamas's battalions had already been dismantled.
Somewhere between 80% and 90% of Hamas was killed by the end of 2024.
Although the IDF took control of 60%-75% of Gaza's territory in 2025-2026, and airstrikes several times a week continue to keep Hamas on the run, the last two years have seen very little change in how close Hamas has come to losing control.
Even if the IDF undertakes another invasion of Gaza, something the Trump administration has consistently blocked, Hamas has shown that it can hide among the civilian population and outwait and outlast the IDF's ability to remain in the area in large numbers.
Netanyahu also invoked the "fortress Israel" metaphor and said he was willing to keep Gaza in ruins, with no rebuilding indefinitely, until Hamas disarms completely. This made it clear that his strategy is to try to keep Gaza miserable long enough for Hamas to simply quit.
But Hamas will not simply quit. It is a fanatical and messianic movement with perverse delusions of grandeur.
In that sense, Netanyahu has no clear plan.
He also seems ready to sacrifice all of Israel's international relations with Europe and perhaps even the US to maintain this uncompromising stance.
In contrast, Eisenkot has no clear plan of his own but is willing to move forward with Trump's cease-fire plan without resistance, including empowering Palestinian Authority-linked technocratic leaders and police, as well as international peacekeepers in Gaza.
He would likely be ready to allow partial rebuilding in exchange for partial disarmament, if for no other reason than to pause, and perhaps even push back, the diplomatic tsunami that is already threatening Israeli national security and economic stability.
This will not eliminate Hamas.
It might weaken the group politically, which could, in the very long term, lead to other groups challenging it. Alternatively, Hamas might manipulate the system, becoming a Hezbollah-style group that controls politics like a puppet master behind the scenes.
Neither of those outcomes will make Israelis feel safer now. But if Hamas is eventually weakened enough to have to share power, that would represent a fundamental shift.
Even if Hamas manages to retain its current power, as it has since October 2024 despite Israel's efforts to crush it, Israel will at least avoid a further deterioration in support from Europe, the US, and elsewhere.
These differences could have implications over the next year and beyond, but Eisenkot has made it clear that he will not move toward a Palestinian state, certainly not during a first term.
So, the differences between them are not as large as those between, say, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, who favors transfer, and Democrats leader Yair Golan, who would push for a two-state solution.
Netanyahu and Eisenkot are worlds apart on the West Bank
If there are strong commonalities between Netanyahu and Eisenkot on Iran and Gaza, with differences largely in the nuances, they are worlds apart on the West Bank.
The only thing they have in common is a strong commitment to fighting Palestinian terrorism as their number one priority.
But on fighting Jewish extremism and expanding Israeli settlements, their second- and third-priority issues, they are far apart.
Eisenkot would immediately reinstate administrative detention for Jewish extremists, which Defense Minister Israel Katz suspended in January 2025 and which Netanyahu has allowed to remain suspended for nearly two years, despite losing control of Jewish extremists.
In addition, Eisenkot would clean house at the police, bringing in officers who would crack down hard on Jewish extremists.
He would likely also fire Shin Bet Director David Zini and replace him with a new chief who would crack down more forcefully on Jewish extremists.
Until recently, most people were not blaming the IDF for the out-of-control situation, so the officers currently in place might be allowed to remain. However, the last few months have blemished their records as well.
It remains to be seen whether Eisenkot might also clean house among senior IDF officers. One major question is whether Maj.-Gen. Dado Bar Kalifa's appointment as the next IDF Central Command chief, scheduled to begin in January 2027, will go through.
That could depend on how strongly IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir backs "Dado" and how much the appointment is perceived as having been dictated by Katz.
Regarding the more than 100 new "farms" that Netanyahu's government established or expanded under the authority of Bezalel Smotrich within the Defense Ministry, Eisenkot would likely clear most or all of them.
He would certainly freeze new settlement construction or limit it to the "natural" expansion of existing settlements.
He would certainly block the expansion of the E1 settlement bloc near Jerusalem, which has intensified European criticism.
Collectively, these actions would help pause or even reverse the diplomatic tsunami that has begun to engulf Israel's national security and economic stability.
However, Eisenkot has no vision for resolving the standoff with the Palestinians in the West Bank, which has persisted since 1967. Once again, he opposes a two-state solution in the near and medium term.
Netanyahu is not prepared to annex the entire West Bank, as Ben-Gvir would like, but his moves to expand Israel's presence in the West Bank have, in a way, forced the final-status issues to the fore.
If he remains in power and continues taking over new parts of Area C, it is not impossible that, at some point, the Palestinians in the West Bank might become concerned enough to offer a new deal under which they receive closer to the 70% of the territory that Trump offered them in 2020.
That would be a significant reduction from the 90%-95% promised to them under the Oslo Accords, but Netanyahu's moves could shift their approach.
Netanyahu, Eisenkot largely aligned on Lebanon and Syria
There do not appear to be any major differences between Eisenkot and Netanyahu on Lebanon.
Both would maintain a security zone. Both are open to partial withdrawals in exchange for the Lebanese army partially clearing Hezbollah from the security zone, and neither trusts the Lebanese army to do its job sufficiently.
Unlike in Gaza, no one believes there is any real chance of removing Hezbollah from power.
Under light pressure from Trump, with heavier pressure likely to focus on Gaza and the West Bank, might Eisenkot agree to partial withdrawals faster than Netanyahu? Maybe.
But Eisenkot has said he would draw a line at eight kilometers to prevent Hezbollah from firing anti-tank missiles into Israel.
Eisenkot might not have destroyed as many homes belonging to southern Lebanese Shiites as Netanyahu ordered destroyed, but that has already happened, so it is unclear whether it would affect future policy.
Whoever is prime minister, there will likely be some partial withdrawals and some degree of a standoff over the security zone.
The only major difference in nuance might be that Eisenkot would try to restore France to a productive role, hoping to score diplomatic points with Paris on other fronts, whereas Netanyahu now relishes public conflicts with the French government.
There also is likely little difference between Netanyahu and Eisenkot on Syria.
Once again, both want to keep a security zone and both have dropped hints at times that they might agree to partial withdrawals, but both have strong doubts about trusting Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa because of his al-Qaeda past.
Once again, Eisenkot might make some partial withdrawals more easily under pressure from Trump, but Netanyahu will to if Trump presses hard enough – and the US president has made it clear that he views Sharaa as an ally, no matter what Israel thinks.
Eisenkot could repair ties with Europe and the US, but faces major challenges
Eisenkot would significantly improve relations with Europe. He might reach new understandings with Middle Eastern countries that once liked Netanyahu but now loathe him.
All of these diplomatic gains could help address various national security and economic stability issues.
Netanyahu would stick to alliances with India, the UAE, Cyprus, and Greece, insisting that if Jerusalem compromises in the way the West wants it to, Israel's national security will be gravely undermined.
But the most crucial prize is the US.
Stunningly, Netanyahu this week invoked a scenario in which Israel loses the US as an ally entirely.
That would mean Israel losing access to US-built aircraft, including the F-35, as well as various other weapons, global diplomatic support, and potentially a major source of economic stability.
This is stunning because, while such a scenario might materialize in January 2029, one would think that any Israeli prime minister would do everything possible to avoid it.
Netanyahu presented this scenario alongside the prospect of two more years of Trump in power, as if anything Israel wants to achieve must be accomplished in the next two years.
And perhaps Netanyahu might achieve things with Trump in those two years that would forever change the playing field.
But Trump's declaration of love and unconditional support for Netanyahu on Sunday was anything but unconditional.
The US president barely made the declaration and has taken numerous potshots at the prime minister over the years.
All it meant was that, given the polling a week before the election, Trump would much rather continue working with Netanyahu, whom he knows well, than have to get to know Eisenkot.
But if Eisenkot is more compliant with some of Trump's demands regarding Gaza, the West Bank, Lebanon, and Syria, the two will likely figure out how to get along.
More importantly, Eisenkot will not give up on the Democratic Party, which has turned against Israel more than at any time in decades.
He will try to hit "restart" on relations in the post-Netanyahu era.
The bad news is that he has no clear plan for doing so, and the gulf between Israeli and American expectations regarding the Middle East is substantial, even if Netanyahu exits stage left.
Whether Eisenkot could bridge that gulf would be one of the key challenges and uncertainties of his premiership.

A black bear &quot;dropped by&quot; a library in the U.S.—enjoyed snacks and ate a jar of honey

A black bear "dropped by" a library in the U.S.—enjoyed snacks and ate a jar of honey
Kyiv • UNN
A black bear wandered into a California library and ate the staff’s supplies, including honey. The animal inspected the shelves and left on its own.
A guest worthy of the pages of a fairy-tale book visited a library in California — especially considering that this very day marked 100 years since the appearance of Winnie-the-Pooh. A black bear entered the building and, according to reports, helped itself to the staff’s food supplies and did not overlook a jar of honey, UNN reports, citing The Guardian.
Details
As library director Joseph Bopp told local outlet KMPH, at around 6:10 a.m. on Wednesday — more than four hours before the official opening at 10:00 a.m. — a black bear wandered into a branch of the Mono County Library System in the town of Mammoth Lakes.
According to the outlet, the animal got to snacks intended for employees: it ate peanut butter, canned peaches, cookies, and a jar of honey. After that, the bear walked around the library, inspected the shelves of new arrivals and the reference desk, and then went outside on its own.
On Wednesday, the Mono County Office of Education released a statement accompanied by surveillance-camera footage showing the bear walking through the library and sniffing books, a chair, and the floor.
"This morning, before the doors of the Mammoth Lakes library opened to visitors, we received a special guest," the statement said. "One might assume that this new ‘bear’ reader was looking for a copy of ‘Winnie-the-Pooh’ — the book that was published exactly 100 years ago!"
Bopp also decided to remind the unexpected guest of the rules: "Although we are always happy to welcome enthusiastic readers and understand how important this centennial anniversary is, we must remind visitors — especially our bears — that food is not part of the library collection."
It should be added
The book "Winnie-the-Pooh," written by A. A. Milne and illustrated by E. H. Shepard, tells of the adventures of the eponymous anthropomorphic bear — a great lover of honey who said of himself that he had "very little brain." Together with his friends — Piglet, Tigger, Eeyore, Rabbit, Owl, Kanga, and Roo — he lives in the Hundred Acre Wood.
The story is based on Milne’s son Christopher Robin’s teddy bear, as well as a real black bear named Winnipeg that lived at the London Zoo. This book and its three sequels remain beloved childhood works for many generations. Many people were also first introduced to Winnie-the-Pooh and his friends when The Walt Disney Company adapted Milne’s works for film and television.
To mark the 100th anniversary of the original Winnie-the-Pooh book, the Mono County public libraries invited local residents to visit any of the seven branches to borrow Milne’s classic work or other books about bears. The library network has more than 180,000 printed works and also offers additional online resources.
Although this encounter resembled a scene from a fairy tale, officials reminded residents that black bears are wild animals that must never be approached or fed.
They also urged people to use bear-resistant trash containers and to keep car doors and windows closed.

Ukraine's EU integration chief slams proposal to pick chief prosecutor in open contest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
17:50:11 UTC
02:50:11 KST

Ukraine's EU integration chief slams proposal to pick chief prosecutor in open contest
Vsevolod Chentsov, Ukraine's deputy prime minister for European integration, spoke out in an Oct. 19 interview against the idea of an open contest for prosecutor general.
The EU has demanded a reform of Ukraine's notoriously corrupt and politicized prosecution service and called for making the procedure for picking the prosecutor general less political and more merit-based. Meanwhile, anti-corruption activists and pro-reform lawmakers have accused the Ukrainian authorities of sabotaging rule of law reforms and resisting the demand for depoliticizing the Prosecutor General's Office.
"I see experts arguing that there should be an open competition for the position of prosecutor general," Chentsov told the Ukrainian media outlet Yevropeiska Pravda. "But that is not something the EU requires, nor is it standard practice in Europe."
He argued that recommendations by Council of Europe experts "clearly emphasize the need to comply with Ukraine’s Constitution, which sets out the roles of the president and parliament in the appointment process."
"How to ensure transparency and select candidates based on their professional qualifications remains open for discussion," Chentsov said. "But personally, I see neither the need nor the possibility of holding an open competition for the position. A balance must be struck between political independence and professional competence."
According to a plan approved in December by Taras Kachka, Ukraine's former deputy prosecutor general for European integration, and EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos, Ukraine should "conduct a comprehensive review of the selection and dismissal procedure of the prosecutor general, with a view to aligning it with European best practice." The plan also envisages reinstating transparent contests for other top prosecutor jobs.
According to Ukraine's interim benchmarks for EU accession, Kyiv "needs to depoliticize the position of the prosecutor general, including by making the selection and dismissal procedures more objective, transparent and merit-based, taking into account European standards."
An EU official who spoke on condition of anonymity told the Kyiv Independent that the EU accession benchmarks "are not calling for it to be an elected position but the process should still change."
"For the EU, the gold standard is to have the involvement of independent, international vetters," the official said. "Separately, the EU and Ukraine launched a task force last week to implement Kachka-Kos and the EU's Rule of Law benchmarks. It serves to identify deficiencies in the current set-up, which would also include the prosecutor general's selection process."
In June, Anastasia Radina, head of parliament's anti-corruption committee from President Volodymyr Zelensky's party, submitted to parliament a bill seeking to select the prosecutor general in a transparent contest with the participation of international experts.
Radina's opponents argue that the Kachka-Kos plan does not envisage a contest involving international experts and that a contest for the prosecutor general's job contradicts Ukraine's Constitution.
Radina has denied the claim that it contradicts the Constitution.
"There may be different interpretations of the benchmark, but I'm not aware of anyone having proposed an alternative approach so far," she told the Kyiv Independent.
Ukraine's prosecutor generals are appointed by the president with parliament's approval and have been seen as closely aligned to whoever is in power. Radina's bill seeks to depoliticize the prosecutor general's appointment.
The debate on selecting the prosecutor general intensified under the previous occupant of the job, Ruslan Kravchenko.
Kravchenko faced scrutiny due to his role in the crackdown on the National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) in 2025.
He was fired by parliament on Sept. 15 amid a major corruption investigation.
Within the investigation, a top prosecutor described as a “confidant” of Kravchenko was charged. Publicly revealed evidence hints at Kravchenko being implicated.
He left Ukraine on Sept. 14, under the pretext of an official trip to a conference in Paris. But the organizers told the Kyiv Independent that they had not expected him to attend, strengthening the suspicions that the trip was a fig leaf for fleeing Ukraine to avoid potential charges.
As Kravchenko left Ukraine, he simultaneously approved charges against the head of the anti-corruption agency investigating him. The charges were later dropped as unfounded.
Kravchenko later moved to Austria, the media outlet Ukrainska Pravda reported on Sept. 23.

Satellite Images Show Two Oil Tanks Destroyed and Bridges Hit in St. Petersburg Drone Strikes
Drone strikes against St. Petersburg on October 18 reportedly destroyed two oil storage tanks, damaged several others, and struck two bridges and a logistics hub, according to the OSINT Telegram channel Absolutely Reliable on October 19.
The channel published an assessment of damage at five locations across Russia’s second-largest city, including the Petersburg Oil Terminal, the Ruchyi oil depot, an OZON logistics hub, and two major transport crossings.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Absolutely Reliable, three storage tanks at the Petersburg Oil Terminal caught fire. These included one 15,000-cubic-meter tank and two 10,000-cubic-meter tanks. The OSINT channel assessed that one tank was completely destroyed, while other tanks sustained exterior damage without catching fire.
At the Ruchyi oil depot in northern St. Petersburg, the channel reported that a 5,000-cubic-meter storage tank was destroyed and a smaller 1,000-cubic-meter tank was damaged. The assessment also identified a fire covering more than 10,000 square meters at an OZON logistics facility.
The reported damage extended to two bridges. Absolutely Reliable identified damage to the road surface of the Southern Fairway Bridge and the surface of the movable section of the Finland Railway Bridge.
Earlier, footage posted online on October 18 showed an explosion at the cable-stayed bridge over the Korabelny Fairway, part of St. Petersburg’s Western High-Speed Diameter highway.
The eight-lane crossing connects Bely Island with Vasilyevsky Island and forms part of a major highway linking the northern and southern sections of the city. The reported strike occurred approximately 4.5 kilometers from the Petersburg Oil Terminal, where a fire also broke out during the attack.

URCS organizes training on IHL for reps of Coordination HQ for POW Treatment, Kyiv Institute of National Guard
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
20:45:06 EEST
02:45:06 KST

A two-day training session on international humanitarian law was held in Kyiv by the Ukrainian Red Cross Society (URCS) for representatives of the Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War and Kyiv Institute of the National Guard of Ukraine.
“The training brought together staff, lecturers and cadets from both institutions. It was delivered by specialists from the Ukrainian Red Cross International Humanitarian Law (IHL) Unit,” URCS said on Facebook Monday.
Participants explored the key rules of IHL governing the conduct of hostilities and protecting people who are not or are no longer taking part in them. Particular attention was given to the principles of distinction and proportionality, precautions in attack, and the protection of civilians during armed conflict.
The training also covered the structure and Fundamental Principles of the International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement, the work of the Ukrainian Red Cross, and the rules governing the use and legal protection of the Red Cross, Red Crescent and Red Crystal emblems.
Following the training, participants discussed opportunities for further cooperation, including developing training programmes tailored to the professional needs of different audiences, delivering specialised training sessions and organising joint seminars.
The Ukrainian Red Cross noted that it continues to work with government institutions to promote understanding of international humanitarian law and encourage its practical application.

ITV’s exposé of racism and misogyny in Reform? Just a few (more) bad apples | John Crace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
17:42:46 UTC
02:42:46 KST

It was the dog that didn’t bark in the night. After Sunday night’s ITV exposé of widespread racism and misogyny within Reform, you might have expected one of its MPs to have taken to the airwaves on Monday morning to defend the party’s honour. To try to persuade viewers that the real problem lay with the journalists who couldn’t stop themselves from investigating Reform rather than the fact that the party’s bigotry was endemic.
Instead, we got nothing. Every Reform MP was otherwise engaged. Were too busy having breakfast. Nothing from Nigel Farage. Nothing even from Robert Jenrick. Maybe he realised he had crashed and burned a few days earlier by suggesting it was just one of those things. One of life’s little mysteries. The BBC was riddled with paedophiles and Reform was awash with racists, said Honest Bob. No big deal. Every organisation had its crosses to bear.
The only MP to post on X in the morning was Richard Tice, who was feeling decidedly grumpy, having only just got married to Isabel Oakeshott. Perhaps he had a hangover. Though his main gripe was that British Airways was yet another failing British institution because it had mislaid at least one of his bags.
Dicky’s social media post had more than a touch of the “don’t you know who I am” to it. You can only imagine the baggage handler may have known exactly who Dicky was and had taken great pleasure in diverting one of the fake Louis Vuitton suitcases from Dubai to Manila. Via Buenos Aires.
The one person out and about for Reform was the one person you would have thought the party would want to keep hidden. Step forward Matt Goodwin, the party’s failed candidate for the Gorton and Denton byelection whose own views could easily pass off as borderline racist in polite circles. Matt is going through his own personal anti-growth agenda. Working hard to deconstruct himself from low-level academic to incredibly dim primate with low social skills. Almost every day, voters in Gorton and Denton thank their lucky stars for having dodged that bullet.
Matt’s defence of Reform was … unorthodox, to put it kindly. So much so that you began to wonder whether he was even conscious. Luckily for him, he was only allowed out on Times Radio. Though that was more than enough. To try to understand Matt is to make a category error. The whole point is to not understand him. That’s the way you stay sane. Because what he wanted listeners to believe was that Nige was a buffer zone against racism. That hordes of would-be racists begged to be allowed to join Reform, only to find out that Nige was a man of peace and love. The one politician who wanted nothing but good things for all immigrants.
It got better. Because Batshit Matt also wanted us to believe that the ITV documentary had just uncovered a few bad apples in the party. So in a way it had done Reform a favour. What were the chances? The ITV journalists had managed to uncover the only seven racists in the Reform ranks. Everyone else was Team Nigel. Never had a bad word for anyone. Except, there was another way of looking at this. That ITV had filmed about 10 Reform councillors and found that seven of them had views that included beheading King Charles for being a Muslim. Some statisticians might put that down as a 70% hit rate. Not so much a few wrong ’uns but a whole army of them. Poor Nige. Always the victim.
Over in the Commons, Wes Streeting was preparing for other threats during departmental defence questions. Though John Healey was not one of them. You’d have thought that Wes might have wanted to schmooze the chancellor before next week’s budget. To try to get the best funding settlement he could. Not a bit of it. Wes began by slagging off his predecessor as defence secretary for wasting money on unnecessary training exercises and then announced he was confident that Healey would reach the necessary 3% and 3.5% targets at next year’s spending review. So, no, Wes wouldn’t be resigning any time soon. Let’s hope his confidence is well placed.
Instead, Wes seemed more interested in persuading himself that there was absolutely nothing unusual in Donald Trump switching the Starlink satellite system on and off at random moments, thereby allowing Russian drones to do untold damage on Ukraine. This was just standard procedure. The only way you could tell the system was working properly was if you turned it off from time to time. Obvious when you think about. Wes was also totally chilled about Trump trying to lower US pump prices by allowing Russian imports of diesel. Fuel that the Russians had also imported from Iran and with whom, coincidentally, the US was at war.
All of this apparently made perfect sense not just to Streeting, but also to Labour and opposition backbenchers. Wes could reassure us because he had had a personal meeting with Pete Hegseth the previous week, during with the secretary for war had reiterated Trump’s claims that Nato forces had been a waste of space in Afghanistan and that the US troops had fought alone. A nice ice breaker. After that, Pete went out of his way to say Washington was totally behind Ukraine, just so long as Russia won the war.
Curiously, the shadow defence secretary, James Cartlidge, didn’t use his questions to talk up the four drones of the “Britannia shield” that the Tories were sure would protect the UK from nuclear war. So it remains a mystery. Almost as if it was a bullshit party conference announcement that was designed to be forgotten within days. Highlight of the day went to Sharron Davies, the former swimmer turned Tory peer, who demanded to know why Andy Burnham hadn’t invaded France to stop the rioting. Can you explain it to her?

Authorities clarified that the curfew applies to the entire population, not just minors. It also announced a ban on demonstrations in certain Paris neighborhoods from 8 pm to 6 am.

Around 550,000 people took part in 110 demonstrations across France on Saturday, including 110,000 in Paris, while about 400 arrests were recorded nationwide, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said Monday that he had asked prefects to introduce localized and partial curfews following the unrest.
He also announced a major judicial operation and partial unemployment measures for businesses affected by the violence.
Authorities have also announced restrictions on gatherings in Marseille.

Chuck Schumer urges FCC to block AI robocalls before elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
17:40:56 UTC
02:40:56 KST

Chuck Schumer urges FCC to block AI robocalls before elections
Chuck Schumer urges FCC to reject petition allowing AI robocalls ahead of key November midterm elections.
United States Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer of New York has urged the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) not to approve a petition by the conservative group Club for Growth to allow AI-generated robocalls ahead of the November midterm elections.
“Under this change, campaigns could use their opponents’ voice to send out a message that is, at best, disingenuous and, at worst, a blatant lie,” Schumer said on Monday.
The petition was originally filed on August 31, and the public comment period began on September 4 and expires on Monday.
Earlier this month, Anna Gomez, the Democratic member of the FCC, urged her colleagues not to allow consideration of the petition brought by the national conservative fiscal policy organisation.
Her concerns echoed Schumer’s. “[If] the FCC allows a dark money group to flood Americans’ phones with AI-generated robocalls they never agreed to receive, it would bring chaos so close to Election Day,” commissioner Gomez told the Reuters news agency at the time.
There is precedent for the concerns being raised. In the 2024 presidential election, ahead of the New Hampshire primary, voters received an AI-generated version in the voice of President Joe Biden, the then Democratic incumbent, telling them not to vote. The FCC said that a political consultant working with longshot primary challenger Dean Phillips was responsible.
At the state level, Louisiana, Tennessee and Vermont passed laws this year requiring disclosures for AI-generated campaign phone calls. While robocalls have been used in political campaigns for years, FCC rules prohibit such calls to cellphones without prior consent, but the restrictions do not apply to landlines.
Club for Growth’s president, David McIntosh, in a statement earlier this month, said that the group is asking for “the FCC to treat First Amendment-protected political speech the same way it already treats wireless calls about package deliveries, bank accounts, and doctor’s appointments”.
“There is no one at the FCC that has expressed any interest in moving to an order on this or any of the petitions, and there are zero plans to do so. The FCC seeks comment on petitions that come in as a matter of normal procedure,” a spokesperson for the FCC told Al Jazeera.

Russia strikes 28 critical energy facilities across Ukraine in latest wave of attacks, Zelensky says
Russian attacks struck 28 substations and other critical energy facilities across Ukraine, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 19, following another wave of missile and drone attacks on the country's energy infrastructure.
At least 550,000 households lost power overnight, Zelensky said, following a coordination meeting on the situation in Ukraine's regions.
Russian forces targeted energy infrastructure in 11 oblasts overnight and on the morning of Oct. 19, First Deputy Energy Minister Artem Nekrasov reported. Additional power outages caused by Russian strikes and ongoing hostilities were reported in four other oblasts.
One energy worker was injured in an attack on an energy facility in Vinnytsia Oblast, Nekrasov said.
Repair crews are working to restore electricity wherever security conditions allow, although prolonged air raid alerts and the threat of renewed Russian strikes are slowing restoration efforts, according to the Energy Ministry.
During the overnight attacks, Russia launched 16 ballistic missiles and more than 200 drones in several waves in what Zelensky described as a "targeted attack on Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast."
Zelensky said Ukraine had "once again" received no advance warning from its partners about the strikes.
Nekrasov said that over the past week, Russia carried out 87 targeted attacks on Ukraine's energy, oil, and gas sectors. Authorities recorded 224 incidents that caused damage to energy, oil, and gas infrastructure during that period.
The attacks come as Ukraine faces a critical shortage of U.S.-made Patriot interceptor missiles, which are essential for defending against Russian ballistic missiles.
"There are political agreements that have not been implemented at the working level. There are also delays in certain types of vital supplies at the level of the U.S. Department of War," Zelensky said.
Zelensky also announced plans to increase production and procurement of anti-drone turrets, which he said have proven "highly effective" against Russian Shahed-type attack drones.
Russia has carried out 2,147 attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure since July 16, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said in an interview with BBC News Ukrainian published on Oct. 19, citing figures as of Oct. 17.
"Not a single day has passed without attacks on energy infrastructure," Koretskyi said.

North Sea strikes could severely disrupt UK fuel supplies, union warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
17:39:13 UTC
02:39:13 KST

North Sea workers are preparing to strike at oil rigs across the ageing basin over the coming weeks in a sign of growing tensions between trade unions and oil companies.
The Unite union said on Monday that more than 160 offshore rig workers would take part in a 24-hour strike from Wednesday that could “severely disrupt” UK fuel supplies.
A 48-hour strike starting on Tuesday was already planned by workers at oil services company Wood Group contracted to Harbour Energy’s Britannia, Jasmine, Judy, Lomond and North Everest platforms.
Trade union leaders are scheduled to continue pay talks with the Apache energy company through the Acas mediation service on Wednesday. But Unite expects the 24-hour strike to go ahead at 6am that morning because, it says, the company has shown “no willingness” to resolve the dispute.
The strike will include workers employed at five Apache oil platforms linked to the Forties Pipeline System (FPS), which is responsible for about 30% of the UK’s oil production. Unite has claimed that a halt in production could lead to a sharp drop in pressure across the pipeline system and disrupt UK fuel supplies.
A spokesperson for Jim Ratcliffe’s Ineos, the owner of the Forties pipeline, did not respond to a request for comment.
North Sea oil companies have been on a collision course with trade unions in recent years as many cut investments in their UK assets, blaming the UK’s energy policies and tax regime.
The industrial action comes ahead of the budget on 28 October and an imminent decision on the fate of the controversial Jackdaw gas project, as the UK faces fresh concerns over its energy supplies this winter because of the global fuel crisis caused by the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine.
Texas-based Apache plans to end all its North Sea operations by the end of 2029, blaming the “onerous financial” impact of the government’s windfall tax, which means oil companies pay a total tax rate of 78% on their profits.
A spokesperson for Apache said it plans to use experienced contractors to continue production during the strike. It added that even if all five platforms were unable to operate, the company would not expect an impact on other oil companies using the Forties pipeline.
The company added: “Our offer provides a 4% pay increase for employees in the bargaining unit, whose earnings already place them among the highest earners in the UK and whose offshore rota averages 153 working days a year.”
Harbour Energy, the UK’s biggest producer of North Sea oil, has also blamed the UK’s tax regime for its decision to scale back investment in UK waters. It said late last year that it would cut 100 offshore jobs, having reduced its workforce by about 600 since 2023.
Wood Group said that only eight of the 150 employees contracted to the affected Harbour platforms took part in strike action earlier this month and that the action did not disrupt operations. A third 48-hour strike is planned for 3 November, according to Unite and trade union RMT.

Saudi Arabia trapped by miscalculations regarding Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
17:35:37 UTC
02:35:37 KST

Saudi Arabia trapped by miscalculations regarding Iran
The Iran newspaper argued that Saudi Arabia misjudged Iran’s broader strategy and the Axis of Resistance regarding Yemen. Riyadh imagined that military action against Yemen would weaken Iran. Instead, the conflict evolved into a strategic advantage for Tehran. Through careful management and without assuming direct control, Iran benefited from developments in Yemen.
The Ansarallah’s ability to threaten the Bab al-Mandab Strait enabled Iran to exercise influence over two major global energy chokepoints: the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab. Iran also positioned itself as a responsible actor by offering mediation and linking the Yemen issue to wider diplomatic negotiations. According to the article, Saudi Arabia failed to recognize this strategic chain of events and found itself in a situation where Ansarallah’s actions ultimately benefited Iran. One of Riyadh’s key mistakes, it argues, was misunderstanding the nature of the relationship between Iran and the Ansarallah.
Ham-Mihan: Trump has already made his final decision
In an interview with international affairs analyst Hassan Hanizadeh, Ham-Mihan examined Donald Trump’s approach toward relations between Tehran and Washington. Hanizadeh said the possibility of conflict remains serious and that Trump could resort to military action in an attempt to reshape regional dynamics in favor of the United States and Israel. Such a course, he warned, could have far-reaching consequences if accompanied by miscalculations. Developments in the Strait of Hormuz and incidents involving large vessels have added further complexity to the situation. According to Hanizadeh, the US president appears to have already decided on Iran, and the possibility of military action has not disappeared. At the same time, Iran is prepared to defend its borders. Given the current sensitive environment, any military move or miscalculation by either side could widen the crisis and produce consequences extending beyond the two countries.
Sobh-e-No: Will a new war break out?
 
Sobh-e-No analyzed possible US scenarios regarding a renewed war with Iran. The paper outlined three possibilities. The first is a large-scale, comprehensive attack. The second is a limited, symbolic strike intended as a signal. The third is postponement until after the midterm congressional elections. It argues that Trump is currently managing tensions in order to get through the election period. However, this delay does not mean the danger of conflict has disappeared; it merely postpones a decision. As a result, the likelihood of a major war in the short term is considered low, though a limited attack or uncontrolled escalation remains possible. According to the article, Trump is reluctant to accept the economic costs, political risks, internal divisions, and strategic uncertainties associated with a new war. He views the conflict as a potential political vulnerability and would prefer to contain it before the election. Nevertheless, mounting pressures could still push him toward either a controlled or unintended escalation.
Javan: Control over Hormuz has significant psychological effects on foes
In an analysis of Iran’s approach toward the Strait of Hormuz, Javan argued that understanding the deeper historical and geoeconomic context is essential. The paper argued that Iran’s decision to impose new management rules over the strait and abandon passivity should not be interpreted as a temporary defensive measure. Rather, it described the move as part of a broader and proactive strategy aimed at signaling the end of American hegemony in West Asia. According to the article, Iran’s determination to maintain sovereign control over the strait has significant psychological and strategic effects on enemies. It argues that this persistence creates frustration within Washington’s decision-making process and could eventually lead US leaders to conclude that efforts to force Iran’s submission through military pressure and war are futile.
Kayhan: US concerned about Iran’s impact on mid-term elections
In an explanation, Kayhan said that the United States is increasingly concerned about Iran’s influence on the American political climate. The paper noted that Donald Trump has repeatedly expressed concern in recent weeks about Iran’s impact on the US Congressional mid-term elections. According to the article, Trump views election results as a measure of success in the war that began against Iran on February 28. It argues that over the past seven months he has repeatedly made claims suggesting that Iran’s military, economic, and political capacities have been severely weakened. However, the paper says that opinion polls in the United States indicate these claims have failed to convince the public. Kayhan contends that Trump’s repeated statements are an attempt to conceal the difficulties that the confrontation with Iran has created for Washington. The article further argues that recent surveys show growing public pessimism regarding success against Iran and increasing concern over the economic pressures associated with the conflict.

Minister says Mahmood’s migration policy will ‘prolong integration’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
17:35:17 UTC
02:35:17 KST

The energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, appears to have criticised Shabana Mahmood’s migration policy in a post on her constituency website, in which she suggested she had concerns that a longer settlement process could affect integration.
Fahnbulleh has since removed the critique, which appeared in a write-up of a community meeting in Peckham, her south London constituency, in September, saying it was not a true representation of her views.
In the original write-up of her comments at the town hall meeting, first highlighted by the Telegraph, Fahnbulleh was reported to have said: “If we continually prolong the time people have to wait for settlement, we can also prolong the process of building cohesion.” Her office said the remarks had been paraphrased, and would be rewritten to reflect a more accurate description of what she had told residents.
The government has proposed increasing the standard qualifying period for indefinite leave to remain from five years to 10, though it is likely to make concessions for some professions, including care workers.
The changes will also mean the pathway to permanent settlement for refugees is extended to up to 20 years, with reviews every 30 months. The government is yet to publish its long-anticipated final response to a consultation on the proposals – though the prime minister, Andy Burnham, has said he is committed to the bulk of the changes.
Tensions in the cabinet have already surfaced over the proposals. Last month the housing secretary, Angela Rayner, said in an interview that the proposed changes – if left unamended – would unfairly penalise care staff who had “moved their lives here to look after our loved ones”.
Fahnbulleh came to the UK as a child after fleeing the civil war in Liberia. Speaking to the Guardian’s Politics Weekly podcast last month, she admitted her family would have found Mahmood’s changes “tough”.
“I represent a constituency which is hugely diverse, where we’ve got first, second, third-generation immigrants, and how we navigate this landscape has been tough,” she added.
With Mahmood believed to be considering changing her plans, Fahnbulleh said she wanted the government to recognise migrants’ contributions.
“I think we ultimately need to get to an immigration system that has control … but actually then recognises the contribution that people have made. And if you’re in this country and you’re working – I say this as a refugee – and you’re doing your bit, and you’re part of your community, you’re working in our health service, then actually this should be a country that welcomes you,” she said.
“I wouldn’t be here if that wasn’t the way that we structured our immigration system. It has always been the case that this country is a welcoming country, and I’m sure it will continue to be that way.”
In her address to her Peckham constituents, Fahnbulleh said the debate had become “increasingly depressing and toxic”. She said there needed to be “a more compassionate immigration system. The asylum process is broken and needs reform. Ultimately, I want to see a system based on control and compassion, with a much stronger focus on integration.”
She continued: “Peckham is a good example of what can happen when communities are built deliberately, and people are given the opportunity to integrate and participate. If we continually prolong the time people have to wait for settlement, we can also prolong the process of building cohesion.
“We need to raise the level of the debate, challenge divisive political rhetoric and make the case for communities like the one we have in Peckham. That means talking about immigration with care, control and compassion.”

Republicans threaten to block Pentagon funding unless Trump takes tougher stance on Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Republicans threaten to block Pentagon funding unless Trump takes tougher stance on Russia
The Hill reports this, according to Ukrinform.
Several pro-Ukraine Republicans are outraged by Trump’s recent foreign policy decisions, including his agreement with Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel fuel into the United States. Reports that Ukraine’s use of the Starlink satellite system has been restricted and that intelligence sharing has been reduced have also sparked anger. Republicans are demanding that sanctions against Russia be reinstated and Starlink restrictions lifted, as the Pentagon and the Trump administration are rushing to secure increased funding.
Congressman Don Bacon warned this week that Congress would not support Trump’s legislative agenda unless he takes action against Russia’s military machine. Congressman Brian Fitzpatrick told The Wall Street Journal that the administration would face “consequences” unless it restores Ukraine’s access to satellite technology.
“The Administration’s decision to reduce intel sharing to Ukraine and access to Starlink equates to aiding the invader & the war criminal who bombs cities,” Bacon wrote on X. He also warned that the Administration’s policy was doomed unless it changed course.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s office declined to comment.
The publication notes that Hegseth has been seeking congressional approval for months of a record $1.5 trillion defense budget proposed by Trump. Last week, he also said the Pentagon would push for approval of a $350 billion supplemental funding package that has stalled in Congress over disagreements about how it should be funded.
The package provides funding for several of Trump’s priorities, including $17 billion for the Golden Dome homeland missile defense system, drones, and $47 billion to expand ammunition production. The Pentagon is also requesting another $36 billion for the Warrior Ethos program, which would invest in housing and infrastructure for service members.
Since Democrats are almost unanimously opposed to Trump’s war against Iran, Republican leaders will need the support of virtually every member of their House caucus to pass the package. Bacon believes the President’s soft policy toward Russia has alienated enough fellow Republicans to make it more difficult to pass defense funding and other legislative initiatives.
The agreement involving Russian diesel fuel has drawn particular criticism. Last week, a bipartisan group of lawmakers sent Trump a letter saying the deal violated, if not the letter, then the spirit of a new law imposing sanctions on Russia.
Some Republicans who spoke on condition of anonymity also criticized the President’s decision amid rising diesel prices, linking the situation to the war against Iran.
“He [Trum] needs to drop this decision. Like, A, it’s illegal. We passed a law saying there’s an energy ban on Russia. But at the same time, why did we get ourselves into a war in the Middle East to upset fuel prices? You want to lower fuel prices, figure that out,” an aide to one House Republican said.
As reported by Ukrinform, the U.S. President said that he did not want to make decisions that could push Russia away from peace talks and accused Volodymyr Zelensky of being “unwilling to end the war.”

Albania on fire: who’s behind the riots?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
17:33:43 UTC
02:33:43 KST

Albania on fire: who’s behind the riots?
Anti-government rioters have torched Albania’s education ministry and supreme court, as protests spread across the Balkan nation. Prime Minister Edi Rama is refusing to step down and blames the unrest on Russia. What’s really going on?
As of October 19, the Albanian capital of Tirana has been rocked by seven consecutive days and nights of rioting, while protests and clashes between demonstrators and police have been reported in the cities of Lezhe, Vlore, Elbasan, and Shkoder. A large group of rioters breached the perimeter of the education ministry in Tirana on October 14, setting the building on fire.
Running battles between demonstrators and police have broken out around the ministry on several occasions since. On October 19, hundreds of demonstrators pelted rocks at riot police, who responded with tear gas and rubber bullets. The previous night, offices of the Albanian Supreme Court were set on fire, and arson attacks on several police stations in the city were reported.
Some 500 demonstrators had been detained and 167 of them formally arrested as of October 17, according to Reuters. 295 people had been injured, including 196 police officers, as of October 19, according to Interior Minister Ervin Demo.
What do the protesters want?
The protests follow more than a year of unrest in Albania, which began when Rama banned TikTok in the runup to last March’s parliamentary elections, following similar measures inposed by the EU during every major election across the bloc since 2024. The ban was lifted in February of this year, but demonstrations broke out again in May after Rama’s government authorized the sale of protected wetlands to a development company operated by US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner.
The protesters demanded the resignation of Rama and his entire cabinet, and the cancellation of a planned twin-phase resort project on the wetlands and on nearby Sazan Island.
The protesters’ core demand – that Rama resign – remains unchanged. However, the movement is now calling for a root-and-branch reform of the entire Albanian establishment, with demonstrators accusing both Rama and opposition leader Sali Berisha of corruption. Unemployment, underfunding of schools, and declining living standards have also been cited by protesters as grievances.
What did Rama say about the protests?
Despite the repeated chants of “Rama resign” heard at the protests, Rama has claimed that the demonstrators do not oppose his government, but Albania’s “mission” of joining the EU.
“I am not being challenged,” he said in a video address on October 18. “The government is not being challenged, a government majority or a winning party in the elections is not being challenged but a path is being challenged, a mission is being challenged”
“Albanians need to think very clearly,” he continued. “Do they want this, do they want that, or do they want the EU?”
Rama has refused to resign, and blamed the protests on “foreign hands that do not wish for Albania to be at peace.” Back in June, Rama accused “the enemies of Albania and of Israel” of waging a “hybrid war” to stop the wetlands development. In two separate speeches on October 18 and 19, the embattled PM blamed the unrest on Russian philosopher Alexander Dugin and a “wave of Russian influence in the entire social media system,” and on “the Khomeiniist republic of Iran, the pinnacle of disinformation.”
Was Russia involved?
In short, no. Rama has not backed up any of his accusations, and they are being treated with skepticism and ridicule by demonstrators and opposition media. Albania’s Publik Media news outlet criticised Rama for “return[ing] to the Berisha, Russia and Iran alibi,” while Pamfleti, an investigative outlet, dismissed his claims as an “ignorant reaction to those protesting his misgovernance”
Even the US-run Radio Free Europe noted that Rama “did not present public evidence” to back up his allegations.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova has rejected Rama’s accusations. “No, Edi Rama,” she said on October 18, “it is the citizens of your country who have taken to the streets in protest.”
“This has all the hallmarks of the ‘highly likely’ British approach,” Serbian journalist Nebojsa Malic told RT on October 19, referring to British Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s failed attempts to blame the 2016 Brexit vote on Russia and a recent ‘terror plot’ at a US airbase on Iran. “We’ll just make an accusation and provide no evidence but say ‘oh it’s highly likely that Russia’s behind this’, and everybody is going to take it for granted.”
Rama is “doing this because he’s hoping it will stick,” Malic said. “He has nothing to lose. He’s seen plenty of leaders in western Europe essentially getting away scot free with covering for their malice and incompetence by blaming Russia.”
“Rama is just as opportunistic as [French President Emmanuel] Macron or any British prime minister in the last ten years,” Malic concluded. “They will say or do whatever, because they think that Russia is not able to defend itself.”
Why did Rama mention Israel?
Rama’s claim that “enemies of Albania and Israel” were behind this summer’s environmental protests stems from the involvement of Kushner in the wetlands project. A close associate of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Kushner has extensive family and financial ties to Israel. His investment firm, Affinity Partners, has funneled Emirati, Saudi, and Qatari cash into multiple Israeli businesses, including five arms manufacturers.
However, all available information suggests that the funding for Kushner’s Albanian projects comes from Albanian, American, and Qatari individuals and entities. Affinity Partners is leading the €1.4 billion Sazan Island project, while Kushner himself is a minority partner in the wetlands development.
Rama visited Israel and addressed the Knesset in January. Less than 24 hours later, Israel’s Channel 12 claimed that the Albanian PM had struck a deal with Netanyahu to accept up to 100,000 Palestinian refugees from Gaza. As speculation spread that the Palestinians would be resettled on land developed by Kushner, Rama clarified that no such deal had been, or would be, made.
Regardless, Rama’s close relations with Netanyahu are at odds with public opinion in Albania, where a 2024 poll found that 73% of the population believe that Israel should be sanctioned over its war on Gaza. Kushner is widely seen in Albania as representing Israeli interests, and Rama’s decision to amend environmental laws and grant “strategic investor” status to Affinity Partners has fueled accusations that the PM is placing Washington and West Jerusalem’s interests above Tirana’s.
Will there be an Albanian Maidan?
Some images emerging from Tirana – burning barricades, police officers set on fire with Molotov cocktails, and smouldering government buildings – are reminiscent of the scenes that played out during the 2014 ‘Maidan’ coup in Ukraine. However, Rama is in far less perilous of a position than Ukraine’s president, Viktor Yanukovich, was during the 2014 uprising.
Unlike the present unrest in Albania, the Maidan coup was planned and directed by foreign actors, namely the US State Department and the British embassy in Kiev. Rama, on the other hand, is a close partner of the EU and US, and neither Washington nor Brussels have backed the protesters. Instead, Rama has apparently been given carte blanche to squash the demonstrations, with columns of military vehicles seen entering Tirana between October 15 and 19.
The EU has condemned the use of violence by protesters, with the European Commission criticizing them for “arson, attacks on State institutions and the destruction of public and private property.” In a statement on October 18, the commission praised Rama’s progress toward EU membership and welcomed his “commitment that the right to protest will be protected.”
One week earlier, an EU delegation in Tirana said that Brussels was “aware of allegations of excessive use of force by the police against protesters and journalists,” adding that the government’s response to protests and riots “must remain within the law.”
The EU took a far more interventionist position in 2014, sending officials to meet with demonstrators in Kiev and endorsing protests even as they devolved into violent riots. Brussels prepared sanctions on Yanukovich, and once he had been toppled, it gifted an €11 billion aid package to Ukraine, which would elect the pro-EU Petro Poroshenko president months later.
The West is still firmly on Rama’s side, and he is unlikely to face any calls for resignation from abroad. However, he is still facing the most sustained public pressure campaign of his 13-year stint in power, and if the protests continue and more buildings burn, he may be left with no choice but to admit defeat and step down.

Mohajerani: Iran’s history of resistance reflects nation’s resolve to defend its sovereignty
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
17:30:19 UTC
02:30:19 KST

Mohajerani: Iran’s history of resistance reflects nation’s resolve to defend its sovereignty
TEHRAN – Iranian Government Spokesperson Fatemeh Mohajerani has praised the Iranian nation’s determination and ability to withstand external aggression, saying past wars demonstrate the country’s resolve to safeguard its independence, territorial integrity and national sovereignty.
Speaking at an event in Tehran on Monday, Mohajerani described the Sacred Defense—the term Iran uses for its 1980–1988 war with Iraq—as a lasting reminder of the nation’s resilience and ability to overcome formidable challenges despite limited resources.
Referring to Iran’s history of conflicts over the past two centuries, she said the Iranian people had achieved significant feats by relying on their determination and collective strength.
Mohajerani stressed that defending the country’s national interests and territorial integrity remained a fundamental principle, adding that Iran had not surrendered an inch of its territory in the wars following the victory of the Islamic Revolution in 1979. She described the preservation of the country’s territorial integrity as one of the Iranian nation’s greatest sources of pride.
The government spokesperson recalled that Iraq’s war against Iran began at a time when the country was grappling with internal challenges in the aftermath of the Islamic Revolution.
Despite those difficulties, she said, the Iranian people demonstrated their determination to defend the country and protect its sovereignty, refusing to compromise on their national rights.
The spokesperson also emphasized the importance of supporting the families of those killed in the war, saying the entire nation stood alongside them.
Mohajerani stressed that the capacity to withstand hardship was not limited by gender, pointing to the experiences of women who have endured profound personal losses while continuing to demonstrate strength and perseverance.

The Guardian view on France’s protests: a polarised country is in a perilous political moment | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
17:30:02 UTC
02:30:02 KST

In Emmanuel Macron’s book Revolution, published ahead of the 2017 presidential election that he went on to win, he promised to restore hope to a country that was losing faith in its future. As Mr Macron’s lame-duck second term enters its last phase against a quasi-insurrectionary backdrop of torched public buildings and looted shops, the failure of that political project appears total.
The worst scenes of urban violence for years overshadowed a weekend of protest that gravely undermined what is left of the French president’s authority. As police lost control of the streets, more than 2,000 shops were ransacked. Far-left groups targeted town halls and local buildings, and engaged in pitched battles with the police, whose disastrously heavy-handed response to last week’s high school protests has succeeded only in escalating tensions.
In a statement on Sunday evening, Mr Macron rightly condemned what he described as episodes of “unbridled violence”. On the far right, Marine Le Pen is already exploiting a national sense of dismay to present herself as the law-and-order solution to the crisis. But the shocking actions of a minority should not obscure the significance of the vast, peaceful demonstrations that took place throughout France on Saturday. Calls to unite the student protests and the yellow vest movement, which disrupted Mr Macron’s first term over cost of living issues, mobilised up to 800,000 people.
The root cause of the unrest is a widespread perception that France’s social contract is broken. The young feel let down by an underfunded and unequal education system, and are fearful of the future impact of AI and the climate emergency. As is increasingly the case across Europe, they no longer trust mainstream politicians to find answers. The scale of the weekend protests showed that gen Z’s discontent has merged with that felt in the country’s neglected towns and banlieues, which have suffered repeated economic shocks since the Covid pandemic.
The obtuse and stubborn response from Mr Macron has been to double down on a cost‑cutting agenda to reduce France’s public debt, in order to appease the financial markets. But in an era where the asset-rich have continued to flourish, and the wealthiest have done best of all, to argue that that there is no alternative to spending less on schools and healthcare won’t wash. The economist Thomas Piketty pointed out during last week’s student protests that the boom in private wealth means that, despite the size of its public debt, “France has never been richer”.
Mr Macron’s reckless decision to call a snap election in 2024, which cost him his majority, left him a diminished political figure. His biggest subsequent error has been to haughtily persist with the economics of austerity, despite clear evidence of deepening political polarisation and rising popular anger. With each week that passes, the social consequences appear more ominous, ahead of presidential elections in six months’ time.
The latest polls suggest that the far right’s huge lead is widening ahead of that contest. Meanwhile, the hard-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon continues to outscore progressive rivals, though the numbers suggest that he would heavily lose a runoff against Ms Le Pen. In an increasingly febrile atmosphere, France is heading towards a seismic reckoning in May. Alarmingly, the civil strife witnessed at the weekend may only be a foretaste of what is to come.

France announces first curfews as government grapples with unrest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
17:30:00 UTC
02:30:00 KST

France announces curfews as government grapples with unrest
PARIS - France announced partial curfews in Paris and other cities on Oct 19 after weekend demonstrations over soaring prices degenerated into some of the worst street violence in recent years.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu did not rule out imposing a state of emergency after the interior minister said police had “lost control”.
Tourists in Paris had a taste of the disruption on Oct 19 when they found the Louvre closed because of a small group of student protesters, while the US embassy in Paris urged American citizens to avoid the demonstrations.
Facing accusations that it failed to anticipate and respond to the violence, the government has vowed to re-establish order, while officials scrambled to contain public anger.
The unrest, erupting just six months before France elects a successor to President Emmanuel Macron, threatened to continue, with organisers calling for a new round of protests on Oct 24.
The authorities said partial curfews would be enforced from the evening of Oct 19 to the morning of Oct 20 in a number of cities including Paris, Lille and Lyon, to protect businesses.
In the capital, a curfew was ordered from 11pm, while demonstrations were banned from 8pm.
“I’m absolutely determined to restore public order”, Lecornu said.
Other European countries have also seen demonstrations over rising prices, with smaller clashes breaking out in Milan and Belgium over the weekend and protests simmering in Spain and Portugal.
Some half a million people turned out across France on Oct 17 to denounce the surging cost of living, a culmination of four weeks of protests that began with students demanding better conditions at high schools.
What started as peaceful demonstrations descended into violence in many cities, as masked groups attacked law enforcement, broke into public buildings and set some ablaze, looted shops, and set fire to cars, bicycles and scooters.
Listings for ‘stolen goods’
