Starshield restrictions  disrupt Ukraine’s drone operations 烏克蘭無人機突遭「星盾」斷網　美國掌控權引發疑慮
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:45:59 UTC
01:45:59 KST

Sudden restrictions on Starshield — SpaceX’s military-grade version of the Starlink satellite Internet service and the backbone of Ukraine’s drone operations and communication — alarmed the country’s military and government officials last week, with commanders reporting lost drones and disrupted missions.
The episode raised fresh questions about Ukraine’s reliance on the Starshield program and who controls access to it.
The episode added to tensions between Kyiv and Washington, a relationship already strained by US President Donald Trump’s reported deal with Moscow on Russian diesel imports, which Ukraine viewed as a betrayal.
Photo: Reuters 照片：路透
What is Starshield?
Starshield is SpaceX’s satellite program for governments and the military. Built on Starlink technology, it is designed for national security missions and includes secure communications, Earth observation and satellites equipped with specialized sensors. It also incorporates additional encryption and security measures for sensitive government operations.
The Starlink system uses thousands of satellites in low Earth orbit to provide broadband connectivity to terminals on the ground, including in areas where conventional Internet infrastructure is unavailable or damaged.
Unlike Starlink, Starshield is tailored to government requirements and can include dedicated satellites and special equipment.
Starshield “is the version where you have much higher speeds, you have better connectivity and it’s not available for civilians; it’s available only for the military,” said Olena Tregub, founder and secretary-general of Ukraine’s Independent Anti-Corruption Commission.
Tregub said reliable, high-speed connectivity was essential for Ukrainian military operations involving drones and units moving rapidly on the ground and in the air. Operators need clear, real-time video feeds to identify what is happening and make decisions, she said.
Ukraine’s increasingly digital battlefield also relies on systems such as Delta, which helps manage and share battlefield data. Transmitting large volumes of information requires fast and reliable connections, Tregub said.
“It’s not just about being able to connect. We need to make sure that this speed is there, that it’s not reduced,” she said, adding that standard civilian Starlink access alone would not meet the military’s needs.
The US government is a major Starshield customer. SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk said last week that the US government owns and controls the system, with decisions about its use resting with the US military and, ultimately, the president. His remarks have fueled questions about who was responsible for the latest restrictions affecting Ukraine.
Photo: EPA 照片：歐新社
How are Starlink and Starshield linked?
Starlink and Starshield are different services, but they share much of the same technological foundation, including SpaceX’s satellite engineering and capabilities.
The difference lies in the customer, security needs and end purpose. Starlink provides commercial services, while Starshield is designed for government and national security missions.
The distinction is not always straightforward. Starshield can draw on the wider Starlink satellite network and related infrastructure, while also drawing on separate and dedicated satellites and systems.
Initially developed for commercial use, Starlink became a crucial communications tool after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Its terminals have helped Ukrainian authorities, emergency services and military units stay connected despite Russian attacks on communications infrastructure.
On the front line, the service supports communications between military units and enables operations requiring a continuous connection between drones and their operators, including missions in which operators need to receive video while aircraft are in flight.
The Starlink and Starshield services are not interchangeable, even when they rely on overlapping technology.
For Ukraine, restrictions affecting particular terminals or military services do not necessarily mean the entire Starlink network has been switched off, neither does the continued operation of civilian terminals guarantee that specialized military connectivity will remain available.
The incident nevertheless reinforced the need for backup communications. Ukraine’s army was preparing alternative solutions, although they would be more expensive and less effective.(AP)
SpaceX旗下的「星盾」（Starshield）—即軍用版的「星鏈」（Starlink）衛星網路服務，是烏克蘭無人機作戰及通訊系統的重要支柱，但這項服務上週突然被限速，讓烏克蘭軍方及政府官員陣腳大亂。多名指揮官通報，部分無人機失聯，軍事任務也受到干擾。
這起事件再次引發外界對烏克蘭依賴星盾系統的疑慮，並質疑星盾的使用權限究竟是誰在掌控。
這也加劇了基輔與華府之間的緊張關係。此前，美國總統川普據報與莫斯科達成協議，開放進口俄羅斯柴油，已使美烏關係陷入緊張，烏克蘭更將這項協議視為背叛。
星盾是什麼?
星盾是SpaceX專為政府及軍方開發的衛星計畫，以星鏈技術為基礎，主要用於國家安全任務，包括安全通訊、地球觀測，以及搭載特殊感測器的衛星。星盾也採用額外的加密及安全措施，以支援涉及敏感資訊的政府行動。
星鏈系統利用數千顆部署在地球低軌道的衛星，為地面終端設備提供寬頻網路連線，涵蓋範圍包括傳統網路基礎設施無法使用或遭破壞的地區。
與星鏈不同，星盾是依照政府需求量身打造的服務，可包括專用衛星及特殊設備。
烏克蘭獨立反貪腐委員會（Independent Anti-Corruption Commission）創辦人兼秘書長歐蓮娜‧特雷古布表示：「星盾是速度更快、連線品質更好的版本，而且不對一般民眾開放，僅供軍方使用」。
特雷古布表示，對於涉及無人機，以及在地面與空中快速移動部隊的烏克蘭軍事行動而言，可靠的高速網路連線至關重要。操作人員需要清晰的即時影像，才能掌握現場情況並做出決策。
烏克蘭日益數位化的戰場，也仰賴「Delta」等戰情系統協助管理及共享戰場資料。特雷古布指出，傳輸大量資訊需要快速且可靠的網路連線。
她說：「這不只是能不能連上網路的問題。我們必須確保連線速度夠快，而且不會被降速」。她補充說，僅靠一般民用星鏈服務，無法滿足軍方需求。
美國政府是星盾的主要客戶。SpaceX創辦人兼執行長伊隆．馬斯克上週表示，美國政府擁有並控制星盾系統，其使用決策由美軍負責，最終決定權則在總統手中。馬斯克的說法也引發外界質疑，烏克蘭的星盾最近遭到限速，究竟是誰該負責。
星鏈與星盾有何關聯?
星鏈與星盾是兩種不同的服務，但兩者共享許多相同的技術基礎，包括SpaceX的衛星工程技術與相關功能。
兩者主要的差異在於服務對象、安全需求及最終用途。星鏈提供商業服務，而星盾則專為政府及國家安全任務設計。
不過，兩者的區別並不總是很明確。星盾可以利用更廣泛的星鏈衛星網路及相關基礎設施，同時也能使用獨立的專用衛星與系統。
星鏈最初是為商業用途開發，但自2022年2月俄羅斯全面入侵烏克蘭以來，已成為烏克蘭至關重要的通訊工具。儘管俄羅斯持續攻擊烏克蘭的通訊基礎設施，星鏈終端設備仍協助烏克蘭政府機關、緊急救援單位及軍事部隊維持通訊。
在前線，星鏈支援軍事部隊之間的通訊，並讓無人機與操作人員持續保持連線以執行任務，因為有些行動需要操作人員在無人機飛行時接收即時影像。
即使星鏈與星盾使用部分相同的技術，兩種服務仍無法相互取代。
對烏克蘭而言，這項區別十分重要，因為特定終端設備或軍事服務受到限制，並不一定代表整個星鏈網路都已關閉。同樣地，即使民用終端設備仍能正常運作，也不保證軍方專用的通訊服務能持續使用。
儘管如此，這起事件再次凸顯建立備援通訊系統的必要性。烏克蘭軍方正準備其他替代方案，但這些方案的成本將更高，效能也較差。
（台北時報林俐凱編譯）

Students need more than answers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:45:57 UTC
01:45:57 KST

In my English classroom at an elementary school in Taitung County, a nod does not always mean understanding. I can ask whether everyone understands, receive reassuring nods and then watch a child wait for classmates to begin before attempting the task. This happens every day.
If nodding were a reliable assessment tool, we could finish the curriculum by Wednesday — just in time for Sports Day.
That gap between appearing to understand and being able to proceed should inform how Taiwan’s schools evaluate artificial intelligence (AI). A clear explanation is valuable, but its educational worth becomes visible in what a student can do.
When I know a student needs support, I pair them with a classmate who understands the task. I become a facilitator, while the helper takes on a similar role. The helper explains, then lets their classmate try, offering guidance along the way.
The work remains the student’s own. The purpose is to help a classmate move through a difficult task, while preserving the opportunity to think through and attempt the task.
This creates two responsibilities. The student must engage with the work. The helper must make an explanation useful to someone else. Knowing an answer becomes the starting point for communication, rather than its conclusion.
My responsibility continues throughout the process. I watch who explains, who attempts the task and where guidance is needed. A correct answer matters, but so does the route by which the pair reach it. If one student supplies the answer and the other merely records it that tells me little about understanding.
There is another distinction to make. Hesitation can signal unfamiliar vocabulary, unclear instructions or uncertainty about how to begin. It does not automatically identify the problem. The teacher must investigate, and remain willing to revise an initial judgement.
These routine decisions are easily overlooked in discussions about educational technology. An explanation can be accurate and still fail to meet a learner’s immediate need. Additional information might help, but sometimes the child needs an opportunity to try with someone nearby.
This leads me to a question for Taiwanese schools considering AI: Does the assistance preserve the student’s opportunity to think, attempt and explain?
A system that supplies a finished response might make an exercise easier to complete. A system used to offer a hint, suggest another explanation or prompt a further attempt could serve a different purpose.
Schools should examine that difference when deciding how a tool should be used in a lesson, if at all. The same principle should shape teacher training. Demonstrating how to generate teaching materials is useful. Teachers also need opportunities to consider what happens after those materials reach children, how misunderstanding becomes visible, when assistance is appropriate and how to check whether a student can proceed.
Peer support is no automatic solution either. Knowing the material does not make a child an effective guide. The helper needs direction, and both students need the teacher’s attention. My classroom offers a perspective on these decisions, rather than a formula for every school.
The wider lesson is that assistance should develop a learner’s capacity to act. In elementary-school classrooms, the value of AI should be judged partly by whether it supports that work. The helper who explains and then allows a classmate to try illustrates something important: Useful knowledge must leave room for the other person’s effort.
AI might know the answer. The educator must still see the person behind the question — and help students learn to see one another.
Casper J.H. Keller teaches English and drama at an elementary school in Taitung County and has more than 25 years of international teaching and leadership experience.

Liberte, Egalite, Misery? Why France is burning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:45:50 UTC
01:45:50 KST

Anyone walking along the boulevards of Paris on Sunday afternoon would have sensed the “shame and anger” described by French President Emmanuel Macron after a weekend of rioting.
Smashed-in storefronts, boarded-up windows and charred makeshift barricades hinted at the looting that hit about 1,500 stores across the country. Dozens of armored cops were still standing guard, shields raised, after a night when 500 people were taken into custody in the French capital alone. Amid the chaos, one lone bystander with a broom quietly sweeping up broken glass.
It is not only France that is feeling the heat. Anger about rising inflation, from energy prices to housing costs, has led to clashes in Italy and Portugal. It might also cost US President Donald Trump the US midterm elections given the impact of his folly in the Strait of Hormuz on oil prices, even as he gleefully tries to deflect attention by pointing fingers at Paris.
Still, France’s propensity to descend into unrest has become scarily regular, as has the inability of Macron’s administration to get a grip. Which begs the question: Why is one of the rich world’s biggest public spenders again on fire? This is after all a highly redistributive country that has racked up an extra 1 trillion euros (US$1.12 trillion) of borrowing since 2019. Yet surveys indicate that French on average lack 500 euros a month to comfortably cover their outgoings, making them vulnerable to sudden changes in their economic situation — and likelier to protest.
On one level, the sparks that lit the flames this time around included multiple short-term political failures that echo the “yellow vest” riots of 2018. The authorities clearly were not expecting more than 500,000 people to take to the streets nationwide, let alone the thousands of looters in Marseille.
The mayor of Limoges, whose town hall was broken into and gutted by fire, has called for more resources for police force he described as outgunned by far-left opportunists. The government’s inability to engage with or defuse earlier protests by high schoolers — driven by a lack of fiscal headroom to throw money at the problem as bond yields, and hence state borrowing costs, rise — fueled the fire.
However, the discontent that provided the kindling was already there. One big reason is that French public spending is allocated in a very lopsided way.
Compare the France of 2024 with that of 1974 — the last year it balanced the budget — and there has been very little change in spending on public services such as security, the courts or education as a percentage of GDP. It has risen by just 0.1-0.3 points, former government adviser Antoine Foucher said.
The biggest beneficiaries, as usual in the West, are pensioners. Spending on them has jumped by about 6.5 points, with successive governments prioritizing a generous and long retirement over the future of young people entering education and the workforce. Almost one-third of France’s education budget goes on pensions, which might explain why teachers’ wages are below the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development average.
Alongside the frustrations of underpaid public servants are signs that adding more jobs in the private sector — the focus of Macron’s labor-market reforms — increasingly does not pay. That 500 euro monthly gap in people’s monthly outgoings is hard to fill via the career ladder as lower productivity, declining education standards and an innovation lag drag wages down while ever-higher social charges eat into take-home pay. The French National Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies has estimated that an employer raising a minimum-wage worker’s salary by about 440 euros would result in a take-home gain of only 100 euros. It is perhaps no coincidence that it took a tax-free bonus of about 500 euros to quell the 2018 yellow vests’ anger. Le Monde estimates that the French median wage has risen 22.8 percent since 2017, outpaced by inflation of 23.4 percent.
That does not excuse the weekend’s violence. French purchasing power is slowing down rather than screeching into reverse. Yet the combination of grievance politics, intergenerational unfairness and an inescapable sense of decline is what makes France feel so fragile despite its size, and its still strengths — such as a nuclear-powered electricity grid and first-class engineering talent. It also makes compromise harder, with the new yellow vests bemoaning low wages and high taxes alongside the masked mobs spray-painting “ACAB,” an acronym for “all cops are bastards.”
With Macron a spent force, the question now is next year’s presidential election. The sight of towns and cities on fire would doubtless create new supporters for far-right leader Marine Le Pen. Her extreme-left opponent Jean-Luc Melenchon is being seen as the instigator of the mayhem on the streets. In a vote dominated by cost-of-living and security fears, the far right holds several cards — including the Trumpian promise of putting hundreds of euros into people’s pockets through cutting payments to the EU.
Still, six months is an age in politics. Le Pen’s plans involve billions in new spending and lack credibility, Bloomberg Economics said. Voters are slowly starting to understand that rising state debt is a problem. Meanwhile, center-left politician Raphael Glucksmann, who has ruled out an alliance with Melenchon, is enjoying a poll surge of his own.
However, what is missing in this crowded race, as elsewhere in Europe, is honesty on the reforms that are needed — from politicians and the aging electorates that are blocking inescapable change.
Lionel Laurent is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist writing about the future of money and the future of Europe. Previously, he was a reporter for Reuters and Forbes. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.

Workers rally in Taipei, demanding better wages
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:45:50 UTC
01:45:50 KST

Hundreds of workers yesterday rallied outside the Presidential Office Building in Taipei, demanding higher wages, increased employer pension contributions and clearer profit-sharing rules, amid a wave of strikes and strike authorization votes across Taiwan.
Participants representing dozens of labor unions from across Taiwan gathered on Ketagalan Boulevard before marching through nearby streets past the Legislative Yuan and returning to the boulevard.
Taiwan Solidarity Front Confederation of Trade Unions chairman Ho Cheng-chia (何政家) criticized what he felt was an outdated labor pension system.
Photo: CNA
Introduced in July 2005, the new labor pension system consists of retirement accounts for individual workers and requires employers to contribute at least 6 percent of an employee’s salary to the account every month.
The employee can voluntarily contribute an additional 6 percent to increase the amount saved. The total built up in the fund can be collected in a lump sum or as a monthly annuity upon retirement as long as contributions have been made for at least 15 years.
Ho said that it was time to increase the employer’s minimum 6 percent obligation, saying it was too low to ensure adequate retirement savings and that an increase would help make up for 21 years of insufficient contributions.
“We hope to raise it to 9 percent first and then gradually to 15 percent,” he said, adding that employers’ annual retirement costs per worker under the old pension system were estimated at about 12 percent of wages.
Government figures show that about 7.87 million workers had contributions made under the new system as of July, while an estimated 115,000 were exclusively under the old system as of December last year.
The new labor pension system is one of the two retirement plans that most workers in Taiwan qualify for.
The other is the “old-age benefits” under the labor insurance system. The current labor insurance premium is 11.5 percent of salaries, capped at NT$45,800 per month, with employers paying 70 percent.
Because of the relatively low salary cap, retirement benefits under the insurance system are limited to less than US$900 a month.
Both systems are run by the Ministry of Labor’s Bureau of Labor Insurance.
Ho also urged amendments to Article 29 of the Labor Standards Act (勞動基準法) to establish clearer requirements for distributing company profits to employees, saying that economic gains should benefit workers beyond the technology sector.
Chunghwa Telecom Workers’ Union chairman Teng Ke-lien (鄧克?) said its Taoyuan and Kaohsiung branches had passed strike authorization votes, with other branches set to hold votes in succession.
The union, which launched the vote to demand higher pay amid what Teng described as record company profits, has about 20,000 members across 26 branches, representing nearly all company employees.
“Striking is just a means, not our goal,” Teng said, urging management to “respond positively” to workers’ demands, adding that a walkout was unlikely before year-end.
Under Article 35 of the Labor Union Act (工會法), employers are barred from retaliating against workers for participating in union activities or labor disputes.
Responding to the protest, the ministry said it remained “open” to raising employer pension contributions, but added that changes required “careful evaluation.”
It also highlighted environmental, social and governance assessment incentives for listed companies that voluntarily increase their contribution rates.
The ministry also pointed to minimum wage reviews and collective bargaining incentives to promote pay raises and profit-sharing, urging employers to consider raising existing employees’ salaries as the monthly minimum wage increases from NT$29,500 this year to NT$30,900 next year.

No. 1 TPBL draft pick Hinton debuts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:45:47 UTC
01:45:47 KST

Adam Hinton, the first overall pick in the TPBL draft, scored 16 points in his regular-season debut on Sunday, but his team, the Kaohsiung Aquas, squandered a 20-point lead, losing 115-114 to defending champions the Formosa Dreamers.
Playing with a protective mask due to a nasal fracture sustained during practice, Hinton added seven rebounds in the Aquas’ season opener at Taichung Intercontinental Basketball Stadium.
He scored his first professional points on two free throws less than a minute into the game, before making his first field goal on a driving layup. He finished the opening quarter with eight points and had 14 by halftime, helping the Aquas build a 63-49 lead.
Photo: CNA
The Aquas almost secured a winning start when Hinton drew a foul on a drive and sank both free throws with about 41 seconds remaining, putting the team ahead 114-113.
However, with about seven seconds left on the clock, Dreamers guard Lin Chun-chi came back with a midrange jumper. Grant Basile missed the Aquas’ final shot, sealing the home team’s comeback victory.
Hinton, a 23-year-old Cornell University graduate who was the TPBL’s first overall pick on July 16, said he regretted the loss and would review his performance, with the hope of improving before his next game.
The intensity of his debut game was as expected, he said, adding that he felt comfortable seeing several familiar faces on the opposing team.
Basile led the Aquas with a game-high 36 points and 14 rebounds. Lin and Brandon Gilbeck shared the Dreamers’ scoring lead with 23 points apiece, with Gilbeck collecting 15 rebounds.
The Dreamers won their first TPBL championship last season after overcoming a 3-1 deficit in the finals with three back to back victories, securing the franchise’s first domestic professional league title.
The TPBL is one of Taiwan’s two professional basketball leagues, alongside the P.League+.
Its seven teams each play 36 regular-season games, split evenly between home and away fixtures.
Four teams advance to the playoffs, with the top three qualifying directly, while the fourth and fifth-place finishers contest a play-in series for the remaining berth.

Rays within a game of heading to World Series
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

16:45:46 UTC

Yandy Diaz has brought the Tampa Bay Rays to the verge of their first World Series trip since 2020.
Diaz had three hits, including a double, and scored the first run in Sunday’s 3-1 win over the Cleveland Guardians that gave the Rays 3-2 lead in the AL Championship Series.
Diaz has hits in seven of eight postseason games and is batting .314 with four doubles, a home run and an .847 OPS as the Rays’ leadoff hitter.
Photo: AFP
“I’m probably a little biased, but Yandy is one of my favorite players to watch,” Rays closer Bryan Baker said. “When he gets going, we’re a different team with the way he works at-bats.”
Game 6 is today in St. Petersburg, Florida, where the Rays are 58-27 during the regular season and playoffs. A potential Game 7 would be Tuesday in the same stadium.
“Momentum is big in this sport and we have it — and we’re going to keep it,” Tampa Bay outfielder Jonny DeLuca said. “Once bats get hot, they say it’s contagious and it’s true. It carried over from yesterday.”
Diaz went 5 for 10 in the last two games with a homer, two RBIs and three runs. The 35-year-old led the AL with 180 hits in the regular season and earned his second All-Star selection. He has played in a franchise-record 33 postseason games.
“I’ve said it for many seasons, as he goes, we go,” Rays manager Kevin Cash said. “We talk about leaders on the team and how they go about their business. And what he does at the top of our lineup, it ignites everybody. He comes up and comes up with a big hit.”
Diaz doubled against Parker Messick in the first and scored on DeLuca’s bases-loaded walk.
“I’m just trying to get on base as much as I can, I’m not necessarily counting the hits,” Diaz said. “A positive mindset is the biggest thing. Just being aggressive with our pitch selection, just jumping on good pitches. Both of those things.”

Group calls for penalties for e-cigarette possession
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:45:46 UTC
01:45:46 KST

The Alliance on Obligatory Education yesterday urged the Legislative Yuan to pass an amendment to the Tobacco Hazards Prevention Act (菸害防制法) that would provide a legal basis for issuing penalties for possessing e-cigarettes.
The act already prohibits the manufacture, importation, sale, supply, display, advertising and use of e-cigarettes.
The Health Promotion Administration (HPA) this year proposed to amend the act to add possession to that list, which was approved by the Executive Yuan and submitted to the legislature for review.
Photo: Rachel Lin, Taipei Times
“The number of disposed e-cigarette devices cannot be used to directly infer the actual circulation volume of e-cigarettes, nor does it mean the problem has been solved,” alliance president Wang Han-yang (王瀚陽) said yesterday, referring to the HPA’s e-cigarette disposal bins set up across the country.
The agency last week said it had collected about 633kg of e-cigarettes since the collection scheme began on Sept. 8.
If the HPA-proposed amendment is approved, e-cigarettes would be confiscated, but no fines would be issued within a one-month grace period, after which people found possessing them would face a fine of NT$30,000 to NT$100,000, Wang said.
An HPA survey from last year found that more than 40,000 adolescents use e-cigarettes, with 2.1 percent of junior-high school students and 5.1 percent of high-school and vocational school students saying them used them.
E-cigarettes can be used as delivery systems for illicit substances, such as etomidate, classified as a Category 1 narcotic in Taiwan, Wang said.
Tobacco use among young people is often driven by factors such as family influence, peer pressure and marketing, Taiwan Medical Alliance for the Control of Tobacco secretary-general Guo Fei-ran (郭斐然) said.
Minister of Health and Welfare Shih Chung-liang (石崇良) said the ministry hopes the legislature would pass the amendments as soon as possible.
As for opposition parties’ concern about not having enough law enforcement personnel to inspect and seize e-cigarettes, he said the ministry has discussed the issue with the Ministry of Education and local governments, and that funding would be allocated to address the shortage.

NTHU to explore research reactor development with NuCube
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:45:42 UTC
01:45:42 KST

National Tsing Hua University (NTHU) signed an agreement with US nuclear microreactor developer NuCube Energy yesterday to explore replacing the university’s aging Tsing Hua Open- pool Reactor (THOR).
The university said the cooperation will assess technology, research applications and deployment feasibility to sustain nuclear education, research and medical services.
Potential applications include boron neutron capture therapy, a cancer treatment, and isotope production, according to an NTHU statement.
Photo: Lo Pei-de, Taipei Times
University President W. John Kao (高為元) and NuCube CEO Cristian Rabiti signed the agreement at a news conference in Taipei, an exploratory step toward possible deployment of a NuCube microreactor to replace THOR, which began operating in 1961 and is scheduled to be decommissioned in 2040.
Speaking afterward, Yeh Tsung-kuang (葉宗洸), dean of NTHU’s College of Nuclear Science, described the partnership as mutually beneficial: the university wanted to understand NuCube’s reactors, while its expertise could help expand their research and medical applications.
Rabiti told the news conference that NuCube planned its first deployment for the end of 2029.
"Today we signed; from tomorrow the real work will start," he said. "We have a lot to do together."
NTHU hopes to install a reactor within two years after NuCube achieves commercial operation in the United States, the university said. Yeh said that contact with Taiwan’s Nuclear Safety Commission was already underway.
NuCube is separately working with Idaho State University on a proposed research and test reactor intended for education and technology demonstration rather than electricity generation.
NTHU said it would invite Taiwanese manufacturers to participate in equipment and component supply, and could share deployment experience and provide technical advice to interested companies.
The agreement follows a podcast interview released last Friday in which President William Lai (賴清德) said restarting existing nuclear reactors would require assurances of safety, a solution for nuclear waste and public consensus.
"We should not exclude any energy source because of ideology, nor disregard environmental sustainability for short-term benefits," Lai said.
Existing reactor restart procedures should proceed and ultimately be decided by professionals, he added.
On workforce development, Yeh said NTHU’s Institute of Nuclear Engineering and Science attracted 66 applicants for 11 places this year, describing the interest as unprecedented in the past decade.
Previously, attracting even 11 applicants had been difficult, he said, attributing the increased interest to a changing policy climate.

Photo: EPA
However, growing confidence in their squad depth a year out from the World Cup could outweigh the concerns.

The Sydney win was another endorsement of Rennie’s up-tempo attacking game, with New Zealand rediscovering the speed, ambition and clinical finishing that were hallmarks of their back-to-back World Cup wins in 2011 and 2015.
“The Greatest Rivalry” tour of South Africa failed to live up to its billing but All Blacks fans may be glad to look back on it as a great turning point if World Cup glory awaits.

Thawing permafrost makes town’s water undrinkable
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:45:41 UTC
01:45:41 KST

Residents of a remote town in Norway that is in one of the fastest-warming places in the world have been told they must no longer drink tap water due to heavy metal contamination that scientists have linked to the thawing permafrost.
Longyearbyen, in the archipelago of Svalbard, gets its main drinking water supply from a 2.5km dammed lake called Isdammen, or “ice pond.” Higher temperatures as a result of the climate crisis have thawed permafrost, leading to newly exposed bedrock leaching metals into the pond.
Longyearbyen, about 1,300km from the north pole, is warming at between five and seven times the world’s average rate, with autumn temperatures rising at up to 4oC a decade.
Heavy metal contamination of the water supply is likely to be linked to two factors, researchers say: the thawing of permafrost — rock-hard ground that remains frozen all year apart from a so-called “active layer” that thaws in summer — and the geology of the former mining town.
“The combination of the thawing permafrost and the shale bedrock, which contains a mineral called pyrite, or fool’s gold, is causing contamination of its water supply,” said Marjolaine Verret, a permafrost expert and associate professor in Arctic geology at the University Centre in Svalbard.
When pyrite came into contact with water and oxygen, it oxidized and generated acidity, she said.
“The acid produced can now leach heavy metals from these rocks into the waterways. The issue we’ve been having here in Longyearbyen is manganese, but other contaminants can be leached out from the rocks,” she added.
The municipality, Longyearbyen lokalstyre, first alerted its 2,600 residents after manganese levels in the water supply were found to be 25 times higher than the 50 micrograms per liter recommended by the Norwegian Institute of Public Health, in September last year.
Longyearbyen Mayor Terje Aunevik said that while drinking water quality had never been good, due to sediment, the manganese levels had “gone ballistic.”
Prolonged exposure to high levels of manganese can cause neurological problems, particularly in children and infants.
Emergency, temporary measures were rolled out, including the installation of a central tank of free purified water, filtered by the local brewery, for residents to refill containers at the local supermarket, and an investigation was launched.
Manganese levels have since dropped, but earlier this year sulfate and nickel levels were found to exceed recommended drinking water limits. As a result, the ban remains in place.
Aunevik said that while manganese levels were “not dangerous,” government guidelines had to be followed.
The drinking water crisis had created a lot of “noise,” with some residents angry at the inconvenience, he said.
The mayor, who has commissioned an investigation into water quality, said a “completely new water mains supply” might be needed.
Potential solutions being considered were installing a filtration system to Isdammen and having a desalination plant as a backup, or the other way around.
Either way was “extremely expensive” and, due to the extreme temperatures of Svalbard, with water temperatures often below zero, would include technical challenges, Aunevik said.
“In Norway, where we have always taken for granted that we can drink the water from the tap, it is challenging to start thinking that we need to carry our water like we do now. Other small communities should be precautious and start thinking of what to do if it happens to their sources,” Aunevik said.
Verret and other scientists have warned that the contamination of water sources in Longyearbyen could be a foretaste of what is to come for Arctic communities.
“These ingredients [bedrock rich in pyrite and heavy metals] and thawing permafrost are present in other parts of the arctic so this could be a first example of how climate change can impact freshwater, for example in northern Canada and Alaska,” Verret said.

NHI bill could bring more harm than good
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:45:41 UTC
01:45:41 KST

The Legislative Yuan on Friday passed the third reading of amendments to Article 22 of the Senior Citizens Welfare Act (老人福利法), which were pushed through by the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and Taiwan People’s Party (TPP).
The move was touted as an expansion of National Health Insurance (NHI) premium subsidies for people aged 65 or older. However, lawyer Lai Chung-chiang (賴中強) said that the hastily passed amendments removed the legal basis for subsidies covering NHI copayments or other medical expenses not covered under NHI for elderly people who cannot afford them.
It is not the additional public spending that should be raising eyebrows, but rather that the legislature appears to have broadly expanded premium subsidies for people aged 65 or older while undercutting other subsidy supports for the most acutely disadvantaged among them.
A legal basis for the administration of subsidies is not just a nice-to-have measure. The original Article 22 of the act was explicit in listing three categories of subsidies: NHI premiums, copayments and medical expenses not covered by NHI. Downstream administrative regulations are based on this legal authorization, so removing two of the three categories in the parent law means that some of the regulatory provisions for subsidy enactments might no longer be legally viable.
Legislators should have ensured that existing protection would remain in place before amending the law, and that social welfare groups and government agencies are not left scrambling to find a fix afterward. Legislation must not be thrown around for campaign propaganda, and lawmakers cannot delete a few words and act like nothing has happened.
This amendment could cost the central government an estimated NT$40 billion (US$1.23 billion) annually. Yet having an income tax rate below 20 percent — the bracket which the original amendment targets — does not necessarily mean someone cannot afford to pay NHI premiums. Conversely, elderly people struggling to make ends meet might be unable to afford even regular medical copayments, let alone necessary expenses such as dentures that are not covered by NHI.
If the KMT and TPP genuinely want to broaden access to healthcare, they should prioritize safeguarding existing protections for low and lower-middle-income people, rather than exempting more people from paying premiums and leaving a gap in subsidies for disadvantaged groups in the process.
With their combined legislative majority, the KMT and TPP are certainly empowered to advance their policy agendas. However, majority rule does not justify bypassing legal scrutiny, nor should the risks be left for government agencies to bear.
The priority should not be to celebrate the amendment’s passage at its third reading, but to immediately publish a comprehensive assessment of its legal and policy implications, and confirm whether subsidies for disadvantaged people can continue. If necessary, the Executive Yuan should seek reconsideration of the bill or an amendment that corrects the problem.
Genuine welfare for elderly people does not mean allowing more people who can afford to pay to save on their premiums while stripping those least able to pay of legal protections. The greatest absurdity of the KMT’s and TPP’s actions is that, despite all the noise about their commitment to caring for older people, they might have ended up cutting protections for precisely those who need them the most.
Elliot Yao is a reviewer.

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:45:40 UTC
01:45:40 KST

The Taiwan High Prosecutors’ Office yesterday indicted four people, including a retired military police captain already facing separate espionage charges, for allegedly helping Chinese contacts pay Taiwanese service members for leaking classified military information.
Retired captain Yu Cheng-yu (尤正宇), who was previously indicted for allegedly accepting tether cryptocurrency in exchange for military secrets, allegedly collected cryptocurrency on behalf of Chinese contacts, converted it into cash and distributed payments to service members who leaked classified information. He allegedly earned NT$430,403 from the scheme, prosecutors said.
The other defendants are two retired servicemen surnamed Lee (李) and Sen (森), and a coast guard member surnamed Tsai (蔡), who allegedly provided a bank account to receive payments. Prosecutors urged the court to impose heavy sentences on all four. The case was yesterday transferred to the High Court.
Photo: CNA
Yu allegedly used a cryptocurrency wallet in his name to receive digital currency from Chinese contacts between March and October 2024, prosecutors said.
He sold the cryptocurrency to dealers for cash and deposited the proceeds into accounts belonging to Lee and Tsai, allegedly concealing the source of the funds, they said.
Yu previously served as a captain at the Reserve Command of the Ministry of National Defense’s All-Out Defense Mobilization Agency. In a separate case, he allegedly accepted tether from a Chinese Internet user using the screen name “Pleasant Voice” (聲音好聽), after seeking money to repay loans.
From early 2022 through the end of 2023, Yu allegedly photographed classified military documents with his cellphone at least five times and sent them to the contact via Telegram in exchange for 4,998 tether tokens with a total value of about NT$150,000. The Ciaotou District Prosecutors’ Office previously indicted him in that case and requested a heavy sentence.
Investigators found that Lee and Sen also allegedly collected and passed military intelligence to China while serving in the armed forces.
Lee allegedly engaged in the activities from around March or April 2024 through August last year, while Sen allegedly did so from around October or November 2023 through March last year. Both have since left the military.
Tsai, a coast guard service member, allegedly lent his bank account to Sen to receive payments from Chinese contacts for leaking classified information. Lee allegedly received NT$884,000, while Sen and Tsai received a combined NT$515,000, prosecutors said.
Prosecutors directed the Investigation Bureau to investigate the case. The four defendants allegedly contravened the Criminal Code of the Armed Forces (陸海空軍刑法), the National Security Act (國家安全法), the Classified National Security Information Protection Act (國家機密保護法) and the Money Laundering Control Act (洗錢防制法), among other laws. The alleged offenses also included leaking and gathering national defense secrets under the Criminal Code and corruption-related offenses under the Anti-Corruption Act (貪污治罪條例).
Prosecutors said Lee and Sen were serving military personnel when the alleged offenses occurred, while Tsai was a public official. The three allegedly participated in the scheme for personal gain, jeopardizing national security, military operational security and national defense interests.
Yu allegedly played a key role by helping Chinese contacts channel payments through an alternative means. Prosecutors also accused him of offering evasive explanations and showing no remorse after the alleged offenses.

Reputation warfare now targets ordinary people
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:45:37 UTC
01:45:37 KST

Attacks on one’s reputation used to be the price that celebrities paid for fame. However, now it is a hazard of ordinary life. Anyone with any standing to lose is vulnerable. If you have an online presence, the damage can spread much further and faster than the truth. Run-of-the-mill bad publicity or harassment might dent your confidence or cause annoyance, but if you become the target of a technologically augmented campaign aimed at destroying your reputation, you could lose much more.
Welcome to the world of reputation operations (rep-ops) — deliberate attempts to erode a target’s credibility and isolate them socially and professionally by strategically amplifying false or maliciously curated information. A rep-op does not aim to persuade one person to distrust another. The primary objective is to change the target’s reputation across networks where credibility, access and influence are the currency of exchange. Success might include colleagues of the victim becoming more guarded, friends pulling back and employers growing suspicious. Reputation is social, and so is the process of destroying it.
Rep-ops use some of the same tactics as Soviet and Russian disinformation and psychological operations (psyops), which were a menace long before the rise of social media. During the Cold War, the Soviets’ Operation Infektion disinformation campaign used fake news to weaken trust in the US and its institutions. In the 1980s, the KGB spread a false claim that the US had covertly engineered the AIDS virus and then blamed Africans for the disease, all part of an effort to tarnish the US’ image as a trustworthy power and sow racial divisions within its borders.
Beginning in 2014, Russia’s Internet Research Agency carried these techniques onto social media. The goal this time was to influence how Americans perceived one another, their political leaders, and their institutions, and ultimately to interfere with the 2016 US presidential election. Far beyond spreading false information, these psyops sought to shape people’s perceptions, attitudes and behavior by creating fake American identities and accounts, posting politically polarizing content, buying advertisements, organizing online groups and staging rallies.
A similar form of manipulation is now used in rep-ops. Just last year, a network of anonymous social-media accounts was mobilized to amplify a false sexual rumor about an 18-year-old University of Mississippi student. Her tragic story confirms that any ordinary person can now be thrust into the limelight, simply because someone wanted it to happen. Reputational warfare is not new, of course. Retaliatory smearing is a common response from powerful institutions that come under attack. If you aim at the king, you should prepare for what might follow, even if you do not miss. After Sinead O’Connor tried to call out child abuse by Catholic clergy, channeling her own household abuse experience into her heart-rending version of Prince’s Nothing Compares 2 U, she was pilloried. It would be another decade before reporters at the Boston Globe exposed the scale of the problem and the Church’s institutional cover-up.
However, O’Connor was a major international star in the 1990s, the face of one of the most iconic music videos of the MTV era. Today, similar reputational costs are imposed on ordinary people through networked amplification campaigns that move between large social-media accounts and anonymous burner accounts, reaching mass audiences in ways that only celebrities were exposed to before.
Rep-ops always create a spectacle, but they do not necessarily require many spectators. They can even occur offline. After Shaakirrah Sanders, a black law professor at the University of Idaho, raised concerns about racial bias, the law school’s administrators told faculty members that her conduct was “unprofessional, demeaning and potentially dishonest.” They said she had “slandered” colleagues and then encouraged complaints against her. As one dean joked to another: “The administration strikes back.”
The administration then doubled down on this reputational signaling in a manner designed to undercut Sanders’ standing with faculty and students, assigning her to courses she did not want to teach, summarizing her teaching evaluations unfavorably and voting against her tenure. A federal judge later characterized these actions as retaliatory, resulting in a US$750,000 settlement. Reputation is a form of social capital that affects a person’s employment, income, social and professional networks, and access to institutions. Destroying a person’s credibility is sometimes just the work of an obnoxious online troll. However, sometimes it is a calculated defensive move by those facing allegations of wrongdoing. Unable to refute the evidence, they try to refute the accuser. Still other times, it is a tool for winning the competition for attention and influence.
Rep-ops pose a vexing problem, because they demonstrate that one’s standing can be irreparably harmed even with false information. Research on the “continued influence effect” shows that misinformation can shape our thinking even after it has been disproven, and a study this year found that repetition itself increases perceived truth.
Although we have all grown more accustomed to spotting fake news and asking whether something we see online could really be true, rep-ops pose a more subtle problem. Is information being circulated to inform us, or, more dangerously, to change how we and others across the network around us treat another person? Because a loss of reputation is hard to rebuild, and false information hard to correct, rep-ops are greatly damaging to their targets. Once the manipulation and falsehoods are exposed, they might ricochet back on their organizers. However, the damage would have already been done. Such campaigns are socially corrosive, further hollowing out our sense of shared truths amid the broader barrage of disinformation, fake news and psyops.
Carla Norrlof is distinguished professor of global political economy, finance and security at the University of Toronto.

UEFA gives Infantino 2-week deadline to release documents on FIFA governance: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:44:46 UTC
01:44:46 KST

Halis Sunnetci
19 October 2026•Update: 19 October 2026
UEFA has given FIFA President Gianni Infantino until Nov. 2 to release key documents and answer outstanding questions concerning FIFA's governance and decision-making, BBC Sport reported Monday.
In a letter obtained by BBC Sport, UEFA General Secretary Theodore Theodoridis said FIFA had failed to address "a number of fundamental questions" about its governance and decision-making following Thursday's FIFA Council meeting.
"Others remain unanswered, and the information and documentation requested have not been provided," the letter said.
The letter included eight pages of questions concerning several FIFA decisions, including the FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) private investment proposal, the FIFA Peace Prize and the suspension of a ban on US international Folarin Balogun during the World Cup.
The demand comes despite Infantino's apology at Thursday's FIFA Council meeting for mistakes in communication and consultation over the abandoned FFE proposal.
The proposal would have created a FIFA-controlled company to manage the commercial rights to FIFA competitions, including the World Cup, with a minority stake sold to private investors.
"The withdrawal of FFE, the acknowledgement of mistakes and the announcement of 'potential governance reforms' do not answer how the relevant decisions were taken or why the FIFA Council was not involved at the appropriate stage," the letter said.
UEFA warned that the outstanding questions could not be deferred until the next FIFA Council meeting and that future reforms could not replace accountability for past decisions.
Infantino is seeking re-election at the FIFA Congress in Rabat, Morocco, in March 2027, amid growing scrutiny of his leadership and calls for his resignation that have persisted since the summer over the now-abandoned FFE proposal.

Bulgaria Courts Chinese Business With New Investment Agreements
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:44:37 UTC
01:44:37 KST

Presidential Candidate Iliana Yotova: The Status Quo
Iliana Yotova will walk into a polling station on October 25 as the only candidate who already holds the job everyone else is competing for
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev has pledged to deepen economic cooperation with China, presenting Bulgaria as a gateway to the European market, while agreements pursued by his government have raised questions about transparency, economic benefits and alignment with European Union policy.
“We see prospects in our relations for building better connectivity between Europe and China, with Bulgaria playing a key role as a gateway to Europe in terms of transport, energy, and digital connectivity. Bulgaria offers excellent conditions for investment in sectors such as electric vehicles, energy, agriculture, and high technology,” Radev said at the start of talks with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi and his delegation at the Council of Ministers.
The meeting took place during Wang’s official visit to Bulgaria, which followed stops in Croatia and Montenegro as part of a tour of Azerbaijan and the Balkans. Radev said he expected the visit to give fresh momentum to bilateral relations and produce practical results. He also welcomed Wang back to Sofia, recalling that the Chinese foreign minister had last visited 11 years earlier.
Radev described the visit as important for both countries and the wider region, expressing confidence that it would expand their longstanding friendship. He recalled that Bulgaria was the second country in the world to recognize China and establish diplomatic relations.
The Bulgarian prime minister also referred to his 2019 visit to China, when he was president, and his discussions with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The two countries adopted a declaration establishing a strategic partnership during that visit, which Radev described as a significant milestone in bilateral relations. He said the partnership should now extend beyond trade to joint projects in key economic sectors.
Wang said China wanted to act as a reliable and responsible partner in Bulgaria’s modernization. “China and Bulgaria share a deep, traditional history of cooperation. We are ready to work with our Bulgarian friends to deepen mutual political trust and deliver more tangible, substantive joint projects that will benefit the peoples of both nations,” he said.
The Chinese foreign minister congratulated Bulgaria on forming its government and conveyed greetings from China’s president and prime minister. He praised Radev’s strategic vision and pragmatic approach, saying he expected Bulgaria to make significant progress under his leadership. Wang also recalled the 2019 declaration on strategic partnership and said Beijing was confident that the new Bulgarian government would take bilateral relations to a higher level.
Wang added that China sought friendly relations with countries worldwide and aimed to build a community with a shared future for mankind. He was scheduled to meet Bulgarian Foreign Minister Velislava Petrova later that day.
During a separate meeting at the Presidential Administration on Dondukov Boulevard, President Iliana Iotova and Wang discussed closer cooperation between Bulgaria and China, as well as the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East. Both said active diplomatic efforts were needed to resolve the conflicts.
“We are living in a time with more conflicts than at any point since the Second World War. Today’s world requires greater trust and responsibility. We must leave our children a secure world in which they can develop their potential,” Iotova said, according to the Presidential Press Secretariat. She also highlighted the damage wars cause to national economies and social systems.
Wang referred to Iotova’s address to the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York in September, which focused on peace and the importance of resolving differences through dialogue.
The two officials also reviewed the 2019 strategic partnership declaration signed by Radev and Xi, agreeing that it had helped advance bilateral ties. Iotova and Wang identified further opportunities for cooperation in the economy, trade, education and culture.
Wang described his meeting with Iotova as evidence of the close friendship between the two countries. He said the formation of a regular Bulgarian government after the April parliamentary elections provided a stable basis for strengthening the strategic partnership and speeding up joint projects already underway. He thanked Iotova for her continued support for relations with China.
Iotova raised the possibility of a direct air connection between Sofia and Beijing, saying it could boost business contacts and cultural ties. Bulgaria also expressed hope that its agricultural products would gain easier access to the Chinese market.
The renewed diplomatic engagement comes as Radev’s government pursues closer economic ties with Beijing, a policy that experts say warrants scrutiny in light of China’s commercial objectives and the EU’s efforts to rebalance trade relations.
In early September, Deputy Prime Minister and Economy Minister Alexander Pulev visited China to sign memorandums intended to strengthen economic ties between Sofia and Beijing. He met Chinese Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang and Vice President Han Zheng, with discussions focusing on new investment opportunities, particularly in the automotive industry.
“We have a strong political will to open a new chapter in bilateral relations with China,” Pulev said during the visit.
The last high-level Bulgarian delegation to visit China had traveled there in 2019, when Radev was president. Experts say he now appears determined, as prime minister, to further deepen his government’s engagement with Beijing.
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang’s visit on October 19 comes as the EU seeks more balanced trade relations with China. The bloc’s trade deficit with Beijing exceeds 1 billion euros a day.
Rumena Filipova, chair and founder of the Institute for Global Analytics, told Svobodna Tochka that both the Bulgarian government and Beijing wanted to expand economic ties. She said China was seeking a production presence within the EU and viewed Bulgaria as a “gateway to Europe.”
Pulev signed four memorandums during his visit, all of which had previously been approved by the Council of Ministers.
The first, between Bulgaria’s Ministry of Economy, Investments and Industry and China’s Ministry of Commerce, provides for a bilateral working group on investment cooperation to support economic and investment relations. It identifies the automotive and energy sectors as priorities and envisages an information-sharing mechanism covering investment legislation, regulations and policies.
A second memorandum was signed with Shanghai Grand Sun Hydrotherapy System Ltd., a supplier of hydrotherapy and spa equipment, including hydromassage bathtub systems and other water-treatment solutions.
The third agreement involves Hangzhou Bosom New Materials Technology Co., Ltd., which researches, develops, produces and sells modified engineering plastics. The company has included Bulgaria in its plans to expand international production capacity. The Bulgarian Investment Agency is to assist with site selection, contact with relevant institutions and the establishment of local production operations.
The fourth memorandum concerns cooperation between the Bulgarian Investment Agency and China Global Advisory. Although the Council of Ministers had approved it in advance, there was no public confirmation that it had been signed during the delegation’s visit. Svobodna Tochka requested confirmation and a copy from the Ministry of Economy and Industry but had received no response by publication.
An intergovernmental Bulgarian-Chinese Commission for Economic Cooperation is already operating, and China is one of Bulgaria’s largest export partners outside the EU.
Radev also inaugurated a second Chinese auto-parts manufacturing plant near Plovdiv on September 8. Later that month, reports emerged that Chinese automaker Great Wall would reopen its vehicle assembly facility near Lovech.
The plant, operated by Litex Motors and Great Wall, began operating in 2012 as the Chinese company’s first European production base. Manufacturing stopped in 2016, and Litex Motors entered insolvency proceedings the following year.
Filipova said the earlier venture had not delivered the expected benefits to Bulgarian industry. “The capital was provided primarily by the Bulgarian side, while the cars were merely assembled in Bulgaria. In other words, the expectations at the time—that this would somehow generate significant added value for Bulgaria’s industrial capacity—never materialized,” she said. She argued that China nevertheless benefited from the arrangement by gaining easier access to the EU market.
Late last year, a Chinese company specializing in energy efficiency established its European headquarters in Vidin.
Chinese investment in Northwestern Bulgaria had previously been attempted in 2011, when state-owned Tianjin Agribusiness Company launched an agricultural project in the municipality of Boynitsa. The plan covered around 20,000 decares of land, but the company withdrew from the area a year later.
Its activities in Bulgaria continued through the associated company Hera Agro, which subsequently carried out agricultural operations in Southern Bulgaria. In 2017, industry publication Agri.bg reported that Hera Agro was among the country’s largest recipients of agricultural subsidies.
Filipova questioned whether Chinese investment had produced clear benefits for Bulgaria, citing experiences in the country and elsewhere. She said research, data and case studies pointed to negative consequences from some Chinese projects, particularly in infrastructure and industry.
According to the Balkan Investigative Reporting Network, Chinese investment in the Balkans totaled 32 billion euros between 2009 and 2021, including 10.3 billion euros in Serbia.
Such investments in the region have frequently been linked to major infrastructure projects, debt and environmental concerns. In Montenegro, the Bar-Boljare motorway brought the country close to bankruptcy. Construction is continuing with European funding, although Chinese companies remain involved. In Serbia, the Linglong tire factory has faced allegations of forced labor and breaches of environmental standards.
Filipova warned that the opacity of agreements and contracts with China created risks, particularly when commercial deals formed part of the Chinese Communist Party’s strategic objectives. She called for all agreements and their clauses to be made public and for economic assessments to be conducted before contracts were signed, establishing whether and how they would benefit the local economy.
Svobodna Tochka asked the Ministry of Economy and Industry to provide details of Bulgaria’s commitments, the expected economic benefits and the transparency of the arrangements, as well as the full texts of the signed memorandums. No reply had been received by the time of publication.
The memorandums state that they comply with Bulgarian and European legislation, but their push for closer ties with China comes as EU institutions call for a more guarded approach to Beijing.
On October 8, 44 European industry associations urged EU member states to act immediately against what they described as “unfair Chinese trade practices.” They warned that these practices threatened production in the bloc and risked further job losses. The signatories included organizations representing the metallurgical, chemical and automotive industries.
The European Parliament adopted a recommendation on October 7 calling for a stronger, more principled EU policy toward China that maintains dialogue while protecting European interests. The recommendation identified excess industrial capacity in China, state subsidies and restricted access to the Chinese market for European companies as key challenges.
Members of the European Parliament said relations with China had reached a critical point because of Beijing’s economic practices and its position on Russia’s war against Ukraine. They called for reduced strategic dependence on China, tighter investment controls and safeguards for critical technologies, infrastructure and supply chains.

The United States will not revoke temporary protection for Ukrainians who fled because of the war for now
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

The United States will not revoke temporary protection for Ukrainians who fled because of the war for now
Kyiv • UNN
Ukrainians with TPS status can remain in the United States and work legally for now. The protection has been preserved for approximately 240,000 registered Ukrainians.
Immigrants from Ukraine and Sudan can retain their Temporary Protected Status in the United States for now. The U.S. Department of Homeland Security announced this on Monday—the day the protection was due to expire. Reuters reports, UNN writes.
Details
A representative of the U.S. Department of Homeland Security said that a notice regarding Ukrainians who have Temporary Protected Status (TPS) would be published "at the appropriate time." Until then, their immigration protection will remain in effect.
Temporary Protected Status allows people who are already in the United States to remain in the country and work legally if armed conflicts, natural disasters, or other extraordinary circumstances are occurring in their homeland.
According to Reuters, about 240,000 Ukrainians who fled because of the war registered for this status in the United States.
What is known about the decision
The temporary continuation of the protection came amid the strengthening of the immigration policies of U.S. President Donald Trump's administration.
In September, his administration allowed Salvadoran citizens with TPS to retain their protection. Earlier, the authorities began procedures to cancel it for citizens of Haiti, Venezuela, Somalia, Yemen, Syria, and other countries.

Art Basel Paris, Metallica lead this week’s global culture calendar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19

Dilara Hamit
19 October 2026•Update: 19 October 2026
From contemporary art in Paris and design showcases in Lagos to Metallica concerts in Las Vegas and jazz performances in Melbourne, cities worldwide will host a wide range of cultural events this week.
 
Art and exhibitions
Art Basel Paris will return to the Grand Palais from Friday through Sunday, bringing together more than 200 galleries from 41 countries and territories.
The fair will be divided into three sections covering established galleries, emerging artists and specially curated presentations.
Its public program will extend across nine Paris landmarks from Wednesday, featuring works by Robert Indiana, Tracey Emin, Niki de Saint Phalle and Yinka Shonibare.
Turkish contemporary artist Kutlug Ataman’s video installation Kuba will be displayed at the Chapel of the Petits-Augustins at the Beaux-Arts de Paris. The work is built around interviews with residents of an Istanbul neighborhood and examines identity, community and displacement.
In New York, the Metropolitan Museum of Art will open Designing the Gilded Age: Drawings from the Studios of Louis C. Tiffany on Thursday.
The exhibition brings together nearly 120 works, including rarely displayed and newly conserved drawings that reveal the creative process behind Tiffany Studios’ stained-glass windows, lamps, mosaics and interiors. It will remain open until Feb. 7.
Design Week Lagos will continue across the Nigerian city until Sunday. Held under the theme Making a New Africa, the festival includes exhibitions, trade showcases, talks and training programs exploring African design, manufacturing and sustainable economic growth.
 
Film and television
The 21st Rome Film Fest will enter its final week before concluding on Sunday at the Auditorium Parco della Musica and other venues across the Italian capital.
The program features international competition titles, public discussions, special screenings and tributes. This week’s events include a Monday screening of Make Some Noise: Mano Negra!, focusing on the French-Spanish rock group, and a Friday program celebrating pioneering women in early cinema.
 
Concerts
Metallica will continue its Life Burns Faster residency at the Sphere in Las Vegas with two performances Thursday and Saturday. The band has prepared separate setlists for the two shows as part of its No Repeat Weekend format, with visuals created for the venue’s wraparound display and immersive sound system.
At Walt Disney Concert Hall in Los Angeles, Andrew Bird will perform with the Los Angeles Philharmonic on Friday. The venue will also present A Symphonic Ballet with Elim Chan on Thursday, Saturday and Sunday, while French organist Lucile Dollat will give a recital Sunday.
Dubai Opera’s program will begin with a symphonic concert by the Gipsy Kings on Thursday. Indian singer-songwriter Prateek Kuhad will bring his Full Moon Chamber Tour to the venue Saturday, followed by the classical program Romantic Masters on Sunday.
The Melbourne International Jazz Festival will also continue through Sunday. Grammy-winning pianist and composer Kris Davis will perform with students from the Melbourne Conservatorium of Music on Wednesday, while South African trumpeter and vocalist Mandisi Dyantyis will appear at the JazzLab on the closing night.
At the Sydney Opera House, the 70th-anniversary staging of the musical My Fair Lady will take place Friday and Saturday. The Sydney Symphony Orchestra will also be performing John Williams’ Star Wars: The Empire Strikes Back score live alongside screenings of the film from Wednesday through Saturday.

Reignited Yemen war brings back prospect of UAE intervention
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:42:33 UTC
01:42:33 KST

Breadcrumb
As Saudi Arabia battles the Houthis in Yemen, could the UAE once again play a role?
As fighting rages on between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthi rebels, reports have emerged of possible intervention by the United Arab Emirates to help their Gulf neighbour.
The UAE officially announced the end of its involvement in Yemen in December 2025, after the Saudi-led military coalition bombed a southern separatist arms depot in Mukalla, and backed the Yemeni government's call for Abu Dhabi's forces to leave the country.
The episode marked a new low in relations between Riyadh and Abu Dhabi, who had both entered Yemen's conflict to oppose the Iran-backed Houthis, who control the Yemeni capital Sana'a and most of northern Yemen.
Less than a year later, however, it appears that the UAE could once again join Saudi Arabia against the Houthis.
How would the UAE re-enter Yemen's war?
Citing unnamed sources in Yemen, The Guardian reported on Saturday that the UAE had agreed to resume payments to some separatist factions it had previously backed in the south, in order to help the anti-Houthi effort.
Maysaa Shujaa al-Deen, a senior analyst at the Sanaa Centre for Strategic Studies, says that while it is unlikely that the Emiratis will jump back in militarily, they could help Saudi Arabia logistically.
"They have experience, which they have through their military intervention in Yemen, and experience in fighting the Houthis and being in charge of some important areas, including the coast and Aden," Shujaa al-Deen told The New Arab.
Shujaa al-Deen notes that it was also "take time" for the separatist Southern Transitional Council (STC), which was backed by the UAE, to mobilise in the south.
Meanwhile, questions hang over whether the southern separatists will take their fight beyond the borders of old southern Yemen.
"There are generally two positions int he south - one is that they should engage in the war before it comes to the south, and the other is that we are not going to engage unless the Houthis attack the south - and this second position is that of most of the STC," Shujaa al-Deen said.
What would be the UAE's demands?
Prior to disengaging from Yemen in late 2025, the UAE had backed southern separatist factions, most notably the STC, which led an offensive into against government forces in the Hadramaut region at that time.
The takeover was one of several moves by the separatists that led to the Saudi-backed call for the Emiratis to leave Yemen.
Shujaa al-Deen says that while Abu Dhabi has backed the separatists, its own interest is not to see the complete separation of the south from the rest of Yemen, as this would reduce UAE leverage in the country. Rather, any Emirati intervention would come with guarantees that "that their political agenda will be enforced in return".
"Aidarous al-Zubaidi has shown up for the first time since the crisis of December/ January, so this is one of the indications that the UAE's conditions [are in play]," Shujaa al-Deen said, referring to the STC leader who fled to Abu Dhabi after the fallout from the Saudi-UAE clash in January 2026.
Al-Zubaidi had attempted to establish STC control across southern Yemen, and called for a referendum on independence, leading to the demand that the UAE disengage from Yemen.
Al-Zubaidi made a video appearance last week after a long hiatus, drawing speculation of an attempted return to the political scene.
If re-engaged in Yemen, the Emiratis would also like to influence which factions are able to rule in the country, Shuja al-Deen adds.
"Another condition would be to oppose the Muslim Brotherhood, who have a really strong presence there, particularly in Taiz and Marib," she said.
Are relations cooling between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh?
The prospect of Abu Dhabi re-entering Yemen's war has also been viewed as a signal of a detente with Riyadh.
Shuja al-Deen says that the presence of a common enemy -- the Houthis -- would defuse tensions between Saudi Arabia and the UAE, adding that relations between them also deteriorated after the Saudi-Houthi truce in March 2022.
However, she notes that Yemen is just one theatre in which Riyadh and Abu Dhabi have clashed.
"They disagreed on Israel, Sudan, Somalia, also there is economic competition between them. So any agreement would only be about Yemen, not a comprehensive agreement between the two countries."

Bonfires of electric bikes burn in Paris riots
Oct 19 - As protests rock France, the sight of electric bikes burning has become commonplace in the unrest.
In Paris, black smoke and flames rose over piles of the e-bikes at the weekend. Elsewhere in the city, a protester threw an e-bike onto a burning car.
Shared-mobility operator Dott said in a statement to Reuters on Monday that about 300 of its electric bikes were destroyed and 120 severely damaged in Paris during the nationwide protests on Saturday, which turned violent in several cities. It has 6,000 bikes in the city.
The company also said 80 vehicles, including bikes and scooters, were destroyed in Bordeaux and 30 to 40 scooters in Lyon. It estimated the damage at around €400,000 ($450,000).
Lime said some of its shared bicycles and scooters in Paris were destroyed or damaged during the protests, with the company losing about 6% of its Paris fleet.
Ahead of the demonstrations, Lime said it worked with police to remove vehicles from designated protest routes and restricted parking and riding in several high-risk areas, adjusting those measures over the weekend as the situation evolved.
Velib, whose bikes are docked, rather than parked on pavements, said in a report in Le Parisien newspaper that around 5% of its fleet of 18,000 e-bikes was destroyed or damaged at the weekend. It did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Reuters.
E-bikes often use lithium-ion batteries, which can ignite and produce intense fires that spread rapidly and produce toxic smoke.
There was no indication that e-bike operators were specifically targeted during the protests over the cost of living and underfunded public services that have descended into riots and looting.
However, with thousands of bicycles available across Paris streets and docking stations, they proved readily accessible to protesters, with many used to build barricades or to set on fire. REUTERS

Halis Sunnetci
19 October 2026•Update: 19 October 2026
The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) announced Monday that it expects to issue its ruling at the end of November on Senegal's appeal against the decision to award Morocco the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) title.
In a statement, the Lausanne-based court said a hearing concerning the Senegalese Football Federation's appeal against the Confederation of African Football (CAF) and the Royal Moroccan Football Federation was held behind closed doors on Oct. 8.
"The Panel have begun and continue their deliberations," CAS said.
The dispute stems from the AFCON final on Jan. 18 in Rabat, where Senegal defeated hosts Morocco 1-0 after extra time following a chaotic conclusion to regular time.
With the match goalless in stoppage time, Morocco were awarded a penalty following a Video Assistant Referee review, prompting Senegal's players to temporarily leave the pitch in protest.
Play resumed after a lengthy interruption, with Morocco's Brahim Diaz subsequently having a Panenka-style penalty saved by Senegalese goalkeeper Edouard Mendy.
Pape Gueye then scored in extra time to secure a 1-0 victory for Senegal.
However, on March 17, CAF's Appeal Board overturned the result following a Moroccan appeal, ruling that Senegal had forfeited the match by leaving the field without authorization.
The board awarded Morocco a 3-0 victory and the continental title, citing Articles 82 and 84 of the competition's regulations.
Senegal appealed the decision to CAS on March 25, seeking to overturn CAF's ruling and be reinstated as African champions.

Search under way for four soldiers missing after gang attack in Haiti
UN official warns of escalating violence in Haiti as security personnel face retaliatory attacks by armed gangs.
The Salvadoran ambassador to the United Nations Security Council (UNSC) has condemned the ambush of four aviation technicians from her country by armed gangs in Haiti.
“During the attack, the criminal groups used firearms and explosive devices, setting the vehicle on fire,” Egriselda Lopez told a UNSC meeting on Haiti on Monday.
International forces in the violence-torn Caribbean nation are trying to find the four Salvadorans who went missing after gangs attacked their armoured vehicle on Sunday.
The soldiers from the United Nations-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF) managed to flee the burning vehicle in Croix-des-Bouquets, a commune north of the capital, Port-au-Prince.
It is the first major attack on the international force since it began operations earlier this year.
Security and elections
The ambush underscored growing risks as gangs retaliate against security operations, according to Carlos Ruiz Massieu, the special representative for the UN Secretary-General for Haiti.
Gangs have fought to increase their influence in the country, particularly since the assassination of President Jovenel Moise in 2021 left a leadership vacuum in the government.
An estimated 70 percent of Port-au-Prince is currently under gang control, as are many thoroughfares in the country.
Massieu told the UNSC meeting that, between July and September, more than a thousand people were killed and over 100 abducted as a result of the gang violence.
In a bid to restore stability, Haiti has sought to hold its first round of national elections in nearly a decade.
But elections have been repeatedly delayed, amid concerns about violence. Earlier this month, the country announced it was postponing the vote indefinitely, after setting a date earlier this year for December 13.
“The repeated announcement of electoral dates without a true assessment of their credibility, of their feasibility, only serves to weaken credibility with Haitian institutions,” Massieu told the session.
He warned that security gains alone cannot deliver lasting peace.
GSF officially began operations on June 1, but has so far operated only in a limited capacity.
Jack Christofides, the GSF special representative in Haiti, said it has deployed over 2,000 personnel from six countries, but the force remains well below its authorised strength and needs equipment, logistics and funding to expand operations.
After Sunday’s attack, the GSF said it is assessing the situation and has advised residents to stay indoors.
The area where the armoured vehicle was struck is controlled by gangs, including Kraze Barye, led by Vitelhomme Innocent and 400 Mawozo, led by Lanmo Sanjou. Both gang leaders have been sanctioned by the UN and US.
“Armed gangs have overrun large parts of Port-au-Prince, the capital, employing tactics including murder, kidnapping and sexual violence amid widespread impunity,” said a UN Security Council report last month.
