POW campaigners keep up fight after cabinet limits compensation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
15:55:36 UTC
00:55:36 KST

POW campaigners keep up fight after cabinet limits compensation
Gordon Darroch
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Campaigners for the widows of former Japanese prisoners of war have said they will keep fighting for compensation after the Dutch government said only surviving partners would be entitled to receive their spouses’ unpaid wages.
Long-term care minister Mirjam Sterk announced last Friday that the partners of civil servants and servicemen who were held captive following the invasion of Indonesia in 1942 would receive 42 months’ back pay, covering the period until the liberation in May 1945.
But Sterk said only widows who are still alive when the compensation scheme is launched on February 1 next year, all of whom are well into their nineties or older, would receive the payouts because a more extensive ruling would be “too complicated”.
The government has also cut the total size of the fund from the €50 mln announced in its last spring budget statement to €11.5 mln, on the basis that only a few hundred widows of the 40,000 men who were captured by the Japanese still survive.
The decision follows decades of campaigning for victims of the camps to be given the same treatment as Dutch government employees who were forced to work in Germany during World War II.
Moluccans
They include Moluccans who later fought on the side of the Dutch during the Indonesian liberation war and were subsequently persecuted by the independent government, prompting them to flee to the Netherlands.
Earlier this year prime minister Rob Jetten apologised to the Moluccan community for the way they were treated when they arrived in the 1950s.
Peggy Stein, of campaign group Indisch Platform 2.0, called for the ruling to be backdated to include widows who were alive when parliament approved a motion by farmers’ party leader Caroline van der Plas on the issue last April.
“That was when these people heard they were going to get their wages, but some of them have died in the meantime,” she told Dutch News.
Stein added that the cabinet appeared to have pushed through the ruling without waiting for parliament to debate the extent of the compensation scheme first.
“We still had to talk to MPs and had asked for a committee debate, but never had a reply,” she said.
“This isn’t about care or morality, it’s purely and solely about the technical settling of a case for the lowest possible cost.”
No official records
Sterk said it was “practically impossible” to compensate relatives of former camp inmates who had died because the government had no central records, but Stein said her campaign group had compiled its own list of detainees and could provide documentation showing they worked for the colonial administration.
“I have a list, but they say the SVB [Dutch social security bank] is legally not allowed to use it,” she said. “But if they have €50 million to spend, why can’t they find other parties to distribute the money who are able to work with us?”
Stein said she was not calling for the regulation to be scrapped, but it should be backdated to 2025 or 2015, when the government first acknowledged that the POWs were in its service. Prior to that it had argued that the colonial government in Indonesia was a separate entity.
Stein said the campaigners would continue to press the cabinet to compensate all victims of the Japanese occupation, including those who were no longer alive. “We have made a promise to these elderly people, we have signed a petition, and we are going to keep fighting for it,” she said.

Israel said Monday it would gradually reopen a vital commercial supply route into the war-battered Gaza Strip after a dayslong suspension, even as fresh Israeli strikes killed at least five Palestinians and the blockaded enclave's population continued to struggle with severe shortages of essential goods.
COGAT, the Israeli military agency overseeing humanitarian affairs in Gaza, said the decision followed reports from merchants that Hamas authorities had withdrawn demands for payments of 10,000 shekels ($3,225) per truck.
The agency acknowledged that the merchants' accounts had not been independently verified but said shipments would resume gradually, with priority given to food and other essential supplies ahead of winter.
Gaza's Government Media Office on Thursday rejected allegations that it imposes taxes or fees on commercial trucks entering the enclave, accusing Israel of using the claims to justify restrictions on goods and calling for the daily entry of 600 trucks.
Israeli authorities also announced tighter financial oversight, requiring payments to be made through documented bank transfers. Merchants found to have paid Hamas would be excluded from the commercial shipment system.
Hamas rejected the characterization of the payments as mandatory fees, saying the 10,000-shekel contributions were voluntary donations from financially better-off Palestinians to a national fund supporting vulnerable families in the war-ravaged territory.
The decision comes amid a deepening humanitarian crisis in Gaza, where much of the population remains dependent on aid after three years of genocidal Israeli attacks, repeated displacement and severe restrictions on the entry of food, medicine and other necessities.
Although a U.S.-brokered cease-fire reached in October 2025 halted the heaviest fighting, Israeli forces have continued carrying out deadly attacks across the besieged Palestinian territory.
Palestinian health officials said at least five Palestinians, including a 14-year-old boy, were killed Monday in separate Israeli strikes in Gaza City and Khan Younis.
The Israeli military did not immediately comment on the latest killings.
According to Gaza health authorities, approximately 1,500 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli fire since the October 2025 cease-fire. Israel says four of its soldiers have been killed by Palestinian resistance fighters in Gaza during the same period.
Despite the cease-fire, Palestinians continue to face deadly Israeli attacks, widespread destruction and severe humanitarian hardship, with access to food and other basic necessities remaining heavily dependent on Israeli-controlled supply routes.

NATO plans to buy jammers that black out GPS for 11 km
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
15:53:36 UTC
00:53:36 KST

- NATO’s Allied Command Transformation plans to buy six portable kits that jam satellite navigation and drone control and video links for training.
- The request for proposals is planned for Oct. 26, with bids due Nov. 30 and contract award expected Dec. 11, 2026.
NATO plans to buy six portable kits that can jam satellite navigation signals and the radio links drones use for control and video, so its trainers can expose ships, aircrews and drone operators to realistic interference during exercises.
Headquarters Supreme Allied Commander Transformation, the alliance command in Norfolk, Virginia, that leads NATO’s training and modernization work, intends to issue a request for proposals on Oct. 26, 2026, according to a notice posted by the U.S. Commerce Department. Bids are due on Nov. 30, and NATO expects to award a fixed-price contract on Dec. 11, using a sealed bidding procedure under its common funding rules. The kits could also be used in operations.
NATO said modern forces depend on satellite navigation for positioning and timing in everything from ships and aircraft to drones and precision-guided weapons, and that jamming or spoofing those signals can leave vehicles without a reliable position or time reference. Small and medium drones are especially vulnerable, since interfering with their navigation or control signals can push them off course, force them to hover, land or fly home, or cut the operator’s video feed. The alliance said its training and evaluation teams need equipment that can create controlled interference on demand, so they can see how crews detect, report and adapt to it.
Each kit must be light enough for one or two people to carry and ready to use within 30 minutes, and must work from a ship, rigid inflatable boat, uncrewed surface vessel, vehicle, tripod or fixed ground site. It must be able to jam the signals of all four major satellite navigation systems, America’s GPS, Russia’s GLONASS, Europe’s Galileo and China’s BeiDou, across multiple frequency bands at once, with each band selectable on its own.
The kits also need to jam drone video links in the 5 to 6 GHz band and drone control links at 400 to 500 MHz and 2 to 3 GHz, as well as several cellular and other bands. Operators must be able to set the area where satellite navigation is denied anywhere from 500 m to 11 km (6 nautical miles), in steps of no more than 500 m, and vendors must provide tables predicting how far the effect will reach at altitudes up to 10,000 ft (about 3,050 m), so exercise planners can keep it away from civilian air traffic.
NATO wants the system run from a laptop with a user interface simple enough for non-specialists, with both omnidirectional and directional antennas and at least four hours of operation on battery power. It must also be controllable remotely anywhere in the world over encrypted satellite links, with a local override and a remote shutdown, and it must include a time-limited mode that cuts off emissions automatically and logs every transmission with a time source that does not depend on satellite navigation.
The winning vendor will deliver the six kits along with a demonstration plan, on-site training at a NATO unit in Europe or the United Kingdom, a user guide with a safety and deconfliction annex, and an emission test report for each kit to support approval from national and NATO spectrum authorities.
Satellite navigation jamming has become a regular problem for NATO members, particularly around the Baltic Sea, where airlines and shipping have reported widespread GPS interference that several European governments have blamed on Russia. In 2025, an aircraft carrying European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen lost GPS signals while approaching an airport in Bulgaria, an incident Bulgarian authorities attributed to suspected Russian interference.
U.S. companies that want to bid must have an active facility in the United States, be approved for NATO competitive procurement, and receive a declaration of eligibility from the U.S. government. The Commerce Department set a deadline of Oct. 23 for U.S. firms to request that declaration and, if they are new to NATO bidding, to submit a one-time application.

Responding to the latest acts of state-driven Israeli settler violence in the occupied West Bank over the weekend, which also targeted a delegation of European diplomats and a Washington Post photojournalist, Amnesty International’s Regional Director for the Middle East and North Africa, Heba Morayef, said:
“Once again, Israel’s apartheid system is turning the olive harvest into a season of horror for Palestinian families across the occupied West Bank. State-driven attacks by settlers on farmers that damage, destroy and steal crops, combined with Israeli military restrictions on access to groves, are causing immense suffering and economic loss for Palestinians.
“The series of attacks by settlers over the weekend against Palestinian residents of Khirbet Abu Falah and Taybeh in the Ramallah area, which also targeted a Washington Post photojournalist and a delegation of European diplomats, offer a glimpse into a reality of relentless aggression against Palestinians. Attempts by senior Israeli officials and electoral candidates across the political spectrum to portray this state-sponsored brutality as the work of a few individuals are a blatant distortion of reality.
“Amnesty International has long been sounding the alarm over the exponential rise in state-driven settler violence against Palestinians, which has sought, through terror-inspiring means, to ethnically cleanse Palestinians from the occupied West Bank. This rise of violence has been fuelled by the international community’s persistent failure to take meaningful action against the very system enabling the continued oppression of Palestinians. These attacks must generate a strong response by states that claim to oppose Israel’s annexation of Palestinian territory, its continuous settlement expansion and state-driven settler violence.
“States must recognize that settler attacks are not isolated acts, but a central policy of the Israeli state and take concrete measures to respect their obligations under international law and to avoid complicity in Israeli violations and crimes against Palestinians by halting all trade, investment and cooperation that contribute to maintaining the unlawful occupation, apartheid and the ongoing campaign of ethnic cleansing.
“States must also impose targeted sanctions against Israeli officials credibly implicated in serious violations of international law and support international justice and accountability efforts. Hiding behind empty rhetoric is not only cowardly, it is enabling further abuses. For Palestinians, it continues to be deadly.”
Background
On 16 October, dozens of masked Israeli settlers attacked Palestinian farmers harvesting olives near the village of Abu Falah, northeast of Ramallah. During the attack, settlers reportedly threw stones, used slingshots, set olive trees on fire and assaulted Palestinians. US photojournalist Heidi Levine, who was covering the olive harvest for The Washington Post, was knocked to the ground, and repeatedly kicked despite wearing clearly marked press protective gear. She also had her camera equipment and phone stolen, and was hospitalized with multiple injuries. On 19 October, Israeli police said they had arrested 10 suspects as part of an investigation into the incidents.
The following day masked Israeli settlers attacked a group that included Belgian, French and Polish diplomats, a French mayor, Catholic representatives and Palestinian residents near the village of Taybeh, also northeast of Ramallah. A Belgian diplomatic vehicle was also reportedly damaged and several members of the delegation were assaulted.
Amnesty International’s 2026 report on the occupied West Bank documented how since late 2022 Israeli authorities have escalated a state-led and state-sponsored campaign of ethnic cleansing, terrorizing and forcibly displacing thousands of Palestinians from Bedouin and herding communities in Area C of the West Bank to permanently alter its demography. In pursuing their goal of formal annexation, they have accelerated settlement expansion, intensified movement restrictions, exponentially increased funding as well as logistical, legal and political support to settlements and outposts, distributed arms to settlers and openly encouraged, facilitated, and condoned settler attacks as a deliberate tool of displacement.
Palestinian communities across the occupied West Bank have faced a sharp increase in settler attacks since October 2023 aimed at forcibly displacing them through physical assaults, threats and harassment against individuals; destruction of property, arson, crop theft; restrictions on access to agricultural and grazing land; and acts of theft and harm against livestock.
Amnesty International is calling on states to suspend all forms of cooperation that contribute to maintaining Israel’s unlawful occupation, ban trade with Israeli settlements, impose targeted sanctions against Israeli officials directly implicated in Israel’s ethnic cleansing campaign and serious crimes under international law against Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza Strip, impose a comprehensive embargo on arms and security equipment to Israel, and support international accountability mechanisms, including ongoing investigations by the International Criminal Court.

Why Mahmoud Abbas keeps postponing Palestinian elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
15:51:56 UTC
00:51:56 KST

Breadcrumb
New deadline, old crisis: Why Mahmoud Abbas keeps postponing Palestinian elections
On 10 October, Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas issued a decree cancelling the legislative elections set for 28 November.
Instead, presidential and legislative polls will be held together on 11 September 2027. The decree followed approval by the Executive Committee of the Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) and consultations with political factions.
The official explanation was Israel's occupation. Fatah officials insist that the movement was ready and that Israeli restrictions made a free, fair, and inclusive vote impossible. While that argument is real, it is also incomplete.
Read closely, the accounts of those around the decision point to three pressures converging at once: external obstacles that have not changed, rivalries inside Fatah that its own leaders acknowledge, and a factional dialogue that gave the leadership a consensual route away from a deadline its critics say it was not ready to meet.
The postponement is less a verdict on Israeli obstruction than a decision about who gets to shape the next Palestinian political order, and on what terms.
The official case
The decree lists various obstacles, including Israel's continuing offensive in Gaza, restrictions on the movement of the Central Elections Commission and observers, and the impossibility of voting in occupied East Jerusalem given Israel's position.
Restrictions on movement, settlement expansion, and settler attacks across the West Bank were also cited, as were the exceptional security and humanitarian conditions in Gaza.
Fatah insists its own machinery was not the problem.
“We prepared seriously for these elections,” Tayseer Nasrallah, a member of Fatah's Revolutionary Council, told The New Arab.
“We mobilised our organisational structures in the West Bank and the Gaza Strip, held meetings and electoral assemblies to choose our candidates, and we were about to register our official list with the Central Elections Commission.”
He rejects the suggestion that internal weakness forced the delay. “Organisational unreadiness and internal disagreements were not the direct reason for the postponement,” he said.
“Creating the right conditions for voting and guaranteeing that our people can take part in every area are among the biggest challenges that must be dealt with before elections are held.”
The obstacles are not invented. But the decree itself describes them as continuing, meaning they were already in place when the November date was set. Nothing in it explains why they should have been lifted by September 2027.
As a full explanation of why this vote was cancelled at this moment, the occupation argument does too little work on its own.
The fault lines inside Fatah
The harder question is what was happening inside the ruling movement.
“The disputes inside Fatah, whether between its leadership centres or with the Democratic Reform Current, have left their mark on the preparations for the elections,” said Noaman al-Abed, a writer and political analyst.
“These disputes came alongside questions about how ready the factions actually are,” he told The New Arab, “and whether they can provide the political, field, and logistical conditions needed, especially in Jerusalem and Gaza.”
Al-Abed's sharpest criticism is aimed at the mechanism Fatah used to pick its candidates. “The experience of the electoral assemblies inside Fatah has deepened the organisational divisions,” he said. “It is doubtful how far they included the different currents within the movement”.
This is where the power dynamics sit. Candidate selection decides who rises inside a movement and who is left out. A process that rival currents see as exclusive does not settle internal contests; it pushes them toward the ballot box, where they can split the vote.
The postponement halted that process: the same decision froze the work of the electoral assemblies for the Palestinian National Council. Folding the presidency into the same ballot raises the stakes further for whoever controls the list.
Fatah's leaders do not deny the rifts. They simply deny that the rifts decide anything.
“Differences within Fatah are not new,” Nasrallah said. “The movement has always dealt with them through internal dialogue”.
Wasel Abu Youssef, a member of the PLO Executive Committee, puts Israel's continuing aggression and the obstacles to the vote first, alongside the need for a comprehensive national dialogue.
Yet even this defence concedes the central point. If the delay was needed to secure consensus, then consensus was missing. The internal divide may not be the only cause of the postponement, but it is part of what made the November date untenable.
Consensus as cover - and leverage
The delay was not announced as a Fatah decision. It was framed as a response to the factions.
“Fatah respected the outcomes of the dialogue held in Cairo with the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine and Hamas,” Nasrallah said, “and conveyed them to the movement's leadership bodies before the procedures for the postponement were completed”.
The decision was presented as answering factional initiatives, above all the PFLP's. On 10 October, the same day as the decree, the PFLP welcomed the change of date and the freezing of the National Council assemblies. It called for a comprehensive national dialogue based on its initiative, "A Roadmap for National Salvation".
That dialogue, it said, should end the division, restore national unity, and rebuild the political system on democratic and participatory foundations, with all forces taking part.
Abu Youssef echoed that agenda. “We need a comprehensive national dialogue that rearranges the internal Palestinian situation, ends the division and produces a consensus guaranteeing that all factions take part in the elections,” he said, adding that contacts with the factions and Egyptian officials were continuing.
“The aim of dialogue must be to end the division and strengthen national unity, so that elections become a means of renewing legitimacy and ordering Palestinian institutions, not an additional cause of fragmentation.”
This framing does two things. A delay requested by a faction outside Fatah reads as national consensus rather than self-interest, which gives the leadership cover. It also changes the question. The debate is no longer only about when Palestinians vote, but about the terms of the political system they vote into, with Hamas at the table in Cairo.
That is a bigger prize, and a riskier one. Whoever shapes the dialogue now shapes the timetable.
“Fatah is ready to abide by the outcomes of the dialogue and the national understandings that are reached,” Nasrallah said. Whether those understandings become concrete, enforceable steps is what the PFLP's roadmap, and the credibility of the delay, will depend on.
The international pressure test
The one clear dissent came from outside. In a statement on 14 October, the European Union expressed regret at the postponement of legislative and presidential elections until September 2027. It stressed the importance of holding them as soon as possible and said it stood ready to support the process, including through an EU observation mission.
Fatah's answer was to redirect the pressure. “Fatah respects the European Union's position rejecting the postponement,” Nasrallah said, “but we ask that this position be matched by political pressure on the occupation government to remove the obstacles hindering the work of the Central Elections Commission, and to guarantee freedom of movement and participation in the West Bank, including Jerusalem, and in the Gaza Strip”.
Abu Youssef framed it as a diplomatic task. “We must keep communicating with European states and the international parties concerned, explain the impact of the occupation's measures on the possibility of holding elections, and work to build an international position that guarantees their integrity and transparency,” he said.
The exchange sets a test for both sides. If Israeli obstruction is the main barrier, European pressure and an observer mission are the remedy Fatah says it wants. If the leadership does not take up that offer with a clear plan, the occupation argument will look more like a shield for internal problems than a reason.
A new deadline, an old political crisis
No single factor explains the postponement. Israeli obstruction is a real barrier to voting across the Palestinian territories. Fatah's internal rifts are real too, and its leaders' insistence on consensus shows the movement was not ready to face voters divided. The factional dialogue gave the leadership a way to turn that weakness into a national project.
The risk is that the delay becomes the outcome. “Repeated postponement of the elections may deepen the crisis of trust between citizens and the Palestinian leadership,” al-Abed warned, “and raise doubts about how serious the commitment is to renewing legitimacy through the ballot box”.
His prescription is simple.
“Overcoming this requires a clear date, early preparation and the political and organisational guarantees needed to hold the elections,” he said.
The postponement has bought eleven months. Its value will be judged by one measure: whether the dialogue produces a national consensus that clears the way for free and fair elections and renews Palestinian legitimacy, or whether divisions and obstacles push the vote back again and deepen the crisis of trust.

Germany to tighten German language exams for migrants — what is the reason
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

Germany to tighten German language exams for migrants — what is the reason
Kyiv • UNN
Starting November 1, Germany will tighten exams for migrants due to the leakage of test questions and answers. The changes will apply to integration courses.
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt plans to tighten German-language examinations for migrants following cases of fraud during testing. The relevant regulation is to enter into force on November 1. Bild reports this, writes UNN.
Details
A spokesperson for Germany’s Federal Ministry of the Interior confirmed this information in Berlin on Monday. According to ministry representatives, the changes are intended to prevent the spread of fraud during examinations.
According to the publication, participants in integration courses illegally obtained written assignments and test answers via the internet and then used them during the “Listening and Reading” part of the examination.
This part requires participants to complete 45 tasks by marking the correct answers.
Another part of the examination involves a written task, during which participants usually have to compose a short message. According to the regulation, this section is often left completely blank.
At the same time, if a participant achieves the required B1 level during the oral part of the examination, the examination is still considered passed thanks to a successful result in the first part.

Israel to resume commercial shipments to Gaza after Hamas fee dispute
CAIRO, Oct 19 - Israel said on Monday it would resume allowing commercial goods shipments into Gaza after a days-long halt over a tax dispute involving Hamas and merchants, restoring a key route for food and other essentials to the aid-dependent enclave.
COGAT, the Israeli military agency overseeing humanitarian affairs in Gaza, said it made the decision after merchants reported that Hamas authorities had withdrawn demands for payments of 10,000 shekels ($3,225) per truck.
"The resumption of coordination is being carried out in accordance with Israel's commitment to the humanitarian provisions of the ceasefire agreement," it said.
COGAT said the merchants' accounts had not been independently verified and shipments would resume gradually, with priority given to essential goods ahead of winter.
Oversight would be tightened to ensure payments are made and received only through documented bank transfers, with any merchant found to have paid Hamas facing exclusion from the system.
Hamas said the 10,000-shekel fee was a voluntary contribution by better-off Gazans to a national fund supporting people in need in the war-ravaged territory.
Most Gazans remain dependent on aid after three years of war, repeated displacement and severe restrictions on aid deliveries. While last year's US-brokered ceasefire halted the heaviest fighting, it has not ended Israeli attacks.
Local health officials said on Monday that at least five Palestinians, including a 14-year-old boy, were killed in separate Israeli strikes in Gaza City and Khan Younis. The Israeli military did not immediately comment.
Israel says Hamas has continued to rearm and carry out attacks in violation of the ceasefire, while Hamas accuses Israel of undermining the agreement.
Gaza health officials say about 1,500 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli fire since the October 2025 ceasefire, while Israel says four of its soldiers have been killed by militants in Gaza over the same period. REUTERS

Kenyan starvation cult leader found guilty of murder of 191 children, 1 adult
More than 400 bodies have been recovered from mass graves discovered at the Shakahola Forest more than three years ago
A Kenyan court on Monday found starvation cult leader Paul Mackenzie and about 30 others guilty of murder over the deaths of 190 children and one adult in one of the world’s worst cult-related disasters in recent history.
Mackenzie and his co-accused will be given their sentence on November 6.
Mackenzie was arrested in 2023 after police received a tip-off, and weeks later authorities began uncovering bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola Forest near the coast in southeastern Kenya.
Prosecutors say Mackenzie and his Good News International Church organised a Christian doomsday sect in which they ordered followers to starve themselves and their children to death to go to Heaven before the world ended.

Zelenskyy says it's Putin who wants an endless war, not him
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
15:50:17 UTC
00:50:17 KST

Zelenskyy says Russia hit Ukraine again with no "warning from partners," U.S. delaying "vital supplies"
Ukrainian President Zelenskyy said Monday that his country had been subjected to another night of Russian missile and drone strikes, "and again there was no warning from partners."
Zelenskyy has accused the U.S. of limiting intelligence, and possibly other assistance to Ukraine amid renewed tension with President Trump, who accused the Ukrainian leader over the weekend of not wanting to end the war. Mr. Trump has significantly softened the U.S. government's policy toward Russia, easing sanctions to allow Russian energy sales in a bid to ease U.S. gas prices.
Zelenskyy says the moves risk emboldening Moscow and enabling it to continue and intensify its four-and-a-half-year, full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The target of the most recent strikes was energy and other infrastructure, Zelenskyy said, adding that a medical clinic, school, metro station and "ordinary residential buildings" were also hit.
Zelenskyy said Saturday that Ukraine was still unable to use Starshield, an upgraded military version of Elon Musk's Starlink satellite technology, to intercept Russian drones. The network is crucial to Ukrainian forces as it enables them to shoot down Russia's jet-powered drones and other weapons.
The Trump administration has denied making any changes to the intelligence it shares with Ukraine, or deliberately slowing down Starshield data.
Asked Saturday if the U.S. government was responsible for the change in Starlink service in Ukraine, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he was "not sure Zelenskyy knows what he's talking about, but it wasn't deliberate … we have nothing to do with that."
"The United States — nobody ordered that Starlink speed to be slowed down. It sort of happened, but my understanding is it's been restored. It's back to where it was before," he said, without elaborating on what he meant by "it sort of happened."
Denys Sienik, Ukraine's chargé d'affaires and current top diplomat in the U.S., told CBS News in a statement later Saturday that Ukraine had still not received a response from the Pentagon or Musk's SpaceX to inquiries about Starlink or Starshield service, "including confirmation that unlimited speeds have been restored and that Starshield is operating as it did previously."
"There are political agreements that have not been implemented at the working level," Zelenskyy said Monday in a post on X, adding that there had also been "delays in certain types of vital supplies at the level of the U.S. Department of War."
He did not expound on his assertion that the Pentagon was delaying shipments of supplies.
The Ukrainian leader issued the statement amid an increasingly terse exchange of accusations with President Trump who, over the weekend, accused Zelenskyy of not wanting the war sparked by Russia's full-scale invasion to end.
In a Truth Social post, Mr. Trump said Zelenskyy "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did."
"He could have made a better deal two years ago than he can now. His country is in shambles, a large portion of his land is lost, his oceans and seas are gone, and his male population is low, wounded, and/or dead," Mr. Trump argued.
The U.S. president has over the last month walked back sanctions on Russia — that had support from a majority of Republicans and Democrats — that were intended to increase financial pressure on Moscow over its assault on Ukraine.
"Ukraine never wanted this war," Zelenskyy said in another statement shared Monday on social media. "We took positively literally EVERY attempt of partners to end this war with dignity."
Just over a week ago Mr. Trump declared in a social media post that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to an "energy ceasefire," which would mean a halt to attacks on the other country's energy infrastructure. Neither Moscow nor Kyiv acknowledged agreeing to any such deal, and within hours Ukrainian authorities reported new Russian attacks on refineries.
Zelenskyy said "again and again Russia's answers" to efforts at diplomacy were new attacks.
"Putin does not want the end of this war, or even any de-escalation steps," he said, adding: "It is very important to call things by their names. Call the aggressor an aggressor and help Ukraine protect lives. When the supply of missiles to Ukrainian air defense is blocked, and Russia receives a weakening or postponement of sanctions, this is, unfortunately, a denial of reality from partners. In reality, the war continues, and continues only because of Russian strikes — the Russian desire to prolong this war."
The Kremlin, meanwhile, has attempted to frame Russia as a willing partner in peace efforts.
Putin's spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Monday that Moscow values U.S. mediation efforts, but that reaching agreements without the participation of representatives from Kyiv is impossible. There have been direct talks, mediated by the U.S., between Ukraine and Russia, but so far the meetings have yielded little more than prisoner swaps, not ceasefires.
The Wall Street Journal first reported Sunday evening that Putin had proposed a meeting between U.S., Chinese and Russian officials to discuss solutions to the Ukraine war, but without a seat for Ukraine at the negotiating table. The newspaper said he proposed the idea for a summit during a call with Mr. Trump on Oct. 9.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said Monday in a post on X that "a trilateral meeting between the leaders of Russia, China, and the U.S. would do only the opposite: encourage Putin to continue this war."

Finance Ministry awaits Industry Ministry stance on steel excise, official says

00:50:13 KST

DUSHANBE, October 19. /TASS/. The Russian Finance Ministry is awaiting the position of the Industry and Trade Ministry regarding the potential introduction of an excise duty on imported steel, State Secretary and Deputy Finance Minister Alexey Sazanov told reporters.
"We are waiting for the Industry and Trade Ministry’s position on this matter. Based on that, we will decide by the second reading whether corresponding amendments to the Tax Code are necessary," Sazanov said.
In early August, Sazanov reported that a draft law on introducing an excise duty on imported steel had been developed and was under discussion with business representatives. At the time, the deputy minister noted that, if an agreement were reached, the tax amendments would be introduced in the autumn, ruling out the possibility of the excise duty taking effect in the fourth quarter of this year.
Earlier, the Finance Ministry prepared and submitted for approval a draft law on introducing an excise duty on imported metallurgical products made from liquid steel.
The calculation formula for the imported steel excise will be tied to the final products that utilize liquid steel in production. Under this approach, the excise duty amount will depend on the characteristics of the finished metallurgical products.

The European Parliament accused Albania of hastily pushing forward Trump&apos;s son-in-law&apos;s luxury resort project
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
18:49:30 EEST
00:49:30 KST

The European Parliament accused Albania of hastily pushing forward Trump's son-in-law's luxury resort project
Kyiv • UNN
MEPs accused the Albanian government of accelerating the promotion of Kushner and Ivanka Trump's resort in a protected area. Protests in Tirana have become more intense.
Members of the European Parliament accused Albania of using "underhanded" methods to accelerate the implementation of a luxury resort project linked to the family of US President Donald Trump. This is happening amid protests that are becoming increasingly violent, reports UNN, citing The Guardian.
Details
Although Prime Minister Edi Rama promised to "listen to the voices of young people" who had taken to the streets, he came under sharp criticism for ignoring demonstrators who had peacefully protested against the controversial project for a long time, the publication notes.
Events unseen in decades unfolded in Tirana: students leading the protest movement engaged in fierce clashes with riot police. Government buildings are on fire in the city, while banks and commercial properties have also been attacked and looted.
In a comment to The Guardian, Dutch MEP Tineke Strik accused Rama of exacerbating the situation through his persistent promotion of plans backed by Jared Kushner — the US president’s son-in-law.
"If the Albanian government had taken the ‘Flamingo Revolution’ seriously, we would not have found ourselves in this situation," she said, referring to the popular movement that emerged in response to the construction of the resort in environmentally vulnerable areas of the Balkan country. — "The students are voicing the dissatisfaction of people who feel that no one is listening to them."
On Monday, the capital saw municipal workers dismantling paving stones while shop owners boarded up their windows with metal sheets. This is the sixth consecutive day of violent clashes, during which protesters even set fire to a police station. Police used rubber bullets and tear gas in an attempt to disperse the crowd. The students said they would continue the protests until the socialist leader resigns — a demand he firmly rejected.
"This terrible idea for a resort was the spark that ignited the flames," says Greta, a student from Tirana. She adds that the slogan young people have been chanting at demonstrations over the past few months is: "Albania is not for sale."
"Now other problems have emerged that are fanning these flames even further. We are genuinely concerned about the state of our democracy, living standards and education."
To add
The article states that the controversial project involves the construction of up to 10,000 villas in coastal areas that were previously protected for environmental reasons. The situation changed after the government adopted an odious law allowing "strategic investors" to build in the Vjosa-Narta landscape — an area surrounding the last intact delta system in the Mediterranean.
In June, the European Parliament called on Albania — a candidate country for EU membership — to repeal the law, stressing that it poses a direct threat to the environmental standards that are a "necessary condition for accession" to the European Union.
The European Parliament’s move came in response to the start of construction work in May. The event triggered a wave of protests across the country, particularly after it emerged that ancient dunes and forest had been destroyed to lay access roads in a nature reserve.
Edi Rama, who was re-elected last year to an unprecedented fourth term, has set himself the goal of bringing this Balkan state — which, even more than three decades after the fall of communism, remains one of the poorest in Europe — into the EU by 2030. In an address broadcast on social media on Sunday, Rama asked: "Albanians should make a clear choice: what exactly do they want — this, that, or EU membership after all?"
However, Tine Strik, a Green MEP who led a fact-finding mission to Albania in June, said it was obvious that the government was rushing to “create facts on the ground” while its activities were not yet governed by EU standards. Albania, one of the leaders in the EU enlargement process, hopes to conclude accession negotiations by the end of 2027.
Citing an environmental impact assessment — whose “scientific findings” Rama recently called the decisive basis for implementing the €4 billion project — Strik said: “The government submitted an environmental documentation package to the European Commission, but it did not repeal the law that allows construction in the protected zone... It is still trying to facilitate the implementation of Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner’s megalomaniacal plans to create a luxury resort. How exactly? By conducting an accelerated impact assessment. If this study had been carried out [more thoroughly], it could under no circumstances have led to the conclusion that such construction was permissible.” This month, speaking at a tourism forum in Brussels, Rama said the landmark project would radically transform the situation in a country that, until the fall of the Stalinist regime in the 1990s, had been “the North Korea of Europe.”
“If construction begins, it will not be decided in the streets but by scientists,” he said at the forum. “The idea that nature will take care of itself if we simply look on is absurd and outdated. We want to create... a high-end tourist destination where nature will be the focus, where people can relax, and where the Albanian people will receive what they deserve: a much stronger economy.”
On 8 October, Kushner described the project as having a single goal: “To build a facility in accordance with the highest standards of design and environmental norms, and to make this extraordinary part of Albania greener, richer in biodiversity and more environmentally sustainable.”
The media outlet notes that private contractors tasked with conducting the environmental impact assessment have been observed mapping, measuring and monitoring the area. In response, environmentalists who initiated the original protests said this week that “science has already spoken.”
“It spoke back in 2004, when experts from the Faculty of Natural Sciences at the University of Tirana decided to place this incredible landscape under protection,” said Aleksander Trajce of the country’s oldest environmental organisation, Protection and Preservation of Natural Environment in Albania (PPNEA). “Their decision was based on very thorough scientific data. Science can no longer tell us anything new. Reviving the discussion is not only insincere but also evidently an attempt to justify construction that should not be taking place at all.”
Emphasising that a proper environmental impact assessment would require “at least two years”, he added: “Several seasons over several years are needed to properly study the species and biodiversity of this region.”
According to Trajce, as the violence continues, Albanians feel deep outrage over the EU’s sluggish stance. “If the EU had intervened earlier and urged Rama to stop, the peaceful phase of the protest movement would not have turned into what we are seeing today.”
Strik, who admitted that she was surprised by the Albanian prime minister’s enthusiasm for creating such a large-scale tourist complex in such a vulnerable area, stressed the importance of protecting similar unique coastal zones on a continent that has already learned from the mistakes of the past. “I accuse Rama of acting in the interests of — his own and Kushner’s — rather than those of the environment or the Albanian people,” she said.
"The government apparently intends to complete all procedures by the time it is legally obliged to comply with EU standards. Such insidious and unscrupulous actions must be firmly condemned by the EU. If Albania genuinely aspires to be a reliable candidate for EU accession, it must respect EU legislation rather than trying to circumvent it." Commenting on Strik’s statements, Rama told The Guardian: "Please tell the honourable lady that the violence in Tirana is very real. Instead of inventing environmental conspiracies that do not exist, she could help Albania by condemning the violence — violence that she appears to endorse, which regrettably makes her resemble a representative of the Kremlin, Ms Zakharova [Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova]."

====================================================================================================

From potential prime minister to election dropout: Gantz's dramatic political downfall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
15:49:06 UTC
00:49:06 KST

Just a week ago, Blue and White chairman Benny Gantz sat in the ynet studio during the "People of the State" conference and confidently promised to remain in the election race until the end. He dismissed calls for his withdrawal, criticized what he described as the cynicism of opposition party leaders and presented polling suggesting that his message of national unity had the potential to win between six and eight Knesset seats.
Gantz appeared determined to stay. But political reality eventually caught up with him, forcing the former defense minister to announce his withdrawal eight days before the October 27 election, or, as he explained, one day before soldiers begin voting. His departure also effectively brings an end to the so-called third bloc, which sought to offer voters an alternative based on unity, reconciliation and political compromise rather than alignment with either Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu or the opposition parties seeking to replace him. The only remaining party in that political space is the one led by Yoaz Hendel and Yaron Zelekha.
Gadi Eisenkot, chairman of the Yashar party and Gantz's former political partner, had planned to meet him and urge him to withdraw. "I'm sure he'll make the right decision and won't run," Eisenkot predicted. But Gantz was unwilling to let Eisenkot claim credit for his departure. He ignored his former ally's calls for a meeting and ultimately decided to withdraw after considerable internal deliberation.
His professional campaign team had urged him to continue, presenting polling that suggested his message could still attract a substantial number of voters. But inside Blue and White, others were increasingly concerned about the consequences of running a campaign that might end below the electoral threshold. Lawmaker Alon Schuster, who held sixth place on the party's candidate list, had remained loyal to Gantz alongside Chili Tropper, Michael Biton and other senior figures. Nevertheless, he established a clear red line: "If it's certain that the party won't cross the electoral threshold, we must not run. We won't throw votes in the trash."
On the other side were the consultants, strategists and pollsters employed by Gantz's campaign, whose work was funded through the party's election budget. Blue and White is not a party short of resources. Based on its eight Knesset seats, it receives eight public campaign financing units, each worth more than 1.8 million shekels, giving it an election budget of approximately 15 million shekels. The campaign also supports paid positions, creating financial interests alongside the political considerations.
One detail illustrated the situation particularly clearly. Shortly before Gantz's dramatic withdrawal announcement, Blue and White issued an official statement declaring that it had filled 100% of its available positions on polling station committees, including committee chairmanships. These are paid positions financed by the party. A party official explained that the appointments would remain in place despite Gantz's withdrawal because the roles concern election integrity, and the activists would continue serving at polling stations even though their party would no longer be contesting the election.
Outside the political blocs
The immediate question is who stands to benefit from Gantz's departure. At first glance, his withdrawal might appear to strengthen the opposition bloc seeking to replace Netanyahu. In practice, however, there is little reason to assume Eisenkot and his allies will gain significantly. Gantz had deliberately distanced himself from that bloc and adopted Netanyahu's line of attack over its potential reliance on Arab parties. He argued that Eisenkot, Avigdor Liberman and Naftali Bennett could form a government with Arab factions, including Balad and politicians such as Ahmad Tibi.
Nor does Netanyahu appear likely to gain substantial support from Gantz's departure. Any movement toward the prime minister's camp would probably be marginal. Gantz's remaining electorate does not constitute a large pool of voters waiting to be redistributed among the major parties.
The politician closest to Gantz ideologically and politically is Yoaz Hendel, who decided at the last minute not to run on a joint ticket with him. Like Gantz, Hendel does not identify with either the opposition bloc or Netanyahu's political camp. He could therefore emerge as the principal beneficiary of the withdrawal, although any potential gain should be kept in perspective. Gantz is not leaving behind several Knesset seats' worth of voters, but rather a few thousand supporters who, according to the latest polling, had left Blue and White well below the electoral threshold.
Gantz has pledged to continue fighting for a national unity government from outside the election race. His decision does not mean that he is resigning from the Knesset. He and the lawmakers elected on his party's list will continue serving until the 26th Knesset is sworn in, approximately two weeks after the election.
The speed of Gantz's decline illustrates the extraordinary volatility of politics. At the beginning of the war, his party was polling at nearly 40 seats, placing him among the country's most prominent potential leaders. Now, just eight days before voters head to the polls, he has been forced to abandon his campaign after a prolonged collapse in public support.
Few political careers have demonstrated such a dramatic reversal in such a short period. From nearly 40 projected seats to a withdrawal before election day, Gantz's latest campaign ends not with the national unity government he envisioned, but with the disappearance of the political alternative he had tried to build.

Kenyan cult leader Paul Mackenzie found guilty over 191 starvation deaths
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
15:49:00 UTC
00:49:00 KST

Kenya: Cult leader found guilty of murdering 190 children, 1 adult
October 19, 2026
A court in Mombasa, Kenya, on Monday found self-proclaimed preacher Paul Mackenzie and 28 associates guilty of murdering 190 children and one adult as part of a notorious Christian starvation cult.
Mackenzie established his so-called Good News International Church in 2003 and was alleged to have incited his followers to starve themselves to death in order to "meet Jesus."
He was arrested in April 2023 after a rights group informed authorities.
Some of his acolytes were rescued but the subsequent police operation exposed hundreds of mass graves at a forest site near the Kenyan beach resort of Malindi.
Local media dubbed the case the "Shakahola Forest Massacre."
Shakahola Forest Massacre: What did the judge say?
"I am satisfied that the prosecution has proved the case against all the 29 accused persons for the murder of 190 children and one adult," said Justice Diana Kavedza Mochache after a hearing which lasted over eight hours.
The prosecution had said Mackenzie "initiated and directed" extreme fasting at his 800-acre (325 hectare) ranch in Shakahola Forest, claiming there was a "structured hierarchy of death" which said children should die first, followed by teenagers, women, and then men.
Post-mortems and police reports revealed that the children mostly died from starvation, but also from "asphyxia, neck compression and traumatic head injury," prosecutors said.
The court in Mombasa also heard that, in some cases, children were isolated and denied food while their parents watched.
"This is a very, very important day," said Francis Wanje, 62, who lost eight family members, including his daughter and two grandchildren, at Shakahola.
"We are expecting a ruling that will be a lesson to the whole public, so that such kinds of things will not happen again," he told the AFP news agency, expressing anger over the government's initial inaction.
Mackenzie facing even more Shakahola charges
Since the initial discovery of the graves, even more bodies of children, women and men have been unearthed, bringing the total to well over 400. The soaring death toll has even required sporadic pauses in excavations as local morgues ran out of space.
In January 2026, Mackenzie was charged over a further 52 bodies found at a nearby village.
There have been calls in Kenya for tougher regulations on religious organizations after it emerged that Mackenzie had been arrested twice in the past but released.
He was arrested in 2017 on charges of "radicalization" but was acquitted. He was arrested again in 2019 in relation to two child deaths at Shakahola, but released on bail.
His sentencing will take place on November 6.
Edited by: Wesley Dockery

The National Bank of Ukraine (NBU) has put into circulation a commemorative UAH 2 coin marking the 100th anniversary of the birth of Bohdan Havrylyshyn, part of its Outstanding Personalities of Ukraine series, the regulator said on Telegram on Monday.

According to the NBU, the coin is made of nickel silver. Its reverse features a portrait of Havrylyshyn, his name and the phrase "Dream boldly."
The obverse features a composition of viburnum, a maple leaf and an edelweiss, symbolizing Ukraine, Canada and Switzerland, the three countries associated with the life of the prominent economist and philanthropist.
The coin was designed by Yurko Hutsuliak, with Volodymyr Atamanchuk and Anatoliy Demianenko serving as sculptors.
The mintage will be up to 50,000 coins in souvenir packaging.
The commemorative coin will be available through the NBU's online numismatic products store and distributor banks.

Carney says cause of fire at Alberta military base still unknown
OTTAWA, Oct 19 - Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Monday that the cause of a fire that killed at least four military members and injured dozens of others in Alberta on Saturday is still unknown.
Carney said in an address to Parliament that soldiers and reserve members were conducting live-fire exercises at an army base in Wainwright while a fire was burning in the training area.
“Driven by ferocious winds, the fire jumped nearly a kilometer in less than a minute to where soldiers were gathered,” Carney said. He added that 50 investigators are currently on the ground, from the army and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, to determine how the disaster happened.
"This loss touches every corner of the nation," Carney said.
Officials said 39 people remain hospitalized, with 19 people in critical condition. The soldiers and reserve members were preparing to deploy to Latvia, where Canadian forces have their largest international military operation.
Kent Moore, a professor of atmospheric physics at the University of Toronto, said the embers from grass fires in dry conditions can spread incredibly quickly. He said there didn't appear to be any rain in the area, so it was unlikely the fire was triggered by lightning.
"The fact that the winds were so strong suggests to me that it wouldn't have taken much to start this fire," he said, speculating that it was likely caused by human error, including sparks from vehicles or live fire, or an errant cigarette from a smoker. REUTERS

U.S. Air Force wants a missile engine that runs on explosions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
15:44:34 UTC
00:44:34 KST

- The U.S. Air Force Research Laboratory is seeking proposals to mature and flight-test a combined-cycle rotating detonation rocket engine over 36 to 48 months.
- The effort supports future High-Speed Affordable Mass Munitions, and white papers are due Nov. 16, 2026.
The U.S. Air Force Research Laboratory wants industry to build and fly a combined-cycle rotating detonation rocket engine, a type of propulsion that runs on a continuous chain of explosions, as a step toward cheap, high-speed weapons that could be built in large numbers.
The lab’s Rocket Propulsion Division at Edwards Air Force Base, California, issued a call for proposals for a Rotating Detonation Rocket Engine-Combined Cycle, or RDRE-CC, flight demonstration under its HERMES Broad Agency Announcement. The notice, published on SAM.gov, sets a Nov. 16, 2026, deadline for initial white papers, with the work expected to run 36 to 48 months.
The program aims to take the technology from early laboratory proof of concept, known as Technology Readiness Level 3, to a prototype demonstrated in a relevant environment, Level 6. The effort is meant to end with a flight test in which a sounding rocket launched from the ground boosts the engine-powered vehicle to its operating conditions, to show the system could work for a future class of weapons the lab calls High-Speed Affordable Mass Munitions, or HAMM.
In a conventional rocket, fuel burns steadily in a combustion chamber. A rotating detonation engine instead creates a detonation wave that races continuously around a ring-shaped chamber at supersonic speed, burning fuel as it goes, which researchers say can deliver more thrust from a smaller, simpler engine with fewer moving parts. A combined-cycle design pairs that rocket mode with air-breathing operation, so the engine can use oxygen from the atmosphere for part of its flight instead of carrying it all on board.
The work laid out in the call covers developing and testing the rotating detonation rocket engine, integrated direct-connect and freejet ground tests that simulate high-speed flight conditions, designing the vehicle and flying it. The technical requirements, vehicle constraints and seven specific test objectives are in a controlled, export-restricted document available only to certified U.S. defense contractors, and the companies doing the work must be able to safeguard Secret-level information.
Selection will happen in two steps. Companies first submit white papers of up to 10 pages, plus an optional five-page technical appendix, describing their design, how they will meet the test objectives, a schedule and a rough cost estimate. The lab expects to review them within six to eight weeks and will invite only the strongest submissions, if funding is available, to send full technical and cost proposals.
Rotating detonation engines have drawn growing attention from the U.S. military in recent years. RTX’s Pratt & Whitney completed a series of tests on a rotating detonation engine in 2025 under DARPA’s Gambit program, which is working toward an air-breathing engine for future long-range weapons, and AFRL’s rocket propulsion researchers at Edwards have been firing rotating detonation rocket engines on test stands for several years.

Rubio in India: What the US secretary’s itinerary signals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
15:41:21 UTC
00:41:21 KST

Rubio in India: What the US secretary’s itinerary signals
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio will meet Indian Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar in Mumbai on Tuesday and visit a major oil refinery in western India the next day as he makes his second visit to the country this year.
Washington’s top diplomat is leaving New Delhi out of his itinerary and is focusing instead on diesel supplies and business deals as high fuel prices weigh on the prospects of US President Donald Trump’s Republican Party ahead of November’s midterm elections.
Rubio is scheduled to visit the Jamnagar refining complex of Indian conglomerate Reliance Industries on Wednesday, where he is expected to meet with its billionaire owner Mukesh Ambani.
The Trump administration is emphasizing business deals over policy and politics as American voters focus on the economy, experts told CNBC.
Why Jamnagar has become important for US
Reliance, India’s largest private company, operates the world’s biggest single-site refining complex at Jamnagar – in Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Gujarat state – which is capable of processing around 1.4 million barrels of crude a day.
The facility’s importance as a major supplier of refined fuels globally has increased as disruptions in the Middle East and Russia squeeze diesel supplies, with ripple effects on US markets.
US diesel prices averaged $6.29 a gallon in September, according to the Energy Information Administration. The International Energy Agency has warned that global shortages could persist into 2027.
Reliance has cranked up increased exports amid the crunch. Its diesel shipments to Europe reached around 4-5 million barrels in July, a ten-month high, while exports to Brazil also rose, Reuters reported.
Any additional Indian diesel flowing to global markets would help ease diesel prices and explain Rubio’s trip to Jamnagar.
Reliance, long a major buyer of Russian crude, has increasingly turned to Venezuela after receiving US authorization to purchase oil directly from the South American country earlier this year.
Jamnagar, unlike many other refineries in India, can process Venezuela’s heavy crude. Venezuelan deliveries scheduled for India could more than double to around 465,000 barrels a day in October, according to ship-tracking firm Kpler. All of those listed Sikka, the port serving Jamnagar, as their destination, Bloomberg reported.
Trump has also waived key sanctions and tariff provisions under a new law targeting the Russian energy trade, potentially making more Russian crude available to refiners. Rubio said that Washington was assessing the economic impact of further restrictions, including on countries dependent on Russian oil such as India.
Ambani has invested in Trump’s dream
Rubio’s meeting with Ambani is significant for another reason.
Reliance is backing a proposed refinery in Brownsville, Texas, designed to process American shale oil. The planned facility would handle 168,000 barrels a day, with the company agreeing to purchase the output under a 20-year arrangement, Reuters reported.
The developer has described it as the first new US refinery in half a century. It will be designed designed for American shale oil. The full investment and construction costs remain undisclosed.
The refinery is key to bringing to the US consumer the benefits of Trump’s efforts – under the political slogan “drill, baby, drill” – to increase domestic fossil fuel production.
The project also adds another strand to the economic ties between New Delhi and Washington, even as both countries inch toward closing a bilateral trade deal following months of negotiations.
The deal’s first phase has entered legal drafting, Indian Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal said last week.
Washington and New Delhi are “very close” to finalizing the deal, Rubio said Monday, adding that trade negotiations were among the factors considered in Washington’s sanctions decisions.
Trillionaire vs. billionaire
Rubio’s expected meeting with Ambani comes on the heels of Elon Musk’s public outbursts attributing delays to the launch of his Starlink satellite internet service in India to the Indian billionaire.
Musk, who has Trump’s ears, accused powerful business interests of obstructing Starlink’s entry and even blamed Ambani for the delay, referring to him as “Prime Minister Ambani” in a X post.
Reliance, whose telecommunications business Jio serves more than 530 million customers in India, has denied blocking competition. It has welcomed Starlink and pointed out that its own satellite venture was awaiting New Delhi’s security clearance.
India has also denied favoring domestic companies in the approval process. Musk subsequently acknowledged Reliance’s response, saying, “Much appreciated.”
Rubio cannot avoid politics
Rubio’s decision to hold talks in Mumbai rather than New Delhi has drawn criticism from India’s opposition Congress party.
Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi snarked that Rubio “summoned his employee to Mumbai,” while senior Congress leader Jairam Ramesh questioned why the American ambassador announced details of Jaishankar’s schedule.
In the US, six Democratic lawmakers urged Rubio to raise concerns over the detention of anti-government protesters in New Delhi and the alleged use of excessive force. Their October 16 letter also sought an investigation into reports that Indian diplomatic missions monitored protesters in the US.
Meetings with foreign dignitaries outside the capital are not unusual, India’s Foreign Ministry pointed out, citing previous engagements in several cities. It confirmed that Rubio and Jaishankar would discuss energy, trade, investment, defense, and emerging technologies.
The Trump administration prioritizes business over politics, and it may well be that the global energy situation – and a billionaire – have placed New Delhi in a sweet spot to benefit from that.

Qatar is preparing a new regional defence partnership while keeping channels open with Tehran, arguing that dialogue and economic ties offer a route to lasting peace. Doha also warned of an energy disruption “peak” with more difficulties on the horizon “in the coming days and months”.
Qatar will soon announce a new defence partnership, Deputy Prime Minister Sheikh Saoud bin Abdulrahman Al Thani said on Monday, while also calling for talks and closer economic ties with Iran to prevent further conflict.
Sheikh Saoud, also minister of state for defence affairs, told the Global Security Forum in Doha that Qatar was using lessons from the Iran war to better protect itself and develop new defence plans with its neighbours.
The planned defence partnership would help Qatar counter ballistic missiles, drones and cyberattacks, he said, also focusing on water security.
He also said Qatar would soon announce a local defence production hub, with local manufacturing or investments in defence companies, working with a regional partner and allies including the United States, Britain and France.
He said that “more than 90% of (Iran’s) attacks” on the region were countered successfully by the Gulf region due to cooperation with the US, through decades of military investments, training and shared experience and that developments of Al Udeid airbase — the biggest US base in the Middle East — would continue in line with their needs.
Sheikh Saoud told the Global Security Forum that Doha had stayed in contact with Tehran at different levels despite Iran’s attacks. “We never stop our communication,” the deputy prime minister said.
The deputy prime minister called for talks between Iran and the six Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries, as well as Pakistan and Turkey, once the US and Iran reach a settlement. International allies should also be consulted, he said.
Until then, he said Qatar was working with Pakistan and Oman on mediation, comparing it to a long-distance race that requires determination and resilience.
Qatar warns of energy disruption
Sheikh Saoud said that the Gulf countries could emerge from the conflict with stronger economies and new partnerships, as they had after previous crises.
“Iran is our neighbour,” he said, arguing that closer economic ties could help prevent another conflict and that the talks should build trust and address security concerns on both sides, with a non-aggression agreement among the possible next steps.
He pointed to France and Germany’s joint work on Airbus as an example of countries building economic links.
Qatar’s deputy prime minister said that Qatar and Iran also share a major offshore gas field, giving both countries an interest in avoiding further disruption.
He also warned that ongoing disruptions in the energy sector continue to send shockwaves worldwide, and that crises in the region can disrupt the “chain of supply from east to west and also from west to east”.
“We haven’t reached the peak with respect to energy,” and warned of more difficulties “in the coming days and months”.
He also rejected transit fees in the Strait of Hormuz and said uncertainty over shipping would raise costs for consumers.
Sheikh Saoud said energy disruptions and other regional conflicts pose an ongoing threat to Qatar and the Gulf countries, and that regional instability can affect Gulf investment toward Europe.

Israel oversaw cash flow to Hamas-controlled Gaza – Time
Israel helped facilitate nearly $2 billion in Qatari payments to Gaza over more than a decade and urged Doha to maintain the funding, even as Israeli officials publicly accused the country of financing Hamas, Time Magazine reported on Sunday, citing official correspondence and testimony from senior Israeli, US, and Arab officials.
Qatari payments to Gaza, long a source of controversy, came under renewed scrutiny after the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack on Israel. Qatar has denied that the funds were intended for Hamas and has argued that Israel was responsible for any money that reached the group, as West Jerusalem oversaw the aid mechanism.
According to Time, Israel’s role went beyond simply allowing Qatar to send aid to Gaza. Israeli officials reportedly determined who received the money, facilitated cash deliveries into the enclave, and pressed Doha to keep the payments flowing.
The report highlights a contradiction between Israeli officials’ public accusations that Qatar was financing Hamas and their private requests for Doha to continue the payments. The discrepancy reportedly angered Qatari officials, according to source in the first administration of US President Donald Trump as cited by Time.
The publication also details how Israel facilitated the payments, including cash deliveries to Gaza in suitcases and a UN-backed payment mechanism. The magazine cited a 2020 letter in which then-Mossad chief Yossi Cohen thanked Qatar’s Emir Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani for the assistance. Two weeks before the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack, then-Mossad chief David Barnea reportedly traveled to Doha and asked Qatar to renew the funding for another two months.
By 2018, Qatar had sent roughly $1.1 billion to Gaza, according to an analysis provided to Israeli ministers. The funds covered humanitarian assistance, fuel, and government salaries. Under the arrangement, Qatar paid for fuel and electricity purchased from Israel, financed projects through the UN, and provided monthly $100 payments to some of Gaza’s poorest families, distributed by the World Food Programme after Israeli authorities vetted recipients.
Netanyahu defended the policy as necessary to avert a humanitarian crisis and maintain essential services in Gaza, the magazine noted. The PM’s office has declined to comment on the latest findings.
Qatar told Time that all its assistance was intended for Palestinian civilians and delivered through mechanisms coordinated with Israel and international partners. At the same time, Doha argued that Israel bore responsibility if any funds reached Hamas because it had overseen delivery and created the mechanism.

Bulgaria Takes Four Medals at World Sumo Championships
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
15:38:02 UTC
00:38:02 KST

Bulgaria has crowned its first world sumo champion in 16 years, with Simeon Stankovic winning gold in the under-115 kg category at the World Championships in Baku, Azerbaijan, on October 17-18.
Stankovic claimed the title after four consecutive victories. He beat Kyrgyzstan’s Sulde Dongak in the semifinals before defeating Hungary’s Marcell Gorica in the final.
Bulgaria’s previous world champion in sumo was Stiliyan Georgiev, who won the title in 2010. Like Svetoslav Binev before him, Georgiev is a two-time world champion.
Stankovic said he had anticipated winning the title, crediting his preparation and the confidence of those around him. "To be honest, I largely expected this title. It might sound immodest, but I trained with the best in Bulgaria, such as Ivan Blagoev, a multiple-time medalist and European champion," he said, as quoted by Sport PR Events Management. He added that Blagoev and his loved ones had believed in him strongly, and that although he was certain he would win a medal, he had also expected to become world champion.
Known by the nickname "The Bull," Stankovic said he would not pause his training after the victory, as he has an MMA bout scheduled in Germany on November 7.
"There is no rest ahead; training continues, because I have an MMA match in Germany on November 7," he said.
Stankovic began wrestling at the age of six and moved to Germany when he was 16, competing in the First Bundesliga. He entered the national sumo championship for the first time in 2017 but subsequently stepped away from the sport for several years.
He returned in 2024 and won silver at the European Championships before finishing as world vice-champion in 2025. This year, he also trained in Japan at the stable run by former professional sumo wrestler Kaloyan Mahlyanov, known as Kotooshu.
Away from competition, Stankovic practices falconry and makes leather accessories and equipment for birds of prey.
Bulgaria finished the World Championships with four medals: one gold and three bronze.
Mihaela Hristova took bronze in the under-65 kg category, while Stanislava Atanasova finished third in the 80 kg division.
Hristova said she was disappointed to have missed the opportunity to win gold, despite securing a place in the semifinals. "My first reaction after winning bronze is a sense of frustration - I was just one step away from the gold. I reached the semifinals; had I beaten the Japanese competitor, I could have been the world champion instead of finishing third," she commented. She added that mistakes could be corrected in future competitions but said she was still proud of her result.
Atanasova also said she had hoped to win the title, while acknowledging the value of her bronze medal.
"I’m both pleased and not. A bronze medal at a World Championship is a significant achievement, but I had come for the gold," she said. Atanasova added that she was proud to be third in the world and grateful for the support of her coaches, parents and friends.
Gabriela Spasova won Bulgaria’s third bronze medal in the under-60 kg category for girls under 18.
Six-time European champion Anna Metodieva returned to the dohyo after a decade away from competition and placed fifth, despite injuring her shoulder in her opening bout.
Ivan Blagoev, competing in the under-100 kg category, and Presiyan Mihov, in the 85 kg division, did not win medals.

Fifteen months ago, Ukraine’s online arms store for front-line units didn’t exist. Now, it delivers 1 in 5 drones that state buys
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
15:38:00 UTC
00:38:00 KST

Ukraine has turned buying weapons into something closer to online shopping. One in five drones bought by Ukraine's Defense Procurement Agency now reaches troops through DOT-Chain Defence, a state digital marketplace established in 2025 that lets combat units order what they need directly, the Defense Ministry says.
Drone technology changes so fast that a weapon ordered through months of paperwork can be obsolete before it arrives, so Ukraine built a marketplace that puts the choice in the hands of the units that fight. Launched in July 2025, DOT-Chain Defence now serves more than 500 combat units.
Unlike the agency’s other channels, central competitive tenders and fixed procurement lists, the marketplace lets commanders pick from a catalog themselves. The system works like an online store, where the military spends state funds to decide exactly what the state supplies them.
From a catalog to the trenches in eight days
Speed is the point of the model. When an item is in stock, the average time from a unit’s order to shipment is eight days, rising to about a month and a half for pre-orders, the ministry notes.
“Delivery speed is especially important for unmanned systems, because technology in this field develops dynamically,” DOT-Chain Defence chief Artem Romaniukov says.
Also, he states that makers and soldiers constantly rework designs to beat new countermeasures.
The catalog spans the main types of unmanned aerial vehicles, FPV drones, bombers and fixed-wing aircraft, along with their munitions, ground robotic systems and electronic-warfare gear.
Who carries the paperwork now
The shift moves the burden off the fighters. A unit builds its own order in DOT-Chain Defence, and the agency handles the procurement side, signing contracts with manufacturers and making payments. That means that purchases are completed in a few clicks.
In the first nine months of 2024, Ukraine’s troops received more than a million drones and other equipment through this system, part of a drone-buying surge that reached about $8 billion in the first half of the year.
