US banning Chinese AI DeepSeek from government agency IT systems
- US Homeland Security has ordered civilian agencies to remove DeepSeek products and services from IT systems, citing risks of sensitive data leaking to the PRC and possible malware.
- The ban also stops agencies buying DeepSeek-based tools. DHS warned the model could create “actionable intelligence” on US people and agencies.
- The move follows earlier bans by some US agencies and states, as Washington steps up pressure on Chinese tech firms. The FCC is also planning new limits on Chinese labs and devices.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – The US Homeland Security Department (DHS) is ordering the removal of DeepSeek products and third-party services using the Chinese AI model from US civilian agency IT systems, according to a notice published on Oct 19.
The department is also banning acquisition of DeepSeek products and third-party services developed using DeepSeek by US civilian government agencies.
DHS said DeepSeek models pose “multiple threat vectors” and raised concerns that use of the product “may result in the transfer of sensitive data to the PRC if used by US government employees or vendors”.
It also said use of DeepSeek by government agencies “could produce actionable intelligence on US persons and/or government agencies. The models themselves may contain malware or other security vulnerabilities”.
In a July memo made public on Oct 19, DHS told federal agencies to monitor flows of traffic in and out of government websites to address potential risks from DeepSeek.
Previously, several US agencies, including the Department of Commerce and the Navy, have banned the use of DeepSeek on government devices. Multiple states including New York, Tennessee, and Virginia have taken similar steps.
The Chinese Embassy in Washington did not immediately comment.
The Trump administration has taken a series of steps to crack down on Chinese tech companies.
The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) will vote on Oct 29 to bar all Chinese labs from testing electronic devices such as smartphones, cameras and computers for use in the US.
In 2025, 82% of US electronics were tested in China.
In December, the FCC banned import of all new models of Chinese drones and also banned imports of new models of Chinese-made consumer routers, the boxes connecting computers, phones and smart devices to the internet.
In July, the FCC voted to bar sales of devices in the US that contain key hardware from Chinese companies deemed to be national security risks and has proposed to prohibit US telecommunications carriers from interconnecting with Chinese telecom firms deemed national security risks. REUTERS

Mandelblit’s testimony raises new questions about Netanyahu’s trial - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

On November 21, 2019, then-attorney-general of Israel Dr. Avichai Mandelblit announced his decision to indict Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for bribery and breach of trust in three cases.
This came four years after the Eran Kamin-Ben Caspit café meeting in late November 2015, which supposedly set things on their way.
The announcement came a day after the Abraham Accords were signed at the White House, where Netanyahu had shared a dais with US President Donald Trump and the foreign ministers of the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain.
Mandelblit was quite the party-pooper.
His performance only repeated a previous one, on February 28 that year, when he announced his intention to indict the prime minister just a month and a half before the April elections.
State Attorney Shai Nitzan was still seeking criminal charges in all three cases instead of just one.
Last week, called by the defense, Mandelblit came to the courtroom and provided testimony that is being continued this week.
If Netanyahu has been undergoing trials, it is obvious now that Mandelblit is undergoing severe tribulations, as are the members of the prosecuting team and police investigators. The public itself is still troubled.
Israelis bothered by the trials
The vast majority of Israel’s citizens have been agitated, bothered, disturbed, and angry. Netanyahu’s admirers and the Likud faithful viewed the entire matter as an attempt to bring down their hero. His opponents led a campaign under the theme “Crime Minister.”
The ongoing street protests began in November 2016, initially involving only a few dozen people, with weekly Saturday-night demonstrations in Petah Tikva, near Mandelblit’s home, and have since increased in number.
A “March of Shame” to protest “government corruption” and delays in the investigations took place on December 2, 2017. A Washington Post headline on February 5, 2018 read, “Israelis have been protesting government corruption for 61 weeks.”
Last week we witnessed an apparent collapse of the prosecution’s professional ethics. Already, in late June 2023, the judges privately told the prosecution and defense that there were difficulties in establishing the bribery offense.
They suggested that the prosecution consider withdrawing it, and three years (!) later, after Netanyahu completed his testimony and cross-examination, the judges repeated that their assessment was unchanged.
Yet, the trial continues.
First, Mandelblit indicated that the police acted behind his back and that specific investigative actions had not been authorized by him, an illegal act. This contradicted previous testimony of police investigators Koresh Barnor and Momi Meshulam, and Mandelblit called their statements “inaccurate.”
He further revealed that he demanded that Barnor remove a wiretap of Nathan Eshel as it was illegally intercepting conversations with Netanyahu.
Moreover, Mandelblit admitted he was kept in the dark concerning the use of Pegasus spyware in the Netanyahu cases and that it angered him.
Furthermore, the improper pressure exerted on the state’s witness Nir Hefetz, the “confidante ruse,” was anathema to him.
Nevertheless, he declared that he did not refer the matter to the Police Internal Investigations Department as that would have stalled the Netanyahu cases. He clarified, “You have to decide which interest you prioritize.”
The priority, of course, was Netanyahu, not justice, as Mandleblit admitted he had not read all the charge sheet items before signing it.
Lastly, Mandelblit admitted that the State Attorney’s Office team (Liat Ben-Ari, Yehudit Tirosh, and Tzipi Gez) concealed from him that they had been privy to the “confidante ruse” while simultaneously participating in a discussion regarding the review of that ruse.
That was apparently a serious conflict of interest: “One would expect them to have updated me,” he testified. “I wasn’t told they had approved the ruse.”
Admittedly, this is but Mandelblit’s version of events. He has yet to be questioned by the prosecution, and a verdict has not been handed down.
Yet, if there has been a public outcry over morals and decency by public officials, one in particular, which for a decade has been based on rumors and unsubstantiated news reports, one would expect some stocktaking and reassessment.
But on October 10, Ben Caspit appeared on Channel 12 and said, “Mandelblit twisted the reality 180 degrees.”
Guy Peleg, justice affairs reporter for Channel 12, informed his viewers that the court sessions with Mandelblit are but a “political happening” and that Netanyahu believes they will serve his election campaign.
Both Justice Minister Yariv Levin and Knesset Constitution and Law Committee chairman MK Simcha Rothman said at the Sovereignty Movement conference in Jerusalem last week that they are undeterred in their plans to continue reforming the judiciary in light of Mandelblit’s statements as a witness.
Former head of the Israel Bar Association, Effi Nave, was blunt in his reaction: “I hoped with all my heart that he would reveal the truth he had shared with me more than once: that he did not believe in the cases against the prime minister that had been forced upon him, and that, in fact, the cases against Netanyahu were trumped-up charges forming part of the persecution of the Right.”
I would entertain the thought that since the trials have not ended, the tribulations of Netanyahu, the prosecution, and the public are far from coming to a conclusion and a resolution. Even when the court delivers judgment, they will not be over.
Adi Ben-Hur, a Likud candidate for the Knesset, was harsh, writing on Facebook, “Mandelblit’s testimony today is nothing short of an earthquake … He [was] unfamiliar with basic details regarding that very indictment …
“We must now enact legal standards that allow for the prosecution of figures like Avichai Mandelblit, Shai Nitzan, Dina Zilber.”
That belief in one camp that Netanyahu is a “crime minister” and the opposing camp’s conviction that those prosecuting him are sinister slime has become such a part of the political performance here in Israel that it is an unfortunate development in our political discourse.
The writer is a researcher, analyst, and commentator on political, cultural, and media issues.

Euronews press review: French newspapers dissect weekend of unrest and rioting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
14:59:37 UTC
23:59:37 KST

French newspapers examine the causes of a weekend of unrest, questioning the police response, violence and examining the role of the ultra-left.
Euronews reviews France’s leading newspapers after a weekend of unrest, with protests over student living conditions turning violent and riots and looting reported in major cities.
Libération: Police fiasco
In its Monday 19 October edition, Libération questions the authorities’ handling of the demonstrations, noting that turnout far exceeded expectations.
“There were five times more of them than the 150,000 demonstrators anticipated by Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez,” the newspaper writes.
It asks whether the government and security forces took the calls for demonstrations seriously enough, describing the events as “the anatomy of a fiasco”.
The paper draws on the analysis of Sébastian Roché, a sociologist specialising in policing practices, who describes how police tactics contributed to the disorder.
“It was barely 12.20 pm on Place de la République in Paris when the tear gas began to spread across the sky, accompanied by deafening grenade blasts,” he says, nearly two hours before the march was due to begin.
Similar scenes unfolded in Marseille and Bordeaux, where gatherings descended into chaos within minutes. Clashes also broke out in Clermont-Ferrand.
Roché argues that police operations split up the marches, scattering demonstrators and making it harder for officers to maintain control — a strategy he says contributed to the damage.
Le Figaro: A scathing editorial
In his Monday editorial, Le Figaro deputy editor-in-chief Vincent Trémolet de Villers condemns what he describes as “a state humiliated in its town halls, its préfectures and its police stations”.
Trémolet de Villers, also a commentator on Europe 1, owned by billionaire Vincent Bolloré, criticises the judicial system, which he portrays as “indulgent towards criminals but merciless towards law-abiding citizens”.
He also attacks what he calls “far-left militias”, “uncontrolled immigration” and the “various forms of socialism that have governed us for the past fifteen years”.
In particularly sharp terms, he targets supporters of Jean-Luc Mélenchon, leader of La France Insoumise, calling them “useful idiots” who “not only wear the keffiyeh but also the tie”. He also denounces what he describes as a “technocratic monarchy, drunk on its own power”.
Le Monde: Organised ultra-left
Le Monde examines the ultra-left, a movement singled out by several political leaders following the unrest.
The newspaper traces its roots to political currents that emerged to the left of communist parties in the 20th century, including council communism, which advocates the direct organisation of workers into councils and rejects political parties.
Historian Sylvain Boulouque, a specialist in anarchism and the far left, explains that the ultra-left originally referred to groups that rejected the French Communist Party’s political model, parliamentary politics and elections.
The article describes a movement whose actions can follow “a logic of confrontation with the symbols of the state, capitalism or authority”.
Historian Gilles Candar, a specialist in the French left, cautions that the term “ultra-left” carries a connotation of excess and is now often used polemically.
He argues that some political leaders’ tendency to equate the ultra-left with the ultra-right creates what he calls a “regrettable and harmful false symmetry”.

Cyber unit flags rise in social media fraud using deepfake videos of PM, ministers to promote fake schemes

Unknown Publisher

Deceptive advertisements on Facebook and Instagram impersonate well-known public figures, including the Prime Minister.
NEW DELHI: The National Cybercrime Threat Analytics Unit (NCTAU) under the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) has flagged a rise in financial fraud through deceptive advertisements on Facebook and Instagram that impersonate well-known public figures, including the Prime Minister, finance ministers and chief ministers, to promote fake govt schemes.“Victims are asked to pay purported fees or taxes to receive the benefits of these fake schemes. In some cases, advertisements offer fake cashback rewards through scratch-cards or spin-and-win contests, tricking victims into approving UPI collect requests from fraud merchants and transferring money to fraudsters,” the NCTAU warned on Monday.Ads, majorly on meta platforms featuring manipulated/deepfake videos ostensibly show the public figures announcing and promoting a welfare scheme allegedly intended to provide financial assistance to the needy. The advertisements listing phone numbers either offer financial assistance under a purported welfare scheme or cashback/rewards through scratch-card or spin-and-win offers.Victims are either directed to a phone number/WhatsApp chat or redirected to a fraudulent website through the advertisement in order to claim the funds/benefits of the purported scheme. In many instances, victims receive calls from international numbers, largely Pakistan-based (+92 numbers), claiming that they have been randomly selected to receive the alleged funds.
Victims are redirected to a website and are coerced to make repeated payments under the pretext of taxes, processing fees, registration charges, verification fees or other administrative expenses in order to receive the funds and benefits.
Victims make multiple payments and suffer substantial cumulative financial losses. In some instances, the victims are redirected to a payment app and induced to enter their transaction PIN on the pretext of receiving the prize money. The transaction, however, results in money being debited from the victim’s account and gets transferred to the perpetrator.NCTAU has asked users to check details of welfare schemes on the official website of the concerned department, before acting on social media advertisements. They have been asked to verify the purpose and recipient of any fee or payment requested in connection with a welfare benefit, as well as identities of the persons claiming to represent the govt, through official channels.“Before approving a UPI collect request or entering a UPI PIN, check the transaction details… A UPI PIN is used to authorise payments, not to receive money,” cautioned NCTAU.

BAKU, October 19. /TASS/. Trade turnover between Azerbaijan and Russia amounted to $2.684 bln in January-September 2026, which is more than 1.3 times lower than in the same period last year, according to figures provided by the State Customs Committee of Azerbaijan.

Exports of Azerbaijani products to Russia equaled $883.587 mln in nine months of 2026 (up by 3.7%), while imports from Russia totaled $2.775 bln compared to $1.767 bln in the same period in 2025 (down by 36.3%), according to figures provided by the customs service.
Russia ranked fifth among Azerbaijan's trading partners in January-September after Italy, the UK, Turkey, and China, according to the report. The share of trade operations with Russia during this period accounted for 7.21% of the republic’s total foreign trade turnover.
In 2025, trade turnover between the two countries totaled $4.92 bln, an increase by 2.5% compared with the previous year.

Egypt postpones Sisi's Saudi troop deployment vote to next week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19

Breadcrumb
Egypt postpones Sisi's Saudi troop deployment vote to next week
Egypt's parliament has postponed a vote on authorising military support for Saudi Arabia until 26 October, amid growing political debate over President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi's request to deploy forces to help Riyadh confront Houthi attacks from Yemen.
The postponement comes as Egyptian political parties and public figures call for a diplomatic solution to the escalating conflict, warning against drawing the country into another regional war without clearly defined objectives or an assessment of the potential costs.
Lawmakers delayed the vote after debating whether Egyptian forces should be sent to Saudi Arabia to support its confrontation with Yemen's Houthi rebels.
Sisi has requested parliamentary authorisation to provide air defence forces and logistical support to help Saudi Arabia counter Houthi missiles and drones.
The Egyptian National Defence Council, chaired by the president, has also expressed Cairo's readiness to provide Saudi Arabia with necessary and available forms of assistance.
However, the prospect of military involvement has divided political parties, with some supporting the proposed authorisation and others demanding clearer limits on any deployment.
Calls for mediation instead of military intervention
The debate has intensified following a call by Al-Azhar's Grand Imam, Sheikh Ahmed el-Tayeb, for an urgent mediation initiative involving prominent Arab and Muslim figures to help end regional conflicts.
Tayeb called on Sunday for an immediate and comprehensive halt to fighting and destruction, proposing the formation of a committee of respected figures from Arab and Islamic countries to defuse tensions and bring opposing parties closer together.
He also expressed Al-Azhar's readiness to support the initiative.
The proposal has gained support from Egyptian political parties and public figures seeking to prioritise negotiations over military intervention.
Egypt's Grand Mufti Nazir Ayyad welcomed the initiative, calling for dialogue and efforts to promote peace.
The Constitution Party also expressed solidarity with Saudi Arabia against threats to its security and sovereignty but urged caution over any decision that could involve Egypt in a regional military confrontation.
It called for the proposed military authorisation to have clearly defined objectives, limits and conditions, while stressing the importance of ending the war through mediation and diplomatic efforts.
The Egyptian Social Democratic Party adopted a more cautious position, instructing its parliamentary representatives to abstain from voting on the request.
While reaffirming its support for Saudi Arabia, the party argued that insufficient information had been provided about the nature of the proposed military missions.
It warned that Egyptian involvement could expose the country's interests and infrastructure to additional risks, particularly shipping through the Red Sea, Bab al-Mandab Strait and Suez Canal.
Lawmaker Reda Abdel Salam proposed limiting any Egyptian deployment to defending Saudi territory and critical infrastructure, including airports and water and electricity facilities, while avoiding combat operations inside Yemen.
Parties divided over risks of involvement
Other Egyptian parties have backed Sisi's request, arguing that Saudi Arabia's security is closely linked to Egypt's national security and wider Arab stability.
The parliamentary blocs of the Wafd Party, the Republican People's Party and the Justice Party have expressed support for the proposed authorisation.
However, even among those supporting assistance to Riyadh, questions remain over the scope of any deployment and the risks of prolonged involvement.
Justice Party deputy leader and MP Mohamed Fouad told The New Arab that a decision of this magnitude required a serious discussion of its objectives, limitations and possible consequences.
He said political parties should move beyond simply supporting or opposing the proposal and examine the circumstances under which Egyptian forces might be deployed.
Fouad stressed that previous regional conflicts demonstrated the importance of establishing clear objectives from the outset, warning against open-ended military operations that could drain human and economic resources.
He argued that supporting Saudi Arabia did not contradict efforts to reduce tensions, and that political and diplomatic engagement remained essential to preventing a wider conflict.

Who is cult head Paul Mackenzie, convicted of convincing followers to die?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
14:54:24 UTC
23:54:24 KST

Who is cult head Paul Mackenzie, convicted of convincing followers to die?
A Kenyan court has handed down the first judgement in the ‘doomsday’ cult case.
A court in the Kenyan city of Mombasa has found a self-proclaimed pastor and his associates guilty of the murder of 191 people, all but one of whom were children.
Paul Mackenzie and several of his followers were charged with murder after his cult was alleged to have forced children to starve so they could “meet Jesus”.
Before Monday’s verdict, the accused had pleaded not guilty and also denied charges in other cases, including terrorism, radicalisation and stopping children from attaining an education.
Here’s what you should know:
Who is Mackenzie?
Mackenzie was the head of the apocalyptic Good News International Ministries, which he established with his wife in 2003 in the southeastern coastal city of Malindi. Before that, he was a taxi driver in Nairobi.
The church drew thousands of followers across its many branches in Kenya, with devotees also following Mackenzie’s fiery sermons broadcast on the church television station, Times TV.
He reportedly convinced followers he could speak to God. Some of them are believed to have sold off property to donate to the church.
Mackenzie preached doomsday conspiracy theories of education as being “evil”, with children forbidden from attending school. He banned his followers from using medication because it was against religious “doctrine” and encouraged followers to burn birth certificates and digital IDs. His preaching was also anti-Western, including condemnation of the United States, the United Nations and even the Catholic Church.
Authorities began to scrutinise Mackenzie’s establishment in the late 2010s.
After his church and TV station were forced to shut down in 2019, he moved to the Shakahola forest in Kilifi County, about 70 kilometres (43.4 miles) from Malindi. Some of his devotees relocated with him to live in mud houses in the vast forest.
What is Mackenzie accused of?
In 2023, authorities were tipped off by a man whose wife and daughter had also relocated to the remote forest.
Police investigations led to shallow mass graves in the forest linked to the cult group. Authorities also found dozens of other emaciated surviving members in the forest. Some told police that Mackenzie had ordered them to starve themselves until they “meet Jesus”.
Most of the bodies exhumed were of children. Some of the victims also died of strangulation or blunt trauma, authorities said, adding that some people who tried to leave the cult were attacked. Others were found with their hands and legs bound together.
A total of 429 deaths were reported, including many others who later died in hospital. Hundreds are still declared missing.
Mackenzie is not believed to have starved himself. Survivors said that according to his orders, children were to starve themselves, followed by unmarried women, men, and last of all, church leaders.
Authorities accused Mackenzie of instigating a mass starvation campaign that led to the deaths. In January 2024, Mackenzie was charged with 191 counts of murder and his church was proscribed as an “organised criminal group”.
What’s happened in the case so far?
Mackenzie, along with 34 others, including other leaders of the church, were arrested and charged with murder and terrorism-related offences.
Enos Amanya Ngala, Mackenzie’s former head of security, was one of the accused, but he entered a guilty plea deal and agreed to stand as a witness for the prosecution.
At a 2024 hearing at the Kenya High Court, the court urged prosecutors to reduce the charges to 12 to speed up the process. Mackenzie and his colleagues pleaded not guilty to the crimes.
Officials also initially arraigned 65 rescued victims on charges of attempted suicide, which carries a two-year sentence in Kenya. A court in Mombasa ordered they be remanded in a rescue centre and monitored, after many reportedly rejected food.
While in jail, Mackenzie was accused of involvement in another 52 deaths after officials said he was luring more victims to their deaths by writing notes from his prison cell.

More than 60% of Ukrainians consider handing Moscow all of eastern Ukraine’s Donbas region in exchange for security guarantees completely unacceptable, according to a new poll by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KIIS).
The survey, conducted Oct. 8-16, found that 61% rejected the proposed concession, while 35% were prepared to accept it, most of them describing it as a difficult condition. Another 4% were undecided.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The institute said the findings showed no statistically significant change from late July and early August.
Opposition stood at 57% among respondents interviewed Oct. 8-9 and 62% among those interviewed Oct. 10-16, a period the institute described as following the announcement of the US’s “diesel deal” with Moscow and subsequent pressure on Ukraine.
KIIS cautioned that the difference fell within the margin of error and did not establish a shift in opinion.
“At least for now, the campaign of pressure on Ukraine has not led to greater willingness to accept this proposal,” the institute said.
Half or more of respondents in every region rejected withdrawing Ukrainian troops in exchange for security guarantees, a Kremlin war goal repackaged as peace terms in earlier US proposals.
Acceptance was highest in eastern Ukraine, where respondents were primarily residents of the Kharkiv region. There, 45% said they could accept the proposal, while 51% considered it completely unacceptable.
Russia Hits 28 Substations in Overnight Strike, Zelensky Says
In other regions, outright opposition ranged from 60% to 66%. In Kyiv, 66% rejected the proposal despite repeated Russian attacks on the capital, KIIS said.
President Volodymyr Zelensky warned in March that Ukraine’s withdrawal from the Donbas – which Russia has failed to capture militarily in 12 years – could free up Moscow’s manpower and pose more threats to the rest of Ukraine.
Who’s the obstacle to peace?
The survey also examined whether Ukrainians see their own government’s negotiating position or Russia’s ambitions as the main obstacle to peace. Researchers divided respondents into two groups to test how different question formats affected their answers.
In the first group, respondents assessed two statements separately. Some 20% agreed that Ukrainian authorities should make more concessions to reach an agreement with Russia, while 73% disagreed.
By contrast, 84% agreed that Russia wants to subjugate Ukraine and is therefore unwilling to accept a peace settlement that leaves it a sovereign state with a strong army. Twelve percent disagreed.
In the second group, respondents were asked to choose which of two statements they agreed with more. Some 78% chose the statement identifying Russia’s desire to subjugate Ukraine as the obstacle to peace. Twelve percent chose the statement that Ukrainian authorities were too uncompromising.
Washington has recently blamed Kyiv and Zelensky for the prolonged war, though the findings suggest most Ukrainians do not share the assessment that Kyiv should make more concessions to reach an agreement with Russia.
KIIS interviewed 1,031 Ukrainian citizens aged 18 and older by telephone, using randomly generated mobile phone numbers.
The survey covered people living in Ukrainian government-controlled territory, including internally displaced people. It excluded residents of Russian-occupied areas and Ukrainians who left the country after Feb. 24, 2022.
The full survey had a maximum formal margin of sampling error of 4 percentage points at the 95% confidence level, accounting for the survey design. For the questions asked separately of roughly half the sample, the maximum margin was 5.7 percentage points.

EXPLAINER - Can the world still protect 30% of the planet by 2030?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
14:51:38 UTC
23:51:38 KST

- Protected areas cover 18.7% of land, 10% of ocean four years before 2030 deadline
- High seas remain largest gap with just 1.7% under protection
Countries are falling short of their pledge to protect 30% of the planet's land and oceans by 2030, with protected areas currently covering 18.7% of land and 10% of oceans as the UN Biodiversity Conference opens in Yerevan.
The conference, known as COP17, is being held in the Armenian capital from Oct. 19 to 30 under the theme "Taking Action for Nature." It marks the first global review of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, adopted at COP15 in Montreal in 2022 with the aim of halting and reversing biodiversity loss by 2030.
A UN report released ahead of the talks shows that most countries have set national targets in line with the framework, yet fewer than half consider themselves on track to meet any of them.
At stake is whether governments can turn four years of commitments into measurable protection on the ground and at sea, with just over three years left before the deadline.
 
30x30: More than a numbers game
The 30x30 goal, formally known as Target 3, is the best-known of the framework's 23 targets. It calls for at least 30% of land and ocean areas to be under protection by 2030.
The target goes beyond simply declaring areas protected. It requires them to be effectively conserved and managed through ecologically representative, well-connected and equitably governed systems.
Other targets in the framework include restoring degraded ecosystems and reducing harmful subsidies by at least $500 billion a year.
 
Climate link: Ecosystems as carbon stores
Ecosystems such as forests, wetlands, oceans and soils store large amounts of carbon, slowing climate change and helping communities adapt to its impacts.
When these ecosystems are destroyed, the stored carbon is released into the atmosphere, linking biodiversity loss directly to global warming.
 
Global picture: Uneven progress
According to October figures from the Protected Planet database, maintained by the UN Environment Programme World Conservation Monitoring Centre (UNEP-WCMC) and the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), there are more than 514,000 protected areas worldwide.
Together, they cover 18.7% of the world's land and 10% of its oceans.
According to an assessment published in September by the Campaign for Nature, government commitments are set to increase protection to approximately 27% of land but only 12% of the global ocean by 2030.
Progress varies sharply by region. Latin America has protected 29% of its land and 26% of its ocean, while Oceania has protected 24% and 41%, respectively. Seychelles leads in land protection at 68%, while Libya, Eritrea and Somalia have yet to protect any.
 
UN stocktake: Commitments outpace action
The State of Biodiversity Action report, released by the Convention on Biological Diversity Secretariat on Oct. 15, offers the first global assessment of progress under the framework.
It found that 162 parties, or 83%, have set national targets aligned with the framework, compared with only about half of parties that set targets under the previous Aichi Biodiversity Targets in 2020.
However, fewer than half of reporting parties considered their national targets to be on track to meet any of the global targets, and negative indicator trends were more common than positive ones.
"We remain off track to meet our collective goals," UN Environment Programme Executive Director Inger Andersen said in the report.
Target 3 reveals a striking contrast. National targets linked to protected areas are among those most frequently assessed by countries themselves as being on track, yet indicator-based data show that Target 3 has made less collective progress than most other targets.
The report also found that marine, coastal and inland water ecosystems consistently show gaps in coverage and remain underrepresented compared with terrestrial ecosystems.
 
Oceans: Widest gap on high seas
The shortfall is most pronounced in international waters. Protection reaches 23.3% in national waters, but just 1.7% on the high seas, which make up 61% of the world's oceans.
Existing marine reserves are not always permanent, as governments can scale back, shrink or strip protections from designated areas. In 2018, Australia scaled back safeguards in its Coral Sea marine park over an area exceeding 740,000 square kilometers, while the US has opened all five Marine National Monuments to fishing over the last two years.
 
Yerevan: Finance, implementation in focus
Countries are expected to review their progress, address finance gaps and discuss how to turn national commitments into action.
Funding remains a major hurdle. The UN report said the 2025 milestone of $20 billion a year in international biodiversity finance was likely not met, though a final assessment will only be possible once complete data are available.
The talks will also test whether the momentum behind the framework can translate into protection that is both broader and more effective.

Mpox continues spreading worldwide, Russia’s sanitary watchdog monitoring situation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
14:50:00 UTC
23:50:00 KST

MOSCOW, October 19. /TASS/. The spread of mpox continues worldwide, Russia’s sanitary watchdog Rospotrebnadzor is monitoring the situation.
"Rospotrebnadzor is keeping the mpox situation under control <…>. Mpox continues spreading worldwide, with Africa remaining the disease’s epicenter. According to the WHO (World Health Organization - TASS), more than 193,000 mpox cases were confirmed worldwide from 2002 to September 2026.
Mpox, formerly known as monkeypox, is a rare viral disease endemic to remote regions near tropical forests in Central and Western Africa. The first case of an animal transmitting the disease to humans was recorded in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 1970. According to the WHO, this virus is usually transmitted to humans by wild animals, such as rodents and primates, while its secondary spread among humans is limited. Usually the lethality coefficient during mpox outbreaks ranges from 1% to 10% with the majority of fatalities affecting younger age groups.
Mpox is most often accompanied by a skin rash or mucosal lesions, which can last from two to four weeks. Additional symptoms include fever, headache, muscle aches, back pain, low energy and swollen lymph nodes.

The comment period expires on Oct 19, which means the FCC could take action on the petition this week ahead of the Nov 3 election.
A spokesperson for FCC chairman Brendan Carr did not comment immediately.
“There is absolutely no excuse to relax these standards and allow special interests to flood our cellphone lines with deepfakes or dark-money-funded AI voices,” Schumer said.

Club for Growth president David McIntosh said in a statement earlier in October that the group wants “the FCC to treat First Amendment-protected political speech the same way it already treats wireless calls about package deliveries, bank accounts and doctor’s appointments”.
The group, which backs conservative economic views on taxes, regulations and cutting the size of government, plans to spend US$175 million (S$224 million) in the midterm congressional elections, it said on its website.
The FCC, in describing the petition, said the system “uses a perfunctory human being for the sole purpose of clicking on a ‘send’ or similarly termed button to transmit thousands of text messages per hour”.
A number of public interest groups have urged the FCC not to grant the petition as has Democratic FCC commissioner Anna Gomez.

Strait of Hormuz scoured for spilt cargo after Iran attacks container ships
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
14:48:56 UTC
23:48:56 KST

People have been scouring the strait of Hormuz for spilt cargo after Iran attacked at least 15 container ships passing through the crucial waterway in the past 10 days.
Some ships have been hit by drones, others by mines. On Sunday, a ship was struck by a rocket-propelled grenade launched from a small boat 75 miles (120km) north-east of the Saudi port of Jubail.
The rise in Iranian attacks appears to have helped resolidify Tehran’s disputed control over the strait, as well as pushing the price of a barrel of Brent crude oil close to $108 a barrel on Monday morning.
Last Wednesday a ship travelling from Karachi, Pakistan, to Fujairah, in the United Arab Emirates, sunk after hitting a mine, according to Iranian state TV. All 21 crew members were evacuated and no injuries were reported. Dozens of its 2,500 containers were seen floating in the water. Rumours that iPhones and other expensive goods were among its cargo – fuelled by fake AI-generated photos published on social media – prompted fishers and others to investigate.
One fisher told an Iranian reporter: “The Arab boatmen, who were closer to the ship, arrived earlier than the Iranians. They used stonecutters to cut the container and took whatever was there.”
Col Javad Mokhtar Rezaei, the deputy head of cultural and social affairs for Iran’s cyber police (Fata), told the Tasnim news agency: “In some cases, the phones offered may actually exist, but exposing electronic components to salt water and extreme humidity can cause corrosion of internal components, damage to the boards, battery and display, and cause hidden malfunctions in the device’s performance.”
Meysam Doost-Mohammadi, a spokesperson for the Iranian mobile phone Aassociation, said it would be unusual for valuable devices to be transported by ship.
The bulk of the recent attacks have occurred close to the coast with Oman, a route that Iran regards as unauthorised. In the seven days to Friday 16 October, 12 vessels were attacked, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations Centre (UKMTO).
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) says it has the right to attack any ship that seeks to traverse the strait without its permission or with its transponders off. Officials have also ordered local fishers not to pillage the sea for luxury items, saying the goods are the property of the state.
Two oil tankers were hit on Saturday, including a supertanker carrying 2m barrels of oil, according to the IRGC. The Fars news agency published a video that appears to show the tanker burning, but which cannot be independently verified. A third tanker was hit late on Sunday.
It is disputed how many ships have been hit by mines or IRGC shelling. UKMTO’s weekly overview recorded 254 transits of the strait (125 outbound, 129 inbound) in the week to 14 October, approximately 70% below pre-conflict levels.
Dr Devaraj Asir Ramesh, of Anna University in Chennai, India, warned that the region’s marine habitats faced threats from toxic debris and oil spills, while noise might have disturbed marine life. Iranian strikes on the Emirates, he said, were likely to have contaminated seagrass beds with hydrocarbons and caused auditory damage to cetaceans – marine mammals such as dolphins and porpoises – which are sensitive to loud noise that travels through the sea.
Oil released by attacks on tankers at Fujairah could have caused ecological harm, he added. “Oil spills, chemical leaks and acoustic disturbances have impaired biodiversity, fisheries, aquaculture, desalination, and eco-tourism,” he wrote in the International Journal of Research and Innovation in Social Sciences.
On Friday, the Iranian president said the conflicts in Gaza and the wider Middle East had inflicted a significant toll on nature that extended beyond borders and required “international solutions”.
“What has occurred in our region as a result of wars of aggression is ecocide, or environmental genocide, and it must be condemned,” Masoud Pezeshkian said. He argued that countries subjected to economic sanctions or military aggression should not be forced to shoulder the financial burden of environmental damage resulting from conflicts they did not initiate.
Successive studies, mainly by US universities using satellite imagery, have warned of the dangers facing the strait.
Meanwhile, the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, visited Tehran offering to act as an intermediary between Iran and Donald Trump, especially over the issue of Iran’s nuclear stockpile, which the US president insists must be addressed before he lifts his threat to attack Iran again.
Iran has offered to open the strait in six days in return for sanctions relief.
Russia has offered to take Iran’s stockpile of highly enriched uranium, but Iran is reluctant to make a commitment on its nuclear programme and has not given the International Atomic Energy Agency access to its bombed nuclear sites since June 2025. Lavrov also proposed a trilateral summit between China, Russia and Iran to agree new security architecture for the strait. He said the region was on the verge of a full-scale crisis.
Tehran is braced for another attack soon, especially after the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, launched a new national security doctrine on Sunday that included an emphasis on prevention and offence, including pre-emptive strikes on potential threats.

Kremlin-installed authorities in Crimea have begun lifting fuel rationing measures introduced months ago in response to shortages caused by Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries and supply routes leading to the annexed peninsula.
Mikhail Razvozhayev, the Russian-appointed governor of Sevastopol, said Monday that purchase limits in the port city had been officially lifted as of midnight as shipments of fuel began to stabilize.
“We’ve removed the restrictions because the logistics situation with gasoline has practically stabilized,” the Interfax news agency quoted Razvozhayev as saying.

“Let’s hope the logistics situation will remain this way from now on,” Razvozhayev said.
Crimea began rationing fuel in May after Ukrainian drone strikes targeted military trucks and fuel tankers that supply the region from the north, triggering local gasoline shortages. The supply crisis later spread into mainland Russia as Ukraine ramped up its attacks on refineries, causing two major waves of nationwide fuel shortages.
On Oct. 12, the average price of gasoline in Sevastopol hit 131.76 rubles per liter ($6 per gallon), according to Rosstat data, which tracks the annexed city alongside Russian regions and lists it as being among the places with the highest gasoline prices nationwide.
Across Russia, the average price of gasoline has increased more than 21% since the start of the year.
Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries began to drive a wedge between the White House and Kyiv this month after U.S. President Donald Trump blamed them for the soaring cost of diesel in the United States, though analysts say the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran is the main cause of high energy prices.
Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine earlier this month, which neither side said they had agreed to beforehand. That apparent pause in strikes collapsed immediately as the Russian army continued its attacks against Ukraine’s power grid.

Heavy rain leaves at least 4 dead in eastern Spain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
14:47:00 UTC
23:47:00 KST

At least four people were killed and others were stranded on rooftops as heavy rain and floods battered Spain's Mediterranean coast, state broadcaster RTVE reported on Monday.
Rescue crews freed dozens of people who had been stranded since early morning, some on rooftops, in flooded buildings, or in vehicles.
Many roads, houses and campsites were underwater in the provinces of Valencia and Alicante. Floods also hit the Balearic Islands of Majorca and Ibiza.
Rescue operations used helicopters and boats, and even a surfboard: Police video showed a 93-year-old woman being brought to safety on one in Gandia.
The regional government declared the second-highest emergency level. Classes were suspended in more than 40 municipalities in the provinces of Valencia and Alicante.
Initially, authorities imposed a curfew of several hours for 145 municipalities with more than 800,000 residents in total.
By the afternoon, the curfew applied to only eight municipalities. However, several places remained cut off from the outside world due to the flooding.
The situation was particularly serious in the coastal town of Oliva, about 70 kilometres (43.5 miles) south of the provincial capital Valencia, where two bodies were recovered on Monday.
Storm system Adam had already caused chaos on the Spanish mainland at the weekend with extreme rainfall. Two people died: One woman in Sagunto in Valencia province, and another woman in Cabrera de Mar in Catalonia.
According to Mayor Yolanda Pastor, about 2,000 people were evacuated from seven campsites in Oliva.
"Many people are still trapped in their homes by the floodwaters," the mayor told the private broadcaster Antena 3. She said some people had climbed onto their roofs to escape.
A spokesperson for the emergency services said all people in life-threatening situations in Oliva had already been brought to safety.
Authorities in the hardest-hit areas in the south of Valencia province and the north of Alicante province urged people to stay in their homes where possible. The coastal regions of La Safor in Valencia and Marina Alta in Alicante were particularly affected.
According to Spain's state weather service AEMET, more than 530 millimetres of rain was recorded in Oliva within 24 hours. In the municipality of Pego in Alicante, just over 620 mm fell.
On Mallorca, the situation remained calm despite the highest red alert level declared for the night. Rescue services registered only three minor incidents: two fallen trees and a risk of collapse, which has since been resolved.
A total of 16 incidents were reported on the Balearic Islands, 11 of them on Ibiza and two on Formentera. Schools on all the islands had cancelled classes for Monday as a precaution.
Over the course of Monday, the rain in Valencia and Alicante and on the Balearic Islands was expected to gradually ease and move further north into Catalonia.
Almost two years ago, the Valencia region was hit by a devastating flood disaster that killed more than 220 people.

Xinhua Commentary: Resilient Chinese economy brings much-needed certainty to the world
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
22:46:58 CST
23:46:58 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- Viewed as an ocean rather than a pond, China's economy may not be immune to headwinds, but it stands firm enough to absorb powerful waves and weather turbulent times. In a world starved of certainty, it remains a stabilizing force in the global economy.
Facts on the ground speak for themselves. China's economy expanded by 4.6 percent in the first three quarters of 2026, landing squarely within the full-year target range and remaining among the fastest of major economies.
Yet to read the economy solely through the lens of headline speed is to miss the more important story. China is in a critical period of accelerating the transition from old growth drivers to new ones. The quality of growth and the direction of structural change matter more.
New quality productive forces are gathering momentum, with new growth drivers including high-end manufacturing, the digital and intelligent economy and modern services contributing more than 40 percent of expansion. In particular, industrial robots, 3D-printing equipment and lithium-ion batteries all registered strong double-digit growth, helping steer the economy toward more innovation-led, quality-driven development.
The foundation of China's economic resilience also lies in consumption, which accounted for nearly half of the GDP growth in the first three quarters. Services retail sales, upgraded goods consumption, new formats, as well as lower-tier markets and inbound tourism, are all picking up steam. With policymakers leaning harder into consumption support, household spending appetite is showing steady signs of recovery, setting the stage to unlock the vast potential of the country's super-large market.
Foreign trade remains one of the brightest spots, with growth reaching its highest level for the same period in five years. From new energy vehicles to photovoltaic products, robotics and innovative pharmaceuticals, Chinese exports are increasingly defined by frontier technology, original innovation capability and complete industrial and supply chains.
Furthermore, China has ample and effective policy tools to shape its economic growth trajectory. Five-year plans, deepened reforms and wider opening up, along with targeted fiscal and monetary measures and considerable room for counter-cyclical adjustment, all provide predictability and stability for the market.
A clear-eyed understanding of the Chinese economy also requires acknowledging the real headwinds: a complex and volatile external environment, insufficient domestic demand, and a structural transition that isn't finished.
As the latest figures have demonstrated, the Chinese economy is resilient. This is contrary to the narratives hyped up by certain pessimists and doomsters in the West. Backed by a domestic market of 1.4 billion people, a solid manufacturing base, well-developed infrastructure, a strong talent pool, and complete industrial and supply chains, the underlying fundamentals and long-term positive trend remain unchanged.
Amid the sluggish global recovery and rising geopolitical risks, China's development continues to offer the world growth momentum and market opportunities. It is both a sustained driver of inclusive and shared growth and a reliable buffer against global economic volatility stemming from factors such as regional conflicts and the rise of unilateralism and protectionism. For many years, China has contributed around 30 percent of global economic growth, remaining a major engine of the world economy.
As the world's largest manufacturer, China continues to provide high-quality, affordable, and reliable product supply globally. No longer just the world's factory, China is becoming a market and a mega-buyer for the world as imports have surged over 20 percent, reflecting a more balanced and open trade structure.
China's commitment to opening up remains unwavering despite rising protectionism globally. This is evidenced by the establishment of more new foreign-invested enterprises, and also highlighted by Apple's executive chairman Tim Cook, who recently noted that the company remains optimistic about China's development prospects and will further expand its business in the country.
China's edge may lie less in its speed, but more in the quality and sustainability of its advance, and in its capacity to hit its full-year targets. "China Opportunity 2.0," boosted by the dividends of innovation and high-standard opening up, will surely create more win-win cooperation outcomes for the world. ■

2026-10-19
22:46:41 CST
23:46:41 KST

TOKYO, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- Japan and the United States began large-scale joint military exercises across multiple locations in Japan on Monday, with Japanese experts warning that the drills would heighten regional tensions and undermine peace and stability in Asia.
The Keen Sword 27 exercises, running through Oct. 29, cover multiple domains, including land, sea, air, space, the electromagnetic spectrum and cyberspace. They involve air defense, anti-ship operations, parachute drops, amphibious operations and electromagnetic warfare, with exercise areas spanning Okinawa, Kyushu and Hokkaido, among other locations.
Japan's Type-25 surface-to-ship missile will take part in the exercises for the first time since its formal deployment in March this year. With a range of about 1,000 km, the missile is regarded as one of Japan's first missile systems capable of striking enemy bases, extending its reach well beyond Japanese territory.
Atsushi Koketsu, professor emeritus at Yamaguchi University, said the missile's participation in the Japan-U.S. joint drills, along with the first deployment of two U.S. weapons systems to Yonaguni Island, would exacerbate regional tensions, calling the developments deeply regrettable.
The Japanese government has repeatedly claimed that the security environment in East Asia is becoming increasingly severe. However, Koketsu said Japan and the United States themselves were contributing to the heightened tensions.
Takakage Fujita, secretary-general of the Association for Inheriting and Propagating the Murayama Statement, also criticized the exercises, describing them as extremely dangerous and calling for an end to military drills that undermine peace and stability in Asia.
According to previous reports by Kyodo News, the Japan Self-Defense Forces and the U.S. military will deploy approximately 45,000 and 12,000 personnel, respectively, for the exercises.
The Type-25 missile will be transferred from its base in Kumamoto Prefecture to the Ohnobaru training ground in the Nagasaki-Saga area for anti-ship drills. The missile will not be fired during the exercises.
Meanwhile, two advanced U.S. military equipment -- the Navy and Marine Expeditionary Ship Interdiction System and the Marine Air Defense Integrated System -- are scheduled to be deployed to Yonaguni Island in Okinawa Prefecture for the first time during the exercises.
The Keen Sword field exercises are generally held every two years. ■

China Focus: China uses digital technology to bring Long March history to life
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
22:46:15 CST
23:46:15 KST

GUIYANG, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- Inside the Zunyi Meeting memorial museum's exhibition hall, visitors are instantly plunged into a Long March battlefield scene after putting on lightweight virtual reality (VR) headsets, feeling as if they are surging across the Xiangjiang River under enemy fire.
Rather than observing history from a distance, they are placed inside it, with smoke filling the horizon, shells churning the water, and the voices of soldiers echoing through the simulated battlefield.
The immersive experience at the museum in Zunyi City, southwest China's Guizhou Province, is part of a broader push across China to use cutting-edge digital technology to preserve and revitalize Long March sites, as this year marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the expedition.
The Long March, a 12,500-kilometer military odyssey from 1934 to 1936, preserved the revolutionary forces and gave the Communist Party of China a new foothold to carry the revolution to victory. Today, sites along the route serve as patriotic education centers. As younger visitors seek more interactive experiences, the museums and memorial halls are turning to digital technology to bring static exhibits to life.
The Zunyi Meeting memorial museum is one such example, featuring a VR experience system. By digitally reconstructing more than 1,000 precious artifacts and using 3D modeling and real-time rendering, it presents panoramic recreations of pivotal moments from the march, including the Battle of the Xiangjiang River.
The technology also serves a preservation purpose. Faded manuscripts and rusted weapons have been converted, through high-precision 3D scanning, into digital archives. To date, the museum has completed 3D scans of 172 artifacts, built digital records for 1,600 two-dimensional items and preserved 8,600 pages of digital artifact archives, with about 80 percent of its collection now capable of interactive digital display.
"It narrows the distance between artifacts and visitors," said Huang Chao, deputy director of the information technology department at the museum.
The impact goes beyond preservation. "Audio-visual and lighting technologies have turned one-way explanations into immersive experiences that move some visitors to tears," said Hong Min, who oversees public engagement at the museum.
Beyond physical venues, a 5G-powered cloud exhibition hall allows users to explore more than a dozen revolutionary heritage sites and thousands of artifacts through a smartphone mini-program, complete with multi-version audio guides and the ability to zoom in on artifact details.
Similar efforts are underway in other parts of the country. In southwest China's Sichuan Province, another key region along the trail, local authorities have built a database containing more than one million pages of archives, alongside a geographic information system covering the Sichuan section of the route.
At a memorial hall in Luding County, visitors wearing VR headsets can virtually step onto the iron chains of the Luding Bridge, recreating the pivotal 1935 battle in which Red Army soldiers crossed it under fire.
"We use VR, digital twin and spatial positioning technologies to engage multiple senses, bringing visitors back to those revolutionary years," said Qu Yongfan, head of the interactive display project, noting that this immersive approach complements traditional static displays and historical documents.
China has been encouraging these local efforts. The National Cultural Heritage Administration has called on 15 provincial-level regions along the Long March route to coordinate the protection, management and use of related cultural relics, with an emphasis on promoting the campaign's spirit. Across the route, museums and memorial sites are increasingly turning to immersive technologies to bring those relics and stories to life.
"We hope to break the boundaries of time and space through technology, making the Long March spirit tangible and accessible, especially for young people," said Wang Zhi'ou, chief designer of the Guizhou Long March Culture Digital Art Museum in Guiyang, the provincial capital. ■

Sinti Auschwitz survivor Hermann Höllenreiner dies aged 92
Hermann Höllenreiner, a Sinti German raised in Bavaria who survived the Nazis' Auschwitz concentration camp as a child, has died aged 92.
Munich's Hanser Verlag publisher and the International Auschwitz Committee said that he had passed away last Friday, October 16, in Mettenheim in Bavaria, surrounded by his family.
Höllenreiner, known as "Mano" to his large Bavarian Sinti family, spent time at the Auschwitz-Birkenau, Ravensbrück and Sachsenhausen camps as a child.
"Only later in his life did he start to tell his story and became a major witness of the era, who hauntingly reported on the horrors of Auschwitz, the perpetrators and the victims, and above all of the still-persistnent discrimination of Sinti and Roma in Europe," Christioph Heubner, executive vice president of the International Auschwitz Committee, said.
"Mano Höllenreiner's biography and tales of suffering were enough for more than one life. What he saw with his own eyes as a child in Auschwitz and what was done to him — for many decades he didn't know how to speak out about it," Heubner said, thanking Höllenreiner for his "courage and humanity" in ultimately telling his story.
Höllenriener managed to flee one of the so-called "death marches" fleeing extermination camps in as Allied armies approached.
Author Anja Tuckermann told his story in a book whose title roughly translates as: "Mano. The boy who didn't know where he was."
He was initially found on a roadside and rescued by liberated French prisoners, who took him home with them. In 1946, he was reunited with surviving relatives in Germany.

German industry shed almost half a million jobs since 2019: Ifo Institute
German industrial businesses employed some 496,000 fewer people at the end of 2025 compared to the start of 2019, according to a survey conducted by the Ifo Institute economic think tank.
The figure represents a 7.1% decline.
Worst-hit has been the automotive industry, a key sector of the German economy, where 123,500 jobs were cut both at carmakers and suppliers, a decline of 13%.
But the metals sector also saw a marked decline in the number of jobs available, dropping 115,600 workers in the period, while the machinery sector bled 64,500 positions.
At the same time, more than 2.2 million additional jobs were created in the service sector, according to Ifo.
It said 391,000 new jobs had been established in the health sector and another 357,000 in social services, including care homes.
Joachim Ragnitz, managing director at Ifo Dresden, said the figures showed an "accelerated structural shift" in Germany.
"Ironically, the very sectors that have sustained our prosperity up to now are shrinking," he said.
"The new jobs are for the most part not being created where Germany is especially productive and innovative. That may slow down our growth potential in the future."

Women well behind men in leadership positions: Destatis
Less than a third of leadership positions in Germany are held by women, a lower level than the EU average, statistics released on Monday showed.
According to the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), citing figures from the EU statistics authority Eurostat, women held just 30.3% of leadership positions in Germany, compared with 35.9% in the whole of the EU.
Only Cyprus, Italy and the Netherlands have lower rates than Germany in the bloc, while Sweden has the highest, at 44.4%, followed by Latvia, Estonia and Poland.
"The low proportion of women in leadership positions in Germany is particularly striking, as almost as many women as men are employed here," Destatis said, comparing the situation with Italy, which has almost the same level of female leadership but a much lower rate of female employment overall.
Destatis defines leadership positions as those involving the management of small companies, the management of large companies or departments within them and high administrative posts.
Merz to open investment conference
A two-day conference entitled "Invest in Germany Summit" is to begin on Monday evening in Berlin as the government seeks to shore up public-sector spending with private money.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz will deliver the opening speech at the conference, which will be attended by an expected 200 representatives from large German and international companies.
The CEO of the US chip manufacturer Nvidia, Jensen Huang, is to be one of the key guests at the conference.
The German government is looking to cooperate strongly with the company, whose products are central to the boom in artificial intelligence, in a bid to help Germany catch up in the sector.
Don't expect too much: Economic institute
The German Economic Institute (IW) has, however, warned against any too high expectations from the summit, saying that high costs for labor, energy and bureaucracy in Germany were a deterrent to investment in the country.
"It would be naive to believe that the summit will change that in the short term. Companies don't choose Germany because of a promotional event. What matters is whether they can make money here," IW director Michael Hüther told the DPA news agency.
He said it would be more effective if the government were to swiftly implement its reform agenda.
A study by Allianz Research has shown that investment in Germany fell by 6.4% between 2019 and 2025, while it grew by 6.7% in the rest of the eurozone and a whole 20.2% in the US.

Kremlin hawks savour Trump-Zelenskiy rift — if it lasts

Unknown Publisher

Kremlin hawks savour Trump-Zelenskiy rift — if it lasts
MOSCOW, Oct 19 - Kremlin hawks are savouring a public rift between Donald Trump and Volodymyr Zelenskiy after a damaging week for Ukraine's president and a beneficial one for Russia, but the champagne is still on ice in Moscow.
While welcoming strains in Kyiv's relationship with its most important ally, Moscow regards the US president's behaviour as unpredictable and European leaders rallied behind Zelenskiy at a summit last week.
There has also been no end to Ukrainian drone attacks on Russia, most US sanctions remain in place on Moscow over Ukraine and Trump's actions can be seen in the light of November's midterm elections to Congress.
On the surface, there was plenty for Russian hawks to revel in after Trump repeatedly criticised the Ukrainian leader, who hit back at him, prompting the US president to say "it's time for Ukraine to get a new president".
"The ‘Man of the Year’ and the ‘new Churchill’ has been branded by his former master as a hindrance to peace and to US interests. After all, he bit the hand that fed him until it bled," former President Dmitry Medvedev, now deputy chairman of Russia's Security Council, wrote sarcastically on Telegram.
Kirill Dmitriev, President Vladimir Putin's point man for economic deals with Washington, reposted an image showing a bear symbolising Russia alongside an eagle representing the US and both creatures confronting Britain — in the form of a lion — and the European Union.
The image was captioned "Things Have Changed."
Dmitriev said he believed Zelenskiy's decision to criticise Trump had backfired, adding on X: "Zelensky overplayed his hand, and his hubris and attacks on President Trump will have significant consequences."
SCEPTICISM
Trump said on October 9 he had reached a deal with Putin to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian fuel and import Russian diesel and last week skipped new sanctions on Russia's oil buyers. In Kyiv, Ukrainian complaints about disruption to US intelligence sharing prompted talk of US betrayal.
But there appears to be a consensus in Moscow that the Trump-Zelenskiy rift has not yet delivered significant benefits.
Sergei Mironov, parliamentary leader of the pro-Kremlin Just Russia party, saw the rift as an attempt to "play to a domestic audience ahead of the Congressional elections."
"The US President needs cheap fuel prices for his voters. He also needs a scapegoat – someone onto whom he can shift the blame for price rises," he said. "But the point is that all this has little to do with Russia’s interests.”
Some Russians are also wary of what they see as frequent U-turns by Trump.
Moscow initially saw Trump's hosting of Putin in Alaska last year as a breakthrough that might lead to a peace deal in Ukraine on Russia's terms. But, like Trump's first term in office, the summit is increasingly seen as a disappointment.
The impact of the diesel deal may also be limited, as the export volumes — at least initially — are relatively small and Moscow taxes fuel production rather than exports, limiting the uplift for Russia's budget.
Trump’s decision to skip sanctions on Russian oil buyers — primarily China and India — is also not seen in Russia as a great gift, or as surprising, as such a move would increase oil prices at the very moment he wants to lower them.
A more tangible benefit to Russia may be Kyiv's complaints that it has not received recent warnings of Russian missile strikes and that there have been limits on the US Starshield system, which Ukraine uses for battlefield communications.
Writing for state media outlet RT, commentator Sergey Poletaev said Russia must be patient.
"For Russia, the task is to recognise this developing reality without mistaking it for an immediate victory," he said. "Zelenskiy has made his choice, the only question left is how long Washington will tolerate the consequences." REUTERS

Drone attack near market kills 80 in Sudan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
14:45:53 UTC
23:45:53 KST

A drone strike near a market in southern Sudan on Sunday evening killed 80 people, mostly commuters catching rides home.
Ahmed Wadi, a witness, said the attack in the town of al-Dibab in West Kordofan state left “50 bodies who I helped bury, one of them my own brother Mohamed”.
Using a satellite internet connection to circumvent a communications blackout, Wadi also said 47 other people were transported to the nearest town, al-Mujlad. A medical source, requesting anonymity for his safety, said 30 of them died from their injuries.
The medic said: “A total of 80 people were killed in the drone strike on al-Dibab, and another drone strike on al-Mujlad injured four who are currently being treated.”
Wadi said the drone struck twice, 10 minutes apart, “on a transport hub where people gather to travel back to their villages after the market day ends”.
The attack is one of the deadliest single strikes since war broke out in April 2023 when a power struggle between the Sudanese armed forces (SAF), headed by Gen Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), led by Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, erupted into violence in the capital, Khartoum.
The RSF-declared administration, known as Tasis, accused the army of carrying out Sunday’s strike. All of West Kordofan state is under RSF control.
Sudan has witnessed an escalation in the use of drones in the war. Between January and April, drone strikes accounted for at least 880 civilian deaths, more than 80% of all conflict-related civilian deaths in Sudan.
After drone strikes on a busy livestock market in Nyala, the capital of South Darfur state, on Friday, the SAF said they had killed RSF fighters, but the RSF accused the military of killing 30 civilians.
The fighting in Sudan has killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced many more. It has been fuelled by foreign powers with vested interests who are supporting sides in the conflict.
Last week, Rosemary DiCarlo, the undersecretary-general for political and peacebuilding affairs at the UN, warned the security council that the conflict and humanitarian crisis was deteriorating “with no breakthrough on the horizon”.
She said: “They [the warring parties] are not moving closer to dialogue. On the contrary, they seem to believe that they can make greater gains on the battlefield and that continued external support will allow them to pursue their objectives by force.”
AFP contributed to this report

The UN World Food Program (WFP) announced Monday that funding shortages have forced it to cut food assistance in the Gaza Strip by around one-third, leaving half a million people without critical support as winter approaches, Anadolu reports.
In a statement, the agency said it is now assisting 1.1 million vulnerable people in Gaza, down from 1.6 million last month, while food rations have been halved.
Families receiving assistance will now get one food parcel instead of two, along with a smaller bag of wheat flour, it said.
The number of daily hot meals has also dropped from 250,000 to 150,000, while families in hard-to-reach areas, including near the Israeli army-controlled “yellow line,” will receive meals every other day instead of daily.
The agency has also reduced the value of cash assistance for 75,000 families.
READ: Winter rains deepen Gaza’s humanitarian crisis as displaced families face severe shelter shortages
According to WFP, an estimated 1.4 million people, or 67% of Gaza’s population, face crisis-level food insecurity or worse, including around 200,000 experiencing emergency conditions requiring immediate food assistance to prevent deaths from hunger.
Only one in five children consumes a sufficiently diverse diet, while unemployment exceeds 80%, leaving many families unable to afford nutritious food.
WFP warned that “modest” improvements in food security since the October 2025 ceasefire remain “fragile” and could quickly be reversed by further reductions in humanitarian assistance.
Funding shortages have also forced the agency to halve its assistance in the occupied West Bank, from 400,000 to 200,000 people.
The agency said it urgently needs $450 million to sustain critical operations across Gaza and the West Bank over the next six months, through March 2027.

PM estimates business losses from Russian attacks at $7.7 bln since start of year, over 1 mln sq m of property destroyed or damaged
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
17:44:51 EEST
23:44:51 KST

Losses incurred by Ukrainian businesses as a result of Russian attacks since the beginning of 2026 are estimated at $7.7 billion, with more than 1 million square meters of real estate, including warehouse and logistics facilities, destroyed or severely damaged, Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhiy Koretsky said in an interview with BBC News Ukraine published on Monday.
"As of now, losses this year are estimated at $7.7 billion. This includes the destruction of premises, businesses, production facilities and goods in warehouses. This is a very large figure, and it continues to grow," he said.
Earlier, Economy and Environment Minister Oleksandr Kravchenko estimated total business losses for the year at around $10 billion.
Koretsky expressed his deep gratitude to small, medium-sized and large businesses for their resilience, prompt problem-solving and conscientious work in the fifth year of the war.
He said the government planned to continue state support programs that had proved effective, including preferential loans under the 5-7-9% program, grants for small and medium-sized businesses, the Svitlodim program and other energy-efficiency initiatives. The prime minister said the government was completing an assessment of which programs had worked.
At the same time, the government is reviewing programs that have not met expectations and setting support priorities for next year in light of limited financial resources, Koretsky said.
"There are programs I would gladly like to continue, and there are others that we will either cancel or significantly scale back. Unfortunately, due to financial liquidity constraints, funding for these programs next year has been substantially reduced," he said.
Among other forms of state assistance, he mentioned making state-owned premises available for the relocation of warehouses and production facilities following an audit of such properties.
"We shared all intelligence and informational briefings with businesses: where strikes were taking place and what the consequences were," he added.
At the same time, he said ongoing dialogue with businesses ultimately came down to requests for compensation: "Provide additional funds," "Refinance," and so on.
"But there will not be enough money for everything. Each time, we respond to new circumstances and new realities, improve our approach, develop new programs and make new proposals," Koretsky said.

Drought and pollution threaten drinking water: Swiss conference

Drought and pollution threaten drinking water: Swiss conference
Drought and environmental pollution are posing an increasing threat to the Swiss population’s drinking water supply, according to experts.
In the search for solutions, numerous experts in wastewater and water protection are meeting in Zurich with representatives from the drinking water and wastewater sectors.
The water sector across Europe is facing major challenges. Climate change, trace substances, rising demands on quality and the financing of infrastructure have made cross-border dialogue more important than ever.
This according to the conference invitation from the Swiss Association for Water, Gas and Heat and the Swiss Association of Wastewater and Water Protection Experts to the Swiss EurEau Water Summit in Zurich.
Around 400 representatives from Switzerland and abroad are expected to attend the main event on Wednesday at the first EurEau Water Summit in Switzerland.
More
Water shortage: Switzerland’s blue gold is under pressure
EurEau is the European water sector association. It represents 38 national organisations of drinking water and wastewater service providers from 33 countries, from both the public and private sectors.
According to the press release, around 60% of drinking water – 80% of which in Switzerland comes from groundwater – can currently be supplied to the population as drinking water either without treatment or after simple treatment.
However, rising concentrations of chemical contaminants in groundwater are putting increasing pressure on local supplies. Chemical contaminants can only be removed – if at all – at great cost in terms of manpower, energy and finance. This makes the protection of groundwater all the more important.
Under these conditions, rainwater is becoming increasingly important in so-called ‘sponge landscapes’, which enhance water retention in soils, water bodies, wetlands, moors, forests and entire catchment areas.
They could help to mitigate peak flows, reduce drought stress, safeguard groundwater, minimise erosion, enhance habitats and increase the climate resilience of our landscape.
This would benefit a range of areas simultaneously: agricultural crops, forests, soil fertility, the drinking water supply, biodiversity and local recreation.

Kenyan athletes set two new records in Tokyo (VIDEOS)
Kenyan runners Agnes Ngetich and Alexander Mutiso set new course records after winning the women’s and men’s races at the Tokyo Legacy Half Marathon in Japan on Sunday.
Ngetich finished the 21.1km race in one hour, four minutes and 23 seconds (1:04:23), cutting three minutes off the previous women’s course record. Her compatriot Tabitha Njeri Kamau came second in 1:08:28, according to the results.
Mutiso won the men’s competition in 59 minutes and 51 seconds, beating the previous course record by one second. He finished five seconds ahead of fellow Kenyan Kiprono Sitonik, who took second place.
Speaking after the race, Ngetich said she that was pleased with her victory and surprised by her finishing time. She also noted that the course had been challenging, with hills and numerous sharp turns. “I didn’t think I’ll get that time. The course was not easy,” she said.
Mutiso said his victory had boosted his confidence ahead of his next marathon. He explained that he made his decisive move on a hilly section of the course between the 17km and 18.5km marks.
“I feel good. I see now I am in a good position to prepare well for [my] coming marathon,” he said.
The course began and ended at Japan’s National Stadium and followed roads used during the Tokyo 2020 Paralympic Games.
Ngetich’s victory came less than a month after she broke the women-only half marathon world record at the World Athletics Road Running Championships in Copenhagen. The 25-year-old completed that race in 1:05:15.
Kenyan distance runners have also recorded major victories in other international competitions this year. In April, Sebastian Sawe became the first athlete to complete an official competitive marathon in under two hours, winning the London Marathon in a world-record 1:59:30. Fellow Kenyan John Korir also won the Boston Marathon that month, setting a course record of 2:01:52.
The London Marathon also saw a record-breaking performance in the women’s race. Ethiopia’s Tigst Assefa set a new women’s-only marathon world record of 2:15:50.
