Houthi ballistic missile strike kills at least 53 Yemen govt troops
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
14:31:00 UTC
23:31:00 KST

Houthi rebels killed at least 53 Yemeni government soldiers in a ballistic missile strike on a military camp Monday, one of the deadliest attacks since fighting surged this summer, military officials said.
The attack wounded an additional 200 recruits at the military camp in the southern province of Shabwa, the provincial government there said. The rebels acknowledged targeting the camp.
The fighting between the Houthis and Yemen’s Saudi-backed government forces is a widening front in the Iran war that began in February. The escalation shattered a 2022 cease-fire deal that largely stopped fighting in Yemen’s civil war.
The Houthis have put their growing military capabilities on display on multiple fronts in recent weeks, repeatedly striking Saudi Arabia’s main international airport hundreds of kilometers away and seizing territory inside Yemen near a key shipping chokepoint.
Iran and its allies in Lebanon and Iraq provide expertise, training and sophisticated weapons to the Houthis, according to U.N. and other experts. Iran denies arming the Houthis, which would violate a U.N. embargo.
The provincial government in Shabwa said in a statement that the death toll is preliminary and may rise. It said the recruits were receiving training to be part of internal security forces.
"This bloody, treacherous attack targeted new recruits in the training and preparation phase and is considered an extremely critical military escalation and a blatant aggression on the security and stability of Shabwa province," the statement said.
It called on Yemen’s president, the Saudi-led coalition and the government to expedite air defense and early warning systems to reinforce Shabwa’s capabilities.
The head of Yemen's ruling Presidential Leadership Council, Rashad al-Alimi, promised a "firm response" and said the attack reflects the Houthis' "approach of resorting to cowardly terrorist attacks whenever they face pressures or their Iranian-backed sabotage plots falter."
One Yemeni military official said the missiles struck while recruits were lining up in formation for a training session. The official spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to talk to the media.
On Sunday, an airstrike blamed on Saudi-led forces killed at least nine people in Yemen’s rebel-held northern province of Saada, the Houthi-run Health Ministry said. Five children and two women were killed in the attack, one of several that killed or wounded more than 30 people over the weekend, according to the rebels.
There was no immediate comment from Saudi Arabia.
The Houthis, a Shiite religious and political movement rooted in northern Yemen, are increasingly attacking Saudi Arabia because it supports Yemen’s internationally recognized government in the civil war. The Sunni kingdom, which has long feared the emergence of a well-armed ally of Shiite Iran on its border, joined the war in 2015 after the rebels seized much of northern Yemen, including the capital, Sanaa.
The rebels have been targeting Saudi airports and oil and military facilities. The headquarters of Saudi oil giant Aramco has been struck as well in a blow to the world’s top oil exporter.
The rebels also recently seized more territory along Yemen’s Red Sea coast and near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a crucial shipping alternative to the Strait of Hormuz.
The Saudi-led coalition this month launched a major military offensive to dislodge the rebels from that strategic perch and retake the territory.

‘Safeguarding exports under sanctions requires operational measures, regulatory reform, private-sect
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
14:27:56 UTC
23:27:56 KST

‘Safeguarding exports under sanctions requires operational measures, regulatory reform, private-sect
TEHRAN- Samad Hassanzadeh, President of the Iran Chamber of Commerce, Industries, Mines and Agriculture (ICCIMA), said on Monday at the National Export Associations Conference, held at the Iran Chamber under the slogan “Capable Exporter, Strong Association, Sustainable Exports”: Foreign trade cannot be examined merely within the framework of export and import statistics, trade balance, or foreign-exchange earnings; rather, foreign trade is directly linked to national production, employment, investment, economic security, access to technology, and the country’s position in regional and global division of labor. From this perspective, any disruption in trade relations affects the country’s production and economic capacities.
Emphasizing diversification of transportation routes, he said: The first necessity for safeguarding trade flows is reducing foreign trade’s dependence on limited transportation routes. Therefore, by assessing the capacity of northern ports, railways, land borders, and regional corridors, alternative routes should be designed appropriate to the type of goods so that disruption on one route does not halt exports and the supply of raw materials.
The President of the Iran Chamber, presenting the Iran Chamber’s proposal to form a Foreign Trade Continuity Task Force, stated: We propose that an operational task force be formed at the earliest opportunity with the participation of the government, the Iran Chamber, Customs, the Central Bank, the Ports Organization, and export associations to develop export programs so that no stoppage occurs in existing minimums.
He emphasized facilitating customs and border formalities and said: When transport time and costs increase, prolonged customs formalities and unnecessary stops at borders impose double damage on trade. Therefore, we recommend that expansion of electronic document exchange, coordination of border working hours, pre-arrival processing of goods, and reduction of repeated inspections be placed at the top of executive reforms.
The President of the Iran Chamber considered securing working capital for exporters essential for the sustainability of the country’s export programs and added: Designing working-capital facilities, accelerating repayment of claims, and financing appropriate to the real export cycle are necessary so that external disruptions do not lead to production stoppage, reduced employment, and loss of markets. The Central Bank and operating banks must devise measures to provide working capital for exporters.
He emphasized the need for flexibility in fulfilling foreign-exchange obligations and said: One cannot insist on the repatriation of export earnings while ignoring operational considerations, differences in market conditions, and real restrictions on financial transfers in designing executive mechanisms. An efficient trade policy is one that links macroeconomic objectives with the operational realities of firms and, instead of continuously transferring uncertainty to economic actors, provides the possibility of risk management and informed decision-making.
Samad Hassanzadeh considered codified insurance support for exports and trade risk management necessary and noted: Increased risk on transportation routes can raise insurance costs and make implementation of export contracts difficult. Therefore, we propose that, with the participation of insurance companies, financial institutions, and economic associations, the possibility of developing insurance coverage, credit guarantees, and risk-management instruments suited to new trade conditions be examined.
He cited diversification of export markets as another necessity for safeguarding foreign trade flows and said: In past years, Iraq was Iran’s largest trading partner, but today, following policies Western countries have applied in Iraq’s economic programs, it is predicted that Iran’s exports to that country will reach a minimum next year, because due to increased export costs, Iranian rates and prices are no longer acceptable for the Iraqi market. India, China, and Turkey send goods to Iraq with zero tariffs and six-month and one-year LCs in a way that neither Iraqi merchants are prepared to buy Iranian goods nor will any volume of Iranian goods exports to Iraq be justified.
The President of the Iran Chamber considered development of economic diplomacy programs key and added: Continuity of foreign trade, in addition to domestic capacities, depends on cooperation with neighboring countries and trading partners. Therefore, economic diplomacy must focus on facilitating transit, customs coordination, developing transportation agreements, and maintaining legal access to international markets, and reducing trade restrictions should also be pursued through diplomatic channels.
Hassanzadeh, stating that the Iran Chamber and the Iran Chamber’s Export Development Commission can be a continuous link between exporters and decision-making bodies, said: Chambers of commerce have made many efforts at all times when problems have arisen for the country, and we believe that in the Iran Chamber, provincial chambers, commissions, and economic associations must present every necessary measure and proposal that helps improve the country’s economic situation to officials with a scientific and expert approach.
The President of the Iran Chamber of Commerce, Industries, Mines and Agriculture emphasized: Systematic collection of problems, presentation of expert solutions, publication of periodic reports, and follow-up of demands through to implementation will help transform firms’ experience into effective decisions and increase the resilience of foreign trade.
He considered revision of the approach toward the private sector one of the prerequisites for improving the performance of Iran’s economy and stated: The private sector is neither a substitute for sovereign responsibilities nor can it alone bear the burden of all the country’s economic problems. The government, without the effective participation of producers, exporters, investors, and specialized associations, will not have sufficient capacity to design and implement efficient economic policies, and officials must take measures to remove ambiguities.
The President of the Iran Chamber, enumerating the responsibilities of the state and the private sector, said: The main issue is creating a clear and constructive relationship between the state and the responsibility of economic actors. The state must focus on macro policymaking, transparent regulation, provision of public infrastructure, legal stability, and guaranteeing fair competition, and the private sector must, within the framework of the law, assume responsibility for investment, productivity improvement, market development, innovation, job creation, and increasing the competitiveness of its firms.
Hassanzadeh, referring to the country’s difficult economic conditions, said: Although managing economic firms has become very difficult, we believe that when the name of Iran and the nation is mentioned, we all have a great responsibility and duty. Today all our country’s officials are making their utmost efforts to solve problems, and good planning is always carried out, but the hostile enemy also always takes actions to neutralize the country’s plans.
The President of the Iran Chamber, stating that today is the time for all of us to stand with all our strength alongside the Iranian nation and cooperate with the government’s policies, noted: The Iran Chamber’s greatest conscientious recommendation under the country’s current conditions is that we must certainly strive to keep economic firms operating, preserve employment for Iranian households’ workforce, and help people’s livelihoods as much as possible so that problems are soon resolved with the dignity and magnanimity of the Iranian nation and the authority of the Islamic Republic of Iran.
The Head of the Iran Trade Promotion Organization, emphasizing the need to increase the volume and value added of the country’s non-oil exports, said: To achieve the real capacities of Iran’s economy in the export sector, while supporting private-sector initiatives, a fundamental transformation in the environment of trade laws and regulations must be created with the participation of responsible institutions and the private sector.
Mohammad Ali Dehghan Dehnavi said on Monday at the Export Conference at the Iran Chamber of Commerce, referring to the impact of sanctions, transportation restrictions, and difficult foreign trade conditions on exporters’ activity: Part of export problems are outside the authority of domestic bodies, but in the area of legal, regulatory, and administrative obstacles, responsibility for solving problems lies with domestic bodies, and more effective measures must be taken in this regard.
He added: Compared with last summer, in some regulatory areas more facilities have been provided for economic actors, including the possibility of agreement between exporter and importer and the possibility of direct transactions, at least for second-group goods, as well as openings in customs and trade agreements.
Dehghan Dehnavi continued: There are reports from economic actors that, due to pressures and existing restrictions, they have abandoned their export activity or faced legal and judicial issues. Such conditions show that the country’s regulatory environment needs transformation and review in various dimensions.
Emphasizing that reforming the regulatory environment is not possible through the action of one body alone, he stated: This transformation must be pursued with the cooperation of legislators, policymakers, regulatory bodies, and the private sector, while economic associations and actors in trade, export, import, and production must also play a demand-making and active participation role in this path.
He added: Part of the obstacles that today face economic actors in the form of regulations can be removed more simply and at lower cost through the participation of associations and the design of voluntary mechanisms.
Dehghan Dehnavi, announcing the Trade Promotion Organization’s readiness to support proposals from economic associations, stated: We welcome any initiative that can help develop exports, including creating export consortia, establishing trade centers in target countries, sending trade delegations, inviting foreign trade delegations, and offering proposed solutions to facilitate settlement of exporters’ foreign-exchange obligations.
He considered creating special paths for exporters and offering practical proposals to facilitate trade activities among areas for association participation and emphasized: The Trade Promotion Organization is ready, in areas where cooperation is possible, to use the capacity of associations and provide the necessary ground for greater private-sector role-playing.
Dehghan Dehnavi, referring to the designation of Mehr 29 (October 21) as National Export Day, stated: The purpose of holding Export Week is to address various issues in this field and to appreciate exporters, economic associations, and entities active in the path of developing the country’s exports.
Appreciating exporters as pioneers in the export field and the Iran Chamber of Commerce and other guild, industrial, and commercial associations, he added: Over the past two years, numerous meetings have been held with associations, federations, commissions, and various organizations, and issues related to exports, programs, and development solutions in this sector have been examined; however, many measures remain to improve the country’s export conditions.
The Head of the Iran Trade Promotion Organization, referring to the country’s non-oil export performance, stated: In the Iranian calendar year 1403 (March 2024-March 2025) the country’s non-oil exports reached $58 billion, one of the highest figures recorded in recent years. In 1404, despite numerous incidents and restrictions, including the Shahid Rajaee Port incident and the 12-day war, the country’s non-oil exports reached $52 billion.
Dehghan Dehnavi noted: Although at first glance a decrease in export statistics may create a negative image, examination of the conditions and restrictions governing trade shows that the private sector has made considerable efforts to maintain export flows.
Stating that about 75 percent of the country’s trade by weight depends on maritime transportation, he added: Despite the restrictions created, the weight decrease in trade during the period mentioned was about 30 to 35 percent, while the decrease in export value was reported at about 20 percent. This difference shows that some goods with higher economic value were still able to be exported.
He continued: Increased transportation costs and other trade costs have caused exports of some goods, especially goods with low value per ton, to lose economic justification. Nevertheless, the private sector has been able to maintain part of the export flow by finding alternative routes and methods.
Referring to Turkey’s export performance, this official stated: In Iran’s neighborhood, Turkey has about $1 billion in non-oil exports daily. This shows the necessity of examining the obstacles and neglected capacities of Iran’s economy to increase exports.
The Head of the Iran Trade Promotion Organization considered increasing export volume and improving the economic value of exported goods as two fundamental axes of policymaking in this field and emphasized: The average value of each ton of Iran’s exported goods is about $300 to $400, and it is necessary to provide the ground for increasing the value added of goods before export.
He added: In some cases, Iranian goods, after entering the destination country, are offered at a much higher economic value after one stage of processing or completing the value chain. Therefore, we must examine why part of this value added is not created inside the country and how, by developing value chains, a greater share of the economic benefits of trade can be retained inside the country.

Norway to extend proposed under-16 social media ban to online games and messaging apps
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
14:27:23 UTC
23:27:23 KST

Online games and messaging services were initially expected to receive broad exemptions, but the government has now decided to assess platforms based on their potential risks to children.
Norway is set to introduce a social media ban for children under 16, with the government announcing on Monday that it is finalising legislation to be submitted to parliament by the end of the year.
The proposed restrictions will also cover potentially harmful online games and messaging services, beyond conventional social media platforms, the government said in a statement.
TikTok, Snapchat and Roblox, a popular online gaming platform where users can create and play games while interacting with others, would likely fall under the proposed law.
"Children's safety must come first," said Lene Vågslid, Norway's minister for children and families, adding that the legislation was nearly complete.
The restrictions aim to protect children from harmful content, addictive features, illegal advertising and unwanted contact from strangers.
Online games and messaging services were initially expected to receive broad exemptions, but the government has now decided to assess platforms based on their potential risks to children.
This means services considered harmless, such as messaging apps used for school communication, could remain accessible.
Vågslid said the government was also safeguarding children's "right to participate," although Monday's announcement did not explain how this would be ensured under the proposed restrictions.
Technology companies would be responsible for verifying users' ages, with systems required to comply with European data protection rules.
Norway's centre-left Labour government published a draft bill in 2025 proposing a minimum social media age of 15 before revising the threshold to 16 in April this year. The legislation has since undergone public consultation in Norway and the European Economic Area (EEA).
Social media restrictions in Europe
Norway joins a growing number of European countries moving to restrict children's access to social media amid concerns about online safety and addiction.
Denmark has adopted similar restrictions, while Spain is pursuing a ban for pupils under 16.
In September, France attempted to ban social media for children under 15, but its Constitutional Council struck it down over freedom of expression concerns.
At the European Union level, the European Commission proposed the EU Kids Act in September, which would also introduce age-based restrictions on social media, online games and other digital services.

A Warm Welcome for US Secretary of State in Central Asia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
14:24:00 UTC
23:24:00 KST

As U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio departed the U.S. capital on October 17, bound for Uzbekistan and India, a journalist asked, “With everything going on in the world and with crisis all over, why are you choosing now, at this time, to go to Uzbekistan?”
Rubio replied that it was the time that worked for the Central Asians. “This is an important relationship,” he added without expounding on that importance.
In response to questions from the Associated Press regarding Rubio’s schedule, the State Department said the secretary’s “responsibility is not to generate a public profile around every challenge; it is to help the president develop and execute a strategy that advances American interests. Some of the most consequential diplomatic work takes place outside the public spotlight.”
The AP’s October 18 article was titled “Rubio heads to Central Asia as some wonder if he’s keeping the most pressing matters at a distance.” Rubio is involved in discussions on a blooming array of international crises, from Iran to China, Gaza to Ukraine, both in his role as secretary of state but also as national security adviser. But he’s not the public face of any of those issues, as the AP argued.
“The Iran, Gaza, and the Russia-Ukraine conflicts each demand serious attention, but they cannot be approached in isolation from the president’s broader national security objectives,” the State Department told the AP, pushing back against the implication that Rubio was avoiding tackling politically risky issues publicly. “The right question is not whether the secretary is visible enough on a particular issue.”
Not only can Rubio avoid the most pressing international crises by jetting off to Central Asia, but he – and the Trump administration more broadly – were guaranteed to receive a warm welcome in the region. There is no free press in Samarkand lobbing difficult questions. There are no allies feeling sour about how much Washington has changed. Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, in particular, have been enthusiastic to endorse Trump administration initiatives, such as the Board of Peace, that traditional U.S. allies have avoided.
In Samarkand, Rubio commented to the media that “Central Asia has simply not received the level of attention from our policymakers over the last 20 years that it deserves. But that’s changing. That’s why we’re here now.” That’s a common refrain from the Trump administration, but it does not match reality.
U.S. foreign policy regarding Central Asia over the last decade has been fairly consistent, as epitomized by the 11-year-old C5+1 format that brought Rubio to Samarkand in the first place to meet with the foreign ministers of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan.
The format was launched in 2015 when then-U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry visited all five regional countries in one trip – a feat Rubio promised to repeat last year during celebrations marking the C5+1’s 10th anniversary. While Rubio did meet bilaterally with the Central Asian foreign ministers, his only regional stop was in Uzbekistan.
The overarching consistency of U.S. policy toward Central Asia does not mean nothing has changed. No longer do U.S. officials mention human rights or press freedom, areas which Central Asia’s autocratic governments score poorly on. And the Trump administration’s transactional style and its focus on business deals resonates with regional states, even as it narrows relations to the economic sphere.
When Rubio’s trip to Uzbekistan was first announced in a late September press release from the U.S. Embassy in India – the U.S. ambassador to India is Sergio Gor, who also wears the hat of special envoy for South and Central Asian Affairs – it remarked that the secretary would be traveling with “a historic business delegation of more than 100 American companies.”
When the trip’s dates were announced in an October 13 press release, the delegation had become “over 200 business leaders.”
In Samarkand, Rubio referred to the commercial delegation as “incredible,” with representatives of almost 300 American businesses joining.
On October 14, The Diplomat had asked the State Department if it had a list of the participating businesses. That question went unanswered.
RFE/RL reported that the delegation would include representatives from Boeing, Citibank, and Franklin Templeton, “as well as businesses operating in critical minerals and other strategic sectors.”
In comments to RFE/RL, Daniel Rosenblum, formerly deputy assistant secretary of state for Central Asia from 2014 to 2019 and then U.S. ambassador to Uzbekistan (2019-2022) and Kazakhstan (2022-2025), noted that the secretary of state’s large business delegation was unusual but “may lead to more successes in terms of deals being signed and new investments.”
He added, however, that “the realities of investing in Central Asia remain the same.” He pointed to “the realities of distance, logistics, financing, finding a good partner. All of those things remain the same, regardless of whether you have 100 companies, 200 companies, or 20 companies.”
The joint statement published on October 19 – titled “C5+1: Historic Partnership, Prosperous Future” – concluded with this: “We envision C5+1 cooperation that continues to deliver regional solutions to global challenges.”
Of course, per usual with the Trump administration, those challenges don’t include climate change, a major complicating issue for regional states bent on building their future economies on the back of AI and mining, both of which are water and energy-intensive industries. And they didn’t touch on human rights, either.
Instead, the statement highlighted trade and connectivity, specifically the Trans-Caspian Trade Route, as well as security. It references “untapped natural resources” and states, “we will combine our strengths to be a collective, powerful driver of regional energy sector development.”

Meta apologises for ‘No Kings’ Instagram blackout as organisers demand answers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
14:23:32 UTC
23:23:32 KST

Meta apologises for ‘No Kings’ Instagram blackout as organisers demand answers
WASHINGTON – Meta apologised for suspending the Instagram account of the “No Kings” protest movement over the weekend, attributing the shutdown to a sharp increase in activity that looked like automated bot traffic rather than human exchanges.
Demonstrators gathered at thousands of events across the United States on Oct 17 decrying President Donald Trump’s aggressive deportation efforts, war in Iran and other policies in the third round of the “No Kings” rallies.
The Instagram account used by organisers and attendees, however, was offline for more than an hour. Meta spokesman Andy Stone wrote in a post on X that it took longer to fix problems with organisers’ access to the accounts.
Stone said network security systems detected the use of a Claude tool reading profiles, posts and hashtags, with the rate sharply increasing in intense bursts on Oct 17.
“These abrupt, high-volume, sequential requests in a short period resembled automated bot traffic rather than an ordinary human browsing our systems. This activity caused our automated protections to incorrectly take the No Kings Instagram account offline,” he said.
“We want to reiterate our sincere apology for the error,” said Stone.
Rally organisers were not satisfied on Oct 19.
“Meta’s explanation still doesn’t add up,” the No Kings Coalition said on the Bluesky platform. “Beyond shutting down our Instagram, we’ve received reports that NoKings and early voting content was inaccessible, restricted or seemed suppressed across Meta platforms.”
“Weeks before an election, an apology isn’t enough. The public needs answers, accountability and concrete safeguards,” the coalition said.
“No Kings” rallies took place in cities from Seattle and San Diego to Chicago, Atlanta and New York.

EU paid Russia 682 million euros for steel in eight months, with slab loophole keeping money flowing, and big consumers lobbying to keep it open — analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
14:20:38 UTC
23:20:38 KST

Four years of sanctions have not closed the door through which Russian metal still reaches Europe. The EU imported 1.6 million tons of Russian iron and steel products in the first eight months of 2026, paying 682 million euros, down 54% in value year on year, GMK Center, a Ukrainian-based consulting company, reports, citing Eurostat data.
Every euro spent on Russian metal is revenue for a state waging war on Ukraine, and the EU has banned most of it: pig iron, direct-reduced iron, iron ore and ferroalloys. Yet one category still flows almost untouched: semi-finished steel, mostly slabs, which made up 97.8% of the imports, or 1.56 million tons worth 670 million euros.
Volumes dropped 55% year on year after the full ban on Russian pig iron and DRI took effect on 1 January 2026, and no pig iron, ferroalloys, iron ore, or DRI reached the EU from Russia in the period, the center found. Iron ore and ferroalloys fall under sectoral limits, and the largest Russian producers are subject to corporate sanctions.
The slab loophole that keeps the money flowing
Slabs are the gap in the wall. Belgium took 767,700 tons of Russian semi-finished steel, nearly half the EU total, and Italy 191,800 tons, the center said.
Demand still outstrips the rules, with a slab quota for the year to September 2026 standing at nearly 3 million tons and effectively used up within four months, the data showed. Scrap was the only other notable inflow, at 41,300 tons worth 11.7 million euros, down about a third.
A ban that keeps getting postpone
The door is closing slowly, and not without a fight. The quota falls to 2.6 million tons for the year to September 2027б and to 2 million for the following year, the center added, yet attempts to halt Russian slab imports early have failed because the biggest consumer countries lobby against it.
Earlier, the Kiel Institute for the World Economy reported that the EU paid Russia €317 billion in goods since February 2022. The sum is €116 billion more than the €201 billion the bloc extended to Ukraine in financial aid over the same period.

Expedition to find Amelia Earhart's missing plane comes up empty
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
14:20:00 UTC
23:20:00 KST

Expedition to find Amelia Earhart's missing plane comes up empty
A mysterious object discovered near a remote Pacific island is not the wreckage of Amelia Earhart's missing plane, researchers said after an expedition to the site, dealing another setback to efforts to solve one of aviation's greatest mysteries nearly 90 years after the pilot disappeared.
"Evidence gathered at the Taraia Peninsula on Nikumaroro confirmed that the visual anomaly first seen in satellite imagery in 2020 was likely a collection of large trees deposited along the peninsula's sandspit," the researchers said. "By the time the team arrived at the site, a good portion of the debris had fragmented and washed away, leaving only a single Y-shaped segment," which they said is what they had initially hoped was the plane.
The researchers said the reflective surface of the anomaly, which had led them to believe it could be metal, was the result of a carbonate veneer, noting other items found nearby were "similarly coated with a shiny concretized amalgam of coral sand."
On Oct. 14, a 17-member expedition team led by Purdue University's Steve Schultz and the Archaeological Legacy Institute's Richard Pettigrew launched an expedition to investigate a mysterious object that in aerial photos appeared to resemble possible wreckage of Earhart's Lockheed Electra 10-E plane.
Severe weather kept the research team aboard their ship for three of the five days allotted for the search, while limited fuel and supplies prevented them from extending the expedition. The search area was so remote, it took the team five days at sea to reach it.
The expedition focused on a lagoon off Nikumaroro, where researchers examined the Taraia Object, an anomaly spotted by a Navy veteran in satellite imagery during the COVID pandemic. Although visible in aerial photos dating back to 1938, the object went unnoticed until 2020. Pettigrew said before reaching it that they believed it could be metal rather than a tree, but further investigation was needed to confirm its identity.
"Amelia Earhart's spirit of courage and curiosity drove every step of the search," Pettigrew said Sunday. "We accomplished our goal to determine what the Taraia Object was, and we're deeply grateful to the private donors who shared our vision and made this journey possible. Our team remains in great spirits and proud of what was accomplished."
The team had developed plans to photograph and film the lagoon and Taraia Object before using magnetometers and sonar equipment to survey the area. Researchers then planned to retrieve the object for identification. The Archaeology Channel documented the expedition through short video updates on its Heritage Broadcasting Service streaming platform.
The research team previously said in a news release that there was "very strong" evidence that the object is Earhart's lost plane.
Earhart and her navigator, Fred Noonan, disappeared on July 2, 1937, roughly 22,000 miles into their trip. Earhart was attempting to become the first female pilot to circle the world, and the first pilot to do so around the equator, Earth's widest point.
Recently, President Trump ordered the declassification of records related to Earhart.
Nikumaroro is part of the archipelago country of Kiribati, located roughly halfway between Australia and Hawaii. The island lies about 400 miles southeast of Howland Island, where Earhart and Noonan were headed when they disappeared during their attempted flight around the world.
Pettigrew believes Earhart and Noonan landed on Nikumaroro and survived there for some time. He points to relics dating to the 1930s and to human remains discovered on the island, which were later lost as possible evidence. However, several competing theories about the aviator's disappearance have emerged over the decades, many of which lack conclusive evidence.
Researchers have spent decades searching for Earhart's plane, hoping its discovery could shed light on her disappearance. In 2024, an expedition team captured a sonar image of what appeared to be an aircraft on the ocean floor, but the object was later identified as a rock formation.

====================================================================================================

Could France’s debt troubles tip Italy into recession?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
14:19:18 UTC
23:19:18 KST

Rising borrowing costs and political uncertainty are putting France’s finances under pressure. Oxford Economics warns that a severe bond-market shock could push both France and Italy into recession in 2027, although a debt crisis remains outside its central forecast.
The eurozone’s second-largest economy saw its bond yields rise further on Monday, following violent street demonstrations in the country over the weekend.
France’s 10-year government bond yield hovered around 4.9% on Monday, near its highest level in more than two decades, as investors demanded a higher premium for holding French debt. Protesters are demanding action on the rising cost of living and declining public services, including education.
The unrest adds to pressure on the government as it battles to get its 2027 budget through a deeply divided National Assembly, the lower house of France’s parliament.
The immediate challenge is to pass a credible budget that reassures investors ahead of the presidential election in spring 2027. But restoring confidence will also depend on whether the next administration can commit to improving public finances over several years.
What is fuelling investors’ concerns?
France is nursing one of the highest public debt ratios in the EU, at 119% of GDP, according to the latest reading from INSEE, the national statistics office. This is coupled with a government forecast for a deficit of 5.4% of GDP in 2026. Public debt stood at €3.596 trillion at the end of June 2026.
The cost of servicing that debt has been rising sharply. The government forecasts public debt interest payments of €91 billion in 2027, up from €79.2 billion this year — an increase of almost €12 billion.
Accelerating inflation and low growth threaten to weaken tax revenues and raise the deficit and debt further.
The current fiscal situation therefore leaves little room for the government to meet protesters’ demands through another large spending package, along the lines of French President Emmanuel Macron’s “whatever it costs” approach when the pandemic hit the country.
The government faces pressure to reduce the deficit and commit to lasting savings to calm nerves on the bond market. If borrowing costs keep rising, France’s debt could become increasingly difficult to control.
And a spiralling crisis could also hit other major eurozone economies, such as Italy.
How France’s debt troubles could hit Italy
Modelling the impact of bond turmoil in France, with some contagion to other high-debt eurozone countries, Oxford Economics found that Italy would be particularly vulnerable because it combines slow growth, high debt and investment that is sensitive to tighter financial conditions.
A key yardstick for measuring market concerns is the gap between a country’s 10-year government bond yield and Germany’s equivalent. The current spread — the extra return investors want to hold French debt instead of German debt — has risen to around 145 basis points (bps). This is still slightly below the peak reached earlier this month, which was the highest since the eurozone debt crisis of 2011–2012.
Oxford Economics sets out a baseline and two adverse scenarios. Its baseline assumes that France’s spread stays below 200bps ahead of the April 2027 presidential election and narrows afterwards. It continues to view a French debt crisis as an unlikely but potentially damaging outcome, rather than its central forecast.
The two adverse scenarios combine higher borrowing costs with a hit to business and consumer confidence. In the moderate scenario, the French spread widens to 250bps from around 140bps when the report was published on 15 October. In the severe scenario, it reaches 400bps.
France and Italy would enter recession in 2027 under the severe scenario. Belgium would also see a jump in its borrowing costs, while Spain, Portugal and Greece would face higher bond yields but less economic damage, with none of the three economies contracting.
Crucially, the eurozone as a whole would avoid recession even under this severe scenario.
According to Andrew Kenningham, chief Europe economist at Capital Economics, a widening of France’s spread to 400bps is a “plausible adverse scenario, (…) which would be comparable to Italy’s spreads in 2012”.
Kenningham agreed that, in that case, there would certainly be a lot of pressure on other high-debt economies, including Italy.
“However, in contrast to the early 2010s, the ECB would be well placed to support countries other than France through its Transmission Protection Instrument,” he said.
With this instrument, the ECB can buy government bonds to help keep borrowing costs under control if the country meets certain conditions.
Kenningham also said that the risks to the banking sector and the risk of a property crash are much lower than in the 2010s.
“So things could get very bad but not as bad as in the 2010s.”
According to Oxford Economics, in its severe scenario, France’s 10-year bond yield would reach 7% in the second quarter of 2027, with the public deficit on track to surpass 6% of GDP. The consultancy warns that yields at such levels could trigger a liquidity crisis.
But expectations of ECB intervention to help France remain low. ECB President Christine Lagarde said last week that the means to stop the surge in French borrowing costs “must first be found in France”, through budget measures to reassure investors.
What France can do to regain investors’ confidence
According to Oxford Economics, the measures needed to calm markets could include gradual spending restraint over several years, accompanied by clear legislative commitments, especially on the retirement age.
But the consultancy warns that “the current minority government will not be able to credibly commit to sustained fiscal consolidation to soothe markets”. Much of the responsibility for carrying out any painful measures could therefore fall to the next administration.
In the meantime, Kenningham said investors are expecting the government to pass a budget that reduces next year’s deficit to around 5% of GDP, “so anything less than that could lead to further loss of confidence in the French bond market”.
Ahead of next spring’s presidential election, far-right leader Marine Le Pen is leading in the polls. In an interview with the Financial Times last week, she promised: “massive reductions in public spending, while reviving the economy”.
She presented her “counter-budget” on 6 October, targeting €140 billion in net savings by 2032 compared with 2026, a deficit below 3% of GDP by 2030 and a constitutional budget rule. Her party proposes cutting administrative and social security spending, immigration-related expenditure and France’s EU contribution.
But economists questioned the figures. Mathieu Plane, deputy director of analysis and forecasting at the French Economic Observatory (OFCE), told Le Monde that more than €80 billion of the proposed savings were questionable, poorly defined and difficult to implement.
In the meantime, France is facing the risk of a vicious circle in which higher borrowing costs force further spending cuts or tax rises, weakening growth and making its debt harder to control.
“France has been heading towards a debt crisis for many years and that moment is now getting closer,” Kenningham concluded.

Russia and India wrap up joint naval drills in Pacific (VIDEO)

Russia and India wrap up joint naval drills in Pacific (VIDEO)
Russian and Indian warships have completed joint naval drills off Russia’s Pacific coast, conducting live-fire exercises and practicing defenses against drone attacks as part of the wider Indra-2026 military exercise.
The maritime phase of the drills took place in the Gulf of Peter the Great near Vladivostok, involving the Russian Pacific Fleet corvette Aldar Tsydenzhapov and the Indian Navy frigate INS Sahyadri, the Russian Defense Ministry said on Saturday.
INS Sahyadri arrived in Vladivostok on October 10 and conducted harbor engagements before operations at sea.
The crews fired naval artillery at surface and aerial targets, carried out coordinated maneuvers, and tested communications between the vessels. They also practiced repelling attacks by unmanned boats and aerial drones representing a simulated enemy. The Russian corvette used 30mm automatic guns, small arms, and electronic warfare systems to counter the simulated threats.
The exercises culminated in a simulated joint operation to rescue a civilian vessel seized by pirates. Russian and Indian naval counterterrorism units boarded the vessel and neutralized the attackers, with drone operators coordinating their movements.
The two navies also practiced helicopter operations, including reconnaissance, cross-deck landings, and medical evacuations.
An Indian helicopter landed aboard the Russian corvette shortly after a Russian helicopter took off. The crews then exchanged mannequins representing wounded sailors as part of a casualty evacuation exercise, RT correspondent Igor Zhdanov reported from aboard the Russian warship.
Indra-2026 began on October 14 and involves land, naval, and air forces from both countries.
The land component will continue in Russia’s Chelyabinsk Region until October 23, with troops practicing joint command and control and operations against simulated armed groups. Russian and Indian aircrews are also conducting exercises involving Su-30SM fighter jets and Mi-8 helicopters.
The previous edition of the exercise was held off the coast of the southern Indian city of Chennai.
The deployment builds on the longstanding defense partnership between Moscow and New Delhi and carries forward cooperation discussed during Russian President Vladimir Putin’s visit to India last December, India’s Defense Ministry said.

Foamy war? St Andrews students play out modern take on ancient ritual
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
14:17:49 UTC
23:17:49 KST

Nobody at the University of St Andrews in Scotland seems to remember how Raisin Monday became a giant foam fight. For 600 years, first-year students have taken part in the ritual of thanking older students for mentoring them through their first few weeks of university life.
Traditionally, freshers would give their elders a pound of raisins – hence the name. This Monday however, hundreds wore fancy dress as they streamed on to St Salvator’s lower college lawn at 11am armed with cans of shaving foam, covering one another in soapy clouds as they have for the past few decades. Groups of students dress as Smurfs, mice, bananas, grandmas, sunflowers and chefs to participate in the annual rite of passage.
The theme for each group is chosen by second- and third-year students, known as “mums” and “dads”, who have been matched with the first years. The proud “parents” stand on the edge of lawn screaming and waving to their “children”. Within minutes, the smell of shaving foam fills the square as cans are emptied over other students. It quickly becomes impossible to distinguish between costumes.
“Traditions like this are much more important because people are less connected face to face than they were before. Getting to do something like this brings everyone together,” says Freya, a first year whose group has been dressed as periodic table elements by their chemistry student parents.
Simon, who is part of the same family, says: “When you are covering each other in shaving foam, how much more bonded can you get?”
Everyone involved recognises that this activity is particularly strange in a crowded field of unusual university rituals. At Merton College, Oxford, students walk backwards around Fellows’ Quadrangle when the clocks go back in October. In Aberdeen, each new rector is carried around campus on the back of a stuffed bull by students.
There is a serious point to the St Andrews ritual at this isolated university on the east coast of Fife, the third oldest in the English-speaking world. More than half of the small town is made up of students – who come from all over the world – and the tradition helps break down barriers between students.
Deborah, an American medical student, is looking out at her academic children in the crowd. Her group has dressed as the blue-skinned supervillain, Megamind, from the animated DreamWorks film. “Because it’s such a small university, we get to have these sort of events. It wouldn’t be feasible at a bigger place. It brings people together. We do not have as many things going on because we are so small, so it helps create community and people you wouldn’t usually meet,” she says.
Sunday has always been a crucial part of the weekend tradition, when first years are woken early, “kidnapped”, and made to take a dip in the North Sea. But in 2026, that is optional. For the Monday foam fight, students are encouraged to donate to a local food bank before they start spraying from their canisters – and appears to be far less alcohol-fuelled than it has in previous years.
After about half an hour, the excited students running around the green begin to slow. The cans of shaving foam are empty and the first years head to the exit to be hosed down despite the single digit temperature. Away from the green, foam-covered students greet their parents with bear hugs, covering them with foam, before heading home for a shower.
“It’s amazing,” says Henry, an American student whose camouflage face paint has been completely covered in foam. “I only really know Americans, so getting to meet people from Singapore, England, South America, Africa and the Middle East through this is great. It’s rare to find a place where you can meet such a diverse group of people.”

Her Tandoori restaurant has been a venue for secret peace negotiations between Israeli and Palestinian representatives.
She was a member of a delegation that accompanied former prime minister Ariel Sharon to India. She was further invited by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the King David Hotel in Jerusalem to cook for Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi when he visited Israel; and she has been a friend and consultant to every Indian ambassador to Israel.
Pushkarna maintains close contact with relatives and friends who are still in India, and she recently received a notice informing her that the High Court of Madhya Pradesh has upheld a previous court decision affirming that the Ranital Jewish Cemetery is a national heritage monument.
Several prominent members of the Bene Israel community are buried there, which is another reason why Indian Jewish community leaders consider the court’s ruling to be a major victory for them and for lawyer Manish Verma.
India's Jewish community made up of around 4,000 to 5,000 members
There are no exact demographic figures for the Jewish communities of India, but the published estimate is somewhere between 4,000 and 5,000 members.
Over the years, the cemetery has been vandalized, but the Jewish community is now in a position to restore tombstones and fix gates.
There are three Bene Israel left in Jabalpur, and they have received support from the municipality, conservationists, and various organizations and individuals.
Other Jewish heritage sites across India are also under threat, but the case of the Ranital Jewish cemetery will make it easier to preserve these historic sites.
Yaniv Revach, the consul-general of Israel to midwest India, based in Mumbai, has offered to help with the restoration project.
Because many Jewish businesspeople and tourists visit India, Chabad maintains several outreach centers across the country, and some of its directors will also help in preserving the history of India’s Jews.

‘Years of hell’: Jewish women describe the fight to obtain a religious divorce
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
14:16:46 UTC
23:16:46 KST

A Jewish marriage requires the consent of both parties under Halacha (Jewish law), and Israeli law prohibits forced marriage. Yet a spouse can still be trapped in a marriage against their will when their partner refuses to grant them a “get,” the religious divorce required to remarry under Jewish law.
According to data collected by Chochmat Nashim, an Orthodox Jewish nonprofit promoting women’s roles in public life, 39.5% of more than 400 divorcees surveyed experienced some form of get refusal, 44% were forced to give up something in exchange for a get, and 21% waited three or more years to receive one.
Although precise figures for the number of agunot (“chained wives”) and agunim (“chained husbands”) in Israel and worldwide are unavailable, the organization estimates that thousands remain trapped in marriages against their will.
A new documentary, Get Up: Breakthroughs in the Battle for Jewish Divorce, examines the devastating impact of get refusal, a practice recognized in many countries as a form of domestic violence.
The Jerusalem Post received an early screening of the film in Jerusalem on Sunday evening, where it spoke with producer Shoshana Palatnik and Caroline Maxwell, who experienced get refusal firsthand.
Documentary explores how get refusal can derail victim's life plans, faith
The emotionally charged 44-minute documentary tells the stories of several agunot and agunim, including people who have been trapped in unwanted marriages for decades and one woman who died without receiving a get. It explores how get refusal can damage victims’ relationships with God, jeopardize their hopes of having children, and intersect with financial and coercive abuse.
While secular Jews in the Diaspora can generally remarry after obtaining a civil divorce, those who adhere to Jewish law cannot remarry until they receive a get. For those hoping to start a new family, years of waiting can mean losing precious time to date, remarry, and have children.
Procreation holds a central place in Judaism. In Genesis 1:28, God blesses Adam and Eve and commands them: “Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth and subdue it.” The command is reiterated in Genesis 9:7, when Noah and his family are instructed to multiply and repopulate the earth after the flood. For women trapped in marriages without a get, the consequences can extend beyond the inability to remarry, as prolonged delays can consume much or all of their fertile years.
In Israel, where marriage and divorce are governed by religious law and civil marriage is unavailable, the absence of a legal separation can leave agunot or agunim burdened with debts accumulated by their abusive spouses.
The non-profit Mavoi Satum documented a case in which a husband who refused to grant his wife a get drained her bank account and amassed hundreds of thousands of shekels in debt. Because the couple remained legally married and held a joint account, the Israel Enforcement and Collection Authority came to the woman’s home to seize her personal belongings.
Other women featured in the documentary described being forced to pay large sums of money, withdraw legal complaints and protection orders, or give up custody arrangements in exchange for their freedom.
'Something has to change,' get refusal victim says
Caroline Maxwell, formerly Caroline Moher, told the audience that the saying “what doesn’t kill you makes you stronger” rang true for her, but that the eight-year fight to obtain her get had brought her dangerously close to breaking point. A court heard how the abuse she suffered at her husband’s hands led her to attempt suicide in August 2015.
Maxwell’s efforts to obtain a divorce in the United Kingdom led to what is widely considered a landmark case. Alan Moher was sentenced to 18 months in prison for controlling or coercive behavior between 2016 and 2021 in connection with his refusal to grant her a get.
“I chose to share my story because I don’t want anybody else to have to go through the years of hell that I went through. I spent eight years trying to get my get and continuing to fight. I want people to understand what it’s like for a woman to try to obtain her get when it’s out of her hands,” she told the Post.
“Something has to change. Someone has to stand up to these bullies. It’s not right that somebody can hold another person captive, denying them their freedom and refusing to let them go.”
Maxwell said she had received support from the vast majority of the Jewish community. She hopes young men and women will be educated about the importance of halachic prenuptial agreements before getting married, helping to challenge the stigma surrounding them. The best time for a couple to discuss such a precaution, she said, is when they are still in love, not because they expect to divorce, but because they care enough about each other to provide that level of security.
Throughout the documentary, Judaism emerges as both a potential source of empowerment for agunot and a system that can be used to keep them trapped.
Communities have organized protests outside the homes of men who refuse to grant a get, seeking to deny them peace while they deny their spouses freedom. Rabbi YY Jacobson also described imposing temporary bans on men who refuse to grant a get.
“I can not [pray] to [God] in good conscience, knowing there is somebody here who is abusing his wife,” Jacobson said.
Religious authorities' role in keeping women trapped
Religious authorities, however, can also play a role in keeping spouses trapped. The documentary highlights a landmark 2014 case in Israel, in which senior religious figures attempted to overturn a get granted to a woman whose husband had been in a vegetative state for seven years.
The High Court ultimately upheld the divorce, agreeing with the original panel of three judges, who had ruled that the husband would fulfill the mitzvah of granting a divorce if he were able to do so. The case has continued to divide the Orthodox world and has followed the careers of the three rabbis involved.
“This documentary is my love letter to the Jewish community,” Palatnik told the Post. “It was an absolute honor to interview the people featured in the film. I was awed by their resilience, and it was deeply touching that they trusted me to tell their stories in a thoughtful and sensitive way.
“It took several years to put this documentary together. We finished production just before October 7, and then paused for quite some time. We filmed in England, Israel, and New York, and it has been an honor to bring these stories to the screen. I’m very happy we’re here.”
Palatnik said she decided to make the documentary because get refusal is an issue that can easily become a thing of the past with a few changes. These include normalizing halachic prenuptial agreements and pressuring batei din (Jewish religious courts) to reject attempts to extort concessions in exchange for a get.
Palatnik also said she hoped to raise awareness of Rate My Beit Din, a platform designed to promote transparency in the religious divorce system. The website aims to help people seeking a divorce identify which courts have faced allegations of corruption and which are more likely to treat agunim with respect.
Shoshanna Keats Jaskoll, an activist who co-founded Chochmat Nashim, insisted that the Jewish community needed to start viewing prenups as the ultimate demonstration of love.
“You’re saying that I will protect you from the very worst of me and the potential that something goes wrong, and that is the most beautiful expression of love that anyone can do for anyone else,” she said.

US Supreme Court snubs bid to revive plea deal for accused 9/11 mastermind
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
14:16:31 UTC
23:16:31 KST

The US Supreme Court declined on Monday to hear a bid by Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the accused mastermind of the September 11, 2001, attacks, to revive a 2024 agreement that would have spared him the death penalty in exchange for a guilty plea - a deal scrapped by former Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin.
The justices turned away appeals by Mohammed and two co-defendants who had also signed plea agreements of a lower court's ruling that upheld Austin's decision to void the deals. The US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit rejected an argument that Austin, who served under former US president Joe Biden, had acted too late.
The Supreme Court's action marks the latest milestone in a military prosecution of the detainees held in Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, that has been beset by two decades of legal gridlock.
In August, a US Air Force judge set the trial for Mohammed and his co-defendants for June 2028.
Mohammed remains the most well-known inmate at the Guantanamo detention facility, which was set up in 2002 by then-US president George W. Bush to house foreign terrorism suspects following the 9/11 attacks, which killed nearly 3,000 people. Mohammed is accused of orchestrating the plot to fly hijacked passenger jetliners into the World Trade Center in New York City and into the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia.
Mohammed, co-defendants accepted agreement before deal revoked
The plea agreements for Mohammed and co-defendants Mustafa al Hawsawi and Walid bin 'Atash had been offered and accepted by the US official overseeing the Pentagon's Guantanamo war court, prompting criticism by Republican lawmakers.
Austin revoked the deals two days later.
A military judge ruled that Austin lacked authority to invalidate the plea deals in a decision that was upheld in December by the US Court of Military Commission Review. The judge then scheduled prompt plea hearings.
The DC Circuit paused those proceedings, and in July 2025, a panel of that court - in a 2-1 vote - backed the decision to scrap the plea deals, saying that Austin "indisputably had legal authority to withdraw from the agreements."
Defense attorneys for Mohammed and al Hawsawi, including lawyers from the American Civil Liberties Union, urged the Supreme Court to hear the case. They said Austin's action violated controlling military law and "prolonged the best chance for finality in the September 11 case in a quarter century."

Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party sent an urgent warning letter to Sport 5 CEO Tomer Turgeman on Monday following reports that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is expected to attend that evening's soccer match between Beitar Jerusalem and Maccabi Tel Aviv at Teddy Stadium in Jerusalem.
The letter, which was also sent to Likud's legal adviser, attorney Ilan Bombach, calls on the Sport 5 to take precautions to ensure that its broadcast of the match and related coverage are not used as a platform for election campaigning.
The match comes just eight days before Israel's October 27 Knesset elections.
The Israeli soccer league administration had previously warned teams against political involvement ahead of the elections.
Yashar argues that the timing of Netanyahu's expected appearance, just eight days before the elections, warrants particular caution. The letter clarifies that the party is not seeking to prevent Netanyahu from attending the match or broadcasters from reporting on his presence.
However, it calls on the channel to avoid "making his presence prominent" through prolonged close-up shots or by providing a platform for speeches, greetings, or campaign-related messages.
Yashar: When necessary, cut away from Netanyahu, switch cameras
The party also wants production, editing, and broadcasting teams to be instructed in advance to switch camera shots or cut away from a segment in real time if, in its view, the coverage crosses the line into prohibited election propaganda.
In the letter, the party's attorneys cite Section 5 of Israel's Elections Law (Methods of Propaganda), arguing that restrictions in place ahead of elections require broadcasters to prevent their coverage from being used for campaign purposes.
The letter nevertheless emphasizes that the party is not seeking to interfere with "legitimate news or sports coverage" of the prime minister's visit.
"We request your confirmation that you will instruct the relevant production, editing, and broadcasting personnel in advance to take reasonable measures to prevent the broadcast of prohibited election propaganda," the letter states.
Yashar warned that if it believes there is a genuine risk of prohibited election propaganda being broadcast, it will consider filing an urgent request for an injunction with the chairman of the Central Elections Committee (CEC).
Eisenkot's party seeks not only to prevent the broadcast of speeches or greetings by Netanyahu, but also to ensure he does not receive disproportionate exposure through close-up shots or prolonged camera focus during the match.

When diplomacy arrived in Jakarta and justice did not
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
14:14:18 UTC
23:14:18 KST

The paradox has acquired a second dimension, and it is written in the ruins of Gaza. Indonesia, a nation that presents itself to the world as a rising democratic power and an indispensable partner for global stability, now positions itself as a moral voice for Palestine while presiding over a domestic order in which liberty is conditional, and dissent is reframed as betrayal.
Under President Prabowo Subianto, this is not a story of isolated abuses. It is the architecture of a state that has learned to speak the language of international responsibility while hollowing out the rights it claims to protect—at home and, increasingly, in its diplomatic conduct abroad. The same logic that shields Jakarta from scrutiny over West Papua now shapes its response to Gaza: a performance of solidarity that stops precisely where material power would be required.
Consider the diplomats’ dilemma. When the United Nations Secretary-General visited Jakarta in October 2026, the official readouts focused on peacekeeping, Palestine, and the reform of the multilateral system. They did not speak of the more than one hundred thousand Indigenous Papuans displaced by military operations, nor of the schools and clinics occupied by security forces, nor of the journalists and activists arrested for documenting the consequences of national development projects.
This silence is not accidental. It is the product of a calculated exchange: Indonesia’s contribution of over fifty thousand peacekeepers to UN missions—including the more than 2,700 currently deployed across eight operations, from UNIFIL in Lebanon to MINUSCA in the Central African Republic—buys it a measure of immunity from scrutiny at home. The moral economy of international institutions rewards what states contribute abroad, not how they treat their own citizens. And Jakarta has learned to spend that credit wisely.
The same exchange now structures the global response to Gaza.
Since October 2023, the United States has used its veto in the Security Council five times to block resolutions demanding a ceasefire, even as the officially confirmed death toll has climbed beyond 56,000, with civilians comprising more than 70 per cent of the dead.
The General Assembly has voted overwhelmingly—164 states in favour, eight against—to affirm the Palestinian right to self-determination and to demand an end to the unlawful occupation.
But the General Assembly cannot enforce its will. Only the Security Council can authorise binding sanctions, deploy peacekeepers, or impose embargoes, and the veto has rendered it structurally incapable of doing so. The International Court of Justice concluded in July 2024 that Israel’s continued presence in the occupied territory is unlawful. The International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Benjamin Netanyahu and Yoav Gallant in November 2024.
Neither ruling has been enforced. The law exists. The enforcement does not. This is the structural paralysis that defines the multilateral order, and it is the backdrop against which Indonesia’s Palestine diplomacy must be assessed.
Jakarta’s rhetorical commitment is genuine and historically grounded. The deployment of the hospital ship KRI dr. Radjiman Wedyodiningrat to El Arish, the dispatch of more than one hundred medical personnel, the airdrops coordinated with the Jordanian Air Force, the offer to evacuate one thousand wounded Palestinians—these are tangible humanitarian contributions, and they deserve recognition.
But they treat the symptoms of the conflict, not its causes. They do not challenge the arms flows that sustain the military campaign, the diplomatic cover that shields it, or the economic relationships that underwrite it. They are politically safe precisely because they leave the structure of impunity intact.
The reason is not mysterious. Indonesia’s economic model depends on Western capital, technology transfers, and access to global markets to fund the nickel downstreaming, infrastructure, and food-estate projects that anchor the Prabowo administration’s developmental vision. To impose unilateral sanctions, to sever commercial ties with states supporting the military campaign, or to take disruptive action outside the parameters of conventional UN diplomacy would risk the investment flows on which that vision depends.
READ: Indonesia slams Israel for discriminating against one of its pilots
And so Jakarta calibrates. It speaks forcefully in the General Assembly, where resolutions are non-binding and symbolic. It sends hospital ships and medical teams, where the gesture is humanitarian, and the political cost is low. It does not weaponise trade, does not lead a sanctions coalition, and does not convert its moral authority into material leverage. The performance is real. The teeth are not.
This calibration is reinforced by a strategic objective that shapes every diplomatic calculation: Indonesia’s campaign for a non-permanent seat on the Security Council for the 2029–2030 term. To secure the votes of a diverse UN membership, Jakarta must maintain functional relationships across geopolitical blocs. Radical or unpredictable positions—precisely the kind that might give its Palestine advocacy enforceable weight—would alienate key voting partners.
The administration therefore prefers the safety of multilateral consensus to the risk of unilateral conviction. The seat is the prize, and the price of the prize is moderation.
The broader Middle East has moved in the same direction. The Abraham Accords, signed in 2020, normalised relations between Israel and the UAE, Bahrain, Sudan, and Morocco, and they have proven unexpectedly resilient even amid the war in Gaza. Regional powers that once framed themselves as guardians of Palestinian rights now prioritise economic modernisation, security partnerships, and supply-chain integration.
The Palestinian cause remains a matter of public rhetoric and domestic legitimacy, but it is increasingly detached from the practical architecture of regional order. Palestine is caught in the gap between the high-level statements that affirm its rights and the material interests that determine its fate.
This is the same gap that defines Indonesia’s domestic order, and it is why the credibility of Jakarta’s Palestine diplomacy cannot be separated from the credibility of its human rights record at home. In West Papua, the machinery of extraction and the machinery of repression are not separate systems; they are the same system.
The legal architecture that prosecutes Indigenous leaders and environmental defenders who contest land grabs is the same architecture that criminalises insult to the president and expands police discretion over digital speech. The state that speaks of Palestinian self-determination while denying it to Papuans is not engaged in hypocrisy for its own sake. It is engaged in a coherent practice of sovereign selectivity: rights are affirmed where they cost nothing and denied where they cost something.
The international community’s willingness to compartmentalise these domains is the condition of Jakarta’s moral voice. Withdraw that willingness, and the voice loses its resonance.
For the international community, the implication is uncomfortable but clear. The implication is uncomfortable but clear. Indonesia cannot be engaged as a credible moral voice on Palestine without confronting the domestic order that sustains its international posture. The shield it has built—of peacekeepers, of non-alignment, of Global South leadership, of humanitarian gestures in Gaza—is not impenetrable.
It depends on the continued willingness of external actors to compartmentalise. That willingness should be withdrawn. Access to West Papua must be a condition of diplomatic partnership, not a concession to be negotiated.
The enforcement of international law in Palestine must be reconnected to the material levers—arms embargoes, trade measures, targeted sanctions—that give law its meaning.
And the reform of the Security Council’s veto must move from aspiration to agenda, because a law that cannot be enforced is not law. It is theatre.
The choice is not between stability and rights. It is between a stability built on silence and a stability built on consent. The ruins of Gaza, the skies over Southeast Asia, and the forests of West Papua suggest that the cost of not choosing is already being paid—by those who have no voice in the capitals where the choice is made.

The Utrecht Conference is a series of Polish–Dutch meetings organised since 1999. Their aim is to strengthen cooperation between Poland and the Kingdom of the Netherlands in the political, economic, and social domains.
This year’s edition of the Conference, a key platform for dialogue at the level of government experts, was attended by several dozen Polish and Dutch representatives from the ministries of foreign affairs, national defence, agriculture, development and technology, climate and the environment, energy, home affairs and administration, justice, as well as family, labour, and social policy.
The Clingendael Institute (Netherlands Institute of International Relations) is an independent Dutch think tank and diplomatic academy based in The Hague. It is tasked with researching global political trends, analysing international security, and providing training for diplomats and experts from around the world.

The spokesperson added: “Our support for Ukraine is unwavering, and I think you saw that in the prime minister’s meeting with President Zelenskyy last week.”

Visegrad Four urge Brussels to ease Russian energy phase-out rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
14:13:10 UTC
23:13:10 KST

The group is calling on Brussels for more funding to cope with the end of Russian energy imports in 2027, amid high electricity prices across Europe.
Slovakia and Hungary called on Brussels on Monday for greater flexibility in phasing out Russian gas, arguing that their landlocked position and reliance on existing supply routes make diversification more difficult and costly.
Bratislava said it had historically served as an entry point for Russian oil and gas but now risks becoming the end of the line, alongside Hungary, as Russian energy supplies to Central Europe are due to end in 2027 under the EU’s plan to phase out imports from Moscow.
“We would like to discuss with the European Commission how the next EU funding period and the availability of EU funds can meet our needs, particularly regarding the expansion of oil and gas infrastructure in the Visegrad Four region,” Slovakia’s Deputy Prime Minister Denisa Saková said on the sidelines of a press conference in Bratislava attended by Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen.
Central European ministers want Brussels to recognise their specific circumstances and take regional needs into account when allocating EU funds for new oil and gas infrastructure and preparing the next EU budget period — another point of contention among member states at the latest European Council summit.
The appeal follows pressure from the Visegrad Group — Hungary, Slovakia, Czechia and Poland — on EU leaders at their 15-16 October summit to reconsider measures to lower electricity bills in the region.
Their demands included greater flexibility in the ongoing review of the bloc’s carbon market, the Emissions Trading System (ETS), and delaying its second phase, ETS2, until 2030.
Energy Commissioner Jørgensen acknowledged the “serious” situation facing people in Central Europe and reiterated the need for “targeted and temporary measures” that would not undermine the bloc’s goal of reducing its reliance on imported fossil fuels.
“We used to be dependent on Russia. We’re moving out of that. Now, that is good. But the current situation shows that we are now dependent on the global market, and events in the Middle East can affect citizens here in Bratislava,” Jørgensen said.
The four EU countries, traditionally more reliant on fossil fuels, argue that high energy prices make it difficult for their industries to commit to investments in electrification. Prices have been driven higher by the US-Israeli war against Iran.
Central European consumers are facing a significantly heavier financial burden, with wholesale electricity futures more than 60% above pre-crisis levels, according to energy think tank Ember.
Ditching Russian energy is raising economic concerns in both countries.
Bratislava and Budapest argue that they face particular challenges in meeting the EU’s diversification requirements and want funding to expand oil and gas infrastructure in the region.
The Visegrad Group has access to several alternative energy sources and supply routes that bypass Russia, albeit at higher cost, with varying levels of integration across the four countries.
“From 2027, we will not be able to import gas from Russia and would like to sign new diversification contracts. Diversification and energy security mean that we have to have prepared rules for the supplies of oil and gas for the V4 region,” Saková added.
Under former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, Hungary challenged the EU’s plan to phase out Russian energy imports, taking the case to an EU court.
Slovakia backed Budapest’s legal challenge, arguing that phasing out Russian energy would put its industrial competitiveness at a significant disadvantage compared with most other EU countries. A first ruling is expected to take months.
