Tehran's dilemma: Is there a growing Baloch insurgency in Iran?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
13:34:43 UTC
22:34:43 KST

Breadcrumb
Tehran's dilemma: Is there a growing Baloch insurgency in Iran?
Armed clashes in Iran’s southeastern province of Sistan-Baluchestan have intensified in recent weeks, reaching their highest level in a decade.
With the US-Israel war threatening to enter an even more volatile phase, such tensions have raised growing concern in Tehran.
At the centre of the escalation is the emergence of a coalition of diverse Baloch militant factions, the Popular Fighters Front (PFF), also known by its Persian acronym JMM (Jebhe-ye-Mobarezin-e Mardomi).
Consisting of Jaish-ul-Adl, PADA Baluch, Harakate Nasr Baluchestan, and the Mohammad Rasulullah Brigade, the militant umbrella was formed in December 2025.
Though they claim to fight for all of Iran, which they say has been “held hostage,” at least one faction among them has advocated Baloch separatism in the past.
But despite their differing political ambitions, the groups share a conservative Sunni Muslim identity, providing common ground in Shia-dominant Iran where the Sunni population is less than 9%.
Tehran's security dilemma
Suddenly, Sistan-Baluchestan has become dangerous.
Since January 2026, at least 37 armed attacks have been reported on police stations, military bases, and checkpoints, while security patrols have been targeted as they move through cities.
Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) personnel are a primary target. There have been high-ranking assassinations, and last month, a regime-linked Sunni cleric was shot dead.
If this continues, the Iranian government may have to send large reinforcements from other parts of the country to contain the unrest, stretching the security infrastructure at a time when it is prepared for a return to war.
Such instability in Sistan-Baluchestan could have consequences for Iran in the coming months.
As per the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED), approximately 70 armed confrontations took place between Iranian security forces and armed groups in Sistan and Baluchestan during 2026, the highest annual level in a decade. Thirteen occurred in the past two weeks alone.
ACLED’s assessments suggest that although Tehran has intensified efforts to dismantle the militant network, raids have often turned into “prolonged battles”, with some lasting as long as nine hours.
Pointing towards a more entrenched insurgency, it says that the “key risk” would be convergence, and a full-scale resumption of the US-Israeli war on Iran could “stretch Tehran’s security forces thin.”
Meanwhile, the human toll is also mounting, according to the US-based Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA), with at least 94 people killed and 33 wounded in 63 armed incidents between 31 March and 10 October.
On 13 October, more than 20 Fatemiyoun brigade members were reported killed or wounded in fighting that lasted for seven hours in the mountainous Taftan area.
The Fatemiyoun are an Iran-backed Shia militia composed largely of Afghan fighters and organised to fight alongside the IRGC. Their reported involvement underscores the extent to which Tehran is drawing on its wider security network to confront the violence.
The use of drones, artillery, and armoured vehicles by government forces in recent clashes further indicates the intensity of the fighting and raises concerns about the consequences of expanded operations in populated areas.
Consequently, Tehran faces a difficult strategic dilemma, and while a forceful response could disrupt militant networks, it may result in deepening local alienation.
While the Iranian government is not losing its grip, chronic instability constrains its ability to respond to war.
Rebranding a Baloch uprising?
Ridden by poverty, plagued by unemployment, and the least developed region in Iran, Sistan-Baluchestan has been tense for decades.
Since their unification as the PFF, however, the region’s militants have changed their narrative, pointing not only to Baloch grievances but also calling for broader political change in Iran.
So far, it cannot be determined whether this consolidation has increased their capabilities, but the ongoing war with Washington has created space for the militants to regroup in Iran.
Dr Farzan Sabet, an Iran expert at the Geneva Graduate Institute, told The New Arab that when “conditions for ordinary people are deteriorating, and the regime is perceived as vulnerable, there are surges of opposition hoping to overthrow the regime, or extract concessions”.
He highlighted the convergence during the 12-day war in June 2025 amid the so-called ‘Lion and Sun’ protests among “leading opposition organisations including the nationwide Pahlavi movement, the coalition of political forces of Iranian Kurdistan in majority Kurdish-speaking areas of Iran, and the PFF in Sistan-Baluchestan”.
Sabet said that Iranian security forces in this province have “historically been poorly equipped and trained, experiencing greater disarray due to the assassination of Iranian security leaders and personnel” during the war.
Militancy in the province has also received a boost from deteriorating material conditions, the dire state of human rights, a disproportionate degree of executions and violations, and, possibly, foreign support.
According to Sabet, the political dynamics in Sistan-Baluchestan are often distinct from those in the core of the country, and there are fewer sensitive population centres and economic hubs.
“It is seen as less of a threat than, say, a comparable event in Tehran or another major city in the core, and there is a lower risk that discontent and instability spread from the periphery to the core than the other way around,” he added.
The impact of such peripheral insurgencies is usually geographically and politically contained in Iran, even though the PFF is “targeting its discourse toward the broader Iranian nation”.
However, “given the recent successes of Balochi militants, the regime may want to surge further security forces into the area,” Sabet said, such as the Fatemiyoun Division - an IRGC-backed militia of Afghan Shia whose members died in recent clashes.
The US-Israel war has added a new dimension to the fragile situation in Sistan-Baluchestan as Iran’s security establishment has diverted away resources and armed groups have seen it as “an opportunity to intensify their activities and test the state’s capacity to respond”, Babak Vahdad, an independent researcher and Iran analyst, told The New Arab.
In his view, the escalation is not an immediate threat to the survival of the Islamic Republic, as Baloch militancy remains geographically concentrated and is not a broader national uprising.
But the situation has exposed “some of the structural weaknesses of the Iranian state, particularly its difficult relationship with ethnic and religious minorities, and a predominantly military response may contain the insurgency in the short term without addressing its underlying causes”.
Meanwhile, according to Iran’s narrative, “certain regional actors” might be encouraging instability there to “divert Tehran’s military and security resources away from the main confrontation in the Gulf, possibly even preparing the ground for a future military attack against Iran”, Vahdad added.
Fractious borders, wider risks
The security issue is made worse by geography. Across mountainous terrain, the porous 900 km Iran-Pakistan border stretches from a tripoint with Afghanistan to the northern Arabian Sea, and policing it is an arduous task for Tehran as deserted, interconnected frontiers with low populations create fertile ground for armed groups and mercenaries.
Even the Pakistani province of Baluchistan across the border has separatist outfits, mercenaries, a smuggling nexus, and long-standing political and socio-economic issues.
Currently, border crossings along the Pakistan-Iran border have been closed by Islamabad.
Naveed Ali Sheikh, an Islamabad-based military analyst, told The New Arab that Pakistan has been facing terrorist attacks originating from the Iranian border region of Sistan and Baluchestan, where banned militant outfits operate and carry out “hit-and-run” [back across the border] attacks.
These groups have targeted Iranian and Pakistani government forces, as well as civilian infrastructure, he said. Noting that a surge in such attacks was observed recently, Sheikh said the border required better security infrastructure, upgraded surveillance systems, and more effective mechanisms to prevent further incursions.
However, border security was not the primary reason behind the recent closure of cross-border trade, as “shadow banking networks are being used by smugglers and black-market operators, which the United States alleges are helping finance Iran's sanctioned military establishment”.
And the temporary closure of border crossings may be intended to manage the anticipated backlog of transactions and documentation if the banking and trade standstill continues.
Sabena Siddiqui is a foreign affairs journalist, lawyer and geopolitical analyst specialising in modern China, the Belt and Road Initiative, the Middle East, and South Asia.
Follow her on X: @sabena_siddiqi

Resisting Erasure: Libraries in Palestine and Palestine in Libraries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
13:32:40 UTC
22:32:40 KST

In the foreword to Resisting Erasure: Libraries in Palestine and Palestine in Libraries (Litwin Books, 2026), Emily Drabinksy writes about the difficulties encountered while indexing articles about settler colonialism and apartheid in the occupied West Bank in 2003. “The thesaurus I was required to use did not include such terms in relation to the territory known as Israel. In fact, Palestine did not exist at all, except as a historical formation.” Indexing anything related to Palestine under Arab-Israel conflict, Drabinski notes, erased the Palestinian experience while lending impunity to Israel’s violence and the US role in arming Israel.
Editors Nora Lester Murad and Mary L. Onorato situate the book within the impact of the metaphor and reality of war: the actual war waged against Palestinians, and the war on libraries and archives in Palestine and the US. Through the contributions in this book, insights are provided as to how librarians are resisting censorship efforts and the erasure of Palestine and Palestinians. Divided in two parts, the first segment of the book deals with resisting erasure in Palestinian libraries and the efforts to preserve Palestinian history. The second segment focuses on resisting the enforced complicity in US libraries and institutions.
The historical background to Palestine since 1948 provides the foundations to understand the trajectories of its libraries, particularly during the Ottoman era. At its end, foreign libraries introduced both administrative organisation as well as Orientalist monopoly. The British Mandate further suppressed Palestinian education and limited school libraries while Palestinians were banned from public libraries in the era – a colonial tactic “to facilitate occupation of their [Palestinians’] land and obliterate their identity”. The Palestinian Nakba of 1948 further entrenched colonial rule and erasure by legitimising the theft of Palestinians’ public and private libraries. The same tactics were repeated during the 1967 Naksa, and in 1982 in Lebanon, when Zionist forces looted the PLO’s Research Centre, seizing all its material which required 35 trucks to transport.
Looting was part of Israel’s colonial violence limiting Palestinian self-determination. The PRC’s stolen material – the majority of it returned in 1983 as part of a prisoner exchange – documented and archived the Palestinian national movement and revolution. Following the massacres of Sabra and Shatila, which were documented in an issue of Palestine Affairs by the PRC, the staff started rebuilding its archives from microfilm copies of book and private collection donations.
Israel’s periodical destruction of Gaza, leading up to the current genocide and its consequences, follow the same colonial trajectory of obliterating libraries. From the destruction of 2014 during Operation Protective Edge to the more recent destruction since 7 October 2023, Palestinians have tenaciously held on to reading, salvaging books from the rubble and maintaining their links to literature. Books were found to have been instrumental in helping Palestinians in Gaza cope with the genocide. At the same time, the genocide also left its mark on Gaza’s libraries and archives. The book states, “archivists and librarians have been repeatedly displaced, injured or killed, making it even more difficult to take stock of the damage to cultural heritage.”
READ: Starvation killed 466 Palestinians since 2024, says Gaza Health Ministry
While the Zionist colonial ideology furthered its war on Palestinian libraries and archives through the decades, the US complements Israel’s efforts with its own manoeuvrings. For example, the book notes the discrepancy between Palestine being constantly mentioned in the media, yet libraries do not stock enough books on Palestine, not even by the most renowned Palestinian authors. The discrepancy in the libraries is further highlighted by statistical data that shows, in August 2025 2,573 books in English about Israel, in comparison to the 650 books about Palestine. The book makes an observation: “the little acknowledge reality that many library workers and policy makers are uncomfortable giving visibility to Palestinian authors, dreading and groundless but potentially devastating accusation of antisemitism.”
The lack of visibility of books on Palestine is reflected in the lack of publicity as most are published by independent publishers or self-published. Another hurdle is the broad categorisation in libraries, which does not use subcategories for the Middle East and North Africa category except for Egypt. The Arab-Israeli conflict, not only a catalogue term but also a normalised reference that avoids the colonial reality, is not only misleading but promotes the erasure of Palestinians in books. The book cautions against bibliographies created by the Anti-Defamation League, which omits the Palestinian experience completely or else chooses titles in which it is misrepresented to further the erroneous concept of ‘both sides’.
The both sides narrative is further explored in the Librarians and Archivists with Palestine’s (LAP) Censorship Tracker through which awareness is raised about Palestine in libraries. Books about Palestine are deemed biased and librarians using the Censorship Tracker stated that “this argument is even applied to discussions opposing genocide, as if supporting genocide was a legitimate ‘side’ that required equal representation.” Embracing the Palestinian narrative also proved hazardous for librarians who have been the target of hate and harassment both online and in person.
Neutrality applied to libraries also results in the erasure of Palestinians. The book gives several examples relating to the dissemination of knowledge and how research guides are misrepresented. When it comes to Palestine, unlike other areas, neutrality was a required component of social justice.
Juxtaposed against censorship, neutrality and erasure is the initiative by Andaleeb Cartonera, inspired by small publishers in Latin America which hold to an independent publishing tradition and which prints material already published online in cardboard cover books. Andaleeb Cartonera describes their press as having started in 2024, stating, “what fuelled the creation of Andaleeb Cartonera was the sense of impotence and rage so many of us felt ten months into the genocide.”
A standard misrepresentation of Palestinian narratives needs to be challenged from within establishments and institutions. Colonialism also reaches into spaces beyond Palestine, as the book shows with its detailed discussions of different aspects of libraries. As the destruction of Gaza continues through forced displacement and therefore increasing fragmentation of the Palestinians and their experience, what happens in the US – resisting the imperialist narrative to make space for the Palestinian one that is shattered by US complicity with Israel – remains an imperative.

Behind the Veil of Religious Harmony in Cambodia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
13:32:00 UTC
22:32:00 KST

On paper, Cambodia often appears as a site of religious tolerance, boasting favorable scores in global indices that measure selected elements of freedom of religion or belief (FoRB). Over the years, these “rankings” have manufactured a facade of harmony that masks realities on the ground. State influence over Buddhist institutions, structural inequalities, and the quiet marginalization of minority groups and the destruction of Indigenous sacred places are routinely obscured by aggregate rankings that mistake the absence of overt conflict and the fear of speaking up for genuine harmony.
This gap in analysis is the central focus of Asia Centre’s report, “Religious Freedom in Cambodia: Unpacking the Rankings,” published on September 28. At its core, the report interrogates what standard metrics capture and, more importantly, what they deliberately or inadvertently leave out.
Several existing reports provide valuable insights into Cambodia’s Freedom of Religion or Belief (FoRB) landscape. The Pew Research Center’s Government Restrictions Index and Social Hostilities Index both offer comparative global measurements of religious freedom and tolerance. In 2023, Cambodia scored 5 out of 10 on the Government Restrictions Index and 0.2 out of 10 on the Social Hostilities Index, indicating relatively favorable performance compared with its neighboring countries.
The U.S. Department of State’s International Religious Freedom Reports provide detailed annual documentation of government policies and religious-freedom conditions. Its 2023 report on Cambodia identified several areas of concern, including state influence over Buddhist institutions and monks’ political affiliations, Muslim representation in local government leadership, and Indigenous Peoples’ land rights.
The report “Diving Deep into Cambodia’s FoRB: An Exploration of Community Hopes and Collective Hurdles” (2024), produced by Women Peace Makers in collaboration with Danmission Cambodia, offers insights into the experiences of different ethno-religious communities in Cambodia, particularly regarding religious education, participation in religious leadership, and access to sacred sites.
Asia Centre’s report builds on this research by examining the institutional relationships. Our report draws attention to power structures that shape how religious freedom is exercised and protected in practice. It also considers developments since 2024, including the leadership transition and the Cambodia-Thailand border conflict. Drawing on the latest cases and consultations with experts and affected communities, the report goes beyond aggregate rankings to examine the political, institutional, and structural conditions underlying Cambodia’s FoRB landscape.
Four findings are particularly significant. First, Cambodia’s appearance of religious harmony obscures the structural inequalities. Existing research pays limited attention to tensions and hostilities between religious communities, particularly between majority and minority groups. This risks mistaking silence and the absence of overt conflict for “harmony.” Asia Centre’s findings instead suggest that “harmony” is a by-product of state influence, structural inequalities and fear that constrain religious expression. By examining these underlying conditions, the report brings greater visibility to grievances and experiences that may otherwise remain unspoken.
Second, state influence over religious institutions constrains religious autonomy and serves political objectives. Buddhism’s central role in Cambodian national identity makes this relationship particularly significant: political influence over Buddhist institutions can shape not only religious expression but also political expression. Institutional and material pressures discourage Buddhist monks from challenging state expectations, while political actors mobilize religious authority to legitimize government objectives, including during the 2025 Cambodia–Thailand border conflict. By examining these dynamics, the report highlights the often-overlooked links between religion and political power.
Third, the intersectionality of rights is obscured. Existing human rights reporting frequently treats religious discrimination, restrictions on fundamental freedoms, and Indigenous land dispossession as separate issues. Asia Centre connects these concerns through a FoRB lens, showing how development projects and land concessions that destroy Indigenous sacred sites can undermine communities’ ability to sustain their religious and cultural practices, while raising broader questions about equal access to institutional protection and accountability.
Fourth, limited FoRB literacy prevents government officials, civil society, independent media, and even some faith-based organizations from recognizing violations. Hence, unequal treatment in administrative procedures, inadequate protection against prejudices, or absences of effective remedies for affected communities are ignored. Asia Centre’s report highlights the need to strengthen FoRB literacy among these stakeholders to ensure that they have the capacity to correctly identify violations, report them, and make sure remedial actions are taken.
Building on these stakeholder capacities, ultimately Asia Centre’s report moves beyond aggregate global indices to expose the institutional and political mechanisms shaping Cambodia’s actual religious landscape.
By examining state influence over Buddhist institutions, the intersectionality of rights, and the systemic challenges faced by minorities and Indigenous communities, the report provides a comprehensive country-level analysis. Its recommendations translate these insights into concrete responsibilities for the Cambodian government, civil society, international organizations, independent media, and faith-based groups.
Rather than treating Freedom of Religion or Belief (FoRB) as an isolated concern, the report connects it to broader social and political dimensions, offering practical guidelines to bridge the gap between formal legal protections and lived realities in Cambodia.
This op-ed is based on Asia Centre’s new report, “Religious Freedom in Cambodia: Unpacking the Rankings.” Download the full report here. For more information about Asia Centre, visit asiacentre.org.

Source: Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi in an interview with the BBC
Details: Koretskyi said that since 16 July, when the reshuffled government began its work, not a single day has passed without attacks on the energy sector. There have already been 2,147 such attacks, which is many times more than last year.

Details: He added that "today there is massive, simply massive destruction of power transmission lines".
"The facilities themselves, the transformers themselves can be protected, but, as you understand, these are thousands of kilometres of switchgear, huge 'football pitches'. It is impossible to protect absolutely everything," he explained.
At the same time, there is a large reserve stock of equipment, and repair crews have the ability and capacity to restore everything in the shortest possible time.
"Thanks to the military, Russia is seeing no results on the front. Therefore, it is directing all its aggression and hatred into terror against civilian infrastructure: electricity, heating, and now water," Koretskyi said, stressing that the Russian goal is to exhaust the people.
He noted that the government's strategy remains unchanged: to protect what can be protected as much as possible and to create distributed generation.
"Together with our partners, we are building up sufficient stocks of backup transformers and equipment to quickly replace damaged ones. We are also strengthening the backup power supply for critical facilities, in particular water pumping stations," he noted.

Wounded Ukrainian Soldier Airlifted by Heavy Drone in World’s First
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
13:29:32 UTC
22:29:32 KST

The Ukrainian military has used a heavy aerial drone to airlift a wounded soldier from the front line in the first known operation of its kind.
The Ground Forces’ Drone Force led the operation alongside the 92nd Separate Assault Brigade named after Ivan Sirko, according to the brigade’s press office, which announced the operation on Monday.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
It said the wounded soldier was an infantryman from the 30th Separate Mechanized Brigade, injured at his position in an unnamed frontline sector. It’s unclear when the operation took place.
The press release calls the rescue a “historic operation” as it marks the first time an aerial drone is used to airlift wounded troops to safety.
The brigade ruled out the usual option, a ground robotic system (UGV), adding that Russian drones were active and the terrain was mined, rendering the use of a UGV impossible.
Specialists from the 92nd Brigade’s unmanned ground systems company then used a heavy hexacopter made by Ukrainian manufacturer Gurzuf Defence, which the brigade said had provided it free of charge.
The brigade wrote that its engineers worked with the manufacturer to keep the drone steady in flight, without flipping or swinging excessively, in order to airlift the soldier
They tested it at sites provided by Gurzuf Defence and planned the mission with neighboring units.
A drone operator from the 30th brigade flew the drone. The 92nd brigade said the rescued soldier is receiving treatment and rehabilitation. It was stated that his life is no longer in danger.
Russian Airports Begin Checking Military Registration Statuses, Activists Report
The 92nd brigade thanked the 30th and 14th mechanized brigades, the 10th Army Corps and Gurzuf Defence for making the operation possible.
Ukraine’s previous rescues using ground drones
Until now, ground robots have largely handled evacuations from positions cut off by active fighting.
In one case that drew presidential awards for the 1st Separate Medical Battalion, a soldier had spent 33 days wounded in a village under Russian control before a UGV reached him. The machine hit an anti-personnel mine on the way but kept moving on a damaged wheel.
The 1st Separate Medical Battalion is now sharing its methods abroad. In September, its combat medics took an armored UGV, the MAUL made by Ukrainian company AIDronesUA, to Sweden. There they met medics from the Swedish Armed Forces’ Livgardet (Lifeguards) regiment.
The battalion used the machine to show how ground robots have changed their ability to reach casualties in the “kill zone,” the corridor between the front lines where strikes, especially by drones, make a conventional evacuation impossible.
Battalion commander Asan Charuhov said every mission requires careful preparation that accounts for the casualty’s condition, the terrain and the combat situation. He added that some of the people evacuated by UGV might not have been evacuated at all by any other means.
Sweden’s commander-in-chief, General Michael Claesson, said the experience and innovation shared by the Ukrainian medics would strengthen his own forces’ ability to operate on the modern battlefield.
The 92nd Brigade’s mission tackles the same problem: a wounded soldier trapped in a zone too dangerous to enter, but from the air rather than the ground.
Gurzuf Defence is best known for its Heavy Shot bomber drones, produced in tens of thousands per year. In a March interview with Ukrainska Pravda, the company said its heavy drones could later evacuate the wounded from the battlefield.
The new mission suggests the air could become a second evacuation route when the ground is too dangerous.

Sudan drone strike kills 11 at displacement camp – official
Unknown

13:29:04 UTC
22:29:04 KST

Sudan drone strike kills 11 at displacement camp – official
Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have killed at least 11 people, including nine children, in a drone attack on a displacement camp in West Darfur, according to the region’s Health and Social Welfare Minister, Babiker Hamdin.
In a statement published on Sunday, Hamdin said that the attack targeted displaced civilians on the Sudan-Chad border. According to preliminary figures, the victims included nine children aged between five and ten and two women aged 23 and 36. Five others were injured.
The victims had reportedly fled their villages last year after RSF fighters allegedly burned and looted their homes. They subsequently sought refuge in Sanakit, near the Chadian border, where they were living in difficult humanitarian conditions before the latest attack.
Hamdin condemned the strike as “a horrific crime and a grave violation of international humanitarian law, reflecting the militia’s indifference to the lives of innocent people.”
He called on the international community to hold those responsible accountable and designate the paramilitary group as a terrorist organization.
Sudan was plunged into a civil war three years ago after a struggle for power broke out between the SAF and the RSF.
Sudan descended into chaos in April 2023 when fighting erupted between the national army, the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). The conflict followed months of tension between their commanders, Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemedti, over a planned transition to civilian rule. What began in the capital, Khartoum, as a power struggle has devastated the country, killing tens of thousands, displacing millions, and pushing parts of Sudan into famine.
Regional and international peace efforts, including African Union mediation and Saudi-US talks in Jeddah, have repeatedly stalled. In September 2025, the Quad group – the US, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, and the United Arab Emirates – proposed a three-month humanitarian truce leading to a permanent ceasefire and a civilian-led political transition. Burhan rejected a subsequent US-led proposal that November, arguing it would dismantle state security institutions while leaving the RSF in place. The paramilitaries said they accepted the truce.
The UAE’s involvement has deepened mistrust of mediation. Sudan’s army-backed government severed diplomatic ties with Abu Dhabi in May 2025, accusing it of supporting the RSF. The UAE denies supplying weapons to the paramilitaries. Relations with Washington deteriorated further in September 2026 after the US questioned both factions’ legitimacy. Sudan rejected the remarks and called for peace efforts free from foreign dictates.
Meanwhile, rival administrations have entrenched Sudan’s divisions. Burhan’s government returned to Khartoum in January 2026 after the army recaptured the capital, having operated from Port Sudan during the fighting. In July 2025, the RSF-aligned TASIS coalition announced a rival government based in Nyala, Darfur, with Dagalo heading its governing council. The UN Security Council and African Union rejected the move.
The RSF has faced similar accusations from rights groups over attacks on civilians. In September, the Sudanese Alliance for Rights reported that five people were killed in an attack on a market in North Kordofan, while the Committee for Justice blamed the group for a courthouse strike that killed ten. On October 9, the Sudan Doctors Network accused the rebels of a drone attack on a displacement camp in Blue Nile state that killed 31 people, including four children.
Earlier this month, Russian diplomat Yulia Zhdanova said that Sudanese troops recovered US-supplied weapons intended for Ukraine from RSF fighters near Bara. Their markings indicated that they had been transferred to Kiev in December 2024, she said, according to TASS.

Kenya confirms eighth Ebola case as outbreak spreads in Congo
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:27:28 EEST
22:27:28 KST

Kenya confirms eighth Ebola case as outbreak spreads in Congo
Kyiv • UNN
Kenya has detected its eighth Ebola case, while 128 contacts remain in quarantine. In the DRC, the outbreak has now spread to eight provinces.
Kenya has confirmed its eighth case of Ebola, while the outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo continues to spread to new areas. UNN reports this, citing Euronews.
Details
Kenyan authorities have detected the country’s eighth case of Ebola after another person who was in quarantine tested positive, a representative of the country’s Ministry of Health said on October 18.
The latest patient is a 49-year-old man who assisted the first Ebola patient. He exhibited symptoms including fever, high temperature, headache, and muscle pain, and was placed in quarantine after likely contact with the virus.
"Today we tested 38 people; one of them tested positive," said Minister of Health Patrick Amoth, adding that the man had been in quarantine since October 9.
Kenya reported its first-ever Ebola death on October 5, when a man who lived in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) died after returning to Kenya.
The other seven cases involve relatives of the first patient or medical workers who treated him; Amoth said their condition is stable.
The ministry said that 128 people who had contact with the first patient remain in quarantine.
The country remains open, with no restrictions on travel, trade, or public gatherings, as recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO). However, the country is intensifying efforts to monitor the spread of Ebola and raise public awareness.
Neighboring Tanzania has tightened border controls and introduced mandatory health declarations and 21-day monitoring for travelers arriving from high-risk countries.
Outbreak reaches eighth province in Congo
Meanwhile, the outbreak continues to grow in the DRC and has reached its eighth province. Two new cases, including one fatality, were recorded over the past weekend in the previously unaffected province of Nord-Ubangi, which borders the Central African Republic.
Authorities reported 9,455 infections and 4,561 deaths as a result of the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history.
"We are seeing Ebola hotspots generally decrease, but unfortunately, geographically, it is spreading," WHO Regional Director for Africa Mohamed Yakub Janabi told the Associated Press.
Janabi noted that one of the biggest challenges is persuading infected people to seek medical care, adding that some deaths occur in communities outside medical centers.
The outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo strain, for which there are no licensed vaccines or specific treatments, although trials are being conducted in the DRC.

How the Protests in France Spiraled as Police 'Lost Control'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
13:27:20 UTC
22:27:20 KST

France’s Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez on Monday admitted that police “lost control” in some cities over the weekend as violent protests erupted across the country, while French President Emmanuel Macron called for a review of the police response to the rioting and looting.
Nuñez said there had been a "lack of anticipation" ahead of the demonstrations on Saturday and acknowledged that policing numbers had fallen short in some areas as hundreds of thousands took to the streets to protest over, what they say are, underfunded public services and rising cost-of-living pressures. The demonstrations followed weeks of student protests that had also seen some violence.
In the wake of the chaotic scenes, Nuñez offered his resignation to Macron because he "felt responsible” for how things unfolded. Macron refused to accept it, due to “the need for a continuous command of the police,” the Élysée Palace told TIME. Instead, Macron has called for the Interior Ministry to “take all necessary steps to ensure transparency over planning and intelligence failures” and to put an end to the barricades and looting.
As France aims to regain full control of its streets, French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has extended local mayors the power to enforce “partial curfews,” in an effort to protect businesses and people. "My determination to restore order is absolute," Lecornu told reporters, emphasizing that localized curfews were preferred over a national enforcement at this time. Paris authorities have since issued overnight curfews in two areas of the capital. The Interior Ministry reported that around 550,000 people had taken to the streets on Saturday. A French trade union put the number at over 800,000. Nuñez on Sunday said that more than 2,000 people had been arrested and over 600 police officers and firefighters injured. In Paris, at least 300 businesses were vandalised, Dominique Restino, the head of the Paris chamber of commerce, told BFM television.
Alongside the violence in the capital, what started out as peaceful protests in Marseille and Lyon also turned violent as rioters descended. Authorities in Marseille on Monday imposed a temporary ban on public gatherings and demonstrations. French unions have already called for a new round of strikes and marches on Nov. 5.
Various buildings and official monuments have been targeted across the country.
Macron condemned the "unbridled violence" as he addressed the nation Sunday evening. “Those who looted will have to pay for the damage, and those who sought to bring down the Republic will be held accountable,” he vowed in a televised speech.
Isa Obradovich, a French-Peruvian American artist living in Paris, has participated in a number of protests since the movement went nationwide in early October. The 22-year-old says the demonstrations have become increasingly charged amid escalating clashes between protesters and police.
“I had to walk through clouds of tear gas to get home and clouds of smoke from fires,” she says of her journey home from the protests this weekend.
Obradovich notes the property damage in her own neighborhood, sharing that some of the stores she regularly visits were impacted by the protests.
“You can also see that there has been more property damage. [Some] grocery stores in my neighborhood were closed yesterday. One of them because they had boarded up the walls, and the other one because the windows of the storefront had been smashed and all the stuff inside had been ruined. I walked past as shop owners and employees were standing there looking at the devastation,” she says.
The Federation of Trade and Retail told TIME that “nearly 3,000 shops and businesses of all sizes across France have been affected by the violence over the weekend.” The French government has said it will create a fund to financially assist shops that were impacted by the riots.
Lawmakers clash over where the blame lies
Lecornu has blamed far-left agitators for the unrest. "There is, after all, a far-left movement that wants to cause—we can’t put it any more strongly—profound unrest in the country in the run-up to the presidential election," he said.
Jean-Luc Mélenchon, leader of France’s far-left party, France Unbowed, pushed back against this framing and insisted the protest movement is “the result of ten disastrous years in which President Macron has disorganized the state and public services.” TIME has reached out to Macron’s offices for comment.
The discord between lawmakers and the uncertainty in the government with Nuñez’s resignation attempt hanging over the proceedings comes just six months ahead of France’s next presidential lection, where Mélenchon will no doubt be hoping to beat centrist contenders to the runoff.
France’s public debt has climbed to a record $4 trillion in Macron’s two terms, according to figures shared by France’s National Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies in late June. The fiscal dilemma has heightened scrutiny on government spending and has sparked questions over “Macronisme,” the right-of-center, top-down governing style that Macron emulates. Further adding to the economic pressures, French government bonds dropped after the weekend of unrest.
Antonio Fatas, a professor of economics at Insead, the European business school, has said the political and economic situation is serious. “I am very worried about the economic situation because growth is low and it is difficult to see how the dynamics change. Then you have the debt numbers, which are bad, and the financial markets are thinking the government is not in control,” he told the Guardian.
Demonstrations spread across France
Throughout September, students across France blockaded schools and demonstrated against, what they say is, a poorly-funded high school system. The protests went nationwide on Oct. 6, when more than 250,000 people took to streets across with teachers, parents, and union activists joining marches.
The demonstrations have drawn comparisons to the May 1968 protests, which were initiated by a student movement and led to millions of workers striking and nearly toppled the government.
In the years since, there have been numerous protest uprisings in Paris, including the Yellow Vest movement of 2018 and the pension reform protests of 2023.
What distinguishes the unrest that unfolded over the weekend is how the pockets of violence dispersed, says Fabien Jobard, a researcher at the French National Centre for Scientific Research. He says that the rioters moved away from the main demonstrations, seemingly catching the police off guard and making it all the more difficult to contain the unrest. That, coupled with the French authorities’ own admittance of failing to anticipate the full scale of the protests, meant that “it was too late to gather enough police forces in different places,” adds Jobard.
On Saturday, as some sought to revive the Yellow Vest movement of 2018, protesters draped a yellow vest over the Marianne statue at the Place de la République.
The group that helped coordinate the action on its website described the mobilization as a convergence of student protests and wider economic grievances, bringing together high school and university students, farmers, firefighters, workers, teachers, healthcare workers, climate activists, residents of working-class neighborhoods, and retirees.
Alongside concerns over school funding and cost-of-living pressures, including concerns over fuel prices, which have significantly increased since the onset of the Iran war after as continued disruption to the Strait of Hormuz sent energy markets spiralling worldwide.
Obradovich describes it as an “intersectional protest movement,” arguing that “the root of all of these problems boils down to this government system taking away funding from public services.”
In his speech addressing the nation, Macron said order must be restored, but also recognized protesters’ concerns. He said his government was working with fuel distributors to ensure a “tangible impact on prices.” Addressing the concerns of students, he said the voices of young people “must be heard” and referenced how the Minister of National Education had set up an online portal to hear concerns. Additionally, he said meetings were being held to develop solutions alongside young people.
Thousands protest in other European cities
France was not alone in dealing with demonstrations over the weekend, as protesters also took to the streets in other European countries.
In Portugal, protesters marched in Lisbon, Porto, and Coimbra as they called for better pensions, improved public services, and affirmative government action to combat rising living costs.
In Milan, police clashed with protesters as some threw stones and looted shops during demonstrations against underfunded services and the rising cost of living.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni condemned "the violence of criminals who, even through organized groups, exploit demonstrations to seek confrontation and sow chaos." There were further clashes between police and protesters in Bologna and Turin.
Unrest also broke out in Brussels, Belgium, on Saturday afternoon, as antifascist activists took to the streets. The demonstrations turned violent, prompting police intervention amid reports of property damage.
In Albania, protests spilled over to a sixth day on Sunday, with student-led demonstrations marching against, what they argue is, an underfunded education system, and allegations of government corruption. Police and protesters clashed in the capital of Tirana, as Prime Minister Edi Rama staunchly rejected calls for his resignation.
Albania’s current demonstrations come months after a protest movement rallied against a planned luxury development linked to Jared Kushner, U.S. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law. The initial marches in May were borne out of environmental concerns, but protests developed amid allegations of corruption and discontent over cost-of-living pressures.

France's unrest lays bare 'slow agony' of Macron's twilight months
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
13:26:32 UTC
22:26:32 KST

France's unrest lays bare 'slow agony' of Macron's twilight months
PARIS, Oct 19 - France’s worst bout of civil unrest in years has plunged President Emmanuel Macron’s final months in office deeper into turmoil, exposing the powerlessness of a leader struggling to contain social anger with little money to spend, scant political capital and an increasingly fragile grip on public order.
The rioting that swept across France on Saturday, leaving a trail of looted shops, torched buildings and defaced public institutions, presents Macron with perhaps the most explosive challenge of his twilight presidency: a country demanding more from a state that can no longer afford to give much.
Macron came to power almost a decade ago promising to upend France’s sclerotic political class, turbocharge economic reforms and restore authority through a more assertive presidency. Instead, with just six months left in office, he finds himself effectively a lame-duck head of state presiding over a country mired in political paralysis, facing acute financial pressures and grappling with unrest that has exposed the limits of state authority.
Unlike during the Yellow Vest uprising of 2018-2019, when Macron sought to defuse public anger with billions of euros in concessions, France’s strained public finances and fractured parliament leave him with precious few levers to pull.
Even former allies are now openly scathing, tracing the country's current impasse to Macron's decision to call a snap parliamentary election in 2024 that weakened his authority.
“The end of this term is a slow agony,” said Loïc Kervran, a former lawmaker from Macron’s camp, on X. “The president paralysed the country with his absurd decision to dissolve parliament in 2024. Arguably the worst decision in the history of the Fifth Republic."
LE PEN'S 'HIGHWAY' TO THE PRESIDENCY
The turmoil may benefit far-right National Rally leader Marine Le Pen, who is already the frontrunner in the 2027 presidential race and stands to gain from both the anger over declining living standards and the fears over law and order unleashed by the weekend’s violence.
"Le Pen no longer needs to spend any money to campaign," Jean-Baptiste Moreau, another former Macron lawmaker, told Reuters. "It's not just a clear path ahead of her — it's a six-lane highway."
Le Pen delivered her own message to the nation in a video statement on Sunday, portraying Macron's administration as a crumbling power and casting herself as the figure capable of restoring order.
When Macron later addressed the country, he offered little concrete action, stopping short of declaring a state of emergency. As he spoke, looting was continuing for a second consecutive night, including in affluent Paris districts, prompting his prime minister Sébastien Lecornu to announce local curfews on Monday.
Opponents and one-time allies alike were underwhelmed. His former prime minister, Edouard Philippe, now preparing his own presidential run, was unsparing in his criticism.
"Mr President, I listened to you last night," he wrote on X. "I would have preferred, like millions of French people, decisions and initiatives to restore order."
"Our country needs to be commanded," he added.
But even Philippe is struggling to shake off his past association with Macron, and most recent polls show far-left firebrand Jean-Luc Melenchon edging ahead of him in the race to qualify for the second-round runoff vote. That outcome would all but guarantee a Le Pen victory, according to opinion polls.
CALLS FOR EARLY RESIGNATION AMID MULTIPLE CRISES
Macron's office on Monday announced that he had refused his interior minister's resignation and ordered a review into apparent failures in intelligence gathering and police preparedness — deepening the impression of a government struggling to regain control.
Investors also took fright. Market analysts say the violence adds another layer of political risk at a time when France is already under scrutiny over its swelling debt burden and struggle to reduce one of the euro zone's largest budget deficits.
The president now finds himself trapped between bond markets demanding spending restraint and protesters demanding the opposite.
Despite calls from opponents to remain in France, Macron arrived in Kuwait on Monday on a Gulf tour he says will help secure fuel supplies and ease some of the economic pressures that have helped swell the ranks of the protesters.
The trip carries risks, reinforcing perceptions of a president disconnected from the public mood. Images of Macron attending a Céline Dion concert with his wife Brigitte on Friday evening, hours before the unrest erupted, prompted ridicule on social media and became an easy symbol for critics seeking to portray him as detached from events.
In a sign of the depth of disenchantment in parts of his political camp, some former allies have begun openly discussing whether he should leave office before the end of his term. Moreau, who spoke to Macron on Sunday, said he urged him to prepare an orderly early departure to break the current political deadlock and avoid another six months of drift.
"He doesn't want to give up, that's not his character. But that's what he should do for the country," he said. REUTERS

How expats tackle Dutch language issues without giving away data
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
13:26:27 UTC
22:26:27 KST

Partner content
How expats tackle Dutch language issues without giving away data
A letter from the Belastingdienst has landed on the doormat, and it might as well be written in code. At work, the team meeting that began in English has drifted into Dutch, and you’re nodding along while hoping nobody asks for your opinion. Sound familiar? We spoke with OmniForge, a tech company helping expats tackle the language barrier online.
Why the usual AI tools fall short
AI assistants promise to help with both of these challenges, but they have their limits. Firstly, many recording and transcription tools only support a handful of major languages, which leaves plenty of expats working in English by default, says Daniel G. Ríos, co-founder and CEO of OmniForge. Secondly, most of them process everything in the cloud, which is less than ideal when it comes to an employment contract, payslip or document with your BSN on it.
The risk is not theoretical. When hackers posted Odido’s customer data online, millions of people were reminded how far personal data can travel. “In the best case scenario, your data might be used to profile you for ads,” Daniel says, “but in the case of data exfiltration from cloud providers, your data might also be used for nefarious purposes.”
A local alternative, built by expats
OmniForge is a privacy-first AI desktop app for macOS and Windows that transcribes meetings and answers questions about your documents, all on your own computer. It was built by a team of expats in the Netherlands who, as Daniel puts it, “experience the exact same bilingual friction our users do.”
https://omniforge.online/dutchnews
“People should not have to compromise on their personal information in order to benefit from a service,” he says. In practice, the AI engine lives on your machine rather than in a data centre. “You could disconnect your WiFi entirely, and it will still securely transcribe your meetings and analyse your documents.” Only account login and subscription management are online.
There’s an environmental upside too, Daniel argues: running AI on your own computer’s spare processing power, what he calls “Green AI at the Edge,” can avoid the electricity and cooling water that big cloud models require from data centres.
When the meeting switches language
Language is where OmniForge stands out. It transcribes audio in 25 languages, including Dutch, English, German, French, Spanish and Polish, and can write summaries and answers in around 200 languages. In other words, a meeting held in Dutch can be summarised in whichever language you read most comfortably.
Then there’s the meeting that starts in English and slides into Dutch. Other tools make you pick a language in advance, Daniel says, whereas OmniForge listens for mid-sentence switches. He admits the transcript does not always get the spoken language right, but because the summary can be generated in any supported language regardless of the input, the gist still comes through.
A typical user, he says, is an international professional in a technical project meeting where half the team defaults to Dutch. Instead of stopping the flow to ask for translations, they record locally, having the assurance that a full English summary will be waiting the moment the meeting ends.
Decoding the paperwork
The same tool works on documents, not just audio. You can drop a Dutch PDF into OmniForge, whether it’s a letter from your landlord or your VvE, a payslip or a notice from the Belastingdienst, then ask questions and get an explanation in English.
Phone calls are covered, too. If you’re talking to the gemeente, put the phone on speaker and record the conversation: even if you feel lost during the call, OmniForge transcribes it so you have a comprehensive summary to review the moment you hang up. “It takes the stress out of local administration,” is how Daniel puts it.
Built for international teams
For employers, the same features make onboarding and internal meetings more inclusive: colleagues who are not fully fluent can follow along through a summary in their preferred language. And because OmniForge records locally, there’s no bot joining your video calls. A project manager juggling several projects can also keep a workspace for each, store meetings and documents together, and ask the assistant for recaps or highlights.
Moreover, local processing represents a win for compliance: HR handles sensitive employee data, and client confidentiality is non-negotiable. Companies are increasingly wary of staff feeding sensitive information to AI chatbots, Daniel explains. “Keeping everything in-house means GDPR compliance by default.” Many cloud tools go to great lengths to get certified, he notes, “but that just means they took steps to secure their customers’ data. With OmniForge, each customer is the sole owner of their data.”
Limitations and next steps
Daniel is upfront about OmniForge’s limits. Because everything runs on your device, transcription speed depends on your hardware: a brand-new machine will get through an hour-long meeting much faster than an older laptop. The assistant is above-average at summaries, highlights and finding information in your documents, “but it cannot compete with the likes of ChatGPT or Claude in terms of raw intelligence,” Daniel concedes, since it has a fraction of the resources.
OmniForge’s next steps will focus on speeding up the models on older hardware and adding more regional dialects. A mobile version is also planned, depending on how many people adopt the app.
Try it on your next confusing letter
The best first step, Daniel says, is to try OmniForge on your next meeting or baffling Dutch letter. Paid tiers start at €9.99 per month for unlimited quotas for individual users. But there’s a generous free tier so you can try before you buy: 40 complimentary minutes per recording and 50 indexed files. All you need to do is download OmniForge for Mac or Windows for free and register.

Five children from same family killed in Russian missile strike laid to rest in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

Five children from same family killed in Russian missile strike laid to rest in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast
Five children from the Voronov family – Dominika, 16, Viorika, 14, Zakharii, 13, Federika, 9, and 18-month-old Artem – have been laid to rest in Radushne, Dnipropetrovsk Oblast. Their lives were cut short on the night of 29-30 July when a Russian missile struck their family home.
Source: Suspilne Dnipro
Details: The children had been considered missing for around two and a half months, but forensic examinations have now confirmed their deaths.
The children's grandmother, Nelia, said all that remained of the house after the strike was the foundation. Throughout this time, she had been praying that all the dead would be identified.
Quote from Nelia: "We didn't know how they would be separated. But now they will all be together as one family there in the cemetery. No miracle was possible. The only thing I asked God for was that they would all be found and identified. There was no one else there, only members of the family – 10 people."
Inna lives near the place where the Voronov family's home once stood. She said she ran outside immediately after the explosion and saw only rubble where the house had been.
Quote from Inna: "The missile hit right in the middle of the house, we were told, in the children's room. We were putting out a fire in the neighbouring house, where two children were trapped under the rubble. When we got them out and went to the [Voronovs'] house, there was no one left to look for… We knew them. All the children were friends with each other. They were good people."
Details: The Voronovs' neighbour Mykola said they had always been a happy, close-knit family.
"In a large family, everyone is like that – they help one another and live as one family. It's hard to comprehend what happened. Such pain," he said.
Dominika's best friend, Karina, also attended the funeral. She said they often spent time together.
Quote from Karina: "[Dominika] was a very kind and sincere person. She really loved beadwork. I even have a pendant from her. She was so wonderful that I just don't have the words. She loved children so much. She was even planning to have a family of her own one day. She wanted two children."
Details: Dominika's classmate Sofiia remembered her as a cheerful, smiling person.
"I didn't know her family, but Dominika was a very cheerful person who was always smiling. I never saw her sad. It is so sad that this happened," Sofiia said.
Ihor Kozachenko, headteacher at the school where Dominika studied, described her as a good friend and an optimistic person who always had a smile on her face.
"She was someone who supported others during difficult times, when some people were in despair. She always had a kind word for others. This is a huge loss for our school. Her family were very close – that is rare these days," he said.
Tetiana Usenko, headteacher at the school attended by Federika, Zakharii and Viorika, said the children's classmates still cannot talk about them without crying.
What is known about the tragedy
On the night of 29-30 July, Russian forces attacked the Kryvyi Rih district. A ballistic missile struck a house in the settlement of Radushne, where the Voronov family lived.
Artem Voronov, 47, and his wife Olena, 41, had 10 children. Seven of them were at home with their parents that night: Mark, 17, Dominika, 16, Viorika, 14, Zakharii, 13, Azarii-Ilai, 11, Federika, 9, and Emiliia, 6.
Their 18-month-old grandson, Artem, was also visiting. He was the son of their eldest son, Danylo, a serviceman based in Mykolaiv. Artem had been due to return home that weekend and had already been enrolled in nursery.
Until the latest forensic findings were released, the deaths of only five family members had been officially confirmed: the parents, Olena and Artem, and three of the children – Mark, Azarii-Ilai and Emiliia.

Russia’s Lavrov to discuss US war and regional security during Tehran visit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
13:22:58 UTC
22:22:58 KST

Russia’s Lavrov discusses US war and regional security during Tehran visit
GCC states have pressed Moscow to help halt Iranian attacks and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
Tehran, Iran – Russia’s Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has met his Iranian counterpart Abbas Araghchi in Tehran, to discuss the war with the United States and efforts to end it.
Lavrov landed in the Iranian capital on Monday afternoon on his first visit to Iran since February 2025. Araghchi said talks with Lavrov had focused on regional developments, including the US-Israeli war on Iran.
He also called out Israel’s “dangerous expansion” in the region, which he blamed for the current hostilities.
“The existing insecurity around the Strait of Hormuz is a direct result of the military aggression by the US and [Israel] against Iran, and it is ongoing in different forms,” he said.
He added that Iran’s policy was to focus on diplomacy, as regional problems have “no military solution”.
“I believe Europe must also open its eyes to some truths,” Araghchi said. “Just like the Americans, the Europeans suffer from miscalculations and wrong interpretations, and have caused many wars and troubles around the world with their wrong policies.”
Meanwhile, Lavrov said Russia is committed to a 20-year strategic partnership agreement with Iran, which officially came into force on October 2. He said Russian specialists would gradually return to the Bushehr nuclear power plant after they left during the war.
The Russian foreign minister also linked restored navigation with protection for Iran against renewed attacks.
Lavrov held a meeting with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian later on Monday. Pezeshkian said that he believes Russia shared “common views and approaches with Iran” when it came to his call for a world based on mutual respect.
Moscow said Lavrov’s trip was part of efforts to ease months of tension, since the US and Israel launched their war on Iran on February 28.
On Sunday, Lavrov was in Bahrain, which was heavily targeted by Iran during the war, to participate in a strategic dialogue session between Russia and the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC).
He was urged by GCC members to use Moscow’s influence with Tehran to press for “serious dialogue” and restore shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, which has been severely disrupted by attacks on commercial vessels.
GCC chief Jasem Al-Budaiwi said member states had faced more than 7,000 Iranian missiles and drones since the start of the war.
In the council’s closing statement, the six Arab countries said they wanted Iran’s nuclear and missile programmes, as well as its support for regional armed groups, to be included in future talks to end the war.
Nikita Smagin, an analyst and researcher on Iran and Russia’s role in the Middle East, said Lavrov’s trip reflects Moscow’s efforts to maintain working relations with all countries in the region.
He said Lavrov also wants to maintain Russia’s status as a mediator, despite the impact of the Ukraine war on its global reputation.
“The timing of visits to the Gulf monarchies and Iran, taking place almost simultaneously, is a deliberate signal: Moscow wants to show that it approaches relations with all these countries on broadly equal terms and is equally interested in cooperation with each of them,” Smagin said.
How does Russia fit in?
Lavrov told GCC ministers in Manama that the region was once again teetering on the brink of a full-scale war and Russia wanted to establish a regional architecture for “collective security”.
He said this could include combining initiatives from countries in the region, along with those put forward by Russia and China, with the aim of restoring maritime traffic and achieving lasting peace. The Russian foreign minister urged other regional states such as Iraq and Jordan, which have also been hit by Iranian strikes, to participate.
Lavrov expressed support for the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) signed between Iran and the US in June, which later collapsed, as a framework for reducing tension.
Iran has said it wants a return to that agreement, and for Washington to honour a finalised bilateral deal between Iran and Oman to manage territorial waters in the Strait of Hormuz. This has been opposed by the US, which has established its own route in the waterway for shipping.
Intelligence reports cited by US media said that Russia and China are providing military support to Iran in the form of satellite imagery for targeting purposes and components for weapons.
But US President Donald Trump contradicted those reports last week, saying Moscow and Beijing would have “too much to lose” if they helped Iran.
Washington has also issued sanctions waivers for Russia in a bid to lower fuel prices driven up by the war against Iran.
Mixed intentions
Russia’s position on the Iran war is somewhat unusual, said Smagin. It has a partial interest in the conflict continuing, as higher oil prices and the severe restrictions on Iranian oil reaching China all benefit Moscow.
“Russia and Iran have been competing primarily for the Chinese market, so China is now effectively forced to buy Russian oil at higher prices because Iranian supplies are largely unavailable,” he said.
Smagin added that Russia does not want the conflict to escalate further, as the consequences could be unpredictable, but its leverage over either Iran or the US to influence the course of the conflict remains limited.
Russia will continue to expand relations with Tehran, Smagin said, including through Caspian Sea trade, and limited military cooperation with Iran.
“These efforts appear to be aimed less at generating economic returns than at expanding Russia’s political influence over Iran and the course of events,” he said.
Military strikes by Iran and the US to wrest control of the waterway have continued, with the US midterm elections approaching on November 3 .
In comments to the media, Trump threatened to “soon finish the job” with Iran, to which Iranian Foreign Minister Araghchi replied: “We have unfinished jobs too.”

LONDON — The British and Polish governments have criticized U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, after he appeared to downplay the role fellow NATO members played in the Afghanistan war.
No.10 Downing Street joined Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski in pushing back at Hegseth, who told an audience at the University of Tennessee over the weekend that few NATO allies were “actually involved in kinetic operations.”
“I was a captain in Afghanistan and we would go to the headquarters in Kabul and there would be 50 flags at the headquarters,” Hegseth recalled. “It was a beautiful thing to see, 50 different countries contributing to the NATO alliance and the ISAF [International Security Assistance Force] mission there.”
Advertisement
But he added: “Except there were maybe five that contributed. It was actually closer to one or two that by the end were actually involved in kinetic operations. In fact the patch ISAF, we joked it meant ‘I Saw Americans Fighting’.”
All of NATO’s then-28 members participated in the U.S.-led war in Afghanistan, after the alliance invoked Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty – NATO’s collective defense clause – on September 12, 2001, a day after the terrorist attacks that took place on 9/11.
It remains the only time the article has been invoked in alliance history.
Asked about his comments Monday, U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s official spokesperson pointed out that “thousands of British and allied families made huge sacrifices to play their significant part in that war and uphold our values,” while “more than 450 British personnel never returned.”
“Their sacrifice and that of other NATO forces was made in the service of collective security and in response to an attack on our ally,” he continued.
“We are incredibly proud of our armed forces, and their service and sacrifice will never be forgotten. And it is wrong to diminish their role.”
Advertisement
Sikorski said in a social media post Sunday that Hegseth should repeat his comments “to the families of 44 Polish soldiers who died who died securing the tough Ghazni province.”
It’s not the first time fellow NATO members’ contribution to the Afghanistan war has been question by the U.S. government.
U.S. President Donald Trump triggered anger in London in January after he said non-American forces “stayed a little back, a little off the front lines” during the war.

Investment in the project totals 1.2 billion yuan, or more than $178 million. The industrial site covers an area of 100,000 square meters. The plant will process food waste into eco-friendly aviation fuel.
The project has received 1.2 billion yuan in investment, which is more than $178 million. The industrial site covers 100,000 square meters. The plant will convert food waste into environmentally friendly aviation fuel.
The article noted that construction is on schedule. Builders have successfully finished laying underground pipelines and constructing key infrastructure and have started finishing buildings and installing equipment. By the end of this year, it is expected that the facility will conduct a pre-startup safety inspection and prepare for the equipment's trial operation.
According to Hainan Ribao, Zhang Zhilong, deputy general manager of the Eco Prime holding company, which is based in Chongqing in southwestern China, stated that the Hainan plant is equipped with units that produce 2,000 normal cubic meters of hydrogen per hour from light hydrocarbons. The facility features a sulfur recovery unit, specialized storage tanks, and loading and unloading facilities. Once operational, the plant will reduce carbon dioxide emissions by more than 400,000 metric tons per year.
A growing number of mainland Chinese companies that focus on foreign markets are establishing production facilities in Hainan. According to the newspaper, they are attracted by the free trade port's preferential terms and advantages, which allow for the expedited shipment of goods to other countries. Yangpu Port is connected by sea routes to Southeast Asia, the Middle East, Oceania, and North and South America. Biofuel produced in China’s southernmost province and certified in accordance with advanced international standards is expected to be shipped directly to Europe and other regions.
