A week in Budapest dedicated to Bulgaria and Bulgarian-Hungarian friendship
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
13:15:26 UTC
22:15:26 KST

Author
Krasimir Martinov
News
A week in Budapest dedicated to Bulgaria and Bulgarian-Hungarian friendship
Monday 19 October 2026 14:10
Monday, 19 October 2026, 14:10
The Hungarian Parliament Building
PHOTO BTA
Font size
The Day of Bulgarian-Hungarian Friendship, the 21st World Meeting of Bulgarian Media, and two anniversaries of Bulgarian cultural organisations make October a month of remembrance, continuity and spiritual ties between Bulgaria and Hungary.
On October 19, when the Bulgarian Orthodox Church honours St. John of Rila, Bulgaria and Hungary celebrate Bulgarian-Hungarian Friendship Day. In 2026, the occasion carries special significance, marking ten years since the date was officially designated as a day of friendship between the two countries. The date connects contemporary relations with a shared historical heritage and the memory of the saint whose relics were taken to Esztergom in the 12th century.
The connection between St. John of Rila and Hungary is part of the historical memory underpinning the celebration. In 1183, during a military campaign through Bulgarian lands, King Béla III of Hungary had the saint’s relics transferred to Esztergom. The relics were later returned to Bulgaria, but the memory of this historical event remains a symbol of the spiritual closeness between the two peoples.
Esztergom remains one of the places where this connection is commemorated. By tradition, the feast of St. John of Rila and Bulgarian-Hungarian Friendship Day are marked at the city’s basilica, where a bilingual memorial plaque dedicated to the saint was unveiled on October 19, 2016.
The commemorative plaque dedicated to St John of Rila at Esztergom Basilica
PHOTO BTA
The 21st World Meeting of Bulgarian Media officially opens today in Budapest, the capital of Hungary. The forum is organised and hosted by the Bulgarian News Agency (BTA).
This year’s edition is mottoed “Media and Leaders”. The event, which will take place in Budapest and Esztergom, is expected to bring together participants from 25 countries, including Bulgaria, both in person and online.
The Bulgarian National Radio is represented by its Director General, Milen Mitev.
21st World Meeting of Bulgarian Media
PHOTO BTA
Today’s programme includes a visit to the Hungarian Parliament and a meeting with MP Márton Hajdu, Chair of the Foreign Policy Committee. At 11:30 a.m., an exhibition dedicated to Bulgarian-Hungarian Friendship Day will open at the Barankovics office building. Bulgaria’s Ambassador to Hungary, Maria Anguelieva, and Simeon Varga, the representative of the Bulgarian community in the Hungarian Parliament, will deliver welcome addresses, the Bulgarian News Agency (BTA) reported.
The 21st World Meeting of Bulgarian Media will begin at 2 p.m. with a wreath-laying ceremony at the memorial plaque dedicated to St. John of Rila at the Cathedral of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary and St. Adalbert, and a prayer service led by Metropolitan Anthony of Western and Central Europe and Father Csaba, the episcopal delegate for the Esztergom Basilica.
The official opening of the 21st World Meeting of Bulgarian Media will take place at 6:30 p.m. at the Bulgarian Cultural Institute in Budapest.
The building of the Bulgarian School and Kindergarten in Budapest
PHOTO Bulgarian School and Kindergarten-Budapest
Behind the official celebrations of Bulgarian-Hungarian Friendship Day, diplomatic meetings and media forums, however, is a community that has kept the Bulgarian language, traditions and cultural memory alive in Hungary for decades. Its cultural life is sustained through schools, theatre, dance ensembles, music and Bulgarian-language publications. These organizations are not isolated from one another but form an interconnected cultural environment where generations come together and pass on their knowledge, skills and sense of identity.
“Bulgarians here are a very close-knit community. We are not just a school, a theatre or a dance ensemble operating separately”, Vanya Kotorova, principal of the Bulgarian School and Kindergarten-Budapest, told Radio Bulgaria.
This is in fact one of the most distinctive features of Bulgarian cultural life in Hungary. Children who study Bulgarian often participate in dance ensembles as well. The school organizes workshops with theatre professionals, while festivals and concerts become shared events for the entire community.
Vanya Kotorova
PHOTO Personal archive of Vanya Kotorova
“We are a small community, yet our cultural life is exceptionally rich”, says Vanya Kotorova, adding that October is a particularly eventful monthfor Bulgarians in Hungary, marked by several important cultural anniversaries.
Jantra-Bulgarian Folkdance Group and The Rositsa Folk Dance Ensemble are among the most iconic representatives of Bulgarian cultural life in Budapest.
On 23 October, Jantra-Bulgarian Folkdance Group will celebrate its 30th anniversary with the music and dance performance JANTRA 30 at the Vígszínház Theatre. The show will feature both dance ensembles, the Pravo and Slavia orchestras, and performers showcasing the richness of Bulgarian folk music and dance.
The Malko Teatro theatre company is also marking 30 years of cultural activity. Founded in 1996, it has established itself over the years as a space where theatre, music, movement and contemporary forms of stage expression come together.
Meanwhile, Hemus magazine continues to showcase Bulgarian literature, art, history and public life, creating opportunities for cultural exchange between Bulgarian and Hungarian authors and readers. The magazine’s 35th anniversary will be marked on 21 October with the opening of Danube-Bridges, an exhibition by photographer Péter Gyukics.
On 23 October, Hungary marks the 70th anniversary of the beginning of the student uprising against Soviet rule. On that day in 1956, a peaceful student demonstration began in Budapest and quickly grew into a mass protest involving more than 200,000 people. The demonstrators called for the withdrawal of Soviet troops, democratic reforms and freedom of speech.

HARARE, October 19. /TASS/. The number of confirmed Ebola deaths in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has exceeded 4,500 since May, with move than 9,400 cases registered in total, the country’s Ministry of Public Health, Hygiene and Social Welfare said.
"Since the beginning of the epidemic in the DRC, a total of 9,455 confirmed cases and 4,561 deaths have been recorded, with the fatality rate standing at 48.2%," the ministry said in its bulletin. It noted that the epicenter "remains Ituri Province, which accounts for 73.2% of all cases and 67.5% of new cases." The epidemic has spread to 66 of the DRC’s 178 health zones across eight provinces. A total of 269 healthcare workers have contracted Ebola.
The current Ebola outbreak began on May 15 in the DRC and Uganda. Ugandan authorities announced on July 28 that the outbreak in the country had ended. The World Health Organization confirmed this on August 25. In neighboring Kenya, the first case of Ebola was confirmed on October 6. The patient was a Kenyan national who had previously lived in the DRC. He arrived in Nairobi via Uganda on October 3 and died on October 5. As of October 19, a total of eight cases had been detected in Kenya.

European telecom companies explore joint satellite bid, pottentially rivaling Starlink
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
13:14:57 UTC
22:14:57 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
19 October 2026•Update: 19 October 2026
Four major European telecommunications companies said Monday they were exploring a joint bid for mobile satellite spectrum to expand connectivity across Europe.
Deutsche Telekom, Orange, Telefonica and Vodafone signed a letter of intent to assess a potential joint bid for the future allocation of mobile satellite services spectrum in Europe, the companies said.
The initiative could provide a European alternative to satellite connectivity services offered by competitors such as Elon Musk's Starlink.
The companies said the project aimed to expand direct-to-device connectivity by integrating satellite services with existing mobile networks and extending coverage to underserved areas.
Under the proposed model, all mobile network operators would receive open and non-discriminatory access, an approach intended to encourage competition and broaden consumer choice.
The four operators would establish ground network infrastructure and critical coordination and monitoring functions in Europe without investing directly in a satellite constellation.
A satellite partner, which has yet to be selected, would provide the constellation, according to the companies.
They said combining their customer reach, network capabilities and technical expertise could accelerate deployment and improve spectrum efficiency.
The initiative also aims to strengthen public network resilience, protect critical communications and support the development of a European satellite constellation.
The companies said the project aligned with the European Commission's ambition to strengthen Europe's sovereignty, security and resilience in critical connectivity infrastructure.
Although the announcement did not explicitly name Starlink, the proposed initiative emphasizes European governance and space infrastructure.
The companies added that the letter of intent would not replace their existing satellite partnerships.

Kyiv faces growing risk of a water crisis this winter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
13:13:55 UTC
22:13:55 KST

'Extremely unpleasant experience' — Why Kyiv faces growing risk of sewage crisis this winter
A man fishes from the shore of the Dnipro River as smoke rises over a residential area following Russian strikes in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Sept. 8, 2026. (Viktor Fridshon / Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images)
As regular Russian strikes on energy facilities leave parts of Kyiv without running water, fears are mounting that further power outages could spark a serious humanitarian and public health crisis in a city whose water and sewage system depends entirely on electricity.
Kyiv’s water system is one of the city’s biggest power consumers, requiring huge amounts of electricity to draw water from the Dnipro river and pump around 700 million liters of clean water daily to households and businesses.
It is also extremely reliant on the central energy grid, making it vulnerable to Russia’s bombing campaign targeting energy facilities.
While some residents have stockpiles of clean water in their homes, water industry experts warn that the main threat comes from the failure of the wastewater system, which needs electricity to transport sewage to wastewater plants.
If left untreated, sewage could flood the city and pose a serious health and environmental hazard.
"Transporting and treating wastewater is a major challenge for utility companies. Equipment is aging, and a lack of electricity for pumping can have serious consequences," Oleksandr Skhin, director of Ukraine’s Association of Water Utilities, told the Kyiv Independent.
Vulnerabilities
While Ukraine’s government has said the country is well prepared for the winter, Kyiv’s residents are growing increasingly skeptical, particularly after Moscow launched one its biggest ever attacks on the capital’s substations on Oct. 14, leaving many households without water and power.
read also
As the Kyiv Independent previously reported, the capital has not prepared sufficiently for the heating season, leaving the city without enough backup power generation. Consequently, recent attacks have not only caused emergency blackouts in the city, but forced the capital to return to scheduled power outages, which haven’t been imposed since the spring.
With the constant voltage fluctuations, Kyiv’s aged electric water utility system simply "burns out," Serhii Horkutsenko, deputy head of Kyivvodokanal, the capital's state-owned water supply company, told Ukrainian media Ekonomichna Pravda in an interview published on Oct. 12.
Moreover, Russia has increased the intensity of its attacks on Ukraine’s energy system fivefold since 2024, Olena Pavlenko, head of the Kyiv-based energy think tank Dixi Group, told the Kyiv Independent. As a result, Kyiv’s energy system is in a more critical state than in previous years, while Russia continues to escalate attacks and deploy new tactics.
A weaker, worn-out energy grid also puts the water system at greater risk because it makes it harder to meet the electricity demands of pumping stations, Oleksii Andriiashchenko, sales manager at Grundfos Ukraine, a major water pump producer, told the Kyiv Independent.
He expects that parts of Kyiv will be left without electricity and water for weeks this winter. In the worst-case scenario, the water system could collapse, leading to overflowing sewage tanks that flood the city.
At the same time, Russia has also directly targeted Kyiv’s only sewage plant — the Bortnychi plant — with drones and missiles on several occasions, Mykhailo Yatsuk, director of the Institute of Water Problems and Land Reclamation, told the Kyiv Independent.
"The destruction of the Bortnychi plant poses the greatest threat. Furthermore, there is a risk of damage to sewage pumping stations. This could create problems for the integrated system and cause significant environmental damage," Yatsuk said.
Preparations
According to Yatsuk, Kyiv’s authorities are much better prepared than previous years and have emergency plans for different scenarios, despite the public perception that the city is not ready.
Authorities have also stockpiled equipment and materials needed to repair damaged water infrastructure, he added.
Ahead of the winter, Kyivvodokanal is already operating 103 generators across its network and is expecting the delivery of more high-capacity generator systems currently being manufactured abroad, Kyiv’s mayor Vitalii Klitschko said on Oct.13. But generators cannot replace the main energy grid, nor can they work continuously, Klitschko said.
What's more, generators can only power smaller pumping stations, not larger, more critical ones, said Andriiashchenko. And Kyiv still needs to construct new high-capacity power generation facilities, like co-generation plants, to fully back up the main water system, Petro Panteleev, first deputy head of the Kyiv City State Administration, said in a public statement.
At the same time, Horkutsenko said that Kyivvodokanal is struggling with staffing and funding shortages. One person is doing the work of four, he stressed. Nonetheless, he promised that the agency would deliver drinking water to residents by truck during severe outages.
But even then, trucking in water deliveries won’t be enough to cover the city’s sanitation and hygiene needs, since the average household consumes 100 liters of water per person per day, according to Skhin.
The lack of water for hygiene and cleaning has been a problem for several Ukrainian cities throughout the war, said Skhin. In Chernihiv, the director of the local water utility could only distribute enough water for drinking to residents from his tractor during a monthlong outage at the start of the full-scale war, he said.
"People had to find their own ways to meet sanitation and hygiene needs, including collecting water from rivers or melting snow," Skhin said.
"It was an extremely unpleasant experience."

A Russian military satellite came critically close to a U.S.-Finnish satellite that may transmit data to Ukraine — media

"Kosmos-2612" reduced the distance to ICEYE-X36 to 26 meters. An expert called the approach critical and warned of rising risks.
The Russian military satellite "Kosmos-2612" approached a critical distance from the US-Finnish ICEYE-X36 satellite operated by ICEYE, which may transmit data to Ukraine, UNN reports, citing Russian media.
Details
According to Russian media, space popularizer Georgy Trishkin said that the distance between the satellites had decreased to 26 meters. According to him, any approach of satellites to within less than a kilometer is considered critical.
The commercial ICEYE-X36 radar satellite can obtain images of the Earth's surface. The data is used for reconnaissance, in particular as part of ICEYE's cooperation with Ukraine.
Trishkin told The Insider that it was impossible to say for certain whether ICEYE-X36 was supplying intelligence data to Ukraine, "but it could quite possibly be used even for that."
According to him, a direct attack on ICEYE-X36 would constitute an attack on the property of the US Department of Defense. He stressed that an accidental collision was "unlikely, since both spacecraft are controlled," but added that "the risks are increasing."

France's leaders vow to restore order after weekend of violent riots across the country
Paris — French officials were considering declaring a state of emergency and implementing local curfews Monday as the nation reeled from a weekend of violence. Widespread anti-government protests in many large cities descended into riots, with damage to historic properties and thousands of arrests.
In hard-hit Marseille, France's second-largest city, all large gatherings were banned Monday in the wake of the violence, which started weeks ago as protests by young people furious over the state of their schools, but quickly snowballed into national demonstrations over the rising cost of living and declining public services.
The 19th-century town hall in the city of Limoges was burned to the ground on Saturday by masked rioters who hijacked marches across France, looting stores, torching cars and buildings and clashing with police as the protests turned violent.
More than 2,500 people have been arrested, France's Justice Ministry said.
The U.S. State Department issued an advisory Monday urging Americans to "avoid the areas of the demonstrations."
In an address Sunday evening, French President Emmanuel Macron, vowed that "those who sought to bring down the republic will be held accountable."
Speaking Monday, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu blamed at least some of the violence on "an ultra-left movement intent on orchestrating profound disorder in the country leading up to the presidential election" in April.
He said police "had lost control" during the unrest, and as the Yellow Vests protest movement, which organized the weekend rallies that turned violent, called for a new round of demonstrations on Saturday, he called for regional authorities to impose "partial" and "localized" curfews to protect businesses.
"I'm absolutely determined to restore public order," Lecornu said, adding that the government was ready to impose a national state of emergency, "if needed."
Speaking of the alleged agitators, Lecornu said there was "an entire network that could be mobilized to challenge the presidential election schedule and the very holding of the presidential election," adding that the government was committed to protecting the country's democratic process.
"There is no way we will allow violent minorities to impose an agenda of violence and, quite obviously, prevent us from holding this election," he said, acknowledging that the protests by high school students over classroom conditions were legitimate, but adding that "the freedom to demonstrate is being undermined."
While French officials have not suggested any link between the unrest and immigration, President Trump claimed one in a brief social media post on Monday, saying: "The migrants have taken over France. They must CLOSE THE BORDERS, FAST!"
Damage to landmarks
Capital city Paris has seen the worst of the unrest, and residents woke up Monday to streets littered with debris and burned vehicles. But severe damage was inflicted across the country, with centuries of heritage being damaged or destroyed by flames.
Video captured the moment the clock tower of Limoges' historic town hall, in southwest France — a landmark that had stood for nearly 150 years, surviving both World Wars — was engulfed in flames and came toppling down.
The tourist office in the eastern city of Lyon stood for years in one of France's most famous, beautiful city squares. But vandals, many of them masked, rampaged around the building and set it on fire, too.
The city hall in Marseille, on the Mediterranean coast, which dates back to the 1600s, was also stormed and vandalized with graffiti.
On Monday, hundreds of protesters gathered outside Paris' iconic Louvre Museum in support of the school students who initiated the demonstrations more than a month ago.
What protesters say they want
The protests began as demonstrations by high school students about a month ago, with thousands taking to the streets peacefully to vent frustration over crumbling schools, overpacked classes and teacher shortages.
But it grew into a nationwide outpouring of anger over the soaring cost of living — salaries that aren't keeping up with inflation, and crumbling public services.
More than 500,000 people took to the streets on Saturday, when the unrest peaked. But as the government alludes to, there have also been opportunists — people and groups looting, vandalizing and attacking police as they try to control the crowds.
"There are so many reasons," Kamil Alahyan, 18, told French news agency AFP. "The politicians who lie, the ultra-rich who've been raking in more and more wealth over the last 10 years … everyone has a different reason."
Anae, a 24-year-old student in Grenoble, told AFP she had completed her studies but now has "no income. I've got no money. I don't necessarily have a secure future. Our planet is burning. And we've got a government that's making a joke out of us!"

His visit comes after Russian President Vladimir Putin told Pezeshkian in early October that Moscow was prepared to contribute to mediation efforts.
Russia and Iran, two of the most heavily sanctioned nations in the world, maintain close ties. Their military and economic cooperation has only increased since the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
In January 2025, Pezeshkian and Putin signed a 20-year strategic partnership treaty in Moscow, covering cooperation in defense, security, energy, trade and transportation.
The agreement also provides for closer coordination on regional and international issues, although it does not establish a mutual defense obligation.
The Middle East war began in February with U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran. Despite a ceasefire in April, followed by a U.S.-Iran memorandum of understanding in June, hostilities in and around the Strait of Hormuz have not stopped.
Iran claims control over the strategic waterway — through which one-fifth of the world’s hydrocarbons pass in normal times — and regularly targets vessels that cross without its authorisation.
In response, Washington has been maintaining a naval counter-blockade on Iranian ports.
The Russian Foreign Ministry said discussions during Lavrov’s visit were expected to focus on “ways to resolve the acute international crisis triggered by the unlawful aggression of the US and Israel against Iran.”
The ministry said the war had been a blow to stability and security “not only in the near and Middle East, but also on a global scale.”
Iran-backed Houthis have declared a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia and captured territory around the Bab al-Mandab strait, the Red Sea chokepoint and vital export route for Saudi oil since Iran blockaded the Gulf’s Strait of Hormuz.
The hostilities were the focus of a meeting on Oct. 18 between the Russian and Saudi foreign ministers on the sidelines of a summit between Gulf states and Russia in Bahrain’s Manama.
They discussed “regional developments, particularly the escalation in Yemen, as well as the persistent threats to shipping in the Straits of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab”, the Saudi Foreign Ministry said on X.
The Houthis have hit Saudi targets including tankers in the Red Sea, oil facilities and Riyadh’s King Khalid International airport.
A Houthi projectile injured at least six people in southern Saudi Arabia on Oct. 18 after it struck a residential area in Najran near the border with Yemen, according to the kingdom’s civil defence agency.
The Saudi-led coalition also said two ballistic missiles were intercepted in the kingdom’s south. Threat alerts for Najran city and As Sulayyil governorate in Riyadh province were issued but quickly cancelled on Oct. 18.

German economy lost 420 bln euro of investments due to crises — research
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
13:11:33 UTC
22:11:33 KST

BERLIN, October 19. /TASS/. The German economy has lost around 420 billion euros in investments since 2020 due to the implications of the coronavirus pandemic and geopolitical crises, the German Economic Institute (IW) said in its research.
According to experts, German businesses invested approximately 470 billion euros less than projected on the basis of historical trends during the reporting period. This decline is equivalent to nearly 12% of the total volume of private investment since 2020. At the same time, Germany's public investments grew by 50 billion euros. The net losses of the investment sector taken together and adjusted for price increases are estimated at 420 billion euros, the institute said.
The research indicates that private investment in Germany will not be able to return to pre-crisis levels until at least the end of 2026. This figure remained more than 10% below the 2019 annual average in the second quarter of the current year. The public sector shows the opposite trend, with public investment volumes exceeding 2019 figures by 20%. Such growth has been driven by the creation of a special infrastructure development fund and the temporary exemption of defense spending from the so-called "debt brake" (a rule that limits the size of the German federal budget deficit), the institute noted.
Public appropriations cannot fully replace private capital to guarantee long-term economic growth, the institute said in its research. Berlin's steps to attract investors as part of the ongoing Invest in Germany summit are viewed positively but experts call them insufficient. According to analysts, the country primarily needs more attractive conditions for doing business. The authors of the study cite deteriorating framework conditions, such as high electricity costs, significant labor expenses, and excessive bureaucracy, as the main factors deterring companies from Germany.
The institute compared the dynamics of Germany's gross fixed capital formation from the first quarter of 2020 to the second quarter of 2026 with a hypothetical baseline scenario that excluded the pandemic and geopolitical shocks, the institute said. Germany's macroeconomic indicators for the period from 1991 to 2019 served as the basis for the calculation.

Morality, social responsibility among Rasul Medal criteria
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
13:09:31 UTC
22:09:31 KST

The head of the Life and Medical Science and Technology judging committee of the Rasoul(pbuh) Medal Gholamreza Hassanzadeh told local Iranian that the laureates are expected to possess strong moral and social qualities in addition to scientific achievements, emphasizing that a person who is not deeply concerned about their society and humanity at large is not fit to be selected for the Medal.
MSTF Media reports:
In an interview with the Mustafa Science and Technology Foundation (MSTF) media, Hassanzadeh elaborated on the judging process for Rasul Medal nominees. The initial evaluation covered 65,000 nominees and was conducted through in-person and online meetings with university professors of medical sciences.
The initial screening, carried out over 16 sessions, narrowed the pool to 20,000 nominees. A final committee meeting was then held to conduct a thorough assessment, resulting in the final shortlist.
“Every indicator was taken into account when evaluating these scientists in terms of qualitative and quantitative criteria,” Hassanzadeh added.
Asked whether the selection criteria were based on a scientist’s overall achievements or on a specific achievement or research publication, he explained, “The winners of the Rasul Medal, unlike the Mustafa(pbuh) Prize, are not selected based on a single outstanding achievement.
“These scientists are under 40 years old and have only recently begun their research careers. Our criterion was therefore more focused on the quality and significance of their achievements. For example, even if a paper they had published had not received many citations, it could still be considered a significant achievement if it had helped solve a problem facing a society.”
Regarding the most important criteria for selecting the final list of laureates, he stated, "Various quantitative and qualitative indicators, such as the H-index, were more relevant in the initial screening. In the later stages, we examined the original articles and the work that individuals had done, as well as patents.”
Hassanzadeh highlighted the importance of the tangible social impact of scientific achievements in selecting candidates for the Rasul Medal. “One of the essential characteristics of universities is social accountability, and every scientist must be accountable to their society and humanity as a whole. Therefore, we carefully considered criteria such as social accountability and individual impact. Every scientific work has inputs and outputs, but the most important question is how much impact it has on society and the extent to which it can help solve societal problems.”
The professor at the Faculty of Medical Sciences at the University of Tehran also discussed the total number of nominations received by the Rasul Medal secretariat. “Many eligible candidates were nominated, and the initial screening proceeded smoothly. Our colleagues at the Mustafa Foundation also provided considerable assistance by supplying accurate information and relevant indicators.”
Asked about the broader message that the final selection conveys to society, Hassanzadeh said, “A person selected as a young scientist for the Rasul Medal must possess strong moral, scientific, and social qualities. Scientific achievements are not the only criteria. A person who is not concerned about their own society and humanity as a whole cannot be considered for the Medal. Various aspects must be taken into account. When selecting candidates for an award named after the Holy Prophet of Islam, their morals and character are also important, and we sought to take these into consideration.”
He emphasized: “Our approach to selecting candidates was not inward-looking; rather, we sought to select everyone who was genuinely deserving. Anyone who met these criteria and passed the initial screening was also considered in the subsequent stages. Our working group did not adopt an exclusively national or international perspective.”
Rasul Medal
Upon the release of the call for nominations for the Rasul Medal, scientific institutions were able to nominate their candidates by January 20, 2026.
The Rasul Medal was founded based on the endowments made by Mustafa Prize laureates, Ugur Sahin, Omid Farrokhzad, and Vahab Mirrokni. It is awarded to scientists under the age of 40 residing in Islamic countries. The inaugural edition of the Medal, called the Young Scientist Medal, was held alongside the 6th Mustafa Prize in 2025.
The Medal is awarded to impactful works in the fields of Life and Medical Science and Technology, Basic and Engineering Sciences, and Computer Science by young scientists from Islamic countries. The candidates must be nominated by a third-party scientific or technological body, such as universities and research centers, reputable scientific and technological associations and institutions, academies of sciences, or science and technology parks.
The candidates for the Rasul Medal must be under 40 years old at the end of the year in which the medal is awarded. This means that candidates for the 2026 Young Scientist Medal must be born in 1987 or later. The winners are bestowed a medal, a certificate, and a $10,000 cash prize in each category.
Established as a symbol of excellence and scientific merit of the young generation of scientific talent, the Rasul Medal promotes scientific and technological breakthroughs by young scientists in the Islamic world and recognizes their influential achievements.

Alaska’s monster tsunami sent water 1,580 feet up a mountain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
13:09:18 UTC
22:09:18 KST

Alaska’s monster tsunami sent water 1,580 feet up a mountain
- Date:
- October 19, 2026
- Source:
- The Conversation
- Summary:
- A massive landslide in Alaska triggered the second-highest tsunami ever recorded, sending water and debris 1,580 feet up a mountainside just hours after tourists visited the area. Scientists discovered that the disaster was preceded by several warning signs, including rapid glacier retreat, heavy rainfall, and thousands of tiny seismic tremors. As glaciers retreat, similar disasters could become a growing danger in mountainous coastal regions.
- Share:
On the evening of Aug. 9, 2025, passengers on the Hanse Explorer finished taking selfies and videos of the South Sawyer Glacier, and the ship headed back down the fjord. Twelve hours later, a landslide from the adjacent mountain unexpectedly collapsed into the fjord, initiating the second-highest tsunami in recorded history.
We conduct research on earthquakes and tsunamis at the Alaska Earthquake Center, and one of us serves as Alaska state seismologist. In a new study with colleagues, we detail how that landslide sent water and debris 1,580 feet (481 meters) up the other side of the fjord – higher than the top floor of the Taipei 101 skyscraper – and then continued down Tracy Arm. The force of the water stripped the fjord’s walls down to bare rock.
It was just after 5 o’clock in the morning on a dreary day, and fortunately, no ships were nearby. In the months after, some cruise lines started avoiding Tracy Arm. However, the conditions that led to this event are not at all unique to this fjord.
Landslides are common in the coastal mountains of Alaska where rapid uplift, caused by tectonic forces and long-term ice loss, converges with the erosive forces of precipitation and moving glaciers. But a curious pattern has emerged in recent years: Multiple major landslides have occurred precisely at the terminus of a retreating glacier.
Though the mechanics are still poorly understood, these mountains appear to become unstable when the ice disappears. When the landslide hits the water, the momentum of millions of tons of rock is transferred into tsunami waves.
This same phenomenon is playing out from Alaska to Greenland and Norway, sometimes with deadly consequences. Across the Arctic, countries are trying to come to terms with this growing hazard. The options are not attractive: avoid vast swaths of coastline, or live with a poorly understood risk. We believe there is an obvious role for alert systems, but only if scientists have a better understanding of where and when landslides are likely to occur.
Signs that a landslide might be coming
The Tracy Arm landslide is a powerful example.
The landslide occurred in August, when warm ocean waters and heavier precipitation favor both glacier retreat and slope failure. The glacier below the landslide area had experienced rapid calving – large chunks of ice breaking off and falling into the water – and it had retreated more than a third of a mile in the two months prior. Heavy rain had been falling. Rain enters fractures in the mountain and pushes them closer to failure by increasing the water pressure in cracks.
Most provocative are the thousands of small seismic tremors that emanated from the area of the slide in the days prior to the mountainside collapsing.
We believe that this combination of signs would have been sufficient to issue progressive alerts to any ships in the vicinity and homes and businesses that could have been harmed by a tsunami at least a day prior to the failure – had a monitoring program existed.
Escalating alerts are used for everything from terrorism and nuclear plant safety to avalanches and volcanic unrest. They don’t remove the risk, but they do make it easier for people to safely coexist with hazards.
For example, though people are still killed in avalanches, alert systems have played an essential role in making winter backcountry travel safer for more people. The collapse at Tracy Arm demonstrates what could be possible for landslides.
What an alert system could look like
We believe that the combination of weather and rapid glacier retreat in early August 2025 was likely sufficient to issue an alert notifying people that the hazard may be temporarily elevated in a general area. On a yellow-orange-red scale, this would be a yellow alert.
In the hours prior to the landslide, the exponential increase in seismic events and telltale transition to what is known as seismic tremor – a continuous “hum” of seismic energy – were sufficient to communicate a time-sensitive warning for a specific region.
These observations, recorded as a byproduct of regional earthquake monitoring, warranted an “orange” alert noting immediate concern. The signs were arguably sufficient to recommend keeping boats and ships out of the fjord.
Our research over the past few years has demonstrated that once a large landslide has started, it is possible to detect and measure the event within a couple of minutes. In this amount of time, seismic waves in the surrounding area can indicate the rough size of the landslide and whether it occurred near open water.
A monitoring program that could quickly communicate this would be able to issue a red alert, signaling an event in progress.
The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s tsunami warning program has spent decades fine-tuning rapid message dissemination. A warning system would have offered little help for ships in the immediate vicinity, but it could have provided perhaps 10 minutes of warning for those who rode out the harrowing tsunami farther away.
There is no landslide monitoring system operating yet at this scale in the U.S. Building one will require cooperation across state and federal agencies, and strengthened monitoring and communication networks. Even then, it will not be fail-proof.
Understanding risk, not removing it
Alert systems do not remove the risk entirely, but they are a better option than no warning at all. Over time, they also build awareness as communities and visitors get used to thinking about these hazards.
Many of the most alluring places on Earth come with significant hazards. Arctic fjords are among them. The same processes that create this hazard – glacier retreat, steep terrain, dynamic geology – are also what make these landscapes so compelling. The mix of glaciers, ice-choked waters and steep mountains is exactly what draws people to these places. People will continue to visit and experience them.
The question is not whether these places should be avoided altogether, but how to help people make more informed decisions. We believe that stronger geophysical and meteorological monitoring, coupled with new research and communication channels, is the first step.
On Aug. 9, visitors unknowingly passed through a landscape on the cusp of failure. An alert system might have given tour companies and people in the area the information they needed to make more informed choices and avoid being caught by surprise.
Story Source:
Materials provided by The Conversation. Original written by Michael E. West and Ezgi Karasözen. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

EU plans March summit in Rome as Italy eyes early election

The EU is preparing to hold its March 2027 summit in Rome to mark the 70th anniversary of the Treaties of Rome, subject to unanimous approval, as Italy faces the prospect of an early spring election.
Preparations are under way to hold a European Council summit in Rome in March 2027 to mark the 70th anniversary of the Treaties of Rome, amid speculation over an early election in Italy.
It would be the first time an anniversary celebration has been combined with a formal European Council summit held outside Brussels.
EU leaders’ summits are normally held in Brussels. In exceptional circumstances, European Council President António Costa can propose another venue, provided all member states agree unanimously.
“President Costa has put forward the idea to organise a formal European Council in Rome in the context of the 70th anniversary of the Rome Treaty. Preparations are ongoing,” an EU official told Euronews, speaking on condition of anonymity.
The move was first reported by Italian daily La Stampa, which said the summit would give Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni a major international platform shortly before the next general election.
Signed on 25 March 1957, the Treaties of Rome established the European Economic Community and the European Atomic Energy Community, laying the foundations for today’s EU.
Italy’s next general election is due by the end of 2027, but an early vote in spring is being openly discussed, with April and May the most frequently cited dates.
The Italian government has welcomed the move.
Costa raised the proposal with Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever during a tour of EU capitals in September, specifically approaching Belgium because Brussels is the usual host of the summits.
De Wever said he would not oppose the one-off exception, an official told Euronews, speaking on condition of anonymity.
Costa’s current term as European Council president expires on 31 May 2027. He is expected to seek a second two-and-a-half-year term, as his predecessors have done. Reappointment requires the backing of a qualified majority of member states.
The change of venue still requires approval from all member states, at ambassadorial or ministerial level. The issue is expected to be discussed in the coming weeks.

Source: Vadym Filashkin, Head of Donetsk Oblast Military Administration, on social media
Details: Filashkin signed the relevant order on 19 October.
In the Oleksandrivka and Cherkaske hromadas, the curfew remains unchanged for now, lasting from 21:00 to 05:00.
Filashkin explained that the decision has been dictated by the security situation. Russian forces are intensifying their attacks on settlements in the oblast, and the risks to civilians are constantly growing.
Quote from Filashkin: "I am asking everyone to take the new restrictions responsibly, plan their movements in advance, and comply with the requirements of military administrations and law enforcement officers.
And I would like to emphasise once again: there have been no safe places in Donetsk Oblast for a long time. I urge people, especially families with children, not to wait for the next attack and to evacuate to safer regions of Ukraine."

Mass killing, when perpetrated by favored allies, becomes foreign policy.
Jeffrey Epstein is a scandal. Benjamin Netanyahu is celebrated. One association invites repudiation; the other earns presidential endorsement. Behold the moral double standard of empire: depravity is condemned when it embarrasses power and defended when it serves it.
Trump’s association with Epstein has become politically radioactive, prompting Republican loyalists to minimize its significance and discourage scrutiny. Yet the same political establishment applauds his endorsement of a leader presiding over Gaza’s devastation, starvation, and mass killing. Netanyahu, subject to International Criminal Court arrest warrants for war crimes and crimes against humanity, is praised as a great warrior and partner for peace.
But the deeper obscenity lies in the racialized mythology surrounding Western civilization itself. Trafficking, sexual exploitation, and predatory depravity have long been depicted as pathologies of the Orient, the Global South, and supposedly backward societies against which the West defines its virtue.
Trump has exploited precisely this vocabulary, portraying Mexico and the darker world beyond America’s borders as exporters of criminality and sexual menace. Epstein punctures that fantasy. His machinery of sexual predation operated not in some supposedly savage colonial backwater but within Western plutocracy, among financiers, celebrities, and political elites.
The horror, in this racialized imagination, is not merely that such crimes occurred. It is that they occurred here, among civilization’s self-appointed custodians.
Netanyahu presents no comparable embarrassment. Why should he? Genocide, dispossession, and mass slaughter are hardly alien to Western imperial history. They are woven into its formation, from Indigenous extermination to colonial conquest. The Zionist extermination campaign in Gaza simply exposes the enduring logic of that tradition.
And Trump, that vulgar spokesman for imperial entitlement, does not merely excuse Netanyahu. He celebrates him.

His loyalists applaud. Republican sycophants parade their devotion to Israel as moral courage. Meanwhile, sections of the Western liberal establishment recoil at Trump’s shamelessness, even as their own political traditions have repeatedly accommodated Zionist ethnic cleansing and violence. Trump embarrasses them by openly advertising the settler-colonial logic their imperial order prefers to disguise beneath humanitarian rhetoric.
Their objection is not necessarily to the barbarism. It is to Trump’s refusal to conceal its pedigree.
Outrage is permitted. Consequences are not.
That is what makes his endorsement so revealing. Epstein represents an association to be explained away; Netanyahu, an allegiance to be proudly proclaimed. One threatens Western moral self-regard; the other reinforces the geopolitical order sustaining it.

Epstein exposed the depravity within institutions claiming to define civilization. Netanyahu exposes the violence those institutions are prepared to finance, defend, and celebrate.
One scandal reveals what powerful men are ashamed to be associated with. The other reveals what they are proud to endorse.

Kazakh President’s Grandnephew Donates Sport University to State Following Investigative Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
13:06:00 UTC
22:06:00 KST

Just one day after an investigation by Radio Azattyq and OCCRP, the grandnephew of Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev announced on Saturday that he is donating the Kazakh National University of Sports (KNUS) to the state.
Framing the handover as a patriotic gesture, Nurassyl Medeu stated the move was not a sale, a transfer into trust management, or a forced step, “but a gratuitous gift to my native country so that it prospers, reaches unprecedented heights, and achieves recognition at the global level.”
“Everything we created must serve our youth, our people, and our country,” he said, adding that it was a great honor to make the contribution. “If you compare KNUS to a ship, I built it to be powerful, reliable, and unbreakable.”
The unexpected announcement of Medeu followed a Friday investigation revealing Medeu to be the grandson of President Tokayev’s sister, Karlyga Izbastina, and detailing how two major educational ventures he founded received substantial state support.
According to the investigation, after President Tokayev has launched an ambitious initiative to establish a “special status” AI research university as a part of his push to transform the nation into a digital state, his 23 years old grand-nephew Nurassyl founded the university “Qazaq AI Research” (QAIRU).
Soon after, the state-owned company QazExpoCongress acquired minority shares in the venture (the company later confirmed to reporters it owns 5 percent stake). At the same time, the institution relocated to a striking, eight-story spherical building in the Kazakh capital, Astana, originally built as the centerpiece of EXPO 2017.
Meanwhile, the for-profit sports academy Medeu founded when he was 18 rebranded last year to KNUS and moved into a $250 million state owned facility. The government also acquired a minority stake in this firm.
Medeu did not respond to requests of either Radio Azattyq or OCCRP prior to publication. However, in a previous interview with state-run Qazsport TV, he sought to quell rumors that his family ties afforded him “special privileges.”
“I do not know where such assertions come from,” he said. “If you wish, you can also open a university and obtain a license. There is nothing extraordinary about it.”
In another interview, with EU Reporter, Medeu defended KNUS’ operations on a state-owned campus, saying the agreement “explicitly prohobit[s] privatization, disposition, or any transfer of the property into private ownership.”
In none of his prior interviews did Medeu mention any intention of gifting the university to the state, and in his Saturday speech, he made no reference to the investigation published a day earlier.
Furthermore, the university’s strategic development plan through 2030, approved last year, contained no provision to transfer full ownership to the state, proposing instead a transfer of only 5 percent. In August of that same year, a state-owned company acquired that exact 5 percent stake, according to publicly available documents.
Medeu also announced the handover on Instagram with a farewell post: “For me, this is not just a goodbye to an important chapter of my life. It is the beginning of a new story for a university that will forever remain close to my heart.”
He did not announce any plans regarding the “Qazaq AI Research University.”

Swiss pharmaceutical group Roche suspends new investments in Germany, division head says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
13:04:45 UTC
22:04:45 KST

BERLIN, October 19. /TASS/. Swiss pharmaceutical group Roche has decided to review its investment strategy for Germany and suspend new projects in the country, Daniel Steiners, head of the company’s German division, said in an interview with the Die Welt newspaper.
He noted that the move was driven by stringent austerity measures introduced by the German government in the healthcare sector.
"We have temporarily put all future investment decisions in Germany on hold. Roche – and by this, I include our global headquarters – wants to see how things develop in Germany. We need to assess whether Germany will remain a partner that provides a predictable framework. We need to know whether or not investments are still welcome here," Steiners said.
"As far as the pharmaceutical sector is concerned, I can say that recent policy has significantly eroded trust," the head of the Roche branch stated. He sharply criticized legislation aimed at stabilizing mandatory health insurance contributions. Steiners emphasized that instead of addressing the sector's systemic issues, German authorities focused on short-term cost-cutting and imposing additional financial burdens on businesses. Without deep structural reforms, the savings achieved will soon be exhausted, and the state will once again face a budget deficit, he estimated.
He added that the tax and regulatory relief planned by the German government for R&D and manufacturing enterprises would only partially offset the industry's losses. In this context, Steiners urged Berlin to develop a predictable regulatory framework and a comprehensive strategy to support the industry.
The Roche representative spoke favorably of US industrial policy, which fosters a highly attractive and straightforward environment for business investment. "Above all, Europe needs to learn how to put in the effort again," he concluded.
The statement from Roche’s leadership coincides with a major investment summit in Berlin, where German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is personally working to attract international capital to the country.
Roche is not the first corporation to scale back its presence in Germany due to government policy. Earlier, US-based Eli Lilly announced it would halve its planned €2.5 billion investment in the state of Rhineland-Palatinate. Germany’s Boehringer Ingelheim has completely scrapped projects worth €900 million, while American pharmaceutical giant Pfizer has frozen its German programs to re-evaluate their viability.

Blue and White party leader Benny Gantz announced on Monday that his party would withdraw from the election race, just over a week before the October 27 election.

“I will not run in the upcoming election. I will continue fighting for unity. It is the only solution that will prevent another disaster and protect Israel against all challenges, at home and abroad,” Gantz said, while announcing his decision.
Later in the evening, he held a press conference in which he took responsibility for his party’s failure to gain sufficient public support.
“Unfortunately, at this time, I have not succeeded in convincing enough of the public of our path, and the responsibility is mine,” he said.
“I remain convinced that our path is the right one,” Gantz added.
He reiterated his calls for a “broad Zionist government,” stating that a Zionist unity government that crosses political blocs “is greater than any individual or party, and it is the only solution in light of the challenges, dangers, and opportunities facing the people of Israel.”
Gantz then stated that he was addressing public leaders from across the political spectrum, saying that for the first time in eight years, he was doing so “not as a political rival but as a citizen of the State of Israel.”
“Do not take us back to October 6. Be brave enough to bring about real change,” he said.
“Set aside old perceptions and do not give in to the old partisan divisions. I warn you: If this does not happen, the nation will continue to be torn apart, and we will face another election or, God forbid, another disaster,” he added.
Gantz’s party had faced a series of departures by lawmakers who are now members of the Yashar party led by Gadi Eisenkot, once Gantz’s second-in-command in the military and a senior figure in the Gantz-led National Unity party bloc.
Blue and White had also distanced itself from the opposition bloc seeking to replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Gantz had called for a “broad Zionist government,” indicating his willingness to sit in a government with Netanyahu. He has been sharply criticized for his back-and-forth approach with the prime minister.
Gantz entered politics with a military background as chief of staff, gained broad public support, and was once seen as one of Netanyahu’s strongest rivals. He held a centrist stance and, in the string of elections between 2019 and 2020, managed to both tie and later surpass the Likud, reaching 33 seats. Gantz went on to serve in two unity governments with Netanyahu.
Gantz’s party launched a new election campaign just last week under the slogan “Choose unity, save the country,” seeking to appeal to voters who identify with neither of the two political blocs.
Gantz also addressed his party’s poor polling numbers in an interview with Yinon Magal and Ben Caspit on 103FM radio on Tuesday, insisting he did not need anyone’s permission to remain in the race.
“I do not need anyone’s permission to continue running,” he said. “It is my democratic right and my duty to tell the people what they need. If you see a Blue and White ballot headed by Benny Gantz, it means I am crossing the electoral threshold.”
Party leaders in the opposition bloc had called for Gantz to withdraw from the elections to reduce the chance of wasting votes if the party failed to pass the electoral threshold.
Opposition party leaders, Gantz's former allies praise his decision to step down, court voters
Eisenkot thanked Gantz for what he called the “correct and responsible decision to withdraw from the most consequential elections since the establishment of the State of Israel.”
“I thank him for his many years of service to Israel’s security and am confident that he will continue to contribute to Israeli society in the future,” Eisenkot said.
Democrats head Yair Golan, who succeeded Eisenkot as Gantz’s deputy chief of staff in the IDF, also praised Blue and White’s departure from the race, saying the bloc had a “shared responsibility to ensure the victory of the change bloc.”
“The Democrats are committed to change and genuine reform and to a Jewish, democratic, liberal, strong, and secure Israel. This is the path we will pursue in the next government as well.”
Additionally, Yoaz Hendel, chairman of the Reservists and Economic Party and former Blue and White member, thanked Gantz for his service to the country while calling on his voters to instead turn to his own party.
“I call on voters from the third bloc to join us. Now, more than ever, it is clear that the only way to establish a Zionist government is to vote for the Reservists and Economic Party.”

LONDON, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- The International Maritime Organization (IMO) secretary-general commended China's expertise in shipbuilding, port infrastructure and maritime technology, as well as its support for developing countries through technical collaboration.
In an interview with Xinhua at the IMO headquarters in London on Friday, IMO Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez expressed enthusiasm about his upcoming visit to China, saying he looked forward to seeing the country's maritime development firsthand and exploring opportunities for closer cooperation.
Dominguez will attend the North Bund Forum and the Global Maritime Forum in Shanghai, which begins on Tuesday.

He said this would enable more countries to play an active role in improving shipping sustainability and using emerging technologies.
"We talked about a lot of AI, but it's also the safety aspects to use this technology the right way," Dominguez said.

Looking ahead to the upcoming North Bund Forum in Shanghai, Dominguez described it as an important platform for building partnerships and advancing international maritime cooperation.

Dominguez added that he had long hoped to attend the forum, as direct engagement with maritime stakeholders offered valuable insights into the practical steps being taken to shape the future of shipping. ■

Külli Taro: When the parliament seems to just get in the way
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
13:03:00 UTC
22:03:00 KST

Külli Taro: When the parliament seems to just get in the way
For every election promise, it is worth asking what problem it solves, who it helps and at what cost, Külli Taro finds.
With political parties leading the charge, we are preparing for elections to the Riigikogu, the country's most important democratically elected representative body. The first campaign ads are already airing, parties are testing the popularity of their election promises and news about who will run alongside whom will soon become a daily occurrence.
Although the Riigikogu is Estonia's most important institution, tasked with debating and deciding all major issues, particularly those involving questions of values, discussions sometimes leave the impression that parliament is an obstacle to making necessary decisions quickly. This seems especially true when following discussions within government agencies where the prevailing attitude appears to be that things would work so much better if only the Riigikogu were not in the way.
A problem needs solving, an idea is on the table, but then come the questions, disputes, negotiations, consultations and proposed amendments. Why can't we just get something done without a time-consuming and exhausting parliamentary debate?
The Riigikogu seems to be getting in the way. If implementing an idea requires changing the law, the preference is to look for ways around that requirement.
Consider the police experiment with "cooling-off stops" several years ago. Speeding drivers were offered the option of waiting by the roadside instead of paying a fine. The experiment effectively introduced a new enforcement measure, with the police taking it upon themselves to shape penalties policy in place of parliament. Only later was the law amended to give police the authority to test cooling-off stops as an enforcement measure.
Or take the infrastructure fees imposed by local governments, which the chancellor of justice has challenged before the Supreme Court because such fees are, in essence, local taxes. We have agreed in the Constitution that local governments may impose and collect taxes and impose obligations only on the basis of law.
Existing laws do not authorize the introduction of infrastructure fees. There is no dispute that building the social infrastructure needed to accommodate new residential developments requires funding. But it is parliament that must make the value judgment about how much of the cost of new schools, kindergartens and other facilities necessitated by new residents should be borne by developers and, ultimately, homebuyers and how much should be funded from municipal budgets as a general public service. Municipal councils cannot take the place of the Riigikogu by invoking their right to manage local affairs independently.
Examples of government agencies taking it upon themselves, rather than leaving it to elected representatives, to decide how medical records, banking information or other data may be used have caused considerable public outrage. And rightly so.
The Riigikogu must decide whose medical records may be accessed, when, under what conditions and to what extent. Information entrusted to doctors must be protected by clear legal safeguards.
It is parliament's responsibility to set limits on government agencies' access to bank account statements through the enforcement register. Bank statements reveal details of people's private lives and even when an agency is pursuing what it considers a noble objective, that does not entitle it to disregard other values.
The purpose of the police's automatic license plate recognition cameras is also understandable. But what caused the greatest outrage was the realization that mass data collection had been organized without broader public debate or even widespread public knowledge.
Technological advances increasingly confront us with the question of whether we, as a society, actually want everything that technology makes possible. Technological solutions must be accompanied by value judgments that distinguish between what we can do and what we want to do. Smart use of data and regulation must not be treated as opposing goals.
These questions require answers enshrined in law. Resolving them means deciding how much power we give the state and how that power may be exercised. The Riigikogu is supposed to debate these issues. That is precisely why we elect a parliament.
Advisory councils and decision-making committees established on any other basis cannot replace a democratically elected representative body. Elected representatives must, of course, listen to outside advice, but parliament cannot be relieved of its responsibility for decisions, its obligation to conduct transparent and wide-ranging debate or its duty to seek additional expertise when necessary.
If the quality of debate in the Riigikogu is unsatisfactory, the solution is not to sideline parliament but to demand more of it. We should insist on more precise questions and clearer answers.
An avalanche of election promises will soon be upon us. That will give us another opportunity to practice holding politicians to higher standards. With every promise, we should ask what problem it solves, whom it helps and at what cost. A catchy idea about "doing something new or exciting" is not enough on its own. We need solutions that genuinely help and whose objectives, costs and limits we can agree on. Reaching that agreement is precisely the job of parliament.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski

China's satellite internet links Arctic, Antarctica, Qinghai-Tibet Plateau for first time
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
21:02:53 CST
22:02:53 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- China's 16th Arctic Ocean expedition team said Monday that its polar icebreaker Jidi had completed a pre-operational application test of domestically developed satellite internet along Arctic shipping routes.
The voyage marked the first successful verification of networked communications across the Arctic, Antarctica and the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, also known as the "Third Pole" of Earth, closing the last communications coverage gap in the world, the expedition team said.
Organized by China's Ministry of Natural Resources, the expedition set off on July 3. The Jidi, meaning "polar region" in Chinese, is one of the expedition's four research vessels.
According to the expedition team, voice and video were clear and smooth during a video link connecting the icebreaker in the Arctic, Qinling Station in Antarctica, the Lhasa River test station in the Xizang Autonomous Region and a ministry bureau based in the eastern coastal city of Qingdao.
The link enabled global low-latency, high-bandwidth communications through the Chinese satellite internet, verifying its stability under harsh conditions such as extreme low temperatures, severe sandstorms, and ice fog.
The voyage also marked the first use of domestic satellite internet for polar medical support. The Arctic Ocean expedition team said the Jidi held high-definition ship-to-shore video consultations with hospitals and experts in Qingdao, enabling timely medical assessment for its members.
Another achievement during the voyage was a homegrown ocean drifting buoy, called Zhigan, which for the first time enabled the Chinese survey equipment to fully control data collection and transmission. Since the transmission speed and quality met practical requirements in the tests, it offered an alternative to the traditional use of international satellites for real-time ocean sensing data transmission.
Zhang Meng, an expedition member and on-site tester, said the Jidi vessel had sent and received more than 300 files totaling more than 100 gigabytes of data and supported more than 40 video consultations during the voyage.
"The communications tests have helped address the information isolation, a challenge in polar expeditions, and verified full-voyage communications support based on China's satellite internet," Zhang said. ■

Feature: Chinese poetry builds bridges of cultural understanding in Riyadh
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
21:02:46 CST
22:02:46 KST

A contestant recites a poem during the university division of the final of the Chinese Poetry Recitation Competition 2026 at Prince Sultan University in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, Oct. 18, 2026. (Xinhua/Luo Chen)
by Xinhua writer Wang Haizhou
RIYADH, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- Basmah bint Saeed, a Saudi schoolgirl, first encountered the Chinese language as a child at her family home, where visitors from central China's Henan Province spoke Mandarin.
Years later, driven by her growing interest in the language, she can sing more than 100 Chinese songs, including those incorporating elements of traditional Chinese opera.
On Sunday, Saeed, a student at No. 69 Intermediate School in the Saudi capital Riyadh, took to the stage at Prince Sultan University in Riyadh, wearing an elegant Chinese traditional outfit and reciting "Xiangxin Weilai" (Believe in the Future), a modern Chinese poem about perseverance and hope.
Her performance won first prize in the secondary-school division of the final of the Chinese Poetry Recitation Competition 2026, jointly organized by the Chinese Embassy in Saudi Arabia and the Confucius Institute at Prince Sultan University.
Saeed was one of 25 contestants from Saudi intermediate schools, universities and the institute that took part in the competition.
Dressed in elegant Chinese traditional attire, the students incorporated music, videos and images of Chinese and Saudi landscapes, cultural landmarks and UNESCO World Heritage sites into their performances, transforming the auditorium into a vibrant meeting place for two cultures.
For some contestants, Chinese poetry and music also reflected personal memories and future ambitions.
Sadeem Mohammad Al Towaim, a Chinese-language major at Princess Nourah bint Abdulrahman University in Riyadh, won first prize with "I Love You, Chinese Characters".
Having spent part of her childhood in Guangzhou, the capital city of south China's Guangdong Province, she has maintained a strong attachment to the country.
"Since I returned to Saudi Arabia, I have always missed China," she said, describing Chinese people as warm and hospitable, qualities she found remarkably similar to those of Saudis.
Now, she teaches her younger brother Chinese every day and hopes to return to China for further studies.
After winning the competition, she smiled when asked whether she had shared the news with her family. "Not yet. If I tell my dad, he will call me immediately," she said.
Another contestant, Jwana Mohammed Al-Amri, recited and sang "Prelude to Water Melody," an ancient Chinese poem written by Su Shi, a famous poet of the Song Dynasty (960-1279).
After studying Chinese for about three years, she has also developed a love for Chinese songs and hopes to pursue university studies in China, although she has yet to visit the country.
The program also featured Arabic poetry and a performance of the classical Chinese music piece "Fisherman's Song at Dusk" on the guzheng, a traditional Chinese zither.
The competition took place amid the expansion of Chinese-language education in Saudi Arabia. Since 2024, Chinese-language education has expanded into public intermediate schools, offering more Saudi students opportunities to study Mandarin.
The event also offered a glimpse of how that learning can extend beyond classrooms into literature, music and personal aspirations.
Zhang Xinying, Chinese director of the Confucius Institute at Prince Sultan University, said that poetry offers a bridge between civilizations. Despite differences in language and literary expression, Chinese and Saudi people share aspirations for family, friendship, peace and a better life.
Zhang hoped that such exchanges would inspire more young people to deepen mutual understanding and carry China-Saudi friendship forward. ■

China Focus: Digital technology helps protect ancient sites, bring history to life
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
21:02:44 CST
22:02:44 KST

HANGZHOU, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- As night falls, 5,000 drones rise into the sky. Their lights trace timber beams and columns, and lost royal palaces slowly take shape overhead. By blending digital technology with archaeological evidence, the spectacle brings Liangzhu, an early regional state that flourished more than 5,000 years ago, back to life.
At the Liangzhu Ruins in east China's Zhejiang Province, a UNESCO World Heritage Site inscribed in 2019, digital reconstructions of ancient palaces are opening a window to the past, bringing the civilization to life while safeguarding its fragile remains.
"Digital technology allows us to transform our research findings into a stunning visual experience, showing how the Liangzhu people lived and worked 5,000 years ago," said Sun Haibo, director of the Cultural Relics and Heritage Administration under the Hangzhou Liangzhu Archaeological Site Administrative District Management Committee.
"The columns traced by drones were placed where they stood 5,000 years ago, allowing us to imagine the structures that once occupied those spots," said Wang Ningyuan, an expert at the Zhejiang Provincial Institute of Cultural Relics and Archaeology.
The Liangzhu case offers a glimpse of how technology is reshaping the way China safeguards and presents its cultural heritage.
TECH PROTECTS RUINS
Preserving earthen ruins in humid climates has long been a global challenge. At Liangzhu, moss and mold grow quickly, and even visitors' footsteps can threaten fragile heritage sites.
The difficulty is compounded by the site's vast scale. Some 316 sites are scattered across a 162-square-kilometer protection zone interwoven with local development. More than 90 percent of the area remains open, making foot patrols alone insufficient.
Liangzhu's solution is to let algorithms stand watch over the ground.
Across the zone, facilities, including 1,006 surveillance cameras and hundreds of ground sensors tracking soil moisture around the clock, form an integrated, intelligent monitoring network. The network issues automatic warnings when abnormalities are detected, cutting response times from three days to 30 minutes.
Researchers have also built a digital twin, a virtual model of the physical site, on a smart management platform. It can simulate extreme weather such as typhoons and downpours, allowing researchers to identify weak points and develop response plans tailored to the areas most at risk.
TECH BRINGS HISTORY TO LIFE
Preserving the remains is only part of the task. Liangzhu is also using technology to help visitors step into the world of this ancient civilization and discover its jade craftsmanship, rice farming and water management firsthand.
At the Liangzhu Museum, visitors can put on augmented reality (AR) glasses and watch a virtual jade cong appear to float out of its display case. The tubular object, with a square exterior and circular interior, can be rotated digitally in midair, revealing intricate carvings from every angle without touching the original.
With a tap on the arm of a pair of AI glasses, visitors can activate an intelligent guide. The device identifies exhibits in the wearer's field of view and provides explanations. Visitors can also ask follow-up questions about whatever catches their interest.
"I can see how it would be appealing maybe to the younger generation and people who are new to archaeology and are kind of learning about this stuff for the first time," said Dorian Fuller, fellow of the British Academy and professor at the Institute of Archaeology, University College London, after trying the AI glasses during a recent visit to the museum.
"I've been visiting Liangzhu since 2004. I visited the previous museum before this one was built," said Fuller. "There's been an improvement, obviously, in the ways in which material is presented at museums with the advent of video screens and touch screens and an additional reconstruction."
Behind the AI guide lies a carefully built knowledge base. The museum has organized its records and archaeological reports into a structured database to support the system. "Every sentence produced by AI can be traced to reliable sources," said Luo Xiaohong, a researcher at the museum.
"Artifacts may age, but data can be preserved forever," said Luo, noting that Liangzhu launched its artifact digitization initiative as early as 2014. A new round of digital collection is now underway, and more than 200 precious artifacts will be given a permanent digital life.
If AR brings individual artifacts closer, virtual reality (VR) at the ruins offers visitors a chance to explore the ancient city as a whole.
Launched in 2025, the VR experience at Liangzhu takes visitors into a digitally reconstructed city. Wearing headsets, they can watch farmers tend rice fields, artisans carve jade and communities work together to manage floods.
At the ongoing fourth Liangzhu Forum held in Hangzhou, Heena Waleed, minister of Arts, Culture and Heritage of the Maldives, said using digital means to preserve the memory of civilization is an important guarantee that cultural heritage will be left to future generations.
"While technology empowers cultural heritage protection, its application must remain anchored to the artifacts' characteristics and intrinsic values," said Xiong Qingbo, an official with the Fujian Provincial Bureau of Cultural Heritage. "Only by doing so can we ensure their proper preservation and transmission amidst rapid technological advancement." ■
