Houthi attack on Yemen army camp in Shabwa kills at least 53: reports
Houthis launch ballistic missiles at camp in southern governorate during training exercise, government forces spokesman says.
A Houthi missile attack on the al-AIam military camp in southern Yemen has killed at least 53 people, according to local authorities.
The Iranian-backed armed group launched three ballistic missiles on Monday at the camp in Shabwa governorate during a training exercise, a spokesperson for Yemeni government forces said.
Officials for the internationally recognised government and medical sources initially said at least 18 people were killed and more than 30 wounded when the strike hit the facility, where new security recruits were undergoing training.
Those numbers increased dramatically later on Monday, when the local authority in Shabwa said 53 people had been killed and 200 injured, news agencies reported.
‘Hostile threat’
The attack was carried out as fighting continued to rage across Yemen. The civil war between the Saudi-backed government and Houthis had eased after a 2022 truce, but the regional impact of this year’s US-Israel war on Iran reignited hostilities.
Fighting escalated rapidly when the Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah – Arabic for Supporters of God – seized strategic territory from forces loyal to the government along the Red Sea coast last month.
Government forces, backed by Saudi Arabia, responded with a counteroffensive and then launched the “Dawn of Yemen” operation, which aims to recapture Houthi-held territory, including the capital, Sanaa, which the Iran-aligned group seized in 2014.
The Houthis, meanwhile, have stepped up attacks on Saudi Arabia, including on Riyadh’s international airport and the state oil company Aramco.
On Monday, Saudi authorities sent alerts to residents of the capital Riyadh warning of “a hostile aerial threat”.
New recruits
Rashad al-Alimi, the head of the Yemeni Presidential Leadership Council, said those killed in Shabwa were new recruits and promised a “firm response”.
“Targeting recruits reflects the Houthi militia’s approach of resorting to terrorist attacks when under pressure,” he said.
Reporting from Sanaa, Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry said the Houthis claimed responsibility for the attack.
“The Houthis said the attack targeted what they called a ‘Saudi-backed’ military base, referring to Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces who are stationed at military camps across the country,” he said.
“The Houthis say they will continue to target those bases. Spokesperson Yahya Saree says anywhere with a Saudi-backed military presence will be considered a legitimate target.”
Earlier, Yemeni government forces said they targeted Houthi gatherings, vehicles and weapons in al-Aqroudh, al-Shaqab and al-Sarari, south of Taiz, which is suffering from fuel shortages and soaring prices.

What's behind Egypt's move towards possible military involvement in Saudi-Yemen conflict?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
12:50:59 UTC
21:50:59 KST

What's behind Egypt's move towards possible military involvement in Saudi-Yemen conflict?
CAIRO, Oct 19 - Egypt's parliament is expected to vote next week on whether to authorise the armed forces to help defend Saudi Arabia against attacks by Yemen's Houthis if Riyadh requests its support.
The move would bring the Arab world's most populous country closer to direct military involvement in the widening conflicts unleashed by the US-Israeli air assault on Iran in February.
President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi requested the approval in a speech on Saturday, saying Egypt would "never, never forget our brothers in the Gulf" and telling Saudi Arabia's leaders that Cairo would "take any measure to protect you".
Like the Gulf states that have come under attack from Tehran in the Iran war, Egypt is a longstanding partner in the US-led security order that is being tested by the conflict.
WHAT IS EGYPT'S STANCE ON THE IRAN WAR?
Sisi's comments marked a clear escalation from the more measured tone authorities have tended to adopt since the Iran war started. Though Egypt has repeatedly voiced strong support for its Gulf allies, Cairo has stopped short of publicly committing itself to a direct combat role in the conflict.
In May, the presence of Egyptian Rafale fighter jets in the United Arab Emirates was disclosed in Emirati state media coverage of an official visit by Sisi. Egyptian coverage of the visit did not mention the deployment. When Saudi Arabia signed a joint defence agreement with Turkey and Pakistan in August, Egypt did not join, though it said it was considering it.
The tone started to shift after the Houthis stepped up attacks on Saudi oil and other infrastructure. Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman last month visited Egypt, where he discussed the need to ensure freedom and security of navigation in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the Red Sea, on which both countries have long coastlines.
WHAT'S AT STAKE FOR EGYPT?
Egypt's economic stability has long been tied up with the oil-producing Gulf. Remittances from Egyptian expatriate workers there are an important source of foreign currency and income for families back home at a time of double-digit inflation worsened by surging food and fuel prices.
Saudi Arabia, the UAE and other Gulf countries have been among Sisi's key financial backers, providing tens of billions of dollars of aid, central bank deposits and investments since the army overthrew President Mohamed Morsi, a senior Muslim Brotherhood figure, in 2013.
"We can never forget how our brothers in the Gulf states stood by Egypt during that period," Sisi said in his speech.
Saudi Arabia has a $5.3 billion deposit at Egypt's central bank due this month along with $267 million in interest, central bank data shows.
WHAT ABOUT SECURITY?
Growing security concerns have also pushed Cairo towards a more active stance, analysts say. A drone strike on two gas vessels at the Mediterranean port city of Damietta in July underscored that Egypt could not expect to keep itself fully isolated from the conflict.
"I think they realise that they can't be on the sidelines about this indefinitely," said H. A. Hellyer, a scholar at the Royal United Services Institute think tank.
For the authorities, the economic and security concerns were "one and the same," he said.
Saudi Arabia and Egypt also have a shared interest in securing shipping through the Red Sea, an outlet for Saudi oil blocked from leaving the Strait of Hormuz. Egypt earns billions of dollars a year from fees on Suez Canal traffic. These overlapping concerns mean "Saudi Arabia's security constitutes a dimension of Egyptian national security," said Sherif Aref, an Egyptian political researcher and journalist.
WHAT SORT OF MILITARY DOES EGYPT BRING TO THE TABLE?
Egypt has one of the Arab world's largest armed forces, with hundreds of thousands of active personnel and large air, land and naval inventories, according to military analysts. Egypt sources equipment from a range of countries, and its air force operates US-made F-16s, French Rafales and Russian-made MiG-29s.
Egypt receives about $1.3 billion a year in US military aid, which helps fund its purchases of American military equipment. Washington waived human rights conditions on a tranche of the funds this year after what it called Cairo's "helpful role" since the Iran war began.
In the years after the 2011 uprising that ousted President Hosni Mubarak, the armed forces fought a counterinsurgency campaign against Islamist militants in the Sinai Peninsula. Egypt also contributed air and naval forces to the Saudi-led coalition that intervened in Yemen in 2015, and conducted airstrikes against Islamic State targets in Libya during that country’s civil war.
Egypt has not undertaken a large-scale foreign ground deployment since the 1991 Gulf War, when its troops joined the US-led coalition to drive Iraqi forces from Kuwait. Nearly three decades earlier, President Gamal Abdel Nasser had sent Egyptian forces into Yemen in a costly intervention later compared to the US involvement in the Vietnam War.
WHAT SORT OF SUPPORT IS LIKELY?
Sisi's speech and subsequent statements have not specified what sort of military forces, if any, Egypt would ultimately intend to send. A deployment of Egyptian troops inside Yemen itself is unlikely, military analysts say.
More likely interventions might include air defence and naval support, said Samir Ragheb, a retired Egyptian military officer who heads the Arab Foundation for Development and Strategic Studies think tank.
"The threats, missiles and drones, require air defence and air forces," he said, adding that the navy could be used for protecting ships, naval operations against piracy and protecting the Saudi coastline.
Still, the entry of another large conventional Arab military would not "suddenly solve the Houthi problem", said Andreas Krieg, senior security studies lecturer at King's College London.
"The Houthis are difficult precisely because they generate disproportionate effect through missiles, drones, dispersed forces and geography. Egypt cannot bomb that problem away," he said.
"What Cairo can do is strengthen Saudi resilience, improve Red Sea control, share the defensive burden and increase the political cost of continued attacks." REUTERS

MOSCOW, October 19. /TASS/. Russia’s Kalashnikov Group has delivered a batch of 9M333 anti-aircraft missiles to the customer earlier than planned, the company told TASS.
"The Kalashnikov Group has successfully delivered another batch of 9M333 anti-aircraft missiles to the customer. As part of meeting its 2026 obligations, the products are being supplied ahead of schedule. It is important to note that these products remain in consistently high demand due to their effective performance in the special military operation zone," the company said in a statement.
The anti-aircraft missile is deployed by the Strela-10 air defense missile system and its versions. Over the past few years, the 9M333 has demonstrated its effectiveness in combat operations.
The missile is designed to hit aerial targets at any time of day under conditions involving the use of dropped, parachuted and modulated organized optical countermeasures, including remotely piloted aircraft and cruise missiles. The missile’s homing head has three operating modes: photo-contrast, infrared, and jam-resistant, giving it a key advantage over other products in this class. The missile’s average speed is 550 m/s, and it can strike targets at altitudes ranging from 10 to 3,500 meters. The munition operates on a fire-and-forget principle.

Roche acquires Chinese antibody-drug conjugate rights for $500m
The Swiss pharmaceutical company Roche has acquired the rights to a portfolio of antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) developed by its Chinese competitor Hansoh Pharma, for $510 million (CHF420 million).
The transaction consists of an initial instalment of $400 million, to be paid upon signing the contract, and a second instalment of $110 million, to be paid one year later.
The contract also provides for funding of $15 billion, subject to the achievement of development, regulatory or even commercial milestones, as well as commissions of an unspecified amount on any revenue, the Shanghai-based group stated in a press release issued today.
ADCs, or antibody-drug conjugates, are preparations that combine, amongst other things, an antibody and a chemotherapeutic molecule. Their purpose is to combat tumours.
More
Personalised cancer vaccines take a leap forward – can Swiss pharma catch up?
Hansoh will retain control over the early stages of development, up to the completion of the first clinical phase. Roche will then take over on a global basis, with the exception of mainland China, Hong Kong, Macao and Taiwan.
Roche first entered Hansoh’s business exactly one year ago, acquiring the rights to the drug HS-20110 for an initial payment of $80 million, which at the time was the subject of a Phase I clinical trial in China and the United States for colorectal cancer and other cancers.

Alongside these popular routes, newer destinations are also attracting growing interest from travelers.
Among domestic flights, Almaty, Shymkent, and Atyrau account for the highest passenger traffic, while Pavlodar is emerging as an increasingly popular destination, with demand for flights to the city rising steadily.
Internationally, Istanbul, Moscow, and Beijing remain the busiest routes, attracting steady demand from tourists, business travelers, and transit passengers.
Meanwhile, newer international routes are also gaining momentum. Astana Airport has reported growing passenger traffic on flights to Ulaanbaatar, Prague, and Guangzhou, reflecting increasing interest in new destinations and expanding international air connections.
Astana currently offers flights to 65 destinations, including 47 international and 18 domestic routes.
Earlier, Qazinform reported that a new Almaty route had connected Hanoi and Prague.

Kazakhstan fits snow leopard with satellite collar for first time in Southern Altai

Kazakhstan fits snow leopard with satellite collar for first time in Southern Altai
A snow leopard named Altai has become the first in Kazakhstan's Southern Altai to be fitted with a satellite tracking collar. The animal, listed in Kazakhstan's Red Book of endangered species, was fitted with the device at Katon-Karagay National Park, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources.
The satellite collar will allow researchers to track the snow leopard's movements, study its travel routes, and identify key areas of its habitat.
The data collected will provide valuable insights into the behavior of snow leopards in the Southern Altai and help improve conservation efforts.
Snow leopards typically inhabit remote, mountainous areas, making them difficult to observe in the wild. Satellite tracking will enable scientists to monitor Altai's movements without having to remain physically close to the animal.
According to conservation specialists, satellite monitoring plays a crucial role in studying rare wildlife, helping researchers identify habitat areas and gather scientific data needed to protect endangered populations.
On October 16, speaking at the COP17 summit in Yerevan, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev announced that Kazakhstan's snow leopard population had reached approximately 190 individuals. He also highlighted the progress made through conservation efforts and scientific monitoring.
The collar was fitted with the participation of Katon-Karagay National Park employees E. Kassymov and Zh. Amanbayev, alongside researchers A. Grachev, M. Bespalov, S. Bespalov, and S. Saparbayev from the Institute of Zoology.
The project is supported by Pernod Ricard Kazakhstan.
Satellite data will be used to map Altai's movements and habitat, helping researchers better understand snow leopard ecology in the Southern Altai and develop more effective conservation measures for this rare predator.
Qazinform previously reported that rare animal populations in Kazakhstan are rising.

Macron begins Gulf tour to secure fuel supplies as cost-of-living protests rock France
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
12:48:33 UTC
21:48:33 KST

French President Emmanuel Macron has begun a Gulf tour to seek additional oil and diesel supplies and help ease soaring fuel costs, following a weekend of violent protests over the cost of living that saw more than 2,500 arrests, according to the supplied report.
Macron arrived on Monday in Kuwait, where he was welcomed by Emir Sheikh Mishal Al-Ahmad Al-Jaber Al-Sabah, hours after condemning what he called “unbridled” violence in an address to the nation on Sunday.
The visit will also take him to the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain and Qatar by Wednesday.
Paris says the trip is intended to strengthen economic and defence partnerships, secure energy supplies and improve the safety of maritime routes disrupted by the US-Iran war.
Fuel supplies and defence deals on the agenda
Macron said before departing that the trip was necessary to “secure our supplies”, pointing to fuel prices as one of the concerns raised by protesters.
In Kuwait, discussions included plans to deliver pre-positioned stocks of kerosene and diesel from Oman to the French overseas territories of Reunion and Mayotte, according to the French presidency.
French armed forces minister Catherine Vautrin also signed a letter of intent on defence cooperation with her Kuwaiti counterpart. Talks included potential arms sales, according to a member of the French delegation.
Airbus separately signed a letter of intent to support the renewal of Kuwait Airways’ fleet and cooperate on maintenance and training.
Macron is accompanied by senior executives from France’s two largest energy groups, TotalEnergies and Engie, as his government seeks concrete commitments on oil and diesel volumes.
Hormuz disruption drives search for alternative routes
The tour comes amid a major disruption to energy shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial route for Gulf oil exports, during the war between the United States and Iran.
The French presidency said Macron would discuss ways to secure maritime shipments and establish “alternative and bypass routes” for energy exports with Gulf leaders, including the UAE president and Qatar’s emir.
The G7 countries, under France’s chairmanship this year, agreed in early October to release 100 million barrels of oil through a coordinated effort to ease pressure on energy markets.
France and Britain have also assembled an international mission to help reopen the Strait of Hormuz, mainly through demining operations, once Washington and Tehran agree on the waterway.
Energy expert Francis Perrin of the French Institute for International and Strategic Relations cautioned that the Gulf tour was unlikely to have an immediate impact on fuel prices, saying exporters may struggle to make firm commitments while regional instability persists.
Macron faces criticism over unrest at home
The overseas trip comes as Macron faces mounting scrutiny over the government’s handling of France’s worst unrest in years. More than 2,500 people were arrested during clashes and looting, with shops and town halls reportedly damaged or set on fire.
Macron acknowledged security and intelligence failures but refused to accept the resignation of his interior minister.
Constitutional expert Benjamin Morel warned that the Gulf tour could project an image of normality but also risk making the president appear disconnected from events at home and suggest a “kind of power vacuum”.
The government now faces the twin challenge of addressing public anger over living costs while pursuing energy commitments abroad that may not translate quickly into lower prices at the pump.

Poland breaks up international criminal group accused of laundering €77 million
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
12:48:31 UTC
21:48:31 KST

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Poland says it has broken up an international criminal group responsible for laundering an estimated 337 million zloty (€77 million) by using currency exchange offices to illegally process money obtained from internet scams.
Nine suspects – eight Ukrainians and one Belarusian – have been detained in a series of raids, which also resulted in the seizure of gold and cash worth over 1 million zloty.
Służby rozbiły międzynarodową grupę zajmującą się praniem pieniędzy z oszustw inwestycyjnych i kryptowalut. Zatrzymano 9 osób, a skala transakcji przekroczyła 337 mln zł. Zabezpieczono złoto i gotówkę wartą ponad 1 mln zł. @Straz_Graniczna @PolicjaCBZC @ABW_GOV_PL pic.twitter.com/g2NQoqaPvP
— Marcin Kierwiński (@MKierwinski) October 19, 2026
The accused – four women and five men aged between 26 and 53 – were arrested in Łódź, Warsaw and Małopolska province, announced Krzysztof Kopania, spokesman for the Łódź regional prosecutor’s office, which is leading the investigation.
The detainees are four female cashiers, three men running the exchange offices, and two couriers used to transport money. All have been charged with participating in an organised criminal group and money laundering. They could face up to 15 years in prison if convicted.
Prosecutors say that the gang, which operated in the cities of Warsaw, Lublin, Wrocław, Katowice and Gdańsk, collected money that had been obtained through internet fraud and transported it to cryptocurrency exchanges. It was then processed without complying with anti-money laundering procedures.
Proceeds were then transferred to bank accounts, sent abroad by car, or concealed in fictitious purchases of gold. Most money was ultimately invested in cryptocurrencies.
“The scale of the operation was enormous,” said Kopania. “It is estimated that between February 2025 and July 2026, members of the group took steps to conceal the origins of approximately 337 million zloty.”
The ringleader was a 34-year-old Ukrainian national who made the key decisions and oversaw the domestic and international channelling of funds obtained from illegal sources, according to the Internal Security Agency (ABW) and border guard, which were also involved in the operation.
Seven of the accused have been placed in pre-trial detention for three (or in one case two) months, while two have been bailed and ordered not to leave Poland.

World will face a serious energy crisis if US launches another war against Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

World will face a serious energy crisis if US launches another war against Iran
IRGC spokesman says Tehran has not yet fully closed the Strait of Hormuz, and could extend that closure to Bab el-Mandeb and Suez Canal
TEHRAN – More than seven months have passed since the United States, together with Israel, launched its war against Iran. What was meant to be a swift campaign to topple the Islamic Republic has instead left American bases across the region in ruins, the Strait of Hormuz still closed, and Washington without an answer to the energy crisis it helped create. With the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding in tatters and American midterm elections approaching, the question now is whether the US will risk another escalation — or accept defeat.
In an exclusive interview with the Tehran Times, IRGC spokesman General Hossein Mohebbi discussed the course of military operations over the past months and what may lie ahead. He also assessed the current state of Iran's armed forces, and spoke personally about succeeding his assassinated predecessor, Martyr General Ali-Mohammad Naeini — and about duty and loss within the faith that sustains Iran's forces on the front lines.
Below is the full text of the interview:
A question that's on a lot of people's minds these days — both in Iran and around the world — is whether the United States and Israel are once again heading toward an escalation of war and conflict, or not. How would you respond to this?
As military forces, we consider every scenario in this regard possible, and from where we stand, no possibility is off the table. That said, based on our assessments, America is definitely not in a position to want to start a new conflict in order to gain some fresh achievement from it. In the past, America came in with everything it had — it had well-equipped bases and vast amounts of equipment at its disposal, it brought fresh, ready-to-fight forces into the field, it pulled out all the stops and drew on every capacity it had — and yet it still couldn't achieve a single one of its declared or undeclared objectives. Not only did it fail, it suffered numerous strategic defeats, the least of which was the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Despite everything America has done so far, it still hasn't been able to reopen that strait, and on top of that, it's suffered enormously significant strategic defeats.
So at this point, America no longer has those capabilities, and it can't use those bases the way it once did. Most of those bases have been shut down, their equipment has been destroyed, and the countries that were most cooperative with America back then no longer offer that same cooperation. American forces today are tired, worn-out forces, and they've pulled back hundreds of kilometers from us. Before the war started, there were at least thirty to forty warships inside the Persian Gulf; but today, not only do they have no ships inside the Persian Gulf, they've also withdrawn roughly seven hundred kilometers away from the Strait of Hormuz. The forces that were stationed at those regional bases have now been moved to distant bases, and even at those distant bases — like Al-Azraq and Al-Tanf in Jordan and Syria — they're no longer safe, because those locations too are within our crosshairs.
So from a military capability standpoint and from a technical perspective, America doesn't have what it takes to carry out a new operation or conflict. But there is a possibility that, with the American elections coming up, it might want to manufacture some kind of achievement — for example, carrying out a limited action so it can exploit the results for the elections. That possibility exists, and since we don't dismiss any possibility, we're ready to respond to any action. Our response this time will be far more severe and will land America in far bigger trouble, and will confront the world with even bigger challenges too. In any case, if America takes a new action — even a limited one — the world will face a serious energy crisis. What's happened so far, in our view, hasn't yet reached the stage of a crisis, and we haven't yet brought all our capacity to bear on fully closing the strait. If America wants to make a new move, it will definitely be facing a massive crisis, and it will also confront the world with a new energy crisis.
With the cold season coming up in Europe, and with America itself and many countries needing energy for heating and daily life, the world will face a new crisis, and a global consensus will form against America — a country that creates problems for the whole world by starting fires. Global public opinion is already against America, and if there's any new move, that opposition will only grow, and America will pay a very heavy price. In our view, rationality dictates that they shouldn't do such a thing; but if one day, based on some illusion or delusion of gaining a new achievement, they want to take action, they'll pay a very heavy price. We haven't yet linked up the Strait of Hormuz, the Bab al-Mandab Strait, and the Suez Canal, and we haven't yet used all the capacities of our region — our material and spiritual potential, our popular strength, the capacity of the resistance front, and the other tools that could create a major challenge for America.
So if we look at the story from America's point of view, this scenario seems unlikely, but it's still possible, and it's precisely on the basis of that possibility that we've prepared our scenarios.
That said, when it comes to the Zionist regime, the matter is different. The Zionist regime is, in any case, looking to take advantage of America's companionship and to act even more aggressively. This possibility is worth thinking about from that angle, and this is where the American people need to think. The letter we wrote to the American people has, in part, this very dimension: Are the American people willing, for the sake of following Zionist policies and helping them reach their vile ambitions, to create massive troubles and enormous challenges — like an energy crisis and even a food crisis — for their own country and for the world? I doubt the American people would be willing to accept such a thing, and we pointed to this in that letter as well.
So if I wanted to sum up my words in one sentence, the answer to your question is that the possibility of any operation — even a limited one — is not entirely ruled out, but our assessments show that they simply don't have the capability needed to carry out an effective operation and achieve their goals. Their capability has become so weakened and scattered that they certainly won't get the results they want, and they'll only box themselves into bigger constraints. They might one day take action for the sake of a limited, tactical gain on the eve of the elections, but they'll certainly run into bigger defeats and constraints, global public opinion will mobilize against them, and there are plenty of options available to deter America. The best path and the best proposal for America is to accept Iran's conditions and declare its defeat by accepting those conditions; that would be the best path for the United States.
The enemy is trying to make it seem as though it was Iran that, by attacking several oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, caused the Islamabad MoU to fall apart. They even claimed that a few rogue forces acted without coordination on July 7. Can you tell us what exactly happened that day?
America is doing a forward escape and resorting to sophistry, when in fact the main violator of this agreement was the United States itself. This breach of promise first happened when, right after the meeting where the memorandum of understanding was concluded and sessions were held to implement its provisions, the US Secretary of State took a trip to the region and issued a statement with the leaders of regional countries that was clearly at odds with the provisions of the memorandum. On the other hand, under Article Five of the memorandum, it had been stipulated that the passage of ships would be conducted according to Iranian arrangements, but America, by threatening certain regional countries, opened a new illegal route through the southern part of the strait and along the coast of Oman in order to effectively nullify that article. Not only did they open a new passage, they also forced ships to pass through it and ignored the Iranian arrangements.
This behavior showed that America had once again broken its word — an approach that had precedent. They once carried out the attack of June 13, 2025 during the negotiations, another time they carried out the attack of February 28 in the middle of the negotiation process, and for a third time — not during the talks but after the Islamabad memorandum was concluded and at the stage of implementing it — they violated the agreement. What should the logical response to such a blatant breach of promise be? A logical, powerful, and fitting response. Any fair and reasonable person, if they look at this sequence, will acknowledge that in the face of America's repeated violations, we were compelled to show our decisiveness and strength — something that, praise God, was achieved.
As was seen, during the 17-day clashes, the greatest losses were inflicted on America. In an interview with the Tasnim News Agency, I announced the exact figures for human casualties, destroyed equipment, and demolished bases, because heavy blows were dealt to them as a result of their latest breach of promise. The claim that the actions taken by our forces were rogue is absolutely untrue. In military structures around the world, discipline and adherence to the organizational chain of command is the first principle, and no one can take unilateral action on a sensitive matter like war without coordinating with the higher levels. So our response was carried out with full coordination and as a decisive reaction to America's breach of promise.
The world needs to know that breach of promise is rooted in the very nature of the United States' statecraft, and that this country doesn't adhere to its signatures and commitments. The America that trampled the JCPOA despite the signature of its then-president and five other countries; the America that, during negotiations, assassinated senior commanders, national leaders, and scientists, and massacred thousands of innocent people — has once again proven that violating agreements is part of the fixed procedures of this country's governance. Breach of promise and disrupting agreements have, as it were, become part of the unwritten doctrine of America's ruling establishment.
On this basis, I declare with certainty that our response to the United States' breach of promise — whether in connection to the JCPOA or the recent agreements — was a strong, powerful, fully appropriate, and timely response. If time were to turn back to the 16th of Tir [July 7] we would do exactly the same thing again, and if such actions are repeated by the other side, our response will be even more crushing than before.
Let's talk a bit more about the events of July 7. Some domestic and foreign experts, attempting to corroborate the United States' claim that the attacks that day were rogue, argue that — given Iran's mosaic defense structure, in which commanders of each unit can act without coordinating with higher authorities if necessary — the occurrence of such an incident is not far-fetched. How would you respond to this analysis?
These two matters are completely different from each other. When we talk about a rogue action, we mean an individual acting without orders and without coordinating with higher bodies, and in conflict with standing directives — something that has absolutely no place in the armed forces. But the matter of mosaic defense and delegating authority to commanders in conditions of severed communications or the martyrdom of a senior commander is a defined doctrine and system, not disorder. In this structure, the chain of succession is precisely specified; that is, if the first commander is martyred or organizational communications are cut off through radio, telephone, or communication networks, the next commanders make decisions based on the requirements of the battlefield and a precise assessment of the enemy's situation. This approach is a military measure, and it isn't called rogue action.
Such measures are even rooted in our epistemic and religious foundations; just as in historical military traditions, specific successors were appointed for conditions in which commanders' communications were severed. So a distinction has to be made between the word "rogue action" and "wartime measure." The enemy raising such claims is part of psychological operations aimed at creating a rift between the body of the armed forces and the country's senior officials, or at suggesting a disagreement between the government and military institutions. They've repeatedly raised these rumors to suggest that the decision-making structure in Iran is unclear, but such atmospherics are merely media tricks whose nature is completely clear to experts, and others too have come to understand this reality well over recent months.
You probably meet with field commanders and also visit military headquarters. What's your assessment of the morale of Iranian forces after more than seven months of war?
Honestly, whatever I say about this might seem unbelievable to you, your colleagues, and your listeners, but the reality is that the morale of our combatants — from commanders to operating forces and equipment crews — is at the highest level; to the point that when we go to visit them, we feel weak and ashamed before their will and character. They're present in difficult conditions, despite certain shortages, in hot and humid weather above fifty degrees and in an insecure environment with minimal welfare facilities, with exemplary morale, and they don't utter a single word of complaint or grievance. We, who have ourselves lived through the era of the Sacred Defense [Iran-Iraq war] and have been in this system for years, feel small before the greatness of their morale, and this situation is truly indescribable. We're ready to arrange the preliminaries for a trip so that you and your respected colleagues can go to those areas in person, talk with them, conduct interviews, and tell their stories to the people. Anyone who's gone to these areas has been astonished by their will, their morale, and their interesting and creative initiatives in the areas of defense and offense. Even foreign journalists who are sometimes sent to visit are deeply amazed by this level of sacrifice, patriotism, love for the people, and idealism.
What's your assessment of Iran's missile, drone, and air defense capabilities compared to the beginning of the war?
Our capability has undoubtedly increased greatly, both quantitatively and qualitatively. Just this morning I was in a meeting where they were reporting that our capability has increased at least one and a half times compared to the past; because we never halted our production — never. The enemy, in its foolish imagination, comes and targets some of our centers and facilities and claims, "I destroyed their air force, their navy, and their missile industries," but that's not the case, and the enemy's imagination is foolish. We never stopped producing missiles, drones, and whatever else we needed in this war and will need in the future; not only did we not stop, we expanded it. Today we've brought many other centers into our organization for producing more weapons, creating greater precision in targeting, increasing destructive power, extending the range of weapons, and producing entirely new armaments. We've brought all our capacity to bear, and praise God, we've succeeded very well.
A very important point that I think many people have experienced is that in special conditions, talents emerge. What we've witnessed and experienced firsthand in this war is that in special conditions we achieve things that might be unbelievable even to ourselves, and are certainly unbelievable to others. This is divine grace, and it's due to the sincerity our forces have — those who have come to the field with all their being and selflessly, and have brought their strong will against the enemy. They fight with will, they fight with sincerity, and naturally divine grace helps too. God Almighty says that whoever strives in Our path, We will surely show him the way. God Almighty has shown and continues to show our combatants ways that are unbelievable — ways a person might not have even imagined before. In bottlenecks, in special conditions, in emergency conditions, and in conditions of connection to the infinite divine source, ways, paths, initiatives, and innovations are found that are wonder-making, and if the war continues or escalates again, these wonder-makers will certainly reveal themselves, God willing.
So, given all this, can we conclude that we possess weapons that we have not yet used?
Yes. Naturally, no country reveals all its weapons in the very first stages of battle. To this day, we have also long used weapons that were produced decades ago, and what has been employed during this period has mainly been older reserves and productions. We never use a weapon that should be reserved for more special conditions in less special conditions; naturally, that is how it will be.
Why do some regional countries, even knowing that American bases on their soil will be targeted if used against Iran, still grant the US this permission?
The first and most important point is that these countries have realized that the bases that were supposed to help their security have not helped at all — they have actually endangered their security. That is, what has the existence of a base, for example in Kuwait or Bahrain or any of them, done for that country so far? Nothing! That base has not even been able to defend itself. For example, what benefit has the so-called American naval headquarters and its Fifth Fleet stationed in Bahrain brought to Bahrain so far? No benefit at all — it has actually been to their detriment. They themselves have realized that these bases cannot provide their security, and beyond that, they have understood that America also cannot provide their security; even America cannot provide security for its own forces, and they have come to this truth.
But your question is: now that they have reached this conclusion, why do they not cut off their relations and abandon them? Naturally, they have contracts with them and have given commitments to America — perhaps as reciprocal commitments — and maybe in the back of their minds they still have some hopes regarding America that stop them from acting quickly; but they will do it, and they will do it gradually. What was the first step in this regard? The Mecca Pact. This pact was concluded among three countries — Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan — without foreign interference; this itself shows that they have become disappointed with pacts with foreign countries like America and have seen that they are of no use to them, and so they have turned to a regional pact.
Such regional pacts, and the possible desire of other countries to join them or even to conclude new pacts, stem from the fact that they have concluded that a foreign country thousands of kilometers away cannot provide their security. So, to answer you specifically: they have concluded that they must gradually separate from America and have these bases removed from their countries; but because of their commitments, their not-so-great hopes regarding America, and the limitations they currently have, they cannot do this quickly — but they will gradually bring it about. If the current generation does not do it — which in my view it certainly will — the next generation will one hundred percent accomplish it.
This is a logical, rational, and experienced process. Based on this understanding, new decisions must certainly be made and we must turn to the regional countries themselves. We too, truly, based on the guidelines of the martyred Imam and the esteemed Leader of the Islamic Revolution, have always wanted to be friends, allies, and to have exchanges with these countries. We have many commonalities in this region — generational, religious, cultural, historical commonalities, historical exchanges, and in some cases a shared destiny.
Now, for example, suppose this region becomes insecure for Iran — will security be created for those countries? Never! There will be absolutely no security in this region without Iran's security, and it will not come about. No security pact will take shape in this region without creating security for Iran; this is a logical matter, and empirical processes have proven it.
So we once again declare to the regional countries — we have fifteen neighbors, apart from those somewhat farther away — that these countries must themselves come together, resolve minor differences, and provide their own security. We too are ready to conclude joint pacts with every single country in which American bases are located, and to provide security regionally and locally, and we certainly have this capability.
Recently, the IRGC published a detailed letter addressed to the American people. What was the purpose behind publishing this letter?
In the first place, our goal was to enlighten and inform the American people. We feel that the American people are unaware of many realities; and the reason for this unawareness is that their leaders and ruling establishment lie to them and do not tell them the truth. Their media too are heavily controlled and subservient to the ruling establishment and cannot express other truths contrary to their views. We have numerous examples of this; even in the case of this very letter's publication, many [Western] media outlets boycotted and opposed it, and this shows that they do not allow the facts to reach the ears of the American people. So we wanted through this letter to clarify part of the realities and explain that the American people themselves are also oppressed by their ruling establishment.
That is, the actions America takes, the aggressions it commits against various countries, the massacres it carries out, the numerous bases it has around the world, and the enormous costs it spends to run these bases and forces and equipment — all of it is paid from the pockets of the American people; but the benefit does not reach the American people — rather, it goes into the pockets of the ruling establishment and the main capitalists of America. In other words, the American people today are in the service of American capitalists and Zionist thinking, and we are certain that a large portion of the American people are unaware of this reality.
By the way, what war or enmity do the American people have with the people of Iraq, that a million human beings should be killed over a lie? What enmity do the American people really have with the people of Iran — or conversely, what enmity could the people of Iran possibly have with the American people — that from thousands of kilometers away, they should martyr our leaders, commanders, and scientists, threaten our country with disintegration, plunder our underground resources, threaten to occupy our islands, and target our missile capability? We truly consider it unlikely that these are the wishes of the American people. What real enmity can our two nations have with each other? These actions are in fact carried out by the leaders and ruling establishment of America, and because of their many lies and their concealment of realities from their own people. Our primary goal was in fact to enlighten, inform, and raise awareness among the American people.
You became the successor to General Ali-Mohammad Naeini, who was assassinated by the US and Israel during the 40-day war. Did this cause any doubt for you, or any opposition from your family, regarding accepting this responsibility?
For me personally, such doubt has never existed and doesn't exist; because we've concluded in our school, religion, Quranic teachings, and religious knowledge that we must carry out whatever duty is created for us. When this matter was proposed to me and I felt it was my duty, I didn't hesitate at all and I said to myself: right now this is my duty and I must carry it out. If, on the path of carrying out this duty, God Almighty grants us martyrdom, that's a great triumph; meaning I've lost nothing — rather, I've attained eternal felicity.
So, based on that well-known teaching in our religious knowledge — "one of the two best outcomes" (one of two good things, both of which are good) — if I can carry out my duty well at this juncture, I've attained one of those good things, and blessed be I; and if I'm martyred on this path, I've attained the second good thing, and again blessed be I. That is, in both cases I've lost nothing and in both cases I've gained something; carrying out one's duty well is one felicity, and martyrdom on its path is another felicity, and whichever befalls me is one of those two good things.
Truly, for my family too there was no doubt whatsoever; because my family is far more revolutionary, stronger, and more spirited than I am myself, and in fact, in many of these arenas, they've been our encouragers from the very beginning until now. So martyrdom for me is felicity, and if it befalls me I'll be very happy; and I advise the survivors too to be happy and to take pride.

Ukraine Develops D·Vision SDR RF Analyzer That Intercepts Drone Video
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
12:46:39 UTC
21:46:39 KST

Ukrainian company CODE380 has developed the portable D·Vision SDR radio frequency analyzer, which scans the airwaves for drone signals and lets users view video transmitted over analog communication channels.
The device’s developers told DOU about the system.
According to the manufacturer’s technical documentation, the device can detect PAL and NTSC analog video signals, as well as compatible digital signals from DJI Mavic drones.
The analyzer uses software-defined radio (SDR) technology, which lets software process and analyze radio signals.
Unlike conventional analog video receivers, D·Vision SDR uses software to search for and identify characteristic drone signals across a wide frequency range.
However, the device can play back footage only from analog video channels. The device cannot decode DJI digital video but can detect the corresponding radio signals.
According to the manufacturer, analog video reception and viewing range at frequencies of 540–6,000 MHz can reach 10 km, while above 6,000 MHz it ranges from 3.5 to 5 km. The analyzer can detect compatible digital video signals from DJI Mavic drones at distances of up to 2.5 km.
The analyzer has two SMA antenna inputs, supports data recording to a microSD card, and includes a built-in screen to display scan results.
Additional features include a waterfall display of radio spectrum activity, EW system testing, and USB remote control.
Depending on the version, the device offers up to three or six hours of battery life. It weighs approximately 290 grams without antennas and measures 130 × 80 × 22 mm.
According to DOU, developing the analyzer’s software and hardware took more than a year, while the entire process, from the start of development to the finished product, took approximately a year and a half.
The developers said the device underwent field testing with the participation of Ukrainian service members, particularly during combat missions.
Ukraine is actively developing portable electronic intelligence systems designed to detect enemy drones promptly.
In March, Militarnyi reported on the development of the Vydun 7.5 detector by Ukrainian company BABAI, which can intercept analog video signals from drones at frequencies of up to 7.5 GHz.
Contra-drone has also introduced the portable SENSE-4 detector, which can identify analog video signals at frequencies of up to 8.2 GHz.
In August, BlueBird Tech also began upgrading its Chuyka 3.0 detectors to expand their capabilities by adding a frequency band from 6 to 8.8 GHz.

India calls out Meta over election protests
India has asked Meta to review how Facebook and Instagram recommend content, citing concerns that their algorithms disproportionately promote certain narratives, amid protests over disputed voter rolls in New Delhi. 
The advisory from India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) calls for changes to content-ranking systems to prevent misleading, manipulated, or out-of-context material from being repeatedly recommended to users, news agency PTI reported on Monday after reviewing the document which was issued on October 10. 
Meta has been asked to act immediately and inform the government of the steps taken. 
The advisory comes amid demonstrations by the youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and opposition parties demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a nationwide electoral-roll revision. 
Opposition groups allege that legitimate voters have been excluded and that the exercise benefits Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). The Election Commission and BJP deny manipulating voter lists. The advisory does not identify any specific protest as the reason for its issuance. 
The document calls on Meta to prevent users from being disproportionately exposed to a “single or limited set of narratives” and ensure greater diversity of credible information. 
India’s IT Ministry has received reports from government agencies suggesting that Meta’s algorithms favor certain kinds of content, PTI reported, citing sources in the ministry.
The ministry has flagged videos, photographs, and graphics relating to public events, particularly police action and restrictions, being promoted without adequate context. It wants stronger checks on old or selectively edited visuals presented as current events and unverified claims about official measures.
Meta has also been asked to identify potentially harmful content gaining significant reach more quickly and cooperate with authorized law-enforcement agencies under India’s information technology laws. The request follows a broader advisory issued to social media companies on October 8, directing them to prioritize complaints from government agencies and label misleading or manipulated content related to public events.
Although the advisory is not legally binding, it amounts to a “continuing censorship directive,” Internet Freedom Foundation founder-director Apar Gupta said. He urged the government to withdraw it and Meta to disclose content removals or reductions in visibility carried out under its provisions.
The ministry maintains that the measures are intended to protect public order while respecting lawful expression.

The Princess of the Netherlands was promoted to the military rank of sergeant

Catharina-Amalia was promoted to sergeant during a ceremony aboard a training sailing ship in the port of Den Helder. She participates in Defensity College.
Princess Catharina-Amalia of the Netherlands has been promoted to the rank of sergeant. The ceremony took place aboard the training sailing ship Statsraad Lehmkuhl in the port of Den Helder. This is stated in a statement by the Dutch Ministry of Defence, reports UNN.
Details
The promotion took place as part of the Defensity College programme, which gives students the opportunity to combine their studies with military work. Programme participants gain practical experience in various units of the armed forces and also take part in military events and training exercises.
The Royal House and the Armed Forces
The Dutch Royal House has historically maintained close ties with the country's armed forces. William of Orange was a military commander, while later Dutch kings held supreme command of the armed forces.
After amendments to the Constitution in 1983, supreme command was transferred to the government.
King Willem-Alexander also has military experience. He completed compulsory military service in the Royal Netherlands Navy and later served in the Royal Netherlands Army and Royal Netherlands Air Force.
As king, Willem-Alexander holds a special position in the armed forces and has a special military status.

Funding shortfall forces WFP to cut food aid to 500,000 Gazans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
12:45:00 UTC
21:45:00 KST

The World Food Programme said Monday it would end monthly assistance to 500,000 people in Gaza due to a funding shortfall, despite acute needs in the war-torn Palestinian territory.
The cutbacks mean 1.1 million Palestinians in Gaza, about half the population, will receive either food or cash assistance each month from the U.N. agency in reduced amounts.
The WFP said its efforts mitigated the effects of a famine last year in Gaza – a description Israel disputed – and warned conditions had not improved enough to withdraw aid.
"People are not safe. Airstrikes continue daily. People remain displaced," Shaun Hughes, the WFP country director, told Agence France-Presse (AFP) in East Jerusalem.
"Almost everyone remains without a permanent home. The humanitarian conditions are brutal," he said.
Latest assessments show 1.4 million people, two-thirds of Gaza's population, are still "acutely food insecure" and need humanitarian aid to survive, he said.
Last August, the U.N.'s Integrated Food Security Phase Classification reported Gaza suffered famine conditions.
Israel, which has blockaded and waged a genocidal war on the territory since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas incursion, described the finding as a lie.
The classification was lifted in December, two months after a U.S.-brokered cease-fire was announced in Gaza. Israel, however, has continued striking Gaza since then.
Since the cease-fire, the WFP stepped up assistance, reaching between 1.5 million and 1.8 million people monthly.
"This has been a lifeline. But now, rather than being able to sustain and scale up that assistance, we're actually having to reduce it," Hughes said.
"That's not because we don't have humanitarian access to deliver food; that's because we don't have funding."
In addition to reducing the number of ration recipients, the WFP also has reduced ration content.
Families receiving food assistance will now get one food parcel instead of two, along with a smaller bag of wheat flour, the WFP said in an operational note.
The 75,000 families receiving cash assistance will see amounts reduced from 1,250 to 750 shekels ($400 to $240) monthly.
The WFP is funded by governments and private donors. It has seen a sharp drop in resources, including when President Donald Trump's administration drastically slashed contributions to U.N. agencies and bilateral aid.
The agency says it needs about $450 million over the next six months for its operations in Gaza and the Israeli-occupied West Bank, but this year it has received only about half the usual funding for the Palestinian territories.
In September, the agency also halved the number of aid recipients in the West Bank, which Israel has occupied since 1967, from 400,000 to 200,000.
"Now is not the time in the history of Palestine and Gaza to turn away from what is happening in Gaza," Hughes said.
The WFP says conditions have moderately improved in Gaza but notes needs could rise again with the onset of winter.
Israel has allowed more goods into Gaza under the terms of a U.S.-brokered cease-fire but still imposes heavy restrictions, turning away shipments of anything with alleged military use – a policy that has included blocking even prosthetic limbs, the United Nations says.
Israel, meanwhile, has ramped up longstanding criticism of the United Nations since the Gaza war, accusing the world body of bias and perpetuating dependency among Palestinians.

Airhub Aviation, an aircraft lifecycle management company specialising in aircraft asset management, maintenance, component repair management and end-of-life solutions, has expanded its base maintenance scope to include Airbus A320neo aircraft powered by either CFM LEAP or Pratt & Whitney GTF engines, as well as Boeing 737 MAX aircraft, following the successful completion of a regulatory audit by Lithuania’s Transport Competence Agency (TKA).
“The aviation market is evolving rapidly, and technical capabilities must evolve with it. Expanding our Airbus A320neo and Boeing 737MAX maintenance scope responds directly to growing demand from lessors, operators and aftermarket players for specialized support across new-generation aircraft platforms. It also strengthens our capabilities across the broader aircraft lifecycle, with a continued focus on technical asset management and residual value preservation,” said Oleg Novak, Managing Director of Airhub Aviation.
“We are seeing growing demand not only for regular 24-month checks but also for the first 12-year checks on new-generation aircraft. A wave of A320neo aircraft is now approaching this milestone, bringing additional challenges for operators, including potentially longer ground times, as these checks are being performed for the first time in the aircraft’s operational lifecycle. Managing these complex maintenance events in the most cost-effective manner requires extensive technical expertise and strong MRO capabilities.
Additionally, over the past 12 months, we have seen the first Boeing 737 MAX 8 undergo an end-of-life management process, while A320neo part-outs are also gaining momentum following several airline insolvencies in 2025–2026,” added Novak.
Airhub Aviation Advances Airbus A220 Service Strategy
Alongside the expansion of its A320neo and 737 MAX maintenance scope, Airhub Aviation is progressing with plans to extend its technical service offering to the Airbus A220 platform.
The company is currently undergoing the approval process and developing capabilities covering line maintenance, aircraft transitions and end-of-life asset management, in cooperation with an established industry-leading partner.
Airhub Aviation sees the expansion of its new-generation aircraft capabilities as part of a broader response to changing market conditions.
“Despite ongoing fleet modernization, the industry continues to face supply chain constraints, limited engine shop capacity and delays in new aircraft deliveries. These pressures are increasing the need for solutions that keep aircraft operational while preserving long-term asset value, and are also driving demand for flexible technical slot availability across the aircraft lifecycle. Demand for specialized technical support is growing across NEO, MAX and A220 fleets, particularly where expertise in complex maintenance, aircraft transitions and asset management is required,” said Oleg Novak, Managing Director of Airhub Aviation.
Airhub Aviation provides independent, asset-focused technical services across the aircraft lifecycle and continues to expand its maintenance scope to cover new-generation aircraft. The company operates a five-bay MRO facility with extensive aircraft parking capacity and maintains partnerships with Airbus and other leading aviation OEMs.

Far-right Ben-Gvir calls on French Jews to move to Israel amid unrest
Israel's far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir has urged the French Jewish community to leave France and move to Israel amid widespread protests over the cost of living, as the Israeli government reportedly prepares a broader campaign to encourage Jewish immigration from the European country.
Ben-Gvir made the appeal during a conference for France's Jewish community in the central Israeli city of Netanya, attended by hundreds of supporters of his far-right Otzma Yehudit party, according to a statement released late on Sunday.
"There are people in France today from various quarters who are seeking to harm Israel," Ben-Gvir claimed, without identifying the groups he was referring to or providing evidence for his allegations.
He urged the French government to reconsider its policies and its treatment of those allegedly seeking to expand their influence in the country.
"All of Europe must wake up, and the whole world must wake up," he declared, before addressing French Jews directly.
"Come home. Come back here. Be here. This is your home, and this is your homeland," he said.
Ben-Gvir, who oversees Israel's police and prison system rather than immigration policy, has long been associated with anti-Palestinian extremism and has previously been convicted of incitement to racism and violence and supporting a banned Jewish extremist organisation.
He has also repeatedly advocated the expansion of Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories and called for the expulsion by force of Palestinians from Gaza.
His appeal comes just days before Israel's 27 October parliamentary elections, amid a campaign in which far-right politicians have increasingly promoted expansionist policies.
It also follows reports that Israeli ministers have been preparing to encourage a potentially significant increase in Jewish immigration from France.
According to Israeli media, Immigration and Integration Minister Ofir Sofer urged the government during a cabinet meeting on 6 October to prepare for potentially "massive" immigration from France.
"We need to remove the barriers in order to allow them to come here," Sofer reportedly told ministers.
Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich also reportedly called for funding to help prospective immigrants, while Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu instructed ministers to develop a joint plan.
The discussions suggest Ben-Gvir's latest appeal forms part of a wider Israeli government effort to capitalise on the unrest in France to encourage immigration, rather than an isolated response to the protests.
Israeli officials have also sought to link the demonstrations to concerns about antisemitism, although the protests themselves have primarily focused on economic hardship, education and public services.
France formally recognised the State of Palestine in September 2025 and joined other Western countries last month in announcing restrictions on trade involving products from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories.
France grapples with mass protests
France has experienced some of its worst civil unrest in years, following mass demonstrations on Saturday against rising living costs, fuel prices and deteriorating public services.
Around half a million people took to the streets, with students, trade unionists and members of the Yellow Vests movement among those protesting.
While many demonstrations were peaceful, clashes erupted in several cities, including Paris, where buildings and vehicles were set ablaze and shops looted.
More than 2,500 people were arrested over the weekend, while nearly 1,000 members of the security forces were injured, according to French authorities.
On Monday, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu called for localised curfews after protesters blocked the entrance to the Louvre Museum, warning that a state of emergency could be imposed if necessary.
President Emmanuel Macron acknowledged failures in the security response but blamed groups on the far left for the violence, while recognising the legitimacy of peaceful protesters' social demands.
Iran's foreign minister takes aim at Macron
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi also seized on the protests to criticise Macron, accusing him of supporting the US-Israeli war against Iran while failing to listen to demonstrators in his own country.
"Mr. Macron brought this situation upon himself when he assured the US President that he welcomed crimes against Iranians," Araghchi wrote on X, according to IranWire.
"Now it is too late to blame the war that people like him helped unleash."
The Iranian minister then offered Macron advice on handling public discontent.
"The French people want fundamental changes, including the freedom of assembly. Mr. President, listen to the voice of France's future," he wrote.
The unrest in France has meanwhile spread to other European countries, with demonstrations and clashes reported in Belgium and Italy, while protests over housing and living costs continue in Spain and Portugal.

Something strange is happening beneath a volcano near 2 million people
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
12:35:09 UTC
21:35:09 KST

Something strange is happening beneath a volcano near 2 million people
- Date:
- October 19, 2026
- Source:
- Penn State University
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered evidence of two hidden magma sources beneath Nicaragua’s Masaya volcano, where satellite observations revealed mysterious ground movements suggesting magma is shifting deep underground. The findings could improve eruption forecasting for the active volcano, which sits near 2 million people and attracts tourists to its spectacular lava lake.
- Share:
A volcano famous for its glowing lava lake is hiding a surprisingly complex system of magma deep underground. Scientists at Penn State have uncovered evidence of two previously unrecognized magma sources beneath Nicaragua's active Masaya volcano, raising new questions about how molten rock moves beneath the surface.
The discovery is particularly important because approximately 2 million people live within 13 miles of the volcano, which is also a popular tourist destination. Understanding its underground activity could help scientists recognize warning signs of future eruptions and better protect nearby communities.
Using six years of satellite observations, researchers tracked subtle changes in the ground around Masaya. They discovered that one part of the volcano initially sank before beginning to rise, possibly indicating that fresh magma was entering a deep reservoir. Meanwhile, the ground around its active Santiago crater and lava lake continued to sink, suggesting that a separate, shallower magma reservoir was behaving differently.
The findings, published in Geophysical Research Letters, reveal that the volcano's underground magma system may be considerably more complicated than previously understood.
"These observations help scientists better understand how magma moves beneath Masaya and may improve monitoring and eruption forecasting in the future," said lead author Lizzie Johnson, who earned her bachelor's degree in geosciences from Penn State in May.
Why Masaya Volcano Is Closely Monitored
Located near Managua, Nicaragua's capital, Masaya is a geologically complex volcano featuring multiple overlapping craters and calderas. Calderas are large depressions that generally form when the ground collapses after magma is removed from an underground chamber.
Although scientists have studied Masaya for years, the movement of magma through its underground reservoirs and passageways remains poorly understood. These systems can change over time, making it difficult to determine exactly what is happening beneath the volcano.
"Having a thorough understanding of Masaya's volcanic activity and its related hazards is critical as around 2 million people live near Masaya and the caldera is a national park and popular tourist destination," Johnson said. "Although Masaya last produced a major lava flow in 1772, its persistent degassing often produces dangerously high concentrations of sulfur dioxide volcanic gas."
Sulfur dioxide is a potentially harmful volcanic gas released as magma approaches or remains near the surface. Even without a major eruption, elevated concentrations can create dangerous conditions for visitors and surrounding communities.
Young Cheol Kim, who completed his doctorate in geosciences at Penn State this summer, explained that monitoring the volcano continuously is essential for distinguishing normal activity from changes that might signal increasing volcanic hazards.
"Doing continuous monitoring allows us to understand the baseline activity and identify see if things are changing," he said, explaining that certain shifts in volcanic behavior could indicate a period of heightened activity or a possible eruption. "And then if there is a need to warn people, we can do that in a timely manner."
Satellites Reveal Hidden Movements Beneath the Volcano
To investigate Masaya's underground activity, the researchers analyzed measurements collected by the Sentinel-1 satellite, which observes the volcano approximately once every 12 days.
The team used a technique called interferometric synthetic aperture radar (InSAR), which can detect extremely small changes in the elevation of Earth's surface. By comparing satellite measurements taken at different times, scientists can identify areas where the ground is rising or sinking.
The technique combines two important capabilities. Synthetic aperture radar sends microwave signals toward Earth's surface, allowing satellites to collect measurements even when clouds obscure the ground. Interferometry compares the returning radar signals to detect changes in distance between the satellite and the surface.
This is especially valuable in tropical regions, where frequent cloud cover can make conventional satellite imagery less reliable.
"Cloud penetration is important for volcanoes because many of them, like Masaya, are in tropical areas where there is often cloud cover," Kim explained. "And when we look at all the different satellite images across multiple years, we can see how the distance between the satellite and the ground changes, where it is uplifting or subsiding."
By examining these subtle movements over time, researchers can investigate processes happening far below the surface without directly observing the magma itself.
Two Magma Reservoirs Behaving in Different Ways
The satellite measurements revealed an intriguing pattern between 2018 and 2024. During the first part of the study, the ground within Masaya's caldera gradually subsided, meaning it moved downward. Later, the same general area began to rise.
Scientists believe this transition could reflect changes in the amount of magma stored underground. When magma drains away from a reservoir, the overlying ground can sink. When additional magma enters and increases pressure within a reservoir, the surface may rise.
The most surprising finding was that the area surrounding Santiago crater did not follow the same pattern. Instead, it continued to sink throughout the six-year study, even as the broader caldera began rising.
"When it's subsiding, that means that there's probably magma draining away from the volcano, but once the ground starts uplifting again, that can mean that there's potentially new magma moving in," Johnson said. "At the same time, the area directly around the active Santiago crater deflated over the entire study period independently of the transition to inflation of the main reservoir. This indicates that the plumbing system is more complex and could be due to decreasing magma in a second, shallower reservoir."
Together, these observations suggest that Masaya may have at least two distinct parts of its magma storage system undergoing different changes. A deeper source could be supplying additional magma to the main reservoir, while a shallower reservoir near Santiago crater may be losing magma.
This would help explain why different sections of the same volcano moved in opposite directions.
What the Discovery Means for Future Eruptions
Understanding these underground movements is important because changes in the ground can provide clues about where magma is accumulating, where it is moving, and how it might eventually reach the surface.
The researchers emphasized that their observations did not reveal any immediate danger to communities surrounding Masaya. However, identifying the volcano's normal behavior and understanding its magma supply system could make it easier to recognize unusual changes in the future.
Continued satellite observations, combined with more detailed computer models, could also help scientists better understand the connections between underground magma reservoirs and volcanic activity at the surface.
"Further long-term geodetic and modeling studies will provide a more thorough understanding and allow for effective hazard monitoring and mitigation at Masaya and other lava-lake hosting basaltic volcanoes," Johnson said.
The findings may therefore have implications beyond Nicaragua, particularly for other active volcanoes that contain persistent lava lakes and complex underground magma systems.
From Undergraduate Research to Volcano Science
Johnson became involved in the project after attending a presentation by Christelle Wauthier, a Penn State professor of geosciences and computational sciences hub director at the university's Institute for Computational and Data Sciences.
She completed the research as part of her Schreyer's Honors College thesis, working alongside graduate researchers, including Kim, to analyze satellite measurements and develop her scientific skills.
"I appreciated learning how a research group works," said Johnson, who has recently started a doctoral program in Earth sciences at the University of Hawaii at Manoa, where she will continue studying volcanoes using seismic waves to image below the surface of Kilauea volcano. "I had never had any experience with research, so it was great to be able to join in the group meetings and get to hear about everybody's work. And learning coding was also useful as I continue with my Ph.D."

Protests over high prices and problems with public services were accompanied by clashes, riots, and looting. 32 people were arrested.
On Sunday, during riots in Milan, Italian police detained 271 young people. This occurred on the second day of protests sparked by the unsatisfactory state of public services and the rising cost of living; during the demonstrations, protesters clashed with law enforcement officers, looted shops and damaged property, UNN reports, citing Reuters.

In addition

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, who faces elections next year, condemned the violence and announced a government meeting on Monday to discuss ways to resolve the situation.
