First Evacuation by Hexacopter: Soldiers from the 92nd Assault Brigade and 30th Mechanized Brigade Rescue Wounded Fighter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
11:20:14 UTC
20:20:14 KST

Service members of the Unmanned Ground Systems Company of the 92nd Assault Brigade named after Kish Otaman Ivan Sirko have carried out their first successful aerial evacuation of a wounded soldier from the front line.
The Company announced this on Facebook.
The operation followed the wounding of an infantryman from the 30th Mechanized Brigade named after Prince Konstanty Ostrogski at the position.
Intense enemy drone activity and dense minefields made evacuation using UGVs impossible.
To rescue the service member, they decided to use a heavy-lift hexacopter from Gurzuf Defence, provided free of charge by a Ukrainian company.
Ukrainian specialists worked with the developers to implement technical solutions that enabled the heavy-lift hexacopter to evacuate wounded personnel without swaying or risking an in-flight rollover. Before the mission, the specialists conducted a series of tests at the manufacturer’s dedicated testing sites.
During the mission, a UAV operator from the 30th Mechanized Brigade controlled the drone. The wounded soldier was successfully transported to a safe location and is now receiving medical treatment and rehabilitation. Specialists from the 92nd Assault Brigade, the 30th and 14th Mechanized Brigades, the 10th Army Corps, and Gurzuf Defence made this unique mission possible through coordinated efforts.

ComBat Vision Develops Gamified Training Tool for Artillery Crews
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
11:16:06 UTC
20:16:06 KST

Ukrainian company ComBat Vision has developed a specialized tool to introduce gamification elements into artillery fire adjustment.
The developers cite changes in training levels among service members joining the Ukrainian Defense Forces as the reason for these adjustments.
According to the developers, the quality of recruits entering the military is declining rapidly, with some artillery crew members being former “TikTokers” or gamers.
To address this problem, the company’s specialists decided to make the firing and aiming process as visually clear as possible for users. The new tool can visualize a projectile’s flight trajectory based on the firing tables for the relevant weapon system.
The system also displays the dispersion area for a specific weapon type and ammunition. This lets the operator assess the probability of hitting the target and potential deviation in advance.
An important feature of the new module is its ability to warn users of potential obstacles along the calculated projectile trajectory.
The system can also simulate a projectile’s flight after a shot is fired, based on the selected charge’s characteristics. A training error is added to the calculations, allowing users to practice subsequent ranging adjustments.
During operation, the module displays simulated or actual impacts and automatically calculates the mean correction based on a series of hits. This simplifies the analysis of firing results and improves the accuracy of subsequent shots.
Operators can enter the necessary corrections in various ways, including through voice commands, and immediately see the updated result on screen.
This approach makes it easier to demonstrate how indirect-fire weapons work and effectively train service members to adjust artillery fire.
The integrated plugin uses the ballistics model from the UkropSoft MyGun app.
ComBat Vision has previously offered to equip UGVs from Ratel and Tencore LLC with an external compass for UAH 3,500.

Swedish appeals court fines ex-national security adviser for gross negligence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
11:15:56 UTC
20:15:56 KST

Swedish appeals court fines ex-national security adviser for gross negligence
STOCKHOLM, Oct 19 - A Swedish appeals court on Monday found former national security adviser Henrik Landerholm, a friend of the prime minister, guilty of mishandling secret information, overturning a lower court ruling.
The case, involving documents left at a hotel in 2023, has embarrassed Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson as it unfolded against the backdrop of a deepening security crisis in the Baltic Sea region following Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Kristersson submitted his resignation after his right-wing government lost its parliamentary majority in a general election in September, but he is leading a caretaker government while a new government is being formed.
Last year, a district court found Landerholm not guilty, saying he had been negligent, but not gravely.
"Unlike the district court ... the court of appeal finds that the man disclosed the information contained in the documents through gross negligence," the Svea Court of Appeal in Stockholm said in a statement.
"The only reasonable explanation for the man having left the documents behind is that he was quite careless when emptying the safe-deposit box where he had kept them," it said.
The appeals court fined Landerholm, Sweden's first national security adviser, 52,000 Swedish crowns ($5,247).
Landerholm, who has pleaded not guilty, stepped down in January 2025 after the investigations began.
His defence lawyer was not immediately available for comment and Landerholm did not immediately respond to a request for comment. REUTERS

The “Week of Italian Cuisine in the World” returns to Athens for its 11th edition, celebrating this year the recognition of Italian cuisine as a UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage. From October 20 to 23, the Italian Embassy, in collaboration with the ICE Office in Athens and the Lombardy Region, will bring the culinary and wine excellence of Lombardy to the Greek capital, presented by Chef Stefano Grandi of the “Il Santa” restaurant in Milan. Fifteen consortia from the region will take center stage at the event, showcasing cheeses, cured meats, and wines that have always reflected the richness of Lombardy’s culinary heritage. Guests will be guided on a journey through traditions and flavors, showcased through the specialties of Lombardy’s provinces. Councilor Alessandro Beduschi will lead the Lombardy Region delegation participating in the events in Athens. The week’s program includes events at the residence of Ambassador Paolo Cuculi and at the Italian restaurant “Sole e Giaguaro” —for industry professionals and media representatives—and will conclude with a masterclass by Chef Stefano Grandi at the IEK-AKMI School of Gastronomy and Hospitality in Athens, dedicated to students. The consortia collaborating on the initiative are: the Provolone Valpadana Protection Consortium; the Grana Padano Protection Consortium; the Gorgonzola Protection Consortium; the Taleggio Protection Consortium; the Quartirolo Lombardo Protection Consortium; the Salva Cremasco Protection Consortium; Valtellina Casera and Bitto Protection Consortium; Bresaola della Valtellina Protection Consortium; Cacciatore Italiano Protection Consortium; Lugana DOC Wines Protection Consortium; Valtènesi Wines Consortium; Oltrepò Pavese Wine Protection Consortium; Franciacorta Protection Consortium; Mantua Wine Protection Consortium; Valtellina Wine Protection Consortium; AS.CO.VI.LO. – Association of Lombardy Wine Consortia

Protesters block Louvre as cost-of-living fury rocks France
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
11:12:27 UTC
20:12:27 KST

French PM calls for curfews as cost-of-living fury rocks France
- Protesters blocked the Louvre in Paris as France faced mass cost-of-living unrest. The Yellow Vests called new protests after a weekend of violence across the country.
- More than 2,500 people were arrested and nearly 1,000 police were injured. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said police “had lost control”, and Macron ordered a security review.
- Rising prices are driving anger across Europe. France faces election pressure, while smaller protests and clashes have also spread to Italy, Spain and Portugal.
AI generated
PARIS – French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu called for localised curfews on Oct 19, as protesters blocked the entrance to the Louvre in Paris, and the authorities scrambled to stem public discontent that over the weekend saw mass cost-of-living demonstrations spill over into some of the worst street violence in recent years.
Lecornu huddled with ministers in a crisis meeting after the interior minister said the police “had lost control” during the weekend’s unrest.
With the Yellow Vests movement, which organised the weekend’s rallies, calling for a new round of protests on Oct 24, Lecornu called for the regional authorities to impose “partial” and “localised” curfews to protect businesses after hundreds of shops were damaged and looted.
“I’m absolutely determined to restore public order,” he vowed, adding that the government was ready to impose a state of emergency “if needed”.
Other European countries, where anger over rising prices has also led to protests, were keeping a nervous eye on the developments, with smaller clashes breaking out in Milan and Belgium over the weekend and protests simmering in Spain and Portugal.
Some half a million people turned out across France on Oct 17 to denounce the surging cost of living, a culmination of four weeks of protests that began with high school students demanding better conditions at their schools.
What started as peaceful demonstrations morphed into violence in some places, as masked groups on the sidelines of the protests attacked law enforcement, broke into town halls and other public buildings, setting many of them ablaze, looted shops, and set fire to cars, bicycles and scooters on the streets.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez offered to resign on Oct 19 after more than 2,500 people were arrested and nearly 1,000 members of the security forces injured. Protesters were also hurt, with one demonstrator’s hand blown off by a police crowd-control grenade.
“On (Oct 17), in some major cities, you couldn’t look shopkeepers in the eye after hundreds of shops had been looted and tell them we hadn’t lost control,” Nunez said.
French President Emmanuel Macron refused Nunez’s resignation, even as he acknowledged security and intelligence failures in the government response, despite the some 60,000 law enforcement personnel deployed across France on Oct 17.
Nationwide, more than 2,330 people were taken into police custody over the weekend, 70% of whom were adults, Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said Oct 19.
More than 2,000 shops were expected to have been affected by the weekend’s violence across France, with damage running into “hundreds of millions of euros”, according to chamber of commerce president Alain Di Crescenzo.
In an address to the nation late on Oct 18, Macron slammed the “unbridled” violence and said the local authorities would be able to ban – “if necessary” – certain rallies in the coming days.
But he stopped short of announcing drastic measures, such as a state of emergency or curfew.
The city authorities in Marseille said on Oct 19 that public gatherings would be banned from noon to 8pm.
The European Union slammed the weekend violence as “unacceptable” but warned that the right to peaceful protest “must be protected” in France.
Germany condemned the violence and updated its travel advice for France, saying “further demonstrations and, in some cases, further outbreaks of violence in the coming days cannot be ruled out”.
Britain said the right to protest “can never excuse violence”.
Discontent spreads
The public discontent showed no signs of subsiding on Oct 19, with demonstrators blocking the entrance to Paris’ iconic Louvre Museum, the most visited in the world.
“We are proud to announce that we are blocking the world’s largest museum,” read a leaflet posted outside the museum, as management and unions said the protest was led by students from Ecole du Louvre.
Rising prices have fuelled anger in France, where diesel prices have jumped nearly 40% and petrol by 25% since March, and where food prices have risen by 25% since 2021.
The unrest in France has flared just months before a key presidential election where centrist Macron cannot stand again and Marine Le Pen, the far-right presidential candidate for the National Rally party, is riding high in the polls.
Ministers have blamed “ultra-left” groups for the violence, while Le Pen claimed that the party of her far-left rival for the presidency, Jean-Luc Melenchon, has “legitimised the violence”.
The left has accused Macron of ignoring protesters’ demands, while the right is calling on him to take a firmer line.
With costs of living rising across Europe, smaller demonstrations have broken out in other countries.
During the weekend, clashes broke out on the sidelines of a cost-of-living demonstration in Milan, with Mayor Giuseppe Sala warning: “I’m very worried because it’s a new phenomenon, which also originates from an international scenario and therefore feeds itself.”
In Spain, hundreds of tents have occupied Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol square since September, when the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her lifelong flat sparked nationwide protests in a country with soaring housing costs.
Dozens of tents have also sprung up in Portugal’s main cities of Lisbon and Porto, with protesters demanding action over rising costs of housing. AFP

PARIS, October 19. /TASS/. The benchmark index of the Paris Stock Exchange, CAC 40, fell by more than 1% amid the widespread unrest that swept across France over the past weekend, raising investors' concerns on the state of the country’s public debt, AFP news agency reported.
As of 10:30 a.m. Moscow time (7:30 a.m. GMT), the index was down by 1.24%, according to the agency. Among the biggest decliners were shares of banks, retail chains, and companies operating in the tourism sector. Shares of BNP Paribas fell by 2.41%, Societe Generale shares lost 2.36%, shares of Carrefour dropped by 3.04%, while shares of the hotel group Accor lost 3.03%.
Deutsche Bank analysts have warned that the recent unrest could negatively affect the willingness of international investors to purchase French government bonds.
France’s national debt is approaching 3.6 trillion euros.
Mass protests against rising fuel prices and the declining purchasing power of the population took place in Paris and across France on October 17. According to organizers, some 800,000 people took part in the protests, while the interior ministry put the number of protesters at 550,000. In a number of cities, protest rallies escalated into riots and clashes with police. Almost 2,400 protesters were detained across the country. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez pledged that the authorities would continue persecuting plunders and looters.

Settler violence threatens Israel’s rule of law, international standing, legal expert tells ‘Post'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
11:11:49 UTC
20:11:49 KST

Unchecked settler violence risks undermining Israel’s rule of law, damaging its international standing and weakening international support for its efforts to curb the Palestinian Authority’s payments to convicted terrorists, Professor Yuval Shany told The Jerusalem Post.
Shany, the Hersch Lauterpacht chair in International Law at Hebrew University and a senior research fellow at the Israel Democracy Institute, also warned the violence could increase the risk of sanctions and travel restrictions against settlers.
Shany’s comments on Sunday came days after extremist settlers attacked a European delegation and an American photojournalist in two separate incidents. Though 10 suspects have been detained for the attack, the issue of growing violence from extremist settlers has been widely discussed by the international community as a cause of concern.
Settler violence in the West Bank has increased in both frequency and severity in recent years. The number of attacks by extremist settlers against Palestinians and Israeli security forces rose by 27% in 2025 compared with the previous year, while severe incidents of nationalist crime increased by more than 50%, according to IDF and Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) data released in January 2026.
The rise in violence comes amid a longstanding record of limited prosecutions. Between 2005 and 2024, 93.8% of the 1,701 police investigation files monitored by Israeli human rights organization Yesh Din were closed without an indictment, while just 3% resulted in a full or partial conviction, according to the organization.
Violence can prevent implementation of court decisions
Shany said that “in principle, Palestinians could go to the Supreme Court and ask for enhanced state protection, and also for the state to compensate them for its negligence in providing them security. And in theory, they could also bring civil cases against identifiable settlers who have damaged their property...
“Many of these Palestinian families do not have the means to actually hire legal [representation]. ... There is a question of whether such legal assistance is available, and also the question of whether they have trust in the Israeli legal system to protect their interests.”
“Even when the court sides with Palestinians occasionally, it’s very difficult to actually enforce these decisions. So, in theory, yes, there are legal avenues that can be utilized. They are sometimes being utilized, but so far the effect has been quite marginal on the ground,” Shany said.
Shany noted that even when Israeli courts rule in favor of Palestinians, violence on the ground can prevent those decisions from being implemented. He pointed to the case of the Tubasi family, whose home the High Court of Justice ordered the IDF to secure after the family was forced to leave in July following harassment by extremist settlers.
When the military attempted to facilitate the family’s return, more than 100 extremist settlers attacked IDF forces, preventing the family from returning home. “Due to the violence, the mission to return the family to their homes was not completed,” the military said at the time.
The refusal of extremist settlers to abide by the law led prominent Israeli journalist and lawyer Ben-Dror Yemini to describe them in a Ynet opinion article as “Israel’s homegrown Hezbollah.” The comparison drew on Lebanon’s struggle to disarm the Iran-backed group and prevent it from dragging the state into wars through attacks against Israel carried out without state approval.
While Shany rejected the characterization, he said that Israel’s failure to uphold the rule of law does not absolve other countries of their own obligations. Nevertheless, he said, “In the court of public opinion, it doesn’t do Israel much favor to have anarchy in territories it controls and criticize other states for also having anarchy in their own territories.”
Shany said that Israel has an obligation under international law to curb the violence, regardless of its position on the legal status of the territories.
“If Israel continues to fail its obligations, it will increasingly face threats of sanctions by third states, which see this as an issue with humanitarian consequences and broader international peace and security implications, because this could send the whole region into a more explosive dynamic,” he said.
“So we will probably see more attempts by European countries to sanction Israel, as we saw last month with the 12 states that took this position.”
In September, the United Kingdom announced a ban on goods imported from Israeli settlements, while 11 other countries said they intended to introduce national restrictions or support broader European measures against settlement-produced goods.
Such measures could have economic consequences for Israel by restricting access to foreign markets and affecting businesses operating in settlements.
Sanctions likely to be placed on Israel
According to the Israel Policy Forum, Israel exported at least $15 billion in goods and services to the 12 countries in 2024. Goods originating in the West Bank, east Jerusalem and the Golan Heights accounted for just short of $45 million of Israeli exports to the UK in 2025.
Shany said that further measures could follow, including initiatives at the UN to impose sanctions on Israel and restrict goods and services originating in the territories, as well as potential legal action through international courts.
Beyond the economic impact, the diplomatic fallout could affect how international actors view Israel’s efforts to curb the Palestinian Authority’s payments to prisoners and families of Palestinians involved in attacks, Shany said.
Israel has withheld clearance revenues collected on behalf of the PA, including deductions linked to payments to prisoners and their families, as well as amounts equivalent to funds previously transferred to Gaza.
Israel has also enacted legislation providing for compensation to victims of terrorism through deductions from PA revenues and advanced plans for new housing units in the E1 area near Jerusalem.
“There would be a growing view among European countries that the combined effect of these measures is not to motivate the Palestinian Authority to take the allegations against it regarding support for families of terrorists more seriously, but rather to bring about its financial collapse and move further away from a two-state framework,” Shany said.
“The E1 construction plans, along with the violence, are seen as part of this pincer movement by Israel. I think this would encounter increasingly stronger resistance and perhaps efforts by European countries to find other ways to support Palestinian sovereignty.”
Shany also predicted growing efforts by grassroots organizations to pursue legal action against settlers abroad, drawing a parallel with the Hind Rajab Foundation’s efforts to bring complaints against IDF soldiers over alleged crimes in Gaza.
“I’m pretty certain that the weak response by the current Israeli government to this violence is going to also put some wind in the sails of those sorts of initiatives,” he said. “So we may see renewed attempts to go directly after settlers in terms of trying to freeze their assets and to introduce movement restrictions on them.”

Overland lifelines under pressure: Iran’s trade with its neighbours
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
11:11:36 UTC
20:11:36 KST

Iran is turning to its land borders for ways to keep trade moving as the U.S. naval blockade constrains shipping. But these routes are best seen as a buffer, not a substitute for maritime trade. They can help move selected goods, give merchants more options, and support businesses in border regions. They cannot make up for lost oil revenue, and they depend on infrastructure and political cooperation that Iran cannot control alone. The recent suspension of trade at two crossings with Pakistan is a reminder that land routes, too, can be disrupted with little warning.
The blockade and the shift to land
The loss of crude exports is at the heart of the problem. Citing Vortexa, Reuters reported that Iran’s seaborne crude exports fell to zero in the second week of September 2026 and were still at zero in early October. Vortexa estimated that 43 million barrels of Iranian crude were trapped west of the Strait of Hormuz. This is more than a shipping setback: oil exports bring in foreign currency, which road and rail trade in food or machinery cannot replace. The figures refer to seaborne crude, however, and do not mean that every kind of Iranian trade has stopped.
Some petroleum products have still made it out. Reuters, drawing on shipping intelligence, reported that eight LPG tankers and one jet-fuel tanker had left the Gulf of Oman since the blockade was reimposed in July. UANI estimated the LPG cargoes at 4.1 million barrels. These shipments show that the restrictions are not an airtight seal, but they are limited and irregular. U.S. officials also cautioned that a ship passing through does not necessarily mean the blockade was breached; vessels are reviewed individually, and some may be allowed through. For now, these cargoes look like exceptions rather than a dependable route for Iran’s energy exports.
Iran’s push to move more goods by land is already straining key crossings. At Gürbulak, on the Turkey–Iran border, the Associated Press reported that truck numbers had risen from about 200 to 1,200.
Waits on the Iranian side reached 12 to 25 days, and an Iranian trade official said the destination side could not process that many vehicles. Trucks can carry food, machinery parts, chemicals, and other goods, but shifting cargo from ships to roads takes more than finding another route. It requires enough lanes, customs staff, scanners, storage, and coordination on both sides of the border.
Corridors: capacity, not just geography
ISNA’s report on the Maku Free Zone shows why it matters to distinguish planned capacity from actual throughput. The zone’s managing director said it could handle 700 to 1,000 trucks a day, while around 300 to 400 trucks were leaving through the Bazargan crossing at the time. Those numbers describe different things: the zone’s stated capacity is not the same as the number of trucks cleared across the border. Raising the latter would require coordination with Turkey and enough capacity at the crossing itself. The figures point to room for growth, but they do not mean trade can immediately increase by the same amount .
ISNA also reports on the proposed Sarakhs–Cheshmeh Sorayya railway. The project could take 12 to 18 months to build if funding is secured and a contractor is selected; its projected capacity is 15 to 20 million tonnes of freight in its first year. These are estimates, not cargo already moving on an operational line. A separate report describes the railway as part of a planned east–west corridor connecting Iran’s network with Turkey’s. If completed, it could offer another way to move goods across the country. Its usefulness will depend on the project being built, border connections working smoothly, and freight costs being competitive.
West Azerbaijan could also benefit from a broader view of Iran’s border network. IRNA highlights the province’s links with Turkey, Iraq, and Nakhchivan, arguing that its role goes beyond a single crossing. With reliable roads, customs facilities, storage, and logistics services, border areas can connect local businesses to several markets and support employment as well as transit.
But geography alone does not make a region a trade hub. Businesses need goods to move predictably, without delays that make the route too costly to use.
READ: Vance acknowledges ‘failures’ in US handling of Iran war
Neighboring markets and political risk
Iraq shows both the promise of regional trade and its exposure to disruption. Reuters reported that Iran–Iraq trade exceeded $10 billion in 2025, driven largely by Iranian food, consumer goods, and other exports. Trade declined in 2026 as the conflict increased security risks, disrupted crossings, and raised transport costs. Iraq remains an important market, but it is not insulated from regional instability. Routes through the Caucasus and Central Asia could add options, though each has its own infrastructure and border constraints. Having more neighbors does not automatically mean Iran can redirect unlimited cargo to them.
The latest suspension of trade at Pakistan’s Gabd–Rimdan and Taftan crossings makes that point especially clear.
Dawn reported that Pakistan suspended commercial traffic through both crossings, with Balochistan officials citing security concerns, smuggling, and border management. Iran’s foreign ministry described the stoppage as temporary and technical and said talks were under way. Hundreds of trucks carrying LPG, rice, fruit, and other goods were reportedly stranded, although passenger traffic through Rimdan–Gabd continued.
The closure may be temporary, but even a short interruption can mean lost sales, delayed deliveries, and higher costs for traders.
Turkey’s incentives and constraints
Turkey has a clear commercial interest in keeping trade with Iran going, but the size and direction of that trade matter. Türkiye’s foreign ministry puts bilateral trade at $5.5 billion in 2025: Turkish exports to Iran were $3 billion, while imports from Iran were $2.5 billion. Turkish exports include machinery, plastics, chemicals, vehicles, and agricultural products; imports from Iran include natural gas, metals, and agricultural goods. The relationship is significant, but the figures show that the balance favors Turkey. Iranian customs figures may not match Turkish data because the two sides can use different periods, categories, and methods; those figures should not be combined as if they were directly comparable.
Turkey has good reasons to maintain commerce with Iran: Turkish firms gain access to a large neighboring market, and transit can bring further business. But commercial interest does not mean Ankara will accept any level of risk. In September 2026, the U.S. Treasury sanctioned a Turkey-based bank and subsidiaries, alleging that they facilitated transactions for Iranian entities. Later that month, Turkey’s banking regulator revoked the operating license of Iran’s Bank Mellat branch. Reuters noted that Turkey’s official notice did not explicitly link the decision to U.S. pressure. These actions do not show that Turkey is ending trade, but they help explain why banks and businesses may be reluctant to handle Iranian payments.
A buffer, not a substitute
The practical value of Iran’s regional corridors will depend on whether goods can move reliably, not simply on how many routes appear on a map. The Maku figures suggest unused capacity, while the railway remains a proposal with a conditional timeline. Keeping border procedures predictable, coordinating customs, improving transport links, and making payments possible are all necessary if trade is to grow. Otherwise, congestion or a temporary closure can erase the advantage of geographic proximity.
Trade with neighboring countries can keep some supply chains functioning and give merchants alternatives when one route is blocked. But it cannot replace seaborne energy exports or the hard currency they generate. Turkey is likely to remain commercially interested, yet any increase will depend on border capacity, payment access, and how much sanctions risk its firms are willing to take.
Iran’s land corridors can reduce dependence on any one crossing; they cannot, by themselves, offset the economic impact of the naval blockade.

Australian lawmaker Helen Haines in critical condition after vehicle ramming attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
11:11:32 UTC
20:11:32 KST

Australian lawmaker Helen Haines was in a critical condition on Monday after being deliberately struck by a car outside her office, with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese saying a terrorism task force would be investigating the suspect arrested.
Albanese said it was too early to determine the motive for the attack but pointed to the changing face of social media having raised the temperature around politics in a country where such violence is extremely rare.
"All of our thoughts are with Helen, her family, her friends, her team, and her community at this extremely difficult time. We are praying for her full recovery," Albanese told a press conference.
Victoria Police said a 43-year-old man had been arrested after the attack on independent MP Haines in Wangaratta, around three hours' drive northeast of Melbourne.
Haines, 65, was airlifted to hospital, Albanese said.
When asked by public broadcaster ABC whether the increased anger around politics had led to worries about attacks on politicians, the prime minister pointed to the anonymity of online content.
"The concern, if you look at anyone's social media feeds and look at the comments, people will say things that they would never say face to face. But the temperature has undoubtedly been increased. Not just here in Australia, of course. We've seen incidents internationally as well," he said.
"Here in Australia, it is a good thing that politicians are able to go about their community and engage with people. I don't want to see a political system in which you can't have conversations with people at the supermarket, in the street, at street meetings, public forums. That's an important part of our democracy."
No further threat to the public reported, Victoria Police say
Victoria Police Acting Superintendent Ashley Mason told a press conference there was no further threat to the public.
Albanese said it was too early to determine the motive for the attack, though a terrorism taskforce would be investigating the arrested suspect.
"We thank the swift assistance of bystanders and the dedicated health workers who assisted her, and police for their response," a statement by Haines' family posted on her Facebook page said.
Haines worked in nursing and midwifery and as an academic before being elected to parliament as an independent in 2019 in the seat of Indi.
Her website says she has opposed proposals including making political donations to the major parties more secretive, banning mobile phones in immigration detention and spending billions on fossil fuel subsidies.

====================================================================================================

After MP 'attacked' in the street, our democracy is facing its biggest test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
11:09:35 UTC
20:09:35 KST

analysis
After Helen Haines attacked in the street, Australian democracy faces its biggest test
"This wasn't an accident."
With those words, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese laid bare the horrifying nature of an attack that has sent shock waves through Australia.
Independent MP Helen Haines was going about her day in the regional Victorian town of Wangaratta when a four-wheel drive struck her outside her electorate office.
The 65-year-old, who has represented the people of Indi since 2019, suffered critical injuries in an attack now under police investigation.
A man is in custody, and while it is too early to conclude whether his alleged actions were politically motivated, the possibility alone is deeply disturbing.
Australians are accustomed to seeing their local politicians in the supermarket, at the footy or simply walking down the street.
They knock on doors, hold mobile offices, attend community events and make themselves available to constituents who want to raise concerns or have a chat.
It's easy to be cynical about politicians, but their accessibility is one of the great strengths of Australia's democracy.
That will now be seriously tested.
Loading...
Shock across political spectrum
Albanese was understandably emotional as he spoke about the attack on Haines just hours later.
He was joined by voices from every corner of Australian politics in expressing his horror at the incident and wishing the MP a full recovery.
While careful not to pre-empt the police investigation, Albanese also took the opportunity to repeat his calls to turn down the temperature of political debate.
He has often said parliamentarians should be able to carry out their work without fear of threats or intimidation, and warned about the consequences of personal vilification and increasingly aggressive political commentary.
Those concerns are not confined to the prime minister.
For years, the Australian Federal Police has been highlighting an alarming rise in threats directed at politicians, their families and staff.
The latest figures show the AFP received 1,067 reports of threatening, harassing, nuisance or offensive behaviour involving federal parliamentarians, high office holders and protected locations in the past financial year.
That was a 12 per cent increase on the previous year and almost double the 555 reports recorded in 2021-22.
Not every report involves a credible threat of violence, and the figures cover more than MPs and senators.
But they demonstrate the scale of the hostility increasingly confronting people in public office.
Loading...
AFP's warning
In March last year, then-AFP commissioner Reece Kershaw delivered a sober warning to a parliamentary committee about the threats facing politicians ahead of the federal election.
He revealed some male politicians had been sent bullets in the mail, while female parliamentarians were subjected to particularly disturbing abuse, including threats of sexual violence.
In some cases, the threats extended to their children.
Just this month, AFP Commissioner Krissy Barrett told the ABC she expected "high office holders and politicians will continue to be targeted by those who hold grievances".
She said while terror investigators were increasingly seeing cases with ideological motivations, another factor was emerging: grievance.
Barrett said people who were feeling distanced and alone were "looking for something to attach to, to give them meaning and purpose".
"We are seeing a bit of a shift there that the grievance is what's actually driving them and then they're looking for some sort of ideological motivation to attach to," she said.
Examples mount across parties
There has been no shortage of examples demonstrating why police are concerned.
One Nation leader Pauline Hanson has spoken publicly about the threats directed at her and her family, and the security arrangements she believes are necessary to protect her.
Liberal MP Andrew Hastie has faced threats serious enough to prompt additional security arrangements at his home and electorate office.
Just last week, Labor minister Anne Aly revealed she had received 19 death threats in a week.
Others have faced criminal threats serious enough to result in charges.
Earlier this year, a Sydney man was charged after allegedly threatening to kill a federal parliamentarian over the phone.
Last year, Victorian men were charged in separate cases involving alleged death threats against federal MPs, including antisemitic abuse.
These are not isolated concerns confined to one political party, one side of an ideological divide or one contentious policy debate.
Nor are they limited to the anonymous abuse politicians have long endured online.
The rise in incidents has raised the question of whether elected representatives can safely do their jobs.
Loading
Warnings come to pass
The AFP has established specialist investigative teams to respond to the growing threat, while security arrangements for individual politicians have come under greater scrutiny.
But there are limits to what even the most extensive protective measures can achieve without changing the way politicians interact with the public.
Police officers stationed outside every electorate office or security checks at every community event would represent a very different Australian democracy.
Voters are entitled to be angry with their elected representatives, but there is an important distinction between robust debate and intimidation or threats.
Police must now be allowed to establish the facts of the attack on Haines.
But the incident has brought into sharp focus the safety concerns that security agencies and parliamentarians have been warning about for years.

Majority of Ukrainians oppose ceding Donbas for security guarantees, ready to endure war – KIIS poll
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
14:08:51 EEST
20:08:51 KST

An absolute majority (61%) of Ukrainians continue to consider it categorically unacceptable to cede full control of Donbas to the Russian Federation in exchange for security guarantees, while 35% are open to such a concession, according to a survey conducted on October 8–16 by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KIIS).
It is noted that compared to late July–early August, when a similar survey was conducted, there were no statistically significant changes. However, on October 8–9, prior to the announcement of the "diesel deal" between the U.S and Russia and subsequent pressure on Ukraine, 57% were categorically opposed to giving up Donbas in exchange for security guarantees.
Across all macro-regions, a half or majority rejects the proposal to withdraw Ukrainian troops in exchange for security guarantees. The highest proportion of those willing to approve such an option is among residents of the East (primarily Kharkiv region), where 45% generally allow for approval, while 51% are categorically against. In other regions, including the South and Lower Dnipro region, 60–66% categorically reject the proposal. In Kyiv, 66% are opposed.
When asked how much longer Ukrainians are willing to endure the war, virtually the same percentage (62%) stated for as long as necessary. Another 4% spoke of 1 year. A shorter timeframe (several months to six months) was cited by 21%, while the remaining 13% were undecided. Among respondents surveyed on October 8–9, 60% answered that they were ready to endure as long as necessary.
Only 10% of respondents expect the war to end by the end of the current year, 2026. Another 13% expect the war to end in the first half of 2027, and 17% by the end of 2027 (bringing the total to 40%). Meanwhile, 39% expect the war to end in 2028 or later, with 21% holding no definite opinion on the matter.
"The results of our survey once again demonstrate that many in both the West and the East still have a limited understanding of Ukraine and Ukrainians (and still seem to view us through the lens of Russian expertise). As we can see, the Russian enemy, through its despicable ballistic missile and drone strikes, is unable to break the spirit and will of Ukrainians; Ukrainians still insist on continuing the resistance. The same applies to pressure from the other side—attempts by some of our partners to pressure Ukrainians into accepting terms of virtual surrender (blushing behind empty and unfulfillable promises of something in the future). Once again, Ukrainians want peace, but between surrender now with an almost inevitable risk of future Russian genocide and resistance now with the hope of achieving acceptable terms, Ukrainians choose to continue resisting," noted Anton Hrushetsky, Executive Director of KIIS.
The survey was conducted via computer-assisted telephone interviews (CATI) based on a random sample of mobile phone numbers across all government-controlled territories of Ukraine, surveying 1,031 respondents aged 18 and older. Under standard conditions, the formal statistical margin of error (with a probability of 0.95 and taking into account a design effect of 1.3) did not exceed 4% for indicators close to 50% and 1.7% for indicators close to 5%, though certain systematic deviations are added under war conditions.

In its announcement, the company said the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund would initially receive 5% of its shares, subject to stockholder approval.

The concert marked the beginning of a new international tour that will take the renowned Kazakh singer across several continents. Blending musical innovation, theatrical performances, and elements of Kazakh cultural heritage, the show offered audiences an immersive journey through the artist’s musical universe.
Dimash opened the concert with an epic performance of the title track, “Dimensions,” sung in Kazakh. The song set the tone for the evening, which featured a series of premieres, original compositions, and performances of some of his best-known works.

The concert also paid tribute to Kazakhstan’s musical traditions through performances of the folk songs “Aqerke,” “Tau Ishinde” and “Durdaraz.” Each piece was accompanied by elaborate choreography, transforming the traditional repertoire into theatrical stage productions.

- Scientists have discovered that severely bleached corals can make a remarkable comeback simply by touching healthy, genetically identical corals. In laboratory experiments, dying corals regained their color and fully recovered within seven weeks, with as little as five days of contact sometimes enough to start the healing process.
- Share:
For the first time, researchers have demonstrated that severely bleached corals can fully recover after spending just a few days in contact with healthy, genetically identical corals.
In laboratory experiments, corals that had turned white and were close to dying regained their health within seven weeks. According to a study published on October 14 in Science Advances, this represents the fastest documented recovery from coral bleaching. The discovery could lead to new techniques for restoring coral reefs, which some estimates suggest could disappear within decades as climate change fuels increasingly severe and frequent marine heat waves.
Coral bleaching occurs when rising ocean temperatures cause corals to lose the beneficial algae living inside their tissues. These algae supply much of the energy corals depend on for growth and survival. Without them, corals lose their vibrant colors, struggle to obtain enough nourishment, and become more susceptible to harmful algae. Even when they survive, regaining their health can take months or years.
"While bleached corals may be dying, they are not dead yet," said lead author Danny Collins, an oceans PhD student at the Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability. "The question we wanted to answer is, once a coral has bleached, what can we do?"
An Unexpected Discovery Reveals a Way to Rescue Dying Corals
Although they may resemble plants or rocks, corals are animals. In most coral species, individual animals reproduce by creating genetically identical copies of themselves. These clones grow together into large colonies that form the foundation of coral reefs.
The idea for the study emerged from an unexpected observation in 2025. Steve Palumbi, a study coauthor and the Jane and Marshall Steel, Jr. Professor in Marine Sciences, noticed something unusual in his laboratory. Two fragments taken from the same coral colony, one healthy and the other bleached, had fallen against each other in an aquarium.
Where the fragments touched, the bleached coral began regaining its color. The change suggested that beneficial algae were returning to its tissues.
At roughly the same time, Collins was investigating how coral diseases develop and spread. He was particularly interested in bacteria carried by plastic debris that lands on corals and can introduce harmful microorganisms through direct contact.
"Harmful bacteria enter corals through physical contact," said Collins, who is also a Knight-Hennessy Scholar. "We were curious about what would happen if we used contact to reintroduce something good - the beneficial algae from healthy corals."
To investigate, Collins designed an experiment using 10 pairs of coral fragments. Each pair consisted of one healthy fragment and one bleached fragment originating from the same coral animal.
Five pairs were positioned so that the fragments physically touched. The other five pairs were separated by gaps measuring only a few millimeters.
The results revealed a dramatic difference. Every bleached fragment that touched its healthy counterpart recovered completely within seven weeks. In contrast, the bleached fragments that were kept apart died.
How a Simple Touch Triggers Rapid Coral Recovery
The researchers discovered that the remarkable recovery depends on a special ability of genetically identical corals to connect their tissues.
"Genetically identical corals recognize one another when they come into contact," said Palumbi, who is a professor of oceans in the Doerr School of Sustainability and of biology in the School of Humanities and Sciences. "Their tissues fuse if they are from the same clone. We see something similar in humans. Organ transplants are often successful if the donor is your identical twin."
Using a powerful microscope, Collins and his colleagues examined what happened when the coral fragments touched. They found that tiny channels within their tissues quickly lined up, forming connections that allowed materials to move between the two fragments.
Through these connections, beneficial algae and the nutrients they produce could pass from the healthy coral into the bleached one. Within just three days, researchers observed algae transferring into the damaged fragments.
The team then investigated how long the corals actually needed to remain connected. By separating pairs after different periods of contact, they discovered that a single week was enough to transfer the algae required for complete recovery. In some cases, just five days of contact produced the same result.
Remarkably, the separated corals still returned to full health within seven weeks, the same amount of time required by corals that remained connected throughout the experiment.
This finding revealed that the rapid recovery was not primarily driven by a continuing supply of algae from the healthy coral. Instead, once enough algae entered the bleached fragment, they reproduced rapidly inside their new host and restored its energy supply.
"Once beneficial algae enter bleached corals, they don't just spread out," said Palumbi. "They flood in and start dividing at the fastest rates seen in corals."
During the second week of contact, the beneficial algae living inside the bleached fragments doubled in number approximately every four days. That growth rate was about ten times faster than what researchers have observed in wild corals.
A Promising Breakthrough for Coral Reef Restoration
Scientists have spent decades searching for ways to protect coral reefs from rising ocean temperatures, disease, increasingly acidic seawater, and other environmental pressures.
Their efforts have included selectively breeding corals that can withstand higher temperatures, raising young corals in nurseries to rebuild damaged reefs, and transferring communities of microorganisms between corals to improve their resilience.
The new findings suggest another possibility: helping bleached corals recover quickly enough to survive the dangerous period following a marine heat wave.
"Bleached corals are often considered a lost cause because recovery after a heatwave is very slow, if it happens at all," said Fiorenza Micheli, the David and Lucile Packard Professor in Marine Science and a faculty advisor of Collins. "We hope this new research will inspire solutions that keep corals healthy long enough to enable full recovery after heat waves through slower processes such as growth, reproduction, and recruitment of new colonies."
However, the researchers emphasize that their experimental approach cannot yet be used to restore reefs on a large scale. For the technique to work as demonstrated, every bleached coral would need access to a healthy, genetically identical counterpart. Finding and supplying those matches across entire reefs would be impractical.
Important questions also remain about how the recovery mechanism could be adapted for broader use.
Over the coming months, the team intends to investigate other ways to introduce beneficial algae into bleached corals without requiring them to remain physically connected to healthy fragments.
One possibility involves collecting beneficial algae from healthy corals well before marine heat waves occur. Researchers could then deliver large quantities of these algae to damaged corals after bleaching events, potentially allowing them to recover much faster.
"These new insights into how corals can naturally recover give us hope for the future," said Micheli, who also co-directs the Stanford Center for Ocean Solutions. "They open the door to what's possible and may lead to the breakthrough we need to accelerate reef restoration."
Study Authors and Research Support
Micheli also serves as a professor of oceans and (by courtesy) of biology. Both Micheli and Palumbi are senior fellows at the Woods Institute for the Environment, which is part of the Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability.
Additional Stanford researchers who contributed to the study include Jana Sipkova, Nathaniel Mollica, Tom Rolander, Courtney Klepac, Gabriel Calistro, and Vanessa Barone.
Mollica is a research scientist in Stanford's Oceans Department, where Calistro works as a research assistant. Rolander is a research engineer in the Fabrication Lab at the Harold A. Miller Library at Hopkins Marine Station, which belongs to the Doerr School of Sustainability.
Sipkova is a postdoctoral scholar, while Klepac is a research scientist. Barone is an assistant professor in the Biology Department of Stanford's School of Humanities and Sciences and is affiliated with Bio-X and the Maternal & Child Health Research Institute.
The Molecular and Cellular Biodiversity Imaging Center, operated by Stanford's Biology Department at Hopkins Marine Station, conducted the coral image analyses.
Financial support came from the National Science Foundation and Stanford University, including seed funding through the Big Ideas for Oceans grant program. The program is organized by the Oceans Department and the Woods Institute for the Environment within the Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability.

'O Captain, my Captain': Should Congress make room for Amarinder Singh again?

2026-10-19

20:04:14 KST

Rahul Gandhi named Captain Amarinder Singh as his favourite BJP leader.
NEW DELHI: Can a party install a new captain, retain the old team and still leave the door open for a former captain who quit the dressing room five years ago? With the leadership chanting 'O Captain! My Captain!' the Punjab Congress seems to be attempting to navigate that question precisely ahead of the 2027 assembly elections.With Pargat Singh at the helm, Raja Warring and Charanjit Singh Channi 'promised' an active role in the campaign; Sachin Pilot has also left the door open to Captain Amarinder Singh's possible return. Can Congress accommodate its old captain without unsettling the new captain and the team?Congress general secretary Sachin Pilot, the party's Punjab in-charge, on October 15 offered a line that will keep speculation alive: "Politics mein 'kuch bhi ho sakta hai' (anything is possible in politics)."Asked about the possibility of former Punjab chief minister Captain Amarinder Singh returning to Congress, Pilot praised him as a leader who had served Punjab "well" and was "a man of a very tall stature". He clarified, however, that he had not spoken to Captain Amarinder about his political plans."I've not spoken to him personally about what his future plans are about joining or leaving any party," Pilot told PTI Videos.
Amarinder Singh on his relationship with Congress leadership.
The remark came less than a fortnight after Congress appointed former India hockey captain Pargat Singh as Punjab Pradesh Congress Committee (PPCC) president, replacing Amrinder Singh Raja Warring on October 2. It also followed Amarinder's public criticism of the BJP, the party he joined in 2022, over its handling of Punjab.So, is Congress merely acknowledging political speculation, or could the old captain's name return to the party's calculations? And if he does return, where would he fit in a state unit that has just changed leadership and is yet to name a CM face?
The 'Uncle Amarinder' connection
The latest speculation began with an unexpected public greeting. On August 6, during an Instagram 'Ask Me Anything' session with students, leader of the opposition Rahul Gandhi was asked to name his favourite BJP politician."Captain Amarinder Singh, definitely. I get along with him, he's cool and he is an expert on military history, so I like him quite a lot," Rahul Gandhi said, before adding: "Hello, Uncle Amarinder!"
The former CM responded that his personal relationship with the Gandhi family would remain, but his political commitment was to the BJP. In a September interview with The Tribune, he said he remained fond of Rahul, Priyanka and Sonia Gandhi, while distinguishing personal relationships from politics."My personal relationship with the Gandhis will always be there, but my political commitment is to the BJP," he said."If tomorrow I tell Rahul, Priyanka or Sonia personally that I'll be there for them no matter what, I mean it and I'm happy to help," he added.The indirect exchange was notable because Amarinder Singh's departure from Congress in September 2021 followed a bitter confrontation with the party's state leadership. "When you've been with somebody for fifty years, they remain your party. I never asked to leave them; they asked me to leave," Captain Amarinder Singh said recently.
Amarinder's BJP discontent
The former chief minister's recent criticism of the BJP has provided the immediate backdrop to the comeback speculation.In an interview published by The Tribune on September 25, Amarinder said the BJP had not consulted him on Punjab politics or policy despite his long experience in the state."I haven't had a single meeting on Punjab policy or politics with them in the last five years," he said.He was more direct about his decision to join the party: "I have gained nothing by joining BJP."
The political career of Captain Amarinder Singh.
Amarinder also argued that the BJP did not adequately understand Punjab and should consult leaders familiar with the state's political and social realities. He advocated an alliance with the Shiromani Akali Dal, pointing to the BJP's historical position as the junior partner in that relationship.In the same interview, he described himself as going through "difficult times", without elaborating.Yet he has also made clear that dissatisfaction does not automatically mean departure. Amarinder Singh said it was his duty to tell the BJP what he thought about Punjab and that criticising the party's approach did not mean he was quitting.
From a 77-seat victory to a bitter exit
Captain Amarinder Singh's record in Congress spans decades, including two terms as Punjab CM, from 2002 to 2007 and from 2017 to 2021.In the 2017 assembly election, Congress won 77 of Punjab's 117 seats under his leadership, returning to power after a decade. But the relationship between Amarinder Singh and the state leadership deteriorated, particularly amid his prolonged confrontation with Navjot Singh Sidhu.Sidhu became Punjab Congress president in July 2021. The conflict intensified over leadership and the government's handling of election promises. On September 18, 2021, Amarinder resigned as chief minister after the Congress high command called a meeting of the party's legislators to discuss leadership.
Sachin Pilot kept the door open to Amarinder Singh's return to the Congress.
He subsequently left Congress and launched the Punjab Lok Congress (PLC). In the 2022 assembly election, the PLC allied with the BJP, but the alliance failed to win a seat for Amarinder Singh's party. AAP swept the election with 92 seats, while Congress was reduced to 18.Amarinder joined the BJP in September 2022, and his PLC was merged with it.The electoral record provides the context for the renewed speculation, but it does not establish that bringing Amarinder back would reverse Congress's fortunes. The party's 2022 defeat followed a wider political shift in Punjab, including AAP's rise and Congress's internal divisions.
Pargat Singh's leadership test
Meanwhile, Pargat Singh's appointment has put a new leader at the head of a state unit that has repeatedly struggled with factional disputes. A former India hockey captain and three-time MLA from Jalandhar Cantonment, he was associated with Sidhu during the 2021 confrontation with Amarinder Singh and had publicly questioned the previous government's delivery on election promises.Pilot called Pargat a "unifying captain", saying the new president has reached out to state leaders and received public support. He has also invoked the team metaphor to describe Congress's approach to the election."You are one captain who's got a fantastic team, and the captain is only as strong as his team," Pilot said he had told Pargat. His appointment, replacing Warring as state chief, was particularly important in the backdrop of an internal tussle between Warring and Channi camps.Punjab Congress has spent months grappling with a bitter power struggle between the camps of state chief Amarinder Singh Raja Warring and former CM Charanjit Singh Channi. The feud spilled into public view through rival sloganeering, poster wars, clashes at party events and boycotts during visits by then state in-charge Bhupesh Baghel. The high command's July compromise, retaining Warring while appointing Channi to head the campaign committee, failed to end the friction. After Sachin Pilot replaced Baghel as Punjab in-charge in September, Warring eventually resigned on October 2, and Pargat Singh was appointed the new state chief.With the Congress leadership now sending the open-door signal to Captain Amarinder, the question is how Pargat's team would accommodate a strong-headed former CM with a history in the party.Moreover, the issue is not limited to Amarinder Singh. In the upcoming months, Congress must also manage the transition from Warring, who led the state unit from April 2022 until October 2026.
No CM face, but several leadership questions
Congress has also decided against projecting a CM face for the 2027 Punjab election.Pilot said the party would fight as a team and decide who should lead the state after securing the mandate, following consultations with workers, leaders and MLAs."We are fighting together as a team. Let the team win. And then we'll decide who gets to do what job," he said.
In June, Amarinder Singh shared that Rahul Gandhi wished him on his birthday.
The party has several experienced leaders, including Partap Singh Bajwa, Sukhjinder Randhawa, Charanjit Singh Channi and Warring. Pargat's appointment adds a new organisational chief to that mix, while the question of Amarinder's possible return remains unconfirmed.For the high command, the practical issue would be defining the role of each leader without undermining the other.
What could Captain Amarinder's return mean
Amarinder Singh's long tenure in Punjab politics, his experience as CM and his association with national security and border-state issues are part of his public political profile. A return could give Congress another experienced voice in its campaign, while his criticism of the BJP could offer a new line of political debate. The Congress may gain from his name, polularity and political history but it is unlikely that he would have any active role owing to his age.But the political costs would depend on the terms of any return. His 2021 exit followed a major leadership confrontation, and Pargat was part of the state leadership aligned with Sidhu during that period. Reconciliation would therefore involve not just Amarinder Singh and the Gandhi family, but a state unit whose leadership has changed since he left.
It would also raise questions about the position of leaders who remained with Congress through the subsequent elections and organisational changes. Warring's emphasis on youth representation, Pargat's task of consolidating the state unit and Pilot's insistence on collective leadership all point to issues that would need to be addressed.For now, there is no confirmed proposal to bring Captain Amarinder back, no announced role for him and no indication that talks have taken place or are under way.Pilot's "anything is possible" may keep the question open, but the party's immediate task remains to get the current team working together before Punjab votes in 2027.

Women may be at greater risk of AI job losses. Telephone switch operators and PCs show why.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
11:02:34 UTC
20:02:34 KST

Decades before Siri or Alexa or ChatGPT, there was a real person, almost always a woman, at the center of the information world. She was so vital, most long-distance communication could not happen without her.
She was the telephone switch operator, and at one time she was part of the single largest occupation for white, U.S.-born women under age 20.
Today, that job doesn't exist.
The world is struggling to figure out what the dawn of artificial intelligence means for society, culture and the economy. A lot of ordinary Americans are just wondering what it means for their jobs.
The history of technological progress — from automated telephone switches to the introduction of the washing machine and the personal computer — can offer some guidance. And that guidance suggests women are likely to be among the most affected by AI.
"AI is focused on routine tasks and numbers and finding patterns, and those types of jobs are the clerical, administrative jobs that a lot of women hold,'' said Ariane Hegewisch, a senior research fellow at the Institute for Women's Policy Research. "It's still 90% of secretaries and clerical workers who are women."
New research backs this up. The International Labour Organization in March concluded that nearly 1 in 10 women in high-income countries work in occupations at the highest risk from AI.
The invention that made operators obsolete
In the 1940s, nearly 95% of America's telephone operators were female. It was a relatively well-paying job for women at the time, and a complicated one: It took months of training to be able to handle the several hundred calls an hour that could come in at peak times. Operators were expected to be speedy, precise — and polite.
These women were hit hard when AT&T introduced the automated telephone switch. It was one of the largest automation investments in history — a close analog to the massive AI investment now underway — and created one of the biggest technological shocks the nation had ever seen.
In the decades after the automated switch was popularized, an estimated 75,000 operator jobs vanished.
Economists James Feigenbaum at Boston University and Daniel P. Gross at Duke University's Fuqua School of Business studied census and paycheck data from the time and followed local employment trends along the path of AT&T's rolling investment in switches across the nation.
"The effect of this shock on incumbent operators was to dispossess many of their jobs and careers," they wrote in 2020. Many switchboard operators wound up in lower-paying jobs — or dropped out of the workforce entirely, they found.
Economist David Autor said this outcome reflects the reality that many workers are already in their highest and best-paying occupation. When the job goes away, the next step is often down.
"Most people are not changing careers very often. They make their career decisions early, and they stick with those careers," he said. "If those careers, if the value of that work ... suddenly goes out of fashion, becomes technologically obsolete, they're going to, in general, do something not as good."
But Feigenbaum and Gross also discovered that the next generation of women fared better.
"Future workers found work in other fields, often taking up similar-quality jobs," they wrote, as the younger workers were "more adaptive to an evolving labor market ... Anxiety over the opportunities available to future generations proved to be somewhat misplaced."
In other words: One type of job went away, but other work emerged over time that was just as good.
'Engines of liberation'
By the 1950s, another technological innovation would come along and have a profound effect on women: the washing machine.
Dubbed "engines of liberation" in a seminal paper on the topic by University of Pennsylvania economist Jeremy Greenwood and others, washing machines and other appliances dramatically reduced the time women spent on unpaid housework. That meant time could be reallocated to a paycheck outside the home, even as women's responsibility for the home remained.
From 1950 to 1980, as gender norms changed, the number of employed women in the U.S. grew by more than 25 million. Their participation rate, or share of the female population in the labor force, grew to 52% from 34%. At the same time, 16 million more men found work, though the male participation rate dropped by 5 percentage points.
The relevant question for the AI boom today: How did the economy suddenly find jobs for these women? If AI creates a vast new pool of available workers, can the economy put them to work?
First, the very entry of women into the workforce meant demand for tasks once done at home moved into the paid economy, services such as childcare and food preparation. Second, as the nation grew wealthier, other employment opportunities for women emerged in the service economy — in retail, restaurants, leisure and hospitality, and even some professional services. And third, as American businesses grew, they needed more people to handle the paperwork — everything from payroll to customer accounts.
Changes to the economy and businesses were partly related to the entry of women into the workforce, but it was also partly random luck that the U.S. was booming and businesses were changing to need more office workers.
"Between 1940 and 1980, there was a ton of new work created in the U.S. economy, and it was in office and clerical work that was accessible to people with a high school education,'' Autor said.
The rise of the PC
The next big revolution affecting women in the workplace was the personal computer.
Before PCs arrived on the scene, women were the backbone of office infrastructure. According to the 1980 U.S. census, nearly 4.7 million Americans worked as secretaries, stenographers and typists. More than 98% were women.
When IBM introduced the personal computer in 1981, followed by the advent of Microsoft Word just two years later, some of the middlemen, or in this case, middlewomen, became obsolete. It didn't eliminate writing, filing or editing. It simply shifted a big chunk of those tasks from dedicated clerical workers to others in the office — executives could type their own reports, book their own travel and print their own papers.
But the PC wasn't entirely bad news for women in the workforce. Studies show women were already more likely than men to be using a computer at work at the dawn of the PC era. The PC put new tools at their fingertips: spreadsheets and databases and general computing power. While many roles were eliminated, many women adapted and found new ways to use the emerging technology to make themselves indispensable to their employers.
That's a potential outcome for AI. In some cases, it will eliminate tasks but not entire jobs, enhancing the time and ability of a worker to do the remaining value-added jobs that only humans can do.
A 2022 paper by Marcus Dillender and Eliza Forsythe found that when companies adopted software to do office and administrative work, it resulted in a 1% decline in employment in the sector but a 3% increase in wages for college graduates.
Many more women have earned college and advanced degrees, and hold managerial jobs, than when other technologies ripped through the economy, offering some potential protection from automation. But maybe not for long: One of the promises of AI is that it will move up the value chain of the jobs performed by humans.
Whatever capabilities the new technology may have now, the outlook is unclear because, Hegewisch says, somewhat ominously, "AI can learn."

Oil tanker temporarily lost power in Baltic Sea due to engine failure — newspaper

BERLIN, October 19. /TASS/. A large oil tanker, the Sled, temporarily lost propulsion in the Baltic Sea due to an engine failure, the Bild newspaper reported.
The incident occurred between the German island of Ruegen and the Danish island of Moen. Late Saturday night into Sunday morning, at around 01:30 a.m. local time (11:30 p.m. GMT), the tanker dramatically reduced its speed and subsequently anchored half a nautical mile from the border of Denmark's territorial waters. Due to strong easterly winds drifting the disabled vessel toward Danish waters, the Vessel Traffic Service Center in Warnemuende dispatched the rescue tug VB Bremen Fighter from the German port of Mukran to the incident scene. By Monday morning, the tanker managed to restore its maneuverability and has currently resumed its westward transit.
The tanker was en route from the Russian port of Primorsk to Skagen in Denmark, the newspaper said.
