Researchers identify female-specific and male-specific genetic risks for anxiety
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
11:00:14 UTC
20:00:14 KST

Men and women share much of the underlying genetic risk for anxiety, but researchers have now identified distinct genetic pathways specific to each sex. These biological differences help explain why females and males often experience and report anxiety in different ways. The findings were published in Psychological Medicine.
Anxiety disorders, which include generalized anxiety, panic disorders, specific phobias, and agoraphobia, are among the most common mental health conditions worldwide. They affect nearly a third of the global population at some point in their lives. Females are diagnosed with anxiety disorders at roughly twice the rate of males.
Men and women also tend to display different symptoms. Females more frequently report internalizing symptoms and experience depression alongside their anxiety. Males often exhibit externalizing behaviors and are more likely to use substances as a coping strategy.
Past research on these differences has often focused on cultural norms, hormonal fluctuations, or differences in brain activation. Studies examining the genetic roots of anxiety have yielded mixed results, with some suggesting stronger genetic influences in females and others finding equal risk. Previous genome-wide studies generally combined data from men and women, an approach that can hide genetic risks applying exclusively to one sex.
Lead authors Jihua Hu and Brittany L. Mitchell, researchers at the QIMR Berghofer Medical Research Institute and The University of Queensland in Australia, conducted a massive study to see if common genetic factors operate differently in men and women. They analyzed genetic and health data from 455,487 individuals of European ancestry using the UK Biobank and the All of Us research programs.
The team first conducted a combined analysis of the entire group. They compared the genetic profiles of individuals with a history of anxiety against those without any mental distress diagnoses. In this group, the researchers identified 56 specific genetic variants associated with anxiety. Genetic variants are slight differences in the DNA sequence that occur naturally between individuals.
Following this initial analysis, the team separated the data to run distinct tests for males and females. The female group included 281,831 individuals, and the male group included 173,656 individuals. The researchers found 21 genetic variants associated with anxiety in females, compared to just five in males. Only a single genetic variant overlapped between the two groups.
The team then calculated the heritability of anxiety for both groups. They found that males exhibit a higher overall threshold for developing the disorder. This indicates that men generally require a greater accumulation of genetic vulnerability and environmental factors to cross the threshold into clinical anxiety. When calculating heritability based on real-world population prevalence, the overall genetic contribution appeared higher in females.
To understand the biological functions of these genetic variants, the researchers mapped them to specific genes. They discovered entirely different biological pathways associated with anxiety in men compared to women. In females, the identified genes were heavily involved in chromatin regulation and olfactory transduction.
Chromatin regulation is a cellular process that packages DNA and controls gene expression, which can influence how sensitive an individual is to environmental stressors. Olfactory transduction involves the body’s ability to process smells.
Evolutionarily, the sense of smell is tightly linked to threat detection and survival. Odor information is processed directly in the amygdala, a brain region central to stress responses. Previous psychological studies have shown that women with anxiety often report heightened sensitivity to smells, a finding that aligns with these genetic associations.
In males, the genes tied to anxiety were primarily involved in lipoprotein metabolism. Lipoproteins help transport and process fats in the body. When a person experiences stress, the body typically mobilizes energy resources, often increasing lipoprotein levels as part of a physical fight-or-flight response. Because male and female metabolisms process fats differently due to sex hormones, these genetic variations provide a biological rationale for why anxiety might manifest differently in men.
The researchers next compared the genetic risk for anxiety against the genetic profiles of 28 other mental and physical health conditions. They wanted to see if the genetic predisposition for anxiety overlaps with the predisposition for other traits. This analysis revealed several sex-specific correlations.
The genetic risk for anxiety in females was strongly correlated with the genetic risk for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and a higher body mass index (BMI). In clinical settings, ADHD and anxiety frequently co-occur in females. The researchers noted that female ADHD might manifest predominantly as anxiety symptoms, which can sometimes result in ADHD being overlooked or misdiagnosed in women.
The link to general body mass index also aligns with past epidemiological studies showing that obesity and anxiety are more strongly linked in women, as well as neuroimaging research finding that higher BMI is associated with stronger stress-related brain responses in women. Conversely, the genetic risk for male anxiety showed a stronger association with waist-to-hip ratio adjusted for BMI. This metric reflects central body fat rather than overall weight.
Central fat distribution is more closely tied to insulin regulation and the specific lipoprotein metabolism pathways identified earlier in the male genetic data. In a final step, the researchers used the genetic variants to create polygenic scores, which are numerical estimates of a person’s genetic liability for a trait. They tested these scores in three independent cohorts, which included a general population group, a symptom-based group, and a clinical cohort of patients with depression.
A score generated from the female genetic data proved best at predicting anxiety in other women within the general population. When attempting to predict male anxiety, the female-derived score and the male-derived score performed similarly. Once the researchers mathematically matched the sample sizes to account for the smaller number of men, the only statistically significant difference was that the female-derived score predicted anxiety in women better than the male-derived score in the general population cohort; the other predictive differences between the male and female scores were not statistically significant.
The study does have a few limitations that require context. The male sample size was smaller than the female sample size, which reduces the statistical power to detect genetic variants in men. The researchers note that larger samples will be needed to clarify sex differences or commonalities.
The dataset also relied exclusively on individuals of European ancestry. As a result, the findings might not accurately reflect the genetic architecture of anxiety in other global populations. The researchers recommend that future genetic studies include larger and more diverse groups of people. By continuing to analyze male and female data separately, scientists can build a more accurate understanding of psychiatric conditions.
Standard approaches that blend male and female data run the risk of oversimplifying human biology and masking important genetic signals. The study, “Unravelling sex differences in the genetic architecture of anxiety,” was authored by Jihua Hu, Michelle K. Lupton, Enda M. Byrne, Nicholas G. Martin, David C. Whiteman, Catherine M. Olsen, Jodi T. Thomas, Sarah E. Medland, Katrina L. Grasby, and Brittany L. Mitchell.

New Philosophy of AI Initiatives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

The London School of Economics and Political Science (LSE) and the University of Toronto have launched new initiatives to support and focus philosophical research on various aspects of artificial intelligence (AI).
The Department of Philosophy, Logic and Scientific Method at LSE has received a $5.3 million donation to launch a new research group—The Global Priorities Research Group (GPRG)—dedicated to “determining which problems matter most and what should be done in trying to realize the best outcomes for humanity and the wider world.”
It’s primary emphasis will be “philosophical research that helps us navigate the largest-scale challenges associated with the impacts of transformative AI.”
Funded by Good Ventures, a philanthropic foundation, the GPRG “will also consider how we should compare and weight the interests of different kinds of beings—be they human, animal, or perhaps even artificial—as well as pursuing foundational research on issues related to value and rational choice with the potential to reorient our priorities across a wide range of issues.”
The group will be led by philosophers Andreas L. Mogensen, who recently joined LSE from the University of Oxford, and Teruji Thomas (Oxford, LSE), and will be based at LSE’s Centre for Philosophy of Natural and Social Science.
Meanwhile, the Artificial Consciousness Initiative is a new project from the University of Toronto Department of Philosophy that “aims to advance foundational research connecting artificial intelligence and consciousness.”
The project’s director, philosopher Andrew Y. Lee, writes:
The initiative’s research agenda focuses on questions about the nature, structure, and indicators of artificial consciousness; the valence and character of potential artificial experiences; the welfare and moral status of artificial systems; and the ethical and safety risks raised by increasingly capable AI. The initiative does not presuppose that current artificial systems are conscious or that future ones will be. But it starts from the view that these questions are worth taking seriously.
The core team of the Artificial Consciousness Initiative includes Karina Vold, Christian Tarsney, and Gwen Bradford.
The initiative’s aims include basic research, partnerships with other institutions, and contributing to public and policy discussions related to AI consciousness. The project is supported by a large grant from Longview Philanthropy.
Both initiatives are currently hiring postdocs.

An Idaho ICE Raid Rounded Up Hundreds. The Fallout Could Change How ICE Operates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

People first noticed the black helicopter in the sky.
It was a chilly Sunday afternoon a year ago at La Catedral Arena, a popular track for horse racing outside the Idaho town of Wilder. Hundreds had gathered at the arena for a festival celebrating horse racing and Mexican culture.
As the military-style helicopter hovered above them, attendees from the rural, predominantly Latino community, began to get nervous.
“Something is wrong,” Ivan Popoca, who attended the festival with his two kids, remembers thinking.
Within minutes, the festival grounds descended into chaos. Backed by armored trucks and snipers, more than 200 members of law enforcement stormed the grounds, some shot rubber bullets into the crowd and hurled flash-bang grenades into vehicles where people had fled to hide. Hundreds of people, including teens as young as 14, were detained and zip-tied.
When it was all over, federal authorities had arrested 105 people for alleged immigration violations. Yet on paper, this wasn’t an immigration raid at all. The only warrant for the Wilder raid was secured by the FBI. Its target: the owner of the track and four others for alleged unlicensed gambling.
Twelve months later, the Wilder raid is at the center of a court fight that could shape ICE operations around the country. Advocates argue that in Idaho, ICE unlawfully piggybacked on an FBI operation, rather than securing their own warrant, as they would be expected to do on this type of operation. A lawsuit brought forth by the ACLU argues that federal authorities violated the Fourth Amendment, which protects against unreasonable searches and seizures, by using an unrelated search warrant as a “cover to go fishing for immigration arrests.”
“That is not what a criminal search warrant execution looks like. That is what a massively violent immigration raid looks like,” says Jenn Rolnick Borchetta, an ACLU attorney who helped bring the resulting lawsuit.
Trump Administration officials insist that the arrests made that day were lawful. “The facts haven’t changed: ICE helped dismantle an illegal horse-racing, animal fighting, and a gambling enterprise operation out of a property known as La Cathedral Arena in Wilder, Idaho,” a DHS spokesperson told TIME. Idaho Gov. Brad Little also defended the raid, saying in a statement at the time that it is “common practice” to detain others present while processing the scene.
For Wilder residents, the La Catedral raid remains an open wound that refuses to heal. Popoca still recalls with anger how he and his 16-year-old son were zip-tied for hours for no apparent reason.
The ACLU and some of the families involved in the case released a documentary online on Monday called Wilder Raids in which they discuss the raid’s impact, and why the legal challenge matters beyond people in Wilder.
“Some community members don't even want to think about this anymore,” says Leo Morales, the executive director of the ACLU Idaho. “But there are also folks who are also realizing how critical it is to be able to push back, to organize and to demand fairness and justice.”
Recurring nightmares
Juana Rodriguez attended the festival with her three-year-old son. Despite both of them being U.S. citizens, they were zip-tied and detained for hours following the raid. Like many others who were detained, she described not being given access to food or water.
“For the longest time, my son begged me for food. He begged me for water,” Rodriguez says. She repeatedly asked the officers she could be untied so that she could feed and console her crying son, she says, but was rebuffed. “I wish I could have done more in the moment, but I couldn't.”
Detainees were eventually taken into a tent and questioned by ICE agents about their immigration status. Among the 105 people who were ultimately arrested, 75 are believed to have been deported to their home countries, according to local media, and 26 were released from ICE custody after their lawyers filed habeas corpus petitions. The whereabouts of the remaining four people are unclear. ICE did not provide an update on their case status.
The day after the raid, the Wilder School District reported absent rates soared, with 20% of students absent, according to The Idaho Statesman. More than half of the district’s student body is Hispanic or Latino.
A year later, Rodriguez says she is still scared to go to Latino cultural and other public events because of what happened at La Catedral. She also has nightmares about ICE officers taking her child away from her.
“I'm from here. My kids are from here,” she says. ”Why should I have to feel that? Like, I shouldn't.”
ICE’s growing legal fights
The ACLU filed a class-action complaint in February, charging that a variety of local, state and federal agencies violated the constitutional rights of those at the festival. Both sides are now waiting for a judge to rule on a motion by ICE and other agencies to dismiss, in which it argued that federal and state law enforcement are protected by qualified immunity, a longstanding legal doctrine when executing a federal warrant.
The Wilder case is one of multiple lawsuits the Trump Administration is fighting over its immigration enforcement operations. In Minnesota, none of the federal agents involved in the deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti have been criminally charged, but a string of civil lawsuits is beginning to emerge. Earlier this month, the family of Renee Good, who was killed last January by a federal agent during the immigration enforcement surge in Minnesota, filed a pair of civil lawsuits against the federal government, according to their legal representative. Marimar Martinez, a U.S. citizen who was shot by a Border Patrol agent during a confrontation on a Chicago street last year, has also filed a lawsuit against the federal government.
Anyone seeking to hold federal agents accountable must be prepared for a long wait, says Borchetta. A lawsuit against the federal government can’t even be filed unless it’s been six months since a complainant filed a claim for compensation and the issue remains unresolved.
“If a federal employee is driving their car negligently on the job and hits you with their car, you can bring a claim for them for that negligence,” Borchetta says. “It also applies where an ICE agent is mistreating you or causing you harm.”
But the law itself imposes many limitations on suing the federal government. Victims can seek compensatory damages for actual losses, but not punitive damages. And unlike state authorities who can be sued for civil rights violations in state courts, federal law enforcement authorities are generally shielded from such lawsuits based on legal precedents.
But Borchetta says the impact of the lawsuits can be bigger than any verdict. She argues that the ongoing Wilder case has already helped change ICE’s conduct as well as how local governments collaborate with them.
“While we don't yet have a decision from the court, we haven't seen more raids like this in Idaho,” she says. “The lawsuit itself exposes both the state and the federal actors to liability, and that can change behavior itself.”

Bulgaria and Hungary will seek closer economic cooperation and work toward greater stability and prosperity in Europe, Bulgarian Foreign Minister Velislava Petrova said during the opening of an exhibition at the Foreign Ministry alongside Hungarian Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Anita Orbán.
The exhibition traces the history of the Lajos Kossuth House-Museum in Shumen and was inaugurated by the two ministers to mark Bulgarian-Hungarian Friendship Day on October 19. This year marks the 10th anniversary of the date being established as a joint holiday for the two countries.
“We will work together - both to strengthen economic cooperation between the two countries and to achieve greater stability and prosperity in Europe,” Petrova said.
She said her talks with Orbán had laid a firm basis for expanding cooperation across several sectors. Petrova stressed that closer ties with friendly countries and the pursuit of common objectives were increasingly important given ongoing conflicts, a complicated security environment, and Europe’s economic situation.
Petrova said shared history and cultural heritage often create the strongest and most lasting connections between nations, describing these as central to the relationship between Bulgaria and Hungary. She recalled that the exhibition documents the arrival of several thousand Hungarian exiles in Bulgaria after the suppression of the 1848 revolution.
To illustrate the close relationship between the two peoples, Petrova quoted scholar Géza Fehér: “Fate has granted me two homelands - Bulgaria and Hungary.”
Orbán said the friendship between Bulgaria and Hungary meant that both countries could depend on each other when confronting current challenges. She added that historical and cultural links had become even more important as overlapping crises brought unprecedented consequences.
“Our strategic partnership provides a solid foundation for us to continue striving together toward freedom, peace, and security in Europe and across the globe,” Orbán said.
The Hungarian foreign minister also described the Bulgarian national minority in Hungary as an important bond between the two countries, welcoming the community’s continued strengthening of its identity. She noted that Bulgarian-Hungarian Friendship Day was also being marked in the Hungarian Parliament, with the participation of the Hungarian culture minister.
Orbán recalled the warm welcome extended to Lajos Kossuth and Hungarian émigrés in Vidin and Shumen, saying the trust and affinity established at that time had survived to the present day.
At the end of her remarks, Orbán thanked Bulgaria for its hospitality and invited Petrova to visit Hungary.

jenny holzer transforms musée d’orsay with monumental light projections and engraved stone

j’ai vu: jenny holzer’s monumental light projections transform the musée d’orsay in paris
the american artist digs into musée d’orsay’s archives, transforming historical writings into monumental LED installations, light projections, engraved stone sculptures, and metallic paintings that confront the conflicts and contradictions of the past.
prefer designboom on google
JENNY HOLZER ILLUMINATES MUSÉE D’ORSAY WITH WORDS FROM THE PAST
The walls of Paris’ Musée d’Orsay have plenty to say, and Jenny Holzer is giving them a voice. For J’ai Vu (I Saw), opening October 20, 2026, the American artist transforms the former railway station into a vast canvas of illuminated words, moving texts, and engraved stone sculptures. Developed in collaboration with the museum, the exhibition draws on writings from the period represented in its collections, bringing together artistic correspondence, political commentary, and historical accounts. Rather than simply revisiting the 19th century, Holzer lets its voices confront the present, proving that some conversations are far from over.
The intervention begins outside, where the museum’s Seine-facing facade becomes the setting for ÉCLAIRÉ, a series of monumental light projections presented from October 18 to 22, between 7 pm and 11 pm. Drawing on approximately 250 excerpts by 34 authors, including writings by Vincent van Gogh, Paul Cézanne, Gustave Flaubert, and Émile Zola, Holzer covers the historic architecture with luminous words that can be experienced freely from the riverbanks. Letters, literary passages, and political reflections unfold across the building, temporarily turning one of Paris’ most recognizable cultural landmarks into a public display of history in motion.
MONUMENTAL LED INSTALLATIONS TRANSFORM MUSÉE D’ORSAY
Inside the Musée d’Orsay, a monumental, site-specific LED installation by Jenny Holzer carries the exhibition through four galleries dedicated to history painting, naturalism, symbolism, and Gustave Courbet. Streams of brightly colored text move through the spaces, introducing historical voices into rooms traditionally dominated by paintings and sculptures. The installation responds to the architecture and the circulation of visitors, recalling the building’s original function as a bustling 19th-century railway station. Once a place for moving passengers, the former Gare d’Orsay now finds itself transporting words instead.
Jenny Holzer also introduces 19 stone sculptures, comprising 17 benches and two columns, distributed throughout the museum’s ground-floor galleries and public spaces. Created specifically for the exhibition, these works feature engraved texts largely dating from 1848 to 1914. Their carefully selected varieties of stone, each researched for its origin and character, establish a material dialogue with the museum’s existing sculptures and pedestals. Unlike the moving LED displays, these inscriptions invite a slower encounter with language, transforming familiar architectural elements into objects that demand a closer reading.
HOLZER CONFRONTS WAR, SECRECY AND CENSORSHIP THROUGH ART
The exhibition takes a more explicitly political turn in the museum’s history painting gallery, where Holzer has developed a new presentation centered on war and conflict. Historical works from the permanent collection appear alongside her own paintings, made with gold, platinum, and palladium leaf, which reference recent international conflicts. Based on partially redacted documents, these metallic surfaces conceal substantial portions of their original texts, leaving visible fragments that raise questions about secrecy, accountability, and the boundaries between legitimate confidentiality and the concealment of wrongdoing. A separate gallery overlooking the Seine extends the presentation, allowing natural light to transform the reflective surfaces throughout the day.
Altogether, J’ai Vu brings together more than 750 distinct texts from 424 sources and 73 authors, potentially making it Holzer’s most extensive selection of written material for a single exhibition. The subjects range from the Franco-Prussian War and the Paris Commune to colonialism, anarchism, labor movements, military corruption, and the everyday realities of Haussmann-era Paris. By bringing these competing perspectives into the same space, Holzer constructs a portrait of history that resists any single interpretation. Projected in light, carved into stone, or partially erased beneath precious metals, the words expose how closely the anxieties of the past resemble those of the present. History, it seems, has never been particularly good at keeping quiet.
project info:
name: J’ai Vu
artist: Jenny Holzer | @jennyholzerstudio
location: Musée d’Orsay | @museeorsay
dates: October 20, 2026 – February 21, 2027

From delivery driver to global fame: A Korean writer's journey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
10:55:00 UTC
19:55:00 KST

From delivery driver to global fame: A Korean writer's journey
October 19, 2026
For ten years, publishers rejected You Yeong-Gwang's book. Yet before it was even printed in South Korea, the once-abandoned manuscript had international publishers flocking to secure translation rights.
"I'm so grateful that the book has now been published in more than 20 countries. Even more astonishingly, it also appeared on the Der Spiegel bestseller list in Germany," he told DW while attending the 2026 Frankfurt Book Fair.
For a debut novel by an unknown author, it was a massive success, securing publication in 15 languages, including English, German, Spanish and traditional Chinese.
"The Rainfall Market" tells the story of a mysterious, hidden shop that only opens when it rains. In the shop, visitors can exchange their deepest unhappiness for a ticket to a brand-new destiny. The plot revolves around Serin, a disheartened young girl who stumbles into the marketplace run by whimsical spirits, finding a warm, comforting space.
"In fact, Serin's story is my story," author You said. "For a long time, I even wondered how wonderful it would be if I could sell my unhappiness and use the money to buy happiness."
While writing the book, he was going through a difficult time himself.
"I had to care for my mother, who had been ill for a long time, and I had also been responsible for supporting my family financially for many years. Life felt incredibly heavy," he reflected.
"But when I was writing, I could immerse myself in the world of the story and, even if only for a short while, forget about those circumstances. That's why writing made me so happy. I truly enjoyed it."
On the creation of 'The Rainfall Market'
The idea of rain is inspired by his own life.
"At that time, my circumstances felt as though it were raining constantly," You said.
The story draws heavily on traditional Korean folklore, serving as a quintessential "healing fiction" tale in which its young protagonist must weigh the true cost of seemingly perfect lives.
"When I was writing, I wasn't consciously trying to write healing fiction. At the time, I didn't even really know that such a label existed."
He initially planned to publish a book independently and started crowdfunding. But as the funding failed, he used all his savings and printed 200 copies, which bookstores refused to take. In a month, he only sold five copies. "I thought that's it. I really have to give up now.”
"At the time, I had undergone eye surgery and due to complications, I couldn't see, so I started working at a call center, where I could work using my voice." You said. "During the week, I worked at a call center, and on weekends I went to a computer academy. I learned how to make books on my own for a few years."
He then taught himself how to use the software needed to create books on his own.
While running one of the crowdfunding campaigns, he started working as a food delivery driver. "The round trip between my home and the area where I delivered food took about four hours each day. So I wrote on my phone's memo app while traveling on the subway."
"Even when I was going through very difficult circumstances, I was able to keep writing because the moments when I was writing were so joyful. For a little while, I could forget about the difficult situation I was in," You explained.
Finally a breakthrough
"I gathered those pieces of writing together and launched what I intended to be my final crowdfunding campaign," he said.
The campaign was intended to fund the publication of "The Rainfall Market."
"To my amazement, the campaign succeeded, and I was able to publish the book commercially for the first time," he said.
Following the crowdfunding success, the novel was acquired by Clayhouse, a prominent South Korean publishing company.
Before it was even published, he had received offers from publishers in five countries and signed international publishing contracts.
And in the first month after publication, the original South Korean language edition sold 30,000 copies across all formats, ranking as the bestselling e-book and third-bestselling physical book.
"I still find it hard to believe that all of this has happened and that I'm here at the Frankfurt Book Fair. I'm incredibly grateful and happy," said You.
A new horizon for Hallyu, or the 'Korean Wave:' K-Comfort Fiction
Korea's newest soft power is K-literature, which sold about 1.2 million translated copies abroad in 2025 for the second consecutive year.
And You's book belongs to a trending genre called Korean comfort fiction.
"When readers closed the book, I wanted them to feel a little warmth in their hearts," he said.
Although Korean literature was first known for darker, more pragmatic books about societal realities, K-comfort fiction is the child of South Korea's pressure-cooker modern society. It offers an answer to the human need for escapism and a transient antidote to the reality of a hyper-competitive education system, brutal job market and intense corporate pressure.
"When I was writing, I was going through a very difficult time myself, and I wished someone would comfort me. So, I thought, why don't I try reading something like that myself? Why don't I write something that can comfort me?" You wondered.
With burnout on the rise globally, more readers are seeking soul-soothing literature with exhausted protagonists they can relate to. Usually without a need to defeat a villain, the stories follow protagonists with a deep desire for rest, community and emotional repair.
The whimsical fiction aspect is the missing element allowing them to step away from reality. The genre originally gained traction through indie productions, online crowdfunding and endorsements from high-profile K-pop artists.
Despite the Korean context, this style of storytelling quickly went global, capturing different international audiences, including those already familiar with cozy K-dramas or those simply looking for a gentle refuge from the anxieties of the modern world.
Last year, the bestselling Korean novel abroad was "Welcome to the Hyunam-dong Bookshop," according to the Literature Translation Institute of Korea. The novel belongs to the same genre as "The Rainfall Market."
While readers embrace the genre, critics view it with literary skepticism. They point out that it relies heavily on a predictable, repetitive formula, often built around a single magical space, with simplistic prose and low-stakes conflicts that prioritize cozy vibes over deep character development.
Reviewing "The Rainfall Market" for the Korea Times, Peter Juhl, a literary critic, described healing fiction as light, feel-good stories and argued the boom reflects a deliberate effort to write global novels for international markets.
Future aspirations and message to readers
"Of course I'm happy that my book is receiving so much love and that I'm able to write. But more than anything, I hope my mother gets better and regains her health," You said after mentioning that his mother underwent surgery a week before his arrival at the book fair.
Beyond the book itself, people seem to relate to and appreciate the story of his own life.
"If I have the opportunity, I'd like to share more stories about hope and dreams with people who are going through circumstances similar to mine," said You. "If my story can help one person even a little, in any way, I don't think anything could make me happier."

US Sends Ukraine Just 12 Patriot Missiles a Month, Holds Back Paid-For Supplies, Zelenskyy Says
The United States is supplying Ukraine with only 12 Patriot air defense interceptor missiles per month—roughly four times fewer than under former President Joe Biden—while withholding approval for additional weapons Kyiv has already paid for, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Bloomberg on October 18, Zelenskyy accused Washington of delaying critical air defense supplies and using restrictions on military assistance to pressure Ukraine into accepting unfavorable terms to end Russia’s war.
“We have paid for the weapons,” Zelenskyy said, referring to purchases that include anti-ballistic missile interceptors under the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) initiative. “A part of the supplies has been authorized” by the US side, “while the rest haven’t been. And this is not a technical issue.”
The Ukrainian president said the current delivery rate represents approximately one-quarter of the number of Patriot interceptors supplied during the Biden administration. Unlike previous US military assistance, which provided interceptors to Ukraine without charge, the Trump administration is selling the missiles to Kyiv.
The restrictions come as Ukraine faces continued Russian ballistic missile attacks targeting cities and critical infrastructure, increasing demand for interceptor missiles capable of countering such threats.
Zelenskyy also proposed suspending Ukrainian strikes against Russian diesel fuel production facilities in exchange for additional Patriot interceptors.
“My latest model was: We don’t target Russian diesel, you give us missiles for Patriot systems to protect our facilities. But they just want us to stop attacking diesel. And if we strike that, they will disconnect us from something,” Zelenskyy told Bloomberg.
The proposal follows US demands that Ukraine halt attacks on Russian oil refineries, which the Trump administration has linked to rising global diesel prices. However, Zelenskyy suggested that Washington’s actions extended beyond disagreements over energy infrastructure.
“I believe steps have been taken to convince Ukraine to capitulate,” he said. “I am not saying that this is the goal our partners are pursuing. I don’t want to think that our American partners believe the war could be ended sooner at Ukraine’s expense. But that’s how it looks.”
According to Bloomberg, the restrictions on Patriot deliveries have coincided with disruptions to Ukraine’s Starlink satellite communications and the absence of advance US warning ahead of a Russian ballistic missile strike on Kyiv on October 18.
Despite the current disagreements, Zelenskyy expressed hope that relations with Washington could improve following the November 3 US midterm elections. “Politics is very aggressive during election time,” Zelenskyy told Bloomberg. “I think it is agony now, but after elections, life will continue and I believe it will be calmer.”
Earlier, on October 16, Zelenskyy warned that Ukraine was facing a severe shortage of PAC-2 and PAC-3 interceptor missiles, noting that most available supplies had been redirected to the Middle East.

President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy would win the first round of the presidential elections if they were held in the near future, according to the results of a sociological survey conducted by New Image Marketing Group with the support of the Dilova Stolytsia publication on October 6–12.
As reported on the publication's website, the incumbent President of Ukraine would gather 29% of voters' support. In second place is Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of Ukraine to the UK and former Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine Valeriy Zaluzhny, for whom 21% of respondents would vote.
The fifth President of Ukraine (2014–2019), leader of European Solidarity party, and MP Petro Poroshenko would secure 9.6% of the vote, followed by a tied result of 5.8% for former Minister of Defense Mykhailo Fedorov, Commander of the 3rd Army Corps Andriy Biletsky, and Head of the Office of the President of Ukraine and former Chief of the Main Directorate of Intelligence (GUR) Kyrylo Budanov. They are followed by independent MPs Oleksiy Honcharenko (5.1%) and Dmytro Razumkov (4.7%).
In the event of parliamentary elections, European Solidarity would win the largest share of the vote with 17%, followed in second place by a hypothetical Zaluzhny party at 16.1%, and in third by Zelenskyy's party with 15%.
Next is a hypothetical Budanov party with 9.6%, followed by All-Ukrainian Union Batkivshchyna and the Azov party with 6.7% each, Razumkov's hypothetical party with 5.1%, Honcharenko's party with 4.6%, and the "3rd Separate Assault Brigade" party with 2.6%. The publication notes that "the hypothesis of whether voters distinguish between the 'Azov' and '3rd Assault' parties requires deeper examination."
Commenting on the survey results, Vadym Denysenko, head of the analytical center at Dilova Stolytsia, noted that traditionally, during periods of tension between Trump and Zelenskyy, the latter's ratings temporarily rise before rolling back. "Zaluzhny's strategy of maintaining a minimal presence in the media landscape, despite all criticism, continues to pay off—he remains unreachable in a second-round runoff for all competitors," he remarked.
Denysenko also suggested that the growth in European Solidarity's party rating was driven by the consolidation of Poroshenko's core electorate amid high media activity from Honcharenko, adding that sustaining this level over an extended period will be extremely difficult.
The survey sampled 1,200 respondents, with a margin of error not exceeding 2.9%.

Japan announces intention to continue contacts with Russia to resolve issues
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
10:51:09 UTC
19:51:09 KST

TOKYO, October 19. /TASS/. The Japanese government remains committed to maintaining dialogue with Russia to resolve outstanding bilateral issues while continuing to assert its claims to the southern Kuril Islands, Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara told a news conference in Tokyo.
The briefing coincided with the 70th anniversary of the Soviet-Japanese Joint Declaration, signed in Moscow on October 19, 1956, which formally ended the state of war between the two countries and restored diplomatic and trade relations.
"We take very seriously the fact that the ‘Northern Territories’ issue (Tokyo’s term for the southern part of the Kuril Islands - TASS) remains unresolved and that no peace treaty has been concluded with Russia," Kihara said. "Japan’s policy on resolving the status of the four northern islands and concluding a peace treaty remains unchanged."
He noted that bilateral relations were currently in a "difficult situation" amid the conflict in Ukraine. "We intend to maintain the necessary contacts with Russia and continue working to resolve the various outstanding issues," Kihara added.
Moscow and Tokyo have held consultations on a peace treaty to formally conclude World War II since the mid-20th century. The main obstacle remains their disagreement over the status of the southern Kuril Islands.
Following the war, the entire Kuril archipelago became part of the Soviet Union. Japan disputes Russia’s sovereignty over Iturup, Kunashir, Shikotan and a group of nearby small, uninhabited islands. The Russian Foreign Ministry has repeatedly stated that Russian sovereignty over these territories, established in accordance with international law, is not open to question.
After Tokyo imposed sanctions on Russia over the conflict in Ukraine, Moscow suspended consultations with Japan on a peace treaty. Russia also withdrew from talks on joint economic activities in the southern Kuril Islands, while visits to the area by former Japanese residents were discontinued.

‘art must reflect the times we live in’: ibrahim mahama on his fondation cartier exhibition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
10:50:18 UTC
19:50:18 KST

‘art must reflect the times we live in’: ibrahim mahama on his fondation cartier exhibition
from abandoned factories in ghana to his major exhibition in paris, the artist uses repair to rethink how we relate to history, labor, and one another, arguing that what we inherit can become a resource for building something new.
prefer designboom on google
Ibrahim Mahama brings Ghanaian industrial histories to paris
Ibrahim Mahama has spent years collecting, dismantling, and rebuilding things that could be considered beyond repair. Old trains, airplanes, factory structures, wooden stools, and industrial materials shape a practice that looks at what societies leave behind and what can be done with it. His work is rooted in northern Ghana, where the history of colonial exploitation continues to shape the region, but his questions reach far beyond it: who gets to shape the future, what do we do with the past, and how can art create something useful for the people around it? These questions come together in The Harvest Season, Mahama’s major exhibition at Fondation Cartier in Paris, on view from October 22nd, 2026, to February 28th, 2027. Developed with nine artists and collectives connected to the Ghanaian art scene, the presentation brings together installations, industrial remnants, and spaces for public activity.
The artist wants the museum to be a space for people to meet, learn, and share ideas. This builds on his work in Tamale, where he has founded three art centers that bring contemporary art into education and community life. For Mahama, this commitment began with a question about the place he comes from. Growing up in northern Ghana, he saw how difficult circumstances could become a reason to leave. An idea from one of his art school mentors offered another way to think about it. ‘We need to see art as a gift,’ the artist recalls being taught during our discussion. ‘Sometimes even the conditions which we inherit or we are born in are a gift in themselves. Sometimes you can inherit a bad gift. But then the question is, how do you transform this gift into a promise for other people?’ This idea is central to Mahama’s practice. He works with what the past leaves behind, finding ways to give old materials, structures, and histories a new role rather than letting them disappear. ‘Contemporary art is not just meant to produce beautiful, fancy exhibitions. The idea is that even if we’re going to deal with the question of aesthetics and beauty, it has to deeply reflect the times that we live in or the question of time itself.’ he tells designboom.
‘The Harvest Season’ at Fondation Cartier
One of the central installations in Ibrahim Mahama’s The Harvest Season at Fondation Cartier is Parliament of Ghosts, an assembly of traditional Asante wooden stools collected in Ghana, some damaged and in need of repair. The stools carry cultural significance beyond their function as objects of everyday use. As Mahama explains, they can mark important moments in a person’s life, from birth to the installation of a chief or queen, and are traditionally carved by craftspeople who inherit these skills across generations. Some African objects, including stools of this kind, were taken during the colonial period and now sit in Western museum collections, where they are often displayed as ethnographic objects behind glass. Mahama argues that removing them from their original contexts changes their status. ‘They no longer lived as they were meant to live,’ he shares with us. To give them another life, he negotiated with their owners to bring the stools to his Red Clay art center in Tamale, where they were repaired with the participation of schoolchildren. The children were invited to watch the process and sit on the stools as the work progressed. ‘We were not thinking of these objects as ethnographic objects. We’re just thinking of them as living beings,’ he reflects. Mahama compares their restoration to the healing of an injured person, who seeks medicine, recovers, and continues living. ‘We wanted these stools to do the same.’
Τhe marks left by damage and restoration are, for Mahama, part of their continuing history. ‘What does it mean for these objects to continue living even in the precarious conditions in which they find themselves in?’ Ibrahim Mahama asks. Bringing the stools to Paris carries a particular significance. As the artist points out, objects of this kind have historically entered European collections through colonial looting. This time, they travel to Europe through a different process, becoming the basis for a parliamentary arrangement where visitors can gather and discuss questions about history, culture, and the present. By giving these objects a new role within the museum, Mahama also challenges what an art institution can be and the kinds of conversations it should make possible. ‘Sometimes, when artists try to present certain ideas in museums, the response sometimes is, “No, we cannot. This is too radical.” But where is art supposed to exist? I thought art was supposed to be the safe space for radicality.’ he comments.
A FORMER GHANAIAN GLASS bottle FACTORY FINDS A NEW LIFE
Mahama applies this approach to architecture, too, working with a former glass bottle factory built in Ghana between 1961 and 1966. Originally designed in Czechoslovakia and manufactured in Germany, the factory formed part of the industrial development of the country following independence. It opened in 1966, just 19 days before Ghana’s first president, Kwame Nkrumah, was overthrown in a military coup. The factory continued operating for decades before being decommissioned and sold for scrap. Mahama used funds from Fondation Cartier to buy back part of the structure and bring it to France, where his team reassembled it as a pavilion. He also acquired approximately 300,000 abandoned glass bottles that were destined for destruction, along with the factory’s sign. Working with metalsmiths, the team restored damaged and rusted components, leaving traces of their previous life visible. For Mahama, the factory connects the industrial ambitions of post-independence Ghana with the political and economic difficulties that followed. ‘What does it mean to confront the decays of history?’ the artist asks. He sees this confrontation as part of art’s role, particularly when the past is painful or difficult to acknowledge. ‘Art is meant to allow us to see the rot that exists within the world,’ he points out, ‘and then when we are confronted by it, maybe we will take a different position on things.’
The structure will serve as a classroom and space for performances and drawing classes, while retaining the marks and imperfections of its former life. ‘We want people to see the scars and learn from them,’ Mahama says, seeing the marks of the factory as traces of its history. ‘Sometimes repair is not just physical. It might also be some kind of historical gap and all that historical deficit.’ In Tamale, the artist has applied this thinking to old trains, airplanes, and other structures, reassembling them for new uses. For him, moving an object from one place to another can be a form of repair too, prompting questions about its history and the relationships it carries. ‘‘Even the act of transferring an object from one place to another, I think, raises the question of repair,’ he highlights. ‘It’s almost as if we’re asking ourselves: how do you repair your relationship with something?’
From the museum to the city
In Tamale, Ibrahim Mahama has established the Savannah Centre for Contemporary Art, Red Clay, and Nkrumah Voli-ni. These three cultural spaces host exhibitions, research, educational activities, and public gatherings. At Fondation Cartier, he wants to bring some of that same energy into the museum, with talks, performances, and workshops taking place alongside the exhibition. ‘I think one of the things I’m most looking forward to is the discussions that would transpire in this period within the exhibition,’ the Ghanaian tells us. He hopes the show will attract people who might not ordinarily visit a contemporary art museum and give them an opportunity to engage with the work on their own terms. He also wants to challenge assumptions about contemporary art from Africa. ‘A lot of people maybe wouldn’t think that in Africa, contemporary art is this significant or this ambitious,’ he continues.
Alongside Ibrahim Mahama’s works, The Harvest Season features nine artists and collectives connected to Ghana’s art scene, including Dorothy Akpene Amenuke, Gideon Appah, James Barnor, Cercle d’Art des Travailleurs de Plantation Congolaise (CATPC), Courage Dzidula Kpodo, Postbox Ghana, Zohra Opoku, Tjaša Rener, and Feda Wardak. Their inclusion also reflects the artist’s interest in collaboration. His experience with the Black Star Lines Collective, which grew out of connections among university professors, students, and other affiliates, shaped his questions about how artists can work together when opportunities and resources are limited. ‘How do we work with each other? How do we help one another?’ Mahama recalls asking as a student. He points to the pressures of an art world where opportunities and resources can be limited and the importance of finding ways to support one another. ‘I might be doing it from a singular artist’s point of view, but the questions that are raised within it are very plural and are very open,’ he argues. ‘Sometimes through the individual artist’s practice, we can be able to ask much more tangible, bigger, collective concerns.’
A future built from what remains
A recent experience in Tamale shows how Ibrahim Mahama’s work can extend beyond the art world. He had been trying to gain access to an old cemetery where Eastern European engineers involved in the construction of grain silos were buried. ‘Some Eastern European engineers who worked in the city, building silos, were buried there,’ the artist explains. The cemetery had long been unused, and his attempts to obtain the land through the state had proved difficult. Eventually, traditional chiefs with authority over the land granted it to him so he could transform it into a public space. ‘It was beautiful to realize that the work we do has developed to a point where people at the local and traditional political levels recognize its significance and are willing to support it,’ he reflects. For Ibrahim Mahama, the gesture demonstrated how contemporary art can become relevant within a local context, where its value is measured through what it makes possible for the community.
An unused cemetery, like an abandoned factory, can become a place for people to gather and reconsider how a community uses its land and remembers its history. This is one of the questions at the center of The Harvest Season at Fondation Cartier: what can be done with what remains, and who might benefit from giving it another life?
project info:

exhibition: The Harvest Season
location:  Fondation Cartier pour l’art contemporain | @fondationcartier, Paris, France

Iran support for Houthis probed as Yemen war re-erupts and Saudi cities hit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Iran support for Houthis probed as Yemen war re-erupts and Saudi cities hit
There have been new reports of Iranian support for the Houthis in Yemen amid a wave of attacks on Saudi cities.
New allegations about Iranian support for Yemen’s Houthis have emerged in media reports and official comments, highlighting the opaque nature of the alliance.
Media outlets have reported that Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) aided the Houthis as they seized swaths of western Yemen and launched their most potent and sophisticated attacks yet on Saudi Arabia, which supports the internationally recognised Yemeni government fighting the Houthis.
Iranian support for the Houthis reported by the media includes training, intelligence, tactical guidance and help in targeting for drone and missile attacks.
If true, this will undoubtedly escalate tensions between Iran and Saudi Arabia, given that the kingdom has been targeted by dozens of Houthi drones and missiles in recent weeks, including an attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh that killed 13 people. Saudi energy facilities and oil tankers have also been targeted by the group.
Iranian backing, according to the reports, contributed to a September offensive by the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God). Those battles saw the Houthis win control of Yemen’s Red Sea coastline and the strategically important Bab al-Mandeb strait.
The Wall Street Journal reported that Iranian Mahan Air flights ferried IRGC paramilitary officers, drone parts, missile guidance systems and impact detonators to the Houthis in Yemen. IRGC officers were also reportedly on the front lines directing Houthi attacks.
The spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen’s government, Major-General Turki al-Maliki, confirmed the presence of an external state actor behind the Houthis’ evolving arsenal but did not mention the state in question.
Al-Maliki noted that the Houthis, who have been at war with the government since 2014, have acquired advanced technologies with regional assistance.
This support has made the Houthis the first nonstate armed group to deploy ballistic missiles, offensive and suicide drones, and explosive-laden, high-speed boats, he said, although other Iranian allies, such as Hezbollah and Iranian militias, also possess such weaponry.
While the Houthis have stressed their independence from Iran, the two groups are ideologically aligned. They have also been accused of collaborating closely on military matters, evident in the Houthis’ missile arsenal.
Operational planning
Analysts who spoke to Al Jazeera all agreed that the “regional assistance” the Houthis are receiving points towards the IRGC although Iran and the Houthis denied this.
One indication of this is the bombing of Sanaa International Airport in July before an Iranian plane carrying a Houthi delegation travelling from Tehran was due to land. The Yemeni government, which said its forces carried out the attack, accused “the Iranian aircraft” of violating Yemeni airspace.
“[Recent reports] confirm what is known to experts for years as the Revolutionary Guard and Hezbollah experts engaged in managing the operational planning of battles against the Yemeni government and neighbouring countries, including the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia,” Ibrahim Jalal, a Yemen-focused analyst, told Al Jazeera.
“For example, the killing of Hassan Irlu [the Iranian ambassador to Houthi-controlled Yemen from 2020 to 2021], in Yemen after the military campaign on Marib in 2021 is one of the important indicators, in addition to Mahan aviation flights that transported more experts ahead of the Houthis’ internal and external escalation during July of this year.”
Ali al-Dahab, a military and strategic security affairs expert, agreed that the advanced weaponry used by the Houthis indicates an Iranian role in recent operations.
“What was leaked about Iranian support for the Houthis through this report did not add anything new except that it confirmed the confirmed, and what it added perhaps is that weapons smuggling, especially precision technologies for missiles and unmanned aircraft, takes place via small submarines,” al-Dahab told Al Jazeera.
“This issue is not everything being smuggled from Iran to the Houthis because there are interceptions of smuggled shipments revealed by the joint forces that were controlling the Mocha coast to Bab al-Mandeb before the Houthis’ control and before its break in September.”
Al-Dahab pointed out that while smugglers historically have used dhows, traditional wooden sailboats, to mislead naval coalitions, employing submarines is a new method used by the Houthis, akin to the tactics used by organised criminal groups in the Americas.
“It indicates that Iran focuses on the Houthis as the centre of military and security gravity south of the Red Sea and, therefore, provides them with these weapons, ammunition, expertise and information in anticipation of a battle that may break out in the Strait of Hormuz,” al-Dahab said. “Therefore, the Houthis play a supporting role for them in the Bab al-Mandeb strait.”
He warned of broader implications for international shipping with the Houthis now in control of Bab al-Mandeb, a narrow waterway linking the Gulf of Aden and the Red Sea.
“The greatest danger now is that substate entities in the southern Red Sea and Gulf of Aden region unite under Iran’s leadership to confront the United States, Britain and Europe in general if a battle breaks out in the Gulf of Aden and the strait,” al-Dahab said.
Diplomatic realities
Saudi Arabia and Iran had appeared to have patched up years of hostilities, including the suspension of diplomatic relations, with a China-brokered reconciliation agreement signed in Beijing in 2023.
Hesham Alghannam, a Riyadh-based fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, said he doubts whether Saudi Arabia ever read the Beijing agreement as reconciliation but as a way of lowering tensions. Differences on geopolitical issues have continued between the two countries since the agreement was signed, including on Yemen, which lies on Saudi Arabia’s southern border.
“That isn’t a breach you can take to a lawyer. It’s keeping two files apart, and it works until someone says it out loud. That’s what’s changed,” Alghannam told Al Jazeera.
“Honestly, the deeper question was never whether Tehran signs [the agreement with Saudi Arabia]. It’s whether anything Tehran signs reaches the people holding the launchers,” he added, referring to Iran-aligned armed groups, such as the Houthis.
“We know how the other sequence ends. In 2014, the [Houthis] were offered seats, special status for Saada [the northern Yemeni stronghold of the Houthis] and a share of the executive authority in Yemen in return for handing the heavy weapons to the state,” he added.
What followed was the Houthis seizure of the capital, Sanaa, in September 2014, forcing the government to flee south, and the later killing of former President Ali Abdullah Saleh.
“What followed was the seizure of the institutions, the president detained, parliament dissolved. The gains were banked, and the guns were kept,” Alghannam added.
“Saleh partnered with them, and he was killed in the street in 2017. Even after taking Sanaa, they didn’t become the state. They built a network of supervisors sitting over every official post. So the Saudi red line is one thing, no armed group or second army inside one state.”
The Saudi-led intervention in Yemen began in March 2015 and led to another direct conflict between Riyadh and the Houthis. Despite the massive support Saudi Arabia provided the internationally recognised government, it failed to retake Sanaa. This highlighted weaknesses within the anti-Houthi coalition, including divisions between the internationally recognised government and southern separatists.
“The lesson of 2015 wasn’t that acting firmly leads to a long war. It was that announcing a goal earlier than you should [do] does because once it’s said out loud, you’re bound to it long before you can deliver it,” he said.
“What Riyadh is trying to do now is easy to say and hard to do, but it’s crucial: tie the money and the weapons to real integration under one command, not to declared loyalty.”
Strategic independence
Hassan Ahmadian, an assistant professor of political science at the University of Tehran, told Al Jazeera that Iran seeks technological independence for partners rather than perpetual reliance.
“This pattern is not like the United States pattern, which keeps whoever follows and allies with it in need of it, meaning [they have] to buy from the United States the weapons he needs, and the main weapon is basically not given to him if it is an Arab or Islamic country specifically,” he said.
“As for Iran, the ally is provided with the technology to create and produce the weapon, and this is not only in Yemen but in other regions and even in Gaza as much as possible where the technology was transferred because the view is different.”
Ahmadian said enabling Iran’s allies to produce their own weapons is a strategic move by Tehran and the Houthis are also motivated by breaking the Saudi siege on territories it controls in Yemen.
“The view is that this technology helps in confronting a common enemy, and therefore, strengthening this capability independently of Iran is in itself a strategic interest for Iran,” Ahmadian said.
“Notice that there is an advance for Ansar Allah [the Houthis] linked to the justice of the cause as there is a siege imposed on the Yemenis affecting 70 percent to 80 percent of the society controlled by Ansar Allah and the Sanaa government. So this cause, breaking the siege, is a just cause. … The regional circumstance gave [the Houthis] a motive that this is the time to pressure Saudi Arabia to break the siege, and this is what actually happened.”

Gate blocked at the port of Naples as truckers' protest spreads
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
12:48:13 CEST
19:48:13 KST

The 'Bausan' gate at the port of
Naples was blocked by truckers, causing disruption and jams on
the A1 highway, as lorry driver protests over soaring fuel
prices spread further on Monday.
                                    
Protests involved truckers blocking roads or sealing off lanes
to slow traffic started in many parts of the country, especially
the south, last week, following strikes and sit-ins by farmers
and fishers.
                                    
They have already had an impact, with shortages of fresh produce
affecting supermarket shelves and market stalls in places
ranging from Catania in Sicily, Scalea in Calabria, Cerignola in
Puglia, Mercogliano in Campania and Sora and Cassino and Fabrica
di Roma in Lazio.
                                    
Pasquale Russo, the head of the Conftrasporto truckers
confederation, said last week that the nation's lorry drivers
may be forced to bring the country to a standstill with a
national strike to draw attention to their plight.
                                    
"We are facing a double risk," consumer association Codacons
said Monday.
                                    
"On one hand, there could be shortages of essential goods in
the coming hours — particularly food products, on supermarket
shelves.
                                    
"On the other, there is a danger that profiteering could occur
along the supply chain, with parties exploiting the current
emergency to implement unjustified retail price hikes.
                                    
"This is a volatile situation, as any increase in retail prices
would only compound already soaring inflation, further
penalizing Italian families.
                                    
"While we fully understand the protests by the haulers, we will
not allow consumers to foot the bill for this situation.
                                    
"For this reason, we urge the government to remain extremely
vigilant against any abuses or profiteering that might arise at
this time; we are also prepared to contact public prosecutor's
offices across Italy to safeguard the interests of Italian
families."
The Ministry of Infrastructure and Transport has called a
meeting with representatives of the road haulage sector for
Tuesday, October 27, at 4:00 PM, at the Ministry's headquarters
in Porta Pia.
                                    
The Ministry stated that representatives from the Premier's
Office, the Ministry of Economy and Finance, and the Ministry of
Business and 'Made in Italy' will also be invited to attend.

Protesters blocked the Louvre amid mass demonstrations in France
Kyiv • UNN
Protesters blocked access to the Louvre, preventing the museum from opening on time. The action took place amid protests over the cost of living and public services.
Protesters blocked access to the Louvre Museum in Paris on the morning of October 19, preventing the world-famous landmark from opening at its usual time, as demonstrations continued across France. UNN reports, citing Newsweek.
Details
"Dear visitors, due to student strikes, the museum is currently closed. We apologize for the inconvenience," the Louvre said in a message on X.
According to the museum management and two trade unions, the blockade was led by students who expressed support for the high school students' movement and condemned what they called "police repression."
In photos from Monday morning's demonstration shared on social media, students from the École du Louvre art and culture school hold banners in front of the museum's glass pyramid bearing the words: "The French civil service is falling apart."
Another leaflet distributed near the entrance read: "We are proud to announce that we are blocking the largest museum in the world."
The Louvre, which usually opens at 9 a.m. local time, remained closed until at least noon on Monday, the CGT trade union said. The union supports the action but is not taking part in it.
"The tourists waiting are aggressive toward us because they paid for tickets," one of the protesters wrote in a post shared on X.
The Louvre blockade is taking place against the backdrop of broader demonstrations across France over the cost of living and public-service conditions, with protests escalating into violence in several cities over the weekend.
In a televised address to the nation on Sunday, French President Emmanuel Macron promised to take a tough stance toward those involved in the riots, while acknowledging the protesters' economic and social grievances. Meanwhile, Marine Le Pen, leader of the far-right National Rally party, accused the administration of being unable to maintain order.
With France's 2027 presidential election approaching, the unrest has also intensified political debate over how the country's government is handling the crisis and who could benefit from growing public discontent.

Israeli police say they have arrested 10 suspects in connection with a wave of settler pogroms in the occupied West Bank over the weekend, including attacks on an American photojournalist and European diplomats.
The suspects were detained early on Monday, on suspicion of involvement in acts of violence, violating a closed military zone order, and illegal construction, Israeli police said on Monday.
Police did not share the suspects’ identities, but Israel’s Army Radio said they were all Israeli citizens.
The arrests coincide with a surge in Israeli settler attacks disrupting the annual Palestinian olive harvest in the occupied West Bank.
Rising settler violence against Palestinians has prompted an international outcry, with the United Kingdom describing it as “ethnic cleansing” and imposing sanctions on products from illegal Israeli settlements.
US praises arrests

On Friday, Heidi Levine was beaten by a group of male settlers in the village of Abu Falah in the occupied West Bank, leaving her with several broken ribs and vertebrae.
She also underwent surgery on a finger that was nearly severed and is recovering from what appeared to be stab wounds to her lower body, which required stitches.
A day later, masked settlers attacked European diplomats visiting the Christian village of Taybeh. France, Belgium and Poland, whose delegates were attacked, also called on Israel to take action.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar and the military have blamed “Israeli rioters” for the attack on the diplomats.
But Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whose religious coalition is projected to lose its governing majority at the October 27 election, has been more vague in his language.
He said the diplomats entered a “sensitive area with a history of confrontations” and without coordinating with the military. He also said that the facts of the attack on Levine in Abu Falah were “unclear”. When she heard about this, Levine said she was “shocked and insulted” about what Netanyahu said.
Settler violence has surged in recent years in the occupied West Bank, with rights groups saying that perpetrators are rarely arrested or punished for their daily attacks on Palestinians.

Defence Minister Theo Francken of N-VA wants to set up a “Gendarmerie 2.0” to reinforce the police with military-trained personnel. Alongside Interior minister Bernard Quintin of MR, he will present a proposal to the government in the coming weeks.
Defence minister wants ‘Gendarmerie 2.0’ to handle crisis situations
Francken’s intention is to set up a mobile brigade under the authority of the Interior ministry. “We want to build up a reserve of people with military training,” he said. “This ‘Gendarmerie 2.0’ can be deployed during major crises, riots or situations that threaten to get out of hand.”
There has been considerable violence during protests in Brussels and Liège in recent days. “The police are doing their very best, but they are failing to restore calm,” Francken said. “That is why we need an additional armed force to support the police.”
If rioters attack paramedics, throw Molotov cocktails and set everything alight, we must have a proportionate response ready
The gendarmerie lost its formal military status in 1992 and was dissolved in 2001, when the country’s police and judicial system was fundamentally reformed in the wake of the Marc Dutroux killings.
“We have a very different society to the one we had 30 years ago,” Francken says. “Mass migration has changed the demographics. A street culture has emerged that leaves the average Belgian bewildered. We need to provide a response to that.”
He is proposing that the ministry of Defence train officers and make them available to the ministry of the Interior. “They will be very useful in cities such as Brussels and Liège. During riots or around New Year’s Eve, we see a constant game of cat-and-mouse involving a great deal of violence. If rioters attack paramedics, throw Molotov cocktails and set everything alight, we must have a proportionate response ready.”
“This is an extension of the already successful cooperation between the police and Defence,” a spokesperson for Quintin’s cabinet said, referring to the security of sensitive locations and joint patrols with the railway police.
“Together, we are looking at how we can strengthen these capabilities to ensure the safety of citizens.”

Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein said Sunday that Baghdad is working to organise a meeting between Iran and Gulf states as part of diplomatic efforts to narrow differences and promote regional stability.
Speaking at the conclusion of the 52nd session of the Council of Foreign Ministers of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), Hussein said Iraq was maintaining contacts with both sides to facilitate dialogue.
“There are ongoing communications between Iraq, the Gulf states, and Iran aimed at bringing their perspectives closer together,” Hussein said, according to the Iraqi News Agency (INA).
“We are working to hold a meeting in Baghdad between Iran and the Gulf states,” he added, without specifying a date or the level of representation expected.
The initiative comes amid regional tensions affecting security and maritime navigation in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz.
In a joint statement issued on 25th August, Oman and Iran linked maritime security in the Strait of Hormuz to recent regional conflicts and emphasised the importance of consultations among countries bordering the Gulf.
On the sidelines of the OIC meetings, Hussein held talks with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Sunday to discuss regional developments and prospects for peace, according to the Iraqi Foreign Ministry.

During the meeting, Hussein reaffirmed Iraq’s support for resolving regional crises through dialogue and diplomatic engagement.
Separately, Hussein announced that the OIC ministerial session had concluded with the adoption of the Baghdad Declaration, following discussions involving 55 countries.
He said the Palestinian issue had been a central focus of the meetings and expressed appreciation for Iraq’s role as host.
“Baghdad was honored to host the 52nd session of the OIC Council of Foreign Ministers,” Hussein said.
OIC Secretary-General Ismail Ould Cheikh Ahmed also reaffirmed the organisation’s commitment to following up on the decisions adopted during the session.
“We will work with Iraq to ensure the implementation of the decisions made during the 52nd session,” he said.

One-year conscripts to join November military exercise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
10:43:03 UTC
19:43:03 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Army’s 584th Combined Arms Brigade will take part in an exercise at the Joint Operations Training Base in Pingtung from November, alongside one-year conscripts and M1A2T tanks, CNA reported.
The Sixth Army brigade loaded, secured, and inspected the tanks in early October for transport to Pingtung. The exercise will run from November to December, testing the tanks’ performance in the field and the brigade’s ability to coordinate its forces.
The M1A2T is a new-generation tank purchased from the US and built to Taiwan Army specifications. The 63-metric-ton tank has a 5.3-meter-long smoothbore cannon and a 1,500-horsepower gas turbine engine.
The brigade will conduct combined arms exercises, weapons assessments, battalion and brigade training, and live-fire tests to evaluate command and fire support. One-year conscripts will also take part in the exercise.
Su Tzu-yun (蘇紫雲) of the Institute for National Defense and Security Research said volunteer soldiers generally perform core specialist tasks, while conscripts take on supporting roles. He cited Sweden’s use of both volunteers and conscripts aboard naval vessels as an example.
In Taiwan, volunteers typically serve as tank commanders and gunners, Su said. They will operate the M1A2T tanks in this exercise, though conscripts could serve as loaders and drivers in the future. In infantry units, some conscripts can also train as drone or Javelin missile operators in addition to serving as riflemen or machine gunners, he said.
Su said that since the restoration of one-year compulsory service, training has progressed from basic combat skills to small-unit tactics and coordination among different types of forces. Conscripts from armored, artillery, and drone units will participate in the upcoming exercise, which he described as an important stage in their training.

Helsinki's 2027 budget targets lower HSL fare increases and more funding for schools and healthcare
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
13:40:59 EEST
19:40:59 KST

Helsinki plans to increase spending on education, healthcare and public transport in 2027 while keeping municipal taxes unchanged, under a budget proposal presented by Mayor Daniel Sazonov on Monday, 19 October.
The proposal includes €470 million for public transport, additional teachers' resources, new healthcare staff and investments worth more than €1.2 billion. The city expects to record a €25 million budget surplus.
Add Helsinki Times as a preferred source on Google (opens Google in a new tab)
One priority is limiting fare increases for Helsinki Regional Transport (HSL). The city wants ticket prices to rise by 1.8% next year, rather than the 3.1% increase outlined in an earlier proposal.
HSL's board will decide on ticket prices later this autumn. Helsinki's proposed transport allocation represents a 14.7% increase compared with 2026.
Education spending would rise by 4.4% to approximately €1.78 billion, with funding directed towards literacy, classroom resources and primary education.
The city plans to reduce the calculated size of classes in the first years of primary school from 20 to 18 pupils, increase mother-tongue lessons and expand funding for schools according to their needs.
Every school would receive at least a basic library collection, while printed learning materials would receive additional funding.
“In next year's budget, we are investing particularly in children and young people,” Sazonov said in a city statement.
Healthcare funding would provide 25 additional doctors and 13 nurses, on top of 52 doctor and 71 nursing positions approved earlier.
Helsinki aims to ensure access to primary healthcare appointments within 14 days. The city also plans to test a healthcare model involving 10 self-employed family doctors and 10 designated nurses.
The proposal introduces grants supporting 1,000 neighbourhood events during 2027 and 2028, intended to encourage residents to organise activities within their communities.
Municipal income tax would remain at 5.3%, while property tax rates would stay unchanged.
The city's municipal services budget forecasts €3.62 billion in external expenditure, approximately €2 billion in tax revenue and €510 million in central government transfers.
Healthcare, social services and rescue operations would receive approximately €3.45 billion in operating expenditure, an increase of 4.8%.
Helsinki and its city-owned transport company plan combined investments of €1.242 billion in infrastructure and public facilities.
Projects include the Jätkäsaari sports centre, Kruunuvuori service complex, Pitäjänmäki school and library, and Myllypuro health and wellbeing centre.
Transport investments include replacing the Junatie metro bridge, renovating the Rautatientori metro station, constructing the Koskela tram depot and developing the western tram network.
Despite the projected operating surplus, the city expects a €786 million deficit in cash flow from operations and investments.
Sazonov presented the proposal to political groups on Monday, beginning negotiations over the 2027 budget.
The proposal will proceed to the city executive board in November before reaching the city council for consideration.
