Türkiye’s short-term external debt stock totaled $176.6 billion at the end of August, rising by $25 million from the previous month, according to central bank data released on Oct. 19.
The stock of external debt on a remaining maturity basis, covering debt falling due within one year regardless of its original maturity, stood at $243.3 billion.
Banks’ short-term external debt declined 1.6 percent month-on-month to $76.3 billion, while that of other sectors edged up 0.1 percent to $74.6 billion.
Short-term foreign currency loans received by banks from abroad fell 3 percent to $9.2 billion.
Foreign currency deposits held by non-resident banks in resident banks slipped 0.1 percent to $19.7 billion, while those held by non-residents outside the banking sector increased 1.7 percent to $22 billion.
Non-residents’ Turkish lira deposits declined 4.8 percent to $25.3 billion.
Among other sectors, trade credit liabilities arising from foreign trade transactions decreased 0.8 percent to $64.5 billion. Cash loan liabilities, meanwhile, rose 6.6 percent to $10 billion.
The U.S. dollar accounted for 34 percent of the short-term external debt stock, followed by the euro at 27.1 percent, the Turkish lira at 25.6 percent and other currencies at 13.3 percent.
On a remaining maturity basis, non-residents’ deposits in resident banks decreased to $67 billion, while loans of banks and other sectors fell to $75.1 billion.

'Permissible, virtuous': Israeli rabbi issues ruling allowing seizure of Palestinian olives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
10:40:37 UTC
19:40:37 KST

A Palestinian research center said on Monday that an Israeli rabbi had issued a religious ruling describing the seizure of Palestinian olive crops in the occupied West Bank as “permissible and even virtuous,” amid widespread attacks on farmers during the annual harvest season.
The Palestinian Center for Israeli Studies (Madar) said in a report that Rabbi Dov Lior, a former rabbi of the Kiryat Arba settlement and a religious authority associated with Israel’s far-right Jewish Power party, issued the ruling on October 16.
Lior declared that taking Palestinian olives in the West Bank is “completely permissible” and even carries “additional virtue,” according to the report.
The rabbi argued that Palestinians prevented from accessing their olive groves for security reasons could be considered to have abandoned their crops, making them available for others to take.
He also claimed that the land belongs to the Jewish people under Jewish religious law and that Palestinians who planted olive trees had already received compensation through harvests collected over previous years.
The Madar report, written by researcher Walid Habbas, examined the ruling as part of broader Israeli policies and practices affecting Palestinian olive harvesting in the occupied territory.
Citing Israeli rights organisation Yesh Din, Madar said hundreds of attacks by illegal Israeli settlers and soldiers had been documented across 171 Palestinian communities since the beginning of this year’s olive harvest season.
It said Palestinians were completely prevented from harvesting olives in 68 cases, while crops were stolen in 119 cases.
Illegal settler violence
The report also highlighted restrictions imposed by the Israeli military on Palestinian farmers’ access to their agricultural land.
Citing a decision reported by Israeli newspaper Israel Hayom in September, Madar said Palestinian farmers would no longer be permitted to harvest olives on land classified by Israel as “state land” across Palestine’s occupied West Bank.
It added that harvesting on privately owned land would also be subject to prior security coordination with Israeli authorities.
Madar said the restrictions, combined with the expansion of illegal Israeli settlement outposts, have increasingly prevented Palestinian farmers from accessing their olive groves.
The report also referred to recent attacks on foreign nationals accompanying Palestinian farmers, including American photojournalist Heidi Levine and a European diplomatic delegation.
Levine, a photographer for The Washington Post, was assaulted by illegal Israeli settlers while covering the olive harvest near Ramallah on Friday.
A day later, masked Israeli settlers attacked vehicles carrying European diplomats during an olive-harvesting visit to the West Bank town of Taybeh, damaging at least one vehicle.
The report cited figures from an Israeli Civil Administration document showing that Palestinian olive groves cover approximately 845,000 dunams (208,800 acres) and contain around 12.6 million trees.
More than 100,000 Palestinian families depend on olive cultivation for their livelihoods, according to the document.
Israeli Channel 13 previously reported Lior’s religious ruling on Friday, saying he had permitted Israeli settlers to take Palestinian olive crops, including from areas beyond the immediate vicinity of illegal Israeli settlements.
Israel has occupied the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, since 1967. Israeli settlements in the occupied territory are illegal under international law.

Science surprises, from honeybees to microplastics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
10:40:12 UTC
19:40:12 KST

Rachel Feltman: Happy Monday, listeners! For Scientific American’s Science Quickly, I’m Rachel Feltman. Let’s get this week off to a great start by catching up on some recent science and tech news you may have missed.
We’ll start with some potentially paradigm-shifting research on the human ovary. According to a new study published in Aging Cell, these aren’t just reproductive organs. Long after ovaries stop producing eggs, the researchers say, the organs continue to evolve.
Building off of previous work in mice, the study examined normal ovarian tissue from 28 postmenopausal women between the ages of 50 and 75. The researchers analyzed nearly 6,000 different protein groups to track not just how postmenopausal ovaries differed from reproductively active ones but to see how they changed over decades of postreproductive life. And they did find changes. While the younger ovarian samples had more proteins associated with maintaining tissue structure, samples from older subjects had more proteins tied to inflammation and immune activity.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
What remains to be seen is whether postmenopausal ovaries are doing something beneficial or something harmful—or whether that’s a scale that can tip one way or the other depending on unknown factors. Given how long the ovaries have broadly been treated as useless bystanders once fertile years are past, we’ll probably be working to uncover their mysteries for quite some time.
Staying on the health beat, let’s talk about microplastics. One of the reasons that plastic has become such a ubiquitous material for things like food packaging and toys is that it’s meant to be really stable, in the chemical sense of the word—it’s a polymer, which is a long chain of molecules that doesn’t really easily react with other molecules it comes into contact with. But the stability of a polymer doesn’t mean the plastic object it ends up in is totally inert. Lots of additives commonly used in plastics, like flame retardants and colorants, are prone to leach out into surrounding materials. Bisphenol A, or BPA, which helps make plastic clear and durable, is just one particularly infamous example of an additive that seeps into food and can interfere with human hormone signalling. We also now know that microplastics—tiny particles that flake away into the environment as factors like heat and UV exposure cause plastic to degrade—have made their way into locations as remote as Antarctica and as intimate as human placentas and brains. While research on the exact impacts of microplastic on human health is very much in its early stages, they’ve been linked to inflammation, cellular damage, altered metabolic function and other serious issues in animal studies.
In a study published last Wednesday in the journal Nature, researchers report that even plastics that aren’t leaching out additives could cause problems. In fact, the very geometry of microplastics could make them more hazardous to human health.
The new study found that when exposed to water, microplastics spontaneously generated the kinds of highly reactive molecules that can damage cells. And more and more of that dangerous chemistry took place as the pieces got smaller. The researchers believe that’s because, as plastic breaks down into smaller pieces, it has more and more surface area. Imagine setting up a banquet hall with nine identical folding tables pushed together to make one big ole square that could fit, say 24 people comfortably. If you split the tables into three rectangles instead, you’d have more potential seats exposed—more surface area—and you’d double your comfortable seating to 48. Set up all nine tables individually, and you’ve got room for 72 place settings. It’s the same amount of table as you started with, but with way more edge exposed.
The same thing happens when plastics break down into micro and nano particles: the total volume of plastic remains the same, but more of it is exposed to whatever surrounds it—including human tissue, which happens to be full of water. While more research is needed to confirm this process and understand its potential impacts, we do know enough to say that you should try to limit your exposure to microplastics. Try to avoid microwaving food in plastic, and keep bottled water away from sunlight exposure which can cause the bottles to degrade.
And while we’re on the subject of avoiding microplastics, let’s shoutout one exposure you might not be aware of, teabags. Research published last week in npj Science of Food quantified microplastics in tea brewed from loose leaves compared to tea bags. Because FYI, those silky looking pyramid-shaped bags are made from plastic, and even many paper tea bags are sealed shut with plastic glue. The new study found that bagged tea could contain more than 1/5th of the European Food Safety Authority’s tolerable daily intake of BPA. So it might be a good time to invest in a tea strainer, preferably one made out of ceramic or stainless steel.
Speaking of hot and dangerous food, hackers have found a new way to wreak havoc on the meatspace. Last week, freezers and fridges in hundreds of French supermarkets were reportedly targeted by a cyberattack aimed at spoiling their wares. The hackers took over software from the Danish firm Danfoss that many major retailers use to regulate their refrigerators remotely. The attack raised temperatures to as high as 122 degrees Fahrenheit and kept them elevated overnight, causing food to spoil.
If you want to learn more on how cyberattacks can target physical infrastructure and how benevolent hackers are working to help protect us from threats like these—check out our September 2 episode.
I know this is shocking but I think I’m gonna wrap us up with a fun animal story. Though this particular study is only fun to think about theoretically and gets pretty unpleasant if it gets too close to home. It has to do with how honeybees do their stinging.
When worker bees sting a target and then fly away, they leave their stingers behind—and those stingers keep, well, stinging. In a study published last week in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, researchers analyzed high-speed videos of honeybee stingers to reveal how they keep pumping venom sans bee.
Now, to the naked human eye a stinger looks like a pretty simple stabbing weapon, but it’s actually a sophisticated instrument. In addition to a venom sac and a pumping chamber, along with muscles and nerves, each stinger contains two sharp lancets that slide on a rail system, kind of like a reciprocating saw. Each lancet has its own attached valve that sits in the pumping chamber. And according to the new study, where scientists had bees sting a clear gel made to mimic human skin, those valves are the key to a stinger’s pumping power. On each downstroke of the lancet the attached valve inflates like parachutes, which creates a pressure seal and pushes venom out. Then as the lancet shoots back up, the valve deflates. The valves are also able to squeeze past one another, so they pump in opposite directions and maintain a continuous flow. Pretty cool, as long as you’re not the person on the receiving end.
That’s all for this week’s science news roundup. We’ll be back on Wednesday to talk to one of my favorite authors of science fact and fiction about their latest book.
Science Quickly is produced by me, Rachel Feltman, along with Fonda Mwangi, Allison Rodgers and Jeff DelViscio. This episode was edited by Alex Sugiura. Marielle Issa and Aaron Shattuck fact-check our show. Our theme music was composed by Dominic Smith. Subscribe to Scientific American for more up-to-date and in-depth science news.
For Scientific American, this is Rachel Feltman. Have a great week!

Last Saturday, the stretch of sea between Larnaca and Ayia Napa became the race course for the “Regatta for Peace,” organized by the Italian Embassy in Nicosia in collaboration with the Cyprus Sailing Federation and the marinas of Larnaca and Ayia Napa. Twenty-four boats lined up at the starting line with over 120 crew members representing 13 different nationalities: an all-time record for participation, making the “Regatta for Peace” the largest amateur regatta ever organized in Cyprus.
                                    
The late-morning start from Larnaca Marina took place in the presence of Larnaca Mayor Andreas Vyras, who welcomed the crews and emphasized the message of peace that the event aims to promote, as well as Tourism Minister Kostas Koumis. 
The “Regatta for Peace” was the first European stop on the international roadshow leading up to the America’s Cup, which will arrive in Italy for the first time in July 2027, in Naples. It helped shine a spotlight on this important event while highlighting the value of sports diplomacy, which is being increasingly promoted by the Italian Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
                                    
“We have dedicated this regatta to peace, the most cherished gift on earth,” said Italy’s Ambassador to Cyprus, Antonella Cavallari, as she opened the event, which—just a few hours before the finish—brought together participants and numerous dignitaries at the Ayia Napa Marina Convention Center. “Peace is the founding value of diplomacy—indeed, the very reason diplomacy exists. And sports diplomacy is one of its most important tools: sports convey a powerful message through their values—fair play, respect for the rules, mutual respect, cooperation, and friendship. Today more than ever, these are the values that should guide relations between nations and their peoples,” the ambassador concluded. 
The Minister of Tourism, Kostas Koumis, expressed great appreciation for the event, having attended from the morning onward and at the subsequent gala dinner. Among the guests in attendance were Cypriot champion Pavlos Kontides, a two-time Olympic silver medalist in the Laser/ILCA 7 class; Ihor Matviienko, the Ukrainian Olympic champion in the 470 class at the 1996 Atlanta Games; and Easy Swiss, the Israeli Olympic champion.
                                    
The day concluded at the Aya Resort, where the awards ceremony took place. The overall winner of the regatta was Typhoon, skippered by Jiovannis Pikis, followed by First Light, skippered by Robert Clunis, and Judith, skippered by Easy Suissa, who also took the top three spots in Class A. In Class B, “Infinity,” skippered by Philippos Haralambous, took first place, followed by “St. Michael,” skippered by Sergej Lysionok, and “Marianna,” skippered by Marios Karpis.

Protecting Earth’s fragile biodiversity takes spotlight at Armenia talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
10:36:51 UTC
19:36:51 KST

Protecting Earth’s fragile biodiversity takes spotlight at Armenia talks
Biodiversity losses continue to upend the lives of billions of people whose future prosperity depends on countries taking urgent action to protect our planet, the top UN official leading talks at the UN Biodiversity Conference in Yerevan, said on Monday.
The aim of the talks in the Armenian capital is to assess progress so far and build on an agreed blueprint for biodiversity protection known as the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, adopted four years ago.
“In 2022, 196 countries made commitments. But we are all accountable to each other and to future generations. What happens here in Yerevan matters. Billions of people whose lives are being upended by the impacts of biodiversity loss depend on progress being made here in the next two weeks,” said Executive Secretary of the UN Convention on Biodiversity, Astrid Schomaker.
Tapping into indigenous ideas
Insisting that “taking action for nature does work”, Ms. Schomaker called for the “untapped energy and ideas” of Indigenous Peoples and local communities, women and youth to contribute to the decisions made at the talks. “We need even greater engagement from cities, businesses and financial institutions…the science is clear. No nation, no economy, no society is immune from the impacts of biodiversity loss,” she said.
The goals of the Convention include tackling the main drivers of biodiversity loss, including changes in how land and seas are used, the unsustainable exploitation of species, climate change, pollution and invasive species.
Perhaps the Kunming-Montreal framework’s best-known ambition is “30 by 30”: conserving 30 per cent of land and sea by 2030, the deadline for achieving the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
To do this, national action plans must align with international goals, finance must match current needs and consumption and production should be in accord with “the finite resources of our planet”, Ms. Schomaker maintained.
Why do these talks matter?
A core aim of the Yerevan talks – also known as COP17, or the 17th Conference Of Parties – is “to turn commitments into measurable progress on the ground”, insisted Armenia’s Permanent Representative to the UN, Paruyr Hovhannisyan.
“We want COP17 to send a clear political signal that addressing biodiversity loss requires coordinated action by governments, international organizations, the private sector and civil society,” he told UN News. “This means strengthening implementation, mobilizing adequate resources, and improving monitoring and accountability.”
Among the big issues governments will grapple with in Yerevan:
- Taking stock: Countries will conduct the very first global review of collective progress under the framework by presenting their national reports and updated national biodiversity strategies and action plans. This will show what has been achieved since 2022 and where faster action is needed.
- Closing the implementation gap: The question is how to translate national targets and plans into measurable results on the ground.
- Finding the money: The framework calls for at least $200 billion annually from all sources by 2030, including at least $30 billion in international biodiversity finance, according to Armenia’s UN Ambassador Mr. Hovhannisyan.
- Making the Cali Fund work: This global financial mechanism established under the UN Convention on Biodiversity was agreed at COP16 in Cali, Colombia. Talks at Yerevan aim to advance practical arrangements for the fund, which was designed to collect funds from companies that use digital genetic data and redistribute these monies to protect biodiversity and Indigenous Peoples.
- Tracking progress: Better monitoring, data, capacity and cooperation are needed so countries can measure whether commitments are actually delivering results.
- Changing the economics: Some of the areas furthest behind require action outside environment ministries, including on finance, business, sustainable consumption and harmful incentives.
The meeting follows warnings from UN chief António Guterres in Yerevan on Friday that more than one million species face extinction.
War on nature
In his call for an end to the “war on nature”, the UN Secretary-General appealed to governments, business and communities to accelerate efforts to protect biodiversity for future generations.
“Every day, humankind saws another branch through the tree of life. Climate chaos, invasive species, overgrazing and overfishing, excessive fertilizers, pesticides, plastics and heavy metals, all these and more are driving the triple planetary crisis of pollution, biodiversity loss and climate chaos,” he said.
The UN chief warned that the world is edging ever closer towards becoming uninhabitable. But he also pointed to international biodiversity action agreed under the Kunming-Montreal Framework. 
It had inspired action worldwide, Mr. Guterres insisted, noting that since 2022, an additional 1.3 million square kilometres of land and six million square kilometres of ocean have received formal protection.
But “progress is uneven and far too slow” and countries risk falling “well short” of the goal of conserving 30 per cent of the world’s land and sea by 2030, the UN chief said.

U.S. Army orders more FD-1 drone interceptors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
10:36:41 UTC
19:36:41 KST

The U.S. Army has placed a second order for the FD-1, a drone interceptor that a single soldier can set up and launch in under two minutes, from Florida-based Mountain Horse Solutions, less than a year after the system first came to the service’s attention.
The order was issued on Oct. 8 by the U.S. Army’s Global Tactical Edge Acquisition Directorate, known as G-TEAD, under an Other Transaction Agreement, a flexible contracting tool that lets the military buy and prototype new technology faster than through traditional contracts. It follows an initial G-TEAD agreement awarded this spring, and the company said the FD-1 is already fielded. Neither Mountain Horse Solutions nor the U.S. Army disclosed the contract value or how many interceptors are being bought.
The FD-1 is designed to destroy Group 1 to Group 3 drones, a range that runs from small quadcopters up to aircraft weighing several hundred kilograms, and can also be used against ground targets. One operator handles the system instead of a crew, and the company says it can work as the strike element behind an existing radar or tracking network or as a standalone system. A soldier stays in control throughout each engagement, and a human authorizes every shot.
The company built the FD-1 to address a cost problem that has strained air defenses in Ukraine and the Middle East, where cheap drones arrive in large numbers and are often shot down with interceptors that cost far more than their targets. It won first prize in the U.S. Army’s xTech Counter Strike competition in November 2025, and the U.S. Army Test and Evaluation Command has completed its technical review.
Soldiers from G-TEAD, the 52nd Air Defense Artillery Brigade and the test command evaluated the FD-1, and after each operational assessment Mountain Horse Solutions delivered user-driven upgrades within five weeks, the company said.
“Soldiers assessed the FD-1 and told us what needed improvement. We turned those updates around within weeks, and G-TEAD provided a way to buy the revised version without waiting on a requirements cycle. That sequence did not exist three years ago,” said Bill Allen, president of Mountain Horse Solutions.
G-TEAD places acquisition teams inside the U.S. Army’s regional commands so field commanders can buy and test new equipment quickly, using events called Accelerated Capability Events that aim to move a technology from concept to transition within 180 days. The FD-1 effort stayed within that timeline from operational assessment through the new award, with the 409th Contracting Support Brigade handling the contracting. The directorate is planning its next such event, focused on counter-drone systems, for spring 2027 in Morocco, where soldiers will test up to 15 drone-defense solutions.
“Soldiers find things a test range never will. G-TEAD built the pathway that turns their feedback into fielded improvements within weeks instead of program cycles and then gave the Army a way to order it,” said Richard Budniewski, director of UAS and counter-UAS programs at Mountain Horse Solutions.
Mountain Horse Solutions, part of Global Ordnance, said it is producing the FD-1 now and has capacity to expand output for further U.S. Army orders as well as for allied and partner nations.

Albanese said on Monday that “the temperature has increased in recent times”.
“I’ve expressed that concern to people in the media,” he said. “If you look at anyone’s social media feeds and look at the comments, people will say things that they would never say face to face.”

Mexico arrests cartel members linked to murders of 10 workers from Canadian mining company
Mexican authorities said on Sunday that they had arrested five men linked to the kidnapping and murder of 10 workers from a Canadian mining company in the country's northwest.
The workers, all Mexicans, were kidnapped at gunpoint on January 23 from a silver mining project belonging to Vancouver-based Vizsla Silver in the violence-plagued state of Sinaloa.
The bodies of the 10 men, two of whom were engineers and one a geologist, were later found buried in clandestine graves.
Mexico's defense ministry said the suspects belonged to a faction of the fearsome Sinaloa cartel. It identified one suspect as Jesus Abraham, alias Taliban.
In June, Mexico announced the arrest of another suspect, identified as Gabriel N., alias Gabito, a hitman for the same faction.
Mines have been the target of organized crime on other occasions in Mexico, as cartels see opportunities to extort or even sell valuable ore themselves.
Abductions by armed groups are common in Mexico, where more than 120,000 people have vanished since the 1950s, many of them abducted and killed by drug cartels.
It is rare, however, for international companies to be targeted.
"We are devastated by this outcome and the tragic loss of life," Vizsla President and CEO Michael Konnert said in a statement after five of the workers' bodies were found. "Our deepest condolences are with our colleagues' families, friends and co-workers, and the entire community of Concordia."
Jaime Castañeda said he identified the body of his brother, José Manuel Castañeda Hernández, on Sunday by viewing photos shown to him by local officials in Mazatlán, CBC News reported.
"In truth, this has been very painful to be here, in a place where we don't want to be," Jaime Castañeda told CBC News in a phone interview.
José Manuel Castañeda Hernández, 43, was a husband and a father to two children, his brother told CBC News.
"It's so hard to see … how they suffer," Jaime Castañeda aid. "There's no justice with what's happening."
The government said the workers were mistaken for members of a rival faction of the Sinaloa cartel, which has been ripped apart by internecine fighting since September 2024.
According to the government, the suspects worked for a faction controlled by the sons of jailed druglord Joaquin "El Chapo" Guzman, who is serving a life sentence in a Supermax prison in Florence, Colorado, which houses numerous high-profile inmates
The Sinaloa cartel has been designated a terrorist organization by Washington.
In July, former Sinaloa cartel co-founder Ismael "El Mayo" Zambada was sentenced in a U.S. court to life in prison, seven years after "El Chapo" was handed the same sentence.

Ebola cases rise in Kenya
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
10:35:11 UTC
19:35:11 KST

Ebola cases rise in Kenya
Kenya has confirmed its eighth case of Ebola after a man tested positive for the virus, health authorities announced on Sunday. Director-General for Health Patrick Amoth announced the latest infection following a new round of testing.
“Today, 38 people were tested, and one tested positive. He is a 49-year-old man who is not a healthcare worker and developed fever, headache and muscle pain,” Dr. Amoth said.
Kenya recorded its first Ebola case in early October 2026, when a man who had traveled from DR Congo to Nairobi was diagnosed with the disease. The patient died at a hospital in the Kenyan capital on October 5. His infection prompted heightened surveillance and contact tracing amid concerns about further transmission.
The authorities have identified 28 contacts, including relatives and healthcare workers, and are tracing another 23 passengers and four crew members who were on the same flight as the patient.
The developments come as DR Congo struggles to contain a major Ebola epidemic. The African state is battling its 17th recorded Ebola outbreak, which was declared on May 15. It involves the Bundibugyo strain of the virus for which there are currently no approved vaccines or targeted treatments available.
According to a situation report by the country’s Health Ministry dated October 16, the outbreak has affected eight provinces, with North Ubangi becoming the latest to report infections. Two cases, including one death, were identified in the province’s Wapinda health zone.
The report put the nationwide toll at 9,415 confirmed infections and 4,536 deaths, representing a case fatality rate of 48.2%. A total of 66 health zones across the eight affected provinces have reported infections.
Earlier this month, Congolese Health Minister Roger Samuel Kamba said the outbreak had passed its peak, citing a decline in new infections and fewer areas reporting active transmission. However, the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) cautioned that the epidemic was not yet under control, warning that insecurity in affected areas had disrupted surveillance.
The DR Congo’s mineral-rich east has been plagued by decades of violence, with dozens of armed groups, including M23, fighting Congolese government forces for power and control of resources such as gold and coltan. Clashes escalated in early 2025, leaving thousands dead and resulting in large-scale displacement, according to UN agencies. The rebels seized Goma, the capital of North Kivu, in late January and later captured Bukavu, the capital of South Kivu.
Ceasefire efforts have repeatedly faltered, including Qatar-facilitated talks in Doha. In February 2026, the parties agreed on arrangements for a ceasefire monitoring mechanism, a step welcomed by the African Union. Congolese authorities have long accused Rwanda of supporting the militants, allegations backed by a UN panel of experts. Kigali has denied the claims.
The accusations have strained Rwanda’s relations with Western partners, including Belgium. In March 2025, Kigali severed diplomatic ties with Brussels, accusing it of harboring “neo-colonial delusions” and interfering in the conflict. The two countries, however, restored diplomatic relations in September 2026.
In December 2025, Congolese President Felix Tshisekedi and his Rwandan counterpart, Paul Kagame, ratified a US-brokered agreement committing Kigali to withdraw its forces from the border and end alleged support for M23, while Kinshasa pledged to curb militias hostile to Rwanda. US President Donald Trump has said the pact, which includes calls for a joint security mechanism, gives Washington rights to local mineral wealth. The fighting has continued despite Trump’s claims that he ended the decades-long conflict.
The Ebola outbreak had also affected neighboring Uganda, which declared itself free of the virus on July 28 after. According to Uganda’s Health Ministry, the outbreak resulted in 20 confirmed cases, including 15 imported infections and five locally transmitted ones. Two people died and 18 recovered.

World Food Programme cuts aid to 500,000 Palestinians in Gaza, citing funding shortages
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
10:34:49 UTC
19:34:49 KST

The UN World Food Programme has said funding shortages are forcing major cuts to its aid program in Gaza, leaving about 500,000 people without monthly food support in a territory where two-thirds of the population struggle to get enough to eat.
The WFP said it was reducing the number of recipients of its monthly assistance to 1.1 million people from 1.6 million.
In addition, food rations have been halved, cash assistance has been cut for 75,000 families, and the number of daily hot meals for those unable to cook has fallen to 150,000 from 250,000, with some families in hard-to-reach areas now receiving a hot meal only every other day.
The WFP said about 1.4 million people, or two-thirds of Gaza's population, face crisis levels of food insecurity or worse, including roughly 200,000 people in emergency conditions.
'Life is still brutal here'
Last year's US-brokered Gaza ceasefire calls for the eventual reconstruction of the territory. But little progress has been made towards implementing a deal to end the conflict that includes terms for Hamas to disarm and Israel to withdraw its troops.
"It's a year into the agreement of this ceasefire. Well, life is still brutal here. There is no proper shelter.. There is no basic services. There is no safety, no security," acting Executive Director of the World Food Program WFP Carl Skau told Reuters in Gaza.
"These cuts are happening just as we are facing the fourth winter. You know, I've been through the winters here, absolutely brutal," he added.
The WFP said it urgently needs $450 million over the next six months to maintain critical operations in Gaza and the West Bank.
"We tell the world now is this is not the time to look away. This is the time to step up to sustain this support, to protect the progress that has been made, but also to push for early recovery," said Skau.

Passenger fares for Malaysia's East Coast Rail Link unveiled
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
18:34:45 CST
19:34:45 KST

KUALA LUMPUR, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- Passenger ticket prices for the East Coast Rail Link (ECRL), a mega rail project in Malaysia built by the China Communications Construction Company, were unveiled on Monday.
A one-way trip from the Gombak station in Selangor state to Kota Bharu in Kelantan state has been set at 125 ringgit (about 30 U.S. dollars), with discounts available for senior citizens, children and students aged between 13 and 24, Malaysia Rail Link (MRL), the ECRL project owner, said in a statement.
The approved fare proposal strikes a balance between public affordability, the value of the services offered, and the long-term operational sustainability of the ECRL, it said.
For the 523-km journey from Gombak to Kota Bharu, economy class fares for transit services start as low as 125 ringgit one-way, while express services start from 147 ringgit one-way, the MRL said, adding that the journey will take approximately four hours.
Ticket sales are scheduled to begin in mid-November, while commercial passenger operations for the Gombak-Kota Bharu route are targeted to begin in mid-December 2026, subject to the fulfillment of safety requirements. Ten sets of electric multiple unit trains will be deployed as the initial fleet, operating at speeds of up to 160 kilometers per hour, it said.
The ECRL will provide 12 trips daily from Monday to Thursday, consisting of six trips in each direction. Service frequency will increase to 16 trips daily from Friday to Sunday, with eight trips in each direction. ■

Xinhua Commentary: Japan must confront its past, not revive the specter of militarism
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
18:34:30 CST
19:34:30 KST

TOKYO, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- More than 80 years after World War II, Japan faces a fundamental question: Will it learn from the catastrophe of militarism and remain committed to peace, or allow historical revisionism and an accelerating military buildup to erode the foundations of its postwar path?
The latest moves by Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and other senior political figures concerning the Yasukuni Shrine, a symbol of Japan's militarist past, have brought the question back into focus. On Saturday, Takaichi sent a ritual offering to the shrine in her capacity as prime minister, while several cabinet members and lawmakers visited the shrine or made similar offerings during its autumn rite.
The notorious shrine honors convicted Class-A war criminals alongside Japan's war dead, making it a longstanding source of concern for countries and regions that suffered from Japanese aggression.
Such actions are not merely private expressions of mourning. When a sitting prime minister makes an offering in an official capacity, the gesture inevitably carries political weight, raising questions about how Japan's leaders view the country's wartime conduct and whether they fully appreciate the historical sensitivities of their neighbors.
This year marks the 80th anniversary of the opening of the Tokyo Trials, which held Japanese wartime leaders criminally responsible for their actions. Fourteen convicted Class-A war criminals are enshrined at Yasukuni. For countries and regions that suffered under Japanese aggression, visits and ritual offerings by senior Japanese officials raise fundamental questions about whether Japan has genuinely confronted its wartime past and acknowledged its historical responsibilities.
The latest controversy has unfolded as Japan, under Takaichi, pursues a sweeping review of its national security policies. The government plans to revise the country's three key security documents by the end of this year, potentially reshaping its future military capabilities and security posture.
Amid rapidly rising military spending, Japan has already taken further steps away from its postwar policy restraints. In April, the government revised its Three Principles on Transfer of Defense Equipment and Technology, lifting a ban on exports of lethal weapons.
Japanese media have also reported that the government may alter the wording of the country's Three Non-Nuclear Principles during the security policy review and consider discussions on introducing nuclear-powered submarines.
When an accelerating military buildup coincides with gestures perceived as downplaying wartime responsibility, Japan's broader political and security direction warrants scrutiny. Its postwar pacifist orientation, enshrined in the Constitution, has shaped regional perceptions of the country's role for decades. Any fundamental departure from this course must be subject to transparent public debate and rigorous scrutiny.
What the region needs is not historical revisionism coupled with unchecked military expansion, but practical confidence-building measures, sustained dialogue and respect for international law.
The Japanese people, who were themselves dragged into the abyss by militarism, have a profound stake in ensuring that their country never again takes the path of militarism. The lessons of history are not obstacles to Japan's future but essential safeguards against repeating past mistakes.
Eighty-one years after the end of the war, Japanese leaders must understand that no pretext can justify attempts to whitewash convicted war criminals, obscure wartime atrocities or distort historical facts. Such actions risk undermining postwar reconciliation and accelerating Japan's remilitarization.
Japan must deeply reflect on its history of aggression, face up to its wartime responsibilities, and exercise prudence on issues surrounding Yasukuni Shrine and other historical matters. A clear-eyed reckoning with the past and an unwavering commitment to peace are essential to preventing the recurrence of historical tragedies and safeguarding lasting peace and stability in Asia. ■

19:34:13 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- China has decided to optimize and adjust its export control measures on certain drone-related items, with the new rules taking effect on Nov. 18, 2026, according to a government announcement on Monday.
Items with specified characteristics cannot be exported without a license, said the announcement, which was jointly issued by the Ministry of Commerce, the General Administration of Customs, and the Equipment Development Department of the Central Military Commission.
These items include autopilots specially designed for unmanned aircraft, some technologies for developing, producing or using unmanned aircraft, some unmanned aircraft or unmanned airships meeting specified characteristics, and engines specially designed for unmanned aircraft or unmanned airships, among others, the announcement noted.
The drone-related items involved have a clear dual-use nature that can be applied for both military and civilian purposes, a spokesperson for the commerce ministry said.
China's move to optimize and adjust the measures in accordance with related laws and regulations aims to safeguard national security and interests, and fulfill international obligations such as non-proliferation, the spokesperson explained.
China is committed to maintaining the security and stability of global industrial and supply chains, and will review relevant export license applications in accordance with laws and regulations. Applications that meet requirements will be approved, the spokesperson said. ■

European governments warn citizens over security in France after riots
Additionally, European governments advised citizens traveling to France to avoid large crowds and exercise caution, warning of a deterioration in security conditions after thousands were arrested and shops looted in protests over the weekend.

Governments warn citizens over security in France after riots
ROME/BERLIN/WARSAW, Oct 19 - Governments in Europe and Asia, including China, on Monday advised citizens travelling to France to avoid large crowds and exercise caution, warning of a deterioration in security conditions after thousands were arrested and shops looted in protests over the weekend.
Demonstrations across France over high prices and declining public services erupted into riots on Saturday, with a town hall torched as violent groups clashed with police.
In response, the foreign ministries of several European countries issued fresh travel warnings.
ITALY
Italy said its citizens should register their presence in France on a website or an app to enable them to be located, as it warned them to avoid large crowds and exercise extreme caution.
GERMANY
The German foreign ministry said further riots in the coming days couldn't be ruled out and urged German nationals to follow instructions from local police. It warned citizens that they could face fines or claims for damages if they failed to leave unauthorised demonstrations when asked to do so.
CZECH REPUBLIC

POLAND
Poland said in its country guidance that visitors should avoid places where demonstrations are taking place, though there was no change to its overall guidance about whether France was safe to visit.
NETHERLANDS
The Dutch government in an advisory last updated on October 7 warned travelers to France to avoid protests.
NORDICS
Denmark, Sweden, Finland and Norway have issued advisories urging their citizens in France to avoid demonstrations and follow the guidance of local authorities.
CHINA

MALAYSIA

Residents trapped as torrential rain floods towns in eastern Spain

Residents winched from rooftops as torrential rain hits eastern Spain
ELS POBLETS, Spain, Oct 19 - Helicopters rescued people stranded on rooftops as torrential rains swept across eastern Spain on Monday, as floods and storms killed at least three people and shelter-in-place orders remained in force for more than 80,000 residents.
The downpour from Storm Adam cut off several towns along the Mediterranean coast as rivers burst their banks and streets turned into torrents, leaving scenes reminiscent of the catastrophic flooding that killed more than 230 people in the Valencia region two years ago.
Members of the Military Emergencies Unit found the body of a woman in the town of Oliva during rescue operations on Monday, bringing the death toll to three, regional broadcaster A Punt reported, citing sources from the unit.
Two other women were confirmed dead over the weekend: one whose body was washed up on a beach in Sagunto, in the eastern region of Valencia, and another who was swept away by floodwaters in Cabrera de Mar, near Barcelona.
'IT'S A DISASTER'
In Els Poblets, northeast of Alicante, cars and vans were piled on top of one another from the force of the water as residents tried to salvage what they could from their homes.
“The village, well, it's a disaster. Some people have lost everything all over again, just like in 2007, when exactly the same thing happened," chef Javier Fornez, 49, said.
Meteorologists say human-driven climate change makes such extreme weather events more frequent and destructive.
National weather agency AEMET said torrential rains linked to Storm Adam dumped exceptional amounts of rain across eastern Spain, with Pego, in Alicante province, recording 632 mm (25 inches) in 36 hours, while several locations in southern Valencia and northern Alicante exceeded 500 mm over the same period.
AEMET issued several red alerts, warning local people to avoid all travel and to seek higher ground. On Monday morning, 800,000 residents were under shelter-in-place orders, but that had been reduced to 87,000 in eight municipalities by late afternoon.
HEAVY-DUTY VEHICLES STRUGGLE TO ACCESS SOME AREAS
More than 2,000 people were evacuated, mainly in Oliva, and authorities carried out nearly 100 rescues in Valencia and Alicante, the Civil Guard police said.
The mayor of Pego, Enrique Moll, told A Punt radio that several people were still waiting to be evacuated by helicopter from their roofs. All access routes to the town were blocked and even heavy-duty military vehicles were unable to move forward in some areas, he added.
The deputy mayor of the coastal town of Oliva, Salvador Llopis, told state broadcaster TVE on Monday that emergency services were rescuing trapped residents, particularly elderly people stuck inside their homes with water up to their waists.
"They have to stay on top of tables and furniture to avoid getting wet," he said, adding that the rains had started to ease after causing extensive damage to infrastructure.
More than 100,000 students in Valencia region have had classes suspended due to the alerts, while the central government has deployed emergency units from the military and national police.
The focus of the storm was expected to shift to Catalonia on Monday afternoon, especially Barcelona and Girona provinces, where more than 100 mm of rain could fall in less than 12 hours. Authorities warned that the risk was heightened because the soil was already saturated from previous storms. REUTERS

OMA dresses faceted French courthouse in coloured glass
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

19:30:45 KST

OMA dresses faceted French courthouse in coloured glass
Dutch studio OMA has completed the Palais de Justice de Lille, a six-sided law court in northern France with a faceted facade lined with coloured glass.
Located in Lille, the project was commissioned by the Ministry of Justice to host the city's high and district courts.
Palais de Justice de Lille occupies a verdant landscape adjacent to a star-shaped fortification, built in 1667 by the French military engineer Sébastien Le Prestre de Vauban.
OMA's design has a pointy, hexagonal form, with each elevation finished in coloured glass, intended to mimic this fortress.
The Palais de Justice de Lille is arranged in three volumes, accessed via a publicly accessible base.
Its first volume is a plinth that holds the major courtrooms, from which a triangular central tower containing minor courtrooms extends. Above, a faceted ring of offices surrounds the tower, which helps draw light into the building.
According to OMA, each volume has "its own material expression and spatial character, reinforcing clarity and orientation throughout the complex".
However, they are unified by light finishes and furnishings, and an ambition to feel welcoming and "free of the intimidation", it added.
Completing the Palais de Justice de Lille is a series of outdoor spaces, distributed across its three volumes.
This includes a public plaza at ground level and a roof garden overlooking the city.
OMA, officially known as Office for Metropolitan Architecture, was founded in 1975 in Rotterdam. It won a competition to design the courthouse in 2018 and was originally due to complete the project in 2023.
The studio's other recent projects include an affordable housing development in San Francisco and a pyramidal building in Hangzhou designed as a "three-dimensional village".
Other law courts featured on Dezeen include one in Toronto by Renzo Piano Building Workshop that aims to display "the identity and values of a modern justice institution" and a 10-storey federal courthouse by SOM currently under development in Florida.
The photography is by François-Xavier Gbré.

France doubles down on its homegrown kamikaze drone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
10:30:31 UTC
19:30:31 KST

- France ordered several hundred more MX-10 DAMOCLES loitering munitions from KNDS and Delair, with deliveries starting in early 2027.
- Luxembourg became the first export customer with a contract worth just over 1.6 million euros, and production has reached 100 units a day.
France has ordered several hundred more MX-10 DAMOCLES kamikaze drones from KNDS France and Delair, and the quadcopter munition has won its first export customer, Luxembourg, which signed a contract worth just over 1.6 million euros ($1.8 million) for an initial capability.
The French Ministry of the Armed Forces activated an optional tranche of its existing contract in early October, covering delivery of “several hundred” of the loitering munitions within 12 months, French defense outlet FOB reported on Oct. 13. The first units from the new batch are due in early 2027. The order follows 460 DAMOCLES delivered to French forces in 2025 and 2026 under the firm part of a framework contract signed in July 2024, which covers up to 2,270 units over seven years.
DAMOCLES is a small quadcopter that carries a 550 g (19-ounce) fragmentation-incendiary warhead made by KNDS and streams live video to its operator up to the moment of impact. It is designed to strike infantry and light vehicles at a range KNDS lists as 10 km (6 miles), with French reporting putting its reach at 10 to 20 km, and can stay in the air for about 40 minutes. If an attack is called off, the operator can abort the dive and send the drone back into a holding pattern until a better moment to strike. The French Army and French Navy both use it.
“This new order makes it possible to increase production capacity,” KNDS said, in remarks translated from French. The company said it had prepared for series production from the start of the first tranche, investing in raw materials and hiring so it could ramp up quickly if needed.
Delair, which builds the airframe, has teamed with the French arm of German automotive supplier Schaeffler to manufacture it. Together, the partners have increased their starting capacity tenfold to 100 drones a day, FOB reported.
Luxembourg’s contract with KNDS Ammo France was signed in June 2026 and gives its small army a first loitering munition capability. FOB reported that DAMOCLES is the only loitering munition in Europe qualified at the government level, and that its five successive safety mechanisms weighed in Luxembourg’s choice, along with closer alignment with France and access to French testing and training facilities that Luxembourg lacks.
KNDS sells DAMOCLES as part of its MATARIS family of loitering munitions, launched in 2025, and is now competing as part of a team for France’s upcoming medium-range loitering munition program, the third phase of the French Army’s “contact drones” effort. France set aside more than 500 million euros ($560 million) in its 2026 budget for that program and other related work, and the winner is expected to be announced soon.
France’s procurement agency, the DGA, has also launched a consultation for tens of thousands of warheads for loitering munitions, buying them separately from the drones themselves so the explosive charges can be stockpiled for years while the fast-changing airframes are updated more often. KNDS said it intends to compete both for drone programs, through partnerships with French or foreign firms, and for different types of warheads.

Trump Endorses Netanyahu Days Before Israeli Election as Iran War Tests Friendship
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
10:30:14 UTC
19:30:14 KST

With days to go before a crucial general election in Israel, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu received a last-minute endorsement for re-election on Sunday from his longtime friend, U.S. President Donald Trump.
“Bibi Netanyahu has been a Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace in combatting the Islamic Republic of Iran,” Trump posted on Truth Social Sunday. “Please let this Letter serve to represent my Complete and Total Endorsement of Bibi Netanyahu in his upcoming Race for Re-Election as Prime Minister of Israel.”
It’s a ringing, albeit late, recommendation for someone Trump hasn’t seen eye-to-eye with in recent months over how Netanyahu’s government has navigated the Middle East conflict. Trump explained his delayed endorsement to Axios reporter Barak Ravid, saying that he’d always meant to endorse Netanyahu because they “have a good relationship, and because we’ll continue to do good things together.”
Trump said in his post that, if Israel were to have “the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi,” the U.S. would be left alone to face the Iran threat. The U.S. and Israel jointly struck Iran in late February, kickstarting a conflict that has not only upended global markets but also thrust Middle Eastern regional security into turmoil.
“Bibi Netanyahu has been Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself,” Trump added, in apparent reference to Netanyahu’s domestic challenges, including a corruption trial, some of which the U.S. President has previously tried to influence. “Despite all of that, he has endured and, in fact, he has thrived!”
Trump’s endorsement comes just before Israelis head to the polling booths on Oct. 27, some three years after the country’s war with terror group Hamas ignited. Since then, Netanyahu has been criticized by opponents for failing to deliver on his promise of restoring regional security.
Public disillusionment with Netanyahu was among several factors that led to the formation of the Yashar! (“Straight!”) Party, whose founder, former Israel Defense Forces Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot, is challenging Netanyahu for the premiership. Eisenkot’s son and nephews were killed in the war in the Gaza Strip.
It’s unclear how big of an electoral boost Netanyahu will get from Trump’s endorsement. An opinion poll from nonprofit The Jewish People Policy Institute in Jerusalem released this month shows that most Israelis still see Trump as a great friend of Israel. A separate opinion poll from JPPI, however, shows their trust in him has eroded. Eisenkot, reacting to Trump’s endorsement, said at an event in Tel Aviv that while he appreciates Trump, only Israelis will decide on their next Prime Minister. Some surveys show Yashar! is in a tight race with Netanyahu’s right-wing Likud party.
Netanyahu nonetheless thanked his “dear friend Donald” in a video posted on social media, saying he was “honored” and “humbled” by Trump’s backing, adding that the U.S. was “fortunate” to have Trump as its leader in the fight to denuclearize Iran.
Trump and Netanyahu’s fraught friendship
Even before Trump became U.S. President, he had publicly endorsed Netanyahu, though Trump, still only a TV personality in 2013, said that the Israeli politician asked for it. Since Trump was first elected, the two have been political allies and friends. Their relationship, however, has seen a number of ups and downs since Trump returned to the White House last year.
Netanyahu was the first foreign leader invited to the White House during Trump’s second-term Administration, and he has met with Trump repeatedly since. Netanyahu pushed Trump to target three key Iranian nuclear facilities in June last year. Last November, Trump sent a letter to Israeli President Isaac Herzog, asking him to pardon Netanyahu on his drawn out corruption trial, which the U.S. President deemed to be “political, unjustified prosecution.”
On Feb. 11, when Trump and Netanyahu met in a closed-door meeting at the White House, Israel and the U.S. failed to reach an agreement on how to proceed with Iran. Netanyahu has long sought to decapitate the Iranian leadership, but Trump at the time insisted on negotiations. Netanyahu, nonetheless, reportedly pressed Trump to launch the Iran operation later that month.
Since their last meeting, their relationship has markedly shifted. Trump has since tried to find an off-ramp to the war in Iran, but Israel’s actions made such peace deal talks thorny.
In March, after Israel attacked Iran’s South Pars gas field in the Persian Gulf, Trump said he told Netanyahu to stop such attacks. Then, on April 17, Trump declared on Truth Social that Israel was “PROHIBITED” from further bombing Lebanon, where it was at war with the militant group Hezbollah. Netanyahu, however, insisted that Israeli troops would remain in southern Lebanon and that security threats persisted—complicating Washington’s efforts toward peace as Tehran indicated that any deal would need to include a halt of the attacks in Lebanon.
When Netanyahu in June ordered strikes on a Hezbollah stronghold in Beirut to retaliate against the group’s alleged attacks on Israel, Trump phoned and excoriated the Israeli Prime Minister, reportedly calling him “f-cking crazy.” Asked by CNBC about the call, Netanyahu said: “We have common goals. Sometimes we have, as in the best of families, you have these tactical disagreements. We always find a way to work them out, and we do so as great friends.”
During Netanyahu’s seventh U.S. visit in July, Trump went public with his frustration. During a telephone interview on Fox News, Trump criticized Netanyahu over reports that the Israeli leader planned to share intelligence showing Iran rebuilding its nuclear program. The U.S. President said: “I don’t need Bibi to tell me that. Bibi is telling me that because he wants me to stay involved.”
Netanyahu is part of Trump’s U.N. alternative called the Board of Peace, though Israel broke again with the U.S. President by rejecting having Turkish and Qatari representatives on the board’s subpanel, the Gaza Executive Board, which is tasked with overseeing post-war reconstruction in the Gaza Strip.
Then Netanyahu rejected the Board of Peace’s 15-point plan to advance a cease-fire in the Gaza Strip and insisted that Israel would not withdraw before Hamas fully disarmed.
In Trump’s extensive interview with TIME in late September, Trump did not answer directly when asked repeatedly if the Israeli population should give Netanyahu another term. “I can only say that I’m not involved in politics anymore,” the U.S. President said.
But despite the lack of clear endorsement then, Trump seemed confident that “Bibi” could still win. “People have written off Bibi many, many times, just like they’ve written off me many, many times,” Trump told TIME. “I wouldn’t underestimate Bibi.”

10:30:03 UTC
19:30:03 KST

The debate about how to control AI and limit its potential for damage is healthy and necessary. It is also unavoidable and urgent.
But this is not the only vital debate. There are also vital questions about how the upsides of AI are shared fairly. Business as usual has left the world's poorest people behind, so far. And for those caught up in conflict—in places like Sudan, Ukraine, Gaza, and Afghanistan—AI can help meet urgent needs.
It is clear to me that the world has more resources to do good than at any time in human history, but too often, we don't distribute them where they are most needed. Now, AI stands to create even more resources in the form of free time, insights, and funds. And they need to be spent in the right places.
The AI revolution is going to mint a new generation of billionaires and millionaires—and with them, a new generation of philanthropists; a term stemming from the Ancient Greek philanthropia, meaning “love of humanity”. It’s a reminder that the act of giving begins with some of the most fundamentally human impulses: care, love, empathy, and selflessness.
Maybe this explains why Effective Altruism—the idea that generosity should be subjected to evidence and calculation—seemed counterintuitive. But I never understood why. After all, who wants ineffective altruism? We should all be asking where our money can do the most good.
Organizations working at the sharpest end of the world’s toughest problems—like the one I lead—need philanthropy to be the smart money: hard-headed as well as big-hearted, focused on outcomes not visibility, concerned to add value not just kudos. Results, not just responsibility, should be the watchword.
Fortunately, there’s been an evidence revolution over the last 20 years. We know a whole lot more about what actually works. This makes giving much easier. Distance no longer needs to be the enemy of confidence.
In fact, there is every reason to think globally, not just locally, about where to make a difference. As the world has become more and more connected, governments have retreated from global problems. For instance, official development assistance funds from Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) countries dropped by a historic 23.1% in 2025. Now, we need new philanthropy to provide some balance in a world that is clearly out of balance.
Around 94% of American philanthropy is spent in the U.S. But the rest of the world is not just where the needs are greatest—from acute childhood malnutrition to violence against women—but where the gains from philanthropy can be greatest.
The 20 countries at greatest risk of a worsening humanitarian crisis, ranked by the International Rescue Committee (IRC) annually in our Emergency Watchlist, represent just 12% of the global population, but 90% of those in humanitarian need. In these places, led by regions like Sudan, Gaza, and South Sudan, children are three times more likely to die before their fifth birthday and 10 times more likely to grow up in extreme poverty than children born elsewhere. The people living here have done the least to contribute to climate change, but face the combined pressures of climate change and conflict—and receive the least support to adapt.
If philanthropy and its “love of humanity” belong anywhere, it is these areas. And just in time, humanitarians have developed increasingly sophisticated tools to transform what we know about how to help people survive through and recover from crisis. Real-time data, randomized controlled trials, cost-effectiveness and cost-efficiency analysis, plus predictive analytics, have transformed the evidence base and the basis for action.
The IRC alone has conducted over 50 impact evaluations since 2020 as well as 500 cost analyses, allowing us to measure not simply whether an intervention works, but how much it costs and how much further each additional dollar can go. So we don't need to be daunted by the big numbers highlighting the 43 million children who are acutely malnourished, the 20 million kids without full immunization, over 300 million people hungry, and hundreds of thousands of women dying in childbirth in fragile states alone. These are problems that we actually know how to solve at manageable, in fact low, cost.
For example, we have learned how to deliver vaccine shots—40 million of them—at just $2 a shot in places like Somalia, South Sudan, and Yemen, negotiating with armed groups along the way to get access to populations otherwise cut off from healthcare. This offers lifelong benefit, not just a short-term palliative.
We’ve shown how local health workers can more simply diagnose and treat acute malnutrition directly in communities where crisis-affected children live. This approach offers a 92% recovery rate, and earlier interventions can catch malnutrition before it becomes severe. The result is that we are 20% more cost-effective, allowing us to help more kids for the same amount of money.
There are more examples. We've demonstrated that violence against women and violence against kids can be reduced by over 70% when they are tackled together. We have also proven the benefits of giving aid in advance of climate disasters, not just in reaction to them: in Afghanistan, our clients were three times less likely to fall further into poverty.
Of course, the contexts stricken by war and state failure are challenging. But that makes the philanthropic imperative towards the people who live there all the more urgent.
The same technology that is delivering fortunes in Silicon Valley can also deliver help to the least fortunate. IRC’s global digital helpdesk, Signpost, has reached 20 million people forced to flee crisis in 12 languages with timely, life-saving information. Leading tech companies helped us develop it. In Somalia, IRC teams employed anticipatory action ahead of last year’s devastating drought, a disaster that typically drives cholera outbreaks. Again, it took partnership of financial support, technical know-how, and NGO savvy.
In all these areas, the traditional aid system is falling short. Too often, climate and humanitarian systems work in separate silos. Despite the evidence, less than 1% of aid is invested in anticipatory action. Every government donor has its own bureaucracy, with different reporting systems, compliance requirements, and measurement metrics.
This is the syndrome that philanthropy can help break. By focusing on what works, measuring what counts, and investing in innovation. The risk does not lie in action; it lies in inertia.
We know more than ever about what works in humanitarian crises, and we have new tools capable of extending those gains. The opportunity for this generation of philanthropists is not simply to give more. It is to take what we have learned and apply it where the stakes are highest. The real test isn't how much they give. It’s where.

How the Xbox’s Disc-to-Digital Program Works
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

After Sony announced plans to abandon physical discs by 2028, all eyes turned to Microsoft to see whether its next-gen console, codenamed Project Helix and described as “an open-platform hybrid PC-console,” will continue to support physical media.
Microsoft has largely stayed silent (though there are plenty of reasons to keep an easily accessible 4K Blu-ray drive for consumers). One big hint that Xbox may be gearing up for a disc-less future, though, is the rollout of a feature called Disc to Digital.
The new tool lets players claim digital copies of their Xbox Series X or Xbox One physical games, making them accessible anywhere they can log into their Xbox account. After a month of beta testing for Xbox Insider users, the feature is now open to everyone, and you don't even need an Xbox Game Pass subscription. In theory, it allows anyone to archive their physical collections—but it’s not without a few complications.
Insert Disc to Continue
So, how does it work? It’s almost as easy as just popping the disc into your console, but not quite. Microsoft says “playing any supported Xbox One or Xbox Series X game disc while signed in will grant you a digital license of that game.” In my experience, this didn’t happen automatically when I launched a game disc.
Instead, pressing the menu button while hovering over the game tile on the Xbox home screen brings up an option to “Claim Digital License.” If it’s supported (more on that in a moment), you’ll get a pop-up showing “Digital license unlocked.” Disc-to-Digital games are tied to your Xbox account rather than your console, and appear in your library with a new icon on the game tile, a disc “disintegrating” into bits of data.
You can then install the game and any updates, then play without the disc in the drive. This will start automatically if you have “Play disc automatically” enabled in your system settings: Go to Profile & system > Settings > Devices & connections > Disc, and turn that option off to keep on top of storage space.
Thankfully, claiming digital licenses isn’t restricted to the current-gen Xbox Series X—it also works on Xbox One consoles with a disc drive. If you upgraded to the disc-less Xbox Series S or the all-digital Series X but still have an Xbox One, this opens a new path for backward compatibility: redeem physical games on the last-gen model, then install them digitally on the newer console. Overall, it's a remarkably simple and welcome process.
Keep in mind you can play digital Xbox One games from an external HDD if you're limited on storage, but Xbox Series games must be installed on either the Series X or Series S internal SSD or an official expansion drive. All storage is pricey right now (thanks, AI), but these proprietary format cards are especially so, ranging from $200 for Seagate’s 1-terabyte model to $550 for 4 TB.
Disc Read Error
The main issue? Disc to Digital is far from universal—not every Xbox Series X and Xbox One game disc is supported, and Microsoft doesn't have an official list of which games are.
First-party titles such as Halo, Gears of War, or Forza Horizon are safe bets, but this doesn’t extend to legacy titles—for instance, Fallout 4, released for Xbox One in 2015, can’t be redeemed as a Disc-to-Digital title yet, despite Microsoft acquiring developer Bethesda in 2021. Third-party games are entirely hit and miss. The Warner Bros. Interactive-published The Lego Ninjago Movie Video Game worked, but Capcom’s Dead Rising 3 didn’t.
The language is also confusing about why you might not be able to redeem a game. One disc gave the error “Digital license unavailable: This game is not participating in digital licensing. You can still play with the disc inserted.” Another showed “This disc doesn’t support a digital license: This disc can’t be used to get access to a digital license. This could be because it is an unsupported disc, or because the disc is damaged. You can still play with the disc inserted.” (And I could, putting the damaged disc theory to rest.)
In many cases, this is likely down to Xbox still negotiating with partners to include their titles. As more publishers come on board, expect more compatible discs. Right now though, the lack of clarity on which games can be redeemed, or what happens when they can’t, makes the whole process a crapshoot.
Sadly, this isn’t a golden ticket for all-encompassing backward compatibility, either. It’s strictly limited to Xbox One and Xbox Series games, likely because those consoles have unique identifiers for those discs. Xbox 360 and original Xbox discs didn’t, which could lead to a literal free-for-all of digital licenses if you could ‘rip’ a game and then pass on or sell the disc for someone to do the same.
This does create another point of confusion, though. When you claim the Disc-to-Digital license for a compatible game, you’re told, “Your digital license is linked to your disc. To ensure your digital license stays in your library, keep possession of your game disc.” That sounds contradictory, given the system also removes the need for a disc to play. After all, after claiming the license for Lego Ninjago on my Series X, I installed and played it on my Xbox One without ever inserting the disc.
Microsoft hasn't clarified whether this means the Disc-to-Digital license will need to be renewed by periodically re-inserting the disc. It’s a big “watch this space” for now, but you probably shouldn’t sell off your disc-drive consoles or physical game collections just yet.
Play Anywhere?
The games you can redeem aren’t necessarily accessible across your devices, either. You still need to keep compatibility in mind—you can play newly digitized Xbox One games on an Xbox Series console, but not the reverse. PC players using the Xbox app can install their Disc-to-Digital games if they’re also included in Microsoft’s Play Anywhere catalog. The same applies to Xbox Cloud Gaming—if it’s not in that catalog, you can't play it, even if it's associated with your Xbox account.
Speaking of which, Microsoft recently capped cloud gaming access, saying that “the cost of providing cloud gaming grows as more people use it,” glossing over the cost and impact of AI infrastructure on server-side components and service provision. Game Pass Ultimate subscribers are now limited to 15 "free" hours per month, 10 for Premium users, and a meager five for those on the Essential plan. Beyond that, users must purchase additional streaming time through the Xbox Store. Even if your Disc-to-Digital game is in the cloud library, you may not get much play time if you want to run it through Cloud Gaming.
That’s a few caveats to keep in mind, but most of them should improve with time, as Microsoft refines the service. For the most part, Disc to Digital works "out of the box" and provides a great way for players to streamline their collections. It feels timely, too—as game install sizes have exceeded disc capacities, the discs themselves have become glorified installation packs, so why not make them a passkey to the digital version that gets installed anyway?
Whether Disc-to-Digital's arrival means the next Xbox will be entirely digital remains to be seen. Right now, it’s a great feature for Xbox players—easy to use, convenient, and surprisingly consumer-friendly. If Microsoft can build toward universal support, this could be its killer feature … at least for the rest of this console generation.

Maricopa County, Arizona, Is Again Ground Zero of Election Conspiracy Theories
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

“Maricopa is a very, very dishonest county,” President Donald Trump told reporters last week.
One could be forgiven for thinking that you had time-traveled back to the chaotic weeks and months following the 2020 presidential election, when Arizona's Maricopa County became the focal point for the election denial movement.
But Maricopa, and election deniers, are back. With just over two weeks to go before the midterms, extremist election activists are trying to undermine trust in the voting process and are ramping up their efforts to confuse and scare people. Central to this is to fall back on well-known tropes that have been used in the past, including the idea that Maricopa County is somehow corrupt.
“At this point, people are tuned into Maricopa as a focus of election rumors,” Kate Starbird, cofounder of the Center for an Informed Public at the University of Washington, tells WIRED. “Sharpie pens bleeding through ballots in 2020. Tabulator machines not reading ballots in 2022. Maricopa has become a familiar setting, a place where election issues arise or are perceived to arise, and where those issues get wrapped into ‘rigged election’ conspiracy theories.”
No evidence of widespread voter fraud in Maricopa County has ever been found, but in March of this year, the administration refocused attention on the county when the FBI seized dozens of hard drives and servers containing data from the Cyber Ninjas audit. The attention was intensified last week, when Trump told reporters that election officials in the county should “be ashamed of themselves” after 3,000 ballots were mailed early in error.
But the rumors went into overdrive last weekend when We the People USA Alliance, an election-denial group central to the baseless claims about voter fraud in Maricopa County in 2020, posted a video on X with the caption “BUSTED.”
The video shows two Maricopa County employees working late at night on October 7 inside the ballot tabulation center. The post insinuated that they were tampering with equipment by “inserting flash drives into computers … during an active election.”
The post also named a Maricopa County employee, who was previously targeted with similarly unfounded claims and threats back in 2021.
The video quickly racked up over 1 million views, boosted by figures like Kari Lake, the former TV star who is now a senior adviser in the Trump administration, who also boosted claims about election fraud in Maricopa County when she lost races in 2022 and 2024 for governor and the US Senate, respectively.
“More shenanigans at the Maricopa county ballot tabulation center,” Lake wrote on X. “Only through God’s intervention was this even discovered.”
But it wasn’t God who provided the video to the group. Jennifer Liewer, the deputy elections director for communications in Maricopa County tells WIRED that the clip was taken from a nonpublic backup livestream camera that is active but not currently one of the livestream cameras available on the county’s website. A source with knowledge of the matter who was not authorized to speak on the record tells WIRED that members of the We the People group had obtained the IP address for the camera years ago, allegedly allowing them to continue to monitor it. We the People did not respond to a request for comment.
The Maricopa County Board of Supervisors issued a statement last week that debunked the claim, clarifying that the employees were “performing authorized and necessary work to update software and upload election data to a computer terminal that is not connected to the internet or ballot tabulation equipment.”
Unsatisfied with this explanation, Shelby Busch, the founder of We The People USA Alliance and a representative for the Republican National Committee (RNC), then contacted the Maricopa County recorder Justin Heap, who is aligned with Trump. His office then contacted the FBI to investigate the issue, according to Heap’s chief of staff.
The FBI asked an investigator from the Arizona attorney general’s office to investigate, and they quickly concluded there was nothing to investigate, according to a copy of their report seen by 12News. “Election integrity is one of the top priorities of this FBI, and we continue to work around the clock to pursue criminal actors who seek to undermine our system and the rule of law,” the FBI tells WIRED.
The RNC and Busch did not respond to a request for comment.
The FBI’s closed investigation has not quelled the conspiracy theories. On Thursday, Busch appeared on Steve Bannon’s War Room podcast repeating claims that something nefarious had happened, and that she had contacted the Department of Homeland Security and Department of Justice to investigate the matter further.
“Can somebody get involved here?” Bannon replied.
The Justice Department, DHS, and the White House did not respond to a request for comment.
“Election rumors contain the same, or very similar, narrative tropes that make them easily digestible for audiences and remixable for rumor producers,” says Starbird, whose group has created a bingo card of such tropes. “Maricopa County has become a trope, a suspicious setting, for election rumors. It’s a ready-to-use building block for a new rumor or conspiracy theory.”

Nearly 38.76 tons of nitrous oxide were seized from three warehouses at the same address in Sofia during joint inspections by the Bulgarian Food Safety Agency and customs officials, the agency said.
