Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
08:17:12 UTC
17:17:12 KST

Thousands Protest Corruption as Clashes Escalate in Albania
Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama has refused to resign despite three days of escalating youth-led protests over corruption, education costs and a lack of job prospects
A fire destroyed much of the 143-year-old city hall in Limoges on Saturday, October 17, during the largest day of protest France has seen in the current wave of unrest. The city’s mayor, Guillaume Guérin, described “a clear, premeditated intention to burn down the town hall,” and the prefect, Maurice Barate, said the roof had collapsed onto the lower floors. By Sunday evening, the Interior Ministry put the national toll at 2,397 arrests and 997 injured police officers and gendarmes, seven of them seriously.
The violence has since turned into a second argument on top of the first. In a televised address on Sunday, President Emmanuel Macron blamed “seditious elements from far-left splinter groups, joined by many delinquents.” U.S. President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance have blamed immigration. The evidence available so far supports neither account in full.
From a school protest to a national one
The movement began in the schools. In late September, students at the Lycée Saint-Exupéry in Créteil, outside Paris, began mobilizing over teacher shortages and poor conditions, and blockades spread across the Île-de-France region. Human Rights Watch dates the start of the protests to September 21. The students’ grievances included unfilled teaching posts, overcrowded classes, buildings with leaking water and broken facilities, and frustration with the Parcoursup university admissions platform. According to TIME, nearly 10% of teaching hours went untaught in the 2024-2025 school year.
Clashes and arrests grew sharply in the first days of October. On October 2, authorities closed about 400 lycées. By early October, the Justice Ministry reported more than 5,000 people held in custody since the movement began, 87% of them minors, and Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said about 85% of those detained were minors, most of them lycée pupils. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu announced five initiatives, including guaranteed classes, repairs to school facilities and a more transparent Parcoursup, with a timeline and funding plan promised by the end of October.
On October 17, the protests broadened to living costs and fuel prices. Authorities counted about 550,000 participants nationwide, and organizers counted about 800,000. Most demonstrators were peaceful, Al Jazeera reported.
What happened on October 17
The worst damage was concentrated in a handful of cities. In Paris, masked, black-clad young men smashed shop windows and fled with stolen goods, Al Jazeera reported, and the base of the Marianne statue at Place de la République was partly dismantled. In Marseille, dozens of shops were looted and a group broke into city hall before being forced out. Bordeaux’s mayor said up to 100 stores were looted in his city. A tourist office in Lyon was set on fire and a Paris restaurant was broken into and burned, according to The Associated Press. Carrefour chief executive Alexandre Bompard said about 20 of the chain’s stores were looted, though reports of his cost estimate range from tens of millions to hundreds of millions of euros.
In Limoges, 17 people were arrested after the fire, seven of them minors, according to local radio, and prosecutors say they are still working to establish “the exact responsibilities.” One person died of a heart attack during the day, and Paris prosecutors are investigating the circumstances.
The police response has drawn criticism of its own. Nuñez announced that France’s police inspectorate had opened 36 investigations into alleged police violence since the school protests began, four of them for mutilating injuries. Human Rights Watch said the protests had been met with excessive force, citing a 15-year-old in Lens who lost a hand after a police stun grenade exploded and a 14-year-old whose jaw was fractured by a tear-gas grenade fired at close range. Amnesty International has also denounced a disproportionate use of force against the student protests. The government temporarily suspended the use of stun grenades.
The far-left accusation
The government’s position is that the unrest was organized or exploited by the radical left. In his Sunday address, Macron said “nothing justifies, nothing explains, nothing excuses” the violence, warned that those who “sought to bring down the Republic” would have to answer for it, and insisted that protesters with legitimate demands must never be confused with those who destroyed and looted. Lecornu blamed the “ultra-left” and criminals.
The claim goes back to the start of October. According to Reuters, a readout of an October 1 crisis meeting, supplied by an anonymous source close to the prime minister, described a “shared assessment by the intelligence services” that the movement was “an operation organised by LFI and its proxies on the far left.” Le Figaro had published an intelligence note dated September 29, which, according to Italy’s Il Foglio, named student unions at the Paris 8 and Nanterre universities, two small far-left groups and La France Insoumise (LFI). The note reportedly said the unrest “could be part of a strategy of escalation” ahead of the 2027 presidential election. The underlying evidence has not been made public. On the same day, the former interior minister and center-right presidential candidate Bruno Retailleau floated banning LFI, while conceding it would be “very difficult in law.”
LFI rejects the accusation. Party coordinator Manuel Bompard said the government was “sinking into conspiracy theories,” and lawmaker Louis Boyard said LFI “has always advocated non-violent demonstrations.” LFI leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who joined the Paris march on October 17, accused Lecornu of “playing with fire” and said that protesters who share his cause should not loot or destroy. Marine Le Pen blamed the rioters for spoiling the protests and criticized Mélenchon.
No published evidence, such as court records or the political affiliations of those charged, yet ties specific acts of violence to LFI or to organized far-left networks. Black clothing and masks, which Al Jazeera observed in Paris, are tactics associated with the “black bloc,” but they do not on their own establish anyone’s politics. An Odoxa-Backbone poll for Le Figaro found that 62% of respondents considered the student movement justified, while 74% believed LFI encourages violence and 78% saw its involvement as an electoral strategy.
The migrant accusation
Trump wrote on October 6 that “this isn’t about schools, this is about Islam wanting to take over a once great Country,” and posted again on Sunday that immigration had “shattered that once great country.” Vance shared a video of the burning Limoges city hall on X on Saturday, writing that “Western liberals imported the third world into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion” and had “ignored fundamental questions of assimilation and compatibility.” French authorities have not made that link. Macron, Lecornu and Nuñez attribute the violence to the far left and to looters, and the students themselves cite schools and living costs.
The numbers needed to settle the question do not yet exist. France has published no breakdown of the nationality of those arrested on October 17, and French law generally bars the collection of ethnic statistics. What is known about the earlier school-protest phase is that the overwhelming majority of those detained were minors, mostly lycée pupils.
The closest precedent is the 2023 riots that followed the police killing of 17-year-old Nahel Merzouk. Gérald Darmanin, then interior minister, said at the time that only 10% of those arrested were non-French. A Senate report published about ten months later put the share of French nationals at 71%, which suggests a larger foreign share than Darmanin had stated. The same report described the typical rioter as a French man with an average age of 23, often a first-time offender. That precedent says nothing certain about 2026.
The protests began in working-class suburbs with many second- and third-generation immigrant families, according to the European Digital Media Observatory, and many of those young people are French citizens. Some of those who damaged property were very likely of immigrant background, as in most large urban disturbances in France, but that is different from a link to recent migration, and no data supports the claim that any ethnic or religious group is more prone to violence.
What the viral videos got wrong
A video that circulated widely online showed a hooded youth firing a flame at a woman’s face in Marseille. The footage is authentic. The attack took place on Thursday, October 1, and the suspect is a 15-year-old pupil at the Lycée Colbert who was not known to police or the courts. He was brought before an investigating judge on October 4 with a view to charges of “acts of barbarity,” and prosecutors asked for him to be held in provisional detention. The victim, a 40-year-old home carer, was treated for first-degree burns to the face after she reportedly stepped in when a group tried to smash a bus shelter. The suspect reportedly admitted the facts. Posts calling him an illegal migrant who targeted a white woman are not supported by any reporting, which does not mention his origin or nationality.
Other clips shared as evidence of the current unrest were recycled from earlier events, including footage of a 2020 Paris protest. Foreign governments have also joined in. On October 7, France summoned Iran’s ambassador over what its foreign ministry called misleading content about the protests spread by official Iranian government accounts.
Why the story looks different from outside France
Inside France, the unrest has followed a familiar pattern. Street protest is part of the country’s political culture to a degree few European democracies share, and much of that history runs through Paris, from the storming of the Bastille in 1789 to the revolutions of 1830 and 1848, the Paris Commune of 1871, May 1968, the yellow vest movement in 2018 and the pension protests of 2023. Most of those movements began with social or political grievances and many produced violence that their critics later used to define them. The students who started this autumn’s blockades were asking for more teachers and classrooms that function and the wider marches of October 17 were about prices and fuel.
Outside France, the same images reached an audience that had little of that context. Footage of a burning city hall or a looted shop travels easily and on platforms that reward the most dramatic reading, it was quickly attached to a ready-made story about the decline of the West and migrants taking over Europe. Recycled videos and foreign state accounts helped spread that story and so did political figures with millions of followers, among them the president and vice president of the United States. The European Digital Media Observatory documented posts presenting the clashes as proof of ethnic incompatibility and promoting “remigration” as the answer. Those narratives existed long before the first lycée was blockaded and the protests supplied them with fresh pictures.
What comes next
Macron has put Lecornu at the head of a crisis cell to speed up aid to damaged businesses, given prefects the authority to ban gatherings where necessary and promised a round table with students, teachers and unions. Prosecutors have not said who set the Limoges fire, and the profile of those arrested on October 17 has not been released. Both camps in the argument over who is to blame are also preparing for a presidential election that Macron, in his address, said is six months away.

Bulgaria recorded the second-highest annual inflation rate in the eurozone in September, at 5.6%, while inflation across both the eurozone and the European Union climbed to 3.8%
Croatia recorded 20.1 million tourist arrivals and 104.9 million overnight stays from January through September 2026, while revenue from foreign visitors rose by nearly 5% in the first half of the year, according to data from the Croatian National Tourist

Iran freestyle win team title of U23 World Championships
TEHRAN – Iran freestyle team won the team title of the U23 World Wrestling Championships held in the Las Vegas.
Ahora Khateri in 65kg and Mahdi Yousefi in 79kg won two gold medals for Iran to seal the title for the Persians.
Khateri's final against Kaiji OGINO (JPN) was spectacular bout with the Japanese leading, 6-1 with 40 seconds left in the bout. But Khateri began the comeback as he used an arm drag to go-behind Ogino and then scored a takedown and turn. The second two points were only awarded after a challenge from Iran.
With 10 seconds left in the match and down 6-5, Khateri snapped Ogino down and tried to go-behind. Ogino managed to remove the grip but Khateri pulled him down on the mat and eventually scored the takedown with 7-6 left.
Khateri burst into instant celebrations as he captured his first world title since 2023, when he won the U17 world title at 45kg. The gold medal will come as a relief after he finished with a bronze medal at the U20 World Championships in August.
"I was able to enter these competitions with a positive mindset," Khateri said. "I’ve changed weight classes, moving up from 60kg to 65kg. Even though I found myself trailing in every match, I managed to turn things around during the second period."
The two gold medals sealed the team title for Iran which also won the Greco-Roman team title. Iran won a total of nine medals, including four gold medals, in Las Vegas.
Yousefi's gold medal over Said Saidulov (RUS), 3-1, clinched the team title for Iran as any slip up there would have cost them the title.
Yousefi managed a takedown in the second period to lead 3-1. Saidulov got on Yousefi's leg in the final 20 seconds but the Iranian defend the position till time expired.
Iran finished with 180 points and Russia was second with 171 points. The United States, which had a underwhelming tournament, finished third with 104 points. Turkey finished a surprise fourth with 99 points and Japan was fifth with 74 points.

Belgian diplomat: ‘West Bank attack is a new escalation’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
08:13:09 UTC
17:13:09 KST

Saturday was meant to be a day of solidarity and peaceful support, in the olive groves of the Palestinian village of Taybeh in the occupied territories. An international diplomatic delegation, comprising Belgian, French and Polish diplomats, a French mayor, the Archbishop of Cambrai and a local priest, joined farmers for the annual olive harvest.
Belgian diplomat: ‘West Bank attack is a new escalation’
Their presence served a specific purpose: what is known in diplomatic circles as a protective presence.
“That means we go with the Palestinians to their olive groves and help with the harvest,” explains Anick Van Calster, the Belgian consul-general in Jerusalem, who was part of the delegation. “We hope that violent settlers will be deterred by our diplomatic presence.”
However, the atmosphere quickly turned. “It was a very violent morning,” Van Calster told VRT. “We’d already heard that the settlers were committing acts of violence elsewhere, but when we heard they were heading our way, we decided to get into the cars. We are diplomats and we do not seek confrontation.”
Before everyone had got safely into the vehicles, a group of attackers appeared. They were young, masked men armed with wooden and metal sticks.
“You could only see their eyes,” says Van Calster. “That didn’t bode well.”
The first vehicle, in which Van Calster was travelling, managed to drive off quickly. The second attempted to pick up members of the French delegation, including Bernard Baudoux, the mayor of the northern municipality of Aulnoye-Aymeries. It was unable to leave before the attackers reached them.
“Mayor Baudoux was physically attacked and thrown to the ground before he could even get in,” Van Calster says. “When the car finally managed to escape, the settlers pelted it with rocks, shattering the rear window.”
The violence has truly reached new heights
Consul-general Anick Van Calster
Once back in the village, the diplomats found a group of Israeli activists in a state of deep shock. “They had also been attacked by the settlers, who had told them: ‘We’re going to kill you’,” says Van Calster.
She stresses that this direct attack on diplomats crosses a dangerous line. “Attacking diplomats is a new escalation,” she says. “Since the start of the olive harvest, there have already been more incidents than there were throughout the whole of last year’s season. The violence has truly reached new heights.”
Many Palestinian farmers no longer dare to go on their own land for fear of their lives, creating economic hardship for many families.
An investigation by Israeli newspaper Haaretz reveals that the army ignored repeated warnings about the impending attack. Urgent calls for help were received at around 13.00, including the exact location and video footage of “at least seven masked settlers, armed with clubs”.
An activist sent the reports to a military helpline, but soldiers ignored the unknown number and did not pass on the information. It was not until around 15.00 that the information reached the army, by which time settlers had already smashed a window of a vehicle belonging to the Belgian delegation.
The army has launched an investigation. It says the helpline was not intended for civilians and that the visit should have been coordinated in advance. According to Van Calster, the latter is not true.
Under the Oslo Accords, diplomats are not required to coordinate their visits in advance, she says. According to reports, the authorities had been aware of their presence and of the threat in the area for hours.
“We must not be blamed for a deterioration in the security situation, the effects of which we are feeling but which have absolutely nothing to do with us,” she says. “Our peaceful presence serves to show just how dire the situation there really is.”
In the wake of the incident, Foreign minister Maxime Prévot of Les Engagés is calling for joint international action. Belgium will continue to press for European sanctions against those responsible for the violence and those who support them, he says.
The European Union, too, has condemned the violence against European diplomats.

In pictures: More than 500,000 took to the streets as France protests erupted into violence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
08:10:26 UTC
17:10:26 KST

Protests in France against rising living costs and declining public services turned violent over the weekend, with more than 500,000 people taking to the streets.
Hundreds of thousands of people marched through various cities and protested peacefully but others set fire to the city hall in Limoges, gutting the 19th-century building.
Lyon's city tourist office was also set ablaze, supermarkets were looted and there were attacks on police officers and vehicles and luxury boutiques, in what was described as the country's worst unrest in years.
Officers used tear gas to restrain the crowds. One protester died of a heart attack, and another lost a hand.
"Those who looted will have to pay back for the damage, and those who sought to bring down the Republic will be held accountable," French President Emmanuel Macron said in a televised address to the nation on Sunday.
He blamed "unrestrained violence" on "insurrectionist elements from radical far-left groups, joined by numerous criminals."
The demonstrations began last month as high school students across Paris lamented poor school conditions, including teacher shortages and unsatisfactory facilities. The demonstrations evolved into a nationwide protest.

‘India is not Bangladesh or France’: Tharoor hits back at BJP, says opposition backs peaceful protest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
08:09:45 UTC
17:09:45 KST

‘We believe in peaceful protest’: Tharoor rejects BJP’s India-Bangladesh comparison
NEW DELHI: Congress MP Shashi Tharoor on Monday rejected comparisons between India and Bangladesh or France amid the political row over the opposition's use of the phrase “regime change”, asserting that the demand was for free and fair elections and not an attempt to topple the government.Responding to Union minister Kiren Rijiju's remarks, Tharoor said India did not support violence and that protests should remain peaceful. He also questioned the relevance of comparisons with unrest in other countries."I think that India is not Bangladesh and India is not France. I don't see these analogies as particularly relevant... We would never condone any of the violence, setting alight buses and police stations and so on, that has occurred in France. We only believe in peaceful protest... that's the kind of protest that I have participated in, and that I believe the opposition in general supports... As far as the larger issues are concerned, there's no point distorting a phrase like 'regime change' and so on... What we are calling for is free and fair elections... What is troubling today is that large numbers of people have been cut from the electoral rolls as the result of a completely troublesome, irregular, and partially illegal process.
This is why we are calling for all this to be undone... It's a constitutional issue. It's not an issue of trying to topple a regime or anything like that..."
Tharoor also defended citizens' right to protect democratic institutions, while clarifying that his criticism was directed at their functioning and not their existence."...Democracy is not a gift of anybody... we, the ordinary citizens of India, are the custodians of it... Every Indian citizen has the right to protect our democracy... All I'm saying is we are asking institutions like the Election Commission to behave themselves, to perform as they are required to by the democratic Constitution of India. That's all it is. I'm not in any way challenging these institutions as institutions. I'm challenging the way they are behaving, the way they are conducting themselves, and that is something that honestly all of us in India should be concerned about..."
Political row over ‘regime change’
The remarks came amid a political exchange over protests against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and allegations of irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.On Sunday, Union Parliamentary Affairs Minister Kiren Rijiju alleged that “anti-India groups” and some politicians had colluded to provoke young people and spread violence, claiming that a conspiracy similar to the unrest in Bangladesh and France had been planned in India.“The violent incident that occurred in Bangladesh and the riots, arson, and looting that took place in France, a similar conspiracy was hatched for India as well,” Rijiju said in a post on X.He further asserted that a change of government in India could take place only through elections.“Regime change in India is absolutely possible, but only through elections, not through Soros,” he said.The row intensified after senior advocate Prashant Bhushan described the agitation against Kumar as a “fight for regime change”. All India Students' Association (AISA) president Neha Bora also referred to the Gen Z-led movement in Bangladesh.Rijiju had earlier accused political rivals and activists of using street protests to create unrest and destabilise constitutional institutions. He said India's youth were focused on nation-building rather than political upheaval.
Separately, Tharoor responded to Elon Musk's recent remarks regarding Starlink, saying the government had maintained that all companies bidding for the service were going through the same process and facing similar delays."I've heard the government's explanation on this issue, which is that there is a process and that all the companies bidding for this are in the same process and are facing the same delays. If that position of the government is taken literally, that means Musk is no further behind in the queue, and Ambani is no further ahead. I think we just have to wait for the process to play itself out... There are several factors. There are questions of the technology, certain security concerns, various kinds of details to do with the uplinking and finally cost.
The last one, the ordinary public will decide. If you are giving me a service and he's giving it to me for 10 times the price, I may take it from you. Or if I really feel that what he's doing is worth 10 times the money, I'll give it to him. Each subscriber will have to decide. Personally, I'm quite happy with my regular connections. I'm not looking for a Starlink myself. But if there are people who feel these things are useful, in a free country, let them have the opportunity."
Ayush Pandey is a journalist at The Times of India, covering breaking news, politics, defence, and major legal and policy developments across India and the world. His reporting focuses on elections, national security, and institutional affairs, tracking the decisions and conflicts that shape public life. Mali’s military and armed groups committing abuses against civilians: HRW
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
08:06:22 UTC
17:06:22 KST

Mali’s military and armed groups committing abuses against civilians: HRW
Soldiers, fighters and separatists in West African country committing grave laws-of-war violations, rights group finds.
Mali’s military and its Russian paramilitary allies have killed civilians in breach of international law, and opposition armed groups have done likewise, Human Rights Watch (HRW) says.
Soldiers and fighters “are committing grave laws-of-war violations while international organisations and governments largely stand by”, the United States-based rights watchdog said in a report released on Monday.
It urged the African Union’s Peace and Security Council to “urgently take action to prevent further atrocities” in Mali.
The West African country has been mired in fighting and attacks since 2012 as the military and its allies have battled an array of armed groups, including Tuareg separatists, and criminal gangs.
The military government that has ruled Mali since back-to-back coups in 2020 and 2021 has turned to Russia for support, enlisting the services initially of fighters from the private Wagner Group, which became the state-controlled paramilitary group Africa Corps in 2025.
‘Scores of civilians’ killed
The rights group said its report was based on interviews with 30 people – witnesses, human rights defenders, community leaders, journalists and a Malian soldier – conducted from late July to mid-September.
“Mali’s military and the allied Russia-controlled Africa Corps … have killed and wounded scores of civilians in attacks and in custody in violation of international humanitarian law,” HRW said.
Armed groups “have also violated the laws-of-war, including torturing and executing captured Malian soldiers”, it added.
HRW said it documented two “apparently indiscriminate” drone attacks by the Malian military.
According to the report, a July 29 attack in the Kidal region of northeastern Mali destroyed part of a health facility, and a second on August 19 hit a market in the central region of Bandiagara, killing six civilians and wounding at least 20.
HRW said it also documented an operation against armed groups in the Segou region in the south, where Malian soldiers shot and killed five girls, and another in the central region of Mopti, where members of the military-allied Dozo militia killed three civilians, “all with impunity”.
Fighters ‘execute’ soldiers
HRW also cited an attack on a military convoy in the Gao region on July 18 by Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM) and allied separatist fighters in the Azawad Liberation Front.
It said the two groups “tortured and executed at least 19 Malian troops” they had taken prisoner.
The JNIM acknowledged that prisoners were killed in the event but denied having ordered the deaths, HRW said.
The Azawad Liberation Front, HRW added, acknowledged fighting with the army and Russian forces in the northeastern region on the day but denied executing soldiers.
The HRW report also drew on research by Armed Conflict Location and Event Data, a nongovernmentsl group that gathers conflict data from around the world.
It said its data show 49 air strikes by Malian forces and the Africa Corps from April to August that killed 89 civilians, “more than double the 22 strikes and 44 civilian deaths reported during the same period last year”.
HRW said it sent a letter to Mali’s defence minister on August 5 with its findings and questions but received no response.

Wei Chuan Dragons take 2-0 lead in Taiwan Series
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
08:05:00 UTC
17:05:00 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Wei Chuan Dragons beat the CTBC Brothers 3-1 on Sunday to take a 2-0 lead in the Taiwan Series.
The Dragons’ pitchers held the Brothers’ first two batters, Chang Shih-lun (張士綸) and Chang Jen-wei (張仁瑋), to a combined 0-for-16 through the first two games, per CNA.
Dragons manager Yeh Chun-chang (葉君璋) said the team’s preparation had paid off after the coaching staff studied the Brothers’ hitters and their tendencies before the best-of-seven Taiwan Professional Baseball League championship series.
Yeh said the Dragons were too anxious early in Sunday’s game. They recorded two hits and a walk in the bottom of the first inning but failed to score after two runners were caught stealing. Yeh said the players wanted an early lead and that the coaches would look into whether the opposing team had picked up on their signals.
Yeh said the Dragons’ strategy against Chang Shih-lun and Chang Jen-wei had been particularly effective. The two hitters can generate significant offense, he said, but the Dragons had studied their strengths and weaknesses, with the results showing through the first two games.
Starting pitcher Cristopher Mercedes threw 85 pitches over six innings, allowing five hits and one earned run. He struck out three batters and walked one, earning the win with a quality start.
Yeh said Mercedes’ performance resembled his strong outings during the regular season. He praised the pitcher’s command, location, and ability to throw a variety of breaking balls, per CNA.
Mercedes was replaced after six innings despite throwing fewer than 90 pitches. Yeh said the pitching coach made the decision, adding, “The pitching coach has faith in our bullpen pitchers.”
The decisive blow came in the bottom of the fifth inning, when Dragons outfielder Zeng Sheng-an (曾聖安) hit a three-run homer to put his team ahead 3-1. The 20-year-old, making his Taiwan Series debut, bounced back from a fielding error earlier in the inning to deliver the go-ahead hit.
The Dragons will return to Taipei Dome on Tuesday for Game 3 after Monday’s scheduled day off, holding a 2-0 series lead.

DPP’s Puma Shen takes Taipei campaign through childhood neighborhood

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — More than 100 relatives turned out to support DPP Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) during a campaign roadshow through Songshan and Xinyi districts Sunday.
The motorcade traveled through both districts before ending at Minquan Park, CNA reported. Shen’s relatives gathered near his childhood home, waving campaign flags and holding banners in support.
Shen said he grew up in Wufenpu, a neighborhood in eastern Taipei known for its wholesale clothing market. He thanked his relatives for their support and said he hoped to bring new ideas to the area, per TVBS News.
Shen said he would announce policies for Songshan and Xinyi after the roadshow. He added that he hoped to spread a positive message throughout Taipei.
Organizers tightened safety measures after supporters followed campaign vehicles and set off firecrackers during Shen’s first roadshow. This time, supporters were asked not to follow the motorcade and instead gather at designated locations along the route, per CTS News.
Shen said organizers had prepared Minquan Park for the event and informed nearby residents in advance. He said the campaign wanted to reach more voters without disrupting local communities.
Shen also denied online claims that he planned to end Taipei’s cash gifts for older residents during the Double Ninth Festival, a traditional occasion honoring seniors. He said the payments would continue and proposed a program to preserve older residents’ memories, per Liberty Times.
Under the proposal, seniors could record personal stories and messages when collecting their cash gifts in person. The recordings would be stored in libraries, allowing younger generations to learn from their experiences, per CTS News.

Taiwan labor groups press for higher wages and share of profits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
08:04:36 UTC
17:04:36 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Labor groups gathered outside the Presidential Office on Monday to call for higher wages, increased employer contributions to labor pensions, a profit-sharing system, and social safety net reform.
Approximately 2,000 people joined the protest, CNA reported.
Under Taiwan’s new labor pension system, employers must contribute at least 6% of a worker’s monthly wages to the worker’s individual pension account. Employers must cover the full contribution and cannot deduct it from workers’ wages.
Ho Cheng-chia (何政家), chair of the Taiwan Solidarity Front Confederation of Trade Unions, told reporters that more than a year had passed since the group called for an increase in the employer contribution rate, but the government had yet to provide a concrete response.
Ho said many unions had recently initiated strike ballots, largely because wages and benefits were inadequate or reasonable profit-sharing systems had not been established. As the government calls for sharing the benefits of AI, it should address gaps in labor regulations and working conditions while Taiwan’s economy is performing well, he said.
Ho said the unions want Article 29 of the Labor Standards Act to clearly specify how companies should share profits and distribute the value created by their workers. The government should give equal attention to the technology sector and traditional industries to help generate better economic outcomes, he said.
Ho added that raising the minimum wage would benefit some service-sector workers, but companies should not use it as the benchmark for employee compensation. With prices continuing to rise, failing to raise wages effectively amounts to a pay cut, he said.

Chiayi Zhongpu Industrial Park’s first plant breaks ground

08:04:32 UTC
17:04:32 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Fluid power equipment maker Hefu Industrial broke ground on a plant at Chiayi County’s Zhongpu Industrial Park on Monday, according to a county government press release.
The Ministry of Economic Affairs worked with Taiwan Sugar Corporation to develop the industrial park. Located near downtown Chiayi, it connects via Provincial Highway 82 to National Highways 1 and 3 and the High Speed Rail.
Hefu Industrial expects to invest NT$45 million (US$1.38 million) in a plant covering 2,310 square meters on a 4,950-square-meter site. It projects annual output of NT$15 million. The plant is expected to be completed in mid-2027, with production slated for 2028.
Hefu Chair Hsu Wen-kai (許文凱) said the firm makes hydraulic lifting equipment for tractors in Australia and car jacks for markets in Europe and the US. He said price competition in China had prompted the firm to focus on high-end equipment.
Hsu said Hefu was in its start-up phase, with new products undergoing testing and samples being sent to customers for evaluation. He hoped the plant would be ready for mass production as the company expanded.
Chiayi County Magistrate Weng Chang-liang (翁章梁), Legislator Tsai Yi-yu (蔡易餘), and MOEA Industrial Parks Bureau Deputy Director Tseng Chu-fen (曾琡芬) attended the ceremony.
Weng said the firm’s hydraulic and pneumatic equipment serves the healthcare, automotive repair, and mining industries. Tsai said flood prevention projects were also underway and expressed hope that more people would settle in the county as companies moved in.

Israel nabs 8 over settler attacks on US journo, European diplomats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
08:01:00 UTC
17:01:00 KST

Israeli police arrested 10 suspects Monday in connection with weekend violence in the occupied West Bank, including separate attacks on a U.S. photojournalist and European diplomats.
The United States, Israel's closest ally, had urged a crackdown on settler violence and the arrest of the perpetrators of the attack on the Washington Post photojournalist.
France, Belgium and Poland, whose diplomats were attacked, also called on Israel to take action.
Police said the suspects were arrested in a predawn operation on suspicion of involvement in acts of violence, violating a closed military zone order and illegal construction.
The suspects, whom police did not identify, were taken into custody for questioning. Israel's Army Radio reported that they were Israeli citizens.
Prosecutions of Israeli settlers, however, are rare.
U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee said on X that the arrests were "a very positive development in finding & punishing those who severely attacked and beat" Washington Post journalist Heidi Levine.
A video released by the police of the predawn operation appeared to show at least one arrested suspect, whose face is not seen, wearing ritual tassels known as tzitzit, which are often worn by religious Jewish men.
The video also appeared to show two slingshots, which can be used to hurl stones, being found at one property. On Friday, when the Washington Post journalist was attacked, dozens of masked settlers, some armed, descended on a Palestinian olive harvest, with some settlers hurling stones with slingshots.
Police, military forces and the Shin Bet domestic security service took part in the operation.
Referring to the West Bank by its biblical name, Judea and Samaria, Israeli Police Commissioner Daniel Levy said the law applied to everyone, "regardless of identity or affiliation."
"The Israel Police is committed to professional, equal, and impartial law enforcement, based on evidence and in accordance with the law," he said in a statement announcing the arrests.
Masked Israeli settlers were filmed Friday assaulting Levine, a U.S. citizen, who was covering a Palestinian olive harvest in the West Bank. Levine was taken to hospital and underwent surgery on a finger.
On Saturday, French, Belgian and Polish diplomats as well as a French mayor were attacked by masked settlers in another part of the West Bank. A Belgian diplomatic vehicle was also damaged.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar and the military have blamed "Israeli rioters" for the attack on the diplomats.
However, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whose far-right coalition is projected to lose its governing majority at the Oct. 27 election, has been more circumspect.
He has claimed the diplomats entered a "sensitive area with a history of confrontations" and without coordinating with the military. He has also said that the facts of the attack on Levine were "unclear."
Levine has said she was attacked by masked men wearing tzitzit tassels. Israel's President Isaac Herzog has apologized, saying the "violent rioters" who "brutally attacked" her did not represent the values of Israel.
Settler attacks on the Palestinians are surging, with at least 170 since Sept. 27, according to Yesh Din, an Israeli human rights group. Journalists, Israeli activists and foreign observers have also been targeted.

Unknown

2026-10-19
08:00:45 UTC
17:00:45 KST

Türkiye will receive a share of the diesel fuel that Russia will supply to the global market under an agreement between Moscow and US President Donald Trump’s administration.
Turkish Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar announced this, Reuters reported.
According to the minister, the agreement is important for Türkiye’s energy security.
Bayraktar noted that Russia had restricted diesel fuel exports in recent months due to supply issues, but Ankara will now be able to receive part of the Russian fuel.
“Thanks to the negotiations we have held, we will receive part of this fuel for Türkiye,” Bayraktar said.
However, the minister did not specify how much diesel fuel Türkiye would receive or the terms of delivery.
On October 9, US President Donald Trump announced an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin to supply 4.8million tonnes of diesel fuel to the US and global markets.
According to Trump, Russia was to immediately deliver more than 300,000 tonnes of fuel, followed by another 500,000 tonnes in November, 1 million tonnes shortly thereafter, and an additional 3 million tonnes within a short timeframe, depending on the capacity of Russian oil refineries.
On the same day, the US Department of the Treasury, through the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), issued a temporary authorization for transactions involving Russian diesel fuel previously subject to US sanctions restrictions.
The document allows the sale, delivery, unloading, and import of such fuel until April 7, 2027.
Following Trump’s announcement, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said that Moscow was beginning to lift its own restrictions on diesel fuel exports ahead of schedule.

Chinese discovery of doughnut-like topology at tipping points breaks physics convention
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
08:00:11 UTC
17:00:11 KST

Chinese discovery of doughnut-like topology at tipping points breaks physics convention
Study bridges critical phenomena and topology, opening new pathways for fundamental science research
Chinese physicists have discovered that a tipping point – a threshold where a physical system rapidly shifts states – can possess a smooth mathematical structure resembling a doughnut’s hole, challenging a belief that the two phenomena must be studied separately.
For decades, mainstream physicists have mostly treated critical phenomena, which describe how physical systems change at critical points, and topology, which studies the properties of geometry, as separate areas of research.
A classic illustration of topology is the difference between a sphere and a doughnut. The two cannot be transformed into each other by stretching or bending alone because they have a different number of holes, unless the surface is cut or glued.
The study by researchers at Singaporean and Chinese institutions was published in Nature on October 7, with Cheng Zheyu and Zhang Xiuhai, both affiliated with Nanyang Technological University in Singapore, as co-first authors.
Cheng and his colleagues set out to investigate whether doughnut-like topological properties could exist at critical points – the thresholds at which physical systems change their behaviour.

European delegation including Belgian diplomats attacked by Israeli settlers in West Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
07:59:26 UTC
16:59:26 KST

A diplomatic delegation including the Belgian consul-general was attacked by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank on Saturday. Violence in the area has escalated since the start of the olive harvest in late September.
European delegation including Belgian diplomats attacked by Israeli settlers in West Bank
The group of Belgian, French and Polish diplomats was taking part in the olive harvest in Taybeh, in the occupied West Bank, a spokesperson for Foreign minister Maxime Prévot confirmed. Their participation was a “symbolic gesture of support for the local population”.
During the visit, the convoy was surrounded by masked settlers armed with sticks, who pelted the vehicles with rocks, breaking a window.
Consul-general Anick Van Calster and a second Belgian diplomat were present at the incident. They were unharmed. Bernard Baudoux, mayor of the French municipality of Aulnoye-Aymeries, was injured.
Prévot condemned the attack on X. “I condemn in the strongest terms the attack by masked settlers in Taybeh, in the occupied West Bank,” he posted. “Palestinians face this violence every day. Settlers also target journalists reporting on it and diplomats ... As the occupying power, Israeli authorities must protect Palestinians, ensure the safety of diplomats and journalists, and bring those responsible to justice.”
He said Belgium would continue to press for European sanctions “against those responsible for this violence and those who support them” and that “the occupation of the Palestinian territory must end”.
I was violently attacked and thrown to the ground. I was quite shaken
Bernard Baudoux, mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries
Baudoux was in the West Bank because Aulnoye-Aymeries is twinned with the Christian municipality of Taybeh. He was visiting to pick olives with locals as a symbolic gesture.
“Suddenly, masked people arrived in cars and started attacking the group,” he said. “I had put on my sash, in the colours of the French flag, in an attempt to protect the people around me. But it was to no avail. I was violently attacked and thrown to the ground. I was quite shaken.”
The Israeli army said in a statement on X that “no Israeli soldiers were present” at the time of the attack. It also stated that the visit had not been coordinated with the army. According to the army, such coordination is “important to prevent incidents such as this”.
Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu describes the incident as a smear campaign against Israel. The army has, however, stated that it is launching an investigation. The Israeli police are also reported to have launched an investigation.
In the nearby village of Abu Fallah, around 80 Israeli settlers attacked Palestinian farmers at the weekend. Wearing masks and dressed in black, they threw rocks and set fire to trees and vehicles.
The situation escalated when the Israeli army intervened. According to the Palestinian news agency Wafa, both Israeli soldiers and settlers opened fire. Several Palestinian farmers were injured.
Human rights organisations have again reported an increase in violence by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank in recent weeks. According to the Israeli human rights organisation Yesh Din, settlers have carried out at least 170 attacks since 27 September, around the start of the olive harvest. The Palestinian Authority reports that at least four Palestinians have been killed and more than 100 injured.
Human rights organisations document a rise in violence almost every year during the harvest, which is a crucial source of income for many Palestinian families. This year, however, it appears to be escalating further in the run-up to the Israeli elections at the end of October.

2026-10-19
07:58:04 UTC

The Philippines has summoned China’s ambassador to Manila after he said Beijing could “easily win” a conflict between the two countries, prompting calls from Philippine lawmakers for his expulsion.
Foreign Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro conveyed Manila’s “serious concern and strong objection” to Ambassador Jing Quan over his public remarks on October 15, which the Philippine Department of Foreign Affairs said amounted to a threat to use force.
The dispute follows a series of incidents involving the two countries’ militaries and coast guards in contested areas of the South China Sea.
China claims most of the strategic waterway, despite an international ruling that found no legal basis for its expansive claims.
Jing made the remarks last week after Philippine Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro described Beijing as a regional “troublemaker”.
Speaking to reporters after a speech at a school in Manila, the Chinese envoy said the Philippines should “feel fortunate” to have China as a neighbour.
“If we want to use force, we may easily win. But no, we will not choose force, and we love peace,” he said.
The comments prompted calls from politicians, including at least two sitting senators, for Manila to expel the ambassador.
In its statement on Monday, the Philippine foreign ministry described Jing’s remarks as “provocative and unacceptable”.
“The Department reserves the right to take further diplomatic action as it deems necessary,” it added.
Jing called for peaceful resolution
Earlier, speaking at the Second Diliman Dialogue in Manila, Jing called for a peaceful approach to maritime disputes, urging both sides to maintain a safe distance, avoid deliberate provocations and prevent incidents from escalating tensions.
He said China and the Philippines should manage their differences through dialogue and consultation, warning against a cycle of reciprocal countermeasures.
Jing also argued that maritime disputes should not define the entirety of bilateral relations, pointing to continued trade, people-to-people exchanges and cooperation in other areas.
“We must not allow a small group of people, backed by forces from outside the region, to steer bilateral relations into a dangerous and uncertain course, or even toward confrontation and conflict,” he said at the dialogue.

Daycare prices outpace benefit cap, hitting low earners hardest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
07:57:09 UTC
16:57:09 KST

Daycare prices outpace benefit cap, hitting low earners hardest
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Seven in 10 daycare centres now charge more than the hourly rate covered by childcare benefit (kinderopvangtoeslag), and parents have to make up the shortfall, parents’ association BOinK reported.
The average hourly rate at the 400 organisations BOinK surveyed is €11.82, while the government only subsidises up to €11.23. The cap goes up to €11.60 in January, which is still less than most centres are already charging, and prices are set to rise again next year.
Low earners will get hit hardest, NU.nl reported on Monday. The state covers 96% of the capped rate for the lowest incomes, leaving them with a bill of a few cents an hour – until the surcharge above the cap is added.
A family on a low income with a child in daycare two days a week could be paying €80 a month next year, up from €70.
“For many parents, this means their own contribution keeps rising,” BOinK chairman Gjalt Jellesma said in a statement.
A social affairs ministry spokesperson told NU.nl that childcare is becoming more affordable overall and that the gap between the cap and actual prices has narrowed since 2023.

World Food Programme cuts aid to 500,000 Palestinians in Gaza, cites funding shortages
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
07:55:57 UTC

World Food Programme cuts aid to 500,000 Palestinians in Gaza, cites funding shortages
- WFP says funding shortages are forcing Gaza aid cuts, leaving about 500,000 people without monthly food support and halving rations for many others.
- The agency says 1.4 million people in Gaza face crisis-level food insecurity or worse, while 200,000 are in emergency conditions.
- WFP needs US$450 million over six months and warns life in Gaza remains “brutal” as winter nears and basic services stay scarce.
AI generated
CAIRO/GAZA – The UN World Food Programme (WFP) has said funding shortages are forcing major cuts to its aid programme in Gaza, leaving about 500,000 people without monthly food support in a territory where two-thirds of the population struggle to get enough to eat.
The WFP said it was reducing the number of recipients of its monthly assistance to 1.1 million people from 1.6 million.
In addition, food rations have also been halved, cash assistance has been cut for 75,000 families, and the number of daily hot meals for those unable to cook has fallen to 150,000 from 250,000, with some families in hard-to-reach areas now receiving a hot meal only every other day.
The WFP said about 1.4 million people, or two-thirds of Gaza’s population, face crisis levels of food insecurity or worse, including roughly 200,000 people in emergency conditions.
The US-brokered Gaza ceasefire in 2025 calls for the eventual reconstruction of the territory. But little progress has been made towards implementing a deal to end the conflict that includes terms for Hamas to disarm and Israel to withdraw its troops.
Life is still brutal in Gaza, says acting head of WFP
“It’s a year into the agreement of this ceasefire. Well, life is still brutal here. There is no proper shelter. There is no basic services. There is no safety, no security,” acting executive director of the WFP Carl Skau told Reuters in Gaza.
“These cuts are happening just as we are facing the fourth winter. You know, I’ve been through the winters here, absolutely brutal,” he added.
The WFP said it urgently needs US$450 million (S$575 million) over the next six months to maintain critical operations in Gaza and the Israeli-occupied West Bank.
“We tell the world now is not the time to look away. This is the time to step up to sustain this support, to protect the progress that has been made, but also to push for early recovery,” said Skau.
Israeli forces still hold more than 60% of the territory and conduct almost daily air strikes, while Hamas controls most of the area where more than two million Palestinians live, mostly in temporary shelters with what aid agencies call inadequate aid supplies.
The Hamas-run Gaza government media office described the WFP announcement as “catastrophic” and said it might accelerate famine in the enclave, calling for more fund to aid agencies to prevent it.
“On top of the circumstances and the difficult life, you want to make it even harder on us,” said Palestinian woman Sabrine Kuhail, standing by a tent shelter at a displacement site in Nuseirat refugee camp in central Gaza Strip.
“You made us hungry for three years with war, destruction, siege, and the bloodshed that is not stopping. What do you want from us? Enough, enough, we are tired.” REUTERS

Singapore sets aside 92 mln USD for bio-based chemicals research
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
15:55:19 CST
16:55:19 KST

SINGAPORE, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- Singapore has set aside 118 million Singapore dollars (about 92.23 million U.S. dollars) for research into producing chemicals from biological materials, the largest public funding commitment of its kind to date, the Economic Development Board (EDB) said on Monday.
The Bioeconomy Funding Initiative, launched under the 37-billion-Singapore-dollar Research, Innovation, Enterprise 2030 plan, aims to address industry challenges and support the transformation of Singapore's energy and chemicals sector, which accounts for one-fifth of domestic manufacturing output, the EDB said in a statement.
The initiative will target chemicals made from biological alternatives to petroleum-based feedstocks, such as yeast and oil palm, the EDB said.
Initial research will focus on converting industrial by-products, or "sidestreams," into usable materials, developing microbe- and enzyme-based production methods, and improving processing efficiency.
Research and development projects will also explore combinations of biological and chemical processes to produce commercially viable goods, including high-grade synthetic rubber.
"There are opportunities for Singapore to grow our capabilities in innovation and production of higher-value specialty chemicals and advanced materials, while supporting the transformation of our existing industrial base towards more sustainable production," said Jermaine Loy, managing director of the EDB.
The latest initiative builds on previous funding commitments and will bring government spending on bioeconomy-related initiatives to about 200 million Singapore dollars over the next five years. ■

China's GDP expands 4.5 pct year on year in Q3

A drone photo taken on Oct. 14, 2026 shows the Yangzhou Port in Yangzhou, east China's Jiangsu Province. China's gross domestic product (GDP) grew 4.5 percent year on year in the third quarter (Q3) of 2026, data from the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) showed Monday. The world's second-largest economy generated about 107.11 trillion yuan (about 15.94 trillion U.S. dollars) in output during the January-September period, according to the NBS. (Photo by Ren Fei/Xinhua)
BEIJING, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- China's gross domestic product (GDP) grew 4.5 percent year on year in the third quarter (Q3) of 2026, data from the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) showed Monday.
The growth rate was higher than the second quarter's reading of 4.3 percent, the data showed. The country's economy expanded 4.6 percent year on year in the first three quarters.
The world's second-largest economy generated about 107.11 trillion yuan (about 15.94 trillion U.S. dollars) in output during the January-September period, according to the NBS.
"The national economy forged ahead against pressure and continued to shift toward innovation-driven, high-quality development, with growing positive changes in major indicators," the NBS said in a statement.
Noting the GDP growth of 4.6 percent in the first three quarters is in line with the country's annual growth target, NBS deputy head Mao Shengyong told a media conference that the economy added 5.7 trillion yuan in output during the period, the largest increase for the same period in the past five years.
In the third quarter, GDP growth picked up 0.2 percentage points from the second quarter, while some international institutions forecasted that major economies were expected to grow more slowly compared to the previous quarter, Mao said.
New growth drivers continued to expand in China, contributing more than 40 percent to the country's economic growth in the first three quarters, according to preliminary estimates. Value-added industrial output rose 5.3 percent year on year, with equipment manufacturing up 10.2 percent and high-tech manufacturing up 14.3 percent. Output of industrial robots, lithium-ion batteries and 3D printing equipment jumped 29.1 percent, 39.5 percent and 62.5 percent, respectively.
Monday's data also showed that the services sector expanded 5.2 percent year on year in the first three quarters, with information transmission, software and IT services up 10.4 percent and leasing and business services up 12.3 percent.
Goods imports and exports rose 18.8 percent year on year to 39.94 trillion yuan in the first three quarters, with imports up 22.3 percent. In September alone, trade grew 27.5 percent.
The surveyed urban unemployment rate averaged 5.2 percent in the first three quarters, unchanged from a year earlier, while September figure stood at 5.2 percent, down 0.1 percentage points from August. In the first nine months, per capita disposable income rose 5.3 percent nominally and 4.4 percent in real terms year on year.
In the first three quarters, retail sales of consumer goods rose 1.1 percent year on year, while retail sales of services grew 5 percent. Mao added that energy consumption per unit of GDP fell 3.1 percent during the period.
China will step up efforts to expand domestic demand, improve supply and make macro policies more effective to sustain the positive momentum of innovation-led and high-quality development, the official said. ■

Feature: Wuhan Open offers glimpse into blossoming Chinese women's tennis
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
15:54:57 CST
16:54:57 KST

WUHAN, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- When China's top player Zheng Qinwen announced to withdraw from the 2026 Wuhan Open due to a right shoulder injury, many home fans were left disappointed.
The 24-year-old had just lifted the China Open trophy and was expected to spearhead the home challenge in central China. Her absence, however, turned attention to the depth and resilience of Chinese women's tennis.
SHI HAN: GROWING THROUGH THE LOWER TIERS
Ranked outside the world's top 200, 21-year-old Shi Han was hardly a household name when she arrived in Wuhan.
She earned her place in the main draw the hard way, qualifying by beating top-seeded American Peyton Stearns and top-100 player Kamilla Rakhimova.
Drawn against 13th seed and world No. 19 Solana Sierra in the first round, Shi admitted she was taken aback by the challenge.
"I had finally made it through qualifying, only to get such a tough draw," Shi recalled after the match.
With little to lose, she decided to give it everything she had. After dropping the opening set 6-4, Shi fought back to win the next two 6-3, 6-3. Her first serve remained reliable, with speeds still reaching around 180 kph deep into the decider. The win was Shi's first over a top-20 opponent and her first main-draw victory at a WTA 1000 event.
Shi then pushed former US Open finalist Leylah Fernandez in the second round, taking a 4-1 lead in the second set before Fernandez closed out the match in straight sets. Shi left Wuhan encouraged rather than disheartened.
"As everyone jokes, maybe I came here to take tuition," she smiled. "The players I've met in Wuhan are all ranked much higher than me. I'll give everything I have, then look back and see where the gaps are between me and them."
This season, Shi has spent much of her time competing on the ITF circuit, away from the WTA spotlight. Yet she has quietly compiled 64 match wins this year, eight more than world No. 1 Elena Rybakina, even though victories at lower-tier tournaments yield relatively few ranking points.
Starting the year outside top 400, Shi has climbed into the top 200 and secured a place in the 2027 Australian Open qualifying draw.
"I've played a lot of tournaments this season. I wanted to improve my ranking as quickly as possible and get back to the Grand Slams," Shi said. "I'm quite satisfied with the effort I've put in. I have nothing to lose. I hope to go further and play better tennis."
GUO HANYU: FIGHTING BACK AGAINST ADVERSITY
Wild card Guo Hanyu, ranked No. 240 in singles but fresh from Wimbledon doubles glory, arrived in Wuhan with modest expectations. Facing 12th seed and world No. 16 Sorana Cirstea in the opening round, Guo lost the first set 6-1 and trailed 0-4 in the second.
"Until the match was over, I didn't think I was going to win," Guo said. "I just wanted to stay on court a little longer and enjoy the atmosphere on the center court. I didn't expect my form to keep getting better."
Trailing 6-3 in the second-set tiebreak, Guo faced three set points. She then seized control, winning five straight points to take the tiebreak 8-6. Trailing 3-5 in the decider, she broke Cirstea when the Romanian served for the match and reeled off four consecutive games to complete a remarkable 1-6, 7-6(6), 7-5 comeback.
She followed that with another marathon win over American Katie Volynets, prevailing 6-4, 4-6, 7-6(3) after more than three hours on court. Guo's run ended against fifth seed Elina Svitolina in the third round, but reaching the last 16 was her best singles result at a WTA 1000 event and made her the only Chinese player to reach that stage in Wuhan.
Her achievement carried extra significance amid personal turmoil. Shortly after returning from Wimbledon, where she partnered Kristina Mladenovic to claim the women's doubles title, Guo learned her father had been admitted to intensive care. She has since struggled to focus and broke down at her post-match press conference when discussing him.
"I can't stand on court and enjoy the match happily like I used to. There has always been a feeling of sadness around me," she said. "I've tried very hard to pull myself out of it, but it's difficult."
"I keep telling myself to leave it to fate. If this is something I have to go through, I can't escape it. All I can do is play point by point, give my best and see where fate takes me."
Last year, Guo recorded her first WTA 1000 main-draw victory in Montreal. At the time, she described it as feeling as if she had "hit the jackpot" by suddenly producing an exceptional performance.
After winning two main-draw matches in Wuhan, she now carries greater confidence into future tournaments.
"At least against players ranked in the top 100, whoever I'm facing, I feel I have a way to compete," she said. "Maybe I won't win every time, but I believe every match brings progress and something to learn."
ZHANG SHUAI: DEFYING AGE TO DREAM BIG
On Oct. 13, 37-year-old Zhang Shuai walked onto center court to face 22-year-old American Ashlyn Krueger.
Zhang began her professional career in 2006, meaning her time on tour almost matches the age of her young opponent.
But on this night, fatigue was evident.
Zhang struggled with her movement, her shots lacked their usual power, and she repeatedly bent over her racket to catch her breath. She eventually lost 6-3, 6-0.
Zhang's heavy workload this year helps explain her fatigue. Since the US Open, she has played at the Billie Jean King Cup, won an Asian Games silver in Nagoya, reached the China Open doubles final and then arrived in Wuhan two days later. Counting singles, doubles and mixed doubles, she has played 128 matches this year.
"At this intensity and at my age, I think I must be a superhero," she said. "Even though I played like this today, I'm still very proud of myself."
As she left Wuhan, the veteran was already looking ahead.
"I'm not young anymore, but I'll give everything I have over the next year and try to come back to the Wuhan Open," Zhang said. "I hope I can perform better next year." ■

Unknown Publisher

15:54:55 CST
16:54:55 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- China has released new guidelines to promote the application of artificial intelligence (AI) and other advanced technologies in commerce, as part of efforts to upgrade consumption and improve commercial distribution efficiency.
These guidelines, jointly issued by nine government departments, including the Ministry of Commerce, outline 18 measures covering goods consumption, services consumption, commercial distribution, innovative business applications and policy support.
To upgrade consumer goods, the guidelines call for integrating AI into product development, design, manufacturing and marketing, expanding the supply of smart devices and robots, and encouraging flexible manufacturing and AI-powered customization.
In the services sector, these guidelines support the application of AI in healthcare and smart elderly care services, the digital transformation of catering businesses, and pilot applications of AI in culture and tourism.
In commercial distribution, the measures include promoting smart warehouses, intelligent logistics equipment and unmanned delivery, alongside digital upgrades in wholesale and retail businesses.
The guidelines also call for developing commercial AI agents for shopping assistance, business operations and logistics, expanding applications of embodied intelligence, and creating virtual shopping experiences. They additionally outline support for technology standards, digital infrastructure and financing.
In June, the Ministry of Commerce and seven other government departments released guidelines containing 17 measures to promote "AI plus consumption," focusing on smart products, AI-enabled services and new consumption scenarios.
China's retail sales of consumer goods rose 1.1 percent year on year to 37 trillion yuan (about 5.5 trillion U.S. dollars) in the first three quarters of 2026, while retail sales of services increased 5 percent, outpacing the 1-percent growth in retail sales of goods, official data released on Monday showed. ■

Australian teens more likely to disclose online sexual harm to AI chatbots than authorities: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
15:54:53 CST
16:54:53 KST

CANBERRA, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- Australian teenagers who experience online sexual abuse are more likely to disclose it to artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots than to authorities, a national study has found.
The study of almost 2,000 Australians aged 16 to 18, conducted in early 2026 by Adelaide University's Australian Cybercrime Observatory, found that 18.7 percent of victims told an AI about their experience, compared with 13.2 percent who reported it to a teacher, doctor, counsellor, police officer or helpline, according to a university statement released on Monday.
More than one in four cases of nonconsensual sharing of sexual images involved AI, while at least one in 25 Australians had experienced, or had a close friend who had experienced, AI-related online sexual victimization before the age of 18, showed the findings published in Child Abuse & Neglect.
Girls experienced higher rates of online sexual victimization overall, but boys were significantly more likely to be targeted when AI was involved, it said, adding that more than one-third of adolescents also expressed concern that AI could be used to create fake images of themselves or people they cared about.
The findings highlighted the need for reporting pathways accessible through AI tools, peer-focused prevention and broader efforts to protect children, researchers said.
"AI involvement in this abuse is worryingly common, and victims are now more likely to tell an AI than teachers, doctors, police or reporting services. We must adapt quickly to protect children," said Associate Professor Timothy Cubitt from Adelaide University, also the study's co-author. ■

boonserm premthada builds coastal office in thailand with reclaimed timber
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
07:45:36 UTC
16:45:36 KST

boonserm premthada builds coastal office in thailand with reclaimed timber
the project combines traditional thai building principles, woven bamboo screens, and a design that allows the structures to be dismantled and rebuilt elsewhere.
prefer designboom on google
reclaimed timber carries its history forward
Designed by Boonserm Premthada of Bangkok Project Studio, Traces by the Sea is a 440.7-square-meter office for Matalay in Khao Lak, Phang Nga, Thailand. The project brings together timber reclaimed from an old rice cooperative building in Phatthalung and a wooden school building in Phang Nga, preserving the paint, joints, and surfaces accumulated through years of use. The architecture makes these traces part of its identity, allowing the histories of the materials to remain visible in their new coastal setting. Differences in dimensions, existing notches, and remnants of painted surfaces guide how each piece is put together. Premthada makes only the changes needed to reuse the wood, allowing its original features to shape the design.
The carpenters assemble the timber by hand on site, examining each piece to find the right position and adapting the connections to fit its existing features. Old joints remain visible alongside new ones, showing how the wood has been worked on before and how the carpenters give it a new purpose.
a cluster of buildings shaped by the climate
The office consists of four timber buildings connected by decks and walkways, drawing on the layout of traditional Thai house clusters. The spaces between the buildings allow breezes to pass through and keep views of the sea open, while the raised floors create shaded areas beneath the structures. Supported by rows of columns, the buildings stand above the sand, providing shelter while remaining open to the surrounding landscape.
The layout draws on traditional Thai architecture, where raised floors and open spaces help keep buildings cool in a hot climate. The design by Boonserm Premthada and his team adapts the principles of a traditional house to a contemporary workplace, allowing familiar ways of building to respond to the needs of an office by the sea. The decks and walkways take people outdoors as they move between workspaces, bringing them into contact with the trees, sea breeze, and changing light. This connection to the landscape makes the coastal setting an everyday part of working at Matalay.
woven bamboo turns traditional craft into a screen
Large woven bamboo trays from northeastern Thailand are used as sunscreens, giving everyday objects a new role in the building. Traditionally used for silkworm rearing, the trays retain their original shapes and woven patterns, keeping their connection to the craft and practices from which they come. Sunlight filters through the weave and the gaps between the trays, casting patterns of light and shadow across the interior. Although their purpose has changed, the trays remain recognizable as traditional tools, showing how local craftsmanship can be incorporated into architecture.
The timber and bamboo elements build on ideas that Boonserm Premthada explored in his artwork at Triennale Milano, now adapted to a building designed for everyday use. Here, the materials must respond to the coastal climate while retaining traces of their previous lives. Throughout the project, the approach is to change as little as possible. Old paint and marks remain on the timber, new joints sit alongside existing ones, and open spaces allow air and views to pass through.
The timber buildings are designed to be dismantled and reassembled elsewhere, extending the project’s interest in reuse beyond its current function. The wood has already moved from a rice cooperative and a school into an office by the sea. Its next life may take it somewhere else, adding another layer of use to its history.
elephant dung bricks extend the material exploration
The wider Matalay development also includes a public toilet building made from elephant dung bricks, extending the project’s exploration of materials and their potential for reuse. The toilet building is a long, low structure with brick walls and timber doorways. Openings above the walls let in natural light and air, while variations in the color of the bricks give the facade a sense of texture. Trees remain visible through the openings and above the roofline, keeping the building connected to its surroundings. Although the toilet building and timber office serve different purposes, both reflect Premthada’s interest in finding value in materials that might otherwise be overlooked. The reclaimed wood retains traces of its previous uses, while the elephant dung bricks turn a natural byproduct into a building material for an everyday public facility.
Visitors arriving at Matalay first encounter Goya Tower, built with the same elephant dung bricks used in the public toilets, before continuing toward the timber buildings by the sea. Together, the structures reflect Boonserm Premthada’s approach to materials, combining reclaimed elements and craftsmanship with new architectural uses.
project info:
 name: Traces by the Sea
client: Matalay
location: Khao Lak, Phang Nga, Thailand
architect: Boonserm Premthada | @boonserm_premthada
design team: Bangkok Project Studio
 gross floor area: 440.7 square meters

The gathering is part of a global initiative led by the Israeli president that brings together Jewish leaders and young people from Israel and the Diaspora to strengthen connections and encourage dialogue about the challenges facing Jewish communities worldwide.
Herzog is expected to conclude his brief visit with a meeting with leaders of Hungary's Jewish community.
The trip comes after a major political transformation in Hungary, where Magyar and his Tisza party defeated Orbán, ending the veteran prime minister's long rule. Orbán had been regarded as one of Israel's closest allies in Europe, regularly supporting Jerusalem in international forums.
Following Magyar's election victory, Herzog was quick to congratulate the incoming prime minister and expressed hope that the two countries would maintain their longstanding relationship. Magyar, for his part, said his government would pursue "pragmatic relations" with Israel.
The change in government has already brought significant adjustments to Hungarian foreign policy, including efforts to rebuild ties with the European Union and international institutions.
Among the most consequential changes was Magyar's decision to reverse Orbán's planned withdrawal from the International Criminal Court in The Hague. Orbán had initiated the withdrawal in response to the court's arrest warrant against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The new government subsequently halted the process, keeping Hungary within the ICC.
Against that backdrop, Herzog's meetings with Magyar and Baka will mark an important early diplomatic encounter between Israel and Hungary's new leadership, as the two countries seek to maintain cooperation despite Budapest's changing foreign policy.

Mystery European buyer signs $235M Israeli rocket deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
07:39:55 UTC
16:39:55 KST

- Elbit Systems won a $235 million contract to supply PULS launchers and EXTRA-MR guided rockets to an unnamed European customer.
- EXTRA-MR is designed to hit high-value targets at up to 80 km, and the deal includes additional launchers and logistics support.
Israel’s Elbit Systems has won a contract worth about $235 million to supply PULS rocket artillery launchers and EXTRA-MR precision-guided rockets to an unnamed European country, along with additional rocket artillery platforms and integrated logistics support, the company said.
Elbit did not identify the customer or say how many launchers and rockets the deal covers, and it gave no delivery schedule.
EXTRA-MR is a medium-range member of Elbit’s EXTRA family of guided rockets, designed to hit high-value targets at up to 80 km (50 miles), and the company says it can work with the command-and-control systems armies already use to find and assign targets.
PULS, short for Precise and Universal Launching System, is a truck-mounted launcher that carries two interchangeable pods, each loaded with a different munition, so the same vehicle can fire 122 mm and 160 mm Accular rockets out to about 35 to 40 km, full-size EXTRA rockets out to 150 km, or Predator Hawk missiles out to 300 km. The launcher can be fitted to a range of wheeled and tracked platforms, which lets armies put it on trucks they already operate.
The system has become one of the main European competitors to the U.S.-made HIMARS. The Netherlands ordered 20 PULS launchers in a $305 million deal, The Defence Blog reported, while Denmark received eight launchers under a 2023 contract and Germany placed a $57 million order in early 2025 for its EuroPULS version, developed with KNDS.
Greece became the latest major buyer in April 2026, when Elbit announced a $750 million contract covering launchers, rockets, loitering munitions and ten years of support for the Hellenic Armed Forces under a defense agreement between Israel and Greece. Outside NATO, Serbia ordered PULS launchers in 2024 in a deal worth about $335 million.
Elbit has kept European customers anonymous before, including in 2025, when it announced a $130 million contract to supply training rockets and precision-guided Accular, EXTRA and Predator Hawk munitions to an unnamed European PULS operator.
Israel’s ground forces have used PULS since 2020 under the name Lahav, mounted on a U.S.-made HEMTT heavy truck.
