World faces nature reality check at UN biodiversity conference
- World leaders meet at COP17 in Armenia to review the Kunming-Montreal biodiversity plan. Countries are off track on 22 of 23 goals, though 27.5% land protection may be reached by 2030.
- Talks are stalled over funding, including how to raise US$30 billion (S$38.39 billion) in public finance and US$200 billion a year by 2030. A draft UN report says 144 countries have made action plans.
- A major focus is reforming US$500 billion in harmful subsidies and boosting private sector support through the Cali Fund. Businesses say clearer rules could improve investment and help stop species loss.
AI generated
LONDON – World leaders, diplomats and nature experts gather in Armenia this week to assess lagging efforts to halt biodiversity loss, with countries off track on most global targets and divisions over funding still unresolved.
The 17th United Nations Conference of the Parties, dubbed COP17, is the first major review of progress under the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, the landmark 2022 agreement that aims to protect 30% of land and sea by 2030.
The climate-focused COP31 begins on Nov 9 in Antalya, Turkey.
While the world is likely to reach an estimated 27.5% of land protection by 2030, scientists say many of the broader goals needed to halt biodiversity loss remain well off track.
From pesticide use to unsustainable fishing and subsidies for a host of damaging activities, the deterioration of ecosystems threatens food production, water security and economic stability across the planet.
Countries are not on track to meet 22 of the 23 goals set out in the Kunming-Montreal framework, a draft UN report showed.
While the UN says that 144 countries including Brazil and China have so far created action plans, who pays and how much towards a US$30 billion (S$38.4 billion) public finance goal is less clear and will be central to two weeks of talks in Armenia’s capital Yerevan.
The broader goal is to mobilise at least US$200 billion annually by 2030.
Subsidy reform
Another major focus is reforming US$500 billion a year of subsidies for activities that damage nature, with governments urged to set a two-year timeline to identify and redirect the most damaging ones.
That could, for example, include those that encourage farmers to cut down rainforest or the offer of state discounts on synthetic fertilisers and chemical pesticides which damage soil and water.
Doing so would help governments address nature loss and related issues like food and energy security without committing more public money at a time of war, energy crises and other inflationary pressures.
“This isn’t primarily a story about conservation,” said Eva Zabey, chief executive of the non-profit Business for Nature, at a media briefing.
“It’s an economic, fiscal, political and competitiveness story, which is grounded in resilience and resource security.”
More than 130 businesses including retailer H&M and consumer goods company Nestle issued an open letter ahead of the talks urging governments to set clearer policies and a plan to reform incentives over the next 12 months, arguing that it would help make it more attractive to invest.
Subsidies ultimately cost governments between US$11 trillion and US$24.7 trillion a year, non-profit Conservation International estimates, as they often pay twice – once for the subsidies and again to patch up the damage that follows, including cleaning up pollution, treating illness and repairing infrastructure.
Bigger role for private sector
With public money tight, many are looking to the private sector to play a bigger role, including through the Cali Fund.
That fund was set up in 2025 to get companies which rely on digital databases of biological samples for their products, such as in the pharmaceutical, cosmetic and commercial agriculture industries, to help pay to preserve nature.
Details still to be ironed out include how funds should be shared between countries and indigenous communities, and whether companies should contribute based on total revenue when only part of their business relies on these genetic resources.
For Cristian Samper, managing director and leader of Nature Solutions at the Bezos Earth Fund, the talks are also an opportunity for governments to do more to halt the extinction of species.
“We know recovery is possible. The decisions we make in Armenia should give more conservation teams the backing to make it happen,” he said. REUTERS

Eyes on the Street: Jane Jacobs’ Concept and Contemporary Residential Architecture in Brazil
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
04:00:00 UTC
13:00:00 KST

The concept of "eyes on the street" is perhaps the most famous within architectural and urban literature when it comes to urban security. Jane Jacobs uses this expression to refer to people who - consciously or unconsciously - use public spaces or observe them from their homes, generating natural surveillance. A movement that, within our discipline, is encouraged both through quality public spaces and through the powerful relationship between the public and private created through building facades. Advocating for this daily control, Jacobs believes in a way of making architecture and cities that condemns excessive verticalization, reinforced by isolated buildings and single-use ones that deny contact with the street.
The concept emerged in the early 1960s and evolved, sparking discussions and implementations across different scales and objectives. An exemplary case of its application and evolution in architectural design can be seen in Vienna during the 1990s. The City's Gender Department championed residential complexes known as Frauen-Werk-Stadt I, II, and III, which were designed with a gender perspective in mind, applying the concept of "social eyes" to a particular end. These complexes featured facades adorned with windows that overlooked central courtyards, specifically positioned in areas where children commonly played. Within each apartment, windows were strategically placed in the kitchen, enabling mothers to keep an eye on their children while tending to household tasks.
Implementing this concept in residential complexes and its vital role in enhancing the quality of life for residents highlights its broad significance. Remarkably, its relevance persists to this day despite the considerable passage of time since its inception.
Related Article
Rereading Jane Jacobs: 10 Lessons for the 21st Century from "The Death and Life of Great American Cities"
The concept not only remains relevant but also continues to be widely discussed and applied. Interestingly, it's evident in some unexpected ways, such as a common practice in Brazilian cities—especially in residential neighborhoods—where residents establish a "shared surveillance network" using signs and images reminiscent of the "eyes on the street" concept. However, this differs from Jacobs' original idea because this "unity against insecurity" not only isolates residents but also fosters empathy exclusively among them, leading to suspicion towards outsiders. It is crucial to note that Jacobs' concept emphasizes that urban safety isn't just about surveillance but also about fostering the vitality and diversity essential for a healthy city.
From the effectiveness of a thoughtfully crafted interface with public spaces to the potentially intrusive surveillance by neighbors, the concept sparks debate. Yet, irrespective of the viewpoint taken, the core lesson is to grasp the significance of architectural elements in shaping public spaces, emphasizing the dynamic interaction between openings and the street. Jacobs' principles serve as a reminder that every architectural decision carries weight, influencing the urban and social fabric of communities. This understanding underscores the necessity of remaining vigilant in our approach to designing architecture and its integration within urban landscapes.
Numerous issues can be explored through Jacobs' concept if we narrow our focus to a specific time frame and examine Brazilian residential architecture. Here, we will highlight some examples where the architectural envelope plays a crucial role in fostering a healthy relationship between interior and exterior spaces.
The Heliópolis Social Housing project in São Paulo, completed in 2014 within the city's largest favela, breaks away from the typical isolated tower design. Instead, it forms a block and establishes an inner courtyard accessible to residents and the wider community, echoing the layout seen in the Austrian examples mentioned earlier. Furthermore, the project integrates with central courtyards and gardens through windows and features a spacious, permeable envelope facing the street, fostering movement and interaction between the public and private domains.
The design of the Paudalho Popular Houses, on a smaller scale and with a horizontal layout, offers an intriguing layout for multifamily housing. Here, residents enjoy a direct visual connection to the street through the living room window and door, unlike the kitchen setup seen in the Frauen-Werk-Stadt. This design choice is enabled by the intentional use of a low wall height. Furthermore, the project incorporates a covered open living space beneath the front porch, which acts as a robust interface between the public and private spheres—a feature of Brazilian culture and other countries.
To wrap up, we have highlighted a few examples of single-family homes that showcase intriguing architectural solutions related to the concept of "eyes on the street." One standout is the House 711H in Brasília, which faces a park. This house employs retractable perforated panels on its front facade, allowing for seamless integration between the private garden and the public area. Another notable example is the Casa 4x30 in São Paulo. Unlike its surrounding homes, it lacks a wall or fence separating the public and private spaces, creating a more open and inviting atmosphere. While the ground floor maintains a closed facade, the absence of walls encourages a closer connection between the upper window and the cityscape.
In contemporary residential architecture in Brazil, unfortunately, most of the examples tend to be disconnected from public spaces. This is especially true for single-family homes not within gated communities, often due to urban planning regulations and further emphasized by the construction of tall walls or fences. This situation leads to complex discussions and debates, as mentioned throughout this article. However, amidst the challenge of balancing security, privacy, and urban integration, some projects manage to shine by actively fostering meaningful connections between architecture and the street. Regardless of the structural and social dimensions of the issue, it is always useful to revisit Jane Jacobs' precepts to understand the way we are designing our architecture and establishing their important relationship with the city.
Editor's Note: This article was originally published on March 13, 2024, and updated on September 20, 2026.

The India Meteorological Department has launched an advanced WebGIS platform designed to boost disaster preparedness against cyclones.
NEW DELHI: As an additional disaster preparedness tool to support ground-level action ahead of cyclones, India meteorological department (IMD) has launched an interactive WebGIS-based platform that will serve as a decision support system (DSS), bringing critical cyclone warnings and marine weather information together in one place.The system will help users, including disaster management authorities, govt agencies and the general public, better understand potential hazards and their likely impacts. It aims to bridge the gap between weather forecasts and their practical application, enabling better preparedness, timely action and enhanced public safety during cyclones and other severe weather events.The launch took place during the bi-annual pre-cyclone exercise meeting for the post-monsoon season (Oct-Dec) under the chairmanship of Mrutyunjay Mohapatra, director general of meteorology, IMD, last week. The DSS platform for the public isavailable on the websites of IMD and regional specialised meteorological centre (RSMC).“Through interactive maps and visualisations of cyclone tracks, intensity, winds, rainfall, storm surge and rainfall forecasts for river catchments, the platform helps users access relevant information and make informed decisions,” said the ministry of earth sciences (MoES) in a statement.
IMD has taken a number of steps in recent years to continuously enhance the capabilities in monitoring, numerical modelling and forecasting of the hazards associated with cyclones, and demonstrated its capability to provide early warning for cyclones with high precision. It has, over the years, emerged as the best in the world for the accuracy of cyclone predictions, reporting zero error on the landfall point and timing.A cyclone is an intense vortex or a whirl in the atmosphere with very strong winds circulating around it in an anti-clockwise direction in the Northern Hemisphere and in a clockwise direction in the Southern hemisphere. The word "Cyclone" is derived from the greek word “Cyclos" meaning the coil of a snake. Tropical cyclones are also referred to as 'Hurricanes' over Atlantic Ocean, 'Typhoons' over Pacific Ocean, 'Willy-Willies' over Australian Seas and simply as 'Cyclones' over north Indian ocean.
On an average, out of five cyclones developing over the north Indian ocean (NIO) comprising bay of Bengal and Arabian sea annually, about three to four of them make landfall causing loss of life and property. Low - lying coastal belts of West Bengal, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and Puducherry are more prone to the impact of these systems.The number of deaths due to cyclones has, however, decreased significantly in the recent past, as a result of the improvement in the early warning capabilities of IMD.

Sao Paulo – Firing off personal attacks, Brazil’s President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and right-wing senator Flavio Bolsonaro held an acrimonious first debate on Oct 18, a week before a tight presidential election run-off.

Bolsonaro, who made several jabs about Lula’s time jailed for corruption on charges that were later annulled, retorted that it was better he stay at a distance “because my wallet could be stolen”.
Lula, who at almost 81 is seeking a fourth term in power, battled to control his irritation at times and repeatedly asked viewers to “look it up on Google” to prove his adversary was lying.
While Bolsonaro has led in polls since the first round, his edge slightly narrowed in two polls this week which showed him with 51% of voting intentions compared to 49% for Lula.

Lula countered by asking Bolsonaro about his plans to emulate the drastic “chainsaw” cuts to public spending implemented by Argentina’s libertarian President Javier Milei, which led to higher unemployment and cuts to benefits.
Throughout the debate, Bolsonaro dodged the question and pivoted to different topics.

Former president Jair Bolsonaro came up several times, including when his son asked Lula why so many prisoners had supported him in the election.

“Vote for me, Bolsonaro, you know your son, you know I’m better than him.”

Ahead of the showdown, tens of thousands of supporters of Lula and Bolsonaro gathered in cities around the country.

“You might have the desire to fight and to grow, but without the means, without social programmes, it’s just not possible. That is why I am here, continuing the fight,” she said. AFP

Basic mobile coverage is now law, but only Starlink can offer it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
03:44:37 UTC
12:44:37 KST

Universal Outdoor Mobile Obligation promises basic coverage. How does it work?
Amid a busy sitting week in Canberra last week, you would be forgiven for missing a new law that could affect the lives of millions of Australians.
For the first time telecommunications companies will be required to provide a baseline level of mobile coverage across the country.
But a lot of the details are yet to be worked out and the timeframes yet to be settled.
What's new?
While 98 per cent of Australians use their mobiles to make calls, coverage is only available across less than a third of country's landmass, and sometimes only through one provider.
Communications Minister Anika Wells said the new Universal Outdoor Mobile Obligation (UOMO) bill would ensure Australians were covered "nearly anywhere" outdoors.
"It requires mobile network operators, who are Telstra, Optus and TPG, to provide baseline outdoor voice and text coverage throughout Australia," she said.
"Secondly, it gives me as minister the ability to set standards regarding mobile services, so things like reliability or fault rectification."
The bill updates the existing Universal Service Obligation, which only mandates access to fixed lines and payphones.
Telcos could meet their obligation using land-based infrastructure, such as mobile towers, but it is expected vast areas will be covered by Low Earth Orbit satellites, known as LEO Sats.
How does it work?
The direct-to-device or direct-to-mobile technology is different to how many Australians might already use satellite to access internet through NBN's Sky Muster or Elon Musk's Starlink, which requires a receiver.
To get reception direct to a mobile it needs to be able to connect directly to satellite, which means you need to be outside.
It is technology that only Starlink can currently provide, but Ms Wells said the new law was about "getting ahead of the game".
"We're hoping to put in place the conditions through these laws that allow Australian entrepreneurship to create, innovate and come up with technology that we can select over things like Starlink," she said.
"But at the moment, regional Australians need connectivity … so we need to get them a better service, we need to ensure that telcos lift their game."
Telstra already provides a direct-to-device satellite text messaging service through Starlink.
But it uses existing spectrum and is available to certain customers on certain phones and cannot be used to contact Triple Zero (000).
Industry and consumer advocates have broadly welcomed the bill, but there are also parts they take issue with, for very different reasons.
"Direct-to-device technology is a very new technology, it has not been widely tested or commercialised," Australian Telecommunications Alliance chief executive Luke Coleman said.
Mr Coleman said the "special spectrum required for satellite services" was yet to be allocated and the technology still needed to be integrated into networks.
"There's still a few things that the industry needs to get through before this becomes a normal operational commercial service," he said.
He said with no plans for Australia to launch its own sovereign LEO Sat capability, telcos would be left to come up with commercial agreements.
"We are talking about services in areas that are by definition not commercially viable," he said.
"So, a real part of the challenge is how these can be sustainably funded."
The Australian Communications Consumer Advocacy Network (ACCAN) took a very different view.
"[The satellite technology] is already being used around the world," the network's chief executive Carol Bennett said.
"We don't want it to become situation where only those who can afford to access this get access because … it'll lock them out of being able to participate fully in the economy if they can't achieve access to this technology."
What's still to be worked out?
There is a lot of ministerial discretion in this bill.
The minister for communications will have the power to determine what the baseline will be in terms of quality of calls and texts, where it will reach, what it will cost, how it is funded, if it will include Triple Zero capabilities, when it will be delivered and fault rectification measures.
Ms Bennett said while ACCAN supported the bill, there were "missed opportunities" by not supporting amendments proposed by the Greens and independent senator Jacqui Lambie.
"Those amendments that ensure that reliability and performance standards and domestic mobile roaming can happen now," she said.
"Both measures would make a huge difference to the uplift in the reliability of telecommunication services, particularly in the regions, and to the safety net that's available to consumers when they don't have a provider that delivers them connectivity and they can roam onto another network."
Loading...
Ms Wells said she wanted to consult industry and stakeholders before setting those standards, but pointed to a separate bill passed last week that increased penalties for telco breaches by 40 times to more than $10 million.
"I don't want to promise things we can't deliver," she said.
"We need to strike a balance between improving mobile services whilst acknowledging that these networks can be complex, can be expensive to maintain."
As for how Triple Zero obligations would interact with the new mobile standards, that is still to be worked out too with a broader review of the Triple Zero Custodian currently underway.
When will it start?
The default start date in the bill is December 31, 2027, but there is discretion for the minister to delay that until the end of 2030.
Ms Wells said she was "ambitious" and wanted it in place by December 1 next year.
The Australian Telecommunications Alliance indicated that was unlikely.
"On the current trajectory, we still need the spectrum to be allocated for this service to become operational," Mr Coleman said.
"Things would weigh in favour of delaying the start date until the market has developed a bit more."

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — TSMC said at an investor briefing on Thursday that it would build another 3-nanometer chip fab in Tainan, CNA reported.

Wei said TSMC expected strong demand for 3-nanometer chips for years and was building three new fabs to meet it. A 3-nanometer fab at Southern Taiwan Science Park is under construction and expected to begin mass production in the first half of 2027. The newly announced Tainan fab is slated to begin production in the first half of 2028.
The 3-nanometer process is used to make chips for AI computing, smartphones, tablets, and automotive electronics that require greater processing power and lower power consumption.
Tainan City Economic Development Bureau Director-General Chang Ting-yuan (張婷媛) said TSMC had built multiple facilities in Tainan for 3-nanometer and 5-nanometer manufacturing and packaging. Its investment had exceeded NT$1.86 trillion (US$57.17 billion) and created more than 11,300 jobs, according to a city government press release. She said the newest 3-nanometer plant would make the city one of the world’s largest chip manufacturing clusters.
On overseas expansion, Wei said TSMC’s 3-nanometer plant in Arizona was ahead of schedule, with equipment being installed ahead of production in the third quarter of 2027. He said its second plant in Kumamoto, Japan, would also use a 3-nanometer process and was expected to begin mass production in 2028.
Wei said TSMC was shifting some 5-nanometer capacity to support 3-nanometer production. The company was also optimizing capacity across its 7-nanometer, 5-nanometer, and 3-nanometer processes, per Liberty Times.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — A series of bribery investigations involving KMT candidates has reportedly affected the party’s grassroots base, weakening its ability to mobilize supporters ahead of the November elections.
On Oct. 8, a court granted KMT New Taipei City Councilor Huang Yung-chang (黃永昌) bail of NT$1 million (US$30,800) amid allegations that he attempted to bribe voters with Guanmiao noodles. Huang denied that the noodles and other items were intended to solicit votes, saying each item was worth less than NT$30, per Liberty Times.
Former Justice Minister Chen Ding-nan (陳定南) established the NT$30 threshold as a reference point for bribery investigations, per Liberty Times. The Ministry of Justice has said the threshold is only a reference: whether an act constitutes bribery depends on whether the parties understood the exchange as an attempt to influence voting and whether the benefit could affect a voter’s decision.
KMT insiders said investigations involving local political figures could undermine the party’s ability to mobilize supporters, per NOWNews. They complained that party workers had become reluctant to distribute even inexpensive items at political events, while DPP activities continued to offer boxed meals and sandwiches.
The insiders warned that if the investigations discourage grassroots supporters from taking part in campaign activities, the effects could extend beyond November and hurt the KMT’s prospects in the 2028 general election.
Opposition politicians have repeatedly accused prosecutors of political bias in vote-buying investigations. TPP Chair Huang Kuo-chang (黃國昌) said candidates could face legal trouble for offering douhua, while DPP Taichung mayoral candidate Ho Hsin-chun (何欣純) had faced no comparable consequences for distributing boxed meals, per CMedia.
KMT Taipei City Council candidate Lai Yi-jen (賴苡任) cited a social media video that allegedly showed a DPP-affiliated candidate in Hualien County sharing sandwiches and drinks with supporters, per UDN. Lai questioned whether authorities were applying the law consistently.
DPP Legislative Caucus Secretary-General Chuang Jui-hsiung (莊瑞雄) rejected concerns about selective enforcement, saying prosecutors could pursue cases fairly based on the evidence, per Rti. Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) likewise said the justice ministry handled bribery investigations impartially and called on lawmakers to support law enforcement, per UDN.
However, prosecutors involved in bribery investigations described a more complicated picture.
Prosecutor B said the backlash against previous investigations had made prosecutors more cautious about cases involving items worth less than NT$100, per Mirror Media. The prosecutor called for law enforcement officials to be shielded from public pressure and for greater consistency in applying potentially ambiguous rules.
Prosecutor A, who had worked in northern Taiwan, rejected the notion that bribery cases were subject to a uniform standard. The prosecutor said similar conduct could lead to different outcomes depending on the social climate and how individual prosecutors interpreted the circumstances.
Prosecutor A also suggested that senior officials’ attitudes could influence whether an investigation proceeded.

Interview: IMF official warns of exacerbated food insecurity in sub-Saharan Africa
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
11:33:06 CST
12:33:06 KST

by Xinhua writer Xiong Maoling
WASHINGTON, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- Sub-Saharan African economies will likely suffer from exacerbated food insecurity if new shocks continue to drive up food prices, an International Monetary Fund (IMF) official has said.
"If you look to grain prices over the past six, seven months, they have increased significantly because of the fertilizers," Zeine Zeidane, director of the IMF's African Department, told Xinhua in a recent interview, noting that there is always "a lag effect" with fertilizers.
"You may not be able to plant in the next season, or plant with limited fertilizers. If you have limited access to fertilizers, you would expect that the yield that you have from agriculture will fall, and that will affect prices," Zeidane said.
The U.S.-Iran conflict and disruptions linked to the Strait of Hormuz drove up fertilizer prices considerably this year, but that's just one factor affecting food insecurity prospects in sub-Saharan Africa, he said, noting that the other factor is the attack on grain shipments from Ukraine and Russia in the Black Sea, due to the ongoing Ukraine crisis.
"If new shocks happen, we'll also have probably low agricultural production in many places in the world, including in Africa," Zeidane said.
El Nino, in particular, could significantly affect agricultural output and push up food inflation, he said.
The official noted that food is a big part of the consumer price index basket in African region. If food inflation rises sharply, the overall inflation will rise with it. "We're pretty concerned about inflation."
"This is why our call in the update is to have kind of tightening bias in terms of monetary policy to make sure that inflation will remain under control," Zeidane said, referring to the IMF's newly released Regional Economic Outlook Update for sub-Saharan Africa.
According to the update, median inflation in the region is projected to rise from 3.4 percent in 2025 to 4.3 percent in 2026 and 5.0 percent in 2027. Growth forecast is 4.5 percent for both 2026 and 2027.
Zeidane said the IMF now has support programs in place for nearly 20 countries in the region and, amid multiple shocks, including the U.S.-Iran conflict, the IMF is in ongoing discussions with some 10 countries on potential new programs, including Senegal and Malawi.
The update noted that pre-war fiscal adjustment and declining debt ratios are important achievements for sub-Saharan Africa, yet "high interest burdens, low reserves in many countries, and falling aid leave limited room for absorbing another adverse shock."
Looking ahead, the update noted that "risks remain decidedly tilted to the downside," including renewed energy supply disruption, sovereign repricing, further aid cuts, and severe weather shocks.
Zeidane expected prolonged impact of the U.S.-Iran conlfict. "As a shock persists, clearly, policy buffers are running thin, and impact will be much worse than over the past six months."
On asset pricing, the official noted that U.S. 10-year Treasury yields have risen by more than 100 basis points since the conflict started, keeping borrowing costs for African countries elevated.
"If it becomes even higher and stays higher for longer, that will be really detrimental to the dynamic of fiscal sustainability because borrowing costs would rise much faster than economic growth," he said.
The 2026 Annual Meetings of the IMF and the World Bank Group was held in Bangkok, Thailand, from Oct. 12 to Oct. 18. Commenting on sub-Saharan Africa's trade relations with Asia, Zeidane sees "good development" over the past few decades, and Asia has become one of the largest trading partners of Africa.
"In particular, China has become the largest trading partner almost everywhere in African countries," he said.
Zeidane noted that in the past decade or two, he has seen more financial support from Asian countries, including China, South Korea, Japan, India and Gulf countries. "This part of the world has been playing a more important role in providing financing to Africa."
Zeidane said he wants to see more foreign direct investment from Asian countries in Africa.
Looking to the future, the official said that he is optimistic about Africa.
"Wherever you have a young population, you will have a lot of creativity, innovation, tech savviness," he said. "I have no doubt that this region will leverage technology to grow faster."
"I think Africa would be the future of the global economy, will be the engine of global growth," Zeidane added. ■

Nearly half of reef-building corals face extinction risk: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
11:32:48 CST
12:32:48 KST

SYDNEY, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- About 44 percent of reef-building coral species face an increased risk of extinction, with climate change-related heat stress as the main driver of population declines, new research finds.
Researchers from organizations including the Australian Institute of Marine Science and the University of Queensland reassessed the status of 774 reef-building coral species on the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List, updating a 2008 assessment, according to a summary of the study published recently on the Australian Science Media Center website.
Of the species assessed, 340 had a higher relative risk of extinction, including 33 critically endangered, 251 endangered and 56 vulnerable species. Heat stress over the next 30 years was the most important driver of risk for 93 percent of the species considered at high risk, according to the study published in Nature.
The proportion of threatened species varied by region, with 43 percent of coral species in the Indo-Pacific, which includes Australia's Great Barrier Reef, classified as threatened, compared with 50 percent in the Atlantic, the research showed.
Coral reefs support diverse marine life and provide economic and social benefits to more than 100 tropical countries. Warming associated with climate change is a major threat to coral reefs, causing bleaching events with increasing frequency, researchers said, adding that in 2008, one-third of reef-building coral species were classified as threatened in the first IUCN Red List assessment.
The researchers warned the proportion of threatened species could be higher following the three hottest years on record from 2023 to 2025, which included a global coral bleaching event, and called for greater efforts to limit global warming to protect the remaining coral populations. ■

The creator of the AI assistant Claude announced the new “Anthropic Public Benefit Fund” on Sunday as tech firms face intense scrutiny over the potential dangers posed by the frontier technology.
In a blog post, Anthropic said it was committing 5 percent of company shares with immediate effect, subject to stockholder approval, with an additional 2 percent to be added “at the board’s discretion” for every 50 percent increase in the company’s value.
“Because of the way the Fund is structured, the more Anthropic grows, the larger the share of the company that can be dedicated expressly to the public good,” the San Francisco-based firm said.
“It is common practice for tech companies to offer escalating compensation awards to their executives. We are instead directing that equity to the public benefit.”
Anthropic said the fund could be used to make donations to traditional nonprofits, as well as “direct distributions to specific populations”.
It said labour market disruption due to AI could be among the causes addressed by the fund.
“Anthropic has already committed $200 million to studying and addressing this issue, but given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed,” the company said.
“The Fund will have the versatility to pursue them.”
Anthropic, officially registered as a “public benefit corporation” in the US state of Delaware, said the fund would not be used for lobbying or political donations, either in the United States or overseas.
Founded in 2021 by former employees of ChatGPT creator OpenAI, Anthropic is preparing for what could be the largest public initial offering in history. It is expected to list on the US stock market before the end of 2026, with analysts forecasting a valuation exceeding $2 trillion.
The company’s charter requires its leadership to balance shareholder returns with responsible AI development.
The breakneck speed of AI development has prompted widespread anxiety about possible negative downstream effects on society, including the job market.
In a report published last month, consulting firm McKinsey estimated that up to 11 million American workers may need to switch careers over the next decade due to AI-driven automation.

China's GDP rebounds to beat expectations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
03:23:15 UTC
12:23:15 KST

China's economic growth rebounded to 4.5 percent year on year in the third quarter, beating expectations and easing the pressure on policymakers for delivering more aggressive stimulus measures to meet the annual target.
The gross domestic product growth rate, released by the National Bureau of Statistics on Monday, beat the forecast for 4.4 percent growth in a poll and was an improvement from the more-than-three-year low of 4.3 percent in the April-to-June period.
The world's second-largest economy generated about 107.11 trillion yuan in output in the first three quarters.
Beijing has leaned heavily on exports for growth this year, but that engine faces growing pressure as domestic demand remains weak and trade tensions with the European Union escalate.
China's strategy of redirecting credit and resources from property towards high-tech industries has created a two-speed economy, where strong factory output and exports mask weak consumption and private investment.
For January-September, the economy grew 4.6 percent, within the range of the government's annual growth target of 4.5 to five percent.
On a quarterly basis, the economy expanded 1.2 percent in the third quarter, surpassing expectations for a 1.1 percent rise and accelerating from 0.9 percent in April-June.
The trade surplus widened more than expected in September as exports surged, keeping the country on track to surpass last year's record surplus of US$1.2 trillion and likely intensifying trade tensions with major partners.
A deal with the EU to rein in Chinese hybrid-vehicle shipments could weigh on the booming auto trade.
Beijing has recently expanded support for home buyers, unveiled measures to steer cheaper credit into sectors such as infrastructure and technology and allocated 550 billion yuan in unused government debt quotas to ease local governments' financial strain and expand infrastructure investment.
Authorities also stepped up fiscal support, including expanding loan interest subsidies for small private firms and consumers and tapping an 800 billion yuan policy-based financing tool to spur infrastructure investment.
Still, infrastructure investment shrank 4.2 percent.
Fixed-asset investment declined 7.2 percent in the first nine months, dropping at the same pace as in January-to-August period.
Retail sales grew 1.1 percent in September, though, improving from the 0.4 percent rise in August and compared with an expected 0.6 percent rise. 
It marked the quickest growth since March.
For the first three quarters, total retail sales of goods and services, a major indicator of the country's consumption strength, increased by 2.6 percent.
Property investment fell 20.6 percent during the period.
Policymakers refrained from releasing large-scale stimulus measures, as strong goods exports, aided by a global AI-fuelled tech boom, should help the country reach its annual growth target.
Industrial output expanded 5.5 percent in September, accelerating from the 5.2 percent growth in August and was in line with expectations. 
It marked the quickest growth in six months.
For the first three quarters, value-added industrial output increased by 5.3 percent. (Xinhua/Reuters)

Lebanon must refuse Hezbollah’s demand to return seized explosives - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
03:21:37 UTC
12:21:37 KST

Lebanese security forces recently seized hundreds of kilograms of explosives from a vehicle at a checkpoint on the highway linking Beirut and the Bekaa Valley. Hezbollah admitted the shipment belonged to the organization and demanded its return.
“The vehicle and its cargo belong to the resistance,” Hezbollah lawmaker Hassan Fadlallah said, also demanding the release of those arrested. The Iran-backed organization said the material was intended for attacks against Israeli forces in Lebanon.
The Lebanese government should reject that demand. Its security forces have taken a concrete step toward enforcing state authority. Returning the explosives would undermine their work and confirm Hezbollah’s assumption that it can overrule them.
Lebanon has repeatedly said that weapons should be held by the state alone. In March, the government specifically banned Hezbollah’s military activities. Lebanese President Joseph Aoun has reiterated the state’s commitment to seizing illegal weapons and combating smuggling. The issue now is whether Beirut will enforce those decisions when Hezbollah openly challenges them.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who pressed Aoun to retain the explosives, was right. According to a US State Department official’s account of their call, Rubio said returning them should be “out of the question” and urged accountability for those who ordered, financed, and directed the shipment.
No sovereign government should accept an armed group moving hundreds of kilograms of explosives around the country without state authorization.
Lebanese military delegation to participate in US-hosted trilateral talks
A Lebanese military delegation is expected to participate on Tuesday in US-hosted trilateral talks in Tampa, Florida. Beirut plans to press for an end to Israeli attacks in Lebanon. Under the US-brokered framework, Hezbollah’s disarmament is linked to a gradual Israeli withdrawal. Hezbollah continues to refuse to disarm while Israeli forces remain on Lebanese territory.
Lebanon’s demand deserves to be taken seriously. Israel should seek a security arrangement that will allow its troops to withdraw. An indefinite military presence carries costs, while repeated strikes cannot provide a permanent solution.
Any withdrawal must also prevent a return to the conditions that existed before the war. For years, agreements intended to keep Hezbollah’s forces away from Israel’s border went unenforced. Hezbollah accumulated missiles, built military infrastructure, and maintained an armed organization stronger than the Lebanese state itself.
Israel cannot responsibly ask residents of the North to return to that reality.
Full disarmament will take time. Lebanon can begin with the weapons already in its possession: retain the explosives, preserve the evidence needed for the investigation, and arrange their safe destruction.
Authorities should investigate the shipment, prosecute anyone proven to have violated Lebanese law, and apply the same policy to future seizures regardless of who claims ownership.
Such action would strengthen Lebanon’s position at the negotiating table. If Beirut wants Israel to cease its strikes and withdraw its forces, it needs to demonstrate that Lebanese territory will remain secure against renewed preparations for attacks on Israel.
Supporting Lebanon to assert sovereignty over its borders
Israel also has a responsibility to support progress. Jerusalem says it wants the Lebanese government and Lebanese Armed Forces to replace Hezbollah as the effective authority in the south.
Sustained, independently verified progress toward disarmament, preventing smuggling, and extending state control should be matched by phased Israeli steps under the agreed framework, consistent with the security of northern communities.
A single seizure cannot establish that those conditions have been met. It can, however, help demonstrate whether Lebanese authorities intend to enforce their decisions consistently.
Verification should include access to suspected weapons sites, clear reporting on confiscations, and evidence that dismantled outposts remain closed. Lebanon’s partners should help its army carry out those tasks and insist that political pressure never determines which shipments pass through a checkpoint.
The European Union’s newly approved mission to train and advise Lebanon’s military and internal security forces offers further support. Its deployment remains pending. Foreign assistance will have limited effect unless Beirut is prepared to uphold its authority against Hezbollah’s demands.
Who decides which armed forces operate on Lebanese soil? If the answer is the Lebanese state, then Beirut already knows what to do with Hezbollah’s explosives.

A 44-year old British mother of two was questioned by two police officers after being referred to Prevent, the United Kingdom's counter-extremism program, due to her advocacy for Israel, the Telegraph reported on Sunday.
Holly Passmore told the Telegraph that the officers asked her about her recent trip to Israel, telling her that she may be "at risk of manipulation." Passmore later obtained police records through a subject access request and found that she'd been labeled as having mental health issues and being "vulnerable to negative influence."
The reports revealed that the referral said Passmore "over-identified with the conflict between Israel and Palestine” and was “supportive of Israel to the point that she has traveled to Israel.”
Passmore has had health concerns she was open about, including severe endometriosis and adenomyosis, as well as ADHD and autism, but told the Telegraph that nobody would describe her as vulnerable.
Visit came despite lack of counter-terror concern
“They knew I’m not vulnerable, but they wanted to monitor me because I was advocating for Israel,” she said.
“When they came to the door, they didn’t discuss my health. They only asked about Israel.”
The police intelligence report acknowledged that "there is no CT [counter-terror] concern with an individual being supportive of Israel as it's a democracy and it would not be a CT concern for a person to travel there."
The report concluded that "no further inquiries are currently necessary to be completed by any other department in respect of this report."
But Passmore, who is currently pursuing a Master's degree in Holocaust studies at the University of Haifa, was visited by police officers weeks after a trip to Israel in June of last year.
“They asked me why I was interested in ‘Jewish issues’, because County Durham is not a Jewish area,” she added. “They even asked me if I’d ever been to Auschwitz, and I said, ‘Yes’.
“I said to them: ‘Look, I get that this is not something that people around here necessarily are interested in, but you know this is something that’s important to me, and it is not illegal’.
Passmore urged not to discuss case online
Passmore had been to Israel on a press trip alongside British journalists and social media influencers after building an online following on X/Twitter.
Originally created to follow gossip about the Duchess of Sussex, the account, which now has over 28,000 followers, turned to campaigning for humanitarian rights, particularly the plight of women in Afghanistan. After the October 7 massacre, she used her platform to speak out against antisemitism and express solidarity with Jewish people.
Passmore said that she was urged by the police to stop discussing the case online after she complained about the visit.
A Counter Terrorism Policing North East spokesman said they could not comment on an individual case.
“All referrals are treated in the strictest confidence and will always prioritize the safety and welfare of those concerned. Where we are notified of concerns for a particular individual, specially trained officers will listen carefully to the concerns and offer any additional support that may be necessary,” they told the Telegram.

US President Donald Trump’s approval rating fell to a record low of 33%, with 66% of US adults disapproving of his performance, according to a Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll released Sunday.
The survey also found that 52% of Americans strongly disapproved of Trump, with the US midterm elections just two weeks away. The poll showed respondents losing faith in the president amid mounting economic fallout from the war with Iran on Americans' everyday lives, according to analysis from the WP.
At 33%, Trump’s approval sank eight percentage points lower than a year ago, dropping below any point recorded during his first term as president.
The WP-ABC poll also revealed that, for the first time in over a decade, voters view Democrats as more trustworthy on the economy than Republicans.
As both major political parties vie for control of the House of Representatives, the polling found Democrats holding an eight-point lead among registered and likely voters, reflecting an upward trend from past surveys, according to the WP.
Iran war central for voters ahead of midterm elections
Affordability and economic concerns continue to be central issues for voters, but Trump’s economic approval rating dropped to 28% in the latest survey, with 48% of respondents saying they were worse off financially than when Trump returned to office in 2025.
The WP reported that this represented the highest percentage of respondents to say so about any president in WP-ABC polling since 1986.
Voters cited the rising price of fuel as the steepest cost concern. Since the outbreak of the war with Iran, gasoline prices have jumped by up to 50% in some states, according to NBC News, with 71% of respondents calling gasoline unaffordable.
Respondents also broadly disapproved of Trump’s handling of the conflict, with 65% saying they believed the war in Iran was a mistake.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Army has issued a public request for information on wheeled unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) that could help evacuate wounded troops.
According to the request, the planned UGVs would have four-wheel, six-wheel, or eight-wheel drive configurations, Liberty Times reported. They must have a minimum payload capacity of 250 kg and an operating radius of at least 30 km. The vehicles must also have a maximum range of 50 km when fully loaded and fully charged.
The vehicles may use electric, hybrid, or conventional fuel-powered systems. They must be suited to Taiwan’s varied terrain, including mountains, hills, urban areas, muddy ground, and damaged roads.
The Army hopes vendors will propose technologies for autonomous navigation, route planning, obstacle detection, and target tracking, per Liberty Times. The vehicles should be able to continue missions even if enemy forces jam or spoof satellite navigation signals.
For medical missions, the request says the UGVs should be able to carry stretchers, oxygen cylinders, and patient monitoring equipment. Modular designs would allow them to be reconfigured for casualty evacuation or medical resupply.
The military primarily relies on medical personnel and ambulances to evacuate casualties, who are then taken to field medical stations or hospitals, according to Liberty Times. UGVs could help transport patients and supplies through high-risk areas near the front lines.
The Army said the initiative is currently limited to market research and gathering technical information.

Samsung to use TSMC process for Nvidia’s next-generation memory chips

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
02:51:30 UTC
11:51:30 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Samsung Electronics will use TSMC’s 3-nanometer process to manufacture base dies for Nvidia’s next-generation custom high-bandwidth memory chips, the Seoul Economic Daily reported Sunday.
The move would mark the first time Samsung has worked with TSMC at the HBM manufacturing stage, according to the report, which cited unnamed industry sources.
Nvidia has asked Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron Technology to use TSMC’s 3-nanometer process for the base dies and a sixth-generation DRAM process for the memory chips’ core dies, the newspaper reported.
Nvidia unveiled its custom memory technology, called Nvidia HBM, in August. The design integrates Nvidia’s custom memory controller into the base die and aims to standardize the architecture across multiple memory suppliers.
Moving the memory controller from the graphics processing unit to the base die is intended to free up space on the GPU for additional computing circuits. Under the reported arrangement, Samsung would continue manufacturing the memory layers while relying on TSMC’s process for the base die.
Samsung agreed to Nvidia’s requirements after an internal review, per Reuters. The South Korean company plans to retain its in-house manufacturing approach for standard HBM products and customized memory developed for other customers.
The arrangement could expand TSMC’s role in Nvidia’s AI chip supply chain beyond manufacturing processors. For Nvidia, using the same process across suppliers could improve compatibility and simplify product validation.
Samsung and TSMC are major competitors in semiconductor manufacturing, making the reported cooperation notable.

Fatty liver disease is actually five different conditions, scientists discover
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
02:35:09 UTC
11:35:09 KST

Fatty liver disease is actually five different conditions, scientists discover
- Date:
- October 18, 2026
- Source:
- Mayo Clinic
- Summary:
- A common liver disease affecting nearly 30% of adults worldwide may be far more complicated than scientists previously realized. Mayo Clinic researchers have discovered that fatty liver disease actually consists of five distinct biological subtypes, each carrying different risks for liver failure, cancer, heart disease, and other serious complications.
- Share:
A common liver disease affecting nearly 30% of adults worldwide is far more complex than previously understood. Researchers at Mayo Clinic have identified five biologically distinct forms of the condition, each associated with different risks of serious health complications, including heart disease, liver failure, cancer, and the need for a liver transplant.
The findings, published in Nature Communications, come from a collaboration between Mayo Clinic and Virginia Tech. Scientists discovered that metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, or MASLD, can develop through several different biological pathways. Some are closely connected to obesity and diabetes, while others appear to be driven by inherited genetic differences.
One of the most important findings involves the genetic forms of the disease. These subtypes are associated with a greater likelihood of progressing to advanced liver damage, even in people who do not have the metabolic risk factors typically linked to fatty liver disease.
By identifying these differences, doctors may eventually be able to recognize vulnerable patients sooner, improve screening, and select treatments based on the specific biological processes responsible for their illness.
"When clinical and genomic data are analyzed together at this scale, you begin to see patterns of disease progression that would otherwise remain hidden," says Shulan Tian, Ph.D., co-senior author and a bioinformatician at Mayo Clinic. "Once you separate these subtypes, you can start to match treatments to the biology that's actually driving the disease."
Why Fatty Liver Disease Can Be Dangerous
MASLD, previously known as nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, develops when excess fat accumulates in the liver. Many people experience no noticeable symptoms, allowing the condition to go undetected for years.
Although fatty liver disease does not always cause serious complications, it can progress to inflammation, scarring, and permanent liver damage. Over time, severe cases may develop into cirrhosis, a condition in which extensive scarring prevents the liver from functioning properly.
MASLD is a major contributor to cirrhosis, liver cancer, and liver transplantation worldwide. Understanding why some patients experience severe complications while others do not has therefore become an important goal for researchers.
Genetic Analysis Reveals Five Distinct Liver Disease Subtypes
To investigate these differences, the research team examined genetic sequencing results alongside extensive medical information from more than 4,600 patients diagnosed with MASLD.
Their analysis included liver enzyme measurements, body mass index, blood lipid levels, and other indicators of metabolic health. The researchers also considered additional medical conditions, including diabetes, depression, and sleep apnea.
Using advanced computer models, they searched for patterns connecting patients with similar genetic characteristics and clinical findings. This approach revealed five distinct groups, each with its own underlying biological features.
The results suggest that patients who receive the same fatty liver disease diagnosis may actually have substantially different forms of the condition, with different risks of developing serious complications.
"What's emerging here is a way to systematically identify meaningful subgroups within complex disease," says Eric Klee, Ph.D., co-senior author and the Everett J. and Jane M. Hauck Midwest Associate Director of Research and Innovation. "It helps us map complex disease with such precision that we can begin to anticipate its course and intervene before the most serious damage occurs."
How Large-Scale DNA Research Made the Discovery Possible
The researchers relied on Mayo Clinic's Research Data Atlas, a system designed to connect patients' genetic information with detailed medical records. By bringing these large collections of data together, scientists can detect relationships that might be difficult to recognize when studying individual patients.
Dr. Klee helped develop the platform, which draws on resources including the Tapestry Study.
That project has produced Mayo Clinic's largest collection of exome data, involving more than 100,000 participants. An exome is the portion of a person's DNA that contains instructions for making proteins, which carry out many of the body's essential functions. Studying this genetic information can reveal inherited differences that influence how diseases begin and progress.
The combination of genetic data and medical histories allows researchers to investigate diseases in much greater detail, potentially uncovering important differences that conventional diagnostic methods cannot detect.
"This is exactly the kind of insight large-scale genomic research was built to deliver," says Konstantinos Lazaridis, M.D., the Carlson and Nelson Endowed Executive Director for the Center for Individualized Medicine who led the Tapestry Study and is a co-author of the research. "When you connect genetic data with detailed clinical information across large populations, you can start to redefine diseases in ways that directly impact patient care."
Surprising Links to Depression, Sleep Apnea, and Migraines
The findings also suggest that the differences between fatty liver disease subtypes extend beyond the liver itself.
For the first time, researchers identified associations between particular MASLD subtypes and conditions such as depression, sleep apnea, and migraine.
These connections suggest that the biological processes underlying certain forms of fatty liver disease may be linked to health problems affecting multiple parts of the body.
Although the findings do not establish that fatty liver disease directly causes these conditions, they highlight how closely liver health may be connected to other biological systems.
Could Personalized Treatments Change Fatty Liver Disease Care?
The discovery could eventually change how doctors assess and treat MASLD. Rather than approaching every patient as though they have the same disease, clinicians may be able to use genetic and clinical information to determine which subtype is present and which complications are most likely to develop.
Such an approach could be particularly valuable for identifying patients with genetic forms associated with severe liver damage, including those who appear to have relatively few conventional risk factors.
The research team now plans to evaluate its findings in larger and more diverse patient populations. Scientists also want to determine whether different subtypes respond differently to available treatments, including GLP-1 receptor agonists, a class of medications used to treat conditions such as type 2 diabetes and obesity.
If future studies confirm these differences, the findings could help move fatty liver disease care toward more precise screening, earlier intervention, and treatments tailored to each patient's underlying biology.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Mayo Clinic. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Tahmina Sultana Priya, Huihuang Yan, Kirk J. Wangensteen, Stephen Wu, Anthony C. Luehrs, Filippo Pinto e Vairo, Fan Leng, Andres J. Acosta, Robert A. Vierkant, Alina M. Allen, Konstantinos N. Lazaridis, Eric W. Klee, Danfeng Daphne Yao, Shulan Tian. Subtyping metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease using electronic health record-linked genomic cohorts reveals diverse etiologies and progression. Nature Communications, 2026; 17 (1) DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-77410-6

APEC sidelines

The Airbus A320, operating as flight OS82 from Tel Aviv, landed in the capital Sofia with 51 passengers and six crew members on board late on Sunday, the airline confirmed.
The Israeli news website Ynet reported that Austrian Airlines received a warning from an Austrian citizen claiming a bomb was aboard the aircraft after it had departed Israel.

Passengers told Ynet they had been informed of an anonymous bomb threat that forced the flight to change course.
Bulgaria’s Transport Ministry said the crew reported receiving the bomb warning while flying near the Romanian border and decided to divert to Sofia.
The Bulgarian Defence Ministry said MiG-29 fighter jets were scrambled to escort the aircraft to the airport.
Passengers disembarked after landing, while Bulgarian authorities launched security checks of the aircraft.
Austrian Airlines, part of the Lufthansa Group, said passengers would be rebooked on alternative flights following the inspections.
Ynet reported that early indications suggested the threat could be a false alarm, although authorities had yet to announce the results of their investigation.
The incident followed a similar bomb scare involving a Delta Air Lines flight from New York that landed at Israel’s Ben Gurion Airport last Tuesday.
Passengers were evacuated, and the aircraft was moved to an isolated area for inspection following an anonymous warning.
Security checks later confirmed the alert was false.

Kenya: Authorities must address economic grievances driving protests, end repressive tactics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Kenyan authorities have increasingly used authoritarian tactics, including arbitrary arrests and detention, abductions, malicious prosecution of protesters, surveillance, and media repression, to crack down on protests against deepening economic hardship and the government’s aggressive fiscal policies, Amnesty International said in a new report today.
The report, “Human Rights Under Siege: Unpacking Authoritarian Practices in an Era of Economic Pressure amid Youth-Led Protests in Kenya”, documents how between 2023 and 2025, increased food and transport costs, levies and tax hikes, high public debt, corruption, rising poverty and inequality, as well as broken electoral promises led to public anger and protests.
“The findings of this report are troubling and paint a stark picture of the Kenyan government’s repressive response to real grievances affecting the day-to-day lives of ordinary people,” said George Morara, Amnesty International Kenya’s Executive Director.
“The state’s attempts to divert attention away from its failure to address its human rights obligations have not worked. Authorities must address the economic grievances underpinning the protests, end the escalating crackdown on dissent, and ensure accountability for human rights violations during the 2023 to 2025 economic and tax related protests.”
The findings of this report are troubling and paint a stark picture of the Kenyan government’s repressive response to real grievances affecting the day-to-day lives of ordinary people.
George Morara, Executive Director, Amnesty International, Kenya
Between April and July 2026, Amnesty International researchers interviewed 102 people, including protesters, lawyers, a medic, journalists, government officials, social media influencers, and civil society activists. The organization also reviewed Hansard reports, budgets, and tax policies for the period 2023-2025.
Amnesty International conveyed the findings to the relevant government agencies. However, no feedback was received as at the date of publishing this report.
Orders from above: arbitrary arrests, abductions and incommunicado detentions
Amnesty International interviewed 36 individuals from five counties who had been arrested by police or abducted by people suspected of being security agents during and after the 2023, 2024 and 2025 protests. Some of them described being held for days.
Many stated that they were beaten, tortured or otherwise ill-treated, and interrogated without legal representation about their alleged financiers, while also being denied access to family.
Benjamin* was accused by his abductors of organizing protests in 2023 and 2024 in Kisumu, western Kenya, against the cost-of-living crisis and controversial Finance Bills. He said: “I was taken to an unknown place and locked for a night. The following day at around 11 am they stripped me naked and dumped me in a room in the middle of Chemelil sugar plantation.”
Ken* was taken from Rongai, placed in the boot of a car with his head covered with a sack and driven around Nairobi and its environs by security agents who also beat him repeatedly- an action that may constitute torture or other ill-treatment.
I was also made to wear a mask, and I was tied with a tape. I was placed on the seat between them. They told me to tell them everything I knew about the protests, or they would deal with me.
Lawrence*
Lawrence*, who was abducted and bundled into a car by unknown individuals in Kitengela, some 30kms south of Nairobi, said:
“I was also made to wear a mask, and I was tied with a tape. I was placed on the seat between them. They told me to tell them everything I knew about the protests, or they would deal with me. The car was speeding and after a while we arrived at a place which was quiet….We entered the place and I found myself in a room with CCTVs which had lights. I was told to take off all my clothes.”
Surveillance of protesters and activists
Amnesty International interviewed people who reported being subjected to unlawful surveillance by the state of their WhatsApp groups and X spaces, mobile phones, residences or the homes of their parents and other relatives.
Journalists were also harassed, physically assaulted and arbitrarily arrested and detained. Six journalists told Amnesty international they were subjected to police use of unlawful force, including being physically assaulted, tear-gassed, sprayed with water cannons, or shot at. Some journalists were ordered to delete footage from their cameras or had their equipment confiscated, tactics intended to cultivate an environment of fear and limit press coverage of protests.
Amnesty International also documented government contempt for the judiciary and the rule of law, including blatant disregard of court orders against security agencies and withdrawal of the security details of a judge.
‘They should deal with corruption and be accountable’
Fifty-four of the protesters interviewed cited corruption as one of the main reasons why they took to the streets, to express their grievances over the continued siphoning of public funds meant for social protection and public services at a time of rising food and fuel costs.
“The issue of increasing taxes is not logical. They should deal with corruption and be accountable,” one protester said.
Another protester from Kisumu said: “Life has become so unbearable for a normal citizen. Once fuel prices are hiked automatically cost of living rises.”
The 2023 and 2024 Finance Bills were passed by parliament despite widespread public disapproval, including protests outside parliament buildings in 2024. Concessions made by parliament in response to memoranda and petitions from the public were too limited to assuage public anger over the Bills and general state of the economy.
Life has become so unbearable for a normal citizen. Once fuel prices are hiked automatically cost of living rises.
Protestor, Kisumu
“The Kenyan Parliament must ensure that public participation is meaningful and not a box ticking exercise; there must be transparency and accountability in public spending. Corruption and wastage of public resources, which undermine the enjoyment of basic rights must be stemmed,” said Tigere Chagutah, Amnesty International’s Regional Director for East and Southern Africa.
Amnesty International calls on the Kenyan government to ensure comprehensive reparations to all victims of human rights violations and their families, including monetary compensation and medical assistance where appropriate, as well as the prosecution of all security agents involved in repressing protests. The organization further calls on Kenya to ratify the International Convention for the Protection of All Persons from Enforced Disappearance, and review and where appropriate, terminate all cases of malicious prosecution of protesters.
Young people are rising up to demand better use of resources, transparency and accountability. The response from the government should not and must not be violent repression.
Tigere Chagutah, Amnesty International’s Regional Director for East and Southern Africa
The government must also enhance transparency in debt management, increase social protection funding to cushion the poor, and ensure that human rights assessment is undertaken prior to any economic reforms or policies.
“Young people are rising up to demand better use of resources, transparency and accountability. The response from the government should not and must not be violent repression.”
*Names have been changed to protect the identity of the interviewees.

New Zealand annual imports from Southeast Asia up 15 pct
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
09:47:36 CST
10:47:36 KST

WELLINGTON, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- New Zealand's imports from the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) rose 15 percent to 16 billion NZ dollars (about 9.06 billion U.S. dollars) in the year to September, driven largely by higher fuel imports, official data showed on Monday.
The total was up 2.1 billion NZ dollars from the previous year, accounting for almost a fifth of New Zealand's total imports of 92 billion NZ dollars in the year to September, according to the national statistics agency Stats NZ.
New Zealand imports mostly refined fuels, including petrol, diesel and jet fuel. Fuel imports from ASEAN rose 30 percent year on year to 5.5 billion NZ dollars during the period, with Singapore contributing 4 billion NZ dollars and Malaysia 1.3 billion NZ dollars, Stats NZ said.
"Fuel imports from ASEAN contributed 42 percent of the total value of New Zealand fuel imports in the year ended September 2026," Stats NZ international accounts spokesperson Shanna Dilworth said in a statement.
The rising value of fuel imports over the period was predominantly driven by higher prices, the agency said.
Imports of mechanical machinery and equipment from ASEAN, including computers, jet engines, turbines and air-conditioners, rose 33 percent to 1.3 billion NZ dollars, while electrical machinery and equipment imports, including phones, transformers and insulation materials, grew 17 percent to 1.5 billion NZ dollars, statistics showed.
This reflects expanding manufacturing of products such as computers and phones in countries including Vietnam and Thailand, the statement said.
Meanwhile, New Zealand's exports to ASEAN rose 11 percent year on year to 9.6 billion NZ dollars in the year ending September 2026, led by dairy products, which increased 14 percent to 5.7 billion NZ dollars, the statement said, adding that Indonesia was the leading ASEAN destination for New Zealand dairy exports, with their value rising 16 percent to 1.5 billion NZ dollars.
ASEAN, comprising 11 member countries, was New Zealand's second-largest dairy export market after China, accounting for almost a quarter of New Zealand's total dairy export value during the period, Dilworth said. ■

Only Robert Lewandowski, who scored in the first 11 rounds of the 2019-20 season, and Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang, who scored in eight consecutive matches in 2015-16, have recorded longer runs.
Leverkusen could have extended its advantage, but Nathan Tella, Maza and Schick squandered late opportunities. Freiburg nearly snatched an equalizer in stoppage time when Lucas Holer headed narrowly wide from close range.

RLWC quick hits: Ponga's power, Tonga's triumph and Fiji's sunny day
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
01:21:13 UTC
10:21:13 KST

Fri, 11 Sept, 7:50 pm, Final score, Rabbitohs 10, Knights 20
Rugby League World Cup quick hits: Kalyn Ponga, Tonga's triumph and Fiji's day in the sun
The first week of the Rugby League World Cup is in the books with stars new and old making statements across the tournament.
From the classic opener between Australia and New Zealand to Tonga's statement win over England and Papua New Guinea's handy victory over Lebanon there's plenty for the international football fan to sink their teeth into.
Here are the quick hits from the opening round.
1. Kalyn Ponga holds New Zealand's hopes in his hands
Over the past few months Kalyn Ponga has made a transformation from someone who can play great into a great player and if his World Cup is over due to a broken arm not only will the tournament be far poorer without him he might take New Zealand's title hopes home with him.
Ponga was magnificent in his Kiwi debut on Friday night, scoring two tries and running for 254 metres as he continued the form that helped drive Newcastle to the grand final earlier this month.
His battles with Australia's Reece Walsh will take some beating as the defining memory from the entire World Cup even as New Zealand fell to a frustrating defeat where they dominated every major stat but the scoreboard.
Ponga has undergone surgery and will remain in camp but if his transcendent year is over, things might have peaked early for the Kiwis.
Keano Kini, a fine fullback in his own right, was terrific in New Zealand's Pacific Championship win last year and has the work rate and running game to break any match open.
But he is not Kalyn Ponga, who is not rare but unique. That means there's nobody else like him.
2. Speed can kill for lightning Samoan backline
It's a measure of the depth Samoa enjoy that Su'a Fa'alogo, Melbourne's player of the year and one of the most dynamic attacking weapons in the sport, could only crack a bench spot for their first match.
Even so, Samoa proved they could strike from anywhere at any time and through almost any player — Jermaine McEwan's 50 metre solo effort will be one of the best efforts of the entire World Cup.
But after Fa'alogo was pitched into the action early following an injury to Deine Mariner and finished with four tries, three try assists and seven linebreaks in this thumping victory it's clear he can act as the Toa's wildcard as they look to emulate 2022's brilliant run to the final.
Just where the Storm fullback fits into the side remains to be seen — Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow is a brilliant fullback in his own right and Fa'alogo's unfamiliarity with playing wing could be targeted by more dangerous opposition.
But speed can kill and when Fa'alogo is out there Samoa have enough to run and gun with anybody.
3. Future is now for Papua New Guinea
The looming presence of the PNG Chiefs is the subtext beneath every Papua New Guinea game in this World Cup and after this impressive win it seems they've landed a good one in Gairo Voro.
The 23-year old five-eighth is coming off a monster season with London Broncos in the English second division, where he scored 39 tries in 31 games to claim the competition's player of the year award.
He took that good form into this victory, scoring a long range try and creating another with his speed and footwork standing out against a Cedars side with plenty of NRL experience.
Tapping into as much local talent as possible will be crucial and if Voro's improvement continues very well could be one of their early success stories.
4. Powerful Tongan statement a long time coming
Tonga's fourth win over a Tier 1 nation is by far their most dominant — the margin of victory is just one point more than the combined margin of all three previous wins.
Even though they've won just one of their past nine matches, have been building to a dominant performance like this for some time.
All nine of those games were against Australia, England, New Zealand or Samoa, and Tonga are now experience the gain from the pain of those defeats.
The attacking cohesion between regulars like Isaiya Katoa, Haumole Olakau'atu and veteran Tui Lolohea was plain to see, as was the defensive combinations that held England to just two tries despite enjoying far better of the field position, and shows that the benefits of regular matches extends beyond than simply winning and losing.
Tonga have hit the ground running but will still have improvement in them. With a semi-final spot essentially at their mercy after this win, it's a good spot to be in.
England, by contrast, have paid the price for the same flaw that cost them in last year's Ashes series — a lack of spark inside the attacking 20. They've scored just 30 points across their past four matches and their inability to strike has them on the verge of their earliest ever World Cup exit.
5. Fiji makes hay while the sun shines
With matches against Australia and New Zealand to come this might be as good as it gets for Fiji in this World Cup but you'd be hard-pressed to find a better day in the sun for the Bati than their opener against the Cook Islands.
After their women's side, the Bulikula, came within a whisker of pulling off a remarkable upset against New Zealand in just their ninth match ever they lined the tunnel to sing the men's team onto the field as they were led out by Fiji legend Akuila Uate carrying the national flag.
It was a potent mix of past and future combining in the present and didn't just Fiji duly responded, they looked good doing it.
Halves Kurt Donogohoe and Brandon Wakeham, who both played in last year's Pacific Bowl tournament together, showed the benefits of their combination with five try assists between them and Manly lock Caleb Navale was excellent in the middle of the field.
There will be harder matches to come but expect Fiji to hold the gloves up.
They haven't played a Tier 1 nation since the last World Cup but they have the talent, experience and cohesion to make Australia sweat for at least a little while.
