FATF Has Declared War on Fraud. Not All Its Allies Can Afford to Fight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
23:00:00 UTC
08:00:00 KST

FATF Has Declared War on Fraud. Not All Its Allies Can Afford to Fight
The UK is right to put fraud at the heart of its FATF presidency. Success will require source countries to have the means to act.
In the week commencing 26 October, the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) will meet in Paris for its first plenary under UK leadership. The organisation’s founding is inextricably linked to the 1980s cocaine boom, which saw unprecedented flows of dirty money pour into the legitimate financial system. In response, FATF drew up 40 Recommendations for countries to implement to protect the global financial system from criminal actors. The more than 200 jurisdictions which have committed to uphold these Recommendations are assessed by their peers through periodic ‘Mutual Evaluations’. Countries found during their assessment to have fallen short of their obligations risk being placed on the ‘grey list’, which can deter investment and raise the cost of banking with other economies.
Over the years, FATF’s Recommendations have helped countries build and use their anti-money laundering infrastructure to make it harder for drug traffickers, terrorists and kleptocrats to abuse the financial system. Yet, in almost four decades of existence, no presidency has built its agenda so explicitly around a single underlying crime as the UK is doing now with fraud.
FATF’s emphasis on fraud reflects the scale of the current global scams industry, which cost an estimated $442 billion in 2025 and now generates profits to rival those of the drugs trade. But whether the UK’s agenda succeeds will depend less on the capabilities of the advanced economies around the table in Paris, and more on the countries outside the room which represent jurisdictions where fraudsters often set up shop. These countries are not FATF members but are held to its standards all the same, and following unprecedented reductions in development assistance many are facing the sharpest fiscal squeeze in decades.
A Threat Rooted Overseas
Fraud is among the most pressing threats developed countries such as the UK, the US, Australia and Singapore face. Sophisticated criminal networks are siphoning billions of pounds from their citizens each year, and in so doing fuelling their ‘polycriminality’ which spill into human trafficking, corruption and even terrorism. Some countries, the UK included, have penned impressive and all-encompassing domestic strategies, but they can only go so far. The UK Home Office estimates that two-thirds of fraud targeting Brits originates overseas, much of it from low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) with the conditions the UN says allow scam operations to take root: high economic informality, weak institutions, established criminal groups and fast-growing use of digital platforms. Dismantling the networks behind the fraud epidemic, therefore, means working with the governments and police forces of the countries where fraudsters operate.
Aid Cuts and Competing Priorities
However, the steepest fall in the history of official development assistance has left many governments in the developing world reeling, and all but crippled their ability to respond to other, more existential crises. By one estimate, LMICs are projected to suffer an additional 9.4 million deaths by 2030, and this year the World Food Programme estimates 266 million people are at risk of acute hunger. No minister worth their salt would divert scarce resources to anti-fraud policies favouring the priorities of the world’s wealthiest economies while facing malnutrition on such a scale.
This is not to say that developed countries are the only victims of fraud; far from it. The Global Anti-Scam Alliance (GASA) estimates citizens of developing countries are more likely to lose money to scams, and that their economies lose a larger relative share of GDP to fraud. Speak to officials in these countries and they know all too well how scams are damaging their economies and shaking their citizens’ faith in institutions. Often, what they lack is not political will, but rather, the means to fight back. Asking them to prioritise fraud without offering tangible support risks producing the kind of box-ticking (whereby countries pass laws in a bid to satisfy assessors without changing much in practice) which FATF has spent most of the past decade trying to stamp out.
Building on Existing Foundations
As our research at RUSI has shown, taking the first steps towards building a more effective anti-fraud response in these countries need not incur massive costs. The financial intelligence units, reporting obligations and central bank powers which FATF itself has spent nearly four decades persuading countries to build can be turned towards fraud, a crime which is far more visible and politically salient than many of the other offences which FATF has exhorted countries to consider.
That said, while the infrastructure FATF has encouraged countries to build provides the means to get started, scaling up efforts is another matter entirely. Freezing the mule accounts moving stolen money is one thing; dismantling the complex web of criminal networks running scam campaigns is quite another. For most jurisdictions, mounting an effective national response capable of plugging into international efforts will require drafting new laws, training specialist investigators and creating new channels for banks, telcos and police to share information safely. It is in these more substantive reforms where the true costs lie, and where cuts to government budgets are likely to hamper ambitions.
Who Should Foot the Bill?
So when FATF asks jurisdictions to treat fraud as a priority this month, it should ask something of its richer members too: help the countries struggling to confront this global epidemic with the associated costs. This is not charity. When the scams emptying British, American and Australian bank accounts are run from abroad, building other countries’ capacity to fight fraud is among the most cost-effective ways to protect people at home.
The mechanism could be a dedicated fund along the lines of the World Bank’s Cybersecurity Multi-Donor Trust Fund. Alternatively, FATF could encourage members to expand their use of bilateral partnerships, such as those the UK already has with Vietnam and Nigeria. To get started, the new presidency should use this month’s plenary to secure a joint commitment from members to put a share of the proceeds they recover from fraud towards building other countries’ capacity, making the scammers pay for their own undoing.
FATF cannot command its members to write cheques, nor should it try; but it can use its influence and importance in the global anti-financial crime community to drive forward the necessary response. If the UK uses its presidency to make the case to its FATF peers that funding other countries’ fight against fraud is one of the greatest acts of self-defence, it will have done more than any domestic strategy could alone. If, however, it declares a ‘war on fraud’ without helping to arm its allies, it risks getting only the bare minimum in return, and the scammers will continue to drain both bank accounts and trust in the financial system along with them.

Zelensky speaks to US envoys as Trump lashes out

Breadcrumb
Zelensky speaks to US envoys as Trump lashes out
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky spoke with top US envoys Sunday to try to ease tensions, as Donald Trump accused his counterpart of not wanting to end the war with Russia.
Zelensky spoke to US officials Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner as both Russia and Ukraine hit each other's energy sites, with Moscow leaving thousands without power and Kyiv carrying out the largest drone attack on Saint Petersburg since the start of the war in 2022.
Trump and Zelensky have clashed as the US president blocked new sanctions on Russia and struck a diesel deal with Moscow, fuelling fears in Kyiv and Europe that the White House was steering towards Moscow.
On Sunday Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform that he was in the process of negotiating a peace between Russia and Ukraine and making "great progress," but claimed: "Zelenskyy doesn't care, and frankly, with all of the money that Europe is famously giving him... he doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did."
"Zelenskyy is using Diesel Refineries in Russia as a target, knowing that these attacks are seriously hurting the world diesel markets, including those in the United States," Trump said.
Earlier, after speaking to Trump's business partner Witkoff and son-in-law Kushner, Zelensky said "a lot depends" on the US position in the war but that "it is clear that there are many things that matter to all of us and that this war must be brought to an end."
Ukraine was ready to work "constructively" and "honestly", he said. "We expect exactly this approach from all our partners -- both from the Europeans and, of course, from the American side."
He said he discussed deliveries of US Patriot air defence systems, as Kyiv struggles to counter Russian missiles.
Zelensky earlier told US broadcaster NBC it would be a "historic mistake" if Washington formally supported Russia and that he hoped Trump would "change his decisions."
But he also said he was "thankful" the US resumed intelligence sharing after a pause that left his country vulnerable to Russian missile strikes.
Thousands without power
A US-led push to end Europe's deadliest conflict since World War II has so far not brought about a breakthrough and Trump has in the past grown frustrated with both Zelensky and Russia's Vladimir Putin because of their lack of progress.
Zelensky spoke to the American officials as he accused Russia of breaking Trump's "energy ceasefire" 76 times and warning Moscow planned to deprive Ukrainians of heat and electricity before winter.
Russian strikes left "tens of thousands" without power in several regions, he said, with Ukrainian officials reporting three people had been killed.
Ukraine's army launched drones at Putin's hometown of Saint Petersburg late Sunday, setting an oil refinery ablaze and killing one person, Moscow said.
Rising smoke was visible from Saint Petersburg's historic city centre on the banks of the Neva River, with Russia saying Ukraine struck an oil refinery and depot.
Saint Petersburg Governor Alexander Beglov said one person was killed and five hospitalised in the city.
Authorities were fighting fires at the Saint Petersburg oil terminal, the Ruchyi oil depot and industrial warehouses, he said.
Russia's VKontakte social network said its data centre was hit and Ozon -- Russia's second largest retailer -- also reported a strike on its logistics centre.
The head of the wider Leningrad region, Alexander Drozdenko, said air defence shot down 144 Ukrainian drones, with state media saying this was the largest attack on the city since the start of the war.
'Dreadful routine of war'
The Kremlin, however, said Ukrainian attacks on its cities will not change its war aims.
Putin has repeatedly said Moscow intends to seize the rest of eastern Ukraine and, in a fifth year of war, few see a way out of the conflict.
"There's a general feeling: they're attacking, we're attacking -- it's become the dreadful routine of war," 58-year-old Galina told AFP in Saint Petersburg.
Moscow has rained drones and missiles on Ukrainian cities daily and Kyiv says its strikes are fair retribution.
Sergei, another Saint Petersburg resident who is also 58, said he felt his apartment block shake and quickly realised it was a drone attack.
"I don't know if I was scared, what must be will be," he said.
Ukrainian strikes caused nationwide fuel shortages in Russia earlier this year.

Venezuela opposition renews support for Maria Corina Machado as leader
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
22:41:49 UTC
07:41:49 KST

Venezuela opposition renews support for Maria Corina Machado as leader
The exiled Nobel laureate has petitioned for new elections in Venezuela and for the country to allow her return.
An alliance of Venezuelan opposition parties has reaffirmed its commitment to exiled Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Corina Machado as its leader.
On Sunday, members of the opposition’s Unitary Democratic Platform (PUD) agreed in a meeting in Caracas to “recognise and support the leadership of Maria Corina Machado”.
The coalition also renewed its demand for free elections in Venezuela, following a series of contested presidential votes in 2024 and 2018.
Sunday’s statement included 14 proposals for a democratic transition, including freedom for political parties, the release of all political prisoners and the safe return of those who went into exile.
The announcement also increases pressure on authorities to allow Machado’s return. She has been living in exile since leaving Venezuela last December to receive her Nobel Prize.
“The will of the Venezuelans must once again govern the destiny of our nation,” the opposition’s former presidential candidate Edmundo Gonzalez wrote on social media supporting the proposals.
“We will not accept political prisoners, persecution or a governing power that disregards the mandate of its citizens. Living in freedom and under a genuine constitutional order is a legitimate demand of our society.”
No election set
Venezuela has yet to declare a date for a new presidential vote. Since January 3, the country has been led by interim President Delcy Rodriguez of the long-governing United Socialist Party of Venezuela (PSUV).
PSUV leaders have been accused of carrying out human rights abuses against political dissidents, including arbitrary arrest, imprisonment and torture.
Still, after the United States launched a military operation to abduct and jail former President Nicolas Maduro, the PSUV has remained in power with the support of the White House.
US President Donald Trump has backed Rodriguez’s leadership, despite her having been Maduro’s vice president.
His administration has maintained an active role in Venezuela, exerting control over its oil resources and pressuring the Rodriguez government for reforms.
But critics point out that Trump has been reluctant to push Rodriguez for new elections, opting instead for a three-phase plan that focuses first on stabilising the country and economic recovery before pursuing a political transition.
Machado, meanwhile, has told The Financial Times she would like to see Venezuela hold elections by July next year.
“The US government and the Venezuelan people all agree that the only way to make this sustainable and a real victory is to turn Venezuela into a stable democracy,” she told the newspaper earlier this month.
A thwarted return
Venezuelan authorities blocked Machado’s repeated attempts to return to the country, according to her party, Vente Venezuela.
Machado has also reportedly attempted to petition the Trump administration for help re-entering Venezuela.
Separately, she gifted Trump her Nobel Peace Prize in January, during a visit to Washington, DC. Media reports, however, have suggested friction between the Trump administration and Machado.
In interviews with Reuters and Axios, US administration officials have anonymously expressed frustration with the opposition leader’s repeated efforts to return home, particularly after a pair of deadly earthquakes in Venezuela last July.
Axios quoted one official as calling Machado’s push “political opportunism”.
Machado, however, remains one of the most popular figures in Venezuela’s opposition.
In October 2023, Machado won the opposition coalition’s presidential primary, but in January 2024, Venezuela’s courts blocked her from running in the upcoming race.
The courts upheld a 15-year ban on her holding public office, reportedly due to her support of US sanctions against the Maduro government.
Gonzalez ultimately replaced Machado as the opposition candidate in the 2024 race. Maduro claimed victory for a third term as Venezuela’s president in that election cycle, despite widespread criticism that the vote did not meet democratic standards.
The opposition released vote tallies that appeared to show Gonzalez had won the race.
The US had recognised Gonzalez as the country’s rightful president-elect and denied the legitimacy of Maduro’s election claims.
Machado was previously removed from the National Assembly in 2014, due to her activism against the Venezuelan government.
A third round of talks between the Rodriguez government and the opposition began in Venezuela this month.
But instead of including Machado, the negotiations have involved members of the 2015 National Assembly, which was led by the opposition and dissolved under Maduro.
Still, in a statement this month, the US State Department praised the talks as aiding the Venezuelan government’s reform.
“Political reconciliation talks between the interim Venezuelan government and 2015 National Assembly representatives are producing tangible reforms in civil liberties and political rights, laying the groundwork for credible elections and a democratic transition,” the State Department said.

Roundup: Houthis, Saudi-led coalition trade fresh strikes as Egypt pledges support for Saudi Arabia

RIYADH/SANAA, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- Fighting between Yemen's Houthis and government forces intensified on Sunday, as a Houthi attack injured six people in Saudi Arabia and Egypt pledged support to the kingdom amid rising regional tensions.
INJURIES, DAMAGES IN SAUDI ARABIA
The Saudi Civil Defense said Sunday that six Saudi citizens were injured, and three houses and three vehicles were damaged after a projectile launched by Yemen's Houthi group struck a residential area in Najran, southern Saudi Arabia.
The civil defense noted that attempts to target civilian objects constitute a "flagrant violation of international humanitarian law."
In separate statements earlier on Sunday, Saudi-led coalition spokesperson Turki Al-Maliki said three drones were intercepted and destroyed, two over the Riyadh region and one over the Eastern Province. He also confirmed that two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis targeting the southwestern Saudi city of Khamis Mushait were intercepted and destroyed.
INTENSIFIED FIGHTING IN YEMEN
Fighting between the Houthis and forces aligned with Yemen's internationally recognized government has intensified on several fronts.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Sarea said in a statement posted on social media platform X that a total of 110 strikes targeted areas in Sanaa and the provinces of Hodeidah, Taiz and Marib over the past 24 hours, leaving more than 30 people killed or injured.
There was no immediate comment from Saudi Arabia or the Saudi-led coalition on the Houthi claims.
Majid Al-Nuzaili, spokesperson for the government forces, said in a statement posted on X that the government forces had carried out 1,326 strikes against Houthi targets across several battlefronts over the past 24 hours, as they pressed ahead with a major offensive against the group.
Government troops and allied fighters captured several positions in the southwestern province of Taiz and seized heavy weapons and other military equipment, according to Al-Nuzaili.
The spokesperson claimed that "about 370 Houthi fighters had been neutralized" and dozens of military vehicles destroyed during the operations.
The figures could not be independently verified, and the Houthis have not immediately commented on the claims.
EGYPT PLEDGES SUPPORT
The escalating hostilities between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia continue to raise growing concerns across the region.
Egypt's National Defense Council decided on Sunday, during a meeting chaired by President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi, to provide Saudi Arabia with "all necessary and possible" forms of support to defend the kingdom's security and stability, the Egyptian presidency said.
The council pledged to help safeguard the kingdom's resources, territorial integrity and Islamic holy sites, according to the presidency's statement, adding that the "escalating" attacks against the Kingdom were unacceptable.
Meanwhile, the council decided to continue and intensify political and diplomatic efforts, in coordination with relevant regional and international parties, to contribute to "de-escalating tensions across the entire region and achieving peaceful resolutions to ongoing regional crises."
On Saturday, Sisi said Egypt was prepared to take "any measures" requested by Saudi Arabia to defend the kingdom's security and sovereignty, calling for an emergency parliamentary session to authorize intervention if requested.
On Sunday, the House of Representatives concluded its session, chaired by House of Representatives Speaker Hisham Badawi, with deliberations set to resume on Monday, according to the local news website Masrawy.
Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said Sunday on X that he and his Saudi counterpart Prince Faisal bin Farhan bin Abdullah Al Saud discussed current regional developments and the importance of de-escalation during a phone call.
President of the United Arab Emirates Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan received Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud in Abu Dhabi on Sunday, with the two sides exchanging views on regional developments and ways to strengthen security and stability and achieve lasting peace in the region, the Emirates News Agency reported.
Also on Sunday, Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) Secretary-General Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi called for effective international action to halt Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia at a meeting of the GCC Ministerial Council in the Bahraini capital Manama.
In the final communique issued after the meeting, the GCC reaffirmed its full solidarity with Saudi Arabia and support for all measures taken by the kingdom to safeguard its sovereignty, security and interests, stressing that the security of GCC member states is indivisible. ■

Jacqui Lambie slams 'nasty' One Nation cartoon mocking vaginal prolapse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
22:20:59 UTC
07:20:59 KST

Jacqui Lambie slams 'nasty' One Nation cartoon mocking vaginal prolapse
In short:
A new One Nation cartoon ridicules outspoken independent senator Jacqui Lambie by mocking her vaginal prolapse.
Senator Lambie says Pauline Hanson's videos are full of "hatred" and "spitefulness".
What's next?
Politicians have condemned the cartoon, while One Nation leader Pauline Hanson says Senator Lambie should "get over it".
Jacqui Lambie has hit back at Pauline Hanson's "nastiness" after a One Nation cartoon mocked the independent senator's health condition.
Senator Lambie gave an emotional speech in the Senate in August, revealing she had a vaginal and bladder prolapse, which required surgery and five months of leave from parliament.
The One Nation cartoon is one in a series of satirical videos that mock politicians and take aim at recent political events.
The latest cartoon uses Senator Lambie's vaginal prolapse as a punchline.
The Tasmanian senator said people were welcome to watch Senator Hanson's videos "if you want more hatred, more spitefulness in your life".
"But what I do know is this: decent leaders don't stir up hatred, pushing us towards bloody anarchy, because that's exactly what she's doing," Senator Lambie told ABC's Radio National.
Senator Lambie said she would not be demanding One Nation remove the video, but called on Senator Hanson's team, especially the men, to ask her to remove it immediately.
"If you think it's a laughable matter about women having problems with their reproductive system, then you be my guest and you stand by her,"
she said.
"But seriously, enough is enough."
Senator Lambie had previously said the condition was directly linked to back injuries she sustained in the army.
On Monday, Senator Hanson said Senator Lambie should "get over it", insisting the video was satirical.
Asked whether the cartoon was appropriate, Senator Hanson said it had "opened" the eyes of women who "may be suffering" and helped raise awareness of women's health issues.
"I think she is taking it to heart, which she shouldn't be," she said.
"Have a bit of a laugh, Jacqui, and lighten up."
Loading...
Politicians stand with Lambie
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Liberal senator Jacinta Nampijinpa Price are among a number of politicians who have publicly condemned the One Nation cartoon.
All praised Senator Lambie's courage in talking about a deeply personal health issue to raise awareness.
In a comment on social media, Mr Albanese thanked Senator Lambie for her "courage which will help others".
Senator Nampijinpa Price said the attack was in "bad taste", and said politicians should "play the ball, not the person".
"I don't like women being ridiculed for very personal issues," she said.
Defence Industry Minister Pat Conroy called for the video to be taken down.
"Senator Lambie, who's a fine public servant committed to serving the public, has been open and honest about her health challenges in a way to raise awareness [of] … these conditions. That's incredibly brave of her," he said.
"So for her to be mocked by One Nation just shows, quite frankly, what they stand for."
Independent MP Monique Ryan said pelvic organ prolapse affected many women and was often linked to physical strain, heavy lifting or past childbirth.
"One Jacqui Lambie is worth 1,000 Pauline Hansons," she wrote.
It is not the first time One Nation's cartoons have sparked a political firestorm.
Last month, Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie slammed One Nation for a cartoon that repeatedly described him as a "traitor".
Mr Hastie, a veteran like Senator Lambie, criticised Senator Hanson and called for the cartoon to be removed, a move that was backed widely across the political spectrum.
"I think that shows Pauline Hanson's hypocrisy. She cried a river for Gina Rinehart when the ABC had a satirical skit played on one of your programs and demanded that it be taken down," he told ABC.
"I think the double standard is ridiculous. It's a cheap, nasty and vulgar attack on Jacqui Lambie's health condition and if she had any decency, she would apologise and pull it down."
Mr Hastie also questioned whether taxpayer funds would be used to roll out cartoons to attack One Nation's political opponents if the party won government.
Pelvic health issues 'not a punchline'
Women's health advocates have slammed the "absolutely disgusting" cartoon, arguing it reinforces stigma surrounding pelvic health issues.
Birth Trauma Australia CEO Amy Dawes said hundreds of thousands of Australian women were impacted by pelvic floor dysfunction.
"Women's health conditions cannot become a subject of public ridicule … [or] a punchline of a joke," Ms Dawes said.
"[This cartoon] sends a message to women that their pain, that their bodies and their health concerns are acceptable targets for humiliation.
"We're working so hard to increase awareness … but this just seems like a gigantic step back."
Health experts have said prolapse and pelvic floor disorders affect as many as one in four women.
Ms Dawes said pelvic organ prolapse and bladder incontinence could have a "profound impact" on a woman's physical health, confidence, quality of life and relationships.
"This is about dignity, it's about health awareness and the message we send to women everywhere," she said.
"If we start to make fun of these conditions, we further exacerbate this stigma, we further increase barriers to people seeking support."

While You Were Sleeping: 5 stories you might have missed, Oct 19, 2026
Macron denounces ‘unbridled’ violence as France hit by new clashes
President Emmanuel Macron on Oct 18 slammed the “unbridled” violence that erupted in cost-of-living protests across France, as police battled protesters and looters in new clashes in Paris.
Nearly 2,400 people were arrested on Oct 17 in unrest that represented some of the worst urban violence in France in years, with almost 1,000 police and gendarmes injured, seven seriously, the interior ministry said.
In an address to the nation, Macron said local authorities would be able to ban – “if necessary” – certain rallies in coming days. But he stopped short of announcing drastic measures, such as a state of emergency or curfew.
“Tonight, we all feel anger and shame,” Macron said of the devastation brought by the protests that include town halls burned down and hundreds of businesses looted or damaged.
Milan police clash with protesters on second day of unrest
Youth and police clashed for a second day on Oct 18 in Milan, where mostly black-clad assailants hurled bottles, ransacked stores, and destroyed property around the central Duomo plaza.
Police in the northern city have arrested more than 200 people since Oct 17, according to Ansa news agency.
Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni called for a security meeting on Oct 19 to address the violence, which resembled some scenes of chaos and looting in Paris.
Kenya confirms eighth Ebola case as regional outbreak spreads
Kenya has confirmed one more Ebola case, bringing the total number of infections in the country to eight, Director-General for Health Patrick Amoth said on Oct 18.
“Today, 38 people were tested, and one tested positive for Ebola,” Amoth said in an interview on Kenya’s Citizen TV.
“He is a 49-year-old man who is not a healthcare worker. He developed fever, headache and muscle pain.”
Trump says Washington golf course renovation to start in November, despite judge’s order
President Donald Trump on Oct 18 unveiled his plans for overhauling a beloved municipal golf course in the US capital, a project already mired in a contentious legal fight.
On Truth Social, Trump posted a mockup of an 18-hole course which would dramatically change the historic East Potomac Golf Links, saying construction is set to start in November.
“When completed, it will be open to the Public while, at the same time, designed to the Highest Level of Golf and able to hold World Class Tournaments such as the US Open, the PGA Championship, the Ryder Cup, and the Presidents Cup,” Trump said.
McLaren to sell five F1 cars, all driven by champions and one by Brad Pitt
McLaren are selling five fully-functioning Formula One cars driven by champions, including Lewis Hamilton and the late Brazilian Ayrton Senna, with one also tested by Hollywood actor Brad Pitt.
The cars, to be sold through high-end dealer Tom Hartley Jr and expected to raise tens of millions of dollars, will be prepared by the reigning constructors’ champions for their next owners.
Hartley Jr also sold the collection of former F1 supremo Bernie Ecclestone and 20 road cars belonging to the late McLaren co-owner Mansour Ojjeh.

Explosive-laden Ukrainian drone crashes in NATO state
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
22:05:09 UTC
07:05:09 KST

Explosive-laden Ukrainian drone crashes in NATO state
An explosive-laden Ukrainian attack drone crashed in Lithuania on Sunday, damaging a passenger car, Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius confirmed on Monday.
The drone triggered a high-level air alert in several Lithuanian regions before crashing in the northern Pasvalys district, near the Latvian border. Debris from the UAV damaged a passing car, but no one was injured, according to National Crisis Management Center head Vilmantas Vitkauskas.
Sinkevicus said the response to the incident was different from standard procedures because the drone arrived from a fellow NATO nation. “The drone entered from the Schengen Area, crossing the border with Poland, so the response was slightly different. Fighter jets were, of course, scrambled and tracked the moving object, but they were unable to see it visually due to adverse weather conditions,” the prime minister said.
On Monday, Sinkevicus confirmed that the UAV had been identified as a Ukrainian strike drone. “There is no doubt that it was carrying an explosive payload,” he said.
According to Lithuanian Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas, the drone was likely a part of a major Ukrainian attack on the Russian city of St. Petersburg. “Some of the drones were diverted off course by Russia’s electronic warfare systems and ended up in our territory. This particular drone is a consequence of the attack on St. Petersburg,” the minister told the LRT broadcaster. He also identified the drone as a Ukrainian FVP-1 model.
The Ukrainian drone attack on St. Petersburg on Sunday night killed one person and injured five others, according to Governor Aleksandr Beglov. It also damaged more than a dozen apartment buildings and sparked a fire at an oil terminal.
Moscow has repeatedly condemned the Ukrainian strikes on Russian civilian and energy infrastructure calling them “terrorist” attacks aimed at compensating for setbacks on the battlefield, where Russian forces have continued to advance.
Despite identifying the drone as Ukrainian, Lithuania blamed Russia for the incident. The case would be investigated as part of a Lithuanian probe into “Russia’s aggression against Ukraine,” a police official told the Lithuanian Elta news agency. Kiev said it regretted the drone incident while calling Moscow’s actions “the root cause of the security threats in our region.”
Kiev has been ramping up its long-range UAV attacks on energy infrastructure in Russia’s Leningrad Region, which surrounds the country’s second-largest city, St. Petersburg, since spring. The campaign resulted in a number of incidents where explosive-laden drones crashed in nearby NATO member states – Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia – while on their way to Russia.
In July, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergey Galuzin said that Moscow had “verified data indicating that Latvia and other Baltic republics have already provided air corridors for Ukrainian drones that have attacked our country’s civilian infrastructure.”
The Baltic nations and Finland, which have been among the staunchest backers of Kiev in the EU during the Ukraine crisis, had previously denied any involvement in the drone attacks on Russia.
Russian Security Council Secretary Sergey Shoigu had previously warned that if it turned out that the Baltic states and Finland “deliberately provide their airspace” to Ukrainian UAVs, Moscow would have the right to self-defense in response to an “armed attack” under Article 51 of the UN Charter.

It was not clear why the demand for consultation was being made repeatedly, Rijiju said
NEW DELHI: Days after Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge called for an all-party meeting to discuss any fresh delimitation proposal, govt on Monday said it had already consulted many opposition parties, including Samajwadi Party, DMK and NCP (SP), and could not hold talks with Congress because of its own unwillingness, refuelling the buzz that Parliament may be called for a short duration to take up the legislation.In a sharp response to Kharge's Oct 16 letter to PM Narendra Modi, parliamentary affairs minister Kiren Rijiju said, "When after repeated requests Congress didn't give dates for discussion, govt's outreach extended to other political parties. Consultations were held with representatives of parties including SP, DMK, YSRCP, NCP (SP), Shiv Sena (UBT), AIMIM and BJD with a view to building a broader consensus in support of the proposed legislation."In these circumstances, it was not clear why the demand for consultation was being made repeatedly, he added, rejecting Kharge's suggestion. World Food Programme cuts aid to 500,000 Palestinians in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
21:54:42 UTC
06:54:42 KST

Breadcrumb
World Food Programme cuts aid to 500,000 Palestinians in Gaza, cites funding shortages
The UN World Food Programme has said funding shortages are forcing major cuts to its aid programme in Gaza, leaving about 500,000 people without monthly food support in a territory where two-thirds of the population struggle to get enough to eat.
The WFP said it was reducing the number of recipients of its monthly assistance from 1.6 million to 1.1 million.
In addition, food rations have been halved, cash assistance has been cut for 75,000 families, and daily hot meals for those unable to cook have fallen to 150,000 from 250,000, with some families in hard-to-reach areas now receiving a hot meal only every other day.
The WFP said about 1.4 million people, or two-thirds of Gaza's population, face crisis levels of food insecurity or worse, including roughly 200,000 people in emergency conditions.
Last year's US-brokered Gaza ceasefire calls for the eventual reconstruction of the territory. But little progress has been made towards implementing a deal to end the conflict that includes terms for Hamas to disarm and Israel to withdraw its troops.
Life is still brutal in Gaza, says acting head of WFP
"It's a year into the agreement of this ceasefire. Well, life is still brutal here. There is no proper shelter...There are no basic services. There is no safety, no security," acting Executive Director of the WFP Carl Skau told Reuters in Gaza.
"These cuts are happening just as we are facing the fourth winter. You know, I've been through the winters here, absolutely brutal," he added.
The WFP said it urgently needs $450 million over the next six months to maintain critical operations in Gaza and the Israeli-occupied West Bank.
"We tell the world now is not the time to look away. This is the time to step up to sustain this support, to protect the progress that has been made, but also to push for early recovery," said Skau.
Israeli forces still hold more than 60 percent of the territory and conduct almost daily airstrikes, while Hamas controls most of the area where more than two million Palestinians live, mostly in temporary shelters with what aid agencies call inadequate aid supplies.
The Gaza government media office described the WFP announcement as "catastrophic" and said it might accelerate famine in the enclave, calling for more fund to aid agencies to prevent it.
"On top of the circumstances and the difficult life, you want to make it even harder on us," said Palestinian woman Sabrine Kuhail, standing by a tent shelter at a displacement site in Nuseirat refugee camp in central Gaza Strip.
"You made us hungry for three years with war, destruction, siege, and the bloodshed that is not stopping. What do you want from us? Enough, enough, we are tired."
